cover.alt: Book cover of Head First Design Patterns

summary: A visual, story-driven course on object-oriented design patterns (Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Factory, Singleton, Command, Adapter, Facade, Template Method, Iterator, Composite, State, Proxy, MVC) and the design principles behind them.

unitSummaries.Chapter 1: Why changing requirements break inheritance-heavy designs, and how encapsulating what varies and favouring composition (Strategy) fix it.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: How a subject notifies dependent objects of changes without being tightly coupled to them.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: How wrapping objects adds behaviour at runtime while keeping classes closed to modification and open to extension.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: How Simple Factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory isolate object creation and invert dependencies on concrete classes.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: How to guarantee one instance with a global access point, and what multithreading does to the classic version.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: How wrapping a request as an object decouples the invoker from the receiver and enables undo, macros, queues and logs.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: How Adapter converts one interface to another and Facade simplifies a subsystem, guided by the Principle of Least Knowledge.
unitSummaries.Chapter 8: How a superclass fixes an algorithm skeleton and lets subclasses supply steps, with hooks and the Hollywood Principle.
unitSummaries.Chapter 9: How Iterator hides how a collection is traversed and Composite treats single objects and trees of objects uniformly.
unitSummaries.Chapter 10: How an object changes behaviour by delegating to state objects, and how this differs from Strategy.
unitSummaries.Chapter 11: How remote, virtual and protection proxies control access to another object.
unitSummaries.Chapter 12: How patterns combine, with MVC as the model case built from Observer, Strategy and Composite.
unitSummaries.Chapter 13: What a pattern really is, how to choose and keep one, and when not to use it.
unitSummaries.Appendix A: Nine further patterns (Bridge, Builder, Chain of Responsibility, Flyweight, Interpreter, Mediator, Memento, Prototype, Visitor) in brief.
unitSummaries.Whole book: Putting the patterns and principles together: choosing among them, telling similar ones apart, and knowing when none is needed.

concepts.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
concepts.title: Inheritance as the first tool for reuse
concepts.question: How does one Duck superclass let a simulator support many duck species with little code?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Many duck species share most of their behavior. Writing that code again in every species class would be slow, and each fix would have to be repeated.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Put the shared code once in a Duck superclass. Each species extends it, receives that code, and adds or replaces only what makes it different. The SimUDuck designers built the game this way.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Reuse is cheap at the start, because a new species needs little new code. But every subclass receives everything the superclass holds, wanted or not, and that sets up the trouble in the next ideas.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The subclasses do not really share the code. Then each one inherits things it should not have.

card.rule: Inheritance reuses code by writing it once in a superclass that every subclass receives.
card.limits: Every subclass receives everything the superclass holds, wanted or not. Reuse by inheritance works while all subclasses really share the code.

concepts.title: One change in a superclass reaches every subclass
concepts.question: Why did adding one fly() method to the Duck superclass produce flying rubber ducks?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Joe had one week to make ducks fly. Adding one fly() method to the shared Duck class looked like the quickest way to get every duck flying.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Every subclass inherited fly(), rubber ducks included, though they are inanimate objects. Joe had not noticed that not all Duck subclasses should fly. The authors call this a localized update with a nonlocal side effect.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Inheritance that looked like a good way to reuse code turned out badly for maintenance, since a change meant for some subclasses landed on all of them. Our reading: list every subclass that will receive a new superclass method before adding it.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A method added to a base class that makes no sense for one of its subclasses, such as fly() on a rubber duck.

card.rule: Adding behavior to a superclass gives it to every subclass, so add it only where every subclass should have it.
card.limits: A new method in a superclass is safe when all subclasses really share it, such as a name every duck has. The risk comes from behavior that only some subclasses should have.

concepts.title: What inheritance costs when behavior varies
concepts.question: Which disadvantages appear when subclasses are the home for behavior that keeps changing?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Behavior that differs between duck types is written inside the subclasses, and the product will keep changing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors list four disadvantages of letting subclasses hold varying behavior: code is duplicated across subclasses; changing behavior at runtime is difficult; it is hard to gain knowledge of all duck behaviors; and changes can unintentionally affect other ducks.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Our reading: the four share one source, since the behavior is fixed in class definitions when the code is written. Ducks that cannot dance, or cannot fly and quack together, are not on the list; inheritance never promised those.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Several subclasses carrying near-identical copies of the same behavior code.

card.rule: When behavior varies, inheritance costs duplicated code, hard runtime changes, scattered knowledge and unintended side effects.
card.limits: The list judges inheritance as the home for varying behavior, not inheritance in general. Stable code shared by all subclasses still belongs in a superclass.

concepts.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
concepts.title: Interfaces fix who gets a behavior but lose the code
concepts.question: Why does making only some ducks implement Flyable and Quackable trade one maintenance problem for another?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Only some ducks should fly or quack, and the executives will keep changing the specification every six months.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Take fly() and quack() out of Duck and put them in Flyable and Quackable interfaces. Only the ducks that really fly implement Flyable, and only those that quack implement Quackable.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: No more rubber ducks flying by mistake. But a Java interface has no implementation code, so each implementing class writes its own and code reuse is destroyed. There may be several kinds of flying even among ducks that fly. The authors call this a different maintenance nightmare.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Many classes implementing one interface with copy-pasted bodies.

card.rule: An interface decides which classes have a behavior but carries no code, so every implementer must supply its own.
card.limits: The lesson is not that interfaces are bad. They name a capability well. The trouble arises when they are the only place a varying behavior can live.

concepts.section: The one constant in software development
concepts.title: Change as the constant of software
concepts.question: What can a developer count on in every project, and what does it mean for design?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Joe's company wants an update every six months, in ways it has not decided yet.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Whatever you build, wherever you work and in whatever language, the one constant is change. No matter how well an application is designed, over time it must grow and change or it will die.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Users want new features, companies change suppliers or data formats, technology moves, and teams learn better ways. Our reading: change arrives unevenly, so the skill is guessing where it will land and judging a design by how well it takes the next change.

card.rule: Software must change to stay alive, so a design should be judged by how well it takes the next change.
card.limits: Not every part of a system changes at the same speed. Treating all of it as in flux wastes effort; the skill is to see where change is likely.

concepts.title: Two failed designs, one shared cause
concepts.question: What do the inheritance design and the interface design have in common that makes both hard to maintain?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two fixes failed in the same way: subclasses holding the varying behavior, and interfaces holding it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Compare the failures instead of repairing each one. In both designs the varying behavior sits inside the duck classes themselves. Whenever it must change, you track down every class that defines it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Our reading: when two repairs fail alike, the thing they share is a better target than either repair, and a third repair of the same kind will fail too.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The failures have different causes. They then need different fixes.

card.rule: When two designs fail the same way, find what they share and change that.
card.limits: Finding a shared cause works only if the failures really are the same kind. Two failures with different causes need different fixes.

concepts.title: Identify what varies and encapsulate it
concepts.question: What does the first design principle tell a designer to do with the parts of a program that change?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Requirements keep changing, and each change risks side effects in code that was working.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Identify the aspects of your application that vary and separate them from what stays the same. Encapsulate the varying part so that you can alter or extend it later without affecting the parts that do not vary.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors promise fewer unintended consequences from code changes and more flexibility in the system.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The fee rule moves out of a class that should stay stable and into classes of its own.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: A part never changes. Pulling it out adds structure with no benefit.

card.rule: Find the parts of the code that change and put them behind their own boundary, apart from the parts that stay the same.
card.limits: The principle says to encapsulate what varies, not everything. Pulling out parts that never change adds structure without benefit.

concepts.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
concepts.title: Pulling fly and quack out of Duck
concepts.question: Which parts of the Duck class are moved out, where do they go, and what stays?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Apart from fly() and quack(), the Duck class works well and nothing else in it seems to change often.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Leave Duck mostly alone and pull out only the two varying methods. Give each behavior its own set of classes: one set for ways of flying, one for ways of quacking. The quack set might hold a quacker, a squeaker and a silent one.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The stable class stays as it was and each varying behavior gets one home. Our reading: what counts as varying rests on today's evidence, so revisit the choice when another part starts to change.

card.rule: Move only the varying methods out, give each behavior its own set of classes, and leave the stable class where it is.
card.limits: Judging what varies rests on today's evidence. A part thought stable may start to vary, so the choice is a judgment, to be revised, not a one-time proof.

concepts.title: Program to an interface, not an implementation
concepts.question: What does the second design principle tell a designer about the type of a variable that holds a behavior?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Duck classes should not need to know how their behaviors work. Before, each duck got its behavior from the superclass or its own subclass, so it was locked into one implementation.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Program to an interface, not an implementation. Each behavior is an interface, FlyBehavior or QuackBehavior, and the behavior classes implement it, not the Duck classes. A Duck holds a variable typed as the interface.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Any class that implements the interface can sit in the variable, and the Duck needs no implementation detail. Our reading: where nothing will ever vary, the extra layer buys little.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Typing the variable with the supertype lets any implementation be assigned.

card.rule: Declare the variable that holds a behavior with a supertype so the code does not depend on which implementation sits in it.
card.limits: Programming to a supertype adds a layer. Where nothing will ever vary, the extra interface buys little.

concepts.title: Interface as a concept versus a Java construct
concepts.question: What are the two meanings of the word interface, and which one does the second principle use?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The word interface means two things, so program to an interface can sound like use the Java keyword interface.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: One meaning is the concept of what an object promises to do. The other is the Java construct. You can program to an interface without the construct. The advice really means program to a supertype, usually an abstract class or an interface.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Any concrete implementation can be assigned to a variable of the supertype, and the class that declares the variable does not need to know the real type of the object.

card.rule: Program to an interface means program to a supertype, which may be an abstract class or a Java interface.
card.limits: The supertype must still declare what the code calls on it. The principle fails if the declared type is a concrete class in disguise.

concepts.title: Assigning the concrete object at runtime
concepts.question: How does declaring a variable as a supertype let the actual object be chosen while the program runs?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Code that names the concrete class of its variable is tied to that class.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Declare the variable with a supertype: Animal animal = new Dog(), then call animal.makeSound(). Better still, do not hard-code new Dog(); assign the concrete object at runtime, as in a = getAnimal().

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The calling code does not know which animal it has. It only cares that the object responds to makeSound(). Our reading: through the supertype variable only methods the supertype declares can be called.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The first line is tied to Dog; the others use the supertype.
blocks.code:
Dog d = new Dog();      // tied to Dog
Animal a = new Dog();   // typed by the supertype
a = new Cat();          // any Animal fits

card.rule: Type the variable as the supertype and let the concrete object be assigned while the program runs.
card.limits: The calling code can only use what the supertype declares. A method found only in a subclass, such as bark(), is out of reach through the supertype variable.

concepts.title: Behaviors as classes of their own
concepts.question: What do the authors gain by putting each way of flying or quacking in its own class?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The new design needs behaviors that other objects can reuse, and new behaviors that can be added without editing old code.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Two interfaces, FlyBehavior and QuackBehavior, each with a class for every concrete behavior. A behavior is no longer hidden inside a Duck class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Other objects can reuse the behaviors. New behaviors can be added without modifying any existing behavior class or any Duck class that uses them. The authors call this reuse without the baggage of inheritance.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Adding rocket flight takes one new class.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: A behavior will never have a second variant. A separate class family is then more structure than it earns.

card.rule: Give every variant of a behavior its own class behind a shared interface, so it can be reused and added to without editing existing code.
card.limits: Each variant adds a class to maintain. For a behavior that will never have a second variant, a separate class family is more structure than it earns.

concepts.title: A Duck delegates to its behavior objects
concepts.question: How does a Duck perform flying and quacking when the code for them has been moved out of it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The flying and quacking code has moved out of Duck, yet a duck must still fly and quack when asked.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: To delegate is to hand a job to another object. Duck gets two variables, flyBehavior and quackBehavior, typed as the interfaces. fly() and quack() are removed and replaced by performFly() and performQuack(), which let the referenced object do the work.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The Duck does not care what kind of object it holds, only that it knows how to quack. Our reading: each behavior costs the Duck one small forwarding method.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The flying code leaves Duck; Duck only forwards.

card.rule: Delegate by holding a reference typed as the behavior interface and forwarding the work to the object it refers to.
card.limits: A Duck can delegate only to an object it has been given. Delegation also adds one small forwarding method per behavior to the delegating class.

concepts.title: Giving a Duck its behaviors in the constructor
concepts.question: How does a MallardDuck get its flying and quacking behaviors, and what does the authors' admission about that tell you?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A mallard must start life flying with wings and quacking like a real duck.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: MallardDuck's constructor sets its inherited quackBehavior to a new Quack object and its flyBehavior to a new FlyWithWings object.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors admit this is a poor way to initialize, since concrete classes are named in the constructor. Flexibility remains because the variables are interface types, so another implementation can still be assigned later.

card.rule: A constructor can give an object its starting behaviors, but naming a concrete class there ties the object to it until the behavior is replaced.
card.limits: Hard-coding new Quack() into a constructor fixes the starting choice in code. Flexibility comes from the variable's interface type, not from the constructor.

concepts.title: The classes the duck code is built from
concepts.question: Which classes make up the working duck code, and what does each quack behavior do when it runs?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The team needs to see the design work, with several small behaviors that a Duck can call in the same way.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Duck and MallardDuck; FlyBehavior with FlyWithWings and FlyNoWay; QuackBehavior with Quack, MuteQuack and Squeak; and a MiniDuckSimulator test class. Each quack class has one quack() method that prints Quack, a message of silence, or Squeak.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Because every class implements the same interface, the Duck calls any of them in the same way. Our reading: a small test shows the design works for a few cases, not that every future behavior will fit.

card.rule: Small classes behind one interface can be mixed and matched, so the Duck's calls never change as behaviors are swapped.
card.limits: A test like this shows the design works for a few cases. It does not show that every future behavior will fit the interface unchanged.

concepts.title: Changing a duck's behavior while the program runs
concepts.question: How can a duck's behavior change after it has been created, and what must the new behavior satisfy?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A duck that cannot fly may need to fly later, and the change should not require building a new duck.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Add a setter method to Duck for each behavior and call it at any time. In the authors' example a ModelDuck is made rocket-enabled by passing a new FlyRocketPowered object to its setter.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The new behavior works because it implements the right behavior interface. Our reading: a setter changes only the one object it is called on.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A grounded duck flies after one setter call.

card.rule: Call a setter with an object that implements the right interface, and the duck's behavior changes while the program runs.
card.limits: A setter changes only the one object it is called on. A rocket-enabled duck does not change the other ducks of the same class.

concepts.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
concepts.title: Behaviors as a family of algorithms
concepts.question: What makes a set of classes a family of algorithms, and where else could the same technique apply?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Calling the duck behaviors a set of behaviors hides what they have in common.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Think of them as a family of algorithms: different ways of doing the same job, each in its own class, all sharing one interface. The authors say the technique could also serve classes that compute state sales tax in different states.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Seeing behaviors as algorithms makes the pattern easier to spot in other problems. Our reading: classes that do different jobs are not a family, even with a shared base, because members must be able to stand in for each other.

card.rule: A family of algorithms is a set of interchangeable ways to do the same job, each in its own class behind one interface.
card.limits: Classes that do different jobs are not a family, even if they share a base. The members must be able to stand in for one another.

concepts.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
concepts.title: IS-A, HAS-A and IMPLEMENTS
concepts.question: What are the three relationships in the reworked class structure, and which arrow stands for each?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The class diagram of the new design uses three kinds of link, and a wrong reading gives a wrong design.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: MallardDuck extends Duck: IS-A. FlyWithWings carries out FlyBehavior: IMPLEMENTS. A Duck has a FlyBehavior and a QuackBehavior, to which it delegates: HAS-A. The authors urge you to label every arrow in the diagram.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A Duck is not a FlyBehavior, so IS-A would be the wrong label between them. The right link is HAS-A.

card.rule: IS-A means extends, IMPLEMENTS means carries out an interface, and HAS-A means holds a reference to another object.
card.limits: Choosing the wrong link gives a wrong design. A Duck is not a FlyBehavior, so IS-A would be a mistake there; the right link is HAS-A.

concepts.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
concepts.title: Composition
concepts.question: What is composition, and how do composed objects get their behavior?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Behavior that is inherited is fixed in the class definition. The ducks need behavior they can be given.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Each duck has a FlyBehavior and a QuackBehavior to which it delegates. When two classes are put together like this you are using composition: ducks get behavior by being composed with the right behavior object, not by inheriting it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors call composition an important technique. It is the HAS-A link put to use, with the held part known by its interface.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Inheritance says a Car is an Engine; composition says it has one.
blocks.code:
class Car extends Engine { }          // inheritance: Car IS-A Engine
class Car { Engine engine; }          // composition: Car HAS-A Engine

card.rule: In composition an object gets its behavior from the objects it holds, not from classes it inherits from.
card.limits: Composition needs a part with a clear interface to hold. If there is no clean way to describe the part by an interface, composing it may be no easier than inheriting.

concepts.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
concepts.title: Favor composition over inheritance
concepts.question: What does the third design principle ask for, and what two benefits do the authors give?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Inheritance ties behavior to a class when the code is written, and the authors want behavior that is easy to change.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Favor composition over inheritance. The duck design was already using this principle before it had a name.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors give two benefits: you can encapsulate a family of algorithms into their own classes, and you can change behavior at runtime, as long as the object you compose with implements the correct behavior interface.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: the code is stable and shared by all subclasses. The principle says favor, not forbid.

card.rule: Prefer giving an object its behavior by composing it with other objects over inheriting that behavior.
card.limits: The principle says favor, not forbid. Inheritance still fits stable, shared code, and the authors say composition has disadvantages as well as advantages.

concepts.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
concepts.title: Why reuse is not the highest aim
concepts.question: Why do the authors say effort should not go into reuse above maintainability and extensibility?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Inheritance promised faster development through reuse, but software gets more time after it is built than before.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In the authors' dialogue the master asks whether time goes into code before or after development ends. After. So effort should not go into reuse above maintainability and extensibility. Inheritance has problems, and other ways reach reuse.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Judge a design by how easily it can be maintained and extended. Our reading: this is the authors' view, and it does not make reuse worthless.

card.rule: Since most time is spent changing software after it is built, a design should be judged by how easily it can be maintained and extended.
card.limits: This is the authors' view, and it does not say reuse is worthless. Reuse that is easy to maintain remains valuable.

concepts.title: The Strategy Pattern in one sentence
concepts.question: What does the Strategy Pattern say in one sentence, and which parts of the duck design match it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A job can be done in several ways, the ways keep changing, and the code that uses them should not be edited when they do.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from the clients that use it. In SimUDuck the behaviors are the family, each has its own class, they share an interface, and the ducks are the clients.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The simulator is ready for any changes the executives ask for next. Our reading: each variant is one more class to maintain.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Our reading: a client with a growing if-chain that picks between ways of doing one job.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The job has only one way of being done. The pattern then adds classes with no payoff.

card.rule: Strategy defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each, and makes them interchangeable so they vary independently of the clients that use them.
card.limits: Strategy suits a job that has several interchangeable ways of being done. Where the job has only one way, the pattern adds classes with no payoff.

concepts.title: A shared vocabulary shortens talk
concepts.question: What does a shared vocabulary between two people save, and what does it do for the listener?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Explaining a design in plain object talk takes many words and leaves the listener a lot to hold in mind.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: At the diner Alice and Flo place the same order. Flo uses far fewer words, because she shares a vocabulary with the cook, who has the diner's patterns in his head and so has less to remember. Design patterns give developers a shared vocabulary in the same way.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Communication is easier, and thinking rises to the pattern level, away from nitty-gritty objects. Our reading: the saving exists only when both sides know the words.

card.rule: A shared vocabulary lets speakers say a complete idea in a few words because both already know what the words stand for.
card.limits: The saving exists only when both sides know the vocabulary. A pattern name said to someone who does not know it carries no meaning.

concepts.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
concepts.title: What a pattern name carries
concepts.question: What is communicated when a team says it uses a pattern, beyond the name itself?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Design meetings slide into implementation details, and junior developers find them hard to follow.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A pattern name carries a set of qualities, characteristics and constraints. Saying we use the Strategy Pattern for duck behaviors tells a listener that the behavior is encapsulated in its own classes, easy to expand and changeable at runtime.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Patterns let you say more with less, keep a talk at the design level, help a team move faster with less misunderstanding, and motivate junior developers to learn, which builds a community of pattern users.

card.rule: A pattern name stands for a whole design with its qualities and constraints, which lets a team discuss design at a higher level.
card.limits: This holds only while both sides mean the same thing by the name. Using a pattern name loosely brings back the misunderstanding it was meant to remove.

concepts.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
concepts.title: Patterns are not libraries
concepts.question: How does a design pattern differ from a library or framework, and where does a pattern first go?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Libraries and frameworks give finished code, but they do not help you structure your own application so that it is understandable, maintainable and flexible.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A design pattern is higher level: it says how to structure classes and objects to solve a certain problem, and it is your job to adapt it. Patterns go first into your brain, not directly into your code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Libraries and frameworks are not patterns, though they sometimes use patterns inside, which helps you understand their APIs faster.

card.rule: A library supplies code you link in; a pattern supplies a design you learn and adapt to your own application.
card.limits: The two are related, not opposed. A library may be built on patterns, and knowing the pattern helps you learn the library.

concepts.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
concepts.title: Knowing OO basics is not enough
concepts.question: Why does knowing abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism not make a designer good at flexible systems?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A developer thinks that knowing abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism already makes a designer good.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: The guru calls this a misunderstanding. Building systems that are flexible, reusable and maintainable is not always obvious and was found through hard work. Design patterns collect those findings.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Knowing patterns puts you ahead, but design is an art and trade-offs remain. When no pattern fits, the principles under the patterns help, and one secret is to think about how a system might change.

card.rule: OO basics are tools; flexible designs come from patterns and principles that were found through experience.
card.limits: Patterns do not guarantee a good design. The guru says design is an art and trade-offs remain, so judgment is still required.

concepts.title: The chapter in one view
concepts.question: What is the chapter's main claim about patterns, change and design, in a few sentences?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A chapter that runs from ducks to diners can leave its main thread hard to see.

blocks.label: Idea
blocks.text: Good OO designs are reusable, extensible and maintainable. Patterns are proven OO experience: discovered, not invented, and general solutions rather than code. Most address change, letting a part of a system vary independently, often by encapsulating what varies. They also give developers a shared language.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Knowing the OO basics does not make a good designer. Our reading: a one-line summary drops the trade-offs, so use it to recall the chapter, not to settle a design.

card.rule: Design for change: find what varies, encapsulate it, prefer composition, and use patterns as proven solutions and a shared language.
card.limits: A one-line summary leaves out the trade-offs the chapter mentions. Use it to recall the chapter, not to settle a design.

concepts.section: What do we know so far?
concepts.title: What the weather station must do
concepts.question: What does the weather application have to do, and what is already given to us?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The client wants three displays now (current conditions, statistics, forecast). It also wants an API so other developers can write displays, and users who add or remove displays. WeatherData supplies getters for temperature, humidity and barometric pressure.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Sort the facts first. Given: the three getters, and measurementsChanged(), which runs whenever new readings exist (nobody on the team needs to know who calls it). To build: displays that update on every change, and room for more of them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The open requirement matters more than the list of three, because the list will grow. The spec is vague, so the list of what is known may be incomplete and should be written down before any design.

card.rule: Before designing, separate what is given, what must be built, and what must stay open to change.
card.limits: A spec can be vague, so a list of what we know may be incomplete; the open requirement matters more than the three named displays, because the list of displays will grow.

concepts.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
concepts.title: Judging the hard-coded first attempt
concepts.question: Why does putting calls to each display directly inside measurementsChanged() make the application hard to extend?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The first attempt fills measurementsChanged() with direct calls to the three displays. It works for today's list. The authors then test it against the chapter 1 principles and a spec that expects new displays.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Their checklist: it codes to concrete classes, every new display means editing code, displays cannot be added or removed at run time, the displays share no common interface, and the part that changes is not encapsulated.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each flaw costs more the more the spec expects change. Here the spec asks for pluggable displays, so every flaw bites. A small system that never changes would pay little. The checklist is a set of questions, not a proof.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: The list of displays is written into the sender's code. A fourth display means another line here.

card.rule: Judge a design by whether adding or removing a part forces edits to code that should stay stable.
card.limits: A small system that will never change may not need more, so the flaws only bite when the spec expects change. The checklist is a set of questions to ask, not a proof of which flaws a particular design has.

concepts.title: The newspaper subscription picture
concepts.question: How does a newspaper subscription work, and which of its parts will we reuse to understand the pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A publisher prints editions. People, hotels, airlines and other businesses keep subscribing and unsubscribing, so the set of recipients changes all the time while the publisher stays in business.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: You subscribe and each new edition is delivered to you. You unsubscribe and deliveries stop. The authors say that if you understand this you roughly understand the pattern: delivery goes to the current list, anyone can join or leave, and editions are produced the same way for everyone.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The picture shows who gets told but not how the telling is coded. In software the publisher calls a method on each recipient, and the analogy says nothing about the interface that makes this possible.

card.rule: Think of a subscription: delivery follows the current list, and recipients can join and leave at any time.
card.limits: The picture shows who gets told, but not how the telling is coded. In software the publisher calls a method on each recipient, and the analogy says nothing about the interface that makes that possible.

concepts.title: Subject, observer and registering
concepts.question: What do the words subject, observer, register and notification mean, and who keeps the list?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Software needs names for the parts of the subscription picture, so that a design can say who holds the data, who wants to hear about it and how they get on the list.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The publisher is the SUBJECT and the subscribers are the OBSERVERS. The subject holds the important state and the list of observers. To register is to ask to be added; to remove is to ask to be taken off. A notification goes to every observer on the list when the state changes. In the book a Duck object asks the subject to make it an observer.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Observers ask to join, so the subject never has to hunt for them. The words name roles, not kinds of class: one object may be a subject for some objects and an observer of others. Swing calls observers listeners.

card.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.
card.limits: These words name roles, not kinds of class: one object can be a subject to some objects and an observer of others. Other systems use other names, for instance Swing calls observers listeners.

concepts.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
concepts.title: Registering, notifying and leaving
concepts.question: In what order do registering, notification and removal happen, and who receives which notification?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The set of observers is not fixed. Objects arrive and leave between one change and the next, and each change must reach the right recipients.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A Duck object asks to be an observer and the subject adds it. When the subject gets a new value, everyone on the list is notified. A Mouse object, tired of the values, asks to be removed. The next new value goes to everyone still on the list, and the Mouse is skipped. The Mouse may later ask to join again.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change's notification. Leaving is not permanent. The walkthrough does not say what happens if the list changes during a notification, so do not assume an answer.

card.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change’s notification.
card.limits: The walkthrough shows the list changing between notifications. It does not say what should happen if the list changes while a notification is being sent, so do not assume an answer from this story.

concepts.title: One object, two roles
concepts.question: Can one object be both a subject for some objects and an observer of another?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The skit has Jill and Lori both watching a headhunter. Jill gets a signing bonus because her company no longer needs to pay a headhunter, so she stops being an observer. Lori stays an observer and does something more.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Lori builds her own call list and notifies her own observers. She is a subject and an observer at once. The roles describe a relationship, so one object can take part in several of them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Notifications can pass through a chain: the first subject tells Lori, and Lori tells those who depend on her. Each link depends on the one before. A chain is a possibility, not advice to build long ones; the skit does not discuss their cost.

card.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.
card.limits: A chain of links is a possibility, not advice to build long chains. The skit does not discuss what long chains cost, so it should not be read as a recommendation.

concepts.title: The formal definition
concepts.question: What does the formal definition of the Observer Pattern claim about dependency and notification?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The newspaper picture is a good way in, but real documentation states the pattern in a formal sentence that must be read piece by piece.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Observer Pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically. One object (the subject) holds the state; many dependents rely on it; a state change is the trigger; every dependent is told without asking again.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Depending on the style of notification, the observer may also be updated with new values. The definition states an intent and not code, so many class designs fit it, though most use Subject and Observer interfaces. Example: a shared calendar event changes and every attendee's view shows the new time.

card.rule: Observer is when one object’s state change automatically notifies all its dependents.
card.limits: The definition states an intent, not code. How notices are sent, and whether values travel with them, differs between implementations, so one definition fits many different class designs.

concepts.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
concepts.title: One owner, many dependents
concepts.question: Why does the pattern speak of one subject and many observers, and what does dependence mean here?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Many objects want the same data. If several of them could change it, they might make conflicting changes and nobody could say which copy is right.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The subject is the object that contains the state and controls it, so there is one subject with state. The observers use that state without owning it. There are many of them and they rely on the subject to tell them when it changes. That reliance is the dependence.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Because the subject is the sole owner of the data, the authors say the design is cleaner than one in which many objects control the same data. The one is per piece of state: a system may hold many subjects, and an observer may depend on several.

card.rule: One object owns and controls the state; many others depend on it for updates.
card.limits: The one is the owner of one piece of state. A system can contain many subjects, each with its own observers, and an observer can depend on several subjects.

concepts.title: Subject and Observer interfaces
concepts.question: What does each of the two interfaces contain, and which classes implement them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Observers are of different types, yet the subject must reach all of them in the same way. It also must let objects join and leave without knowing who they are.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Most designs use two interfaces. The Subject interface has methods to register an observer, remove an observer and notify observers. The Observer interface has one method, update(), which the subject calls. WeatherData implements the first and keeps the list; each display implements the second.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each interface lists what the other side may call: observers call the Subject interface to join or leave, and the subject calls the Observer interface to deliver news. The two-interface layout is common, not part of the definition itself.

card.rule: The Subject interface offers register, remove and notify; the Observer interface offers update.
card.limits: The book says there are a few ways to implement the pattern and that most use these two interfaces. The two-interface layout is common, not part of the definition itself.

concepts.title: Loose coupling
concepts.question: What does loosely coupled mean, and what does a subject know about its observers?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Objects that must interact often end up knowing each other's classes and details, so a change to one forces changes to the other.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: When two objects are loosely coupled they can interact but have very little knowledge of each other. In Observer, the only thing the subject knows about an observer is that it implements the Observer interface. It needs to know neither the concrete class nor what the observer does.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The design principle: strive for loosely coupled designs between objects that interact. They build flexible systems that handle change, because they minimise interdependency. Loose is not zero: the subject still relies on the interface, and observers still rely on the subject to tell them.

card.rule: Loosely coupled objects interact while knowing as little as possible about each other.
card.limits: Loose coupling shrinks what each side knows, not whether they depend on each other. The subject still relies on the interface and observers still rely on the subject to tell them.

concepts.title: What loose coupling buys
concepts.question: Which changes can be made to subjects and observers without breaking the other side?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A design is only as good as the changes it survives. Observers come and go, get swapped, and may be wanted in other programs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The subject depends only on a list of objects that implement the Observer interface. So new observers can be added at any time, an observer can be replaced at run time, and observers can be removed at any time. A new kind of observer needs no change to the subject: implement the interface and register.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Subjects and observers can be reused independently, and changes to either do not affect the other, as long as both still meet their interface obligations. The freedom ends where the interface itself changes, which reaches both sides.

card.rule: While both sides keep to the interfaces, either can be changed, added, removed or reused without touching the other.
card.limits: The freedom lasts only while the interface contract is kept. Changing the interface itself reaches both sides, so this is not permission to change anything at all.

concepts.title: Three principles at work
concepts.question: How does the Observer Pattern apply the earlier principles of encapsulating variation, programming to interfaces and composition?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Chapter 1 gave three principles: separate what varies, program to an interface, and favor composition over inheritance. The authors ask how Observer applies each.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: What varies is the state of the subject and the number and types of observers; the pattern lets you vary the dependents without changing the subject. Subject and observers both use interfaces, which keeps things loosely coupled. Observers are attached to subjects by composition, set up at run time and not by an inheritance hierarchy.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: One structure satisfies all three principles at once. Using the pattern in name does not guarantee this, though: the chapter later finds that java.util.Observable falls short on some of them.

card.rule: Observer separates what varies (the observers), programs to interfaces, and links subject and observers by composition.
card.limits: The chapter later finds that the built-in java.util.Observable falls short on two of these principles, so using the pattern in name does not guarantee the principles are followed.

concepts.title: Applying Observer to the weather station
concepts.question: How do we apply Observer to the weather station: who is the subject, who are the observers, and how do they get the data?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Mary and Sue know the definition but must turn it into classes. They also have to decide how the measurements reach the displays, which is left open for now.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Mary reads the definition: WeatherData is the one and the displays are the many, and the measurements are the state that changes. Sue adds that displays register with WeatherData, which then calls a method on each. Displays differ in type, so they share an interface with an update() method.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Passing the measurements as arguments to update() is the team's first, simplest answer, and the authors return to that choice later in the chapter. The mapping is a start, not the end of the design.

card.rule: Make WeatherData the subject and each display an observer behind a common interface with update().
card.limits: This is the team’s first answer. How the measurements travel to the observers is left open and revisited later in the chapter, so the mapping is not the end of the design.

concepts.section: Implementing the Subject interface in WeatherData
concepts.title: WeatherData as a subject
concepts.question: What changes inside WeatherData when it implements the Subject interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: WeatherData must tell any number of displays about new readings, including none, without naming them in its code.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: WeatherData implements the Subject interface. It keeps the list of registered observers and offers the methods to register and remove them. measurementsChanged() no longer names displays: it goes through the list and calls update() on each observer with the new measurements.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: One loop covers any number of displays. How the list is stored and the loop written are the implementer's choices. The chapter's own listing is not copied here.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The loop replaces the named calls.

card.rule: WeatherData keeps the observer list and, when measurementsChanged() runs, tells every observer on it.
card.limits: How the list is stored and how the loop is written are the implementer’s choices. The chapter’s code is not reproduced here, and the same idea fits other storage.

concepts.section: Now, let’s build those display elements
concepts.title: Displays that register themselves
concepts.question: What does a display do when it is built, and why does it keep a reference to the subject?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A display must get onto the subject's list and may later need to leave it. The subject should not have to know about displays in advance.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Each display implements the Observer interface. In the current conditions display the constructor receives the subject and registers the display with it. The display also stores the subject, although it does not use it again, because it may want to unregister in future. Its update() stores the new values and calls display().

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The display chooses to join, so nothing else needs to know it exists. Calling display() inside update() suits a small example; the authors say there are much better ways, which Model-View-Controller shows later.

card.rule: A display registers itself with the subject when built and keeps the subject so it can unregister later.
card.limits: Calling display() directly inside update() suits a small example only. The authors point to Model-View-Controller for a better separation of receiving data from presenting it.

concepts.title: Adding a display late
concepts.question: How can a new display, such as the heat index, be added to the weather station?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The CEO says the station cannot ship without a heat index display, which combines temperature and humidity into how hot it feels. The formula comes in a supplied file.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Write a new HeatIndexDisplay class that implements the Observer interface and register it with WeatherData. It takes temperature and humidity from each update, computes the index and shows it, and ignores pressure.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The subject is not touched, which is the payoff of the design. It holds only while the new display needs data the subject already provides; a value the subject does not hold forces a change to the subject. A display that ignores part of what is pushed shows a cost of pushing one fixed set.

card.rule: To add a display, write one new observer class and register it; leave the subject alone.
card.limits: This works when the new display needs only data the subject already provides. A display that needs a value the subject does not hold forces a change to the subject.

concepts.title: Push and pull
concepts.question: What do push and pull mean for getting state to observers, and what does each cost?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An observer needs the new state, and the state has to get there somehow. The book stages a chat between a subject and an observer who disagree.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: With push, the subject sends the state along with the notification, as the weather update() does with temperature, humidity and pressure. With pull, the subject only notifies and each observer fetches what it wants from the subject through getters.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The subject likes push: one notification carries everything. It fears that pull opens it up through public getters and takes several calls. The observer prefers pull: observers differ, each takes only what it needs, and new state needs only a new getter, not new update calls on every observer.

card.rule: Push sends the state to every observer; pull lets each observer fetch what it needs.
card.limits: Each style has a price. Push gives all observers the same set and ties update() to it. Pull needs public getters and may need several calls to collect what an observer wants.

concepts.title: Is pull really better?
concepts.question: The authors call pull more correct than push: how sound are their reasons, and when do they hold?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The chapter summary says you can push or pull data, and that pull is considered more correct. That is a claim the reader can test, not a definition.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Their reasons come from the chat: observers differ and the subject cannot predict their needs; each fetches only what it needs; adding state later does not force changes to every update call. To judge the claim, test each reason against the case at hand.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Pull is strong when observers are varied and state is likely to grow. It is weaker when one small state is used in full by every observer, so the subject's points about convenience and private state count for more. This is a considered view, not a law.

card.rule: Weigh the claim that pull is more correct by checking whether its reasons fit the situation.
card.limits: The authors give pull as a considered view, not a law. The subject’s counterpoint, that push is convenient and keeps state private, is real and wins in some cases.

concepts.title: Java’s built-in Observer support
concepts.question: What are java.util.Observable and java.util.Observer, and how do they differ from the hand-built version?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Java ships its own Observer Pattern, so a team may reuse it and not write list handling by hand.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The most general support is the Observer interface and Observable class in java.util, which resemble the hand-built interfaces and work with either push or pull. The subject, WeatherData, extends Observable and inherits its add, delete and notify methods. An observer implements java.util.Observer, calls addObserver() to join and deleteObserver() to leave.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The subject no longer writes its own list, but it must extend a class. The chapter later shows that this brings problems that limit the class's use.

card.rule: Extend Observable to be a subject; implement java.util.Observer and call addObserver to observe.
card.limits: Observable is a class, so a subject must extend it. The chapter later shows this brings problems that limit its use.

concepts.section: How Java’s built-in Observer Pattern works
concepts.title: The changed flag
concepts.question: What must a built-in subject do before notifyObservers() actually notifies, and why does that rule exist?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A sensitive subject may change by tenths of a degree many times a second. Telling every observer each time would flood them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: With the built-in Observable, notifying takes two steps: call setChanged() to signal that state has changed, then call one of the two notifyObservers() methods. If notifyObservers() runs without setChanged() first, the observers are not notified.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The flag lets the subject choose which changes deserve a notification, for example only when the temperature moves by more than half a degree. It is also easy to forget: when notifications go missing, check it first.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Without the flag nobody is told.

card.rule: No notification happens without setChanged(); use it to decide which changes deserve one.
card.limits: The flag is a gate that is easy to forget to open. If observers are not notified when you expect them to be, the missing setChanged() call is the first suspect.

concepts.section: Reworking the Weather Station with the built-in support
concepts.title: Push and pull with the built-in classes
concepts.question: How does the built-in support let a subject push or pull data to observers?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The built-in classes must serve both push and pull, but their update() has to be one fixed method for every observer.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The built-in update() receives the Observable that notified it plus a data object. To push, pass the data to notifyObservers(arg). To let observers pull, call notifyObservers() with no data, and each observer reads what it wants from the Observable it was handed.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The book reworks the displays to pull temperature, humidity and pressure through getters. Either style needs setChanged() first. Pulling needs the subject to expose getters, and pushing needs observers to know what the data object holds.

card.rule: Pass a data object to notifyObservers(arg) to push, or notify without data and let observers pull from the Observable they receive.
card.limits: Pulling needs the subject to expose getters, and pushing with a data object means observers must know what the object contains.

concepts.title: Do not rely on notification order
concepts.question: Why can the output order differ between the hand-built and built-in versions, and what should our code assume about it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two implementations of the same pattern may visit the observers in different orders. Code written against one order is at risk when the other is used.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The reworked weather station gives the same calculations, but the text appears in a different order, because the built-in notifyObservers() notifies in a different order than the hand-built one. The authors ask which is right and answer: neither, they were just implemented differently.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Writing code that depends on a specific order is incorrect: if the Observable or Observer implementation changes, the order could change and the application could give wrong results. That is not loosely coupled. The advice concerns order between observers.

card.rule: Do not depend on the order in which observers are notified.
card.limits: The advice is about order between observers. It does not claim that notifications happen in no order, only that the order is not part of what the pattern promises.

concepts.title: The dark side of Observable
concepts.question: What problems come from Observable being a class with a protected setChanged(), and which principles does that cut against?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The authors call it the dark side: java.util.Observable is a class and does not implement an interface, and the pattern it supports is meant to follow the principles of chapter 1.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Because it is a class, a subject must subclass it, so it cannot be added to a class that already extends another. With no interface you cannot write your own implementation that works with Java's Observer, nor swap in another, such as a multithreaded one. Also setChanged() is protected, so you cannot compose an Observable instance.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: These problems cut against program to an interface and favor composition over inheritance. The authors say Observable still has some utility and may serve if you can extend it; these are potholes to watch for, not a ban.

card.rule: Judge a library class by whether it lets you follow the principles; Observable’s class form and protected method block reuse and composition.
card.limits: The authors say Observable still has some utility and may serve if you can extend it. These are potholes to watch for, not a ban on using the class.

concepts.title: Built-in or hand-built?
concepts.question: When should you use the built-in Observable, and when should you build your own?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A team that needs observer behaviour must pick between the built-in class and its own version. Constraints such as an existing superclass decide.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Observable may serve your needs if you can extend it. If you cannot, roll your own implementation as the chapter did at the start. The authors add that in a lot of cases it is more flexible to build your own and that it is not all that hard.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A hand-built version costs writing the list handling and does not plug into Java's built-in Observer API. Knowing the pattern well puts you in a good position to work with any API that uses it. The advice is the authors' view; the constraints of the project decide.

card.rule: Use the built-in class when you can extend it and its limits are tolerable; otherwise write an interface-based version of your own.
card.limits: This is the authors’ view. A hand-built version costs writing the list handling and does not plug into Java’s built-in Observer API, so the right choice depends on the constraints.

concepts.section: Other places you’ll find the Observer Pattern in the JDK
concepts.title: Observers in Swing
concepts.question: How do Swing listeners relate to observers, and what happens when a button is clicked?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: GUI toolkits must react to user actions without knowing in advance what the program will do. Swing solves this with the same pattern under other names.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A JButton, through its superclass AbstractButton, has many add and remove listener methods. The listeners are the observers, and an ActionListener listens for actions such as a press. The book's example has a button with an AngelListener and a DevilListener, each answering in its own way.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The match is by role: frameworks rename the parts and use their own method names and event objects. Listeners appear all over Swing, and many other GUI frameworks use the pattern heavily.

card.rule: In Swing, a component is the subject and its listeners are observers added and removed through add and remove methods.
card.limits: Frameworks rename the roles and use their own method names and event objects. The match is by role, so a different toolkit may call the same thing by another name.

concepts.section: The updated code, using lambda expressions
concepts.title: Lambdas as observers
concepts.question: How can a lambda expression act as an observer, and does it change the pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An inner class for a listener is a lot of ceremony when the listener is one line long.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Lambda expressions were added in Java 8. A lambda creates a function object, and that function object is the observer. Passed to addActionListener(), it is matched to actionPerformed(), the one method in the ActionListener interface, and the button calls it on a click like any other listener.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: You are still using the Observer Pattern: you only skip creating an ActionListener object. This works where the observer interface has one method. Readers unfamiliar with lambdas can keep using inner classes.

card.rule: A lambda that fits a one-method observer interface is an observer, and the pattern is unchanged.
card.limits: This applies where the observer interface has a single method, as ActionListener does. The pattern itself does not need lambdas, and inner classes still work.

concepts.title: One subclass per combination
concepts.question: What goes wrong when a shop gives every drink-and-extras combination its own subclass?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each drink can take any mix of extras, and every extra has its own price. Prices change and new extras such as caramel arrive. Pricing each combination in a class of its own ties every price to many places.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The starting design: an abstract Beverage, one subclass per drink, and then one more subclass for each drink-and-extras combination. Every combination class works out its own total.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors call the result a maintenance nightmare. When milk gets dearer, every class that includes milk is edited, and a new topping means yet more classes.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Each combination class repeats the prices of its parts.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Class names that list every extra, and one price constant repeated in many classes.

card.rule: One subclass per combination multiplies the classes and scatters every price change across many of them.
card.limits: With a few fixed combinations that will not change, one subclass for each stays manageable; the trouble starts when options multiply or change.

concepts.title: Flags in the base class
concepts.question: Why does keeping a true-or-false flag for each extra in the base class still leave Starbuzz with problems?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Fewer classes would help, yet each extra still needs a price and a place in the order. The base class is the one spot every drink shares, so it looks like the natural home for the extras.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: One Beverage base class keeps a true-or-false flag for each extra. Its cost() adds the price of every extra whose flag is on, and each drink subclass adds its own price on top.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The class count drops, but the trouble remains: a price change edits the base class, and a new extra means a new flag and more changes to existing code. The authors add that base-class functionality may not suit some subclasses.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Skip it when extras would keep arriving or differ by subclass. It is a fair choice when the options are few, stable and suit every subclass.

card.rule: Flags in the base class shrink the class count, yet every new or changed extra still edits existing code and burdens some subclasses.
card.limits: If the options are few, stable and fit every subclass, flags in the base class can be a reasonable, simple choice.

concepts.title: Static inheritance, runtime composition
concepts.question: How does behaviour gained by composition differ from behaviour inherited by subclassing, and when is each fixed?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: New behaviour must be added without breaking code that already works. Inheritance fixes behaviour in the class tree, so each new combination seems to demand editing or a new subclass.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Composition and delegation: one object holds others and hands work on to them. Behaviour inherited by subclassing is set at compile time and is shared by every subclass. Composed behaviour can be assembled at runtime.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: New responsibilities, even ones the superclass designer never imagined, arrive as new code and not as edits, so existing code is less likely to gain bugs or side effects. The price is more objects to create and coordinate.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Plain inheritance is enough when all variants share the same behaviour and nothing varies at runtime.

card.rule: Subclassing fixes behaviour at compile time for all subclasses; composition lets you add behaviour at runtime by writing new code.
card.limits: Composition adds more objects to create and coordinate, and when all variants share the same behaviour and nothing varies at runtime, plain inheritance is enough.

concepts.title: The Open-Closed Principle
concepts.question: What does the Open-Closed Principle ask of a class, and what does it buy?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Requirements change, yet code that has been written and tested is valuable. Editing it risks new bugs, while refusing all change makes the system rigid.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. Others may add new behaviour, while the working source stays as it is.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors say the reward is a design that is resilient to change and flexible enough to take on new functionality when requirements change. It is a goal, not a guarantee that every class can be extended.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: A class with no likely change gains little from extension points; the principle is pursued where change is expected.

card.rule: Design classes so new behaviour arrives as new code, while working code stays unchanged.
card.limits: A class without extension points is not broken; the principle is a goal pursued where change is expected, not a rule for every class.

concepts.title: Open and closed without contradiction
concepts.question: How can a class be open and closed at the same time without contradicting itself?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: Open means others can add behaviour to a class. Closed means the finished, tested source is not edited. Each word describes a different thing, so the phrase asks for one result: extension by new code.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Without this reading the principle sounds self-contradictory and is easy to dismiss. The authors point to techniques that allow extension without direct modification, such as the Observer Pattern: new observers extend a subject without new code in it.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: A design is open only along the extension points it supplies. Any other kind of extension still means editing its code.

card.rule: Open means behaviour can be added; closed means existing code is not edited, so the words do not collide.
card.limits: A design is open only along the extension points it provides; extending it any other way means editing its code.

concepts.title: Apply it where change is likely
concepts.question: Why do the authors say not to apply the Open-Closed Principle to every part of a design?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Making a design extensible takes time and effort, and every extension point adds abstraction. Effort is limited, and nobody can predict every change.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Aim the Open-Closed Principle at the parts of a design most likely to change. Finding them comes partly from experience of object-oriented design and partly from knowing the domain.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors say you usually cannot make every part follow the principle, and doing so would probably be wasteful. Applied everywhere, it can lead to complex, hard-to-understand code. The principle gives no formula, so some guesses will be wrong.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: An extension point on a part of the design that has never changed and has no sign of changing.

card.rule: Spend extensibility effort on the parts of the design most likely to change.
card.limits: Judging what will change takes experience and domain knowledge, so you will sometimes guess wrong; the principle gives no formula.

concepts.title: Decorating by wrapping
concepts.question: How do you build a Dark Roast with Mocha and Whip by decorating, without a new subclass?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Customers combine drinks and extras in any mix at order time. A class for every mix does not scale, and extras added after the drink is built cannot come from inheritance.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Start with a plain beverage and decorate it at runtime. For a Dark Roast with Mocha and Whip, take a DarkRoast, wrap it in a Mocha, wrap that in a Whip, then call cost(). Each decorator holds the object it wraps.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A new extra is one new wrapper class, and no existing class changes. Orders can combine extras in any way. The cost is many small objects, and code that must choose the extras and their order correctly.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Wrapping replaces a combination class.

card.rule: Start with the plain object and wrap it, one decorator per extra, at runtime.
card.limits: Wrapping builds an order from many small objects, and the code that assembles the chain must choose the extras and their order correctly.

concepts.section: Constructing a drink order with Decorators
concepts.title: Delegating inward
concepts.question: When cost() is called on the outermost wrapper, how does the total price come about?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A price made of several parts must be added up without the client knowing how many extras sit around the drink or which ones.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The client calls cost() on the outermost decorator. It delegates to the object it wraps, and so on inward to the plain drink. As each result returns, each decorator adds its own charge. A decorator may act before delegating, after it, or both.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each decorator needs to know only the one object it wraps, so the chain can be any length. Where wrappers work on one another's output, the order of wrapping can change the result.

card.rule: Call the outermost decorator; each decorator delegates inward and adds its own part.
card.limits: The order of wrappers can matter when each step works on the previous step's output, such as encrypting before or after adding a watermark.

concepts.section: Okay, here’s what we know so far...
concepts.title: Same supertype, so substitutable
concepts.question: Why can a decorated object be used anywhere the plain object was used?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A wrapped drink must still work wherever a plain drink worked, or every caller would need to know about wrappers.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A decorator has the same supertype as the object it decorates. A DarkRoast wrapped in Mocha and Whip is still a Beverage, so it can be passed on and priced like any other. Wrappers can wrap wrappers, and objects can be decorated at any time.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Client code written against the shared type cannot tell a wrapped object from a plain one. The authors flag runtime decoration with any number of decorators as a key point.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Substitution does not extend to code that checks for one specific concrete class; such code does not see through the wrapper.

card.rule: A decorator shares its component's type, so the wrapped object can replace the original anywhere.
card.limits: The substitution holds for code written against the shared type; code that checks for a specific concrete class will not see through the wrapper.

concepts.title: The pattern in one sentence
concepts.question: How does the book define the Decorator Pattern, and what does it offer instead of subclassing?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Behaviour must be added to some objects, chosen while the program runs, without a subclass for each variant.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The book defines the Decorator Pattern as attaching additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Dynamically means at runtime. Decorators are a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: New behaviour comes from composing the object with a decorator, so a single object can gain responsibilities. The definition names the role only; the class structure in the beverage example shows how to build it.

card.rule: The Decorator Pattern attaches extra responsibilities to an object at runtime, as a flexible alternative to subclassing.
card.limits: The definition describes the role only; it does not tell you how to structure the classes, so use it together with the class structure, not alone.

concepts.title: Roles in the design
concepts.question: What do component, concrete component, decorator and concrete decorator each name in the beverage design?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: The abstract component is the shared type, Beverage. A concrete component is a real item that can be decorated, such as HouseBlend. The abstract decorator, CondimentDecorator, extends Beverage. A concrete decorator, such as Mocha, adds one extra.

blocks.label: Why it matters
