blocks.text: Component names the thing being wrapped and decorator names the wrapper. These are jobs, not kinds of product, so naming a class by its role tells you what it holds and what it may replace.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: Roles are jobs, not fixed classes. A decorator can itself be wrapped by another decorator, so one object can play both parts.

card.rule: Name each class by its role: abstract component, concrete component, abstract decorator or concrete decorator.
card.limits: Roles are jobs, not fixed classes: a decorator can itself be wrapped by another decorator, so one object can play both parts.

concepts.title: Inherit the type, not the behaviour
concepts.question: Why does CondimentDecorator extend Beverage when decorators do not get their behaviour from it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Decorators must be interchangeable with the objects they wrap, yet their added behaviour should not be fixed at compile time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: CondimentDecorator extends Beverage only so that decorators match the type of what they wrap. Behaviour is not inherited. It comes from composing a decorator with a component and with other decorators.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Decorators can be mixed and matched in any way at runtime, and new ones added later. Behaviour set by inheritance is fixed at compile time and limited to what the superclass supplies or what is overridden.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A decorator that depends on inherited code for its added behaviour is getting that behaviour by inheritance again.

card.rule: Decorators inherit the component's type, not its behaviour; the behaviour comes from composition.
card.limits: This reading holds when the superclass supplies only the shared type; if decorators also rely on inherited code, behaviour is coming from inheritance again.

concepts.title: Abstract class or interface for the type
concepts.question: Why did Starbuzz keep an abstract Beverage class when an interface could also supply the shared type?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Decorators need a shared type, and Java can supply it with an abstract class or an interface. Starbuzz already owned a working abstract Beverage.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors note that the pattern traditionally specifies an abstract component, though in Java an interface could be used. Starbuzz kept Beverage because the team tries to avoid altering existing code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Decorators are written against the type that already exists, and nothing old is edited. Our reading: this applies the Open-Closed Principle to the team's own habits.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: the argument for keeping the abstract class covers code you already have. With a fresh design the choice is open, and an interface may be the lighter way.

card.rule: A decorator needs the component's type, supplied by an abstract class or an interface; keep the existing one if it works.
card.limits: When designing from scratch, the choice is open and an interface may be the lighter way to give the type; the argument for keeping applies to code you already have.

concepts.title: What a concrete decorator holds and does
concepts.question: What must a concrete decorator hold and implement to wrap a beverage and add its own extra?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each condiment must add its own charge and description without knowing which drink, or which other condiments, it is wrapping.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A concrete decorator, such as Mocha, holds a reference to the beverage it wraps, given when it is built. Its cost() asks the wrapped beverage for its cost and adds its own. Its getDescription() asks for the description and adds its own name.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Beverage and the concrete drinks do not change. Each new condiment is one class written to the same recipe. A decorator can build only on what the wrapped object returns, so it cannot reach deeper into the chain.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: One condiment class follows the recipe.

card.rule: A concrete decorator stores the component it wraps and implements each method by delegating to it and adding its own part.
card.limits: A decorator can only build on what the wrapped object returns; it cannot reach deeper into the chain, so reorganising descriptions needs extra code.

concepts.title: Code that checks concrete types
concepts.question: What happens to code that checks for a specific concrete component once decorators wrap it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Code that gives a discount to a HouseBlend must recognise a HouseBlend. Decorators put another object in front of it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Decorators are transparent to code that uses only the abstract component type. Transparency stops when code relies on a concrete component type: wrapping a HouseBlend makes the outer object a decorator, so the test fails.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors say that once you write code against concrete components, you should rethink your application design and your use of decorators.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Type tests, casts or class-name comparisons on a value that might be wrapped.

card.rule: Write client code against the abstract component type; checks on concrete components break once decorators wrap them.
card.limits: The problem arises only for code that inspects concrete types; when all code uses the abstract type, decorators can be added with no change.

concepts.title: Chains, outermost objects and creation
concepts.question: Why is a decorator that needs to know every layer of its chain stretching the pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A decorator is meant to add behaviour to the one object it wraps. Features that need a view across the whole chain, or a client holding the wrong layer, strain that design.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Each decorator works with the single object it wraps, and clients hold the outermost decorator. If a decorator must look several layers in, the authors say you are pushing it beyond its true intent, though it is possible.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: More objects are in play, so errors such as holding an inner decorator are more likely, and its charge is lost. A CondimentPrettyPrint decorator could parse the final description to tidy it.

card.rule: Let each decorator work with the one object it wraps, and hand clients only the outermost decorator.
card.limits: Features that need knowledge of the whole chain are possible with extra decorators, but they strain the pattern, so consider whether a different design suits better.

concepts.title: Decorators in Java I/O
concepts.question: How does the java.io package use the Decorator Pattern to add features when reading a file?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Reading a file needs optional features such as buffering and line numbering. A class for every combination of source and feature would be huge.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The java.io package is largely based on the Decorator Pattern. A basic input stream is wrapped in decorators. BufferedInputStream and LineNumberInputStream extend FilterInputStream, the abstract decorator. Output streams, Readers and Writers follow similar designs.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Features are mixed by wrapping. The package has many small classes that can overwhelm newcomers, and Reader and Writer mirror the byte streams only closely, with a few inconsistencies.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Wrap the source, then add features.

card.rule: In java.io, decorators such as buffering wrap an input stream; read the API by asking what each wrapper adds.
card.limits: The package has many small classes that can overwhelm newcomers, and the Reader and Writer streams mirror the byte streams only closely, with a few inconsistencies.

concepts.title: Weighing the costs of decorators
concepts.question: Which costs of the Decorator Pattern do the authors admit, and how should you weigh them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The pattern gives flexibility and keeps classes closed to modification, but a fair judgment also weighs what it costs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors name three costs. Decorator designs often have many small classes. Code relying on concrete types can break. The code to create an object grows, since the component must be wrapped in several decorators.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors state these costs openly, and in the interview point to Factory and Builder to ease creation. A fair critique shows a specific cost that outweighs the benefit for the case at hand.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: skip wrappers when a feature is fixed for years and nothing varies at runtime.

card.rule: Weigh decorators' flexibility against many small classes, breakage of concrete-type checks and heavier creation code.
card.limits: Naming a cost is not a reason to reject the pattern; criticism must show that the costs outweigh the benefit in the case at hand.

concepts.title: When you see new, think concrete
concepts.question: What does a new expression tell you about the code that contains it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Code that picks a class from run-time conditions names every candidate class. The authors say new itself is fine. The trouble is change: the list of candidates keeps moving, and each move sends you back into that code.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: When you see new, think concrete. You are instantiating one specific class, an implementation rather than an interface. Code written to an interface keeps working with new implementing classes through polymorphism.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Code that names many concrete classes may have to be reopened whenever one is added or removed, and the same choice often sits in several places. A fixed set of classes causes no such trouble.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The first line is tied to two classes; the second asks a factory and names neither.

card.rule: When you see new, think concrete: the code is tied to that class and must be reopened whenever the set of choices changes.
card.limits: The cost appears only where the choices vary. A class that is very unlikely to change can be created directly without harm.

concepts.title: Concrete choices break closed for modification
concepts.question: Why does code that picks among concrete classes fail to be closed for modification?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A design should be open for extension and closed for modification, as the previous chapter reviewed. Code that chooses among concrete classes must be opened up each time a variant comes or goes, so it fails this test.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Closed for modification means new behavior arrives by adding code, not by editing code that already works. The authors turn to their first principle for the clue: identify the aspects that vary and separate them from what stays the same.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Choosing code has to be examined for what to add or delete on every change. Because the same chain tends to be repeated in several parts of the application, maintenance and updates become harder and more error-prone.

card.rule: A piece of code is closed for modification only if adding a new concrete type needs no edit to it.
card.limits: Closed does not mean frozen. Bug fixes and genuinely new requirements still reopen code; the aim is that routine additions of variants do not.

concepts.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
concepts.title: Finding the lines that vary
concepts.question: In an ordering method, which lines change as the menu changes and which stay the same?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The ordering method does two jobs. It decides which pizza class to build from the type requested, then it prepares, bakes, cuts and boxes the pizza. The menu changes often; the processing steps do not.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Apply the first principle: the creation lines are the aspect that varies, so separate them from the processing steps that stay the same. Once you know what varies, the next move is to encapsulate it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The creation lines keep the method from being closed for modification, because Clam and Veggie arrive and Greek leaves. The authors conclude that dealing with which concrete class to instantiate is what is messing up the method.

card.rule: Find the lines that change with the menu and separate them from the steps that stay the same.
card.limits: Separate only what really varies. Moving stable code out adds indirection and gives nothing in return.

concepts.title: A factory handles creation
concepts.question: What is a factory in this chapter, and what does the old ordering method become?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Creation code mixed into the ordering method forces that method to know about Greek versus Clam pizzas. The authors want a place whose only concern is creating pizzas.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Move the creation code into a separate object, which the authors call a Factory. Factories handle the details of object creation. The old method becomes a client of the factory: it asks for a pizza and works with whatever implements Pizza.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The client no longer names concrete pizza classes. It cares only that the result implements the Pizza interface, so it can prepare, bake, cut and box it.

card.rule: A factory is an object whose only job is to create other objects, so its clients ask for a product instead of building it.
card.limits: A factory does not remove concrete classes from the program. Some code, usually the factory, still names them; the gain is that the naming is gathered in one place.

concepts.title: Why one creation class helps
concepts.question: How does moving creation into one class help when it only seems to push the problem elsewhere?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A critic says that moving creation into another class only pushes the problem elsewhere. The authors need a reply that explains why one creation class still helps.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: SimplePizzaFactory has a createPizza(type) method holding the old chain of decisions. Clients such as the ordering code ask it for a pizza and call the pizza methods on the result.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The factory may have many clients, for example a menu class and a home-delivery class. Encapsulating creation in one class leaves one place to modify when the implementation changes, and removes concrete instantiations from the client code.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, each store creates its pizza itself; after, it asks the factory.

card.rule: Put creation logic in one class so many clients share a single place to change.
card.limits: With one client, a short menu and no expected change the gain is small. The factory's own create method still changes when the menu does.

concepts.title: Static factory: convenient but fixed
concepts.question: What do you gain and lose by making the simple factory's create method static?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Callers want to use a simple factory without building a factory object first. Some designs therefore make its create method static, an approach often called a static factory.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A static create method is called directly on the class name, so no instance is needed. An ordinary factory object is an instance that can be handed to a client, which lets a different factory be passed in.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors name the disadvantage: you cannot subclass the factory and change the behavior of the create method. You gain convenience and lose the ability to swap or specialize creation.

card.rule: A static factory is convenient to call, but its creation behavior cannot be subclassed or swapped.
card.limits: If the creation rule will not need replacing, the convenience may outweigh the loss. The cost appears only when a different creator is needed.

concepts.title: The store holds its factory
concepts.question: How does the store hold its factory, and what could be swapped in?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Franchises will want pizzas in different regional styles, yet the store's ordering code should stay the same. The store needs a way to be given different creation behavior.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Rework PizzaStore so it receives a SimplePizzaFactory and keeps it in a field. Its orderPizza() calls factory.createPizza(type) instead of building pizzas itself.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Because the store is composed with the factory, a different factory can be swapped in. The authors suggest New York, Chicago and California style factories. The ordering code is unchanged; only the factory it holds differs.

card.rule: Give the client a reference to its factory so a different factory can be swapped in.
card.limits: Swapping the factory changes only how products are created. The store can still run its own steps its own way, which proves a weakness later.

concepts.title: Simple Factory is an idiom
concepts.question: Why do the authors give Simple Factory only an honorable mention instead of calling it a design pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Developers often say Factory Pattern for any class that builds objects. The authors want readers to separate a widely used coding habit from the two true factory patterns coming next.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: The authors say Simple Factory is not actually a design pattern but a programming idiom. It is commonly used, so it gets a Head First Pattern Honorable Mention.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Some developers mistake the idiom for the Factory Pattern. The authors treat it as a warm-up before two heavy-duty patterns that are both factories, and still call it a simple way to decouple clients from concrete classes.

card.rule: Treat Simple Factory as a handy idiom, and do not confuse it with Factory Method or Abstract Factory.
card.limits: The label is the authors' judgment about what counts as a pattern, and the idiom is useful whatever it is called. Other writers may draw the line differently.

concepts.title: What implementing an interface means
concepts.question: What does the phrase implement an interface cover in design patterns, beyond the Java keyword?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Design-pattern books say a class implements an interface even when no Java interface is in sight. A reader who takes the phrase literally will misread many diagrams.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: In general use, a concrete class that supplies a method from a supertype is implementing that supertype's interface. The supertype can be a class or a Java interface.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: A subclass that provides the methods of an abstract class counts as implementing that class's interface, though it writes extends. In Java code, the keyword implements still names a Java interface.

card.rule: To implement an interface is to supply the methods of any supertype's public contract, whether the supertype is a Java interface or a class.
card.limits: The broad sense is for reading design talk. In Java code the keyword implements still names a Java interface, so check which sense a speaker means.

concepts.title: Two needs at once
concepts.question: What two needs pull against each other when the pizza store becomes a franchise?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The store succeeds and franchises spread. The franchiser wants every franchise to use its time-tested code, while each region wants its own style of pizza (New York, Chicago, California) to suit local taste.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: State the problem as two needs before choosing a design: freedom to vary the pizza style by region, and consistency in the way the store operates.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A solution has to satisfy both needs. A design that gives the regions their own styles but loosens the franchiser's procedures meets only one of them.

card.rule: State a design problem as its competing needs before choosing a solution.
card.limits: Naming the needs does not choose the solution, and some designs satisfy only one need well.

concepts.section: But you’d like a little more quality control...
concepts.title: Judging one factory per region
concepts.question: Does giving each region its own factory meet both of the franchiser's needs?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Franchises need regional pizza styles, and the franchiser needs a consistent process. The first idea is one factory per region: NYPizzaFactory, ChicagoPizzaFactory and CaliforniaPizzaFactory.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Remove SimplePizzaFactory and compose each PizzaStore with the factory for its region. Each franchise then creates its own style of pizza.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Test-marketing showed franchises using the factory for creation but inventing their own procedures for the rest: baking differently, forgetting to cut and using third-party boxes. Variety was met; consistency was not. The authors want a framework that ties store and creation together.

card.rule: Judge an approach against every stated need: this one varies creation but leaves the process uncontrolled.
card.limits: The test-market report is the authors' story, not data. The weakness exists only where franchises are free to edit or bypass the process.

concepts.section: A framework for the pizza store
concepts.title: Keep the process, vary one step
concepts.question: How can the pizza store keep its ordering process fixed yet let each region choose its pizzas?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The franchiser wants one well-honed ordering routine shared by every franchise, and wants the pizza style to vary by region. Nothing yet ties the two together.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Put createPizza() back into PizzaStore as an abstract method, and create a PizzaStore subclass for each regional style. The shared orderPizza() routine stays in the base class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: All the variation among stores is pushed into createPizza(), and the ordering procedure stays consistent across franchises. Each subclass determines the pizza, all inside the PizzaStore framework.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The ordering routine stays in the base class; only one step is left open.

card.rule: Keep the fixed process in a base class and leave the varying step as an abstract method for subclasses.
card.limits: Inheritance fixes each variation when the subclass is chosen. Changing style while the program runs needs a different object, not just a different call.

concepts.title: What decide means here
concepts.question: When the pattern says subclasses decide which class to instantiate, who actually decides and when?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The pattern's official wording says subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Read literally, that suggests a run-time decision made inside the subclass.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: orderPizza() is defined in the abstract PizzaStore, and concrete pizza types are created only in the subclasses. When orderPizza() calls createPizza(), the subclass of the store you chose is called into action.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: There is no real-time decision by the subclass. You decided by choosing the store, and that subclass determines which pizza gets made. The authors say the subclasses are not really deciding.

card.rule: When the book says subclasses decide, it means the chosen subclass determines the product, not that code picks at run time.
card.limits: A creation method can also choose among several products using a parameter. That picking is separate from the sense of deciding by subclass.

concepts.title: The shape of a regional store
concepts.question: What does a regional store inherit, and what must it supply?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each franchise should get the whole ordering routine for free and write only what is regional.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A regional store subclasses PizzaStore and supplies a createPizza() method that implements its style. NYPizzaStore returns New York style pizzas; the Chicago and California stores do the same with their own.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The superclass orderPizza() has no clue which Pizza is created. It knows only that it can prepare, bake, cut and box what comes back.

card.rule: A regional store inherits the whole ordering routine and supplies only the creation method for its style.
card.limits: If a regional store feels it must override the ordering routine, the framework is not doing its job. Style is what varies.

concepts.title: Declaring a factory method
concepts.question: What is a factory method, and what does it decouple?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The ordering code in the superclass needs a Pizza, but it must not contain the code that builds a concrete one.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Declare an abstract creation method in the base class, such as abstract Pizza createPizza(String type). Subclasses implement it. This is the factory method; it returns a product and holds no creation code in the base.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A factory method handles object creation and encapsulates it in a subclass, which decouples the client code in the superclass from the object creation code in the subclass.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The factory method is the one abstract line; the caller uses only the result.

card.rule: A factory method is an abstract creation method that subclasses implement, keeping the superclass code ignorant of concrete products.
card.limits: It decouples the superclass from products, not from the subclass choice: someone must still pick which subclass to instantiate.

concepts.title: Tracing an order step by step
concepts.question: In what order do the pieces run when a customer orders a pizza in the factory method design?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Readers need to see where the work happens when two customers order in different cities from the same code.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Joel instantiates a ChicagoPizzaStore and Ethan a NYPizzaStore. Each calls orderPizza() with a type. orderPizza() calls createPizza(), defined in the subclasses, which returns a Pizza; orderPizza() then prepares, bakes, cuts and boxes it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: orderPizza() has no idea what kind of pizza was created. It knows only that it has a Pizza. The same call gives a New York or Chicago result depending on the store.

card.rule: Trace an order as: choose the store, call orderPizza, let the subclass create, then process the product.
card.limits: The trace shows the normal flow only. It does not show where the choice of store came from, which sits outside the pattern.

concepts.title: Creators and products
concepts.question: What are the four players of the pattern, and which one holds the factory method?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A pattern is easier to recognize when each class has a named role. This one has two sides: the classes that create and the classes that are created.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The abstract Creator gives an interface with a factory method, and its other methods operate on the products. Concrete creators implement the factory method. On the other side, Pizza is the abstract product and the regional pizzas are concrete products.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Only the subclasses of the creator implement the factory method and create products. The creator is written against the abstract product, so it never needs to name a concrete one.

card.rule: Name the roles: the abstract creator holds the factory method, concrete creators implement it, and the abstract product is what the creator works with.
card.limits: Real designs rarely use these textbook names. Identify roles by what each class does: who declares creation, who implements it, who is created.

concepts.title: Two hierarchies side by side
concepts.question: How do the creator classes and the product classes mirror each other?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each region needs its own way of making its own products. That knowledge has to live somewhere without leaking into the shared routine.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Seen as a framework, the pattern encapsulates product knowledge in each creator. Draw the creators on one side and the products on the other: the two hierarchies run in parallel, linked by the factory method.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: NYPizzaStore knows how to make New York style products and ChicagoPizzaStore the Chicago ones. A new California region needs a new creator and its matching products, one more strand in each hierarchy.

card.rule: Pair every concrete creator with its concrete products; adding a region adds a strand to both hierarchies.
card.limits: Parallel hierarchies cost classes: each variation adds a creator and a product set. If variants are few, the extra structure may not pay off.

concepts.title: The Factory Method definition
concepts.question: What does the official definition of Factory Method say, and what does defer mean in it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A class wants to use a product while leaving the choice of concrete class open to whoever extends it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Factory Method Pattern defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Factory Method lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Like every factory it encapsulates the instantiation of concrete types. The abstract Creator's other methods operate on products from the factory method, and only subclasses implement it. Defer means the creator postpones the choice to a subclass.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The authors present it as one way to encapsulate creation. Abstract Factory is another, and it uses object composition rather than inheritance.

card.rule: Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object and defers the choice of class to subclasses.
card.limits: It is one form of encapsulating creation, not the only one. Other factories, such as Abstract Factory, use composition instead of inheritance.

concepts.title: Forms a factory method can take
concepts.question: What forms can a factory method take, and why does it help even with one concrete creator?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The pizza stores use one parameterized, abstract factory method, and a reader may take that for the only shape allowed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The factory method need not be abstract: a default factory method can produce a concrete product, so the creator works without subclasses. It may be parameterized to build several products, or build one product and take no parameter. Both forms are valid.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: With only one concrete creator the pattern still decouples a product's implementation from its use, so changing products does not affect the creator. A plain String parameter is not type-safe; typed alternatives such as constants or enums catch errors earlier.

card.rule: A factory method may have a default, may be parameterized or single-product, and still decouples use from implementation with one creator.
card.limits: A string parameter pushes mistakes to run time. If many products are created from one method, a typed parameter keeps errors visible before the program runs.

concepts.title: Simple Factory versus Factory Method
concepts.question: How do Simple Factory and Factory Method differ, given that the concrete stores look like a simple factory?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The concrete stores look very like SimplePizzaFactory. A reader asks whether the two are the same thing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Simple Factory is a separate object composed with the store. In Factory Method, the concrete stores extend a class that declares createPizza() abstract, and orderPizza() is a general framework that relies on the factory method.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors call Simple Factory a one-shot deal: it encapsulates creation but gives no way to vary the products. Factory Method lets the chosen subclass decide which products go into the pizza.

card.rule: Simple Factory composes a separate creator object; Factory Method places the creation step in subclasses of the class that uses the product.
card.limits: The two can look the same when written out. The difference is the relationship: a separate object versus an inheriting subclass.

concepts.title: Creation cannot be avoided
concepts.question: Is a factory merely hiding the concrete classes, and what does the master reply?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A student worries that a factory still uses concrete classes to instantiate objects. Is he fooling himself?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The master replies that creation is a fact of life: we must create objects or we will never write a Java program. The answer is to corral the creation code, like the sheep whose wool you would pull over your eyes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Once corralled, the creation code can be protected and cared for. If it is left to run wild, you can never collect its wool.

card.rule: Concrete creation cannot be eliminated, only gathered in one place where it can be maintained.
card.limits: Corralling works only when the corral is the single place. Creation code that still lives elsewhere keeps the problem alive.

concepts.title: Counting what a class depends on
concepts.question: How do you count the concrete classes a piece of code depends on, and what happens when a variant is added?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The very dependent PizzaStore creates every pizza object inside the store instead of delegating to a factory. Directly instantiating an object makes you depend on its concrete class.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Draw the store with every pizza class it creates: there is one arrow from the store to each concrete class, so the store depends on all of them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The count grows with the menu: adding California style pizzas makes the store depend on the new California classes as well. Reducing these dependencies is the goal the next principle formalizes.

card.rule: Count a class's dependencies by counting the distinct concrete classes it names; each new variant adds one.
card.limits: A count shows exposure, not damage. A dependency on a class that is very unlikely to change costs little.

concepts.title: Depend on abstractions
concepts.question: What does the Dependency Inversion Principle say, and how does it differ from program to an interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Reducing dependencies on concrete classes is a good thing. The authors want a formal, memorable statement of it.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The Dependency Inversion Principle: depend upon abstractions; do not depend upon concrete classes. It is stronger than program to an interface, because high-level components should not depend on low-level ones; both should depend on abstractions.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A high-level component is a class whose behavior is defined in terms of other, low-level components. PizzaStore is high-level because its behavior is defined in terms of pizzas, the low-level components.

card.rule: Depend upon abstractions, and let both high-level and low-level components depend on them.
card.limits: The principle does not say that concrete classes disappear. It says the arrows between components should point at abstractions.

concepts.title: Where the inversion happens
concepts.question: How does applying Factory Method invert the dependencies, and what is inverted in your thinking?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The very dependent store depends on every pizza type because orderPizza() instantiates concrete types. Pizza exists as an abstraction, but the store gets little leverage from it.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Apply Factory Method to move the instantiations out. Afterward both the high-level store and the low-level pizzas depend on the abstraction Pizza. Factory Method is not the only technique for this, but it is a powerful one.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The dependencies are inverted: low-level classes now depend on a higher abstraction. Thinking inverts too: instead of starting at the store and going down, start at the pizzas and ask what you can abstract.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, the store holds a concrete class; after, it holds only the abstraction.

card.rule: Start from the low-level classes, abstract what they share, and let both sides depend on that abstraction.
card.limits: Factory Method is one technique among others. It also adds classes, so for a stable class that is unlikely to change it can be more than needed.

concepts.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
concepts.title: Three guidelines for spotting violations
concepts.question: Which three guidelines help you avoid designs that violate the Dependency Inversion Principle?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The principle is easy to agree with and hard to spot in a design. The authors give three checks for designs that violate it.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: No variable should hold a reference to a concrete class. No class should derive from a concrete class. No method should override an implemented method of any of its base classes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Using new holds a reference to a concrete class, so use a factory. Deriving from a concrete class depends on it. Overriding an implemented method suggests the base class was not really an abstraction, because those methods are meant to be shared.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A field typed to a concrete class, a parent that is not abstract, or a subclass redefining an inherited method.

card.rule: Check three things: concrete references held, concrete parents extended, and implemented methods overridden.
card.limits: These are warning signs, not proofs. A hit on one guideline marks a place to look, and calls for a judgment about whether the class is likely to change.

concepts.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
concepts.title: Guidelines to strive for
concepts.question: Must every program obey the Dependency Inversion guidelines, and when is breaking them acceptable?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The three guidelines would forbid code that every Java programmer writes daily. Should they be treated as laws?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The authors say they are guidelines to strive for, not rules to follow all the time. Every Java program ever written violates them, and the value is knowing when you are violating the principle and having a good reason.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A class that is not likely to change may be instantiated directly: String is created constantly because it is very unlikely to change. A class that is likely to change should be shielded with a technique such as Factory Method.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: A class you know is unlikely to change can be instantiated directly; the authors say that is not the end of the world.

card.rule: Treat the guidelines as aims, and break them knowingly, only for classes unlikely to change.
card.limits: Knowing a class is stable is itself a judgment that can be wrong. A class once thought permanent can start to vary, and the cost of reopening code returns.

concepts.title: Keeping ingredients consistent
concepts.question: How can the franchiser guarantee that every franchise uses quality ingredients?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The framework works, but some franchises substitute inferior ingredients to lower costs and raise margins, which will hurt the Objectville brand in the long term.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The franchiser builds a factory that produces the ingredients and ships them to the franchises.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: One problem remains: regions differ, and what is red sauce in New York is not red sauce in Chicago. One set of ingredients must ship to New York and a different set to Chicago.

card.rule: Control quality by supplying the inputs yourself, in a form that still allows regional variation.
card.limits: Supplying inputs controls what goes in, not how it is used. The other controls, such as the shared process, are still needed.

concepts.title: A family of ingredients
concepts.question: What is a family of products, and why does each region need its own?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: New York uses one set of ingredients and Chicago another. California and perhaps Seattle will want theirs, so the design must handle several complete sets.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: In the authors' case a family is all the things needed to make a pizza: dough, sauce, cheese, meats and veggies. Each region uses one family.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Ingredients inside one family belong together: New York's thin crust dough goes with its marinara sauce and Reggiano cheese, not with Chicago's plum tomato sauce.

card.rule: A product family is the set of related parts needed to make one whole thing, and a region chooses one family.
card.limits: Family is about parts that belong together. A group of unrelated products that are merely made by the same company is not a family in this sense.

concepts.title: Building the ingredient factories
concepts.question: What three steps build the ingredient factories and hook them into the store?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The franchiser must supply each region its own matching ingredients, and every store should get its set from one place.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Define an interface for the factory with a create method for each ingredient. Build a factory for each region as a subclass that implements each create method. Implement the ingredient classes, which can be shared among regions where appropriate. Then hook the factories into the old PizzaStore code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: An abstract class could replace the interface if there were common machinery to implement. The authors' interface has methods for dough, sauce, cheese, veggies, pepperoni and clam.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: One interface, one factory per region.

card.rule: Define the factory interface, build one factory per region, then hook the factories into the client.
card.limits: Adding an ingredient to the family changes the interface and so every regional factory must be updated.

concepts.title: Pizzas built from the factory
concepts.question: How do pizzas use an ingredient factory, and why does one class per pizza suffice?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With Factory Method alone there were NYCheesePizza and ChicagoCheesePizza classes that differed only in regional ingredients. The pizzas are made the same way: dough plus sauce plus cheese.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Rework the abstract Pizza so it only uses factory-produced ingredients. A pizza is composed with an ingredient factory, and its prepare() method asks that factory for the dough, sauce and cheese.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: There is no need for two classes per pizza: the ingredient factory handles the regional differences. The Pizza class is decoupled from them and is ready for new regions such as the Rockies or the Pacific Northwest.

card.rule: Give a product the factory that makes its parts, so one product class serves every region.
card.limits: This works when the products are built the same way and differ only in their parts. If the regions assemble differently, separate classes are still needed.

concepts.title: The Abstract Factory definition
concepts.question: What does the Abstract Factory Pattern provide, and what does the client stay free of?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Franchises must get matching ingredients, and the code that builds pizzas should not name any regional ingredient class.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Abstract Factory Pattern provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. A client uses the abstract interface to create a set of related products without knowing which concrete ones are produced.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: From the abstract factory you derive concrete factories that produce the same products with different implementations. Passing in a different factory gives different implementations while the client code stays the same.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The client is written against the interface only.

card.rule: Abstract Factory gives clients an interface for creating a whole family of related products, so they never name the concrete ones.
card.limits: The pattern pays off for families that vary together. For a single product, a plain factory method is lighter.

concepts.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
concepts.title: Following an order through the ingredient factory
concepts.question: In what order do the store, pizza and ingredient factory act when a customer orders?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The ordering flow from earlier is unchanged at first. Readers need to see exactly where the ingredient factory steps in.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Ethan gets a New York store and calls orderPizza(), which calls createPizza(). That is where the ingredient factory gets involved. When prepare() is called, the pizza asks that factory for its dough, sauce and cheese.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The prepared pizza is returned, and orderPizza() bakes, cuts and boxes it. The first part of the order process has not changed at all.

card.rule: Trace the flow: choose a store, order, create the pizza with the factory, prepare from the factory, then bake, cut and box.
card.limits: The trace fits the chapter's code. A real system may pass the factory through other routes, but the idea that the product asks the factory for its parts holds.

concepts.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
concepts.title: Two factory patterns side by side
concepts.question: How do Factory Method and Abstract Factory differ in how they create objects and what they create?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Both patterns keep clients from depending on concrete classes, so people mix them up.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Factory Method creates objects through inheritance: extend a class and implement its factory method. Abstract Factory creates them through object composition: pass a factory object to code written against the abstract type.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Factory Method usually makes one product and needs one method. Abstract Factory makes a family, so its interface is larger, and its methods are often implemented as factory methods. In Factory Method the creator often holds code that uses the products.

card.rule: Factory Method creates one product by inheritance; Abstract Factory creates a family of products by composition.
card.limits: The two often appear together, and an Abstract Factory's methods are frequently factory methods. Real code rarely labels itself as one or the other.

concepts.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
concepts.title: Costs and choices
concepts.question: What does Abstract Factory cost when the family grows, and when should each factory pattern be chosen?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the authors' interview, each pattern teases the other about a cost. Abstract Factory needs a large interface; Factory Method needs a subclass per variation.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use Abstract Factory when you have families of products and want clients to create products that belong together. Use Factory Method to decouple a client from concrete classes, or when you do not know ahead of time all the classes you will need.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: If new products are added to Abstract Factory, its interface has to change, and that means changing every subclass. Abstract Factory replies that creating whole families needs a big interface, while Factory Method creates one product with one method.

card.rule: Choose Abstract Factory for matching families and accept the cost of changing its interface; choose Factory Method when one product or unknown classes are the issue.
card.limits: The advice is a pair of speaking characters in an interview, not a measured study; for real work, consider how often the family grows.

concepts.title: Objects that must exist only once
concepts.question: Which kinds of objects should exist only once, and what goes wrong if a second copy appears?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some objects stand for one real thing or one shared set of facts: preference and registry settings, logging, drivers for devices such as printers and graphics cards. A second copy could disagree with the first or compete with it for the same device.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Let the class itself guarantee that only one object of it exists. The chapter calls this arrangement the Singleton pattern and spends the rest of its pages on how to build it correctly.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Without one copy, the authors warn of incorrect program behavior, overuse of resources and inconsistent results. With it, all parts of the program share the same object. The authors add that Singletons are meant to be used sparingly.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: the object is an ordinary record or a per-request helper, where many copies are normal and nothing is shared.

card.rule: Give a class a single instance when a second copy would cause wrong behavior, wasted resources or inconsistent results.
card.limits: Having one object is a cost as well as a benefit. The authors say Singletons are meant to be used sparingly, and a design with many of them deserves a hard look. Not every shared object needs to be one.

concepts.title: Why new cannot limit instances
concepts.question: Why can an ordinary class not promise that only one instance of it exists?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A class that anyone can instantiate has no control over how many objects exist. Making it non-public only narrows who may call new: every class in the same package can still build as many as it likes.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Our reading: access rules answer who, not how many. To limit the count, the class must be the only code that can call its own constructor.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Our reading: an agreement such as only startup code builds this object is a convention the compiler cannot check. This is why the next step is a constructor nobody else can reach.

card.rule: Calls to new cannot be counted from outside, so limiting instances has to start with limiting who may call the constructor.
card.limits: Package-level access narrows who can call new but does not cap how many times they call it. Restricting callers is necessary for a single instance but not sufficient: something must also hand out the one object.

concepts.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
concepts.title: A private constructor plus a static method
concepts.question: How can a class with a private constructor ever produce an object, and who may ask for it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A private constructor shuts out every outside new, yet then nobody can get an object: calling the constructor would need an object, and none exists yet. The class needs a way in that does not depend on an instance.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Declare the constructor private and add a public static method. A static method belongs to the class, so callers reach it through the class name, and because it sits inside the class it may use the private constructor.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Outsiders can ask for an object but cannot create one on their own. A side effect the authors mention: a class whose only constructor is private cannot be extended.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Our reading: a class with a private constructor and no static method that builds or returns an object can never be used.

card.rule: Make the constructor private, then expose a static method so outsiders must ask the class for the object.
card.limits: Private construction closes the front door only. It says nothing about how many objects the static method builds, so a careless method could still return a fresh object on every call.

concepts.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
concepts.title: The classic implementation
concepts.question: What three pieces make up the classic Java Singleton, and what does getInstance do on the first call and later calls?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The one object must be held somewhere that exists before any object does, and it should be built only when somebody asks for it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Three parts work together: a private constructor, a static variable that holds the instance, and a static method getInstance. On the first call the variable is empty, so the method builds and stores the object. Later calls return the stored one.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The object is created lazily, only if requested. The authors warn that this plain version has problems later in the chapter, especially with several threads.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, any caller could write new Settings(); after, only getInstance can build one.

card.rule: Private constructor, static variable, static getInstance: build on the first request and return the stored object afterwards.
card.limits: The book itself marks this version as having issues that appear later in the chapter, so treat it as a starting point rather than finished code.

concepts.title: Why the chocolate boiler needs one instance
concepts.question: What can go wrong if a program holds two controller objects for one physical chocolate boiler?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The boiler controller protects the plant: it avoids draining unboiled mixture, filling a boiler that is already full, and boiling an empty one. Those checks depend on the controller remembering the boiler state.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Make the controller a Singleton, so one object keeps one record for the one physical boiler.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: With two controllers each keeps its own record and neither sees what the other did, so a check that should stop a fill passes. Our reading: shared mutable state is what makes a second instance dangerous; a stateless class would suffer far less.

card.rule: Safety checks that depend on an object's state only work if every caller shares the one object that holds the state.
card.limits: One instance protects the state only inside one running program and one copy of the class. The chapter later shows two ways the one-instance promise can still break: several threads, and several class loaders.

concepts.title: The Singleton pattern defined
concepts.question: What are the two promises in the Singleton definition, and who keeps them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two needs pull at once: only one instance of the class, and an easy way for any code to reach it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Singleton Pattern ensures a class has only one instance, and provides a global point of access to it. The class manages its single instance, stops other classes from creating one, and hands it out on request.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The class diagram is a single class, yet the code has pitfalls. Our reading: the definition fixes the count and the access point, not when the object is built, so lazy and early creation can both qualify.

card.rule: Singleton means one instance, controlled by the class itself, plus one well-known way for anyone to reach it.
card.limits: Both promises are needed. A global variable offers the access without the one-instance guarantee, so reachability alone does not make a Singleton.

concepts.title: Lazy creation versus an up-front global
concepts.question: Why might building the single object only when first requested beat building it at startup?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A global variable that holds a heavy object is usually filled when the program starts, even in runs that never touch it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Lazy creation: build the object the first time getInstance is called, and keep it for every later call.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A run that never asks pays nothing; the first caller pays the building cost. The authors stress this for resource-intensive objects. Lazy creation also introduces a check-then-create step, which the next ideas show to be risky with threads.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: the program always uses the object at startup, so waiting saves nothing.

card.rule: Create the single instance on first request when it is expensive and may never be needed.
card.limits: Lazy creation is not free: the first request pays the whole cost, and the check that decides whether to build must stay correct when several threads call at once. When the instance is always needed, building early costs nothing extra.

concepts.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
concepts.title: How threads break the classic version
concepts.question: How can two threads running getInstance together end up with two different boiler objects?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Lazy getInstance checks the variable and, if it is empty, builds the object. Two threads can interleave these steps.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Thread A finds the variable empty. Before A stores anything, thread B also finds it empty. Each builds an object and stores it, so two boilers exist and the later store replaces the earlier one.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Tests on one thread pass, yet production can fill a boiler twice. The authors say to treat every application as multithreaded.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A shared variable is tested and then assigned, with nothing preventing another thread from acting between the two steps.

card.rule: A check-then-create sequence can be interrupted, so two threads may both see no instance yet and each build one.
card.limits: The problem arises only when threads actually overlap during the first call, which makes it rare and hard to reproduce. A single-threaded program is safe, but the authors tell readers to consider every application multithreaded.

concepts.title: Synchronizing getInstance
concepts.question: What does making getInstance synchronized fix, and what does it cost on later calls?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The check and the creation must not overlap with another thread running the same two steps.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Mark getInstance as synchronized, so only one thread executes it at a time.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Straightforward and effective. Protection is needed only on the first call, though; every later call still waits for the lock for no benefit. The authors call that unneeded overhead.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The only change from the classic version is the keyword synchronized.

card.rule: Declare getInstance synchronized to make the first-time check and creation safe, accepting a lock on every call.
card.limits: Synchronization is needed only until the instance exists, so the price buys nothing afterwards. Where getInstance is called rarely this is harmless; on a busy path the cost matters.

concepts.title: When the lock's cost is acceptable
concepts.question: Under what conditions do the authors say to leave a synchronized getInstance alone, and when to reconsider?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Locking takes time, and a lock on every call can matter when getInstance is called often.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: First option the authors list: do nothing if getInstance is not performance-critical. They warn that synchronizing a method can decrease performance by a factor of 100, so reconsider if a high-traffic part of the code starts using it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: You keep the simplest correct code and pay only by watching where the method is called. Our reading: call frequency changes the speed, not the correctness.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: a hot path calls getInstance thousands of times a second; then a lock on each call is the cost the authors warn about.

card.rule: Keep the synchronized method while getInstance is off the busy path, and revisit the choice when traffic grows.
card.limits: The factor of 100 is the authors' warning about what can happen, not a measured cost for every program. Examine your own performance constraints before changing code that is correct.

concepts.title: Eager creation at class loading
concepts.question: How does building the instance up front remove the thread race, and when is it a good fit?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Laziness creates the race. If the program always needs the object, or building it is cheap, laziness buys nothing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Create the instance where the static variable is declared. The JVM builds it when the class is loaded, before any thread uses it, so getInstance only returns it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: No lock and no check, so no race. The object exists even if never used. The authors say it suits programs that always create and use the instance, or where creation overhead is not onerous.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: getInstance shrinks to a plain return.

card.rule: Initialise the static instance when the class loads, so the JVM guarantees it exists before any thread uses it.
card.limits: Eager creation gives up laziness: a costly object is built even if never used. It is the wrong choice for a resource-intensive Singleton that the program might not need.

concepts.title: Double-checked locking
concepts.question: How does double-checked locking limit synchronization to the first calls, and which Java versions break it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: You want lazy creation without paying for a lock on every call.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Check for the instance with no lock. Only if it is missing, enter a synchronized block, check again, and then build. The static variable uses the volatile keyword.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Only the first calls synchronize, so overhead drops drastically for busy callers. It does not work in Java 1.4 or earlier; before Java 5 choose another approach.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The second check inside the lock matters: another thread may have built the object while this one waited.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: You must run on a JVM earlier than Java 5, or getInstance is not performance-critical and a plain synchronized method is enough.

card.rule: Check without locking first, lock only when the instance is missing, check again inside the lock, and use Java 5 or later.
card.limits: On Java 1.4 and earlier, many JVMs make the technique unsafe, so choose another method there. It also adds complexity, which is not worth paying when getInstance is not on a busy path.

concepts.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
concepts.title: Choosing a fix for the boiler
concepts.question: Does the authors' ranking of the three fixes follow from the facts they give about the boiler?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The boiler facts: no performance concerns, the instance is always created, and double-checked locking would need at least Java 5.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors weigh the three fixes against those facts. Synchronizing is straightforward and guaranteed to work. Eager creation works as well, perhaps less obvious to a developer who knows the standard pattern. Double-checked locking looks like overkill.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The ranking follows from these facts. Our reading: with a hot path or a costly object that is rarely needed, the same reasoning would favour a different fix.

card.rule: Choose the simplest fix whose cost your actual constraints can bear.
card.limits: These verdicts hold for this boiler's constraints. Heavy traffic, or a costly object that may never be used, would change the ranking.

concepts.title: Singleton versus a global variable
concepts.question: On what grounds do the authors say a Singleton beats a global variable or a plain convention?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Code wants global access to one object. A global variable offers access, but nothing stops a second instance from being built.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Singleton gives both promises: one instance and global access. The authors name its edges over a global: lazy creation instead of startup creation, and the one-instance guarantee. They add that globals tend to pollute the namespace with many references.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: You gain control over count and timing. The authors also say Singletons can still be abused, so the pattern is a tool, not a licence.

card.rule: Judge a Singleton against a global by the stated reasons: lazy creation, a real one-instance guarantee, and less namespace clutter.
card.limits: These grounds are the authors' argument, not proof that globals are worse everywhere, and Singletons can be abused too. Weigh the reasons themselves instead of your taste for or against globals.

concepts.title: A class made only of static members
concepts.question: Why do the authors advise against replacing a Singleton with a class where everything is static?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: It can look simpler to make every method and variable static, so the class itself acts as the one object.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors say this works when the class is self-contained and has no complex initialization.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Static initialization in Java can get messy when several classes are involved, giving subtle bugs about order of initialization. Unless there is a compelling need, the authors prefer to stay in the object world.

card.rule: According to the authors, prefer a real Singleton object over an all-static class unless something compels otherwise.
card.limits: The warning concerns complex initialization or several classes. For a self-contained class with simple setup, the authors concede the two are equivalent.

concepts.title: Class loaders and the one-instance promise
concepts.question: How can two class loaders produce two instances of a Singleton?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each class loader defines a namespace, so the same class can be loaded once per loader.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Two loaded copies of a Singleton class mean two static variables, and therefore two instances.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Locking inside one copy cannot help, since each copy is separate. The authors tell you to be careful with several class loaders and suggest specifying the class loader yourself.

card.rule: Remember that the one-instance promise holds per loaded copy of the class, so several class loaders can defeat it.
card.limits: The risk exists only when more than one class loader loads the class. In a program with a single loader the promise is unaffected, and the authors advise care rather than avoiding Singletons.

concepts.title: The garbage collector bug before Java 1.2
concepts.question: What did an old garbage collector bug do to Singletons, and when does it still matter?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Before Java 1.2 a garbage collector bug could collect a Singleton whose only reference was held by the Singleton itself.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The workaround on such a JVM is a registry of Singletons that keeps a global reference to each.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: After a collection, the next getInstance quietly built a new object, so state and connections reset with no error. Since Java 1.2 the bug is fixed and no global reference is required.

card.rule: On Java 1.2 or later a Singleton needs no extra global reference to survive collection.
card.limits: On a pre-1.2 JVM the problem is real, and the authors advise a registry of Singletons there. On any modern JVM no precaution is needed.

concepts.title: Singleton and one responsibility
concepts.question: Does a Singleton break the one-class-one-responsibility principle, and how do the authors weigh that?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A class should do one job. A Singleton does its main role and also manages its own instance and global access.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors agree that you can argue it has two responsibilities. They defend it: a class managing its own instance makes the overall design simpler, and many developers know the pattern.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Some developers still choose to abstract the Singleton functionality out of the class. Our reading: that trades the simplicity of self-management for a cleaner split of jobs.

card.rule: Weigh the extra responsibility against the simplicity and familiarity, and state which reasons carry your decision.
card.limits: The authors' reasons are about usefulness and familiarity, not a proof that the principle does not apply. Wide use does not make a design correct, so test their case instead of accepting it.

concepts.title: Subclassing a Singleton and using it sparingly
concepts.question: Why is subclassing a Singleton awkward, and what do the authors suggest asking before attempting it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A private constructor blocks subclasses. Loosening it to protected or public lets other classes instantiate the class, so it is no longer a Singleton.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The instance sits in one static variable, so straightforward subclasses all share it. To make subclassing work, the base class needs a registry of sorts.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Before building that, ask what subclassing gains you. The authors note the Singleton code is trivial to add to any class, that it is not meant to fit a library, and that a design with many Singletons deserves a hard look.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: You are tempted to turn many classes into Singletons; the authors say to use them sparingly.

card.rule: Before subclassing a Singleton, ask what the subclass gains, since the cost is a weakened guarantee or extra machinery.
card.limits: The advice is about subclassing, not about the pattern itself: the authors still say to use it wherever you must control the number of instances. Sparing use means counting your Singletons, not avoiding them.

concepts.section: Free hardware! Let’s check out the Remote Control...
concepts.title: Wrapping a method call in an object
concepts.question: What does it mean to encapsulate a method invocation, and what does the caller gain from it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A caller wants work done but should not carry out the steps itself. If it runs every step directly, it cannot postpone the work, hand it to someone else, record it, or take it back later.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Wrap a method call, meaning the action together with the object that performs it, in an object of its own. The caller holds the wrapper and triggers it. The wrapper knows how the work gets done.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The calling object no longer worries about how things are done. A call that is an object can be stored, passed around, saved away for logging, or reused to implement undo. The chapter builds on these uses.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: for one direct call whose result is used at once, a wrapper only adds an object and gives nothing back.

card.rule: Wrap a request, together with the object that will carry it out, in an object so that the caller can trigger it without knowing the details.
card.limits: The wrapper pays off when the caller should stay ignorant of the details, or when requests must be stored, queued, logged or undone. For a single direct call that needs nothing of these, it only adds an object.

concepts.section: Taking a look at the vendor classes
concepts.title: Vendor classes with no shared interface
concepts.question: Why is a remote control hard to design when every vendor class has its own methods?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The customer sends vendor classes for lights, fans, hot tubs and audio gear. Beyond on() and off() they offer methods such as dim(), setTemperature(), setVolume() and setInputChannel(). There is little industry effort towards a common interface, and more such classes are expected.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Treat future variety as a requirement. The remote must work with the devices on the disc and with any the vendors supply later, so it cannot depend on any particular vendor class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: No shared method exists for the remote to call. The authors call the design job interesting for this reason: it has to cope with variety it has not yet seen, not only with the classes on the disc.

card.rule: Treat future variety as a requirement: the remote must not depend on any particular vendor class.
card.limits: The difficulty is variety plus growth, not the number of classes. If the classes shared one interface, calling it would be enough and most of this problem would go away.

concepts.title: Keep the remote ignorant of the devices
concepts.question: What should the remote know, and what should it leave out, according to the team in the cubicle?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Mary wants the remote to know how to interpret button presses and make requests, but not how to turn on a hot tub. Yet a press still has to switch on a light or open a garage door.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Separate the concerns. The remote turns presses into requests, and device know-how lives elsewhere. Mary rejects a remote built from if statements that test which class sits in a slot and call that class own method.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Sue spells out the cost of the if-statement remote: every new vendor class would mean going into the remote and editing it, with the risk of new bugs and more work. The principle says who should know what, but not yet how a request reaches a device.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The same decision in code, with made-up devices.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A branch for each vendor class inside the remote, so that each new device type forces an edit there.

card.rule: Give the remote only the job of turning button presses into requests, and keep device knowledge out of it.
card.limits: Separating concerns says who should know what, not how a generic request reaches a specific device. The team still needs a mechanism for that link, which the next ideas supply.

concepts.title: A command object wraps a request and its target
concepts.question: What does a command object hold, and what does the remote do with it when a button is pressed?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Every button must trigger a different action, yet the remote must stay ignorant of what the action is and which device it touches.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Joe proposes command objects. A command object encapsulates a request to do something, such as turn on the light, on a specific object, such as the living room light. The remote stores one per button and, on a press, asks that object to do its work.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The remote has no idea what the work is, so it is decoupled from the light. Command objects load into button slots and the remote code stays simple, since each command holds how to do a task together with the object that does it. Joe and Mary admit the pattern is hard to picture at first.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A button class with a field for one particular device and a call to that device own method.

card.rule: Store in each button an object that holds both the action and its target, and let the remote only ask that object to act.
card.limits: The remote stays simple only because the knowledge moved: some command object must still know the device own methods. Joe and Mary admit the pattern is hard to picture at first.

concepts.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
concepts.title: The order slip as a request object
concepts.question: Why can the waitress handle any order without knowing what is on it or who cooks it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A waitress must pass on any customer order, yet she should not have to know what is on it or who will cook it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Order Slip encapsulates a request to prepare a meal. It has one method, orderUp(), which encapsulates the actions needed, and it holds a reference to the object that prepares the meal, the cook. The waitress passes the slip through the order window and calls Order up.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The slip is an object, so it can be passed from the waitress to the order counter or to the next waitress taking over her shift. She needs to know neither the order nor the cook. The authors note that a real waitress would care; in Objectville she does not.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Our reading: a waitress who checks which dish was ordered and calls the matching cook method has taken over the job of the slip.

card.rule: A request object carries its content and its performer inside it, behind one method, so whoever passes it on needs to know neither.
card.limits: The diner is a deliberate simplification: the authors note that a real waitress would care what is on the slip. Treat the picture as a model of the decoupling, not as advice that requesters never read content.

concepts.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
concepts.title: The waitress invokes, the cook performs
concepts.question: How are the waitress and the cook decoupled, and what links them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The object that takes requests and the object that carries them out should be able to change without disturbing each other.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The waitress takes order slips and invokes orderUp() on them. Her takeOrder() method is parameterized with different slips through the day, and she is not fazed, because every slip supports orderUp(). The cook knows how to prepare meals and takes over once orderUp() is invoked.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors stress that waitress and cook are totally decoupled: she holds slips, and he gets his instructions from the slip. The diner models separating the object that makes a request from the objects that receive and execute it. Our reading: the slip still points to the cook, so the link moved into the request.
