card.rule: The requester only calls the one shared method on whatever request it holds, and the performer receives its instructions only through the request.
card.limits: The decoupling is between waitress and cook. The slip still refers to the cook, so the link has not vanished; it has moved into the request object.

concepts.section: From the Diner to the Command Pattern
concepts.title: Matching the diner to the pattern roles
concepts.question: Which pattern role matches each diner player, and in what order is an invoker loaded and used?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To use the diner as a guide, each player needs a name in the pattern, and the order of loading and use must be clear.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Customer becomes client, order becomes command, waitress becomes invoker and short order cook becomes receiver. The method orderUp() becomes execute() and takeOrder() becomes setCommand(). The client creates a command, stores it in the invoker with setCommand(), and later asks the invoker to execute it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Once loaded, a command may be used and discarded, or it may stay in the invoker and be used many times. Our reading: the roles name jobs rather than classes, so in a small program one object can fill more than one role.

card.rule: The client builds a command, loads it into the invoker with setCommand(), and the invoker later calls execute() on it, which makes the receiver act.
card.limits: The roles describe jobs, not classes: one object can take more than one role in a small program. Check the jobs, not the names.

concepts.title: The Command interface has one method
concepts.question: Why do all command objects share one single-method interface, and what is that method called?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An invoker must be able to run any request, so every request needs the same way of being started, whatever device is behind it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: All command objects implement the same interface, and it has a single method. In the diner it was orderUp(); in code it is usually called execute(). No device appears in it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The invoker needs to know only that execute() exists. The variety of the vendor classes does not leak into the interface; names such as setVolume() or dim() appear only inside concrete commands. Our reading: adding a method to the interface, such as undo, changes what every command must provide.

card.rule: Give every command the same one-method interface so that an invoker can run any of them without knowing which one it holds.
card.limits: The no-argument, no-result shape fits requests whose details are fixed when the command is created. A richer interface, such as one that adds undo, changes what every command must provide.

concepts.title: A concrete command binds a receiver to an action
concepts.question: What does a concrete command store, and what does its execute() method do?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The shared interface names no device, yet some class has to call the vendor own methods, such as on() on a light or up() on a garage door.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A concrete command implements Command. LightOnCommand takes a Light in its constructor and keeps it, and its execute() calls on() on that light. GarageDoorOpenCommand keeps a GarageDoor and its execute() calls the door up() method.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The command name states the request while the vendor method name stays hidden inside. One concrete command ties one receiver to one action behind the common execute(). Our reading: it adds nothing to the receiver, so a new receiver method needs a new command.

card.rule: A concrete command stores its receiver when it is constructed and, in execute(), calls the receiver own method.
card.limits: The command is the one place that knows the vendor method name. It adds nothing to the receiver, so a new method on the receiver, such as dim(), is not reachable until someone writes a command for it.

concepts.title: Loading and swapping a command in a one-slot remote
concepts.question: What happens when the one-slot remote is loaded with a command, pressed, and then loaded with another?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To see the pattern run before building the full remote, the authors start with a remote that has one button and one slot.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The simple remote stores a command in its slot through setCommand(), and buttonWasPressed() calls execute() on whatever is there. In the test, a light command is loaded and the button pressed, then a garage door command is loaded and the button pressed again.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The same remote code serves two different requests. The slot does not care which command it holds, as long as it implements the Command interface. Our reading: a new command replaces the old one, so several commands at once need several slots.

card.rule: An invoker holds one command in its slot through setCommand(), and a button press calls execute() on whatever is there now.
card.limits: The slot keeps only the latest command, so loading a new one replaces the old one. Holding several commands at once needs more slots, which the seven-slot remote provides.

concepts.title: The Command Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the Command Pattern do, and what four abilities does it give?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With the roles known, the team needs a precise statement of what the pattern is and what it offers beyond the remote.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Command Pattern encapsulates a request as an object, letting you parameterize other objects with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations. A command binds actions to a specific receiver and exposes one method, execute().

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: From outside, no object knows which actions run on which receiver, only that execute() services the request. Parameterizing means loading an object with different requests: the waitress with orders through a day, a remote slot first with light on and later with garage door open. Queuing, logging, undo and macros come later; logging would make no sense for a remote.

card.rule: Wrap a request as an object and you can parameterize invokers with it, queue it, log it and undo it.
card.limits: A given use need not employ all four abilities. The authors say that logging would make no sense for a remote control, though it suits other applications.

concepts.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
concepts.title: Where the decoupling comes from
concepts.question: How does the structure of the pattern keep the invoker and the receiver apart?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The invoker must run requests without being tied to the objects that perform them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The invoker knows only the Command interface and calls execute(). The concrete command holds the reference to the receiver and calls its actions. The client creates the concrete command and gives it its receiver.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The invoker never refers to the receiver, so the two can change independently, with the commands as the only link. Our reading: coupling moves rather than vanishes, since commands depend on receivers and the setup code depends on the concrete classes.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: An invoker class that imports or names a receiver class.

card.rule: Keep the receiver reference inside the command so that the invoker depends on the Command interface alone.
card.limits: Coupling does not vanish; it moves. The command class depends on the receiver, and the client or setup code depends on the concrete classes. The gain is that the invoker is free of both.

concepts.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
concepts.title: Binding each command to its own receiver
concepts.question: How does the remote tell the living room light from the kitchen light?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A seven-slot remote may drive several objects of one class, such as a living room light and a kitchen light. How can it tell them apart?

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: It cannot, and need not. Each slot has an on and an off button, and commands are assigned to them, for example onCommands[0] and offCommands[0]. When the commands are created, one is bound to the living room light and another to the kitchen light.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The receiver of the request gets bound to the command that encapsulates it, so by the time a button is pressed no one cares which light is which. Our reading: a command acts on the receiver it was given, so another receiver means another command object.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Our reading: a command that creates its own receiver instead of receiving the one it should control.

card.rule: Choose the receiver when you create the command, and the invoker then needs no idea which receiver it drives.
card.limits: A command acts on the receiver it was given. To act on another receiver you need another command object.

concepts.title: Seven slots: the remote as invoker
concepts.question: How does a seven-slot remote store its commands, and what happens when a button is pressed?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Seven slots with an on and an off button each need somewhere to store what the buttons do, and the remote code must stay the same whatever is plugged in.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Assign each slot a command, which makes the remote the invoker. The remote keeps two arrays of commands, one for on buttons and one for off buttons, indexed by slot. A press calls execute() on the matching entry.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: That command invokes actions on its receiver, which may be a light, a ceiling fan or a stereo. The remote code is the same for every device because it never learns what is in a slot. Our reading: the client code loads the commands, not the remote.

card.rule: Keep one command per button in arrays indexed by slot, and make a press call execute() on the matching entry.
card.limits: The arrays hold only commands, and their size fixes the number of slots. The remote does not decide what a slot controls; the client code that loads the commands does.

concepts.title: A command can do several things
concepts.question: Can one command make several calls on its receiver, and what does the invoker see?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some requests take more than one call on the receiver: playing a CD needs the stereo switched on, the CD input selected and the volume set.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: StereoOffCommand binds the stereo to its off() method. StereoOnWithCDCommand makes three calls inside execute(): turn the stereo on, set the CD, set the volume to 11. The invoker still sees one method and makes one call.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The other vendor classes follow the same shape, so writing their commands is routine. The authors expect vendors to have no trouble writing such simple classes in future.

card.rule: Let execute() make as many receiver calls as the request needs, and name the command for the whole request.
card.limits: A command stays small only while it delegates to the receiver. Commands that grow their own logic are the smart commands discussed later, which cost some decoupling.

concepts.section: Now, let’s check out the execution of our remote control test...
concepts.title: NoCommand: a command that does nothing
concepts.question: Why does the remote start every slot with a do-nothing command instead of leaving it empty?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If a slot could be empty, the remote would have to test on every press whether a command is loaded, and every handler would repeat that check.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: NoCommand implements Command and its execute() is empty. The remote constructor puts a NoCommand in every on and off slot, so there is always a command to call.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: This is an example of a null object, useful when there is no meaningful object to give and the client should be spared handling null. The authors add that Null Object is sometimes listed as a design pattern itself.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Checking for an empty slot versus filling every slot in advance.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: when an empty slot should be reported to the user, a silent default hides the problem.

card.rule: Fill unused places with an object that obeys the interface and does nothing, so the caller needs no check.
card.limits: The do-nothing object makes an empty slot silent: a press has no visible effect and gives no sign that nothing was loaded. Use it when doing nothing is an acceptable answer.

concepts.section: Putting the Remote Control through its paces
concepts.title: Judging the design against its stated goal
concepts.question: Does the design meet the goal the documentation states, and how would you check the claim?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The remote documentation must tell the customer what the design is for. It states a primary goal, a means and a hoped-for benefit.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Judge a design against its stated goal. The goal was to keep the remote code as simple as possible so that it needs no change when new vendor classes appear. The means was the Command Pattern, decoupling RemoteControl from the vendor classes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors believe this will reduce the cost of producing the remote and of maintaining it. That is an expectation. The test is concrete: add a new vendor class and see whether the remote must be edited. The authors also note that the pattern brings many small classes.

card.rule: Judge a design by its stated goal: ask whether the chosen means delivers it, for example whether a new device needs no edit to the remote.
card.limits: A belief about lower cost is not a measurement. The authors also point out costs of the means, such as extra small classes, so weigh the benefit against them.

concepts.title: Undo mirrors execute
concepts.question: How does a command support undo, and what must the remote remember?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The remote has a global undo button, but it cannot know how to reverse every kind of device.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Add an undo() method to Command that mirrors execute(): whatever execute() last did, undo() reverses. LightOnCommand.undo() calls off() and LightOffCommand.undo() calls on(). The remote tracks the last command invoked and calls its undo() when the undo button is pressed.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The remote does not know how to reverse anything; each command knows how to reverse itself. Our reading: remembering one command gives one step of undo, and a single opposite call is enough only when the earlier state is certain.

card.rule: Add undo() to the command so it reverses what execute() did, and have the invoker remember the last command to call it on.
card.limits: This version remembers one command, so it undoes one step. And a single opposite call works only when the earlier state is certain: a fan that could have been at any speed needs more.

concepts.title: Undo that needs remembered state
concepts.question: How can a command undo a change when the earlier state could have been any of several values?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A ceiling fan has several speeds and an off setting. Reversing a change to high means returning to whatever speed it had before, which is not one fixed opposite.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The command tracks the fan last speed setting and, when undo() is called, restores it. Each fan command, for high, medium, low and off, does this for itself.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Typically a command has to manage some state to support undo, so it holds the receiver and the earlier state of that receiver. Our reading: it restores only what it recorded.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Guessing an opposite versus recording the earlier state.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Our reading: an undo() that makes a fixed opposite call on a receiver that could have been in several states.

card.rule: When a command changes a receiver, have it remember the earlier state and put it back in undo().
card.limits: A command can restore only what it recorded. If something else changes the receiver between execute() and undo(), undo puts back the old record, not the newer situation.

concepts.title: A stack of commands for repeated undo
concepts.question: How can the remote undo several steps in a row instead of only the last one?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Users want to press undo many times, but the remote remembers only the last command.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The invoker keeps a stack of previous commands instead of one reference to the last. When undo is pressed it pops the first item off the stack and calls its undo().

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The most recent command is reversed first, then the one before it, and so on. Our reading: only commands that went through the invoker are on the stack, and the commands themselves do not change.

card.rule: Keep executed commands on a stack and, on each undo, pop the top one and call its undo().
card.limits: Only the invoker changes; the commands stay as they are. The history holds only commands that went through the invoker, so an action performed directly on a receiver cannot be undone this way.

concepts.title: A macro command runs many commands
concepts.question: How can one button run several commands at once, such as a party mode?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A Party Mode button should dim the lights, switch on the stereo and TV set to a DVD and fire up the hot tub in one press, but a slot holds a single command.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Create the commands for the parts, load them into an array and hand it to a MacroCommand whose execute() steps through the array. A second array of off commands makes the matching off macro. The macro is assigned to a button like any other command. The authors call this extension the Meta Command Pattern.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The macro is itself a Command, so the remote cannot tell it from a single command. Our reading: the macro has no receiver of its own, since its parts do the work.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A hard-coded combined command versus a command holding a list.

card.rule: Make a command that holds a list of commands and runs each of them in its execute().
card.limits: A macro holds no receiver of its own: its parts do the work, and the client chooses the parts when the macro is built. The macro is only as capable as the commands inside it.

concepts.title: Undoing a macro in reverse order
concepts.question: In what order should a macro undo its commands, and why?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: After a macro runs, pressing undo must reverse everything the macro did.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: MacroCommand.undo() calls undo() on its parts. In the authors solution it loops from the last command down to the first, the opposite of execute().

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Because a macro is a command, it can be undone as one unit, whether it holds two commands or twenty. Our reading: a later step may rest on an earlier one, which is why it is taken back first, and a part that cannot reverse itself leaves its effect in place.

card.rule: Undo a macro by calling undo() on its parts from the last to the first.
card.limits: A macro can restore the earlier state only if every part can reverse itself. A part whose undo() does nothing leaves its effect in place.

concepts.title: Smart commands and macros: the authors view
concepts.question: What do you give up when a command does the work itself, and why do the authors favour macros?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A command can delegate to a receiver or carry out the request itself. Party mode could be a hard-coded PartyCommand or a MacroCommand.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: According to the authors, aim for dumb commands that just invoke an action on a receiver. Smart commands implement most or all of the logic of a request themselves. For party mode the authors prefer a MacroCommand: you decide dynamically which commands go in, and less new code is needed.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: With a smart command the invoker and receiver are less decoupled, and you can no longer parameterize commands with receivers. Smart commands are not uncommon in practice.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Our reading: a command whose execute() computes results itself and holds no receiver.

card.rule: Prefer dumb commands that delegate and macros built from parts, and accept a smart command only when you can afford the lost decoupling.
card.limits: This is the authors recommendation, not a law. A smart command is legitimate where the decoupling it costs is not needed.

concepts.section: The Command Pattern means lots of command classes
concepts.title: The cost: many small classes
concepts.question: What is the main cost of the plain pattern, and why are the extra classes so alike?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each request on each receiver needs its own concrete command, and every one of them shares the same interface.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In the remote there are two command classes per receiver class: LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand for the light, GarageDoorUpCommand and GarageDoorDownCommand for the garage door, and so on.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The result is a lot of extra small classes. Each is a little bit of packaged-up computation that gives the remote a common interface to the behaviour of many different receivers. Our reading: the cost counts distinct requests, not invokers.

card.rule: Expect about one small class per request and receiver when the pattern is written in its plain form.
card.limits: The cost counts the distinct requests, not the invokers. It is a cost of the plain form: a language feature that packages computation more compactly can reduce it, as the next ideas show.

concepts.section: Simplifying the Remote Control with lambda expressions
concepts.title: Lambda expressions as commands
concepts.question: How can a lambda expression take the place of a concrete command class?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The many command classes are only packaged computation. If the computation could be passed in directly, the classes could go.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A lambda expression, added in Java 8, writes a method exactly where it is needed. Instead of LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand objects, pass lambdas holding their execute() code to setCommand(). It fits because Command has exactly one method, with no arguments and no result, and the compiler checks the match.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The slot then holds a function object, and execute() runs the lambda. The concrete command classes can be deleted, but the Command interface stays, since it gives the lambdas their type.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A concrete class versus a lambda, with made-up devices.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The interface has more than one method, since a lambda replaces a method, not a whole object.

card.rule: Where an interface has exactly one method, pass a lambda with a compatible signature instead of writing a class.
card.limits: It works only for an interface with a single method. A lambda replaces a method, not a whole object, so it cannot stand in for an interface with two.

concepts.section: Simplifying even more with method references
concepts.title: Method references and named lambdas
concepts.question: When can a method reference replace a lambda, and what do you do when the command has several steps?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Many lambdas only call one method, while some commands must do several things.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: When a lambda passes just one method call, pass a method reference instead, such as stereo::off. When a command does more, like turning on, setting the CD and setting the volume to 11, write the lambda inline or create it separately, give it a name and pass the name.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A method reference is a convenience for the simplest case; a command with several calls needs a lambda body. A separately created lambda has the type Command, which matches the parameter it is passed to.

card.rule: Use a method reference when the lambda only calls one method, and a lambda body, inline or named, when it does more.
card.limits: A method reference names one method, so it cannot cover a command with several calls. It is a convenience for the simplest case.

concepts.section: Test the remote control with lambda expressions
concepts.title: When lambdas are the wrong tool
concepts.question: Why do the authors advise against lambdas once the Command interface has an undo method?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Once undo is added, the Command interface has two methods, execute() and undo(). One lambda cannot replace two methods.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Lambdas suit functional interfaces, those with a single method. The authors say you could probably find a way with two kinds of commands, but the code would probably be more complex than command objects. If you work around the rule, lambdas are probably not the right solution.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Lambdas also get names assigned by the Java runtime, so a display built on class names shows odd text. Fixing it means adding a name parameter for each slot.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Command has both execute() and undo(): keep command classes.

card.rule: Use lambda commands while the interface has one method; keep command classes when it has more, such as execute() and undo().
card.limits: This is the authors judgment, worded as probably. Dropping the undo feature restores the single method. A workaround is allowed, and the question is whether it costs more than it saves.

concepts.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: queuing requests
concepts.title: Queuing requests
concepts.question: How do commands let a job queue and worker threads handle work they know nothing about?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A computation may need to run long after the client created the command, even on a different thread, as in schedulers, thread pools and job queues.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Commands go in at one end of a job queue. Threads at the other end remove a command, call its execute(), wait for the call to finish, discard the command and fetch another.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The queue classes are totally decoupled from the computation: one moment a thread does a financial computation, the next it retrieves something from the network. They just call execute(). Our reading: since each command is discarded after its run, the queue serves work done once.

card.rule: Put commands in a queue and let worker threads take each one and call execute(), whatever it computes.
card.limits: The queue runs only objects that implement the command interface. A worker discards each command after its run, so the queue serves work to be done once, not requests to be kept.

concepts.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: logging requests
concepts.title: Logging requests for crash recovery
concepts.question: How can a log of command objects restore an application after a crash?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some applications must log every action and recover after a crash, yet some data structures are too large to save on every change.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Add store() and load() to commands; in Java, serialization could implement them, with its usual caveats. Store a history of commands on disk as they execute. After a crash, reload the command objects and invoke their execute() methods in batch and in order.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Save the operations since the last checkpoint and apply them to it after a failure; a spreadsheet is the authors example. This suits applications with large data, not a remote. Extended to sets of operations, it gives transactions in which all operations complete or none do.

card.rule: Log executed commands since the last checkpoint, and after a failure reload the checkpoint and execute the logged commands in order.
card.limits: It pays only when saving the whole data on each change is too costly. It does not suit a remote control, and serialization has its usual caveats as a way of storing commands.

concepts.title: What an adapter does
concepts.question: What does an adapter change, and what does it leave alone, when two things do not fit together?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A US laptop plug does not fit a British wall outlet, and neither the laptop nor the building's wiring can be altered. Two sides disagree about the interface, meaning the set of connections or calls that one side offers and the other relies on.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A travel adapter sits between plug and outlet and presents the outlet in the shape the plug expects. Object-oriented adapters play the same role: they take one interface and adapt it to the one a client, the code making the calls, expects.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Both ends stay as they were. Some adapters only reshape the connection and pass the current straight through; more complex ones also step the power up or down, as a software adapter may convert data as well as calls.

card.rule: An adapter changes the interface one side offers into the interface the other side expects, and leaves both sides as they were.
card.limits: An adapter only bridges a difference in interface. If the wrapped thing lacks what the client needs, the adapter cannot invent it.

concepts.title: The new vendor problem
concepts.question: How can a new vendor's classes join an existing system when neither your code nor theirs may be changed?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Your system already works with one vendor's classes. A new vendor offers the same kind of service through a differently designed interface. You do not want to change your working code, and the vendor's code is not yours to change.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Write a class that receives your existing calls and converts them into calls that make sense on the new vendor's classes. This middleman is the adapter. The book also notes a route needing no code from you: make the vendor supply the adapter class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Your code and the vendor's both stay untouched, and the translation lives in one place. The price is one more class to write and keep up to date, unless the vendor provides it.

card.rule: When you cannot change either side, put a middleman class between them that speaks your interface in front and the vendor's behind.
card.limits: An adapter is extra code that someone must write and maintain, so it earns its place only when changing the callers or the vendor is not realistic.

concepts.title: Client, target and adaptee
concepts.question: In an adapter design, which part is the client, which is the target interface, and which is the adaptee?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Talking about a mismatch needs names: who makes the calls, which interface do they expect, and which class does not fit? Without them it is easy to adapt in the wrong direction.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The client makes the calls. The target interface is the one the client is written against. The adaptee is the existing class with the mismatched interface. The adapter implements the target and is composed with the adaptee, holding a reference to it. The book's example wraps a turkey so it can stand in where a duck is expected.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Client and adaptee are decoupled, since neither knows about the other. Only the adapter knows both interfaces.

card.rule: The client talks to the target interface, the adapter implements that interface, and the adaptee sits behind the adapter.
card.limits: The roles only matter when interfaces differ: a client that already speaks the adaptee's own interface has no use for the adapter.

concepts.section: Here’s how the Client uses the Adapter
concepts.title: How a request travels through an adapter
concepts.question: What happens, step by step, when a client uses an adapter, and what does the client know about it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A client should be able to use the adaptee without learning anything about it. So who does the translating, and at what moment?

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Three steps. The client calls a method on the adapter through the target interface. The adapter translates that request into one or more calls on the adaptee, using the adaptee's interface. The client receives the result and never learns that an adapter did the translating.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: One request on the target can turn into several calls on the adaptee, and the adapter decides the mapping. The client stays unaware only while the translation stays faithful.

card.rule: The client calls the adapter through the target interface, the adapter makes the matching calls on the adaptee, and the client never sees the translation.
card.limits: The client is unaware of the adapter only while the adapter keeps up its end. When the translation is imperfect, the client may notice, as the remove() case later shows.

concepts.title: How much work an adapter needs
concepts.question: What decides how much work an adapter takes, and what shapes can an adapter have beyond wrapping one class?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A large target interface means many methods to map, and writing an adapter can look like a lot of work. New and old parts of a system may also expect different interfaces.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The job is proportional to the size of the target interface. The alternative, reworking all the client-side calls, means a lot of investigative work and code changes, while an adapter puts every change into one class. An adapter may hold two or more adaptees, and a Two Way Adapter implements both interfaces so it can act as either.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The cost is paid once, in one class, instead of across every client. A Two Way Adapter lets old and new parts of a system share one object.

card.rule: Adapter effort grows with the size of the target interface, and an adapter may wrap several classes or serve two interfaces at once.
card.limits: Our reading: an adapter that must map a huge target interface may cost more than editing a few callers. The comparison in the text assumes the callers are many.

concepts.title: The official definition
concepts.question: What is the Adapter Pattern's official definition, and what two benefits follow from it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Classes whose interfaces are incompatible cannot cooperate, even when one could do the other's work. The interface a client needs may also keep changing over time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Adapter Pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface the clients expect, and lets classes work together that could not otherwise. The conversion says what the pattern does; the cooperation says why.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The client is decoupled from the implemented interface. If the interface is expected to change, the adapter encapsulates that change, so the client does not have to be modified each time.

card.rule: The Adapter Pattern converts a class's interface into the one clients expect so that otherwise incompatible classes can work together.
card.limits: Converting an interface does not make a class's behavior suit the client. Two classes can match in signature and still disagree about what the calls mean.

concepts.title: Composition and coding to the target
concepts.question: Which design principles does the object adapter use, and what do they let you do?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An adapter must reach the adaptee somehow, and the client should not end up tied to one particular backend.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The object adapter wraps the adaptee by object composition, giving it an altered interface. The client is bound to the target interface, not to any implementation.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The adapter can be used with any subclass of the adaptee. Several adapters can each convert a different backend, and new implementations can be added after the fact as long as they adhere to the target interface.

card.rule: Wrap the adaptee by composition and code the client to the target interface, so any adaptee subclass or new backend can be fitted behind it.
card.limits: A backend that does not implement the target still needs its own adapter. Composition also adds one more object and a line of delegation per method.

concepts.title: Object adapter and class adapter
concepts.question: How does a class adapter differ from an object adapter, and why did this chapter cover only one of them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An adapter can reach the adaptee by holding it or by inheriting from it. Which is possible depends on what the programming language allows.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: An object adapter uses composition: it holds the adaptee and passes requests to it, and this chapter built that kind. A class adapter subclasses both the target and the adaptee.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A class adapter needs multiple inheritance, which the book says is not possible in Java, so Java gets object adapters. In a language with multiple inheritance a class adapter may become an option.

card.rule: An object adapter composes with the adaptee; a class adapter inherits from both the target and the adaptee and needs multiple inheritance.
card.limits: The book works through object adapters only, so details of class adapters here are only sketched. Which form is available depends on the language.

concepts.title: Weighing the two adapter forms
concepts.question: Before choosing between the object adapter and the class adapter, what does each side claim and what does each give up?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each form has a case to make, and a reader who picks a side after hearing only one will judge badly. Restate each claim before agreeing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The object adapter claims that composition lets it adapt the adaptee and any of its subclasses, and that a little delegation code buys flexibility. The class adapter claims it need not reimplement the adaptee, can override its behavior, and is one object instead of two, while admitting it is committed to one specific adaptee class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Our reading: neither side wins in the abstract. The choice rests on your language and on whether you need reach over subclasses or the ability to override. The book asks how composition versus inheritance affects flexibility.

card.rule: Restate each form's claims and what it gives up, then weigh them against your language and your needs before taking sides.
card.limits: A debate staged between the two forms is not evidence by itself, since each speaker argues for itself. The book leaves the weighing to the reader.

concepts.section: Adapting an Enumeration to an Iterator
concepts.title: Adapting Enumeration to Iterator
concepts.question: What do Enumeration and Iterator each offer, and how does an adapter let new code use legacy Enumerations?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Early collections such as Vector, Stack and Hashtable return an Enumeration from elements(). Newer collections use Iterator, which also adds the ability to remove items. Legacy code still produces Enumerations while new code wants Iterators.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Build an EnumerationIterator adapter. It implements the Iterator target and is composed with an Enumeration adaptee. The hasNext() and next() methods are straightforward: they pass straight through to the adaptee.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: New code sees only Iterator while the legacy code stays untouched. Iterator has one operation that Enumeration lacks, so the adapter cannot be perfect.

card.rule: To let new code use a legacy Enumeration, write an adapter that implements Iterator and wraps the Enumeration.
card.limits: The mapping works for the calls both sides have. Iterator offers an operation that Enumeration cannot support, which makes the adapter imperfect.

concepts.title: When the adaptee cannot do what the target asks
concepts.question: What can an adapter do when the target has an operation the wrapped class cannot support?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Iterator has a remove() method, but Enumeration is a read-only interface, so the adapter has no way to implement a fully working remove().

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The best that can be done is to throw a runtime exception. The designers of Iterator foresaw the need and defined remove() so that it supports an UnsupportedOperationException.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The adapter is not perfect, and clients must watch for potential exceptions. As long as clients are careful and the adapter is well documented, the book calls this a perfectly reasonable solution.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: if the target promised that the operation always works, throwing from it would break the promise.

card.rule: When the adaptee cannot do what the target allows to fail, throw the exception the target's contract permits and document it.
card.limits: This works because the Iterator contract was written to allow it. If a target promised that an operation always works, throwing would break the promise.

concepts.title: Is an adapter just a decorator?
concepts.question: Both adapters and decorators wrap an object. In what sense is 'an adapter is only a decorator' right, and in what sense wrong?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Adapters and decorators both wrap an object, so one can be mistaken for the other. A claim such as 'an adapter is only a decorator' needs testing, not a nod.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: In the book's fireside chat the Decorator says adapters are fancy decorators, since both wrap. The Adapter replies that it always converts the interface of what it wraps and a decorator never does. The Decorator answers that it extends behaviors or responsibilities and is not a simple pass-through.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: They end by agreeing that they look somewhat similar on paper but are miles apart in intent. Shared structure does not make two patterns the same.

card.rule: A claim that one pattern is just another is judged by asking in what sense it holds: both wrap, but an adapter converts an interface while a decorator adds behavior.
card.limits: Similar structure does not mean the same purpose. The structural match makes the claim tempting, so check the intent before agreeing.

concepts.title: Adapter, decorator and facade by purpose
concepts.question: Which of adapter, decorator and facade converts an interface, which adds responsibility and which simplifies?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Adapter, decorator and facade all wrap something, so wrapping cannot be what tells them apart.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A decorator does not alter the interface but adds responsibility. An adapter converts one interface into another. A facade makes an interface simpler, hiding the complexity of one or more classes behind a clean, well-lit front.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Ask what the wrapper does with the interface: keep it, convert it or simplify it. The chapter's summary puts it as an adapter changing an interface, a decorator adding behaviors and responsibilities, and a facade wrapping a set of objects to simplify.

card.rule: An adapter converts an interface, a decorator adds responsibility while keeping the interface, and a facade simplifies.
card.limits: All three wrap something, so wrapping cannot tell them apart. Only what each does with the interface, and why, can.

concepts.title: The home theater problem
concepts.question: Why does using a collection of well-working components still become hard, as in the home theater example?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The home theater has a DVD player, projector, automated screen, surround sound and popcorn popper. Every part works, and weeks went into wiring and tuning. Even so, the whole is awkward to use.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Watching one movie takes thirteen tasks in a fixed order. Turning everything off means doing them again in reverse, a CD or the radio would be as complex, and an upgrade brings a slightly different procedure.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The complexity has moved from building the system to using it, and it recurs with every new use and every upgrade. Our reading: the book gives no threshold for when a sequence is long enough to need help.

card.rule: When using a group of components takes many ordered calls that repeat and change with upgrades, the use itself has become the complexity.
card.limits: The example is a motivation, not a count. A short sequence on a few parts is usually not worth a new layer, and the book gives no threshold.

concepts.title: What a facade is for
concepts.question: What does a facade do for a complex subsystem, and what stays available to clients who need more?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A subsystem is a set of related classes that work together, and using them as a group is hard. Clients that want only the common job should not have to learn every part.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A facade class provides one, more reasonable interface to the subsystem and gives the long sequence a short name. A client that just wants to watch a movie calls the facade and never meets the individual components.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The subsystem becomes easier to use, and it is still there: clients that need its full power can use it directly.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: a facade that tries to expose every feature of the subsystem stops being simple.

card.rule: A facade gives a complex subsystem one simpler interface while leaving the subsystem itself available.
card.limits: A facade makes using the subsystem simpler, not the subsystem itself. A facade that tries to expose every feature stops being simple.

concepts.title: A facade can be smart, and there can be several
concepts.question: Can a facade do more than forward calls, and can one subsystem have more than one facade?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: It is tempting to think a facade only forwards calls and that each subsystem gets exactly one.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A facade is free to add its own smarts in addition to using the subsystem. The home theater facade, for example, knows the popper must be turned on before it can pop. The pattern also allows any number of facades for a given subsystem.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Knowledge about how to use the subsystem lives in one place. Our reading: more smarts and more facades mean more code to keep correct.

card.rule: A facade may hold its own knowledge, such as ordering, and a subsystem may have several facades.
card.limits: More smarts and more facades mean more code to keep correct. A facade also stays a client of the subsystem and does not repair it.

concepts.title: Building a facade by composition and delegation
concepts.question: How is a facade built, and why does a client coded to it survive a change of components?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Clients want a few high-level calls such as watchMovie() and endMovie(), not a dozen calls on separate parts.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The first step is composition: the facade holds the components of the subsystem. Then it implements simplified methods that bring the components together into a unified interface, and does the work by delegation, calling the components in the right order.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A client coded to the facade does not change when the components are upgraded to ones with different interfaces; only the facade does.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: one method hides the order. Clients call watch() and meet one friend instead of two components.

card.rule: Compose the facade with the subsystem's components, delegate through a few high-level methods, and code clients to the facade.
card.limits: Only clients that go through the facade are protected. A client that calls the components directly still depends on them.

concepts.title: Adapter or facade: count or intent?
concepts.question: Is the number of classes wrapped what separates an adapter from a facade, and how would you test such a claim?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A tempting rule of thumb says an adapter wraps one class and a facade wraps many. Does it hold?

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The book says no. An adapter may adapt many classes to one interface a client expects, and a facade may simplify a single class with a very complex interface. The difference is intent: the adapter alters an interface to match what a client expects, and the facade provides a simplified interface to a subsystem.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A rule of thumb can be tested by looking for a counterexample, and one is enough to refute it. Our reading: the class count remains a hint in textbook examples but cannot define the difference.

card.rule: Tell an adapter from a facade by intent, converting versus simplifying, and not by how many classes are wrapped.
card.limits: The count is a fair hint in textbook examples, where adapters wrap one class and facades several. A hint is not a definition.

concepts.title: Talk only to your immediate friends
concepts.question: What does the Principle of Least Knowledge ask of an object, and what problem does it prevent?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: When an object depends on many classes, and they on others, changes in one part cascade to other parts. The book calls such a system fragile, costly to maintain and complex for others to understand.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Talk only to your immediate friends. For any object, be careful of the number of classes it interacts with and of how it comes to interact with them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A small circle of friends limits how far a change can travel. The slogan does not say who counts as a friend; the next idea does.

card.rule: Principle of Least Knowledge: talk only to your immediate friends.
card.limits: The slogan does not by itself say who counts as a friend. The guidelines in the next idea do.

concepts.section: How NOT to Win Friends and Influence Objects
concepts.title: Who counts as a friend
concepts.question: From inside a method, which objects may you call, and which objects are off limits?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A slogan about friends is of little use until it says exactly which objects a method may call.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: From any method, invoke only methods that belong to the object itself, to objects passed in as parameters, to any object the method creates or instantiates, and to any components of the object. A component is any object referenced by an instance variable, a HAS-A relationship.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Objects returned from calling other methods are not friends. Calling into one is a request to another object's subpart and increases the number of objects you directly know.

card.rule: Inside a method, call only the object itself, its parameters, objects it creates and its own components.
card.limits: The guidelines concern reach, not whether the code works: a call on a returned object is out of bounds even when it is convenient.

concepts.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
concepts.title: Why a call chain through a returned object breaks the principle
concepts.question: What does a chain like station.getThermometer().getTemperature() cost the caller, and how is it fixed?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The code station.getThermometer().getTemperature() asks the station for a thermometer, then calls a method on what came back. The caller therefore knows two classes.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Ask the object you already know to make the request for you. The station makes the inner call, so the caller does not have to know about the station's component objects.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The caller now knows only the station. The book's Car class shows the ways of calling methods that stay within the principle.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before: the caller reaches through the station. After: it asks the station, which uses its own component.

card.rule: Replace a chain through a returned object with a request to the object you know, and let it make the inner call.
card.limits: The rewrite shifts knowledge instead of removing it: the station still knows its thermometer. A method may freely call objects it creates itself.

concepts.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
concepts.title: Weighing the principle's costs and benefits
concepts.question: Should the Principle of Least Knowledge always be applied, and what does applying it cost?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A guideline that cuts dependencies also has costs. The authors say that no principle is a law, since all design involves trade-offs.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The Principle of Least Knowledge and the Law of Demeter are one and the same, and the terms are used interchangeably. The authors prefer the first name because it is more intuitive and because 'law' suggests it must always be applied. Principles are used when and where they are helpful.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The benefit is fewer dependencies between objects, which studies have shown reduces software maintenance. The cost is more wrapper classes to handle calls to other components, with more complexity, more development time and decreased runtime performance.

card.rule: Treat Least Knowledge as guidance to weigh: it cuts dependencies, but costs wrapper methods, complexity and some speed.
card.limits: The authors report the benefit but give no figures in this passage, so how large it is in your case is for you to judge.

concepts.section: The Facade and the Principle of Least Knowledge
concepts.title: How a facade supports Least Knowledge
concepts.question: How does a facade help a client keep to the Principle of Least Knowledge?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A client that calls each component of a subsystem has many friends, and every component change can reach it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A facade avoids tight coupling between clients and subsystems and helps follow the Principle of Least Knowledge. A client that uses a facade deals with one friend, and the facade may call every component because the components are its own, held in instance variables.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Knowledge is concentrated in the facade rather than removed. Our reading: a client that bypasses the facade gets no benefit.

card.rule: A facade lets a client talk to one friend instead of every component, which keeps the client within the Principle of Least Knowledge.
card.limits: Knowledge is concentrated, not removed: the facade still knows every component. Clients that bypass the facade get none of the benefit.

concepts.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)
concepts.title: Duplicated recipes in Coffee and Tea
concepts.question: What problem is the author trying to solve by redesigning the Coffee and Tea classes?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Coffee and Tea each hold a recipe method, written separately. The two are so close that a lot of code appears twice, in a form that differs only in a few details.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors want the repetition gone. A first redesign moves the steps that are identical, boiling water and pouring into the cup, into a common base class. The steps that differ stay in the subclasses.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Part of the repetition disappears. The authors then ask whether this first cut was enough, and whether another likeness between the two classes is still unused.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Two classes whose methods list the same actions, with only a few details changed from one to the other.

card.rule: When two classes carry the same code, find what they share and move it to one place.
card.limits: A first cut that moves only the identical methods up removes some duplication, not all of it; what remains may be a repeated pattern around the steps that differ.

concepts.title: The recipes are one algorithm
concepts.question: What do the two recipes share beyond the methods they already have in common?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: After the first cut the two recipes still read alike. Both boil some water, use the hot water to extract the coffee or tea, pour the result into a cup, and add the appropriate condiments.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Two of those four steps already sit in the base class. The other two have the same role in both drinks and differ only in which beverage they serve. So the next thing to abstract is the recipe method itself, the steps in their order.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Seen as one algorithm, the recipe can be written once instead of once per drink. Our reading: this holds only when both drinks really run the same kinds of step in the same order.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Subclass methods that run the same kinds of step in the same order, each step written for its own kind of item.

card.rule: Look for a shared sequence of steps, not only for shared methods.
card.limits: The sequence is shared only when the classes really run the same kinds of step in the same order; matching helper names called in different orders do not form one algorithm.

concepts.title: One neutral name for analogous steps
concepts.question: How does giving analogous steps one name let a single recipe method serve both drinks?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Coffee calls brewCoffeeGrinds and addSugarAndMilk, while Tea calls steepTeaBag and addLemon. Since the method names differ, one recipe method cannot call both.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors reason that steeping and brewing are analogous, and that adding sugar and milk is much like adding lemon. They invent a neutral name for each pair, brew and addCondiments, so the recipe reads boilWater, brew, pourInCup, addCondiments.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The recipe no longer mentions coffee or tea, so it can be written once. Our reading: a name that describes one kind of drink would bring the problem back.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Step names that spell out one variant, such as one drink or one file format, in code meant to serve several.

card.rule: Give analogous steps one general name so a shared sequence can call them without knowing the specific kind.
card.limits: A name should say what the step is for, not how one kind does it; if two steps are not truly analogous, a forced common name hides a real difference.

concepts.title: The recipe lives in the superclass
concepts.question: Which class holds the recipe, and what do Coffee and Tea still have to supply?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A recipe copied into each subclass repeats the order of the steps, while the subclasses differ only in how two of those steps are done.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Move prepareRecipe into the superclass, CaffeineBeverage. It calls boilWater, brew, pourInCup and addCondiments in order. The first and third are written there; Coffee and Tea supply brew and addCondiments. The authors say they have built the Template Method Pattern, with prepareRecipe as the template method.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Coffee and Tea shrink to the two steps that really differ. They hold no recipe of their own, and the superclass controls the order of the steps.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The superclass after the change; each subclass only fills in the two abstract steps.

card.rule: Write the algorithm once in the superclass and leave the varying steps to subclasses.
card.limits: The superclass can only call steps it has named in advance, so every variation must fit one of them; a variation that needs a different sequence calls for a different design.

concepts.title: Tracing a Tea through the template
concepts.question: Which class's code runs at each point when a Tea object makes its drink?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To trust the design you need to know which class's code runs at each point when a Tea object makes its drink.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Calling prepareRecipe on a Tea starts in CaffeineBeverage, where the template method lives. boilWater and pourInCup run there. brew and addCondiments run in Tea, because only the subclass knows how to steep and what to add.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The superclass runs the show and decides which step comes next. The subclass is called only when its turn arrives.

card.rule: In a template method the superclass calls every step, and the subclass code runs only when the superclass reaches it.
card.limits: The trace holds when a subclass supplies only the steps left open; if it overrides a shared step or the template itself, the path through the code changes.

concepts.section: What did the Template Method get us?
concepts.title: What the template buys
concepts.question: What does the Template Method design give that the first Coffee and Tea design did not?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the first design Coffee and Tea each ran their own algorithm. Code was duplicated across them, and a change to the algorithm meant opening several classes.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In the Template Method design the CaffeineBeverage class runs the show: it has the algorithm and protects it. The subclasses reuse that algorithm.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The book's table lists the gains. Reuse is maximised, a change to the algorithm is made in one place, and the class is a framework where a new beverage implements only a couple of methods. Knowledge of the algorithm is concentrated in one class.

card.rule: The template keeps the algorithm in one place, so reuse grows and changes stay local.
card.limits: These gains depend on the algorithm being really shared; if every new variant needs its own sequence, the central algorithm becomes a constraint instead of a help.

concepts.title: The pattern defined
concepts.question: How does the book define the Template Method Pattern, and what exactly is a template in it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Several classes follow one procedure whose steps differ in detail from case to case. The procedure's structure should stay put while the details vary.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a method and defers some steps to subclasses. A template, the authors explain, is just a method that defines an algorithm as a set of steps. One or more of the steps is abstract and implemented by a subclass.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Subclasses can redefine certain steps without changing the algorithm's structure. The structure stays unchanged while the subclasses provide part of the implementation.

card.rule: A template method is a method that fixes the steps of an algorithm and defers some of them to subclasses.
card.limits: The pattern lets subclasses change how a step is done, not which steps exist or in what order; a change to the structure itself belongs in the superclass.

concepts.title: Concrete, abstract and hook methods
concepts.question: What kinds of method can the abstract class hold, and who supplies each?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The steps of one algorithm differ in who should write them: some are the same for every subclass, some must differ, and some are extras that only a few need.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The abstract class that holds the template method may define three kinds of method. A concrete method is written there and shared, as boilWater is. An abstract method is left for each subclass to implement. A hook has an empty or default body there, and a subclass may override it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Abstract methods are the steps a subclass has to supply, hooks are optional extras, and concrete methods are the shared work.

card.rule: The abstract class mixes shared concrete steps, required abstract steps and optional hooks.
card.limits: The kind is a design choice made step by step: moving a step from abstract to concrete removes a decision from subclasses, and moving it to a hook makes it optional.

concepts.title: Protecting the template with final
concepts.question: How can the template method be protected from subclasses that would change the algorithm?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The pattern promises that subclasses do not change the structure of the algorithm. Without a guard, a subclass could replace the whole sequence with its own.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The book's safeguard is to declare the template method final, so that subclasses cannot override it. They still supply the abstract steps and the hooks, but they cannot rewrite the template.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The promise of an unchanged structure no longer rests on trust. Our reading: the language enforces it. The book lists this among its summary points for the pattern.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The template method marked final; subclasses can only fill in scan and pay.

card.rule: Declare the template method final so subclasses supply steps but cannot rewrite the algorithm.
card.limits: Final guards the sequence only; it does not stop a subclass doing poor work in its own steps, and it suits only an algorithm whose structure should be fixed.

concepts.title: What a hook is
concepts.question: What is a hook, and what does a subclass gain from it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some points in an algorithm are worth offering to subclasses, but not worth forcing every subclass to write something there.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A hook is a method declared in the abstract class with only an empty or default implementation. A subclass can override it to hook into the algorithm at that point, or ignore it. The template method decides where each hook is called.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The algorithm gains optional extension points. A subclass that does not care leaves the default in place and writes nothing.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A hook with an empty body, called by the template at a fixed point.

card.rule: A hook is an empty or default method in the abstract class that a subclass may override to join the algorithm at that point.
card.limits: A hook is optional, so the algorithm must still work if every subclass ignores it; a step the algorithm cannot do without belongs among the abstract methods.

concepts.title: Three uses of hooks
concepts.question: In what ways can a hook be used inside the algorithm?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Subclasses want different things from a hook: an optional extra step, a chance to react to the algorithm's progress, or a say in what the algorithm does.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The book names several uses. A hook can make a part of the algorithm optional. It can let a subclass react to a step about to happen or just done, as justReOrderedList lets a subclass redisplay a list after reordering. It can also answer a question for the abstract class, such as whether the customer wants condiments.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: In each use the subclass takes part without owning the algorithm: the template method still places every hook call.

card.rule: Hooks let a subclass take an optional step, react to an event, or make a decision for the template.
card.limits: In each use the template still decides where the hook is called and what to do with its answer; the hook cannot reorder the algorithm.

concepts.title: Abstract method or hook?
concepts.question: When should a step be an abstract method and when should it be a hook?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A step may be one that every subclass has to supply, or one that only some subclasses care about. The two cases call for different declarations.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: According to the book, use an abstract method when the subclass must provide an implementation of the step, and a hook when that part of the algorithm is optional. A concrete subclass must implement all the abstract methods; with a hook it may choose to implement it, but does not have to.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The choice therefore sets how much each subclass has to write.

card.rule: Make a step abstract when every subclass must supply it, and a hook when it is optional.
card.limits: The test is whether the step is truly required: a step with a harmless default is a hook, but a step the algorithm cannot do without stays abstract even if some subclasses find it dull.

concepts.title: How fine to cut the steps
concepts.question: How fine should the steps of a template method be?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Every abstract step is work for each subclass, so an algorithm cut into many abstract steps makes every subclass a big job.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors suggest keeping the number of abstract methods small. One way is not to make the steps of the algorithm too granular. Another is to turn optional steps into hooks.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors call coarser steps a trade-off: they are easier to implement but give less flexibility. Hooks ease the burden on subclasses.

card.rule: Balance step size: fewer abstract steps are easier to implement, and more steps give more flexibility.
card.limits: There is no fixed number; the right size depends on how much subclasses really need to vary, and steps cut too coarse make the template too rigid to be useful.

concepts.title: The Hollywood Principle
concepts.question: What problem does the Hollywood Principle protect a design from?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Dependency rot sets in when high-level components depend on low-level ones, which depend on high-level and sideways ones, and so on. Then no one can easily understand how the system is designed.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The Hollywood Principle: Don't call us, we'll call you. Low-level components may hook themselves into a system, but the high-level components decide when they are needed and how.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Control sits with the high-level components, which the authors offer as a way to prevent dependency rot.

card.rule: High-level components decide when and how to call low-level components, not the other way round.
card.limits: The principle settles who is in charge; it does not remove every upward call, so judge the explicit dependencies between levels rather than each single call.

concepts.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
concepts.title: Template Method as Hollywood in action
concepts.question: How does Template Method apply the Hollywood Principle, and how does that differ from Dependency Inversion?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A framework class wants subclasses to take part in its computation without the two sides becoming tangled in each other.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Template Method applies the principle: CaffeineBeverage is the high-level component. It controls the algorithm and calls Coffee or Tea only when a step is needed. The subclasses do not decide when brew or addCondiments run.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The book relates this to the Dependency Inversion Principle. Both aim at decoupling, but Dependency Inversion is the stronger, more general statement: avoid concrete classes and work with abstractions. The Hollywood Principle is a technique for hooking low-level components into a computation without creating dependencies from them to higher layers.

card.rule: In Template Method the superclass decides when to call the subclass's steps.
card.limits: The Hollywood Principle is narrower than Dependency Inversion, and Template Method is only one of its uses; a design can follow it without following the pattern.

concepts.title: Arrays.sort in the wild
concepts.question: Is Arrays.sort a true Template Method, and why does it depart from the textbook form?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Arrays.sort needs a way to compare two items. A Java array cannot be subclassed, and the designers wanted sort to be useful across all arrays.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: They made sort a static method that holds the algorithm, and deferred the comparison to the items being sorted. Those items implement the Comparable interface and its compareTo method, which says whether one object is less than, greater than or equal to another.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: It is not the textbook pattern, since nothing is subclassed. The authors judge it in the spirit of Template Method: the algorithm is in one place and incomplete without the missing step. They add that it is in some ways more flexible.

card.rule: A method that owns an algorithm and defers one step to something supplied is in the spirit of Template Method, even without subclassing.
card.limits: Judging whether code counts as a pattern means asking what the pattern is for, not only whether it matches the textbook diagram; a look-alike can fit another pattern better.

concepts.title: Hooks in JFrame and applets
concepts.question: Where do hooks appear in Swing's JFrame and in applets?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A framework such as Swing runs the process of putting a window on screen and has to leave room for your own drawing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: JFrame inherits a paint method that does nothing by default, because it is a hook. Overriding paint inserts your graphics into JFrame's algorithm for displaying its area. An applet is a small program that runs in a web page and subclasses Applet, which provides several hooks.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The framework runs the process and your code joins in at the hooks. Because an applet's methods are hooks, it is not required to implement them.

card.rule: In a framework, override the hooks to add your behaviour; the framework decides when they run.
card.limits: Overriding a hook changes what happens at that point, not when it happens; and spotting hooks in real code means looking for methods the framework calls with an empty or default body.

concepts.title: Template Method versus Strategy
concepts.question: How do Template Method and Strategy differ, and what does each give up?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Both patterns encapsulate algorithms, so the choice between them depends on how the variation is to be supplied.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Template Method uses inheritance: it defines the outline of an algorithm and lets subclasses do some of the work. Strategy uses object composition: it defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, each implementing the whole algorithm.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: In the authors' fireside chat Strategy claims more flexibility, since a client can change algorithms at runtime. Template Method claims to be a little more efficient, with fewer objects, and to keep control of the structure.

card.rule: Template Method varies steps through inheritance; Strategy swaps whole algorithms through composition.
card.limits: These contrasts come from a playful dialogue and give the authors' view; real designs can blend both, as the sort method does.

concepts.title: Factory Method as a specialization
concepts.question: How is Factory Method related to Template Method?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some steps of a template exist to create objects, and which class gets created depends on the subclass.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The book says Factory Method is a specialization of Template Method. The primitive operations that subclasses supply are used to create and return objects.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: In Template Method, subclasses decide how to implement the steps of an algorithm. In Factory Method, subclasses decide which concrete classes to instantiate.

card.rule: Factory Method is a Template Method whose varying step creates an object.
card.limits: Specialization points one way; the two patterns are not interchangeable, and the pair cannot be read as one pattern with two names.

concepts.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge
concepts.title: Two menus, two ways of storing items
concepts.question: What difficulty arises when two merged menus keep their own different ways of storing items?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two kitchens merge, and each has years of code built around how its menu stores items, so neither chef will rewrite. Both menus share the MenuItem class; only the container differs: an ArrayList in one, a plain array in the other.

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: One client now needs both menus. The method that hands out the items has a different return type in each, so the client cannot treat the two menus alike. The design question is how each storage choice can stay while the client stays manageable.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The client inherits every difference it can see. With nothing hiding the difference, whoever reads both menus must deal with two kinds of container.

card.rule: When two parts hold their data differently, any client that uses both inherits the difference unless something hides it.
card.limits: If only one menu existed, or both stored items the same way, there would be no difference to hide. The problem also assumes the owners refuse a rewrite; if one side could change cheaply, unifying storage might be the easier fix.

concepts.title: A client that must use both menus
concepts.question: What does a client have to do to print every item from menus stored in different structures?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The new Java-enabled waitress must print a custom menu and say whether an item is vegetarian. To do either she asks each menu for its items, and the two menus return different container types.

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: Printing needs one loop for the ArrayList (size() and get()) and another for the array (length and subscripts). Every other Waitress method follows the same theme: fetch both menus, then run two loops.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each acquisition with a new storage type adds another loop to every method; a third restaurant means three loops.

card.rule: Each distinct storage type forces its own traversal code into every client method that reads the items.
