card.limits: The cost appears only when the client reads storage directly. If the client received items through one shared way of stepping through them, extra storage types would not add loops.

concepts.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?
concepts.title: Three faults of a client that sees inside
concepts.question: Which design faults show up in a client that reads two storage types directly?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The Waitress reads both menus directly. Checked against design principles, her code shows three faults, and all of them come from her seeing inside the menus.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Fault one: she codes to the concrete PancakeHouseMenu and DinerMenu classes, not to an interface. Fault two: she must know how each menu represents its items, which breaks encapsulation. Fault three: the two loops are duplicate code, and a third menu would add a third loop.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: If the Diner switched to a Hashtable, a lot of the Waitress's code would have to change.

card.rule: A client that sees how its collaborators store things is tied to them, repeats code and breaks when they change.
card.limits: These are faults of the client's design, not of the menus: each menu's storage is fine inside its own class. Blaming the storage choice would point the repair at the wrong place.

concepts.title: The goal: one shared interface
concepts.question: What would the two menus need to share so the client can stop depending on either one?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The chefs refuse to rewrite, yet the Waitress will be hard to maintain and extend. The menus are already close: each has a method for the items, and the return type is the only difference.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Aim for one interface that both menus implement. The Waitress would then hold fewer concrete references and might lose the repeated loops. The goal is to decouple her from the concrete menus completely, so she can focus on being a waitress.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Her code would refer to the interface instead of the concrete menu classes, and she would no longer need to care what type of menu she holds.

card.rule: Make the client depend on one shared interface so it need not know which concrete variation it holds.
card.limits: A shared interface helps only when the variations really do the same job. These menus already offer nearly the same operations; classes with unrelated jobs cannot be unified this way without more work.

concepts.title: Encapsulate the iteration
concepts.question: What is the part that varies in the menu code, and what can we do with it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The book's earlier advice is to encapsulate what varies. Here the varying part is the iteration: the ArrayList is walked with size() and get(), the array with its length field and subscripts.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Create an object called an Iterator that hides how one collection is walked: one for the ArrayList, another for the array. The client asks the iterator for items one at a time and never touches the collection's own stepping.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each iterator carries the knowledge of one collection, so the client's loop stops depending on the container type.

card.rule: Put the varying way of stepping through a collection into its own object, and let the client talk to that object.
card.limits: This helps when the stepping varies between collections. With a single collection type the iterator hides nothing worth hiding, and the iterator itself must still know the one collection it serves.

concepts.title: The Iterator interface
concepts.question: What operations does the Iterator interface offer so that one client loop can serve any collection?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A client loop should work for any collection, yet each collection is stepped through differently. The loop needs a small, common set of operations to depend on.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Iterator interface offers hasNext(), which reports whether more items remain, and next(), which returns the next item. Write one implementation per kind of collection: arrays, lists, hash maps, whatever you favour. The client uses only the interface, so one loop serves all.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each concrete iterator holds the knowledge of one collection, and the client holds none of it.

card.rule: Define a small interface for stepping through items and write one implementation for each kind of collection.
card.limits: The interface says nothing about order, so an iterator over an unordered collection promises none. A collection that cannot supply an iterator, like an array, still needs one written by hand.

concepts.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator
concepts.title: Each menu builds its own iterator
concepts.question: Who should create the iterator for a menu, and in what type should it be handed to the client?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A client needs an actual iterator object, and it should not have to know which concrete iterator class fits which storage.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Add one method, createIterator(), to each menu. It builds the iterator that suits that menu's storage and returns it as an Iterator. The Waitress calls createIterator() and never names the concrete iterator class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each menu keeps its own storage and now also knows how to be walked. The cooks only had to add this one method, because the iterator classes were provided for them.

card.rule: Let each collection create the iterator that suits it and hand it out through the shared interface.
card.limits: The collection now depends on its iterator class, a small price paid in the one class that already knows the storage. A client that wants a different traversal needs the collection to offer it.

concepts.title: One printing method that takes an Iterator
concepts.question: How does the Waitress print any menu once she receives an Iterator instead of a menu?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With iterators available, the Waitress still carries a printing loop for each kind of menu.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Give her one printMenu() that takes an Iterator. To print a menu she calls createIterator() on it and passes the result in; inside, a single loop takes the next item while hasNext() is true.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Printing both menus becomes two calls to the same method, and the duplicate loop is gone. Test drive code then confirms that she works with both menus.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, a method needs a loop per container. After, one method serves any iterator.

card.rule: Write the client's work once against the Iterator and feed it the iterator each collection produces.
card.limits: The Waitress still fetches each menu through its concrete class, so she is only partly decoupled, and each new menu still needs its own call. Fixing the loop did not fix those.

concepts.section: What have we done so far?
concepts.title: Before and after the Iterator
concepts.question: How do the Waitress's dependencies differ before and after iterators were added?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To judge the change, compare the design before and after along the same points: what the Waitress can see, how many loops she needs, and what she is bound to.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Before: the menus were not encapsulated (an ArrayList in the Diner, an array in the Pancake House), two loops were needed, and she was bound to the concrete collection types. After: she has no idea how the menus hold items, one loop handles any collection that implements Iterator, and she uses an interface.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: One problem remains: she is still bound to two concrete menu classes.

card.rule: Compare a design before and after a change along the same dimensions: what is visible, how many loops, and what the client is bound to.
card.limits: A before-and-after table can hide what the change left alone. Here the Waitress still depends on two concrete menu classes, so the table must be read for what remains as well as what improved.

concepts.title: What the iterator solution leaves unsolved
concepts.question: Which problem is still open after adding iterators, and how can we describe it precisely?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Judging a solution means asking whether it solved every problem it set out to solve. The iterators fixed the exposed storage and the duplicate loops.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Mark each original problem as solved or open, and name the open ones precisely. Here one is open: the menu classes share no declared common interface, so the Waitress still names two concrete menu classes. The authors fix that next.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A fair review says what is missing and where, instead of calling the work incomplete without saying how.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A verdict such as it feels unfinished, which names no specific gap and gives nobody a next step.

card.rule: Judge a solution by listing the original problems, marking which are solved, and naming precisely any that remain.
card.limits: This only works if the original problems were stated fully at the start. A problem nobody wrote down can be marked neither solved nor open, so an incomplete list gives false comfort.

concepts.title: A small shared Menu interface
concepts.question: What does a shared Menu interface with one createIterator() method give the Waitress?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The Waitress still depends on two concrete menu classes, although the menus are nearly identical.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Define a small Menu interface with a single method, createIterator(), and have PancakeHouseMenu and DinerMenu implement it. The Waitress refers to menus through the interface, programming to an interface and not to an implementation.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each menu class remains responsible for creating the iterator that suits its own storage, so the Waitress no longer depends on how menu items are held.

card.rule: Give the variations a small shared interface that exposes only what their clients need.
card.limits: A shared interface covers only what clients share. Anything a client needs beyond it must come from elsewhere, or the interface must grow, which couples more clients to more detail.

concepts.title: Use the standard java.util.Iterator
concepts.question: Why swap a homegrown Iterator for java.util.Iterator, and where must we still write our own?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The authors built their own Iterator interface to show how it works, but the standard java.util.Iterator offers a lot more leverage.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Switch to java.util.Iterator, whose methods are hasNext(), next() and remove(). ArrayList already has an iterator() method, so PancakeHouseMenuIterator is deleted and one line changes. An array offers no iterator, so the DinerMenu keeps its own iterator class, now written to the java.util interface.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: One homegrown class disappears. The array-based menu still needs a hand-written iterator.

card.rule: Prefer the platform's standard iterator interface, and write your own iterator only for collections that lack one.
card.limits: The standard interface fits only if its operations suit you. If your aggregates need more, you can extend the Iterator interface rather than abandon it.

concepts.title: Optional and unspecified parts of Iterator
concepts.question: What does the Iterator interface leave optional or unspecified, and how should a careful client react?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The standard Iterator interface declares remove(), yet not every iterator can or should delete from its collection.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors call remove() optional. An iterator that will not allow removal should still provide the method and throw the runtime exception UnsupportedOperationException.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A good client checks for that exception when it calls remove(). The interface is a contract with gaps, so a careful client reads what it promises before relying on it.

card.rule: Read an interface for what it leaves optional or unspecified, and write clients that survive those gaps.
card.limits: Gaps in a contract are not to be filled by guessing. A client that assumes removal works, or that iteration is safe while the collection changes, may break; check the documentation instead.

concepts.title: The Iterator Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the Iterator Pattern provide, and what does it keep hidden?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Clients want to go through a group of objects without learning how the group is held.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The pattern gives sequential access to the elements of an aggregate while keeping its underlying representation hidden. An aggregate is any object that holds a group of elements, such as an array, a list or a hash map.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The Waitress steps through items one after another and never learns whether they sit in an array or an ArrayList. The aggregate creates the iterator, and the iterator does the traversal.

card.rule: Access an aggregate's elements one after another through an iterator, without exposing how the aggregate holds them.
card.limits: Sequential access is what is promised, not any particular order or random access. A client that must jump to the fortieth element or sort by price gets no help from the pattern as defined.

concepts.title: Polymorphic iteration
concepts.question: What does a uniform way of stepping through every aggregate allow us to write?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Once every aggregate offers the same way of being stepped through, code can be written once for all of them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Polymorphic iteration means writing methods that take an Iterator as a parameter. Such a method iterates over any collection that supports Iterator, with no concern for how the collection is implemented. printMenu() is the example.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A new kind of collection costs existing iterator-taking code nothing, provided the collection can supply an iterator. That code sees only what the Iterator offers.

card.rule: Write methods that take an Iterator, and they serve any collection that can supply one.
card.limits: Polymorphic code sees only what the Iterator offers. If a method needs something the interface lacks, such as the number of items in advance, the iterator alone cannot supply it.

concepts.title: Traversal belongs to the iterator
concepts.question: Which object should carry the job of traversal, and what does moving it do to the aggregate?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An aggregate that also carries traversal has more to maintain than its real job, which is managing a collection of objects.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The pattern gives the job of traversal to the iterator object, not to the aggregate. The aggregate stays focused on managing its objects.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The aggregate's interface and implementation become simpler, and the responsibility sits where it belongs.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, the shelf holds books and walks them. After, it only holds books and hands out an iterator.

card.rule: Give traversal to the iterator so the aggregate does only the job of holding and managing its elements.
card.limits: The move works when traversal can be separated from managing the elements. The iterator still needs to know enough about the aggregate to step through it, so the two are separate but not strangers.

concepts.title: Classic names and Java names
concepts.question: How do the classic iterator methods map onto the methods of java.util.Iterator?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Other books draw the Iterator with first(), next(), isDone() and currentItem(), while java.util.Iterator has next(), hasNext() and remove().

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Map the names by job. The classic next() and currentItem() were merged into one next(). isDone() became hasNext(), with its meaning turned around. first() has no counterpart, because in Java you usually get a new iterator to start the traversal over.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: There is very little difference between the interfaces. remove() is an extension in java.util.Iterator, and the range of behaviours you can give an iterator is wide.

card.rule: Read different iterator interfaces by mapping their methods onto the same few jobs: start, advance, read and test for the end.
card.limits: Mapping names works because the jobs agree. A method with no counterpart, like remove() in java.util.Iterator, is an extension, and the range of behaviours you can give an iterator is wide.

concepts.title: External and internal iterators
concepts.question: What is the difference between an external and an internal iterator, and which did the menus use?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Who drives the traversal? Sometimes the client needs to steer, and sometimes handing over a task is enough.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: With an external iterator the client controls the iteration by calling next(); the menu example used this kind. An internal iterator steps through the elements itself, so you must pass it an operation to apply as it goes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Internal iterators are less flexible, because the client does not control the iteration. Some argue they are easier to use: you hand over the operation and the iterator does all the work.

card.rule: Choose an external iterator when the client needs control of the pace and path; consider an internal one when handing over the operation is enough.
card.limits: Neither style wins everywhere: the external one gives the client control, the internal one saves the client work. Choose by whether the caller needs to steer the traversal.

concepts.title: A class should have only one reason to change
concepts.question: Why does giving a class a second responsibility make it harder to keep stable?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If an aggregate handled both its collection and the iteration, it would change when the collection changes and also when the way of iterating changes. That is two reasons to change.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A class should have only one reason to change. Every responsibility is an area of potential change, so give each responsibility to one class, and only one class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Fewer areas of change leave fewer chances for problems to creep in when code is modified. Spotting several responsibilities inside one class is hard.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, one class stores the rows and decides how they look. After, each job has its own class.

card.rule: A class should have only one reason to change, so give each responsibility to exactly one class.
card.limits: Separating responsibilities is one of the hardest jobs in design, because our minds group behaviours that are really two responsibilities. Only careful examination, and watching for signs that a class changes in more than one way, will find them.

concepts.title: Cohesion
concepts.question: How does cohesion relate to the Single Responsibility Principle, and what makes it high or low?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: Cohesion measures how closely a class or module supports a single purpose or responsibility.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: A class has high cohesion when it is designed around a set of related functions, and low cohesion when it is designed around a set of unrelated functions.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: Cohesion is a matter of judgement, not a count of methods. Ask whether the parts of a class serve one purpose.

card.rule: Aim for high cohesion: build each class around functions that belong together.
card.limits: Cohesion is a matter of degree and judgement, not a count of methods. A short class can be incoherent and a long one tightly focused; ask whether its parts serve one purpose.

concepts.title: Fitting a third menu into the framework
concepts.question: What three changes fit the Café menu, which stores items in a HashMap, into the framework?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A third menu arrives. The Café keeps its items in a HashMap, and it should slot into the iterator framework.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Three changes: implement the Menu interface, get rid of getItems(), and add createIterator() that returns an iterator over the HashMap's values. A HashMap holds keys and values, so first retrieve its values (the MenuItems), then get the iterator from them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: It is easy because HashMap is one of the Java collections that supports Iterator, though not quite as ArrayList does.

card.rule: To fit a new collection into the iterator framework, implement the shared interface and return an iterator over the part that holds the elements.
card.limits: The route to an iterator differs by collection: a hash map gives one only through its values. Fitting a collection still needs someone who knows how it holds items to write its createIterator() code.

concepts.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress
concepts.title: Decoupled and extensible
concepts.question: What did adding the Café menu show about the Waitress after the iterator work?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The Café menu is added to the Waitress. How well does the iterator design absorb a new menu?

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Waitress expects Iterators, so adding the Café takes one more menu and one more call to printMenu(). The test drive prints breakfast, lunch and the Café's dinner.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: She is decoupled from how the menus are built, and extensible: a menu with any storage can be added by giving it createIterator(). The authors then look at what still remains in her code.

card.rule: Test a design by what it costs to add the next variation: a good design takes a small, local addition.
card.limits: Easy extension is relative. Adding the Café still meant opening the Waitress and adding a call, and the authors count that as a remaining cost; the design is extensible only up to that point.

concepts.title: The Collections Framework and Collection
concepts.question: What do ArrayList, Vector and similar classes share through java.util.Collection, and how does HashMap differ?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To use iterators well you need to know where they come from in the standard library.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Java Collections Framework is a set of classes and interfaces including ArrayList, Vector, LinkedList, Stack and PriorityQueue. Each implements java.util.Collection, which has many useful methods for manipulating groups of objects.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Hashtable and HashMap support Iterator only indirectly. They hold keys and values, so you first retrieve the Collection called values and then obtain its iterator.

card.rule: Find the Collection that holds the elements you want, and get the iterator from it.
card.limits: Not every class takes the same route: maps hold two sets and need the extra step. Check which part you are iterating over before you ask for the iterator.

concepts.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?
concepts.title: The Waitress is still not ready
concepts.question: What weakness remains in the Waitress even though her menus are decoupled?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Every new menu forces the Waitress to be opened and another printMenu() call added. The authors name this a violation of the Open Closed Principle.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: It is not her fault, since the menu implementation was decoupled and the iteration extracted. What remains is that the menus are separate, independent objects, and we need a way to manage them together.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The chef suggests putting the menus into a collection and looping over it. That removes the repeated calls, though it does not settle everything.

card.rule: After decoupling, check what still forces edits to the client when a variation is added, and look for a way to manage the variations together.
card.limits: Grouping the menus in a collection fixes the repeated calls but not everything. Names are lost unless each menu carries one, and a flat collection cannot hold menus inside menus, which is the next challenge.

concepts.section: Just when we thought it was safe...
concepts.title: When menus must hold menus
concepts.question: Why can the array-based Diner menu not take a dessert menu as one of its elements?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The Diner wants a dessert submenu, so the design must now support menus within menus.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The dessert menu would best be an element of the Diner's collection, but the Diner stores its elements in an array of MenuItem, and a menu is not a MenuItem, so it cannot be assigned.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Patching around this would not carry further acquisitions or submenus. The structure itself must become general enough for all menus and submenus.

card.rule: When a new requirement breaks the container's type assumptions, treat it as a sign the structure must change, not a case for a patch.
card.limits: Not every requirement justifies a rework. The authors reach for one because the complexity has risen so far that patching could not take further acquisitions or submenus; a one-off case may deserve a smaller fix.

concepts.title: Requirements for the new design
concepts.question: What three requirements must the new menu design meet?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The complexity has risen so far that the authors stop patching and ask what the new design must provide.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Three requirements. First, a tree-shaped structure that holds menus, submenus and menu items. Second, traversal at least as convenient as the iterators in use now. Third, more flexible traversal, such as iterating over only the Diner's dessert menu, or over the whole Diner menu including the dessert submenu.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Menus, nested submenus and items fit naturally into a tree.

card.rule: Before choosing a solution, list what it must provide: the structure, the convenience of access and the flexibility of traversal.
card.limits: A list of requirements reflects what is known now. This one comes from the dessert case, and later cases might add more, so treat it as a current outline rather than a final one.

concepts.title: The Composite Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the Composite Pattern define, and what is a part-whole hierarchy?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Menus must now hold menus, a new dimension that Iterator alone does not solve. The authors keep Iterator in the solution but step back to another pattern.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Composite Pattern composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies, and lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly. A menu tree is such a hierarchy: made of parts (menus and items), yet usable as a whole, one big uber menu.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Menus, submenus and items live in one structure, and one operation can be applied to the whole tree or to any part of it.

card.rule: Compose objects into a tree of parts and wholes, and let clients treat any node in the same way.
card.limits: The pattern fits only data that really is a hierarchy of parts and wholes. For a flat collection with no nesting, an Iterator is enough.

concepts.title: Treating parts and wholes uniformly
concepts.question: What does it mean to treat individual objects and compositions uniformly?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A tree of menus, submenus and items mixes containers with plain items, and the client should not have to ask which it holds.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Any menu is a composition, because it can contain both menus and menu items. The individual objects are the menu items, which hold nothing else. Give both kinds the same operations, such as print, and an operation can be applied to the whole structure or to just a part.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: In most cases the client can ignore the difference between compositions and individual objects. Some operations still do not suit one of the kinds.

card.rule: Give compositions and individual objects the same operations so a client need not ask which one it holds.
card.limits: Uniformity has gaps: some operations make no sense on one kind, such as asking a leaf for its children. The pattern accepts this and handles such cases by design choices.

concepts.title: Component, composite and leaf
concepts.question: How are component, composite and leaf related in a composite structure?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A hierarchy of parts and wholes needs names for its positions, or it is hard to talk about.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A composite contains components. Components come in two flavours: composites and leaf elements. A composite holds a set of children, which may be other composites or leaves, while a leaf has no children.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The definition is recursive, and the data forms a tree drawn upside down, with a composite at the root and branches of composites ending in leaf nodes. A Component is any object in the structure.

card.rule: Name the three roles: component for any node, composite for a node that holds children, leaf for a node that holds none.
card.limits: The roles describe positions in the structure, not kinds of thing in the world. If a leaf later needs to hold children, it has to become a composite, and its parent must still be able to treat it the same way.

concepts.title: The MenuComponent interface
concepts.question: What does the common component class offer, and what happens to operations a node cannot support?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Menus and menu items must answer the same calls, yet some methods make no sense on every node, such as getChild() on a leaf.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Create the abstract class MenuComponent as the common interface of leaves and composites, with a default implementation for each method. The default throws UnsupportedOperationException. A MenuItem or Menu implements only the methods that suit it and inherits the rest.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Uniform calls mean a client can reach an operation its node does not support, and it learns this only when the code runs. Sometimes the best a default can do is throw a runtime exception.

card.rule: Put every operation any node may need into one component type, with defaults that signal unsupported operations.
card.limits: Throwing defaults trade compile-time safety for uniformity: a client may call an operation its node does not support and learn only at run time. Sometimes the best a default can do is throw a runtime exception.

concepts.title: The leaf and composite classes
concepts.question: How do MenuItem and Menu differ in which MenuComponent methods they implement?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The shared component class lists every operation, but each concrete class should supply only the ones that make sense for it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: MenuItem, the leaf, implements the behaviour of the elements, such as getPrice() and isVegetarian(), and leaves child management at the defaults. Menu, the composite, holds MenuItems or other Menus and implements child management. It does not implement getPrice() or isVegetarian().

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Operations a class leaves out fall back on the exception default. Which operations a Menu should support is a design choice, taken up later in the chapter.

card.rule: Let each class implement the operations that fit it and inherit the defaults for the rest.
card.limits: This split is a design choice. A Menu could have defined isVegetarian() in some way, but the authors leave it unsupported and discuss the alternatives later in the chapter.

concepts.title: Printing by recursion
concepts.question: How can a Menu print everything beneath it without the client walking the tree?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If a Menu's print() handled only its own name, the client would have to walk the whole composite and print each item itself, which defeats the point of having a composite.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Each component can print itself. A Menu's print() iterates through its children and calls print() on each; if a child is another Menu, that Menu's print() starts its own iteration, and so on.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: One call prints the whole structure, whatever its depth, and the client does no walking.

card.rule: Let each composite perform an operation by asking its children to perform it, so the operation spreads over the whole tree.
card.limits: The recursive walk assumes every node can perform the operation. If one cannot, the call fails there unless the design supplies a default or a way to skip it.

concepts.section: Getting ready for a test drive...
concepts.title: Transparency traded for safety
concepts.question: What does the Composite Pattern trade away by putting child management and leaf operations in one interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Putting child management and leaf operations into one component interface can look like a breach of the Single Responsibility Principle.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors agree there is some truth in it: the pattern trades that principle for transparency, meaning a client treats composites and leaves uniformly and cannot tell which one it holds. The other way is to split the responsibilities into separate interfaces.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The shared interface costs some safety, because a client might try something meaningless, such as adding a menu to a menu item. Separate interfaces catch such calls but lose transparency and need conditionals and instanceof. The authors call it a design decision.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Transparent: add() sits on the shared type. Safe: add() sits only on the composite.

card.rule: Weigh transparency against safety in the component interface, and choose knowingly.
card.limits: Neither design is right everywhere. The authors call this a design decision and a classic tradeoff, and note a leaf can be seen as a node with zero children, which softens the apparent violation.

concepts.title: Iterating over a whole composite
concepts.question: Why does an external iterator over a composite need more than a simple loop, and what does it use?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The Waitress may want to walk the entire composite, for example to pull out the vegetarian items.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Add createIterator() to every component. The CompositeIterator steps through the items of a component and also includes child menus, their child menus, and so on. As an external iterator it must keep its position, so a client can drive it with hasNext() and next().

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Over a recursive structure it keeps that position in stacks as it moves up and down the hierarchy. The code is short but can be mind-bending.

card.rule: To iterate externally over a tree, keep your position in stacks as you move up and down the hierarchy.
card.limits: Recursion inside print() is easier because the program's own call stack keeps the place for you. An external iterator gets no such help, which is why its code is hard to follow; the authors warn it can be mind-bending.

concepts.title: The Null Iterator
concepts.question: What should createIterator() return for a node that has nothing to iterate over?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A MenuItem has nothing to iterate over, yet every component must answer createIterator().

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: There are two choices: return null, which forces conditional code on the client, or return an iterator whose hasNext() always returns false. The authors prefer the second and call it NullIterator, a no-op iterator.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Clients never have to check for null.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, the leaf hands back null. After, it hands back an iterator that is already finished.
blocks.code:
static Iterator<String> leafBefore() { return null; }
static Iterator<String> leafAfter() { return Collections.emptyIterator(); }

card.rule: When there is nothing to return, return an object that safely does nothing instead of null.
card.limits: This choice fits where having nothing to iterate is a normal answer, as it is for a leaf.

concepts.title: Unsupported operations: exception, false or type check
concepts.question: How did the authors handle isVegetarian() on a Menu, and what were the alternatives?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The Waitress goes through the whole composite calling isVegetarian() on each element, but a Menu does not support that operation.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Menu's inherited method throws UnsupportedOperationException, which the Waitress catches before moving on. The authors agree that try/catch is meant for error handling, not program logic, and still prefer this to the alternatives.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The alternatives are an instanceof check first, which loses transparency, or having Menus return false, which is simple and keeps transparency. The exception says plainly that the operation is unsupported, which is different from false.

card.rule: When an operation does not apply to some nodes, choose among an exception, a default value and a type check by weighing clarity and uniformity.
card.limits: The authors' choice is a position, not a proof. It keeps uniformity and clarity but uses exception handling as part of program flow, which they concede is not its intended use.

concepts.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...
concepts.title: Implementation issues for composites
concepts.question: Which further issues can arise when implementing a composite, beyond the basic tree?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Beyond the basic tree, the imagined interview with the Composite Pattern lists further issues to decide.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Parent pointers: a component can point back to its parent, which eases traversal and deleting a child. Ordering: a composite that must keep its children in order needs a more careful scheme for adding, removing and traversing. Caching: store a result at the composite nodes when the structure is expensive to traverse and is traversed constantly.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: These are options to weigh, not requirements. A menu whose items need no particular order needs no ordering scheme.

card.rule: When building a composite, decide about parent links, child order and caching, as well as the shape of the interface.
card.limits: These are options to weigh, not requirements. A menu whose items need no particular order needs no ordering scheme.

concepts.title: Iterator and Composite among the patterns
concepts.question: How do Iterator and Composite differ from the other patterns met so far, and what do they have in common?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With two more patterns in the toolbox, you need to tell them apart from the earlier ones by purpose.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Iterator traverses an aggregate without exposing its representation and takes iteration off the aggregate. Composite holds individual objects and compositions in one structure and treats them uniformly. Others: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable behaviours and uses delegation, Adapter changes the interface of classes, Facade simplifies the interface of a group of classes, Observer notifies objects of a state change.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Both new patterns deal with collections of objects. Each has tradeoffs the chapter spells out, such as the optional remove() in Iterator and transparency against safety in Composite.

card.rule: Know each pattern by its purpose: Iterator for traversal without exposure, Composite for uniform treatment of parts and wholes.
card.limits: A one-line purpose is a pointer, not the whole pattern. Each has tradeoffs the chapter spells out, such as an optional remove() in Iterator and transparency against safety in Composite.

concepts.title: States and transitions
concepts.question: What do the circles and the arrows of a state diagram stand for?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A device acts differently depending on where it is in its life, and a team needs one shared picture of that before anyone writes code. Prose alone hides the odd cases.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Draw each configuration as a circle, a state, and each move that an action causes as an arrow, a transition. In the gumball machine, inserting a quarter takes No Quarter to Has Quarter; turning the crank takes Has Quarter to Gumball Sold; ejecting returns to No Quarter.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors count four states, four actions and five transitions: dispensing ends in Out of Gumballs or No Quarter depending on how many gumballs remain, so the machine must keep that count. The picture is silent on pointless actions, such as ejecting with no quarter in.

card.rule: Read a machine as states, which say how it behaves now, and transitions, which are the actions that move it between states.
card.limits: A diagram shows only the moves someone drew. It does not say what should happen when an action makes no sense in a state, and it does not hold the numbers, such as gumballs left, that pick between arrows.

concepts.title: A state machine with conditionals
concepts.question: How does a procedural state machine keep its current state and decide what each action does?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A state diagram has to become code. The nearest tool is a number for the current state plus conditional statements, which is quick to write for a small machine.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Four steps: gather the states; hold the current one in an instance variable with a constant value per state; gather the actions; write one method per action that uses conditionals to pick the behavior for the current state.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The code is grouped by action, so one state's behavior is spread over every action method. It works and passes the in-house tests, but each new state or action means reopening all those methods.

card.rule: In a procedural state machine, one variable names the current state and every action method branches on it.
card.limits: The recipe works for small machines and the gumball tests passed. Its cost shows later, when states or actions are added and every branching method must be revisited.

concepts.title: Every action in every state
concepts.question: What must the code decide for each pairing of a state with an action, including pointless ones?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Customers do silly things: eject a quarter that is not there, insert two, turn the crank without paying. Joe and Frank accept that the machine cannot ignore them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Decide the response to every action in every state, pointless pairings included. A typical reply to a nonsensical action is a message and no change of state, as in the sold-out state.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: With S states and A actions there are S times A pairings to define. Most refuse rather than move, but each still has to be written, so the grid grows whenever a state or an action is added.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: An action method that has a branch for some states and silently does nothing in the others.

card.rule: Give every action a defined response in every state.
card.limits: The grid grows with each new state or action: a machine with S states and A actions has S times A pairings. Many pairings simply refuse the action, but each still has to be written somewhere.

concepts.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!
concepts.title: The change request tests the design
concepts.question: Why does the 1-in-10 request put a working design under strain?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Passing every test says little about tomorrow. Mighty Gumball's testers were happy, then asked for a contest: one sale in ten releases two gumballs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Test a design with a change request. Draw the new behavior as a changed state diagram first, then ask how many places in the code must change and how much working code those edits touch.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The request shows how costly extension is, and every edit to working code risks a bug. One request is a sample, not a verdict on all code.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The program is a one-off that will never change after delivery; judging its structure by an extension test pays little.

card.rule: Judge a design by how a new requirement changes it, not only by whether it passes today's tests.
card.limits: One change request is a sample, not proof of a bad design. A program that will never change need not be judged on this, and the authors' verdict applies to the structure of this code.

concepts.title: Behavior scattered across states
concepts.question: What fault in the first design leads Judy and Frank to conclude that it must be refactored?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the conditional design the behavior of every state lives in shared methods, and transitions are buried in the branches. The authors list worries: the Open Closed Principle, nothing encapsulated, bugs from further additions.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Refactor: keep what the machine does and change how it is built. Localize the behavior of each state so that changing one state does not put the others at risk.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Separation gives more pieces to manage. It pays when behaviors change independently of each other; if they stay fixed, shared code can be left alone.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A change to one behavior forces an edit inside code that other behaviors share.

card.rule: When one change must edit code that other behaviors share, separate the behaviors.
card.limits: Separation has a price in structure and in the number of pieces. It helps most when the behaviors are likely to change independently. If they stay fixed, the shared code can be left alone.

concepts.title: Two principles behind the redesign
concepts.question: Which principles do Frank and Judy invoke, and which design move does each one justify?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: What differs from state to state is behavior, yet it is tangled into the machine. Frank and Judy want changes to stay local.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Encapsulate what varies: each state's behavior goes into its own class. Favor composition: the machine holds the object for its current state and delegates to it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Judy expects a new state to need a new class and perhaps a few edited transitions. The gain is a smaller area of change, not zero change.

card.rule: Pull what varies into its own classes, then let the main object hold one of them and delegate to it.
card.limits: Adding a state still means writing code, and some neighboring transitions may need edits. The gain is a smaller area of change, not zero change.

concepts.title: The three-step redesign
concepts.question: What are the three steps of the redesign, and what happens to the conditional code?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The conditional code must go, but the machine still has to answer every action. The cubicle ideas need a concrete plan.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: One: define a State interface with a method for every action. Two: write a State class for every state, responsible for the behavior in that state. Three: delete the conditionals and delegate to the current State object.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The machine stays as the object that clients use. The real work moves to deciding what each state does for each action, including the ones that make no sense there.

card.rule: Make one State interface with a method per action, one class per state, and have the machine delegate instead of branching.
card.limits: The three steps are quick to state; the real work is deciding what each state does for every action. An action that matters in one state only still needs a reply from all the others.

concepts.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes
concepts.title: One interface, a class per state
concepts.question: What does each state class provide, and what does it need from the machine?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each action must be answered differently depending on the state, and the machine must be able to call any state without checking which one it holds.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Every state class implements all four actions of the interface and answers for its own state. The sold-out state refuses a quarter with a message; the no-quarter state accepts the same call. It also has a toString that names the state.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The same method name means different behavior in different classes, so a method read alone can mislead. A state that mostly refuses still has a method for every action.

card.rule: Each state class implements every action of the State interface, answering correctly for its own state.
card.limits: A method name means nothing without its class: insertQuarter in one state and in another are different behavior. Reading a single method in isolation can mislead.

concepts.title: How a state moves the machine on
concepts.question: How does a state class change the machine's state, and how does it learn which state comes next?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some moves depend on run-time data: after the sold state dispenses, the next state is No Quarter or Sold Out depending on the gumball count.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A state class does the part of the first version that belongs to its state. When the machine should move on, it asks the machine to set the current state to the next state object, which it gets through a getter on the machine instead of naming a concrete class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: States choose their successors, so they come to depend on one another. Getters on the machine soften the coupling but do not remove it.

card.rule: A state class answers an action for its own state and, when the machine should move on, sets the machine's current state to the next state object.
card.limits: Because states choose the next state, they come to depend on one another. Fetching state objects through the machine's getters softens this, but does not remove it.

concepts.title: The machine just forwards
concepts.question: How does the reworked machine replace its integer state and its branches?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The machine's integer state and its branches are what made the first version hard to change.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The machine holds one object per state and a variable for the current one. Each action method forwards the same action to that object, so the class of the current state decides what happens.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Branching is replaced by polymorphism. One wrinkle: an unsuccessful crank turn still calls dispense. The state refuses it, so nothing breaks, but the call is unnecessary.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, the method tested a number. After, it forwards the call.

card.rule: The context holds one object per state and a variable for the current one, and each action method calls the same action on that object.
card.limits: Forwarding looks the same whatever the state, so the cost shows up elsewhere: extra calls such as dispense after a failed crank turn are harmless only because the states refuse them.

concepts.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...
concepts.title: Same behavior, new structure
concepts.question: What did the rework change, what did it keep, and which gains do the authors claim?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: After a long rework, the authors check that it paid off. Customers must see no change, and the code must be easier to work with.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Refactor by changing structure and keeping behavior. The reworked machine is structurally quite different from the first but functionally the same.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Gains the authors list: each state's behavior is localized in its own class, the troublesome if statements are gone, and the structure maps more closely to the state diagram, so it reads more easily. The price is more classes.

card.rule: A good refactoring keeps behavior and changes structure so that behavior is localized, branching shrinks and extension is easy.
card.limits: The gains are the authors' claims for this redesign, and the price is more classes. Easier to read is a judgment: someone used to the first version may disagree.

concepts.title: The State Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the State Pattern's definition say an object can do?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An object's behavior has to follow its internal state without a tangle of conditionals in the object.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The State Pattern allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object is the Context; the classes behind it are ConcreteStates. The Context delegates to the current state object, which is replaced over time.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The same request gets different answers at different moments: a quarter is accepted in the no-quarter state and rejected in the has-quarter state.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: A behavior is picked from outside and kept for life; that is the situation Strategy covers.

card.rule: The State Pattern lets a context change its behavior by delegating to a current state object that is replaced as its internal state changes.
card.limits: The pattern suits behavior that changes along with the object's own state. A behavior picked from outside and kept for life is another situation, the one Strategy covers.

concepts.title: Appearing to change class
concepts.question: What does it mean that an object appears to change its class, and what produces the appearance?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A client that sees an object change its behavior completely may conclude that the object has become something else.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The definition says the object appears to change its class. In reality the Context uses composition and references a different state object; its own class stays the same.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Clients usually know little about the state objects, so the swap stays out of their sight. The class change is only an appearance, seen by someone who watches behavior.

card.rule: A client sees one object whose behavior changes; the change comes from swapping referenced state objects, not from changing a class.
card.limits: The class change is only an appearance, visible to a client that watches behavior. The context's real class stays the same throughout.

concepts.title: Same diagram, different intent
concepts.question: The State and Strategy patterns have the same class diagram; how do they differ?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The State and Strategy patterns have essentially the same class diagram, so a picture cannot tell them apart.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: They differ in intent. In State, behaviors sit in state objects and the current one changes over time to reflect the context's internal state. In Strategy the client usually specifies the strategy object the context is composed with.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Strategy can change its object at run time, but often one strategy suits a given context. State moves along well-defined transitions, built into how it works. Real code can sit between the two.

card.rule: Same structure, different intent: in Strategy the client configures the behavior, in State the context moves itself through states.
card.limits: Because the diagrams match, only the intent tells the patterns apart: who picks the object and why. A picture alone cannot name the pattern, and real code can sit between the two.

concepts.title: What each pattern replaces
concepts.question: What problem does each pattern solve, and when would you reach for each?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Inheritance fixes behavior when an object is created. Conditionals on internal state grow large and hard to maintain.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Strategy is a flexible alternative to subclassing: change behavior by composing with a different object. State is an alternative to lots of conditionals in the context: change the state object to change behavior.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Without separate objects, a program with a lot of state ends up with very large conditionals that are hard to understand. Both patterns rest on composition and delegation, so they overlap.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Behavior never needs to change and no conditionals are piling up; neither pattern is called for.

card.rule: Reach for Strategy when inheritance locks a behavior in place, and for State when conditionals on internal state pile up.
card.limits: Both rest on composition and delegation, so they overlap. If behavior never needs to change and no conditionals are piling up, neither is called for.

concepts.title: Who decides the transitions
concepts.question: Where should state transitions live, and what separates reasonable positions?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Someone has to decide which state comes next. The gumball states decide, because the choice depends on the gumball count at run time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The alternative is to let the Context decide the flow. The authors' guideline: fixed transitions suit the Context; more dynamic ones usually go in the state classes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The choice decides which classes stay closed to modification as the system evolves. It is a guideline, so two designers can defend different placements; the useful move is to state the issue and weigh reasons.

card.rule: Put fixed transitions in the context and dynamic ones in the states, and weigh the dependencies that each choice creates.
card.limits: The authors give a guideline, not a rule, and leave the choice open. Two designers can defend different placements, so the useful move is to state the issue and give reasons.

concepts.title: Clients, and sharing the states
concepts.question: Who talks to the state objects, and when can several contexts share them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An application may create many contexts, and a full set of state objects for each is wasteful.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Clients do not talk to the states; every request to a state comes from the Context. Many contexts can share state objects, typically kept in static variables, if the states keep no internal context of their own.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Sharing fails if a state remembers anything about one context. What varies per context must stay in the context and reach the state through a reference passed in.

card.rule: Clients talk only to the context, and state objects can be shared among contexts if they keep no context data of their own.
card.limits: Sharing fails when a state remembers anything about one particular context. Whatever varies per context, such as a count, must stay in the context and be reached through the reference passed in.

concepts.title: The price of more classes
concepts.question: Is the larger number of classes worth it, and how do the authors answer the objection?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each state becomes a class, so the design has many more classes than the first version had.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors grant the objection: more classes are often the price of flexibility. They advise building with them unless the code is a one-off you will throw away, and they point out that the extra classes can be hidden from clients.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The alternative is very large conditionals. Objects make the states explicit and cut the effort to understand and maintain the code. The advice rests on a prediction that the code will change.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The code is a throwaway demo that will never gain states.

card.rule: Accept the extra classes when the code will live and change, and keep them out of the clients' sight.
card.limits: For a throwaway one-off the authors accept that the extra classes may not pay back. The advice also rests on a prediction that the code will change, which could turn out wrong.

concepts.title: Interface or abstract class
concepts.question: When would the State type be an abstract class instead of an interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The pattern's diagram shows State as an abstract class, but the gumball machine used an interface. States may repeat the same replies.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use an interface while the states share no code, as in the gumball machine. Consider an abstract State class when states repeat default behavior, or when methods may be added later.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: An abstract class lets you add methods without breaking the concrete states. Generic inherited replies are acceptable because the authors reason that customers will not see those error messages.

card.rule: Use an interface while states share no code, and an abstract State class when they repeat default behavior or methods may be added later.
card.limits: The gumball machine had nothing to share, so the interface was enough; the abstract class is something the authors suggest considering, not something they built.

concepts.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game
concepts.title: Adding the contest as a new state
concepts.question: How does the 1-in-10 game fit into the state design, and what does that show?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The contest needs a second gumball released one time in ten. In the conditional design that meant a tangle of edits.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Add a WinnerState class, almost the same as the sold state but dispensing two gumballs, and a state variable for it on the machine. Put the random draw and the transition to winning in the has-quarter state, where the crank is turned.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors call the change simple and say the design is paying off. It is small, not absent: the has-quarter state is edited.

card.rule: To add behavior to a state-based design, add a state class and change the transitions that lead into it.
card.limits: The change is small, not absent: the machine gains a new state variable, and the has-quarter state is edited. Changes that affect every state, such as a new action, still touch every class.

concepts.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.
concepts.title: One state class or two
concepts.question: Should the winner behavior be its own state or part of the sold state, and how is such a trade-off judged?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The sold and winner states are almost identical: the winner dispenses two gumballs instead of one. Two considerations pull in opposite directions.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Keeping them as two classes avoids one class standing for two states and keeps each class to one responsibility. Merging them removes duplicated code. The authors call the choice a design decision.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Merging sacrifices clarity and gives the sold state two responsibilities. The authors ask what happens when the promotion ends or the stakes change.

card.rule: Treat one state class or two as a trade-off between duplicated code and a class with two responsibilities, and decide with reasons.
card.limits: The authors do not name a winner. Their two considerations, clarity and single responsibility, favor a separate class, but they leave it as a design decision for the situation.

concepts.title: Adding an action: refill
concepts.question: How does the refill action get added to the state design?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A sold-out machine can do nothing until someone refills it, so the design needs a new action, refill, that takes the number of gumballs added.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Add refill to the State interface; every state implements it. The machine's refill adds to the count and then calls the current state's refill. Only in the sold-out state does that move the machine to No Quarter.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Data lives in the context and the decision lives in the state. In the other states refill does nothing. Another design might refuse with a message or reject a refill mid-sale.

card.rule: A new action goes into the State interface and every state answers it, while the context updates its data and then delegates.
card.limits: The authors' version leaves refill as a quiet no-op outside the sold-out state. Another design might refuse with a message, or reject a refill when the machine is mid-sale.

concepts.title: A monitor that reports on machines
concepts.question: What does the first gumball report need, and where does each piece of its data come from?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The CEO wants a printed status report for each gumball machine. The machine already offers a gumball count and a current state, so the only missing piece is a location to tell machines apart. The team wants a very fast turnaround.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Add a location field to GumballMachine. Write a separate GumballMonitor class that is handed a machine, asks it for location, inventory and state, and prints them as a report. Reporting stays out of the machine class.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Quick to write and easy to read. The monitor holds an ordinary reference to its machine, so the design is only as wide as one running program. The next page shows where that stops working.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A fresh case: the report logic lives in its own class and reads the kiln only through its methods.

card.rule: Keep reporting in a separate monitor class that is given a machine and reads it through the machine's existing methods.
card.limits: This design relies on the monitor holding an ordinary reference to the machine, so it works only while both live in the same running program.

concepts.title: Right code, wrong place
concepts.question: Why does a correct monitor still fail to satisfy the CEO, and what does Joe propose to keep the code?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The first monitor works in testing, but the CEO wants to sit at his desk and watch machines remotely. The monitor runs in the same JVM as the machine, so it cannot see machines elsewhere. The team would like to keep the code that already works.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Joe proposes leaving GumballMonitor as it is and handing it a proxy: a stand-in for a real object. It acts like a gumball machine but, behind the scenes, talks over the network to the real, remote machine. A JVM is one running Java environment with its own memory.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The reporting code is kept instead of rewritten. The proxy itself still has to be built, and Frank doubts that will be easy. The rest of the chapter does that building.

card.rule: When working code is in the wrong place, keep it and give it a stand-in for the distant object.
card.limits: A stand-in saves rewriting only when the existing code uses just the methods the stand-in can offer; code that reaches inside the object still needs changes.

concepts.title: The remote proxy
concepts.question: What is a remote proxy, and what do 'remote object' and 'local representative' mean in that definition?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A client wants to call methods on an object that lives in a different address space, such as another JVM's heap, yet the developer wants to write only ordinary local calls.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A remote proxy is a local representative of the remote object. The client calls local methods on it; the proxy forwards each call to the real object and hands back the answer. The low-level details of network communication are the proxy's business, not the client's.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Client code stays short and free of networking detail. The proxy exists only because the real object is elsewhere, and the calls it makes still travel over a network.

card.rule: A remote proxy is a local object that forwards each call to an object in another JVM.
card.limits: The idea applies only when the real object lives in another address space; a stand-in for an object in the same JVM is not a remote proxy.

concepts.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
concepts.title: Why a reference cannot cross heaps
concepts.question: Why can't a program hold a variable referring to an object in another heap, and what does Java offer instead?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A variable such as Duck d can refer only to an object in the same heap as the code running the statement. A client therefore cannot simply grab a reference to an object living in another JVM.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use Java's Remote Method Invocation, RMI. It gives a way to find objects in a remote JVM and to invoke their methods, which the missing direct reference cannot do. A proxy built on RMI takes the place of that reference.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The remote object is reached by a call across the network, not brought into the caller's heap. The authors first take a detour to learn RMI before applying it to the gumball machine.

card.rule: A reference works only within one heap; to reach beyond it, use a mechanism such as RMI that finds and calls remote objects.
card.limits: RMI finds and calls remote objects, but the call still crosses a network; it does not bring the remote object into your heap.

concepts.title: Client helper and service helper
concepts.question: How do two helper objects let a client call a remote service as if it were local?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The client should call a remote service as if it were local, with the developer writing as little code as possible. The real method logic, however, lives on the server.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Two helpers do the communicating. The client helper has the service's method but none of its logic: it sends the method name and arguments to the server and waits. The service helper receives the request through a socket, unpacks it and calls the real method on the real service.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each side believes it is making or receiving an ordinary call. The price is two extra objects, plus packing and shipping on every call.

card.rule: The client calls a look-alike helper that ships the call to a second helper, which makes a plain local call on the real service.
card.limits: The client helper holds no service logic, so it can only forward; if the server is unreachable it has nothing of its own to answer with.

concepts.title: One remote call, six steps
concepts.question: In what order does a remote call travel from the client object to the service object and back?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A call must reach the service object and its result must return, all without the client object noticing the trip.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Six steps. The client calls the method on the client helper. The helper packages the call and ships it over the network. The service helper unpacks it and invokes the real method. The service returns a result to its helper, which packages and ships it back. The client helper unpackages it and returns it to the client.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: To the client object the whole trip is transparent. It is one round trip that uses the network in both directions and passes through several hand-offs.

card.rule: A remote call is a round trip: call, package, ship, unpack, run, package, ship, unpack, return.
card.limits: The six steps describe one successful round trip; they do not say what happens when the network fails part way.

concepts.title: What RMI builds for you
concepts.question: What does RMI build for you, and what are the client and service helpers called in RMI?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Writing both helper objects and all the networking and I/O code by hand for every service would be a lot of work.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: RMI builds the client and service helpers for you, including a client helper with the same methods as the remote service, and supplies a lookup service for finding remote objects. In RMI's own words, the client helper is a stub and the service helper is a skeleton.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: You call remote methods like normal ones and write no network code. The network itself does not go away, so remote calls can still fail.

card.rule: RMI generates the stub, the skeleton and a lookup service, so you write ordinary calls instead of network code.
card.limits: RMI removes the networking code, not the network: calls still travel over a wire and can fail.

concepts.title: A call that looks local can fail
concepts.question: Should a remote call be fully transparent to the client, and what must the client still acknowledge?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A remote call looks local to the client, but the client helper sends it across the network. Networking and I/O are risky: they can fail and throw exceptions all over the place.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Make the risk visible instead of hiding it. The client must acknowledge it by handling or declaring the remote exceptions, rather than treating the call as plain local code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The call is less seamless than first hoped but honest about the network. The authors ask whether remote calls should be totally transparent; this card's answer is that the call looks local yet is not.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Our reading: a client that calls a proxy with no thought for failure treats the proxy's look as the whole truth about the call.

card.rule: A remote call looks local but is not; the client must acknowledge that it can fail.
card.limits: Acknowledging the risk means handling or declaring the failure; it does not mean the failure can be predicted or prevented.

concepts.title: The remote interface
concepts.question: What three rules must a remote interface follow so that RMI can use it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The client needs one type to call the service through, RMI must recognise the methods as remote, and every call crosses a network where things can fail and data must be shipped.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Step one: a remote interface. It extends java.rmi.Remote, a marker interface with no methods. Every method declares RemoteException. Arguments and return values are primitives or Serializable; strings, arrays, collections and most API types already qualify, and your own types must implement Serializable. The stub and the real service both implement it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Clients are typed against the interface and never see the implementation. Each custom type in a signature must be made Serializable by you.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Marking a local interface as remote-ready.

card.rule: A remote interface extends Remote, declares RemoteException on every method, and uses only primitive or Serializable types.
card.limits: Remote is a marker: extending it adds no behaviour, only meaning for RMI, and the interface declares what clients may call, not how.

concepts.title: The remote implementation
concepts.question: What must the class that does the real work do to be usable as a remote service?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The class that does the real work must also take on the machinery of being a remote object.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Step two: implement the remote interface and extend UnicastRemoteObject from java.rmi.server, the simplest way to get that machinery. Add a no-arg constructor that declares RemoteException, because the superclass constructor throws it and every superclass constructor runs when a class is instantiated.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Little code is needed beyond the real logic. The constructor can look pointless since it does nothing, yet it is required to carry the declaration.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A remote implementation of the Probe interface.

card.rule: A remote implementation implements the remote interface, extends UnicastRemoteObject and declares RemoteException on its constructor.
card.limits: Extending UnicastRemoteObject is described as the simplest way, not the only way; the constructor rule follows from the superclass constructor throwing.

concepts.title: Registry first, then the service
concepts.question: What does the rmiregistry do, and in what order are the pieces of a remote service started?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Clients must be able to find the service by name, and the service must offer itself to them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Step three: start rmiregistry from a directory that can reach your classes. Think of it as the white pages of a phone book, where a client goes to get the proxy. Step four: start the service, which instantiates itself and registers with the static rebind() method of Naming.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Registering needs a running registry, so the order is fixed: registry first, then service. Once registered, clients can look the service up by name.

card.rule: Start the registry before the service, then register the service by name so clients can find it.
card.limits: The order is fixed by the registration line needing a running registry; the registry only helps once the service has registered.

concepts.section: How does the client get the stub object?
concepts.title: Getting the stub
concepts.question: How does the client obtain the stub it will actually call?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The client needs the stub, since that is the object it calls methods on, but it does not have one yet.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The client asks the registry for a stub by name, like looking in the white pages. Naming.lookup takes an address and a name, such as rmi://127.0.0.1/RemoteHello. The client then invokes methods on the returned stub as if it were the real service.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Client code is one lookup followed by ordinary calls. The lookup yields something only when a service registered that name.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Looking up a stub for the Probe service and using it.
blocks.code:
