Probe p = (Probe) Naming.lookup("rmi://127.0.0.1/Probe");
double t = p.read("A");

card.rule: Look up a name in the registry to get the stub, then call the stub as if it were the service.
card.limits: Lookup returns something only if the service registered that name; over the Internet the notes say some kind of locator service would be needed.

concepts.section: How does the client get the stub object?
concepts.title: Two common RMI mistakes
concepts.question: Which two mistakes do programmers most often make with RMI, and when does each show up?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two slips catch RMI beginners. Neither is hard to avoid, but one of them gives no warning before the program runs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Mistake one: starting the remote service before the rmiregistry, so rebind() finds no registry. Mistake two: leaving an argument or return type non-serializable, which the compiler does not detect.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The first shows when the service starts, the second when a real call is made. Plan for both: registry first, and every remote type Serializable.

card.rule: Start the registry first, and make every remote argument and return type serializable.
card.limits: These are the two mistakes the book names; it does not claim they are the only ones.

concepts.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
concepts.title: Making GumballMachine a service
concepts.question: Which three things must be done to turn GumballMachine into a service that remote clients can call?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: GumballMachine already works locally. It should become a remote service without being redesigned.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Three tasks. Create a remote interface for the machine, giving a set of methods that can be called remotely. Make sure all the return types in that interface are serializable. Implement the interface in a concrete class. The machine itself needs only a couple of additions, as in the RMI detour.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The existing class is reused. After these steps the machine can receive calls, but no client can find it until it is started and registered.

card.rule: Give the existing object a remote interface, make its return types serializable, and implement the interface in the existing class.
card.limits: These steps prepare the machine to receive calls; no client can find it until it is started and registered.

concepts.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
concepts.title: Serializing drags references along
concepts.question: Why is making State Serializable not enough, and what extra problem does its reference to the machine cause?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: getState() returns a State, so State must be Serializable. But each State object keeps a reference to a gumball machine, so it can call the machine's methods and change its state.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Serialization follows references. Serialized as it is, a State would drag the machine it points to along and transfer it too. The authors do not want the entire machine sent with the State, and they say an easy fix exists in the code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Making a type Serializable is a decision about everything it points to. This card names the problem only; the fix is left to the book's code.

card.rule: Before marking a type Serializable, check what it points to, because shipping it can ship them too.
card.limits: The concern is the references the object holds; this card claims only the problem, and the fix is left to the book's code.

concepts.title: Registering the machine
concepts.question: What must a finished gumball machine service do before the monitor can find it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A finished service cannot be reached until clients can locate it, and the CEO's monitor needs more than one machine to find.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Register each machine with the RMI registry as it starts, then run several machines with the new code. The authors add this start-up code to the test drive.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Registered machines can be looked up by name. Registration needs the registry to be running and does not look anything up for the client.

card.rule: A finished service is invisible until it is registered with the registry.
card.limits: Registration only makes lookup possible; a client still has to look up the stub, and the registry must be running.

concepts.title: Reusing the monitor with proxies
concepts.question: How does the original GumballMonitor keep working when the machines are remote?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The CEO wants to monitor many machines, but the authors want to reuse GumballMonitor instead of rewriting it for a network.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Make a few changes and let the test drive get proxies to the remote machines. The monitor calls methods on a proxy, which makes a remote call across the wire and returns a String, an integer and a State object.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Because it uses a proxy, the monitor does not know or care that calls are remote, apart from having to worry about remote exceptions. The reporting code keeps its shape.

card.rule: Hand the unchanged client proxies instead of local objects, and let it deal with remote exceptions.
card.limits: The monitor ignores where its machines live, but not that a call can fail; the book also says a few changes were still needed.

concepts.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
concepts.title: Following one request
concepts.question: What happens, step by step, when the CEO's monitor asks a remote machine for its state?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To understand why the demo works, follow one request and see which object does what on the way.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The monitor gets proxies to the remote machines and calls getState(), along with getCount() and getLocation(). The proxy forwards the call to the remote service. The skeleton receives it and passes it to the gumball machine. The machine returns the state to the skeleton, which serializes it and sends it back; the proxy deserializes it and returns an object to the monitor.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The monitor sees an ordinary return value. All of the transport work happens in the two helpers between the monitor and the machine.

card.rule: Proxy forwards, skeleton delivers, the machine answers, the skeleton serializes, the proxy deserializes.
card.limits: The walk-through follows getState(); the calls to getCount() and getLocation() take the same path.

concepts.title: The Proxy Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the Proxy Pattern provide, and what does it mean for a proxy to control access?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A client sometimes cannot or should not reach an object directly: it may be remote, expensive to create, or in need of securing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Proxy Pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it. The authors also call the proxy a representative. In the gumball case, the proxy controlled access by handling the network details the monitor could not.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The variations of the pattern mostly differ in the way the proxy controls access. Control of access does not have to mean refusing a request.

card.rule: A proxy is a representative of another object that controls access to it, whether by hiding the network, delaying creation or checking rights.
card.limits: Control of access does not always mean refusing a request; in the gumball case it meant making a remote object reachable.

concepts.title: Subject, RealSubject and Proxy
concepts.question: How do the Subject, the RealSubject and the Proxy relate in the pattern's structure?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A client coded against one type should be able to use either the real object or its stand-in without change.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Subject is the interface for both. RealSubject does the real work. Proxy implements Subject, holds a reference to the RealSubject and controls access to it; clients reach the RealSubject through the Proxy, which may also create and destroy it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Because both implement Subject, the Proxy can be substituted for the RealSubject anywhere it occurs. The price is one more class and one more hop for every call.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A guard stands in for file-based lab results behind the same interface.

card.rule: The Proxy and the RealSubject implement the same Subject interface, and the Proxy holds a reference to the RealSubject.
card.limits: Substitution works through the shared interface; a stand-in without the Subject interface cannot be dropped in.

concepts.title: Three ways to control access
concepts.question: Which three ways of controlling access does the chapter name, and what does each guard?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: What a proxy has to control differs from case to case: distance, cost of creation, or who may call what.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Variations revolve around the way the proxy controls access. A remote proxy controls access to a remote object. A virtual proxy controls access to a resource that is expensive to create. A protection proxy controls access to a resource based on access rights.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Choose the variant by what is being guarded. The remote proxy is only one implementation of the general pattern, and the three named here are not the whole family.

card.rule: Pick the proxy by what it guards: a remote object, an expensive resource or a resource needing rights.
card.limits: The three named forms are not a closed list; the book mentions further variants such as caching proxies.

concepts.title: The virtual proxy
concepts.question: How does a virtual proxy treat an object that is expensive to create, before and after it exists?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some objects are expensive to create, yet the client may need something to work with before the object is ready, or may never need it at all.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A virtual proxy represents an object that may be expensive to create. It often defers creation until the object is needed, and acts as its surrogate before and while it is being created. After that it delegates requests directly to the real subject.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Start-up stays cheap and an unneeded object is never built. The proxy behaves differently before and after the real object exists, so it must know which phase it is in.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A planner proxy builds the slow planner only when a route is first asked for.

card.rule: A virtual proxy stands in until the costly object is needed, creates it then, and afterwards passes requests straight through.
card.limits: A virtual proxy hides the cost of creation but does not remove it: the real object must still be built when it is needed.

concepts.title: Waiting for a CD cover
concepts.question: What must a CD cover viewer show while an image downloads, and why does a virtual proxy fit?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A viewer lists CD titles and fetches each cover from an online service. Retrieval time depends on network load and bandwidth, yet the application must show something meanwhile and must not hang while it waits.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Put a virtual proxy in place of the Icon. It manages the loading in the background and shows the message Loading CD cover, please wait... until the image has arrived. Then the proxy delegates the display to the real icon.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The interface stays responsive and tells the user what is happening. The wait itself is not made shorter.

card.rule: When something slow must appear on screen, put a proxy in its place that shows a message and loads it in the background.
card.limits: The proxy hides the wait but does not shorten it; the real image still has to arrive before it can be shown.

concepts.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
concepts.title: How ImageProxy works
concepts.question: What are the four steps ImageProxy follows from the first request to a new image?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: ImageProxy must show something while an image downloads, show the image once it has arrived, and cope with the user choosing another cover.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: One: create an ImageIcon and start loading it from a network URL. Two: while the bytes arrive, display the loading message. Three: when loading is complete, delegate all method calls, including paintIcon(), getWidth() and getHeight(), to the icon. Four: for a new image, create a new proxy and begin again.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each proxy serves a single image and changes behaviour once, at the moment loading completes. A new request means a new proxy rather than reuse of the old.

card.rule: Start loading, show a message, delegate every call when loaded, and start over with a new proxy for a new image.
card.limits: The four steps describe one proxy's life; a new request does not reuse the old proxy.

concepts.title: Conditionals inside ImageProxy
concepts.question: What weakness do the conditionals in ImageProxy reveal, and how would the State Pattern address it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: ImageProxy has two situations, image loaded and not loaded, and conditional statements choose between them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors' Design Puzzle suggests the State Pattern. Create two states, ImageNotLoaded and ImageLoaded, and move the code from the if statements into them. The proxy begins in ImageNotLoaded and moves to ImageLoaded once the ImageIcon has been retrieved.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The conditionals leave the proxy and live in the states. The book offers this as a possible clean-up, not as a repair of something broken.

card.rule: When one internal condition is tested in several methods, consider moving each condition's behaviour into a state.
card.limits: The puzzle offers a possible clean-up; the version with conditionals still works, and the book does not call it wrong.

concepts.title: Running the viewer
concepts.question: What happens from the first paint to the moment the real image appears?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Loading must not freeze the window, yet the real image has to replace the message once it has arrived.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: On the first paintIcon(), ImageProxy fires off a thread that retrieves the image and creates the ImageIcon. After the icon is created, the next paintIcon() delegates to it, so the image takes the place of the message.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The window stays usable while loading; the authors suggest resizing it to see this. The image appears at the next paint after loading ends, not at the instant it arrives.

card.rule: The first paint starts a background load; the first paint after it finishes shows the real image.
card.limits: The image shows at the next paint after the load completes, not at the instant of arrival.

concepts.title: Proxy or Decorator?
concepts.question: How do Proxy and Decorator differ when both wrap an object and forward calls?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Proxy and Decorator can look very similar: both wrap an object and share its interface.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Judge them by purpose. A decorator adds behavior to a class; a proxy controls access to it. ImageProxy's loading message looks like added behavior, but its more important job is decoupling the client from the ImageIcon, so the client need not wait for each image before painting.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Structure alone cannot settle which you have. Saying that a proxy wraps its subject is also inexact: a remote proxy's subject is on another machine, and a virtual proxy's subject may not exist yet.

card.rule: Ask the intent of the wrapper: if it adds behaviour it is a Decorator, and if it controls access it is a Proxy.
card.limits: Structure alone cannot tell them apart, since both implement the same interface and forward calls; only the purpose does.

concepts.title: Proxy, Adapter, Decorator and Facade
concepts.question: How do Proxy, Adapter, Decorator and Facade differ in what they do to the objects they wrap?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Adapter, Decorator, Facade and Proxy all sit in front of other objects and forward requests, so they are easy to mix up.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A proxy implements the same interface and controls access. A decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior. An adapter changes the interface of the object it adapts. A facade wraps a bunch of objects to simplify their interface.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A protection proxy that offers only part of an interface to a role can resemble an adapter. To make clients use a proxy, a factory can wrap the subject before returning it.

card.rule: Same interface and access control is Proxy; different interface is Adapter; added behaviour is Decorator; simplified interface is Facade.
card.limits: A protection proxy offering only part of an interface can resemble an adapter, so purpose, not shape, has to settle it.

concepts.section: Using the Java API’s Proxy to create a protection proxy
concepts.title: Java's dynamic proxy
concepts.question: What is a dynamic proxy, and where does the code that says what the proxy does belong?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Java creates the proxy class for you, so you cannot put the access logic inside that class as the classic pattern does.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The java.lang.reflect package creates a proxy class on the fly that implements one or more interfaces. Its behaviour goes in an InvocationHandler: the object the proxy asks to do the real work after receiving a call. Because the class is made at runtime, this is a dynamic proxy.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The generated class carries none of your logic. The class diagram differs slightly from the classic one, since the handler, not the proxy, holds the behavior.

card.rule: A dynamic proxy is a class that Java makes at runtime, and its behaviour is supplied by an InvocationHandler you write.
card.limits: The generated proxy holds none of your logic, so everything the proxy should do must live in the handler.

concepts.title: The protection proxy
concepts.question: What is a protection proxy, and which access rules does the matchmaking service need?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the matchmaking service any client can call any PersonBean method. A customer could rate himself or change another customer's data.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A protection proxy controls access to an object based on access rights. Owners may set their own information but not their own Hot or Not rating. Other customers may set the rating but nothing else. Anyone may call the getters, since they return nothing private.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Rights depend on who is calling and which method is called. One rule for every caller cannot work, so more than one proxy is needed.

card.rule: A protection proxy lets each caller reach only the methods their role allows.
card.limits: The rules concern who is calling and which method, not the values passed; a proxy decides by role.

concepts.section: Big Picture: creating a Dynamic Proxy for the PersonBean
concepts.title: One bean, two proxies
concepts.question: How many proxies does the matchmaking service need, and which three steps build them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Customers must not change their own Hot or Not rating, and must not change other customers' personal information. A single rule set cannot satisfy both.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Create two proxies: one for access to your own PersonBean and one for access to another customer's. Steps: create two InvocationHandlers, write the code that creates the dynamic proxies, and wrap any PersonBean in the appropriate proxy. Using your own bean makes you the owner; looking at someone else's makes you a non-owner.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Java builds the proxies and you supply the handlers. Each relationship's rules sit in one place, but something must choose the right proxy for each situation.

card.rule: Make one proxy for the owner and another for the non-owner, and wrap the bean in whichever fits the situation.
card.limits: Which proxy applies depends on who is looking at whom; the same bean may need either one at different moments.

concepts.title: How a handler decides
concepts.question: How does a call on the proxy reach the handler, and how does the handler decide what to do?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Java's generated proxy has no logic of its own, yet something must decide, call by call, what is allowed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The InvocationHandler interface has a single method, invoke(). Whatever method is called on the proxy, invoke() is what the proxy calls on the handler. It usually examines the method's name and perhaps its arguments, then forwards the call or throws IllegalAccessException. The non-owner handler lets get methods and setHotOrNotRating through.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: All access rules sit in one method. Our reading: because the decision rests on method names, a method named off the convention would be judged by the wrong rule.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: A guest handler for a document proxy lets view methods through and refuses the rest.

card.rule: Every call on the proxy arrives at invoke(), which looks at the method name and either passes the call on or refuses it.
card.limits: The handler decides only from what the call reveals, such as method name and arguments; it does not know who the caller is unless it was built with that information.

concepts.section: Step two: creating the Proxy class and instantiating the Proxy object
concepts.title: Creating the proxy
concepts.question: What does Java need to create a proxy for a PersonBean, and why is it called dynamic?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With a handler written, you still need an object that implements the bean's interfaces and routes every call to it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Proxy.newProxyInstance takes three things: the class loader of the person's class, the interfaces of that class, and a new handler given the person. Cast the result to PersonBean. The non-owner method has the same shape with the non-owner handler.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A few lines produce a protected object. The proxy is dynamic because its class is created at runtime from the interfaces you pass; before the code runs there is no proxy class.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Protecting a thermostat with the same three arguments.

card.rule: Proxy.newProxyInstance takes a class loader, the interfaces to implement and a handler, and returns an object you can use as any of those interfaces.
card.limits: Dynamic refers to the class being created at runtime, not to the instance being set up at runtime.

concepts.title: Dynamic proxy fine print
concepts.question: What restrictions apply to the interfaces passed to newProxyInstance, and how can you tell a proxy class?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Dynamic proxies have restrictions that appear when you pass unusual input.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Proxy.isProxyClass() answers whether a class is a dynamic proxy class; otherwise the proxy acts like any class implementing those interfaces. newProxyInstance takes an array of interfaces only, no classes. Non-public interfaces must all come from one package, and two interfaces may not have methods with the same signature.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: These are the major restrictions; the book sends you to the javadoc for further nuances. Check them before relying on an unusual combination.

card.rule: Pass only interfaces, keep non-public ones in one package, and avoid interfaces with clashing methods.
card.limits: The restrictions listed here are the major ones; the book points to the javadoc for further nuances.

concepts.title: A family still growing
concepts.question: What do the Proxy Zoo and the toolbox suggest about the list of proxies and about its costs?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A pattern learned from three examples can mislead you into thinking those three are all there is.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Proxy Zoo shows many mutations of the pattern and asks readers to catalogue more they meet. The toolbox adds caching, synchronization, firewall and copy-on-write proxies to the three studied.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Like any wrapper, proxies increase the number of classes and objects in a design. Their control of access has to be worth that price.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: when the client can reach the object directly and nothing needs controlling, a proxy only adds classes.

card.rule: Treat the three named proxies as examples of an open family, and weigh each proxy against the classes and objects it adds.
card.limits: The book states the cost in one line and gives no measure, so claim no more than that proxies add classes and objects.

concepts.title: Patterns working together
concepts.question: How can several patterns live in one design, and what does that look like?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A design meets several separate needs at once: a class that does not fit, a feature to add, a group to manage. No single pattern answers all of them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Meet each need with the pattern that fits it and let the patterns sit side by side. In the rebuilt duck simulator each new request got its own pattern, and the earlier patterns kept working.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each part answers one request and stays small. The authors add a caution: patterns are used where and when they make sense, and parts of the simulator may be overkill.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: One ordinary class with clear methods already solves the problem. According to the authors, good object-oriented design principles can be enough on their own.

card.rule: Several patterns can share one design, each solving its own part of the problem.
card.limits: Using many patterns is a means, not a goal. A pattern earns its place only when it answers a real need in the design.

concepts.title: Compound pattern or plain combination
concepts.question: What turns a group of patterns used together into a compound pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Patterns often appear together, so the words need a boundary. A design built for one scenario differs from a combination that has proved useful across many designs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A compound pattern combines two or more patterns into a solution to a recurring or general problem. The duck simulator is only patterns working together; Model-View-Controller is the authors' real compound pattern.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Naming the combination lets people reuse it and talk about it as one thing. Our reading: the count of patterns does not decide it; how general the problem is does.

card.rule: A compound pattern is a combination of patterns that solves a general, recurring problem.
card.limits: Generality, not size, decides. A combination of six patterns built for one app is not compound, and a pair that answers a widespread problem can be.

concepts.title: A common interface for the flock
concepts.question: Why does the rebuilt simulator start with a Quackable interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A simulator must treat mallards, duck calls and a rubber duck alike, yet each one sounds different. The patterns added later need one type they can all hold and wrap.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Give every quacker the same Quackable interface with a quack() method. Callers use the interface, and each class quacks in its own way. Every later pattern in the chapter works through this one shared type.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: New kinds of quacker plug in without changing the caller. Our reading: a class with an unrelated method set, such as the goose with honk(), does not fit until something adapts it.

card.rule: A shared interface lets different things be used alike while each behaves in its own way.
card.limits: A shared interface only covers what it declares. A class with an unrelated method set, like the goose, does not fit until something adapts it.

concepts.title: Adapting the goose
concepts.question: How can a goose that only honks join a simulator that expects Quackables?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The simulator expects Quackable, but a Goose honks and has no quack() method. We still want a goose wherever a duck can go.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Adapter Pattern: a goose adapter implements Quackable, holds a Goose, and turns each quack() call into a honk.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The simulator treats the wrapped goose as one more Quackable, and neither Goose nor the simulator changes. Our reading: the adapter only translates calls; it cannot give the goose abilities it lacks.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: the goose is wrapped once and can join any list of Quackables.

card.rule: An adapter implements the interface the client expects and translates each call into calls on the wrapped object.
card.limits: An adapter changes the shape of the call, not what the wrapped object can do. A goose still honks; it is only reached through quack().

concepts.title: Counting quacks with a decorator
concepts.question: How can we add quack counting without touching any duck class?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Quackologists want the total number of quacks made by a flock. Editing every duck class to count would be heavy and invasive.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Decorator Pattern: a QuackCounter implements Quackable, holds another Quackable, adds one to a count on quack(), and delegates the quack to what it wraps.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The duck code never changes. The counter only counts objects that it wraps, so a duck created without the wrapper is not counted.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: the counter wraps a duck, quacks through it, and keeps a count.

card.rule: A decorator wraps an object of the same interface, adds behavior around the call and delegates to the wrapped object.
card.limits: A decorator adds behavior only to the objects it wraps. Any duck created without the wrapper escapes the counting.

concepts.title: You must wrap to get the behavior
concepts.question: What goes wrong when decorated behavior depends on every object being wrapped?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Decorated behavior exists only if the object is wrapped. The wrapping code is scattered wherever ducks are created, so one forgotten wrap leaves uncounted quacks.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors localize creation and decoration in one place instead of trusting every creation site to remember the wrapper.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The weakness disappears once only one place creates ducks. Our reading: the weakness matters most where creation is spread over many places.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before: b is created without the wrapper, so only one quack is counted.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Several places build the same wrapped object by hand, and nothing stops a new place from skipping the wrapper.

card.rule: When behavior comes from wrapping, make sure the wrapping cannot be forgotten.
card.limits: This weakness matters where objects are created in many places. If one place creates every object, the wrapping can be put there once.

concepts.title: A factory that always wraps
concepts.question: How does a factory guarantee that every duck is created already wrapped?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The counter must never be forgotten, and the simulator should not know which kind of duck it is getting.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Abstract Factory Pattern: an AbstractDuckFactory declares a create method for each duck. DuckFactory makes plain ducks and CountingDuckFactory wraps each one in a QuackCounter. simulate() takes a factory and uses it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Passing a different factory gives a different product family through the same method, and counted ducks come from one place. A duck created directly with new bypasses the factory.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: the factory decides whether a duck is wrapped.

card.rule: Pass a factory into the code that makes objects, and the factory decides which family, wrapped or plain, is produced.
card.limits: A factory protects only objects it creates. Anything created directly with new, as the geese still were, bypasses it.

concepts.title: The geese the factory missed
concepts.question: What gap does the duck factory leave, and how might it be closed?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The duck factory covers ducks, but the simulator still creates geese by calling concrete classes directly, so they slip past the factory.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors ask for an Abstract Factory for geese that creates goose ducks, meaning geese already inside their adapter. They suggest adding createGooseDuck() to the existing duck factories, or building a separate factory for families of geese.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Both fixes close the gap, so everything that needs the treatment is created through a factory. Our reading: a separate factory fits better when the products are a very different family.

card.rule: A factory design is complete only if every object that needs its treatment is created through it.
card.limits: Extending a factory with new methods is sensible when the products are one family. A very different family may deserve its own factory.

concepts.title: A flock as a composite
concepts.question: How can a whole flock be treated like a single duck?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A ranger asks why ducks are managed one by one. We need to talk about collections of ducks, and sub-collections for families, and to apply an operation across the whole set.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Composite Pattern: a Flock implements Quackable and holds a list of Quackables. Its quack() passes the call to every member, and a member can itself be a flock, so flocks nest.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A client treats a flock like a single duck. Our reading: the pattern does not itself say in what order members are called.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: one call to the outer flock reaches the nested flock and its members.

card.rule: A composite implements the same interface as its parts and passes each call down to its children.
card.limits: The pattern says nothing about order or about who owns the children. Calling a method on a flock affects members only in the way the composite is written to pass it down.

concepts.title: Safety versus transparency
concepts.question: What does a composite gain and lose by keeping add() only on the composite?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the Composite chapter, menus and menu items shared every method, including add(), so a client did not need to know what it held. That also allowed meaningless calls, such as add() on a menu item.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Here the authors keep child-management methods off the leaves: only Flock has add(). Nobody can call add() on a Duck.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The design is safer, but less transparent: a client must know it holds a Flock to add to it. The authors say there are always trade-offs and you must weigh them in your own composites.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: add() exists only on Flock, so it is called on a variable typed Flock.

card.rule: Choosing which methods leaves share with composites trades safety against transparency.
card.limits: The authors do not call either choice the right one. The better choice depends on whether mistakes or uniform treatment hurt more in your design.

concepts.title: Letting Quackologists observe
concepts.question: How can the Quackologists be told every time a particular duck quacks?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Quackologists want to observe the behavior of individual ducks and be told each time one quacks, without polling the ducks.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Observer Pattern. An Observable is the object being observed, with methods to register and notify observers. Quackable extends this interface, and a Quackologist implements Observer and registers with the ducks. The authors leave out a removal method to keep it short.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each quack notifies all registered Quackologists. Our reading: an observer that has not registered hears nothing.

card.rule: An observable lets observers register, and tells all of them when something happens.
card.limits: Observers learn that a quack happened only if they registered. An unregistered Quackologist hears nothing.

concepts.title: Putting observer code in a helper
concepts.question: How do many Quackable classes become observable without repeating the registration code?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Every Quackable class could write its own registration and notification code, as in Chapter 2, which means the same code repeated many times.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Encapsulate the code in a helper class named Observable. Each Quackable is composed with an Observable and implements QuackObservable only by delegating to the helper.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The real code is written once. Because Quackable now extends QuackObservable, every class that implements Quackable must change, including the QuackCounter decorator.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: Mallard holds a helper and only delegates to it.

card.rule: Put shared observer code in one helper and have each class delegate to it.
card.limits: Delegating to a helper avoids duplicate code, but every class must still hold and call the helper, and a changed interface forces every implementer to follow.

concepts.title: Observing a whole flock
concepts.question: What does it mean to register an observer with a composite flock?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A Quackologist may want to observe an entire flock, which holds ducks and other flocks. Registering with every duck by hand would be tedious.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Two patterns on one request. If you observe a composite, you observe everything in it, so when you register with a flock, the flock makes sure you are registered with all its children, nested flocks included.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Any quack by any member notifies you, and your code looks the same as for a single duck. Our reading: only members the registration reaches are covered.

card.rule: Registering with a composite registers the observer with all its children, nested flocks included.
card.limits: Registration covers the members at the time it is passed down. Members that are created without going through the flock are not covered.

concepts.title: The pattern nobody mentioned
concepts.question: Where did the Iterator Pattern appear in the simulator without being announced?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A flock must apply quack() to each member, and the Observable helper must notify each observer. Both need to walk a collection.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors admit they snuck in the Iterator Pattern: both use java.util's iterator over an ArrayList. Iterator lets code walk a collection without knowing how it stores things.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A pattern can be present without being named, so a count of patterns can include ones nobody announced. Our reading: naming a pattern matters only when it helps you reason.

card.rule: A pattern can be at work in a design without being named, and the collection class often provides it.
card.limits: Naming a pattern is useful only when it helps you reason; using a language's own collections does not make a design more clever.

concepts.title: The simulator in one pass
concepts.question: Which request in the simulator was answered by which pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: After many steps, a reader needs the unity of the design: which request led to which pattern, and why they fit together.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A chain: a bunch of Quackables; a goose wants in (Adapter); quacks are counted (Decorator); the decorator must not be forgotten (Abstract Factory); flocks need managing (Composite); Quackologists want notice (Observer). Iterator runs underneath Composite and Observer.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The patterns cooperate because they all present the Quackable interface. The authors warn that you would never design a real system this way.

card.rule: State the unity of a design as a short chain: each need and the pattern that answered it.
card.limits: The chain shows how patterns can fit together, not how to design: the authors say you would not approach a real design this way.

concepts.title: Patterns are not the goal
concepts.question: Is applying patterns until a problem is solved a good way to design?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: After the simulator, a reader may think design means applying patterns to a problem until a solution appears.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The authors say that is wrong. The exercise showed how patterns work together. Apply patterns where and when they make sense, never just for the sake of it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Parts of the simulator may be big-time overkill, and the authors call the design forced and artificial, though it is useful for learning. Good OO principles sometimes solve a problem well enough.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The only reason for a pattern is to use a pattern. Start from the need, not from the pattern.

card.rule: Use a pattern when the problem calls for it, never in order to use a pattern.
card.limits: This is the authors' opinion, and it does not forbid patterns: where a need recurs, the pattern is often the best answer. The caution is against starting from the pattern.

concepts.title: The three roles of MVC
concepts.question: What does each of the model, the view and the controller do in a music player?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A music player manages songs and playlists, plays them, and keeps its screen current. Mixing data, display and input handling in one place makes the program hard to change.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Model-View-Controller. The model holds the data, the state and the application logic. The view is your window onto the model. The controller takes your actions, works out what they mean and manipulates the model.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each part has one job. The authors' secret for learning it is that MVC is just a few patterns put together. Our reading: the roles are responsibilities, not necessarily three files.

card.rule: The model holds data and logic, the view displays it, and the controller turns user actions into changes to the model.
card.limits: The roles describe responsibilities, not necessarily three separate files. Small programs may place two roles in one class, at the cost of mixing their concerns.

concepts.title: How an action moves through MVC
concepts.question: In what order do the user, view, controller and model react to a click?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Changes arrive from the user and also from inside, such as the next song starting. Both must reach the screen without the parts knowing too much about one another.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: You interact with the view; the view tells the controller; the controller asks the model to change and may also ask the view to change, for example by disabling a button. When the model changes, it notifies the view, which asks the model for the state it displays.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The screen follows the model whatever started the change. Our reading: this is the classic flow, and the web version differs.

card.rule: Action flows from view to controller to model, and updates flow from model to view, which then asks for state.
card.limits: This is the classic flow. The authors note that the controller may also observe the model, and in other settings such as the web the update path differs.

concepts.title: Why keep a controller
concepts.question: Why not put the control logic directly inside the view?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If the controller mostly calls a method on the model, why not do that in the view code? The authors give two reasons against it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Keep a controller. It interprets the input and manipulates the model, so the view manages only the interface.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Otherwise the view would have two jobs, and it would be tightly coupled to the model, so reusing it with another model would be out of the question. The controller keeps the two loosely coupled and the design flexible.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: Our reading: a throwaway screen with one fixed model and no reuse gains little from the extra class.

card.rule: A controller keeps the view free of control logic and decoupled from the model.
card.limits: The reasons apply when a view might change or be reused. For a throwaway screen with one fixed model, the extra class may buy little.

concepts.section: Looking at MVC through patterns-colored glasses
concepts.title: MVC is Observer, Strategy and Composite
concepts.question: Which three patterns make up MVC, and which part uses each?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Learning MVC from the top down is difficult, and not many developers succeed. A list of three roles does not explain how they stay decoupled.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: See MVC through patterns. The model uses Observer to keep views and controllers updated. The controller is the strategy for the view and can be exchanged for another controller. The view uses Composite internally to manage windows, buttons and other components.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The three patterns together decouple the three players. The authors call this the best path to learning MVC. Our reading: real systems adapt the mapping.

card.rule: MVC is Observer in the model, Strategy for the controller, and Composite in the view.
card.limits: This is the classic reading. Real systems adapt it, as Model 2 does for the web, and not every framework shows each pattern as plainly.

concepts.title: The model as Observer
concepts.question: How does the model keep views updated yet stay unaware of them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The model must keep any number of views and controllers current, yet it should not depend on what they are.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The model is an Observable. It notifies registered observers when its state changes, and knows only that it has observers. Observers may pull the state themselves, or the model may push it with the notification.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The model stays decoupled from views and controllers. The authors note that the Observer chapter lists disadvantages of push. A controller may also register as an observer, for example to enable or disable controls.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: the model announces a change and the registered view reads the new value.

card.rule: The model announces changes to registered observers and knows nothing else about them.
card.limits: Pull and push are both possible. Push saves the view a call but ties the notification to what the observers want to know.

concepts.title: The controller as Strategy
concepts.question: In what sense is the controller a swappable strategy for the view?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The view should concern itself with presentation only, yet its behavior on input must be changeable without editing the view.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Strategy Pattern. The view holds a controller through an interface, ControllerInterface in the DJ example, so any controller that implements it can be plugged in. The controller is the behavior of the view.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Swapping the controller gives different behavior and the view does not change. A controller written against a different set of calls cannot be dropped in unchanged.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: the view holds only the interface, so any Controller can be passed in.

card.rule: The view holds a controller through an interface, so swapping the controller swaps the view's behavior.
card.limits: A controller can only be swapped for another that fits the interface. A controller written for a different set of calls cannot be dropped in unchanged.

concepts.title: The view as Composite
concepts.question: Where does the Composite Pattern sit in the view of an MVC program?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A display is windows holding panels holding buttons and labels. The view needs to treat a container and a single component alike.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The view uses the Composite Pattern to manage this nested set, so asking a container to display itself makes it ask its members to do the same.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Today GUI packages such as Swing, and browsers turning markup into an interface, hide the structure. In the early days of MVC the pattern was more obviously part of it. Our reading: not seeing it in your code does not mean it is absent.

card.rule: The view is a tree of nested components that are treated alike, which is the Composite Pattern.
card.limits: Composite is easy to miss because GUI libraries manage it for you. Not seeing it in your own code does not mean it is absent.

concepts.title: The BeatModel
concepts.question: What does the BeatModel hold, expose and leave out?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The DJ tool needs a model that keeps the beat and drives the speakers with MIDI, and that can serve different views.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The BeatModel holds the current beats per minute and the code that generates MIDI events. It exposes an interface for the controller to manipulate the beat and for view and controller to read state, plus methods for observers to register and be notified.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: It makes no assumptions about the view, so a lightshow driven by the beat, or a text view naming the genre from the BPM, could use the same notifications.

card.rule: A model holds state and logic, offers an interface to change and read them, and lets observers register.
card.limits: A model shaped this way serves many views, but its interface is also the only door in; whatever the view needs must be offered there.

concepts.title: The DJ view
concepts.question: How is the DJ view built, and what does it do with the model and controller?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The tool must show the BPM and the beat pulse, and must let the user act, without the view changing the model itself.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: DJView registers as an observer of the model and reads the BPM through the model's interface when notified. When a control is used, the view tells the controller what to do, and the controller tells the model.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The display follows the model alone. The two windows, one for the display and one for the controls, are two parts of one class, split to show that they differ. Our reading: the roles are about responsibility, not files.

card.rule: The view displays what it learns from the model and reports user actions to the controller.
card.limits: Splitting the display and the controls into two windows is a teaching choice. Both live in one class, which shows that the roles are about responsibility, not about files.

concepts.title: The DJ controller
concepts.question: What does the BeatController do between the view and the model?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Input such as Start must become an action on the model, and the controls must reflect what is now possible.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The controller sits between view and model. It turns a menu choice into a model call. After Start it disables the Start item and enables Stop; after Stop it does the reverse.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The controller implements behavior for the view and holds no application logic. It may work out which model calls to make, but the code that manages and manipulates the data lives in the model.

card.rule: The controller translates view actions into model calls and adjusts the controls, but keeps no application logic.
card.limits: The line between interpreting input and application logic can blur. The authors say a little work to choose the model calls is not application logic.

concepts.section: And now for a test run...
concepts.title: Tracing a change through the DJ tool
concepts.question: When the BPM is changed, which parts react and in what order?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: When the display looks wrong in an MVC program, you need a quick way to find which part is at fault.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Follow the change: control, controller, model, notification, view. In the test run the BPM display follows the controls although it has no logical link to them, because it observes the model.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The beat bar keeps up with the beat for the same reason. Our reading: the trace works when the model is the single source of state.

card.rule: To trace any change, follow it from control to controller to model to notification to view.
card.limits: Tracing works when the model is the single source of state. If a view kept its own copy of state, the trace would break.

concepts.title: Adapting a model to an existing view
concepts.question: How can the DJ view be reused with a heart monitor that has a different interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The DJ view displays a beat rate and a pulse, much like a heartbeat. The HeartModel offers getHeartRate() where the view calls getBPM(), so the view cannot use it as it stands.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use the Adapter Pattern, which the authors call a common technique with MVC: adapt the new model to the existing controllers and views. The adapter's getBPM() calls getHeartRate().

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The view needs no change. Our reading: the adapter only translates, so calls such as setting a heart rate have nothing real to call.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: the adapter lets the old view read the heart model.

card.rule: Adapt the new model to the interface the existing view and controller expect.
card.limits: An adapter only translates. Where the new model cannot do what the old one did, such as set a heart rate, the adapter has nothing real to call.

concepts.section: Now we’re ready for a HeartController
concepts.title: A controller for the heart
concepts.question: What does reusing the view with a HeartController show, and what does it leave unfinished?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A new controller must plug into the existing view for a model that cannot start, stop or be set.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The HeartController is plugged into the same view with the HeartAdapter. It disables Start and Stop. The other buttons still appear, but the controller implements no-ops for them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The view shows the heart rate and the beat bar looks like a pulse. The dead buttons are left, and the authors note the view could be changed to support disabling them.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: the controller ignores calls that mean nothing for a heart.

card.rule: A swapped-in controller can reuse a view fully, though controls it ignores remain visible.
card.limits: Reuse worked, but the result is not finished. The view still offers controls that do nothing, which the authors suggest fixing in the view.

concepts.title: Model 2: MVC on the web
concepts.question: How do a browser, a servlet and a JSP split the roles of MVC?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Soon after the Web appeared, MVC had to fit the browser and server model, where the browser sends a request and the server returns a page.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Model 2, using servlet and JSP technology. A servlet receives and parses the HTTP request and acts as the controller, working on the model, usually a database. The result goes into a JavaBean, and control is forwarded to a JSP view, which returns a page.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The same separation of model, view and controller as a desktop GUI. Our reading: updates reach the view with each response, not at any time.

card.rule: In Model 2, the servlet is the controller, the model is usually a database, and the JSP is the view.
card.limits: Model 2 fits the request and response style of the web. It differs from the desktop flow, where the model notifies the view at any time.

concepts.title: Why Model 2 helped web teams
concepts.question: What did Model 2 give web teams beyond a clean design?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the old days, anyone with access to the JSPs could write any Java code they liked, including people who knew HTML but not software.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Model 2 separates components and also production responsibilities. Developers who know servlets keep the controller work, and web producers work on simple JSPs.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors say it saved many web shops from sinking into chaos. Producers have access only to HTML and simple JavaBeans.

card.rule: Separating model, view and controller also separates who works on what.
card.limits: The benefit is the authors' own account of the web shops of that time. It depends on view files being kept simple enough for non-programmers.

concepts.title: Reusing the model unchanged on the web
concepts.question: Why did the BeatModel need no change to move to the web?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Moving the DJ tool to the web should not mean rewriting the beat logic.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In MVC the model knows nothing about views or controllers, only that it may have observers to notify. The BeatModel depends on no outside classes, so it was used on the web off the shelf. The servlet translates HTTP input into model actions.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: No work was needed on the model. The view uses the model's state and does not alter it, as in desktop MVC. Our reading: one hidden reference to a desktop screen class would break the reuse.

card.rule: A model that depends on no view or controller can be reused unchanged in a new setting.
card.limits: Reuse without change holds only while the model really has no dependencies on the old setting. One hidden reference to a screen class would break it.

concepts.section: Model 2 is an adaptation of MVC to the Web
concepts.title: Where the patterns went in Model 2
concepts.question: Are Observer, Strategy and Composite still present in Model 2?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Model 2 does not look exactly like textbook MVC, so a reader wonders where Observer, Strategy and Composite went.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: All the parts are still there, adapted to the browser model. The view no longer registers with the model, but gets the equivalent of notifications from the controller, which passes it a bean. The servlet is still the strategy, and the view is a nested set of components built from HTML, most likely a composite.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: On the web, state is only needed when a response page is made, so notifications at other times would be pointless. The servlet is not composed directly with the view, yet it still provides the view's behavior.

card.rule: Model 2 keeps all three patterns, adapted: indirect notification, a swappable servlet, and a browser-built composite.
card.limits: Model 2 departs from the classic form, so the patterns are less visible. The idea of the role remains, even when the original wiring is gone.

concepts.title: What MVC buys, and where it is loose
concepts.question: What does MVC achieve, and where do the authors admit it is looser than it looks?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: MVC is presented as clean, but the DJ code leaves some access wider than it should be.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Observer, Strategy and Composite together decouple model, view and controller. Adapter can fit a new model to an existing view and controller, and Model 2 adapts MVC to the web.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The authors admit loose ends. Some call the controller a mediator, but the view reads the model's state directly, so it is not a pure mediator. The view has access to every model method, and a narrower interface is a job for a pattern.

card.rule: MVC decouples its three parts, but judge a design by what each part can actually reach.
card.limits: These loose ends are the authors' own admissions in a simplified example. They do not make MVC unsound; they show where a real design should tighten.

concepts.title: Context: the recurring situation
concepts.question: In the definition of a design pattern, what is the context and what must be true of it?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: The book defines a pattern as a solution to a problem in a context. The context is the situation in which the pattern applies, and it should be a recurring situation. Its example: you have a collection of objects.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Naming the context tells you where a pattern might apply at all. It only sets the scene; it does not say what goes wrong or what to do about it.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: A situation that will not come back is a poor context for a pattern.

card.rule: Name the recurring situation first, because the context is where the pattern applies.
card.limits: A context is only a setting. Describing it tells you nothing about what to do, and a situation that will not come back is a poor context for a pattern.

concepts.title: Problem: goal plus constraints, called forces
concepts.question: What two things make up the problem part of a pattern, and what do pattern writers call them?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: The problem is the goal you want in the context plus any constraints found there. The book's example: step through a collection without exposing how it is stored. Stepping through is the goal; hiding the storage is the constraint.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: Pattern writers call goals and constraints the forces, since they shape and control the solution. A useful pattern balances the light side (the goal) and the dark side (the constraints).

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: Reaching the goal while breaking a constraint is not a solution. The word force is lingo; do not let it get in the way.

card.rule: A problem is a goal plus its constraints, and a useful solution balances both.
card.limits: Reaching the goal while ignoring a constraint is not a solution. The term is lingo, though, and the book says not to let the word get in your way.

concepts.title: Solution: a general design anyone can apply
concepts.question: What kind of thing is the solution part of a pattern, and how does the book's collection example show it?

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: The solution is what you are after: a general design that anyone can apply, which resolves the goal and the set of constraints. The book's example: encapsulate the iteration into a separate class.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: The word general matters. A design is an arrangement of parts, not the code of one program, so another developer can use it on a different collection.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: A fix that works only inside one program is not yet a general design. One that reaches the goal but breaks a constraint does not count either.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: After: callers loop with for-each, and the storage inside Shelf can change without touching them.

card.rule: A pattern's solution is a general design that resolves the goal and constraints.
card.limits: A solution that only fits one program is not a general design. A design that resolves the goal but breaks a constraint does not count as the solution either.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: Why the car-window fix is not a pattern
concepts.question: A description has a context, a problem and a working solution. Why might it still fail to be a pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Someone locks the keys in the car and must get to work on time. The fix is to break the window, get in and drive. A context, a problem and a working solution are all present.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The book still says this is not a pattern. A pattern needs a recurring problem, and this solution is not one you can apply over and over. Having the three parts is necessary but not enough.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Check recurrence before calling a description a pattern. Two further tests (a name and a description others can use) come in the next idea.

card.rule: Before calling something a pattern, check that its solution can be applied again and again, not only that context, problem and solution are present.
card.limits: Recurrence is one test among several; the next idea adds two more.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: A pattern needs a name and a transferable description
concepts.question: Besides recurrence, what two further weaknesses does the book find in the car-window description?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The keys-in-the-car write-up has two more faults. It is hard to hand to someone else so they can apply it to their own unique problem, and it has no name.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A pattern needs a name so it can join a vocabulary shared with other developers, and a description someone else can apply. Real catalog entries say more than a bare problem, context and solution.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A named, transferable description lets developers talk about the design in a word. The name alone is not enough; recurrence and a general solution are still required.

card.rule: Give a pattern a name and describe it so that someone else can apply it to their own problem.
card.limits: A name alone does not make something a pattern, since recurrence and a general solution are still needed. A name also helps only as far as other developers share it.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: Patterns are guidelines you may adapt
concepts.question: May you change a pattern's structure to fit your design, and what should you do when you do?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A well-known pattern almost fits your design, but a class or two does not suit your case. Real-world examples often depart from the classic designs.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Patterns, like design principles, are guidelines, not laws, so you may alter them to fit. The book adds that it never hurts to document how your version differs from the classic design.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Other developers can recognise the pattern at once and see where yours differs. Without a note, they may misjudge which pattern is in use.

card.rule: Treat a pattern as a guideline you may adapt, and write down how your version differs from the classic one.
card.limits: Adapting is allowed, but undocumented changes leave the next developer unable to tell which pattern is in use or how it differs.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: How a catalog entry is laid out
concepts.question: Which sections does a pattern catalog entry have, and which question does each answer?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A growing set of patterns is hard to search and compare unless every entry is laid out the same way.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A catalog describes each pattern by a template: name; Intent; Motivation and Applicability; Structure and Participants; Implementation and sample code; relations to other patterns; Consequences.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: You know where to look for what, how a pattern relates to its neighbours, and what using it will cost. An entry describes the classic design; yours may differ.

card.rule: Match your question to the section: intent says what, motivation and applicability say when, structure and participants say how, consequences say what it costs.
card.limits: The entry describes the classic design; your adapted version may differ. Catalog entries are also richer than the bare problem, context and solution definition, but they do not replace judgment about your own case.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: Working through a catalog entry
concepts.question: In what order does the book's patterns user check a catalog entry before building the pattern into a design?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: You have a catalog full of entries and a design problem, and you want to avoid the wrong pattern or a surprise in your design.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Jim's routine: know the patterns and their relationships beforehand. Check Motivation and Applicability, then Consequences. Only then study Structure and Participants, work the pattern in with alterations, and read Implementation and sample code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Fit and effects are confirmed before any class is drawn. The routine is one practitioner's habit, not a rule of the catalog.

card.rule: Confirm the fit and the consequences first, then study structure and participants, then adapt and read the implementation notes.
card.limits: This is one practitioner's routine, not a rule of the catalog. The fixed points are to confirm the fit before adopting and to adapt the structure to your own design.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: Fundamental and domain-specific catalogs
concepts.question: What kinds of patterns catalogs exist, and how big is the classic one?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Different areas of software have different recurring problems, and no single book can hold all the patterns.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Catalogs of fundamental patterns sit beside catalogs of domain-specific ones, such as EJB patterns. The classic fundamental catalog is Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, with 23 patterns, by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Choose a catalog by its scope. The fundamental catalog does not cover a domain's own problems, and a domain catalog does not teach the fundamentals.

card.rule: Pick a catalog by its scope: the GoF catalog for the 23 fundamental patterns, a domain catalog for the patterns of one area.
card.limits: A catalog's scope is also its limit. A fundamental catalog does not cover the specific recurring problems of a domain, and a domain catalog does not teach the fundamentals.

concepts.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer
concepts.title: Patterns are discovered, not created
concepts.question: Where do patterns come from, and who can write one?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A developer may feel that a solution they keep using deserves to be called a pattern, or may want to contribute to the community.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The book says patterns are discovered, not created. Anyone can discover one and write its description, but it is not easy and does not happen quickly or often.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Most people use patterns and never write one. Becoming a patterns writer takes commitment, so ask first why you would want to.

card.rule: See a pattern as something found in recurring practice, and write one only if you are ready to commit.
card.limits: Finding a solution you like is not the same as having found a pattern. It still has to recur and to pass the tests the next ideas describe.

concepts.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer
concepts.title: The Rule of Three
concepts.question: When does the book say a candidate has earned the right to be called a pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Anyone can believe a solution is good. The community needs a test that separates a real pattern from a personal favourite.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: You do not have a pattern until others have used it and found it to work. In general it must pass the Rule of Three: it can be called a pattern only if applied in a real-world solution at least three times.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Two successful uses are not yet enough. The words in general mark it as a rule of thumb, not a proof.

card.rule: Call a candidate a pattern only after it has been applied in real-world solutions at least three times.
card.limits: The phrase in general marks it as a rule of thumb. Three uses is a minimum, not a proof, and the uses must be real-world solutions in which the pattern worked.

concepts.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer
concepts.title: Study first, then reflect
concepts.question: What two things does the book tell a would-be patterns writer to do before writing anything down?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A designer thinks she has found a new pattern. New-looking designs are often old ones in disguise.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Do your homework: be well versed in the existing patterns first. Then reflect on your own experience, the problems met and the solutions used, and comb it for designs that recur.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Most apparently new patterns are variants of existing ones, and a real find may have too narrow an applicability. Study also helps you recognise patterns and relate them to each other.

card.rule: Study the existing patterns first, and expect most apparently new patterns to be variants of known ones.
card.limits: Most is not all: variants are far more common than new patterns, but new ones can appear. A find that does recur can also be too narrow to qualify as a real pattern.

concepts.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer
concepts.title: Write it down, let others try it, refine
concepts.question: How does the book say a pattern candidate should be written up and improved?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A pattern candidate stays in its author's head unless others can read, understand and apply it.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Get the idea on paper in a way others can follow. Use the GoF template instead of inventing a format. Then have others try the candidate, give feedback, and refine again.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Think of the pattern as a work in progress that improves over time.

card.rule: Write the candidate in an established template, let others try it, and refine it until they can read and apply it.
card.limits: The description will never be perfect; it needs to be solid enough for others to understand. Refining does not replace the Rule of Three, which still decides whether it counts as a pattern.

concepts.title: Why patterns are put into categories
concepts.question: Why do catalogs partition patterns into categories, and what does a reader gain?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: As discovered patterns multiply, a flat list becomes hard to browse and hard to compare.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Partition patterns into classifications. The book gives three reasons: to organise them, to narrow a search to a subset, and to compare patterns within a group.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The Master adds that any large collection invites categories because they let us think at a more abstract level. The book still says knowing the patterns and their relationships matters most.

card.rule: Group a large collection into categories so that you can organise it, narrow a search and compare like with like.
card.limits: A classification is a tool. The book says the most important thing is to know the patterns and the relationships among them, and to use categories when they help.

concepts.title: Creational, structural and behavioral
concepts.question: Which three-way classification does the best-known scheme use, and what is it based on?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The first catalog needed one scheme to divide its patterns into groups that readers could carry in their heads.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The best-known scheme partitions patterns by purpose into Creational, Behavioral and Structural. Structural patterns describe how classes and objects are composed into new structures or functionality; Behavioral patterns concern communication and interconnection between objects.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Many patterns seem to fit more than one category, and everyone has trouble placing them. The scheme is a convenience, not a law.

card.rule: Classify a pattern by its purpose into creational, structural or behavioral.
card.limits: Many patterns seem to fit more than one category, and the book says everyone has trouble placing them. The scheme is a convenience, not a law.

concepts.title: Why Decorator is structural: look at intent
concepts.question: Decorator adds behavior, so why is it a structural pattern, and what is the key to placing a pattern?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Decorator adds behavior, so many developers expect it among the behavioral patterns.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The Gang of Four filed it under structural. Decorator composes objects by wrapping one in another to provide new functionality, so its focus is how objects are composed, not how they communicate. The intent of a pattern is often the key to its category.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Read a pattern's intent, not just its visible effect. Intent usually settles the matter but not always, and some readers still disagree.

card.rule: Decide a pattern's category from what its intent is about, not from whether its effect adds behavior.
card.limits: Intent usually settles the matter, but not always cleanly. Many people stay confused by the three categories, and a reasonable reader may disagree with a placement.

concepts.title: Other ways to classify patterns
concepts.question: Besides purpose, what other ways of classifying patterns does the book mention?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: One scheme cannot answer every question a reader has about a pattern.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Patterns are often classified by a second attribute: whether they deal with classes or with objects. Some schemes start from the three categories and add subcategories such as Decoupling Patterns.

blocks.label: Consequences
