questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A team wants to benefit from other developers' experience of structuring classes and objects. Which of these is a design idea to learn and adapt, not code to link in?
options: A networking library with a published API
A named way of structuring classes to let one behavior vary
A GUI framework with ready-made windows
A file-handling package that is added to the build
optionExplain: A library is code that you link into your program.
Right: a pattern is a design idea you learn and adapt.
A framework is also code written by someone else.
A package is code added to a build, not a design idea.
questions.explain: Libraries and frameworks are code; a pattern is a way of structuring classes and objects. The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Code is linked in; a pattern is learned.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: Design patterns don't go directly into your code, they first go into your ____.
questions.explain: Patterns are applied by a developer who knows them, not added to the program as files.
questions.rule: Patterns go into your brain first.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A developer asks for a library of design patterns so as not to have to learn them. What do the authors say?
options: A library of patterns will be published soon
Patterns are the same as libraries, so any library will do
Patterns are too small to need adaptation
Patterns are higher level than libraries, and each must be adapted to the application
optionExplain: The authors say there is no library of patterns, only catalogs that list them.
The authors say libraries and frameworks are not patterns.
The authors say it is our job to adapt them.
Right: the authors say patterns tell us how to structure classes and objects, and we adapt them.
questions.explain: A pattern is a design to adapt, not a part to import.
questions.rule: Adapt the design to your application.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: The authors say libraries and frameworks are not design patterns, yet may use them. What benefit follows for a developer who knows patterns?
options: They no longer need to read documentation
They understand APIs built around patterns more quickly
They can replace the library with a pattern
They can predict every bug in the library
optionExplain: Documentation is still needed.
Right: the authors say pattern knowledge speeds up understanding of such APIs.
A pattern is not a replacement for code.
Pattern knowledge does not reveal bugs.
questions.explain: Recognizing the pattern in a library tells you how its parts fit.
questions.rule: Patterns help you read other people's code.
questions.teaches: Recognizing a pattern inside a library lets you predict how its parts relate before reading its details.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A student learning to cook asks whether a recipe book is the same as the technique of emulsifying. By analogy with the card, which answer fits?
options: No: the book supplies finished recipes, and the technique is a method you learn and adapt
Yes: both are ingredients to add to the dish
Yes: the technique is a smaller recipe book
No: the technique cannot be adapted to new dishes
optionExplain: Right: finished recipes parallel libraries, and the method parallels a pattern.
Neither is an ingredient.
A technique is applied across dishes, which is its strength.
A technique can be adapted.
questions.explain: Finished parts and general methods differ in every field.
questions.rule: Parts are used; methods are adapted.
questions.teaches: Finished code gives you a result; a pattern gives you a method for reaching results in many situations.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: True or false: according to the authors, libraries and frameworks are themselves design patterns.
questions.explain: The authors say libraries and frameworks are not patterns; they are specific implementations that we link into our code, though they sometimes use patterns inside.
questions.rule: Libraries implement; patterns guide.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A programmer knows classes, inheritance and polymorphism well. What can be said about the flexibility of their designs?
options: Knowing these basics does not by itself guarantee flexible, maintainable designs
It guarantees them, since the basics are the whole of design
It guarantees them, but only for small programs
It makes patterns useless for them
optionExplain: Right: the guru says the basics are not enough on their own.
The guru calls this a misunderstanding.
Size of program is not the guru's point.
The guru presents patterns as the collected experience.
questions.explain: Knowing tools is different from knowing how to use them to make flexible designs. The card next gives the guru's view.
questions.rule: Basics are necessary, not sufficient.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: The guru says design is an art, and it involves ____ between competing goals.
questions.explain: Even with patterns, choices cost something and must be weighed.
questions.rule: Design involves trade-offs.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: Two developers face a design problem and neither can find a matching pattern. According to the guru, what should they use?
options: Nothing; without a pattern no design is possible
A library that happens to be close
The first design that comes to mind
The OO principles that underlie the patterns, including thinking about how the system might change
optionExplain: The guru says principles can guide them.
The authors say libraries are not patterns and do not cover design.
A first guess ignores the principles.
Right: the guru says principles help when no pattern is found.
questions.explain: Principles are the layer under the patterns.
questions.rule: Fall back on principles.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: The developer asks whether knowing patterns lets him skip the hard work and reach designs that are certain to work. How does the guru answer?
options: Yes, completely, so no judgment is needed
Yes, to an extent, but design is an art and trade-offs remain
No, patterns have nothing to offer
No, because patterns are discovered, not made
optionExplain: The guru adds a caution about trade-offs.
Right: patterns save effort but do not remove judgment.
The guru says well-tested patterns put you ahead.
The discovery of patterns is not the point of the answer.
questions.explain: Patterns shorten the path but do not do the choosing.
questions.rule: Patterns inform judgment; they do not replace it.
questions.teaches: The value of a pattern is that others have already paid for its lessons; the cost of choosing among patterns remains with the designer.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: An experienced pilot tells a student: 'Knowing the controls does not make you a good pilot. The checklists and the rules of flying came from hard experience.' Which part of the guru's view matches?
options: Anyone who knows the controls can fly well
Checklists remove the need for judgment
Basic knowledge is not enough; collected experience and principles add what is missing
Experience matters only for beginners
optionExplain: This is the misunderstanding the guru names.
The guru says trade-offs remain.
Right: the structure matches the guru's view.
The guru does not limit patterns to beginners.
questions.explain: The same relation between basics and experience appears in any craft.
questions.rule: Basics plus experience, not basics alone.
questions.teaches: In any craft, collected experience records what basic skills leave out; it speeds learning without removing the need for judgment.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: True or false: the guru says a designer who knows the OO basics will automatically build flexible, reusable systems.
questions.explain: The guru calls that one of the true misunderstandings of object-oriented development.
questions.rule: Basics do not automatically give flexibility.

questions.q: Which sentence best sums up the main thread of a chapter on SimUDuck, Strategy and shared vocabulary?
options: Expect change, separate what varies, and use proven patterns as a shared language
Use inheritance wherever two classes share code
Never change working code after release
Write code first and decide the design later
optionExplain: Right: this captures the thread from the problem to the pattern.
The chapter shows the limits of inheritance.
The chapter says software must change.
The chapter shows the value of design thinking.
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a problem to principles to a pattern. The card next gathers the threads.
questions.rule: Change, separation, patterns.

questions.q: Match each idea from the chapter's summary to the sentence that expresses it.
questions.explain: The summary points: patterns are discovered, give general solutions rather than code, address change, and provide a shared language.
questions.rule: Know the chapter's summary points.

questions.q: A team builds a fitness app. Workout types differ, and new types are expected every quarter. Using the chapter's thread, what should the team do first?
options: Create a subclass for each workout and copy shared code
Write one big class with a branch for each type
Find what varies, the workout types, and put it behind an interface
Wait for the first change request before designing
optionExplain: Copying shared code multiplies the cost of change.
Branches make every addition risky.
Right: expecting change, they separate what varies.
The chapter says to plan for change, not wait for it.
questions.explain: The chapter's main thread, applied to a new domain.
questions.rule: Expect change; separate what varies.

questions.q: Which statement about patterns would the chapter's authors accept?
options: A pattern is a finished class to be copied into the code
A pattern is a general solution that must be adapted to the application
A pattern is a law that settles every design choice
A pattern is a new invention for each project
optionExplain: The authors say patterns do not give you code.
Right: patterns give general solutions, not code.
The guru says trade-offs always remain.
The authors say patterns are discovered, not invented.
questions.explain: A pattern is a discovered, adaptable solution.
questions.rule: Adapt the pattern; do not copy it.
questions.teaches: The authors say constructing OO systems with these properties is not obvious and was discovered only through hard work.

questions.q: True or false: according to the chapter's bullet points, patterns give you code that you paste into your application.
questions.explain: The bullet points say patterns don't give you code, they give you general solutions to design problems, which you apply to your specific application.
questions.rule: Patterns give solutions, not code.

questions.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
questions.q: Duck declares sound() and move(). RubberDuck overrides only sound(). What does this program print?
options: Squeak swims
Quack swims
Squeak
A compile error, since sound() is declared twice
optionExplain: Right: the override replaces sound(), and move() is inherited unchanged from Duck.
This is the Duck version of sound(). The object is a RubberDuck, so its own version runs even through a Duck variable.
Inheritance gives the subclass move() as well, so a second word is printed.
Overriding is allowed and is the usual way for a subclass to differ.
questions.explain: RubberDuck replaces sound() and receives move() from Duck. It writes code only where it differs.
questions.rule: A subclass receives the superclass code it does not replace.

questions.q: RubberDuck declares no fly() of its own. What does this program print?
options: An exception, since rubber ducks are inanimate
Nothing, since RubberDuck has no fly() of its own
A compile error, since a rubber duck cannot fly
flap, since RubberDuck inherits fly() from Duck
optionExplain: Nothing in the code checks what the object is, so no exception is thrown.
A subclass with no fly() still has the inherited one, so something is printed.
The compiler knows nothing about which objects should fly; it only follows the class structure.
Right: every subclass receives the superclass methods, so the rubber duck flaps.
questions.explain: The inherited method runs. This is the flying rubber duck of the book, in six lines.
questions.rule: A method added to a superclass runs in every subclass.

questions.q: Which new Duck superclass methods are safe, because every subclass, rubber ducks included, should have them?
options: getName()
swim()
fly()
layEggs()
optionExplain: Right: every duck type, rubber ones too, can have a name.
Right: the game shows all its duck species swimming, so a shared swim() fits.
This is the book's mistake: rubber ducks are inanimate and should not fly.
Inanimate rubber ducks do not lay eggs, so they would inherit a method that makes no sense.
questions.explain: A method is safe in a superclass when all subclasses really share it. fly() and layEggs() are meant for only some.
questions.rule: Put a method in the superclass only if every subclass should have it.

questions.q: Which two items are NOT on the authors' list of disadvantages of inheritance for duck behavior?
options: Code is duplicated across subclasses
We can't make ducks dance
Changes can unintentionally affect other ducks
Ducks can't fly and quack at the same time
Runtime behavior changes are difficult
optionExplain: This is on the list: the same behavior code is copied into several subclasses.
Not on the list: inheritance never promised dancing, so its absence is no disadvantage of the design.
This is on the list: a change meant for one duck can reach others.
Not on the list: nothing in an inheritance design stops one duck from doing both.
This is on the list: behavior fixed in class definitions is hard to alter while the program runs.
questions.explain: The four listed costs all concern how behavior is stored and changed. Dancing and doing two things at once are different complaints.
questions.rule: Judge a design by the costs it causes, not by things it never promised.

questions.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
questions.q: Joe puts the shared flying code inside Flyable, as shown. What does the Java compiler do?
options: It rejects the code, since an interface method has no body
It accepts the code and every implementer shares the flying code
It accepts the code, but only winged ducks may implement it
It warns about the body, then ignores it and compiles the rest
optionExplain: Right: javac reports that interface abstract methods cannot have a body.
This is what Joe would like, but an interface in the book's sense holds no implementation code.
The compiler does not care which ducks have wings; the error is about the body.
There is no such warning; the code is an error.
questions.explain: The book's point is that a Java interface carries no implementation code, so each implementer must write its own. Our reading: Java 8 added the default keyword, which allows a body, but the plain interface method in the book does not.
questions.rule: An ordinary interface method declares a behavior but cannot supply its code.

questions.section: The one constant in software development
questions.q: Executives want an update every six months, in undecided ways. What must Joe do for each new Duck subclass under inheritance?
options: Nothing, since subclasses inherit the right behavior automatically
Rewrite the Duck superclass from scratch each time
Look at fly() and quack() and possibly override them
Write a new interface for the subclass
optionExplain: Inherited behavior is automatic, but it is not automatically right, as the rubber duck showed.
The superclass is not rewritten each time; the work is in the subclasses.
Right: with a spec that keeps changing, every new subclass must be checked and its fly() and quack() possibly overridden.
The interface idea was a different plan, and it has its own cost.
questions.explain: The authors say Joe will be forced to look at and possibly override fly() and quack() for every new Duck subclass, for ever.
questions.rule: Under inheritance, every change pushes work into every subclass.

questions.q: A retail app has 8 store classes, each holding its own discount code. A rule changes, and a developer edits all eight. What does the authors' account predict?
options: The edits are safe, since each class is edited only once
A new interface would make the edits unnecessary
The compiler would update the copies of the code
The hunt through every class probably introduces new bugs
optionExplain: Each class is edited once, but the risk lies in finding and changing every copy correctly.
An interface names the behavior but does not hold it, as the interface design already showed.
A compiler does not synchronize copies of code written by hand.
Right: tracking down every class that defines the behavior probably introduces new bugs along the way.
questions.explain: Having to find and change the same behavior in many classes is the shared failure. Each missed or mistyped copy is a new bug.
questions.rule: Behavior spread over many classes costs a hunt, and the hunt breeds bugs.
questions.teaches: Tracking down and changing a behavior in every class that defines it probably introduces new bugs along the way.

questions.q: A new fee type, drone, is sold, but fee() is not edited. What does this program print?
options: A compile error, since drone is unknown
optionExplain: Right: no branch matches drone, so the default 4 is returned and printed as 4.0.
14 is the same-day fee, which applies only to that kind.
The kind is only a string, so the compiler cannot know which kinds exist.
9.5 is the express fee, which applies only to the kind express.
questions.explain: The varying rule sits inside Order, so a new fee type either needs an edit there or silently gets the default. Encapsulating the fees in their own classes removes this trap.
questions.rule: If adding a variant means editing a stable class, the varying part is not yet encapsulated.

questions.q: A student studies one pattern for payments and another for chat messages. Which feature do the authors say nearly all patterns share?
options: Both are libraries that are linked into the program
Both replace inheritance everywhere in a design
Both need exactly one interface and two classes each
Both let one part of a system vary independently
optionExplain: Patterns are designs to learn and adapt, not libraries to link in.
Some patterns use inheritance, and the authors say the principle favors composition rather than banning inheritance.
Patterns differ in size; no fixed count of classes is required.
Right: the authors say patterns let some part of a system vary independently of the others.
questions.explain: Because most patterns address change, nearly all of them isolate a part that varies. That is why this first principle underlies almost every pattern.
questions.rule: Ask of any pattern which part it lets vary on its own.
questions.teaches: Nearly every pattern lets one part of a system change without touching the rest.

questions.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
questions.q: A team moves fly() and quack() out of Duck, and also swim(), which all ducks share, into behavior classes. What is the error?
options: Nothing; the more methods are moved out, the safer the design
swim() should have been moved out before fly() and quack()
swim() does not vary, so moving it adds structure for no gain
Methods may be moved out only into one shared behavior class
optionExplain: Moving everything out would leave an empty class and add structure where no change is expected.
Order is not the issue; the question is whether the method varies at all.
Right: the authors pulled out only the parts that vary and left the rest of Duck alone.
Each varying behavior gets its own set of classes, so more than one set is normal.
questions.explain: The authors found nothing else in Duck that seemed to change, so they left it. Our reading: moving a stable method out costs a class and buys nothing.
questions.rule: Move out only what varies.

questions.q: Which part of this Duck code breaks the second design principle?
options: flyBehavior is declared as the class FlyWithWings
FlyWithWings implements an interface of the behavior
The fly() method prints a message instead of returning
performFly() forwards the call to another object it holds
optionExplain: Right: declaring the variable with a concrete class locks Duck to that implementation; it should be typed FlyBehavior.
The behavior class implementing the interface is exactly what the principle asks for.
What the method prints is an implementation detail and not a type choice.
Forwarding is delegation, which the design wants.
questions.explain: The principle concerns the declared type of the variable. With the type FlyWithWings, no other behavior can be assigned.
questions.rule: Declare behavior variables with the interface type.

questions.q: Logger is an abstract class, and the variable has that type. What does this program print?
options: file:hi
A compile error, since Logger is not an interface
hi
screen:hi
optionExplain: FileLogger is declared but never created; the object assigned is a ScreenLogger.
A supertype may be an abstract class; the Java keyword interface is not needed.
Both classes add a prefix, so the text alone is never printed.
Right: the object is a ScreenLogger, and the abstract supertype lets it be used through the Logger variable.
questions.explain: The variable is typed with a supertype, so programming to an interface works without the interface keyword. The actual object decides which write() runs.
questions.rule: An abstract class is a supertype too.

questions.q: The array is typed Animal. What does this program print?
options: Woof Woof Woof
Woof Meow Woof
Meow Meow Meow
A compile error, since Animal is abstract
optionExplain: The first and third objects are Dogs, but the second is a Cat.
Right: each call runs the version of the actual object stored in that slot.
The declared type is Animal; the objects inside are what decide each sound.
An abstract class can be the declared type; only creating an Animal directly is forbidden.
questions.explain: The loop knows only that each element is an Animal. At each step the actual object supplies its own makeSound().
questions.rule: One call on a supertype variable runs the code of whatever object it holds.

questions.q: Route planning moved from Vehicle into RouteBehavior classes. Vehicle's other members are shared by all vehicles. Must Vehicle become an interface?
options: Yes, since every class with varying parts must become an interface
Yes, since a class cannot hold a reference to a behavior object
No, it can stay a class that subclasses inherit shared members from
No, since interfaces cannot be used for vehicles
optionExplain: The varying part was moved out; that is what lets the remaining class stay a class.
A class can hold a reference typed as an interface; that is how delegation works.
Right: like Duck in the book, it keeps its common properties and methods without the old problems.
Interfaces can describe anything; the reason to keep the class is the shared code.
questions.explain: Asked whether Duck should become an interface, the authors say no: with the varying behavior removed, specific ducks still gain from inheriting the common parts.
questions.rule: After the varying part is moved out, inheritance for the stable part is fine.
questions.teaches: Duck stays an ordinary class after the redesign: with the varying behavior removed, specific ducks still inherit common properties and methods from it without the old problems.

questions.q: ModelDuck's constructor replaces the quack behavior it inherited. What does this program print?
options: << Silence >>
Quack
Quack, then << Silence >>
A compile error, since quackBehavior is assigned twice
optionExplain: Right: the field holds the silent behavior by the time performQuack() runs, and Duck forwards to it.
Quack is the starting value from Duck, but the constructor replaces it before performQuack() is called.
Only one object is held at a time, so only one message is printed.
A variable can be assigned more than once; the second assignment simply replaces the first.
questions.explain: Duck's code is unchanged. Which text appears depends only on the object in quackBehavior.
questions.rule: A delegating class does whatever the object it holds does.

questions.q: Duck holds a flyBehavior that prints stay. What does this program print, and what is the delegation error?
options: stay, since performFly() uses the held variable correctly
flap, since the interface forces FlyWithWings to run before the lambda
A compile error, since a Duck may not hold a lambda
flap, since performFly() ignores flyBehavior and builds a FlyWithWings
optionExplain: That would be correct delegation, but the method never touches the variable.
Interfaces never force one class to run ahead of another.
A lambda is a valid object for a one-method interface; the compiler is satisfied.
Right: it creates a concrete object each time, so the held behavior is never used and cannot be swapped.
questions.explain: Delegation means forwarding to the object the Duck holds. Creating a concrete class inside the method brings back the lock to an implementation.
questions.rule: Forward to the held variable, never to a new concrete object.

questions.q: A teammate complains that new Quack() in MallardDuck's constructor is a poor way to initialize. What do the authors say about this?
options: They agree it is poor, and say later patterns will help fix it
They deny a problem, since interface-typed variables remove it completely
They say constructors must not assign behavior objects
They recommend replacing the behavior classes with if-statements
optionExplain: Right: they admit it and promise that more patterns in the toolbox will help later.
Interface-typed variables keep flexibility, but the concrete class is still named in the constructor.
They use the constructor in their own code; the point is to name classes there, not to avoid it.
That would bring back the problems the design was made to remove.
questions.explain: The authors say the choice is made this way for now and that later patterns will help fix it.
questions.rule: A hard-coded concrete class in a constructor is a known weak spot.
questions.teaches: The authors say the hard-coded constructor choice is for now, and that later patterns in the book will help fix it.

questions.q: A developer adds a times parameter to the QuackBehavior interface and leaves Quack as shown. What happens when this compiles?
options: Quack compiles, and quack() is skipped at run time
Only the interface is rejected, and Quack compiles
javac rejects Quack, as it lacks quack(int)
Quack compiles and prints Quack twice
optionExplain: A class that misses an interface method does not compile, so there is no run time.
The interface is fine; the class that implements it is the one in error.
Right: Quack must implement every method of the interface it names.
Nothing in the code repeats the print.
questions.explain: Adding a new behavior class touches nothing else, but changing the interface itself forces edits in every class that implements it. Our reading: that is why the interface should describe the job in a stable way.
questions.rule: New classes are free; a changed interface is not.

questions.q: Sprint keeps a counter. What does this program print?
options: run1 run1 walk
run1 run2 run3
walk walk walk
run1 run2 walk
optionExplain: The same Sprint object answers both calls, so its counter keeps counting.
The behavior is replaced before the third call, so the counter does not reach 3.
The first two calls use the Sprint object before the replacement.
Right: the Sprint object counts 1 and 2, then the variable is given the walking behavior.
questions.explain: The variable holds one behavior at a time. Swapping it changes what the next call does, and a behavior object keeps its own state.
questions.rule: Assigning a new behavior object changes what the next call does.

questions.q: setFlyBehavior() takes a FlyBehavior, and Squeak implements QuackBehavior. What happens when this is compiled?
options: javac rejects it, since Squeak does not implement FlyBehavior
It compiles but fails at run time when fly() is called
It compiles, since setFlyBehavior() accepts any behavior object
javac rejects it, since Duck has no QuackBehavior variable
optionExplain: Right: the new behavior must implement the correct behavior interface to be accepted.
Type errors of this kind are found by the compiler, before anything runs.
The parameter type is FlyBehavior, so not every behavior object is accepted.
Duck needs no QuackBehavior for this call; the error is the argument type.
questions.explain: A behavior can be swapped in only if it implements the interface the setter expects.
questions.rule: A swapped-in behavior must implement the right interface.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: Three tax rules share one interface. What does this program print?
optionExplain: Each member of the family computes tax its own way, so the three results differ.
The loop runs over all three rules, so three values are printed.
200 is the price, not the tax on it.
Right: the same call tax(200) gives 10 percent, 5 percent and no tax in turn.
questions.explain: The loop calls the same method on every member. Each member supplies its own result, which is what makes them a family.
questions.rule: Members of a family answer the same call in their own ways.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: Match each Java line to the relationship it expresses.
questions.explain: extends gives IS-A, a field that holds another object gives HAS-A, and implements gives IMPLEMENTS.
questions.rule: Read the keyword or field to find the relationship.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: Sort each item: does it use composition, or inheritance?

items.t: class Radio { Speaker speaker; }
class Radio extends Device
A Camera that calls the flash object it holds
A Mallard that receives fly() from Duck
A Printer given a PaperTray object
class Kayak extends Boat

questions.explain: Composition means holding another object and using it. Inheritance means receiving code from a superclass.
questions.rule: Held object means composition; extends means inheritance.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: A Cell has 3 data types and 2 display styles, one subclass for each pair. A third style, Percent, is added. What does each design need?
options: Inheritance: 1 new subclass; composition: 3 new classes
Inheritance: 1 new subclass; composition: 1 new class
Inheritance: 3 subclasses; composition: 1 display class
Inheritance: 3 new subclasses; composition: 3 new classes
optionExplain: This has the designs the wrong way round: composition needs only the new display style.
One subclass would leave two data types without the new style.
Right: inheritance needs a Percent subclass for each of the 3 data types, composition one new display class.
Under composition the display style is held separately, so the data types are untouched.
questions.explain: Our reading: when two choices vary together, inheritance multiplies classes, while composition adds one class per choice.
questions.rule: Composition adds, inheritance multiplies.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: A module is copied into 5 products. A rule changes twice a year, and each edit takes one person-day per copy. How many person-days of edits in a year?
optionExplain: Two is the cost for one shared copy; here there are five copies.
Five covers one change, but the rule changes twice.
Right: 5 copies times 2 changes is 10, against 2 for a single shared module.
Twenty would count each copy four times.
questions.explain: Our reading: the week saved by copying is paid back many times, because maintenance takes most of a program's life, as the master points out.
questions.rule: Count the cost of the changes, not only of the first build.

questions.q: Checkout holds a Discount object that can be replaced. What does this program print?
optionExplain: Right: 10 percent off 100 is 90, then subtracting 5 gives 95.
The first call happens before the replacement, so it uses the 10 percent discount.
The first value was stored before the strategy was replaced, but the second call uses the new one.
The second discount returns the reduced price, not the amount taken off.
questions.explain: Checkout is the client and never changes. Its results change because the algorithm it holds is interchangeable.
questions.rule: A strategy can be swapped without editing the client.

questions.q: Design A has a Shop subclass per country, each with its own tax code. Design B has one Shop holding a TaxRule object. Which can switch tax rule while running?
options: Design A, because each subclass already contains the rule
Neither, because tax rules are fixed when a shop is created
Both, because either design can change its class while running
Design B, because the held TaxRule can be replaced
optionExplain: A subclass fixes its rule when the code is written, so the object cannot trade it for another.
In Design B the rule is held in a variable that can be reassigned.
An object cannot change its own class while the program runs.
Right: Design B is Strategy, and a setter can give the Shop a different TaxRule.
questions.explain: Strategy puts the algorithm in a held object, so it can be exchanged. Subclassing fixes the algorithm in the class.
questions.rule: A held algorithm can change at runtime; an inherited one cannot.

questions.q: A team lead says Strategy in a design talk, and a newcomer does not know the word. What can the lead hope for, according to the authors?
options: The newcomer is shut out, since the term hides the design
The newcomer is inspired to start learning the pattern
The newcomer must already know every pattern to attend
The newcomer needs a library of patterns before the talk can go on
optionExplain: A term can exclude a listener, but the authors present the vocabulary as something to share and spread.
Right: the authors say using patterns can inspire those who do not know them to start learning.
Nothing in the text asks listeners to know all patterns first.
The authors say there is no library of patterns to install.
questions.explain: Pattern names do more than save words for those who know them. They also give colleagues who do not know them a reason to learn.
questions.rule: Using the names in front of others invites them to learn.
questions.teaches: Using pattern names in talk can inspire colleagues who do not know patterns to start learning them.

questions.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
questions.q: A team says its Report class uses the Strategy Pattern, but the code is one long if-statement on the report type. What is wrong with the claim?
options: Nothing, since a pattern name only needs to be said aloud to count
Strategy forbids any if-statement anywhere in a program
Strategy implies behavior in classes of its own, which an if-statement lacks
Strategy applies only to games that simulate animals
optionExplain: A name carries qualities and constraints, so a false claim misleads the listener.
An if-statement elsewhere is no problem; the claim fails because the structure is missing.
Right: the name promises encapsulated behavior in classes of its own, which listeners will assume.
The pattern applies to any family of interchangeable algorithms.
questions.explain: Because a pattern name carries a whole set of qualities, using it for code that lacks them brings back the misunderstanding the vocabulary was meant to remove.
questions.rule: Use a pattern name only for a design that has the pattern's structure.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: Sort each item: is it a library or framework, or a design pattern?

items.t: Java's networking classes
A GUI toolkit's window classes
A way to structure classes so one behavior can vary
Strategy
A package of file input and output code
A reusable design you adapt to your own application

questions.explain: Libraries and frameworks supply code you link in. Patterns supply designs you learn and adapt.
questions.rule: Code you link in is a library; a design you adapt is a pattern.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A reviewer approves a design only because it uses a named pattern. According to the guru, what does the reviewer overlook?
options: That judgment is still needed, since design has trade-offs
Nothing, since time-tested patterns settle a design
That a library containing the pattern must still be added
That knowing encapsulation and inheritance is enough on its own
optionExplain: Right: the guru says there will always be trade-offs, so the choice still needs judgment.
The guru says following proven patterns puts you way ahead, but not that they settle everything.
The authors say there is no library of patterns to add.
The guru calls the idea that the basics are enough a misunderstanding.
questions.explain: A pattern is a proven starting point, not a verdict. The designer still weighs the trade-offs for the application.
questions.rule: Patterns inform design decisions; they do not replace them.

questions.q: Sort each statement: does the chapter say it, or does the chapter not say it?

items.t: Patterns are discovered, not invented
Patterns are code you paste into your application
Most patterns let one part of a system vary independently
Knowing the OO basics makes you a good designer
Patterns give developers a shared language
Libraries and frameworks are design patterns

questions.explain: The bullet points describe patterns as discovered general solutions that address change and give a shared language. They reject the other three statements.
questions.rule: Patterns are general solutions to apply, not code to paste.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: A client wants a dashboard whose panels refresh when sensor readings change, and wants outside developers to add panels later. What is the main pressure on the design?
options: Sensor readings must be saved in a database before any panel is shown
All panels must look identical to each other
Panels must be added and removed without rewriting the sensor code
Panels must refresh on a fixed timer, once a second, whatever the sensors do
optionExplain: Storage may be useful, but nothing in the request mentions saving readings.
Looks are not mentioned; the request is about who can add panels.
Right: the wish for outside developers to add panels is a demand about change.
A timer is one way to refresh, but the request is about reacting to changes, and a timer says nothing about adding panels.
questions.explain: The request stresses that new panels will come later from other people, so the design must absorb them without edits to the sensor code. The card next lays out this kind of requirement.
questions.rule: Before designing, separate what is given, what must be built, and what must stay open to change.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: WeatherData has getters for temperature, humidity and ____.
questions.explain: The three tracked values are temperature, humidity and barometric pressure.
questions.rule: Know the data the subject owns.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: The team cannot see the code that calls measurementsChanged(). What does the chapter have them do about that?
options: Rely only on the fact that it runs when new readings arrive
Rewrite it so that the displays themselves control when it runs and how often
Study the caller and copy its timing into each display
Replace it with a loop that checks readings repeatedly
optionExplain: Right: the contract is enough, and the callers are not their concern.
The team is asked to fill the method, not to take over its scheduling.
Copying the caller’s timing ties every display to details nobody asked them to know.
Polling is a different design and the spec gives no reason to change how the method is triggered.
questions.explain: The authors say we do not know or care how the method is called; we only know that it is, when data is available. A design can lean on a stated contract without knowing the code behind it.
questions.rule: Rely on the stated contract, not on the unseen internals.
questions.teaches: A design should depend on what a trigger promises (it fires when new data exists), not on how the code behind it works.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: A greenhouse object has getters for temperature and moisture and runs readingsChanged() when its sensors report. Sort each item by whether the spec gives it or leaves it to our team.
groups: Left for our team to build

items.t: The getters for temperature and moisture
The sensors calling readingsChanged()
A moisture dashboard that updates itself
A fan panel that updates itself
A way for a grower to add a custom panel later
The sensor hardware that takes readings

questions.explain: The greenhouse object, its getters and the sensor calls are supplied. Every screen, and the ability to add more, is the team’s work.
questions.rule: Name what is supplied before deciding what to build.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: A client says: we need email and SMS alerts now, and other teams may add chat alerts later. Which statement should shape the design most?
options: The statement that email comes first in priority for the client
The statement that two channels exist today
The statement that alerts go to customers
The statement that more alert channels may be added later
optionExplain: The order of priority is not stated, and it would not change how new channels are added.
Today’s two channels are a snapshot; designing only for them is the trap in the first attempt.
Who receives alerts is a detail; it does not decide how channels are added.
Right: it tells the designer the set of channels is open, so a fixed list would break.
questions.explain: A requirement about future change outweighs the current list, because a design fitted to today’s list has to be reopened when the list grows.
questions.rule: Requirements about future change shape a design more than the current list.
questions.teaches: A requirement that says more variants will come tells the designer what to keep open, and outweighs the list of variants known today.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: True or false: Suppose the spec said only three displays would ever exist and nobody could add or remove them. The requirement that outside developers can plug in displays would then no longer be part of the spec.
questions.explain: That requirement is exactly the one the spec states for the real project; with the three displays frozen it would disappear. The change tells you which requirement was driving the design.
questions.rule: Ask which requirement would vanish if conditions changed.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: A teammate says: we know the three displays, so design exactly those three. What does this overlook?
options: That the displays must be written in the same language as WeatherData
That other developers must be able to add displays, so the set will grow
That measurementsChanged() has to be rewritten to find out who calls it
That the three displays must each store the readings in their own database
optionExplain: The spec says nothing about language; the open point is who adds displays.
Right: the open-ended requirement is what the three-display plan ignores.
The authors say the team does not know or care how the method is called.
Storage is not mentioned in the spec; the displays only show conditions.
questions.explain: The spec also says other developers write their own displays and users add or remove them. A design fitted to three displays would be reopened as soon as the list grows.
questions.rule: Requirements about future change shape a design more than the current list.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: True or false: A class that calls three named display classes one after another whenever its data changes is easy to extend with a fourth display.
questions.explain: Each added display needs another line in that class, so the class must be edited every time. The card next shows how the authors judge such a design.
questions.rule: Judge a design by whether adding or removing a part forces edits to code that should stay stable.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: Which problem comes from hard-coding the calls to three display classes inside measurementsChanged()?
options: The displays can no longer read the temperature
Each new display means editing that method
The method runs too slowly on every reading
WeatherData loses its getter methods
optionExplain: Reading values is unaffected; the displays receive them in the calls.
Right: the display list is fixed in the method body, so every change touches it.
Speed is not the issue the authors raise.
The getters stay; they are not touched by this choice.
questions.explain: The list of displays lives inside the code, so adding one means changing and recompiling that code.
questions.rule: The list of recipients should not be written into the sender’s code.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: With the hard-coded design, a user wants to switch off the forecast display while the program runs. Which flaw does this expose?
options: Displays do not store the measurements they are shown
No way to add or remove displays at run time
Humidity values are shown in the wrong units on screen
The getters return the wrong type of value to the caller
optionExplain: Storing is not at issue; the displays receive the values they show.
Right: the update calls are fixed when the code is written.
Units have nothing to do with who is updated.
Types of the getters are not the issue.
questions.explain: Because the calls are compiled into the method, the set of displays cannot change while the program runs. Changing it at run time needs the list held as data that can be altered.
questions.rule: A list fixed in code cannot change at run time.
questions.teaches: Whether recipients can change at run time depends on whether the list is data held by the sender or calls written into its code.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: A ticket system calls the concrete classes SmsSender and EmailSender by name whenever a ticket changes. Select the flaws that apply.
options: It codes to concrete classes instead of a shared interface
It keeps ticket text in a database
A new channel means editing the ticket class
It cannot reply to the customer
optionExplain: Right: the ticket class names the two concrete classes directly.
Where the text is stored is not part of the checklist.
Right: each new channel is a new edit to the ticket class.
Replying is a feature question, not a design flaw of this kind.
questions.explain: Naming concrete senders in the ticket class mirrors the weather example: concrete classes, and an edit for each new variant.
questions.rule: Concrete names in the sender mean edits for each new variant.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: True or false: A teammate defends hard-coded calls for a calculator with exactly two screens that are fixed for good. By this chapter’s reasoning, the flaws cost as much there as they do in the extensible weather application.
questions.explain: The flaws were judged against the weather spec’s demand for added displays. Where no change is expected, the same hard-coding costs little.
questions.rule: Weigh each design flaw by how much change the spec expects.
questions.teaches: A design flaw has a price that depends on how much change is expected; where change is not expected, the same hard-coding is cheap.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: A reviewer says: the hard-coded design is fine because each display really does receive its update. What is missing from this judgement?
options: It ignores that displays should be fast enough for readings arriving often
It forgets to count how many getters the measurement class has
It assumes the client’s CEO has already approved the whole design
It tests today’s behaviour, not what happens when displays are added or removed
optionExplain: Speed is not part of the argument.
The getter count is irrelevant to the judgement.
Approval is not a design criterion in the chapter.
Right: the design is judged against the demand for change, not for working once.
questions.explain: A design that works for the present list can still fail the spec’s requirement that the list change. Judging soundness means testing against the whole spec.
questions.rule: Judge a design by whether adding or removing a part forces edits to code that should stay stable.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: Select the statements that are true of this method and its fields.
options: The calls run in an order that loses some of the readings
It names concrete display classes, not a shared interface
Adding a third display means editing measurementsChanged()
A display cannot be removed while the program is running
The getters of the measurement class are missing
optionExplain: The order of two calls does not lose readings; each receives the same values.
True: the fields are typed CurrentDisplay and StatsDisplay.
True: the list of displays is written in the method body.
True: the calls are fixed in the code, so the set cannot change at run time.
Not shown here and not a flaw of this design; the values arrive as parameters.
questions.explain: The fields are typed by concrete display classes, a fourth display needs another line in the method, and the calls are compiled in, so nothing can be unplugged while the program runs. The order of calls and the getters are not the problem.
questions.rule: Judge a design by whether adding or removing a part forces edits to code that should stay stable.

questions.q: Which everyday arrangement is most like objects being told automatically whenever something changes?
options: A magazine subscription, with each issue sent to those signed up
A library catalogue, where you look up a book each time you need one
A phone book, where you search for a number when you want to call
A vending machine, where you ask for an item on each visit
optionExplain: Right: the source reaches out to its current list when something new exists.
In a catalogue the reader must go and look; nothing is sent.
A phone book is consulted on demand, not delivered.
A vending machine responds only to a request each time.
questions.explain: The source of change pushes news to those who signed up, instead of each person checking. The card next builds on this picture.
questions.rule: Think of a subscription: delivery follows the current list, and recipients can join and leave at any time.

questions.q: True or false: Once you unsubscribe from a publisher, new editions stop being delivered to you.
questions.explain: Deliveries follow the current subscription list, so leaving the list ends them.
questions.rule: Delivery follows the current list.

questions.q: Hotels and airlines subscribe to the same paper as individuals. What does that suggest about how the publisher treats subscribers?
options: It prints a different edition for each type of subscriber it has
It checks each subscriber’s kind of business before delivering
It delivers the same edition to anyone on the list
It lets the subscribers decide when each edition is printed
optionExplain: Different editions per type would add knowledge about subscribers that the picture does not need.
Checking each subscriber is extra knowledge the picture never calls for.
Right: being on the list is all that matters to the publisher.
Subscribers receive editions; they do not control printing.
questions.explain: The publisher does not need to know what kind of recipient it has, only that the recipient is on the list. This is the seed of loose coupling.
questions.rule: The sender needs to know only who is on the list.
questions.teaches: The sender can treat every recipient alike because membership of the list is the only thing it has to know about them.

questions.q: Match each part of the newspaper picture to its counterpart in a podcast app.
pairs: A listener who follows the show
Tapping follow on the show page
questions.explain: The producer plays the publisher, followers are subscribers, following is subscribing and each episode is an edition.
questions.rule: Map the roles, not the surface details.

questions.q: A shop posts a sign saying come and check whether there is news. Customers drop in to look. How does this differ from a subscription?
options: It is the same, since customers still hear the news in the end
It is a subscription with a very large list of customers
Customers must check by themselves; nobody reaches them
It delivers news to some customers but not others on purpose
optionExplain: Hearing the news is not the point; who acts is.
There is no list and no delivery in the sign model.
Right: in a subscription the source reaches out; here the customer does the checking.
Selective delivery is not what the sign does.
questions.explain: A subscription flips who acts: the source reaches those on its list, rather than each interested party repeatedly checking the source.
questions.rule: Subscriptions put the work of telling on the source.
questions.teaches: In a subscription the source does the reaching out; with a notice board each interested party has to keep checking.

questions.q: A thousand more people subscribe to a newspaper overnight. What changes in how the publisher produces each edition?
options: Nothing about producing the edition; only the delivery list grows
The edition has to be redesigned for a much larger audience
The publisher must ask each new subscriber what it wants
Each existing subscriber must be told about all the newcomers
optionExplain: Right: producing the edition is independent of who receives it.
Content could change for other reasons, but a longer list does not require it.
The picture has no step where the publisher asks subscribers anything.
Subscribers do not need to know about each other.
questions.explain: Production and delivery are separate in the picture, so a longer list does not touch how editions are made.
questions.rule: Think of a subscription: delivery follows the current list, and recipients can join and leave at any time.

questions.q: What does this code print?
options: deliver to Ann, then deliver to Bo, then deliver to Cy
deliver to Bo, then deliver to Cy
deliver to Cy only
deliver to Bo only
optionExplain: This ignores the remove call: Ann has unsubscribed.
Right: the list holds Bo and Cy when the loop runs.
Bo never left the list.
Cy joined before the deliveries, so Cy is on the list too.
questions.explain: Ann is removed before the deliveries run, and Cy was added before them. Delivery follows the list as it stands when the loop runs.
questions.rule: Think of a subscription: delivery follows the current list, and recipients can join and leave at any time.

questions.q: A thermostat object changes its reading and several screens refresh. Which word best names the thermostat’s role in the Observer Pattern?
options: Observer, because it is watched by the screens
Listener, because it hears the room temperature
Client, because the screens use its reading
Subject, because it owns the state that changes
optionExplain: The screens are the observers; the thermostat is the thing being observed.
It listens to the room, but in this pattern “listener” is a synonym for observer, the receiving side.
“Client” is not one of the pattern’s role names.
Right: the thermostat holds the changing state the screens depend on.
questions.explain: The object that owns the changing state is the subject. The card next defines it with its partner term.
questions.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.

questions.q: Match each term of the pattern to its meaning.
pairs: The object that holds the state and the list
An object that wants to hear about changes
Ask to be put on the list
Ask to be taken off the list
questions.explain: Subject and observer are the two roles. Registering and removing are how observers join and leave the subject’s list.
questions.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.

questions.q: Who asks for an object to become an observer?
options: The subject searches for objects that look interested
The object itself asks the subject to register it
A third manager object assigns observers to subjects
The state is copied to every object automatically
optionExplain: The subject has no way to know who is interested without being told.
Right: the Duck tells the subject it wants in.
The card describes no manager; the observer asks.
Nothing is copied to objects that have not registered.
questions.explain: Registration is requested by the observer, so the subject only has to keep its list and does not need to find observers.
questions.rule: Observers sign themselves up.
questions.teaches: Registration is the observer’s request, which means the subject keeps no knowledge of who might want to join.

questions.q: A stock price feed tells a chart widget, an alert bell and a logger whenever a price changes. Sort each description by role.

items.t: The object that holds the current price
The object that keeps the list of who to tell
The object that asks to join the list
The object that receives each notification
The widget that redraws on a new price
The object that sends the notifications

questions.explain: The feed owns the price, keeps the list and sends notifications. The widget, bell and logger ask to join and receive notifications.
questions.rule: Subject owns and sends; observer joins and receives.

questions.q: In a smart-home app a door sensor reports open and a lamp and an alarm react. A teammate calls the lamp the subject because it is the visible part. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the visible object is always the subject
The subject is the sensor, the object that holds the changing state
The alarm should be the subject because it matters most
Neither lamp nor sensor is a subject; only the app is
optionExplain: Visibility does not decide the role; the sentence overgeneralises.
Right: roles follow who owns the state and who depends on it.
Importance does not decide the role either.
The sensor owns the state here; the app is only the setting.
questions.explain: The subject is picked by what it holds: the changing state. The lamp and alarm depend on it, so they are the observers.
questions.rule: Roles follow who owns the state, not who is most visible.
questions.teaches: Roles in the pattern are defined by who owns the changing state and who depends on it, not by importance or visibility.

questions.q: A new display object is created but does not ask to register. The subject’s state then changes. What happens?
options: The subject registers it as soon as its own state changes
The display receives the change after a short delay of some kind
The display is told once about the change and is then removed
The display receives nothing, since only registered observers are notified
optionExplain: The subject does not add objects by itself; observers ask.
No delay mechanism exists; being off the list means no notification.
Removal only happens when an observer asks.
Right: notifications go to the list, and the display is not on it.
questions.explain: Being on the list is what earns a notification, and joining is the observer’s own step.
questions.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.

questions.q: A tutorial says: the observer holds the state and keeps the list of subjects. Which correction is right?
options: The observer keeps the list and subjects ask to be added to it
Both hold state, but only the subject holds a list of observers
The subject holds the list and the observers hold the state
The subject holds the state and the list of its observers
optionExplain: This swaps who keeps the list.
Observers use state; the subject is its owner.
State and list both belong to the subject; observers only use the state.
Right: the subject owns both the state and the list.
questions.explain: The roles are the other way round: the subject holds the state and the list of observers, and observers ask to join that list.
questions.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: An object has asked a subject to stop sending it updates, and then the subject’s state changes. What is the most likely outcome?
options: It is skipped for this change but can ask to join again later
It still gets this change but none of the ones after it, either
It is told about the change by a different object instead
It is blocked from ever observing that subject again
optionExplain: Right: removal takes effect for later changes, and rejoining is allowed.
Removal takes effect immediately, not after one more update.
The subject does the telling, and only to its list.
Nothing in the story bars a second registration.
questions.explain: Leaving ends notifications from then on, and joining again is possible. The card next walks through the story.
questions.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change’s notification.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: Put these events from the book’s walkthrough in order.
items: An object asks the subject to make it an observer
The subject adds it to its list of observers
The subject gets a new data value
The subject notifies every observer on its list
The object asks to be removed
Later changes skip the removed object
questions.explain: The sequence is: join, be added, state changes, everyone on the list is notified, leave, and be skipped afterwards.
questions.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change’s notification.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: True or false: Once an observer has removed itself, it is barred from observing the same subject again.
questions.explain: The Mouse may ask to be an observer again some day, and from then it would be notified of later changes.
questions.rule: Leaving can be undone by registering again.
questions.teaches: Removal is reversible: an object that left the list can register again and then receives later notifications.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: A chat channel notifies members of each post. Ana joins at 9:00 and Bo at 9:05. Ana leaves at 9:10, then a message is posted at 9:15. Who is notified?
options: Ana only
Both Ana and Bo
Bo only
Nobody, since the membership changed recently
optionExplain: Ana left before the post, so she is skipped.
Ana was removed, so she is not on the list.
Right: Bo is on the list at 9:15 and Ana is not.
Membership changes do not suspend notifications; the current list is used.
questions.explain: The list at 9:15 holds Bo alone, because Ana was taken off at 9:10.
questions.rule: Notify the list as it stands at the moment of the change.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: A flash-sale subject sends an update at 10:00. Cy registers at 10:30. Does Cy receive the 10:00 update?
options: Yes, since Cy is on the list now, past updates are re-sent
Yes, but only the update that came right before registering
No, Cy hears only about changes that happen after registering
Only if Cy also removes itself and joins again
optionExplain: Nothing in the story replays history to new observers.
There is no step in the story that sends one previous update.
Right: the walkthrough sends a notification when the state changes, to those on the list then.
Rejoining does not replay anything either.
questions.explain: Notification happens at the moment of a change, so a late observer misses earlier changes. Our reading: a new observer may need another way to learn the current state.
questions.rule: A new observer does not hear about past changes.
questions.teaches: An observer can also un-register later, so it helps to keep a reference to the subject.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: A student summarises the walkthrough. Select the two statements that are wrong.
options: The subject notifies only the newest observer
A removed observer is skipped on later changes
An observer can register again after leaving
A removed observer still receives later notifications
optionExplain: Wrong: every observer on the list is notified.
Correct as told: the Mouse is skipped after removal.
Correct as told: the Mouse may ask again.
Wrong: removal ends later notifications.
questions.explain: Notification goes to the whole list, and removal ends it. The two wrong statements each break one of these facts.
questions.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change’s notification.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: What does this code print?
options: X 1 then X 2
X 1 then X 2 then Y 2
X 1 then Y 2
Y 2 only
optionExplain: X was removed before the second round.
X is not on the list in round two, so it receives nothing.
Right: each round goes to the list as it stands then.
X was on the list for round one and was notified.
questions.explain: X is on the list for the first round and gets 1. Then Y joins and X leaves, so the second round reaches Y only.
questions.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change's notification.

questions.q: In a group chat, the group object notifies members of new messages, and each member object also notifies a status bot when the member goes online. Is a member breaking the pattern?
options: No, a member can be an observer of the group and a subject for the bot
Yes, because an observer can never also serve as a subject for other objects
Yes, since the bot should observe the group object directly
No, because group members are neither subjects nor observers
optionExplain: Right: roles belong to relationships, so one object can hold several.
The pattern places no such ban on an object.
The bot may observe the group too, but the pattern does not require it.
Members are observers of the group, so they do take a role.
questions.explain: The roles are about relationships, so an object can have one role in one and another elsewhere. The card next shows the book’s example.
questions.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.

questions.q: True or false: In the skit, Lori ends up only as an observer, with no observers of her own.
questions.explain: Lori keeps observing the headhunter and builds her own call list, so she is also a subject.
questions.rule: Lori is both.

questions.q: A news agency tells a regional paper, which tells its readers. If the agency stops publishing, what do the readers receive?
options: New items, since the paper itself becomes the subject for the readers
Items from the agency, delayed by the paper’s own work
The paper’s own items, which are unaffected by upstream
Nothing new, because the paper has nothing from upstream to relay
optionExplain: The paper stays a subject, but only has what it receives or produces itself.
There is nothing to be delayed once the agency has stopped.
The paper might produce its own items, but this chain is about relayed ones.
Right: each link depends on the one before it.
questions.explain: In a chain, each object depends on the one upstream, so a break upstream silences what depends on it.
questions.rule: In a chain every link depends on the one above.
questions.teaches: A chain relays changes through layers, and each layer depends on the one before, so an upstream break silences everything below it.

questions.q: A warehouse sensor tells a stock tracker when a shelf is empty. The tracker tells a purchasing screen and a supplier emailer when stock runs low. Select the true statements.
options: The stock tracker is an observer of the sensor
The stock tracker is a subject for the screen and the emailer
The purchasing screen is a subject for the sensor
The sensor is an observer of the stock tracker
optionExplain: True: it depends on the sensor’s reports.
True: it keeps its own list and tells them.
False: the screen only receives what the tracker sends.
False: the sensor does not depend on the tracker.
questions.explain: The tracker sits in the middle with both roles. The screen and emailer are only observers; the sensor is only a subject.
questions.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.

questions.q: A spreadsheet cell B1 depends on A1, and cell C1 depends on B1. Which description fits B1?
options: A subject for A1 and an observer of C1
An observer of A1 and a subject for C1
A subject only, since it holds a value
An observer only, since it depends on A1
optionExplain: This reverses both directions.
Right: it follows A1 and is followed by C1.
It holds a value, but C1 depends on it too, so it also observes.
C1 depends on B1, so B1 is also a subject.
questions.explain: A chain of dependent values lets a change ripple through layers, and each layer chooses what to pass on.
questions.rule: Chained dependencies let one change ripple through several layers.
questions.teaches: Chained links let a change ripple through several layers, and each middle object is both an observer and a subject.

questions.q: Lori stops observing the headhunter but keeps her own call list. What happens to her observers?
options: They keep hearing the headhunter’s news through her anyway
They hear nothing about the headhunter, though she can announce her own news
They are removed from her own list automatically, as well
They become observers of the headhunter directly at once
optionExplain: She has stopped receiving it, so there is nothing to relay.
Right: she no longer receives it, so she cannot relay it.
Nothing removes observers except their own request.
Nothing moves them; they stay on her list.
questions.explain: What she relays depends on what she receives, while her own news is still hers to announce.
questions.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.

questions.q: What does this code print?
options: B got hi, then C got hi!
B got hi only
C got hi!, then B got hi
B got hi, then C got hi
optionExplain: Right: B receives hi, then tells its own list the message with an exclamation mark.
B passes the message on to its own list, so C is told too.
C hears only after B has received the message and passed it on.
B adds an exclamation mark before passing the message on.
questions.explain: The first list holds an object that is an observer of the first source and a subject for the second list. It prints its own line and passes on a changed message.
questions.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.

questions.q: The Observer Pattern defines a one-to-____ dependency between objects.
questions.explain: One object, the subject, has many dependents. The card next gives the full definition.
questions.rule: Observer is when one object’s state change automatically notifies all its dependents.

questions.q: True or false: In the Observer Pattern, the dependents are notified when the state of the one object changes.
questions.explain: The trigger in the definition is a change in the state of the one object.
questions.rule: The trigger is a change of state.

questions.q: Does the definition require the subject to send the new values along with its notification?
options: Yes, a notification must always contain the new values themselves
No, because observers never need any values from the subject at all
Yes, but only for the very first notification that is sent
No, it leaves open how the values reach the dependents
optionExplain: This treats one common style as the definition itself.
Observers usually do need values; the point is how they get them.
Nothing in the definition separates a first notification.
Right: the definition leaves the style of notification open.
questions.explain: The definition fixes that dependents are told about a change, not how the data reaches them. Sending values along and letting observers fetch them are two styles.
questions.rule: The definition fixes who is told and when, not how the data travels.
questions.teaches: The definition leaves open whether the new values travel with the notification or the observer fetches them afterwards.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it fits the Observer Pattern or not.

items.t: A fitness tracker refreshes a watch face and phone widget when steps change
A calendar event update refreshes every attendee’s view
A calculator returns a result when asked
A function sorts a list and hands it back
A group chat pushes each new message to every member
A converter turns one file into another on request

questions.explain: The fitting cases have one changing source and many dependents told automatically. The others are on-demand requests with a single caller.
questions.rule: Look for one changing source and many dependents told automatically.

questions.q: An operations room has staff who must refresh their screens by hand after a change. Which word of the definition does this arrangement fail?
options: Automatically, because the change itself does not cause the update
One-to-many, because there are many screens on the wall
Dependency, because the screens depend on the data they show
State, because the shared data has no state of its own
optionExplain: Right: here a person must act after every change.
There are many screens, so this part holds.
The screens still depend on the data.
The data has state; the failing part is how the screens learn of changes.
questions.explain: Automatic means the change itself causes the notification, with no manual step or checking by the dependents.
questions.rule: Automatic means no manual step by the dependents.
questions.teaches: Automatic in the definition means that the notification follows from the change itself, with no manual step or polling by the dependents.

questions.q: A student restates the pattern: many objects change state and one object is notified. What is wrong?
options: It leaves out the word dependency, which is the only word needed
It says state where the definition says value, which changes the meaning
It reverses the direction: one object changes and many are notified
Nothing is wrong, since both directions describe the same pattern
optionExplain: Dependency matters, but the main fault is the reversed direction.
The definition uses state; this is not the fault.
Right: the one is the source of change and the many are notified.
The directions are not interchangeable.
questions.explain: The subject is the one source of change and the observers are the many dependents who are told.
questions.rule: Observer is when one object’s state change automatically notifies all its dependents.

questions.q: Which situation is an instance of the Observer Pattern as defined?
options: A report tool runs a query and prints the rows when a user presses a button
A checkout page calls a payment function and waits for its single answer
A price ticker updates a chart, an alert bell and a log whenever a price changes
A teacher asks each pupil in turn for a page number, one pupil at a time
optionExplain: A button press starts one request; no dependents are told about a state change.
One caller asks and one function answers: no one-to-many dependency.
Right: a change of state tells many dependents automatically.
The teacher polls each pupil; nobody is told automatically.
questions.explain: Only the ticker has one source of change and several dependents told automatically. The others are single requests and answers, or a manual loop.
questions.rule: Look for one changing source and many dependents told automatically.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: A playlist is edited by its owner and shown on several devices. Where should the playlist data be controlled?
options: In every device, each one editing and keeping its own copy
In whichever device made the latest edit, switching over to others as time goes on
In one object that owns it, with the devices depending on that object
In a copy per device, with none treated as the real one
optionExplain: Many editable copies would drift apart.
The owner would change from edit to edit, and no one could rely on it.
Right: one owner means one place where the truth lives.
Without an authoritative copy, devices cannot agree.
questions.explain: A single owner gives the other objects one place to rely on. The card next names this relationship.
questions.rule: One object owns and controls the state; many others depend on it for updates.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: Because the subject is the ____ owner of the data, the observers depend on it for updates.
questions.explain: The subject alone owns and controls the state, so every observer relies on it.
questions.rule: One owner, many dependents.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: Why do the authors call one owner a cleaner design than many objects controlling the same data?
options: Only one place can change the state, so none disagree
Fewer classes are needed in total, so the design is smaller overall
Observers become faster at reading the data they depend on
The data can be stored in less memory than before
optionExplain: Right: a single owner removes conflicting changes by different objects.
The count of classes is not the argument.
Speed is not what the authors claim.
Memory is not what the authors claim.
questions.explain: With one owner there is one place where changes are made and one source of truth. Shared control would let objects change the same data in conflicting ways.
questions.rule: One owner, one source of truth.
questions.teaches: A single owner means one place to change the data and one source of truth, while shared control lets objects make conflicting changes.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: One flight record is shown on a gate screen, an airline app and an airport board. Select the true statements.
options: The flight record is the one that owns the state
Each screen edits its own copy of the status
The screens depend on the flight record for changes
Adding a fourth screen creates a second subject
optionExplain: True: it owns the status.
False: that would give many owners.
True: they rely on it to be told.
False: a new screen is one more observer; the subject stays one.
