questions.explain: The authors write that decorators are the same type as the components they decorate, either through inheritance or interface implementation.
questions.rule: Same type by inheritance or interface.
questions.teaches: Either route, extending a class or implementing an interface, gives a decorator the same type as its component; what matters is the shared type.

questions.q: True or false: Pat says the Decorator Pattern cannot be used in Java unless the component type is an interface.
questions.explain: The Starbuzz design uses an abstract class, and the authors say an interface could also be used. Both give the shared type.
questions.rule: Both routes work.

questions.q: A new project has no legacy code. Someone argues that it should be an abstract class because working code should be left alone. How strong is that argument here?
options: It applies fully, because abstract classes are required
It does not apply, since there is no existing working class to protect
It applies fully, because interfaces cannot supply a type to the program
It applies, because the authors forbid interfaces
optionExplain: Neither choice is required.
The reasoning protects existing code; a new project has none.
Interfaces can supply a type.
The authors say an interface could be used.
questions.explain: The argument for keeping the class rests on existing code. Without it, the choice rests on design preferences.
questions.rule: Reasons for leaving code alone need code to leave.
questions.teaches: The advice not to fix what works presumes working code to protect; with a blank slate, the decision rests on design preferences.

questions.q: The shared type here is an interface, not an abstract class. The program prints ____.
questions.explain: Each Milk calls cost() on what it wraps and adds 0.25: 1.5 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 2.0. An interface supplies the shared type just as an abstract class does.
questions.rule: The pattern works the same whether the shared type is an interface or an abstract class.

questions.q: A Mocha decorator's cost() must return the price of the whole drink so far. How does it most plausibly get the drink part of that price?
options: It asks the beverage it wraps for its cost
It reads the price from a global price list for every drink
It calls cost() on every drink in the shop
It stores the drink's price when the program starts
optionExplain: The wrapped beverage already knows its own cost.
A decorator would then ignore the object it wraps.
Only the wrapped drink is relevant.
Prices of wrapped objects must come from the objects themselves.
questions.explain: Delegation to the wrapped object is the natural source. The card next shows the recipe.
questions.rule: Ask the wrapped object.

questions.q: A concrete decorator keeps a reference to the ____ it wraps.
questions.explain: Without that reference the decorator could not delegate.
questions.rule: A decorator holds what it wraps.

questions.q: A Book has the description Book. A GiftWrap decorator wraps it, then a Card decorator wraps the GiftWrap. Each decorator returns the wrapped description, a comma and its own name. What does getDescription() on Card return?
options: Card
Card, GiftWrap, Book
Book, GiftWrap, Card
Book, Card
optionExplain: This is only the outermost decorator's name.
The names are added on the way out, so the plain item appears first.
Card asks GiftWrap, which asks Book, and each adds its name on the way out.
GiftWrap sits between Book and Card and adds its name too.
questions.explain: Each layer appends its own name to what the inner one returned.
questions.rule: Append your name to what came back.

questions.q: The same Mocha class is used to wrap an Espresso in one order and a Whip-wrapped DarkRoast in another. Can one Mocha class do both?
options: No, a decorator class can wrap only one kind of drink, never a different kind afterward
Yes; it holds a reference of the shared Beverage type, so it accepts any beverage
Yes, but only if Mocha extends both drinks
No, because Mocha cannot wrap another decorator
optionExplain: Wrappers are written against the shared type, not a single drink.
The reference is typed to the shared type.
Mocha extends the shared type only.
Decorators wrap decorators.
questions.explain: Since the reference is of the shared type, the same wrapper works over any beverage or chain.
questions.rule: One decorator class, any component.
questions.teaches: Because a decorator's reference is typed to the shared type, one decorator class can wrap any component or chain of components.

questions.q: True or false: A Whip decorator whose cost() returns only its own charge, leaving the other classes to add theirs, still gives the correct total price.
questions.explain: The wrapped drink's cost is never included, so the total is wrong. A decorator must add its charge to what the wrapped object returns.
questions.rule: Delegate, then add.

questions.q: Mocha is written to accept any Beverage. What does that imply about odd combinations, such as mocha on a drink where it makes no sense?
options: The type does not prevent them, so the code that builds orders has to enforce sensible combinations
The compiler will refuse any odd combination
The Beverage class will refuse the wrapper at runtime
Odd combinations are impossible with decorators
optionExplain: Any Beverage fits, so rules must come from elsewhere.
The shared type allows every combination.
Beverage has no such checks in this design.
Any wrapper can wrap any component of the shared type.
questions.explain: The authors note that decorated objects are typically created by other patterns, so combinations are managed in creation code.
questions.rule: Creation code decides sensible combinations.
questions.teaches: A decorator accepts any component of the shared type, so nothing in the pattern prevents odd combinations; the creation code must manage them.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: Latte, Mocha, Mocha 3.5
Mocha, Mocha, Latte 3.5
Latte, Mocha, Mocha 0.5
Latte 2.5
optionExplain: The description grows outward from Latte, and the cost adds 0.5 twice to 2.5.
It puts the wrappers before the drink, but each decorator appends to the inner description.
It reads only the added charge, forgetting that Mocha adds to the wrapped cost.
It ignores the wrappers; each Mocha changes both the description and the cost.
questions.explain: Each Mocha asks the wrapped drink for its description and cost, then adds its own part. Two Mochas around a Latte give Latte, Mocha, Mocha and 2.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 3.5.
questions.rule: A decorator builds on what the wrapped object returns, so the innermost part comes first.

questions.q: What happens when main calls cost() on this Whip?
options: It prints 2.6, because the latte is passed to the constructor
It prints 0.1, because a missing drink counts as zero
It throws NullPointerException, because the wrapped drink was never stored
It does not compile, because the constructor ignores its parameter
optionExplain: Passing the argument is not enough; the constructor never keeps it.
Java does not treat a null reference as zero; calling a method on it fails.
The field in is still null when cost() calls in.cost().
Java allows a constructor to ignore its parameter, so it compiles.
questions.explain: The constructor ignores its parameter, so the field in stays null. cost() then calls in.cost() on null and throws a NullPointerException. A concrete decorator must store the component it wraps.
questions.rule: A concrete decorator must keep the reference to the object it wraps.

questions.q: A discount rule applies when a drink is a HouseBlend. The HouseBlend is then wrapped by a Mocha decorator. What most likely happens to the rule?
options: It still applies, since the HouseBlend is still inside the Mocha wrapper
It stops applying, because the outer object is not a HouseBlend
It applies twice, once for each layer
It raises an error when the wrapper is created
optionExplain: The HouseBlend is inside, but the rule looks at the outer object.
The test looks at the object it receives, which is now a decorator.
Only one object is tested.
Creating a wrapper does not run the rule.
questions.explain: The check inspects the outer object. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Checks see the outer object.

questions.q: True or false: Decorators are transparent to client code that is written against the abstract component type.
questions.explain: Such code calls the shared methods and does not care what is inside.
questions.rule: Abstract-type code does not notice decorators.

questions.q: A music player shows a Live banner when a Track is a LiveTrack. A Gain decorator is then wrapped around a LiveTrack. What happens to the banner?
options: The banner stays, since a wrapped LiveTrack is still a LiveTrack
The banner appears twice
The banner disappears, since the outer object is a Gain wrapper
The player crashes at startup
optionExplain: The wrapper shares the Track type, but it is not a LiveTrack.
Only one check is made.
The check tests the object received, which is now the wrapper.
The failure is silent: the check simply is not met.
questions.explain: The wrapper is a Track, but not a LiveTrack.
questions.rule: Concrete checks see the wrapper.

questions.q: Before wrapping existing objects with a new decorator in an existing program, which check protects you most?
options: Check that the decorator has a short and clear name
Count the number of existing subclasses
Confirm the decorators have no methods
Search the client code for tests of concrete types
optionExplain: Names do not affect behaviour.
The count says nothing about concrete type checks.
Decorators must have methods to add behaviour.
Such tests are what stop working after wrapping.
questions.explain: Concrete type tests are the ones to find and rethink before introducing decorators.
questions.rule: Look for concrete type checks first.
questions.teaches: Before introducing decorators into existing code, search that code for checks on concrete types, because those are the places that stop working.

questions.q: After a drink is wrapped in decorators, which client code keeps working and which can break?

items.t: Calls cost() on a Beverage
Prints the result of getDescription()
Passes the drink to a function that accepts any Beverage
Checks whether the drink is a HouseBlend before discounting
Casts the drink to Espresso to read an espresso-only setting
Compares the drink's class name with the text HouseBlend

questions.explain: Code that uses only the shared type is unaffected; code that inspects the concrete class sees the wrapper instead.
questions.rule: Shared-type code survives wrapping.

questions.q: A team's code does not check concrete types. They plan to insert three new decorators and later remove one. How much client code must change because of the type?
options: All of it, because every new decorator changes the type the client sees
Only the code that calls cost()
None, since the client uses only the shared type in both directions
All of it, when a decorator is removed
optionExplain: Decorators keep the shared type.
Calling shared methods needs no change.
Insertion and removal are both invisible to shared-type code.
Removing a decorator leaves the shared type unchanged.
questions.explain: Transparency works both ways: adding or removing a layer does not disturb shared-type code.
questions.rule: Shared type means free to add or remove.
questions.teaches: Transparency works in both directions: for shared-type code, adding, removing or reordering decorators needs no change.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: true
A compile error, because Gift is not an Item
ClassCastException
false
optionExplain: It assumes the test looks inside the wrapper, but instanceof sees only the outer object.
Gift implements Item, so the code compiles.
instanceof never casts, so it cannot throw ClassCastException.
The outer object is a Gift, so the test is false.
questions.explain: x holds a Gift, and a Gift is not a Book, even though it contains one. instanceof checks the outer object only, so it prints false.
questions.rule: A type test sees the outer wrapper, not the object inside it.

questions.q: True or false: A decorator is normally expected to inspect all the other decorators in its chain.
questions.explain: A decorator adds behaviour to the object it wraps; looking through several layers goes beyond its intent. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Work with the object you wrap.

questions.q: To get the effect of every decorator, a client should hold a reference to the ____ decorator.
questions.explain: The outermost layer reaches all the layers inside it through delegation.
questions.rule: Hold the outermost layer.

questions.q: A chain is Plain, wrapped by Tax, wrapped by Tip. A function receives the Tax layer by mistake and calls price() on it. What is missing from its result?
options: The Plain amount
The Tax charge
Both Tax and Plain
The Tip charge
optionExplain: Tax delegates to Plain, so its amount is included.
Tax adds its own charge to Plain's amount.
Tax delegates to Plain and adds itself.
Tip is outside Tax, so the function never sees it.
questions.explain: The function sees only layers from Tax inward, so the Tip charge is lost.
questions.rule: Missing an outer layer means missing its effect.

questions.q: According to the authors, how are worries about holding the wrong layer in the chain eased?
options: Decorators cannot be wrapped more than twice
The compiler warns about any inner reference
Decorated objects are typically created by other patterns, such as Factory and Builder, which keep creation well encapsulated
Clients are told to avoid decorators
optionExplain: There is no such limit.
No such warning exists.
These patterns hand out finished chains.
The authors recommend the pattern.
questions.explain: The authors say creation is well encapsulated by Factory and Builder, so clients seldom assemble chains.
questions.rule: Let creation code hand out finished chains.
questions.teaches: Creation patterns such as Factory and Builder hide the wrapping, so clients receive a finished chain and the risk of holding a wrong layer is reduced.

questions.q: True or false: If getDescription() returns a list of descriptions rather than one string, a pretty-print decorator finds it easier to turn Mocha, Whip, Mocha into Whip, Double Mocha.
questions.explain: The authors suggest returning a list so that a decorator can count repeats and reorder entries more easily.
questions.rule: A list is easier to rearrange than a string.

questions.q: Which signal suggests the design is asking too much of one decorator?
options: The decorator adds a charge to the result returned by the object that it wraps
The outer decorator must parse or inspect what several inner layers did
The decorator is placed in the outermost position
The decorator shares the type of its component
optionExplain: This is the pattern's normal use.
Needing to see through layers is the authors' sign of stretching the pattern.
Position alone is normal.
Sharing the type is required.
questions.explain: A decorator is within the pattern when it works with the output of the one object it wraps.
questions.rule: Within the pattern: one wrapped object.
questions.teaches: A quick test of whether a decorator stays within the pattern is whether it needs only the output of the one object it wraps.

questions.q: Match each problem to the remedy the authors give or mention.
pairs: A client holds an inner decorator and loses the outer charge
Build decorated objects with Factory or Builder patterns
Code tests for HouseBlend and fails after wrapping
Write code against the abstract component type
Mocha, Whip, Mocha should read Whip, Double Mocha
A CondimentPrettyPrint decorator that parses the description
questions.explain: The authors say Factory and Builder encapsulate creation, that code should use the abstract component type, and that a CondimentPrettyPrint decorator could parse the final description.
questions.rule: Each decorator-chain problem has a remedy in the text: encapsulated creation, the abstract type, or an extra decorator.

questions.q: In Java's java.io package, how is a feature such as buffering most likely added to an input stream?
options: By editing the stream class's source
By wrapping the stream in a buffered stream class
By creating a subclass for each combination
By passing a setting to the file system
optionExplain: Library users cannot edit the library.
The buffered class wraps the original stream and adds the feature.
A subclass per combination is the design decorators replace.
Buffering is added by a wrapper, not by the file system.
questions.explain: The library uses wrappers. The card next shows which classes.
questions.rule: Add features by wrapping.

questions.q: Match each java.io class to its role in the pattern.
questions.explain: The authors describe the stream classes as wrappers around an InputStream, with FilterInputStream as the abstract decorator.
questions.rule: Map familiar roles onto java.io.

questions.q: You find a class GzipWrapper that takes an InputStream and extends FilterInputStream. What does that suggest about it?
options: It is a plain file reader with no wrapped stream
It replaces InputStream for all programs
It is an output stream
It adds behaviour to whatever stream it wraps, like a decorator
optionExplain: A class that takes a stream as input wraps it.
It decorates InputStream; it does not replace it.
It extends an input stream class.
It extends the abstract decorator and wraps a stream.
questions.explain: Extending the abstract decorator and holding a stream are the marks of a decorator.
questions.rule: Spot the wrapper by its shape.

questions.q: A developer wants a stream that converts uppercase characters to lowercase. Which approach fits the library's design?
options: Write a new class extending the abstract decorator that wraps a stream
Edit the library's FilterInputStream class
Write a subclass of every existing stream class, one for each possible source
Switch the file to lowercase before reading
optionExplain: The library is built so that new wrappers can be added.
This modifies library code.
This is the class-per-combination design again.
This is a different job from writing a decorator.
questions.explain: The authors suggest writing your own decorator for this task, with no change to the existing classes.
questions.rule: Add your own wrapper to a library built on the pattern.
questions.teaches: A library built on the pattern can be extended with your own wrapper, which needs only the shared type and no change to the library.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the large number of small classes in java.io shows that the Decorator Pattern was misapplied there.
questions.explain: The authors say many small classes are a known downside of the pattern, which can overwhelm developers, not a sign it was misused.
questions.rule: Many small classes are a cost of the pattern.

questions.q: You meet an unfamiliar image library with classes Image, FileImage, ImageFilter, Blur and Sharpen. What is a sensible way to read it using the java.io lesson?
options: Read each class alone, ignoring how they connect
Assume each class is a separate subclass of FileImage
Find the base type and abstract wrapper, then ask what each wrapper such as Blur adds
Avoid the library, because decorators are always confusing
optionExplain: Without the wrapping roles, the structure is hard to see.
Wrappers share the base type; they are not subclasses of the concrete image.
The same roles can be traced in any decorator-based library.
The authors say understanding the pattern makes such APIs easier.
questions.explain: Seeing the roles turns a pile of classes into a set of wrappers.
questions.rule: Trace the roles in any wrapper-based API.
questions.teaches: Any library made of many wrappers can be read by locating the base type and the abstract wrapper, then asking what each wrapper adds.

questions.q: Up is a decorator over an input stream. What does this program print?
options: h
H
HEY
optionExplain: It forgets that Up changes the byte it reads from the wrapped stream.
read() delegates to the wrapped stream for h, Up turns it into H, and the cast prints the character.
This call reads one byte only, not the whole text.
72 is the code for H, but the cast to char prints the character, not the number.
questions.explain: Up extends FilterInputStream, the abstract decorator, and changes the result of read(). The first byte is h; Up returns the upper-case code, and the cast to char prints H.
questions.rule: A new java.io decorator extends the filter class and changes what read() returns.

questions.q: Which of these are costs of the Decorator Pattern that the authors admit?
options: Code that relies on concrete types can break
Decorated objects cannot be passed to code expecting the component type
Creating an object needs more code, to wrap it in decorators
Many small classes can overwhelm developers
Behaviour can only be fixed at compile time
optionExplain: Wrapping hides the concrete type.
Decorated objects share the component's type, so they can be passed.
Instantiation must also build the chain.
The authors cite Java I/O as an example.
Decorating happens at runtime.
questions.explain: Three of these are costs the authors list; the other two get the pattern wrong. The card next gives the full list.
questions.rule: Three costs: many classes, concrete types, creation code.

questions.q: Decorator-based designs often result in a large number of small ____, which can be overwhelming to a developer.
questions.explain: The authors cite java.io as the example of many small classes in a decorator-based API.
questions.rule: Many small classes is the first cost.

questions.q: True or false: A small internal tool needs one optional feature that stays fixed for years, and given the costs the authors list, wrappers would add more structure than that feature needs.
questions.explain: Without a need for runtime flexibility, the costs of many small classes and heavier creation code are paid for little gain.
questions.rule: Costs count against a low-benefit case.

questions.q: The authors state the weaknesses of the Decorator Pattern as well as its strengths (for example, many small objects). What does that suggest about their account?
options: It is weaker, since an account should only describe benefits
It is irrelevant to judging the account
It is a sign the pattern should not be used
It is more complete, because relevant costs are on the table
optionExplain: Hiding weaknesses would make the account less complete.
Whether costs are included is central to completeness.
Naming costs does not show they outweigh the benefits.
Stating costs fills the picture a reader needs.
questions.explain: An account that names the costs of its own proposal is harder to call incomplete on that point.
questions.rule: Look for what an account leaves out.
questions.teaches: When authors name the costs of their own proposal, their account is more complete; leaving out relevant costs is a common way an account falls short.

questions.q: A critic says: 'The chapter only shows benefits of decorators, so it is incomplete.' Which reply is accurate to the text?
options: The chapter also lists many small classes, concrete-type breakage and heavier creation code
The chapter hides all costs, but that is acceptable
Costs are not relevant to a design pattern
The costs appear only in other chapters
optionExplain: These costs appear in the chapter.
The chapter does state costs.
Costs are relevant to a fair account.
The costs are stated in this chapter.
questions.explain: The critic's claim can be checked against the chapter, and it fails.
questions.rule: Check the claim against the text.

questions.q: A reader says that wrappers are unpleasant to look at, so decorators are a bad idea. By the standard of fair criticism, what is missing?
options: Nothing; a strong dislike is enough to reject a design
A vote from other readers
A specific shortcoming, such as a cost the account omits or one that outweighs the benefit
A longer description of the pattern
optionExplain: Dislike is not a reason.
Counting opinions does not test the claim.
Dislike alone shows no fault in the account.
Description does not supply a criticism.
questions.explain: Criticism should name what is wrong or missing, not only how the reader feels.
questions.rule: Dislike is not disagreement.
questions.teaches: Dislike is not a criticism: to fault a design fairly, point to a specific cost, omission or contrary evidence.

questions.q: A new teammate is overwhelmed by a library of many small classes that all wrap one base type. Which view do the authors offer to ease this?
questions.teaches: Seeing the many small classes of a Decorator-heavy API as a set of wrappers around the base component makes the API much easier to understand.
options: Treat each class as a separate tool with no link to the base type
Replace the library with a single large class that has every feature
See the classes as a set of wrappers around the base type, each adding one thing
Wait for a Factory to hide every class so that nobody needs to read them
optionExplain: Ignoring the shared base type hides the very structure that explains the classes.
A single large class gives up the flexibility that the authors credit to the pattern.
The interview says the I/O classes are easier to grasp as wrappers around an InputStream.
The authors mention Factory and Builder for the creation burden, not as a way to hide the classes.
questions.explain: In the interview the pattern says that seeing the classes as a set of wrappers around the base type, such as InputStream, would make life much easier.
questions.rule: A Decorator-heavy API is easier once its classes are read as wrappers around the base type.

questions.q: A method contains the statement new ReportPdf(). What does that statement tie the method to?
options: Only an interface that ReportPdf implements, because the compiler hides the class
Nothing in particular, because new is only a language feature
The concrete class ReportPdf, which the method now names directly
The caller of the method, which must also create a ReportPdf
optionExplain: A variable may be typed to an interface, but the new expression itself still names the class.
It is a language feature, but using it creates a link to the class it names.
Right: the statement names one specific class, so the method depends on that exact class.
Callers are not involved; the link sits inside the method that uses new.
questions.explain: Creating an object names its exact class, so the code depends on that class. The card next shows why this matters when choices change.
questions.rule: new names a concrete class.

questions.q: The authors' reminder is: when you see new, think ____.
questions.explain: Using new instantiates a specific class, which is an implementation rather than an interface.
questions.rule: new means concrete.

questions.q: A game spawns monsters in one method: level 1 builds a Goblin, level 2 an Ogre, and so on. Next month the team adds a Dragon and drops the Goblin. What is the main cost of this design?
options: The spawning method must be reopened for every change to the monster list
Monsters run more slowly because new is a slow operation
The Dragon class cannot be written until the spawner method has been finished
The spawner can no longer call methods shared by all monsters
optionExplain: Right: the method names each class, so each addition or removal is an edit to it.
Speed is not the concern the authors raise; they point at how change affects the code.
Classes can be written separately; the trouble lies in the code that picks among them.
It still can; the damage is limited to the code that creates them.
questions.explain: The method names each concrete monster, so changing the list means editing it. Code that only used a Monster interface would be unaffected.
questions.rule: Many concrete names mean many reasons to reopen the code.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, new is a flaw in the language that should be avoided wherever possible.
questions.explain: The authors say technically there is nothing wrong with new. The trouble is how change interacts with it, so a creation site whose choices stay fixed costs nothing.
questions.rule: The cost comes from change, not from new itself.
questions.teaches: The expense of a concrete class is paid only when the set of choices changes; with fixed choices, new causes no maintenance problem.

questions.q: A checkout method contains PaymentMethod p = new PaypalPayment(); and then calls p.charge(). Which statement is accurate?
options: The method depends only on PaymentMethod, since the declared type is all that later lines use
The method has no dependency because charge() is called polymorphically
Only the PaypalPayment class depends on anything, because the method receives its payment from outside
The method still depends on PaypalPayment, because new names it despite the interface-typed variable
optionExplain: The declared type covers the later calls; the new expression is the dependency that remains.
Polymorphic calls are fine, but the creating line still ties the method to one class.
The method builds the object itself with new, so the dependency runs from the method to the class.
Right: the declared type protects later lines, but the creating line still names the class.
questions.explain: An interface-typed variable only protects the lines that use it. The line that creates the object still names a concrete class.
questions.rule: Look at the creating line, not the variable type.
questions.teaches: Declaring a variable with an interface type does not remove the dependency; every new on a concrete class is a dependency of the code that holds it.

questions.q: A developer reasons: our date-formatting helper is built with new in forty places and the class has not changed in years, so we must refactor all forty immediately. Where does the reasoning go wrong?
options: It confuses forty creation sites with forty classes, so the count is overstated
It overlooks that a stable class costs little, since the pain comes from choices that change
It assumes refactoring is free, when a change across forty sites carries real risk
It treats new as harmless, when the authors say each use of new damages the design
optionExplain: The reasoning fails on stability, not on counting.
Right: the concern is varying choices; a stable class needs no urgent change.
Refactoring does have a cost, but the flaw lies in the premise that stability does not matter.
The authors say technically there is nothing wrong with new; the culprit is change.
questions.explain: The problem is new meeting change. Where the class is stable, creating it directly is acceptable.
questions.rule: Fix creation sites where the choice varies.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: sms
mail
push
It throws an exception because no push class exists
optionExplain: A reader assumes any non-matching string defaults to sms; the code does the opposite.
Right: pick tests only for sms, so push falls through to the Email branch.
A reader expects the argument to be echoed; no class named for push exists.
A reader expects an unknown kind to fail; the conditional quietly supplies a default.
questions.explain: pick returns an Sms only for sms and an Email for everything else, so the call prints mail. Every new kind of sender would mean reopening pick.
questions.rule: A chain of conditions around new is code you must reopen for each new variant.

questions.q: True or false: A method that picks which concrete class to build with a chain of if statements can gain a new option without being edited.
questions.explain: Each option is a branch in the chain, so a new option is a new branch. The card next explains the principle behind this.
questions.rule: Adding a branch is an edit.

questions.q: Which description fits code that is closed for modification?
options: Its source file is locked so that no developer may open it again
Adding a new variant needs no edit to its existing code
It contains no if statements anywhere in its body
It uses abstract classes and no concrete ones
optionExplain: Closed refers to the design, not to file permissions.
Right: extension happens by adding code, not by editing code.
Branches may exist; the test is what happens when a variant is added.
Something must still create objects; closure is about edits when variants change.
questions.explain: The principle asks that new variants arrive as new code. Existing code that must be edited for each variant is not closed.
questions.rule: New variants should mean new code, not edited code.

questions.q: A log shipper has a ship(destination) method with branches for file, syslog and cloud destinations. The team plans a fourth. Which change best lets the next destination arrive without editing ship()?
options: Add a comment above the branches listing every supported destination
Replace the if chain with a switch statement that handles each destination in turn
Make ship() final so that no subclass can change how it behaves
Move the choice of destination out of ship(), so it only calls an interface method
optionExplain: Documentation helps readers but each addition is still an edit.
A switch is the same list of branches in another syntax.
Final prevents overriding but does nothing about the branch list.
Right: the varying choice leaves, and the remaining method no longer changes when a destination is added.
questions.explain: Separating what varies from what stays the same removes the branches from the stable method.
questions.rule: Separate the varying choice from the stable method.

questions.q: If the same chain of type checks is repeated in four methods, adding one new type means editing ____ methods.
questions.explain: Each copy of the chain is a separate place to open, so the edit sites multiply with the copies.
questions.rule: Duplicated choices multiply the edit sites.
questions.teaches: Being closed for modification is about how many places must be opened for one change, and duplicated creation logic multiplies that number.

questions.q: A mobile app picks a map provider with new GoogleMaps() or new OpenMaps() inside every screen. The product owner asks for a third provider. What follows?
options: Each screen that makes the choice must be edited, so none is closed for modification
Only the new provider class must be written, because screens use whichever provider exists
Nothing changes, because the providers share a common interface that screens already use
Only the first screen changes, and the other screens copy its choice automatically
optionExplain: Right: every screen names the concrete providers, so each must be reopened.
The new class is new code, but the screens that choose still need changes.
A shared interface helps code that uses a provider; the creating lines still name classes.
Nothing copies automatically; each screen has its own choice.
questions.explain: The domain is new but the situation is the same: choice logic repeated in many clients, each of which reopens.
questions.rule: Count the places that name concrete classes.
questions.teaches: Moving the choice into one place means a single edit reaches every client, which is why separating the varying part benefits all of them at once.

questions.q: A developer says: our create method is closed for modification, because we only add new cases at the bottom of its switch statement. What is wrong with that claim?
options: A switch statement is closed once it has been tested, whatever cases it contains
Cases at the bottom run slower than cases placed at the top of the switch
Adding a case at the bottom is still an edit, so the method is not closed
The method should have been written with if statements instead of a switch
optionExplain: Testing does not close a method; each new case still edits the method's source.
Speed is unrelated to the principle.
Right: where the new line goes does not matter; the method's source changes.
Syntax is not the issue; the edits are.
questions.explain: The test is whether adding a variant touches existing code. Appending a case still touches the method.
questions.rule: Appending is still editing.

questions.q: True or false: Editing a closed-for-modification method to fix a rounding bug in its arithmetic violates the principle.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the principle is about adding variants without editing working code, so correcting a defect is a different kind of change.
questions.rule: Closure targets routine variants, not bug fixes.

questions.q: Sort these changes by what happens to the existing code that builds or uses the classes.

items.t: Adding a case to a chain of if statements that builds classes
Handing a client a new class that implements an interface the client already calls
Deleting a class that a client creates with new
Replacing one concrete class with another inside a client that builds it with new
Adding a class that implements the interface of a client that only calls interface methods

questions.explain: Code that names concrete classes must be edited when those classes come and go. Code that only calls an interface keeps working with any new implementation through polymorphism.
questions.rule: Naming a concrete class opens the code; calling an interface keeps it closed.

questions.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
questions.q: In a method that first chooses which product class to build and then runs a fixed series of steps on the product, which part is most likely to change as products come and go?
options: The fixed series of steps
The names of the methods called on the product
The order of the steps
The choice of which class to build
optionExplain: The steps are the same for every product, which is why they are stable.
Those names come from the shared interface and stay constant.
Order is part of the stable process.
Right: the product list changes, and the choice follows it.
questions.explain: Product lists change, while the process applied to every product stays steady. The card next shows this in the pizza store.
questions.rule: The choice varies; the process stays.

questions.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
questions.q: Sort these parts of orderPizza() by whether they change as the menu changes.

items.t: Choosing between Clam and Veggie pizza classes
Adding a branch for a new pizza type
Removing the Greek pizza branch
Calling prepare() on the pizza
Calling bake() and cut() on the pizza
Calling box() on the pizza

questions.explain: Everything about choosing a class follows the menu. The processing steps apply to any pizza.
questions.rule: Creation varies; processing stays.

questions.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
questions.q: A ticket printer has printTicket(kind) which picks a Concert, Sports or Theatre ticket class, then formats the header, adds a barcode and prints. New ticket kinds keep arriving. Which lines should be separated from the rest?
options: The lines that choose and build the ticket class
The lines that format the header of the ticket
The barcode and print lines that finish the job
None, because every line in one method belongs together
optionExplain: Right: they change with the ticket kinds; the formatting and printing steps do not.
Formatting is the same for every ticket, so it is stable.
Those steps apply to every ticket kind and stay put.
Lines in one method can have different reasons to change; that is the point of separating them.
questions.explain: Ask which lines must be edited when a new ticket kind is added: only the lines that choose and build the Concert, Sports or Theatre class. Formatting the header, adding the barcode and printing stay the same for every kind.
questions.rule: Separate lines by their reason to change.

questions.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
questions.q: True or false: If the menu stays fixed for years but the boxing step changes every season, the creation lines are still the part to separate from the rest.
questions.explain: The dividing line follows the change that actually arrives. With a fixed menu the creation lines are stable, and the box step is what varies.
questions.rule: Separate what actually changes.
questions.teaches: Creation code is the usual suspect, but the dividing line between varying and stable code follows the real source of change.

questions.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
questions.q: A video app has playVideo(source), which builds a YoutubeStream, VimeoStream or FileStream, then buffers, decodes and renders it. After the varying lines are separated, what remains in playVideo?
options: The choice among stream classes, since that is the main purpose of the method
Nothing, because the whole method moves into a new class
Buffering, decoding and rendering, applied to whatever stream it receives
A list of the stream class names for documentation
optionExplain: The choice is the varying part and is the piece that moves out.
Only the varying lines move; the steps stay.
Right: the stable steps stay and work through a shared stream type.
A list of names would still tie the method to those classes.
questions.explain: After separation the method treats the stream through its shared type and no longer names concrete streams.
questions.rule: The stable method works through the abstract type.
questions.teaches: Once the creation lines leave, the remaining method sees only the abstract type, so it no longer needs an edit when the list of concrete types changes.

questions.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
questions.q: A developer says: I will move prepare, bake, cut and box out of orderPizza() because they are the most important part. What is the flaw?
options: Those steps cannot be moved out of a method without breaking the calls that use them
Importance is not the test; the steps are the stable part and the creation lines vary
The steps are too short to be worth moving, so the effort would not pay off
They belong in the Pizza class in every design, so moving them elsewhere is wrong
optionExplain: Steps can be moved; moving them would not address the change.
Right: separation is driven by what changes, not by what matters most.
The length of the steps is not the test for moving them; what matters is whether they vary.
That is one possible design, but it does not respond to varying creation.
questions.explain: The first principle separates the varying aspect from the stable one. Moving the stable steps leaves the problem in place.
questions.rule: Separate by change, not by importance.

questions.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
questions.q: The menu drops Clam and adds Pesto. Which part of this method must be edited?
options: The if chain and the calls to prepare, bake and box
Only the three calls to prepare, bake and box
Only the if chain that picks the class
The return statement, because the return type changes
optionExplain: A reader assumes a new pizza needs its own steps; here every pizza is processed the same way.
A reader mixes up the stable and varying parts; the calls stay as they are.
The choosing lines vary with the menu, while the three processing calls apply to any pizza.
The method returns the Pizza type either way, so nothing there depends on the menu.
questions.explain: Swapping Clam for Pesto changes only the branch that chooses the class. The processing steps are the part that stays the same.
questions.rule: Find the lines that change with the menu and leave the stable steps alone.

questions.q: An object whose only job is to create other objects is called a ____.
questions.explain: Naming creation as its own responsibility is the move the chapter makes. The card next shows what happens to the code that used to build objects itself.
questions.rule: Creation gets its own object.

questions.q: After creation moves to a factory, orderPizza() needs to know only that the pizza implements the ____ interface.
questions.explain: The method relies on the Pizza interface for prepare, bake, cut and box, and on nothing more.
questions.rule: The client sees only the interface.

questions.q: A ReportJob picks a CsvWriter or XmlWriter with new, then writes rows. Creation moves to a WriterFactory. What does ReportJob do afterwards?
options: Keeps choosing the writer itself and hands the choice to the factory afterwards
Builds the writers itself but registers them with the factory
Asks WriterFactory for a writer and uses it through the Writer interface
Asks the factory for a class name, then calls new on it
optionExplain: Then the factory would have no job; moving creation into WriterFactory means ReportJob must stop choosing the writer.
Registration is not creation; the job would still name the classes.
Right: ReportJob becomes a client of WriterFactory, asking it for a writer and using the result only through the Writer interface.
That keeps a concrete creation inside the job.
questions.explain: Once creation lives in WriterFactory, ReportJob only asks for a writer and uses it through the Writer interface. It no longer names CsvWriter or XmlWriter, so a new format does not touch the job.
questions.rule: Ask the factory, do not build.

questions.q: True or false: When PestoPizza replaces GreekPizza on the menu, orderPizza() needs an edit but the factory does not.
questions.explain: Only the factory holds the knowledge of which classes exist, so the factory changes and orderPizza() does not.
questions.rule: Menu changes land in the factory.
questions.teaches: Because the client holds only the interface type, a product class that did not exist when the client was written can be returned to it without any edit to the client.

questions.q: A game's EnemySpawner has a switch that picks Zombie or Skeleton, then positions and animates the enemy. A developer moves the switch to an EnemyFactory. What is the factory now responsible for?
options: Choosing and constructing the right enemy
Choosing, constructing, positioning and animating the enemy
Positioning and animating the enemy only
Deciding when each level starts
optionExplain: Right: the factory takes over only the decision and the construction, which leaves positioning and animating with the spawner.
Positioning and animating are the follow-up steps that stay with the client.
Those are the stable steps, not the creation.
Deciding when each level starts has nothing to do with choosing or building an enemy, so the factory takes no part in it.
questions.explain: Moving the switch gives EnemyFactory the choice of Zombie or Skeleton and the construction, and nothing more. EnemySpawner keeps the positioning and animating, because a factory's responsibility ends once the product is handed over.
questions.rule: Creation ends at hand-over.
questions.teaches: A factory takes over the creation step only; the follow-up steps stay with the client, so the split follows the line between building an object and using it.

questions.q: A teammate says: now that we have a factory, no class in the whole program names a concrete pizza. What is wrong?
options: Concrete pizzas cannot be named inside factory classes at all
The Pizza interface still names them
The client must name them to cast the result
The factory itself still names the concrete pizzas
optionExplain: Factories are exactly where concrete pizzas are named, so this cannot be the flaw.
The interface names none; the factory does.
A client that cast the result to a concrete class would defeat the design, but nothing here requires that.
Right: creation has to name concrete classes somewhere, and the factory is that place.
questions.explain: The factory gathers the naming of concrete pizzas into one place, but it does not abolish it, because something must still say new on a specific class. The gain is that the clients no longer do.
questions.rule: Naming moves; it does not vanish.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: clam baked, greek baked
clam baked, null
A compile error, because Greek has no class
clam baked, veggie baked
optionExplain: A reader assumes a class exists for every name; the factory has no Greek class.
A reader expects an unknown type to yield null; the conditional always returns some pizza.
A reader expects the compiler to check the type string; it is only an ordinary string.
Right: make returns Clam only for clam; any other type, greek included, falls to Veggie.
questions.explain: The factory still contains the chain of decisions; it only moved there from the client. For greek the conditional falls through to Veggie, so the second call bakes a veggie pizza.
questions.rule: A factory gathers the choosing code; it does not make the choosing disappear.

questions.q: Four classes of a mailing app each repeat code that builds an SmtpSender or SesSender. Moving that code into a SenderFactory adds which benefit?
options: Each of the four classes can stop calling methods of the Sender interface
Four copies of creation code become one, leaving one place to maintain
The factory never needs editing, since new senders are added elsewhere
SmtpSender and SesSender become abstract classes, so no code needs new
optionExplain: A reader thinks the factory replaces the interface; clients still call its methods.
Right: the duplication disappears along with the scattered class names.
A reader moves the edit away; the factory itself still changes when senders do.
A reader confuses the factory with abstraction; concrete senders still exist.
questions.explain: The student in the master-and-student dialogue says that placing creation in one object avoids duplication and gives one place to perform maintenance. That benefit comes on top of hiding class names.
questions.rule: One creation place means one maintenance place.
questions.teaches: Gathering creation in one object also avoids duplicated creation code and gives one place to perform maintenance.

questions.q: A critic says moving creation code into another class only pushes the problem elsewhere. What is the strongest reply?
options: The new class runs faster than the old method, which makes the move worth it
Several clients can share that one class, so a change is made once
The code is easier to read because it is spread over more classes
The problem disappears, because a class is not allowed to hold creation logic
optionExplain: Speed is not the argument; the reply has to be about how a shared class limits the cost of change.
Right: several clients can share that one class, so a change is made once, which is the benefit the authors point to.
Spreading code over more classes does not by itself make it easier to read or change.
Classes can hold creation logic; the logic still exists in the factory.
questions.explain: A pushed problem is still a problem unless the destination is shared. The card next shows the authors' answer.
questions.rule: Share creation so one change reaches all clients.

questions.q: True or false: In the simple factory version, the code that picks between cheese, clam and veggie pizza classes lives in the factory rather than in orderPizza().
questions.explain: The factory's create method holds the type checks, and orderPizza() only asks for a pizza.
questions.rule: Choosing lives in the factory.

questions.q: A parcel firm had three classes, each with its own chain choosing between Ground, Air and Sea carriers. A CarrierFactory now holds the one chain. How many places need editing to add a Rail carrier?
options: Three: each of the old clients
One: the factory's create method
Four: the three clients and the factory
None, because the factory writes itself
optionExplain: The three clients no longer contain the carrier chains, so none of them needs editing for Rail.
Right: only CarrierFactory's create method holds the chain, so the Rail branch is added there once.
The clients just ask the factory for a carrier and stay unchanged, so they are not edited.
Someone must still add the Rail branch and class; the factory does not write itself.
questions.explain: The three clients stopped naming Ground, Air and Sea once the chain moved into CarrierFactory. Adding Rail therefore means one edit, in the factory's create method, rather than one per client.
questions.rule: One creation place, one edit.

questions.q: The factory's create method is declared to return the abstract ____ type, so no client sees a concrete class name.
questions.explain: Returning the abstract Pizza type means callers only ever see the interface, so the concrete class names stay hidden inside the factory.
questions.rule: Return the abstract type.
questions.teaches: The factory's create method is declared to return the abstract product type, so no client ever sees a concrete class name.

questions.q: A spreadsheet app has an ExportMenu, an AutoSave and an EmailAttach, all building a Writer for xlsx, csv or ods. The team creates a WriterFactory. What happens to the clients' concrete instantiations?
options: They stay in the clients, and the factory keeps a second copy
They move into the Writer interface that all clients share
They are replaced by a comment in each client explaining the choice
They disappear from the clients; each calls the factory
optionExplain: Keeping a second copy would duplicate the choices, which is the problem a factory removes.
Interfaces describe behavior and do not build objects, so the Writer interface cannot hold the instantiations.
A comment explains a choice but does not create an object, so the clients would still need the code.
Right: the clients drop their concrete instantiations and each simply calls WriterFactory.
questions.explain: Centralizing creation means ExportMenu, AutoSave and EmailAttach no longer name the xlsx, csv or ods writers. Each one asks WriterFactory for a Writer, so only the factory knows the concrete classes.
questions.rule: Clients lose their concrete names.
questions.teaches: Beyond sharing one place of change, centralizing creation removes concrete class names from every client, which lets them stay closed for modification.

questions.q: In which case does extracting a simple factory give the least benefit?
options: One client, one fixed product type, and no expected changes
Many clients and a product list that keeps growing
Several clients repeating the same type chain of checks
A menu that changes every month, used by several different classes
optionExplain: Right: with one client, one fixed product and no change, there is nothing shared or varying for a factory to absorb.
This is the case that pays off most.
Repetition is what the factory removes.
Change is what makes a factory useful.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a factory pays off through sharing and change. With one client, a fixed product and no expected change, extracting it adds a class without removing any repeated edits.
questions.rule: No change and no sharing means little gain.

questions.q: What undermines the factory's benefit in this shop?
options: Greek is built with new in the shop, so dropping Greek reopens the shop
The factory is kept in a field of the shop rather than in a local variable
create returns the abstract Pizza instead of naming a concrete pizza class
bake is called on the pizza only after the factory has made it
optionExplain: Right: one concrete class is still named in the client, so a menu change reaches it.
A reader treats the field as the problem; holding a factory in a field is how the shop is composed with it.
A reader sees the abstract return type as a flaw; it is what keeps clients free of concrete names.
A reader doubts the order of steps; processing a product after it is created is the intended flow.
questions.explain: The shop gets most pizzas from the factory but still instantiates Greek itself. A menu change that touches Greek must reopen the shop.
questions.rule: Every concrete creation left in the client keeps the client open to change.

questions.q: True or false: With one SimplePizzaFactory shared by a menu class and a delivery class, adding Pesto means editing both classes.
questions.explain: Both clients ask the factory for pizzas and do not name concrete classes, so the new pizza is added in the factory alone.
questions.rule: One place to modify.

questions.q: True or false: A factory whose create method is static can be subclassed to override how it builds objects.
questions.explain: Static methods are bound to their class and cannot be overridden by subclasses. The card next explains the trade-off.
questions.rule: Static methods are not overridden.

questions.q: True or false: A static factory method can be called without first creating a factory object.
questions.explain: A static method is called through the class name, so no factory object has to be created first. That is the convenience of the static form, though it gives up the ability to subclass the factory.
questions.rule: Static means no factory object is needed.

questions.q: A theme-park app creates tickets with TicketFactory.create(kind), a static method. The owner wants a holiday variant with different rules, chosen when the app starts. Which design suits that?
options: A second static method with the same name in a holiday subclass
Keep the static factory and add an if inside it
An instance factory that can be replaced when the app starts
Make the static factory final so it cannot be misused
optionExplain: A static method in a subclass hides rather than overrides, so it would be a separate method and could not replace the first.
Adding an if inside the factory reintroduces an edit to it for every new variant.
Right: an object can be swapped when the app starts, while a static call is fixed to the class it names.
Final stops subclasses from changing a method, but it does not make a static call replaceable.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a static call is bound to the class named in it, so the holiday rules cannot be swapped in at start-up. An instance factory is an object, so the app can be given the holiday version instead of the usual one.
questions.rule: Swapping needs an object.

questions.q: With a static factory, where must you edit to use a different creation rule?
options: Nowhere, because the new rule can be supplied from outside
In the Pizza interface that the products implement
In the build settings used to compile the project
At each call site, which names the static class
optionExplain: Supplying a new rule from outside is only possible when the factory is an object, not a static class.
The Pizza interface describes the products and takes no part in choosing the creation rule.
Build settings are not where a factory is chosen; the code itself names the class.
Right: a static call is bound to the class named in it, so every call site must be edited.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a call to a static method is bound to the class named in the call. To use a different creation rule you must edit each call site that names the static factory.
questions.rule: Static means bound.
questions.teaches: A static call is bound to the class named at the call site, so replacing the behavior means editing every such call.

questions.q: Sort these conditions by which kind of simple factory they favor.

items.t: The creation rule is fixed and used everywhere
Callers want to avoid creating an object first
Convenience in calling matters most
Each region needs its own creator
A franchise supplies its own creator
Creation behavior must be replaced by subclassing

questions.explain: Need for replacement points to an object; fixed rules and convenience point to static.
questions.rule: Choose by the need to replace.
questions.teaches: The choice between static and instance is a trade between convenience and replaceability, driven by whether the creator must ever be replaced.

questions.q: A developer says: I made the create method static so each region's subclass can override it. What is wrong?
options: A static method cannot be overridden by subclasses
Regions rarely need different creators
Subclasses cannot exist for factories
Static methods are slower than instance methods to call
optionExplain: Right: static methods cannot be overridden, so the regional subclasses cannot supply their own versions.
Regions often do need different creators, which is exactly why a static method is a problem.
Subclasses of a factory can exist; static only blocks overriding the create method.
Speed is not the issue here; the problem is that static prevents overriding.
questions.explain: The developer wants each region's subclass to override create, but a static method cannot be overridden. Static and subclass overriding do not mix, so the method has to be an instance method.
questions.rule: Static cannot be overridden.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: fancy
A compile error, because a subclass may not declare a static method with the same signature
An exception, because m is declared as Maker but holds a FancyMaker
plain
optionExplain: A reader assumes the FancyMaker object's version runs; that happens only for instance methods.
A reader thinks the redefinition is illegal; it is allowed, and it only hides the parent's method.
A reader expects a type mismatch; a subclass object may be held by a superclass variable.
Right: static methods are not overridden; the call is bound to the declared type Maker.
questions.explain: m is declared as Maker, and a static call is resolved from the declared type, so the program prints plain. A subclass cannot change what a static factory method does.
questions.rule: A static factory method cannot be overridden, so its creation rule cannot be replaced by subclassing.

questions.q: A store needs to make pizzas in three regional styles using the same ordering code. Which technique changes the style without editing the ordering method?
options: Copy the ordering method for each region
Add a region flag to the Pizza interface
Pass the store a regional factory object
Make the store a static class
optionExplain: That duplicates code and multiplies edits.
A flag would not remove the concrete choices.
Right: composition lets a different regional factory be handed to the store without touching its ordering method.
Making the store static does not help, because a static class cannot be given a different factory.
questions.explain: The store can be given different helpers. The card next shows this in the pizza store.
questions.rule: Compose, then swap.

questions.q: Because the store keeps a reference to its factory, the store is ____ with the factory.
questions.explain: The store holds a reference to its factory, which is composition. Because the factory is held rather than hard-wired, a different one can be supplied.
questions.rule: Composition allows swapping.

questions.q: A music app's PlaylistBuilder is constructed with a TrackSourceFactory. In offline mode the app should use local files. What is the smallest change?
options: Edit the builder's code to check for offline mode
Construct the builder with a local-file factory
Make TrackSource a static class
Subclass the builder for offline mode
optionExplain: Then the builder would be reopened for each mode.
Right: pass a local-file factory to the builder and leave the builder's code alone.
A static TrackSource could not be swapped for a local-file version.
A subclass of the builder would work, but swapping the factory needs no new class.
questions.explain: PlaylistBuilder already receives a TrackSourceFactory, so offline mode only needs a local-file factory passed in. The builder never changes; the factory does.
questions.rule: Swap the factory, keep the client.

questions.q: True or false: If the store builds its own factory with new inside its constructor, a franchise can still swap in a different factory without editing the store.
questions.explain: The store would name the concrete factory, so swapping means editing the store again.
questions.rule: Receive the factory; do not build it.
questions.teaches: Composition only helps when the factory is supplied from outside the client; a client that constructs its own factory with new is tied to that factory again.

questions.q: An alarm-clock app plays sounds through a SoundPlayer built by a PlayerFactory it is given. A new device needs a vibration player. What changes?
options: The alarm code is rewritten for the new device's player
The factory is removed so the alarm can build players itself
A different factory is passed in; the alarm code stays
All players become static so that the alarm can find them
optionExplain: Composition exists so that the alarm code need not be rewritten for each device's player.
Removing the factory would put creation back inside the alarm and lose the ability to swap players.
Right: supplying a different factory changes the player while the alarm code stays as it is.
Making the players static would block swapping them, not help the alarm find them.
questions.explain: The alarm depends on PlayerFactory, not on a particular player. A vibration device is handled by passing in a different factory, so the alarm code stays unchanged.
questions.rule: The client stays the same.
questions.teaches: The same client code can behave differently solely by which factory it is given, so variety is introduced at assembly time rather than inside the client.

questions.q: Which problem does swapping the factory not solve?
options: Franchises baking, cutting and boxing in their own way
Franchises wanting different pizza styles from one another
Adding a new region to the franchise network later
Hiding the concrete pizza classes from the store itself
optionExplain: Right: the factory only creates pizzas; how a franchise bakes, cuts and boxes is outside its job.
A regional factory handles different pizza styles for different franchises.
Another factory covers a new region without any change to the store.
The factory already hides the concrete pizza classes from the store.
questions.explain: Swapping the factory changes only which pizzas get created, so it cannot change how a franchise bakes, cuts and boxes. Those steps are not part of what the factory varies.
questions.rule: A factory varies creation only.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: box:thin box:thin
box:thick box:thin
box:thin box:thick
A compile error, because Factory has only one method
optionExplain: A reader assumes the first factory sticks for all stores; each store keeps its own.
A reader reverses the order; the stores are ordered in the order written.
Right: each Store uses the factory it was constructed with.
A reader doubts the lambdas; an interface with one method can be implemented that way.
questions.explain: The same Store class produces different results solely by which factory it was handed. The variation is introduced where the store is assembled.
questions.rule: Swap the factory you give a client to swap what it creates.

questions.q: True or false: The authors count Simple Factory as one of the official design patterns.
questions.explain: The authors call Simple Factory an idiom and give it only an honorable mention, not the status of an official pattern. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Simple Factory is an idiom.

questions.q: The authors call Simple Factory a programming ____, not a design pattern.
questions.explain: An idiom is a commonly used coding habit; the authors give it an honorable mention only.
questions.rule: Idiom, not pattern.

questions.q: A junior developer says our code uses the Factory Pattern, describing one class with a method that switches on a type string and returns products. According to the authors, what is the most accurate description?
options: The Factory Method Pattern
The Abstract Factory Pattern
Not a factory at all
The Simple Factory idiom
optionExplain: Factory Method needs a creator whose subclasses supply the creation.
Abstract Factory needs an interface for a family of products.
It does encapsulate creation, so calling it no factory at all overstates the point.
Right: there is no subclass-supplied creation and no family interface, so it is the Simple Factory idiom.
questions.explain: A single class that switches on a type string and returns products encapsulates creation, but it has no subclasses supplying creation and no family interface. The authors call that the Simple Factory idiom, not a pattern.
questions.rule: Match the structure to the name.

questions.q: True or false: Because Simple Factory is only an idiom, the authors advise against using it.
questions.explain: Their summary calls it a simple way to decouple clients from concrete classes. The label says how to classify it, not how useful it is.
questions.rule: Idiom is a label, not a verdict.
questions.teaches: Whether something is called a pattern is separate from whether it is useful; the authors recommend the idiom for decoupling clients from concrete classes.

questions.q: A developer says our OrderRouter class chooses a carrier class from a string. According to the authors, what would turn that into a real pattern?
options: Making the string that selects the carrier longer and more descriptive for readers
Structure around the choice, such as subclasses supplying creation or a family interface
Renaming the class so its name ends in Factory Pattern, matching the book's terms
Adding more carriers until the choosing class is large enough to count as a pattern
optionExplain: The structure is what matters, not the string.
Right: those are the structures of Factory Method and Abstract Factory.
A name ending in Factory Pattern changes nothing about the structure, so it stays an idiom.
Adding more carriers just lengthens the same single choosing class, which stays an idiom.
questions.explain: A lone class that picks a carrier from a string is still the Simple Factory idiom. The authors reserve pattern status for structures with more than a single choosing class, such as subclasses supplying creation or a family interface.
questions.rule: Structure makes the pattern.
questions.teaches: What turns a factory into a pattern in this chapter is structure around it: subclasses supplying creation in Factory Method, or an interface for a family of products in Abstract Factory.

questions.q: True or false: The authors note that some developers mistake Simple Factory for the Factory Pattern.
questions.explain: The authors write exactly that some developers mistake Simple Factory for the Factory Pattern, and suggest using the mix-up as a conversation starter.
questions.rule: Know which name is which.

questions.q: According to the authors, sort these by whether each is an official pattern or the Simple Factory idiom.

items.t: Factory Method
Abstract Factory
A class whose create(type) method picks a product class
A static create method that a whole program calls
An abstract class whose subclasses implement a creation method

questions.explain: The authors treat Factory Method and Abstract Factory as the two heavy-duty patterns. A separate class or static method that builds products from a type is the Simple Factory idiom.
questions.rule: Two real factory patterns; one useful idiom.

questions.q: True or false: A class that extends an abstract class and fills in its abstract methods has implemented that class's interface in the general design-patterns sense.
questions.explain: Design talk uses interface for the set of methods a type offers, whether it is a Java interface or a class. The card next gives the authors' note.
questions.rule: Interface means the contract.

questions.q: In general design-pattern use, a concrete class that supplies a method from a supertype is said to ____ that supertype's interface.
questions.explain: The supertype may be a class or an interface; supplying its methods is implementing its interface.
questions.rule: Implementing means supplying the contract.

questions.q: Java code has an abstract class Notifier with send(), and a class EmailNotifier extends Notifier and supplies send(). Which statement fits design-pattern vocabulary?
options: EmailNotifier implements nothing because it uses extends
EmailNotifier implements Notifier's interface in the general sense
Notifier must be a Java interface for the phrase to apply
EmailNotifier implements nothing until it adds the implements keyword
optionExplain: That is the narrow reading the authors warn against.
Right: EmailNotifier supplies the supertype's send(), which is what implementing an interface means in the general sense.
The phrase is not limited to Java interface types; it also covers a supertype that is an abstract class.
The implements keyword is not required for the general sense; supplying the supertype's methods is enough.
questions.explain: In design-pattern talk, a class implements a supertype's interface when it supplies the supertype's methods, even if the keyword used is extends. So EmailNotifier implements Notifier's interface.
questions.rule: Supply the methods, implement the interface.

questions.q: True or false: Code that uses a variable typed as an abstract class is programming to an interface in the broad sense.
questions.explain: An abstract class offers an interface of methods without a concrete implementation, so coding to it counts.
questions.rule: Abstract types count as interfaces.
questions.teaches: Coding to an abstract class's methods counts as coding to an interface in the broad sense, so the guidance about interfaces applies to abstract classes too.

questions.q: A language has no interface keyword, only classes. A design book says a Logger class must implement the Sink interface, where Sink is a base class with write(). What does that sentence ask for?
options: That Logger be declared with a Java interface file
That Logger be renamed Sink so that the two names match exactly
That Logger be declared final so nobody can change it
That Logger supplies the methods of Sink's public contract
optionExplain: The language has no interface keyword, so a Java-style interface file cannot be what is asked for.
Renaming Logger to Sink would not supply Sink's methods; the two names need not match.
Declaring Logger final prevents subclassing but has nothing to do with supplying Sink's methods.
Right: Logger must supply the methods of Sink's public contract, which needs no particular keyword.
questions.explain: The sentence asks Logger to supply the methods of Sink's public contract, which works in any language. Without an interface keyword, Logger does this by subclassing the Sink base class and supplying write().
questions.rule: Interface means contract.
questions.teaches: The idea is independent of language keywords: an interface is the set of methods clients can call on a type, however the language expresses it.

questions.q: A developer reads the authors' note and decides: so I can write class Circle implements Shape even when Shape is an abstract class. What is wrong?
options: In Java code, implements names a Java interface; a class extends an abstract class
An abstract class has no methods for a subclass to implement, so the phrase cannot apply
Circle must itself be abstract before it can use the implements keyword
Java forbids naming a class Shape, since that word is reserved for interfaces
optionExplain: Right: the broad sense is for talking, not for code syntax.
An abstract class can declare abstract methods for a subclass to implement; the trouble is the keyword, not the idea.
Circle need not be abstract to use implements; the real problem is that Shape is not a Java interface.
Java does not reserve the name Shape for interfaces; the problem is which keyword goes with which kind of type.
questions.explain: In Java code, implements names a Java interface and a class extends an abstract class. The broader sense of implementing an interface is for talking about design, not for syntax, so the two senses must be kept apart.
questions.rule: Words versus keywords.

questions.q: In design-pattern vocabulary, what does Square do with respect to Shape?
options: It does not implement the interface, because no implements keyword appears
It implements Shape's interface by supplying area(), though it writes extends
It only inherits, since area() is abstract and Square adds nothing of its own
It implements the interface only if Shape is rewritten as a Java interface
optionExplain: A reader takes the phrase literally as a Java keyword; the broad sense covers any supertype.
Right: supplying a supertype's method counts, whether the supertype is a class or an interface.
A reader overlooks that Square supplies the body of area(), which is exactly what implementing means.
A reader ties the idea to the keyword; the authors say the supertype can be a class.
questions.explain: Square supplies the method declared by its supertype, so in the general design-pattern sense it implements Shape's interface. The Java keyword implements is a narrower matter.
questions.rule: Implementing an interface means supplying a supertype's methods, however the language spells it.

questions.q: A company licenses its shop software to local owners. Local owners want regional menus; head office wants one checkout procedure. What kind of problem is this?
options: A problem with only one need, since head office makes the decisions
A problem solved by removing the regional menu from the software
Two needs that must both be met: menu variation and consistent process
A problem of speed, since checkout delays are what annoy owners
optionExplain: Both needs are stated, so both must be met.
That loses the variation the owners want.
Right: owners want regional menus and head office wants one checkout, so a design has to deliver both.
Nothing in the scenario mentions speed; the stated needs are menu variation and one checkout procedure.
questions.explain: Good design starts by naming each need. The card next shows this for the pizza store.
questions.rule: List the needs first.

questions.q: Which needs does the franchiser have for the franchises? Select all that apply.
options: Regional pizza styles
Use of the franchiser's tested code
A single national pizza style
No ordering procedure at all
optionExplain: Right: local taste varies, so the franchises need regional styles.
Right: the franchiser wants consistent operation through its tested code.
This removes the regional freedom the franchises want.
The franchiser wants one proven ordering procedure, so having none would contradict its aim.
questions.explain: The franchiser wants regional pizza styles to vary and wants every franchise to use its tested ordering code. A single national style or no ordering procedure would each contradict one of those needs.
questions.rule: Name both needs.

questions.q: A mobile-banking vendor sells its app to banks, each wanting its own colors and logo, while the vendor needs one audited transfer routine. Which pair of needs matches the franchise problem?
options: Variation of both the look and the transfer routine
Consistency of the look and variation of the routine
No variation and no consistency, so any design would do equally well
Variation of the look and consistency of the transfer routine
optionExplain: Varying the transfer routine would give up the single audited routine the vendor needs.
That reverses the needs: the banks want their own look, and the vendor wants the routine held constant.
With no variation and no consistency, neither the banks' branding nor the vendor's audit need is met.
Right: the look varies per bank while the transfer routine stays constant, like regional menus with one ordering procedure.
