Right: start at the low level and ask what the concrete classes share, then abstract it.
Comments do not change dependencies.
questions.explain: The bottom-up step is to look at the concrete checkouts and ask what they share; that shared part becomes the abstraction OrderScreen depends on.
questions.rule: Abstract from the bottom.

questions.q: True or false: A store that uses a factory method but still casts the returned Pizza to NYStyleCheesePizza has inverted its dependencies.
questions.explain: Casting the returned Pizza to NYStyleCheesePizza names a concrete class again, so the store depends on it once more and the dependencies are not inverted.
questions.rule: Do not cast to the concrete type.
questions.teaches: Using a factory method does not by itself invert dependencies; the client must also work only through the abstraction, because a cast to a concrete class re-creates the dependency.

questions.q: A music app's Player builds a Mp3Decoder directly. Which design inverts the dependency?
options: Mp3Decoder extends Player so that the decoder inherits its settings
A Decoder type that Player uses and Mp3Decoder implements, with a factory
Player stores decoder names as strings and converts them when needed
Player gets a second concrete decoder class to share the load
optionExplain: Subclassing makes the coupling tighter.
Right: Player uses a Decoder type that Mp3Decoder implements, so both sides rely on Decoder.
Strings still require creation by class somewhere in the player.
A second concrete decoder only adds another dependency for Player to carry.
questions.explain: Player and Mp3Decoder both depend on the Decoder abstraction, so the arrow from Player to the concrete class is gone.
questions.rule: Introduce the shared abstraction.
questions.teaches: The inversion applies to any pair of components: introduce an abstraction that the higher level uses and make the lower level implement it, so the arrows point at the abstraction.

questions.q: A reader says: Factory Method is the only way to follow the Dependency Inversion Principle. What does the book say?
options: It is the only technique the authors give for the principle
It has no connection to this principle, which is about subclassing
It is not the only technique, though it is one of the more powerful
It is a weak technique that the authors recommend against
optionExplain: The authors say it is just one technique, not the only one.
It is a technique for following the principle, which is about depending on abstractions, not merely subclassing.
Right: the authors say it is not the only technique, though it is one of the more powerful.
The authors call it one of the more powerful techniques, not a weak one.
questions.explain: The book presents Factory Method as one technique for following the Dependency Inversion Principle, and one of the more powerful, but not the only one.
questions.rule: One powerful technique among others.

questions.q: Put the steps of the authors' inverted thinking for the pizza store in order.
items: Notice that the store would depend on every concrete pizza
Start from the pizzas and ask what they share
Abstract that into a Pizza type
Rely on a factory to get the concrete classes out of the store
The store and the pizzas both depend on Pizza
questions.explain: The authors begin at the pizzas, abstract them and then use a factory so the store never names a concrete class. The result is that both sides depend on Pizza.
questions.rule: Start from the low-level classes and abstract.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: Which of these does the Dependency Inversion Principle's guidance advise against? Select all that apply.
options: Holding a reference to a concrete class in a variable
Deriving a class from a concrete class
Calling a method through an interface
Declaring a method in an abstract class
optionExplain: Right: a reference to a concrete class ties the code to that class.
Right: the child depends on its concrete parent.
Calling a method through an interface is the preferred style, so the guidance does not advise against it.
Abstract declarations are what the principle favors.
questions.explain: The guidance disfavors depending on concrete classes: holding a reference to one and deriving from one both do that. Calling through an interface and declaring methods in an abstract class are the preferred style.
questions.rule: Avoid concrete references and parents.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: No class should derive from a concrete class; derive from an ____ such as an interface or abstract class.
questions.explain: Deriving from an abstraction such as an interface or abstract class keeps the new class depending on a stable contract instead of on a concrete implementation.
questions.rule: Derive from abstractions.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A SmartLamp extends a concrete BasicLamp, overrides its turnOn(), and a Controller holds a field of type SmartLamp. How many guidelines does this break?
options: Three: a concrete reference, a concrete parent and an overridden method
One, since only the field holding the SmartLamp reference counts
Two, since overriding a method is allowed for any subclass
None, since the guidelines were written about pizza stores only
optionExplain: Right: a concrete reference, a concrete parent and an overridden method each break one guideline.
The field is only one issue; the concrete parent and the override also break guidelines.
Overriding an implemented method is what the third guideline advises against, so it counts.
The guidelines are general advice for any design, not only for pizza stores.
questions.explain: Checking each guideline in turn: Controller holds a reference of the concrete type SmartLamp, SmartLamp derives from a concrete class, and it overrides an implemented method. That breaks all three guidelines.
questions.rule: Check all three.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: True or false: If a subclass has to override an implemented method of its base class, the base class was not really an abstraction to start with.
questions.explain: Implemented methods in a base class are meant to be shared by all subclasses; overriding shows they were not.
questions.rule: Overriding signals a leaky base.
questions.teaches: Having to override an implemented method suggests the base class does not capture what its subclasses share, so the abstraction itself may be the thing to repair.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: In a spreadsheet tool, a ChartPanel keeps a field of type ConcreteBarChart. Which guideline does this break, and what fix do the authors suggest?
options: A class derives from a concrete class; make ChartPanel final to stop it
A method overrides an implemented method; delete the overriding method
None, because a field is allowed to hold a reference to any class it uses
A variable holds a concrete class; type it as Chart and use a factory
optionExplain: ChartPanel is not deriving from a concrete class; it holds a field, so that guideline does not apply.
The scenario describes no overriding method, so that guideline is not the one broken.
The guideline explicitly covers variables holding references to concrete classes, so a field is not exempt.
Right: this is the guideline about variables holding concrete classes, and the fix is to type it as Chart and use a factory.
questions.explain: ChartPanel's field of type ConcreteBarChart breaks the guideline against holding a reference to a concrete class. The fix is to type the variable as the Chart abstraction and obtain the object from a factory.
questions.rule: Variable type reveals dependency.
questions.teaches: Guidelines are symptom checks: each points at a different place, field types, parent classes or overridden methods, where a hidden concrete dependency can be found.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A developer says: I derive from an abstract base class and override its concrete helper methods all the time, so I follow the guidelines. What is wrong?
options: Abstract parents are not allowed under the guidelines, so the design fails
Overriding implemented methods breaks the third guideline, abstract parent or not
Helper methods cannot be concrete in an abstract parent, so the design fails
The guidelines apply only to interfaces, so this code is outside their scope
optionExplain: Abstract parents are encouraged by the guidelines, so that is not what fails.
Right: overriding implemented methods breaks the third guideline, whether or not the parent is abstract.
An abstract parent can contain concrete helper methods; the guidelines caution against overriding them.
The guidelines apply to all classes and not only to interfaces, so this code is in scope.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Deriving from an abstract base class is fine under the guidelines, but overriding its implemented helper methods breaks the third guideline. The abstraction is not the problem; the overrides are.
questions.rule: Overrides are the warning.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: Match each design smell to the guideline it breaks.
pairs: A field typed to a concrete class
No variable holds a reference to a concrete class
A class extends a concrete class
No class derives from a concrete class
A subclass redefines a method its base already implements
No method overrides an implemented base method
questions.explain: Each guideline points to a different place to look: field types, parent classes and overridden methods.
questions.rule: Three guidelines, three places to look.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A developer calls new String() inside a method. How should this be judged by the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: It does not violate the principle, since String is part of the language
It violates the principle but is acceptable, as String is unlikely to change
It is a serious fault, so String creation should go behind a factory
It is acceptable because strings are small and cheap to create anywhere
optionExplain: It names a concrete class, so it does.
Right: it violates the principle but is acceptable, since String is unlikely to change.
The cost of a violation depends on how often the class changes, and String rarely does.
Size and cheapness do not decide; what matters is how likely the class is to change.
questions.explain: String is a concrete class, so new String() technically violates the principle, but it is unlikely to change, so the violation is harmless. The cost depends on how often the class changes; the card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: Judge by likelihood of change.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, every Java program ever written violates these guidelines.
questions.explain: The authors say every Java program violates these guidelines, to stress that they are guidelines to aim for rather than absolute rules.
questions.rule: Guidelines are aims.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: Sort these creation sites by what the authors' reasoning suggests.

items.t: A String built inside a method
A list built inline in a helper
A small value class that has not changed in years
A pricing rule that changes every quarter
Payment provider classes that vary by country
Enemy types added every release

questions.explain: Classes unlikely to change can be created directly; classes likely to change deserve a technique such as Factory Method.
questions.rule: Shield what changes.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: True or false: A factory placed around a class that later proves stable for ten years was a serious design error.
questions.explain: Likelihood of change is a prediction made in advance; a protective factory that turned out unnecessary is a small cost.
questions.rule: Judge by what was known then.
questions.teaches: Whether a class is likely to change is a prediction made in advance, so a protective factory around a class that later proves stable is a small cost, not an error.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A game developer creates Vector2 objects directly everywhere but puts Enemy creation behind a factory. A reviewer wants Vector2 behind a factory too. What reply fits the authors' reasoning?
options: Vector2 is unlikely to change, so direct creation is fine; Enemy varies
The reviewer is right, since no concrete creation is acceptable
The developer is wrong to use any factory at all in the game
Both should be created directly, since factories add needless classes
optionExplain: Right: Vector2 is unlikely to change, so direct creation is fine, while Enemy varies.
The authors accept violations for stable classes, so not every concrete creation must be removed.
Classes that vary, like Enemy, do need a factory, so using one is right.
Enemy varies, so it does benefit from a factory and should not be created directly.
questions.explain: Vector2 is unlikely to change, so creating it directly is acceptable by the same reasoning the authors give for String. Enemy varies, so it belongs behind a factory.
questions.rule: Stable classes can be created directly.
questions.teaches: The test for dropping the guideline is the class's expected stability, not its category; a small value class is usually stable, while a domain class with many variants is not.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A reader concludes: the authors admit all programs violate the guidelines, so the guidelines are worthless. Where does the conclusion fail?
options: The authors themselves said the guidelines are worthless in practice
The authors only meant that a few programs violate them, so the admission is narrower
It ignores that guidelines tell you when and why you are breaking them
The guidelines apply only to String objects, so they say nothing else
optionExplain: The authors never called the guidelines worthless; they present them as guidelines to follow where reasonable.
The authors say every Java program violates them, so the admission is not narrower; the flaw lies elsewhere.
Right: guidelines tell you when and why you are breaking them, and that awareness is the value.
The guidelines apply to class design generally, not only to String objects.
questions.explain: The guidelines are valuable because they tell you when and why you are breaking them, so you break them knowingly. Admitting that violations are common does not make that awareness worthless.
questions.rule: Guidelines give awareness.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A PricingRule class changes every quarter and is created with new at twelve sites. What will the next change cost?
options: None, because pricing rules are as stable as the String class
Up to twelve edits, unless creation is first gathered behind a factory
One edit, because the compiler updates every new call by itself
Two edits, the class itself and a single factory that already exists
optionExplain: A reader borrows the String exception; this class changes every quarter.
Right: each new names the class, and this class is likely to change.
A reader expects tooling to fix call sites; each site still names the class.
A reader assumes a factory exists already; the scenario says creation is spread across twelve sites.
questions.explain: A class that is likely to change deserves shielding. With creation spread over twelve places, each change reaches each place.
questions.rule: Shield classes that are likely to change.

questions.q: A franchiser finds that some franchises use cheaper ingredients than agreed. Which response gives the franchiser direct control over ingredient quality?
options: Ask franchisees to be more careful with their ingredients
Remove the regional styles from the franchise menu
Let each franchise choose its own supplier of ingredients
Supply the ingredients from the franchiser's own source
optionExplain: Asking franchisees to be careful is only a request, and requests do not enforce quality.
Regional styles are not the cause of the cheaper ingredients, so removing them fixes nothing.
Letting each franchise pick its own supplier invites exactly the cheaper-ingredient problem.
Right: supplying ingredients from the franchiser's own source gives direct control over their quality.
questions.explain: Controlling the source controls the quality, so the franchiser supplies the ingredients itself. The card next shows how the book does it.
questions.rule: Control the supply.

questions.q: True or false: In the book, the ingredient problem appears after the ordering framework was already in place.
questions.explain: The franchises were following the procedures, but some were substituting inferior ingredients.
questions.rule: Process was fine, inputs were not.

questions.q: A pharmacy chain finds some stores buying cheaper packaging than agreed. The chain wants one supplier but needs different labels per country. What does the pizza solution suggest?
options: Supply the packaging from head office, with a set for each country
Ban country-specific labels so one packaging set fits every store
Let each store decide on quality, since stores know their customers
Ship one identical set everywhere and ignore the labeling differences
optionExplain: Right: head office supplies the packaging, with a regional set for each country.
The regional differences are real.
Letting each store decide brings back the original problem of stores buying cheaper packaging.
One identical set ignores that labeling rules differ by country.
questions.explain: As with the pizza ingredients, head office supplies the packaging centrally and provides a set for each country. That keeps one supplier while allowing the labeling to differ.
questions.rule: Central source, regional sets.

questions.q: True or false: If every region could use exactly the same sauce, the book's design would still need a separate sauce set for each region.
questions.explain: The need for several sets comes from regional differences; one shared sauce needs only one set.
questions.rule: Sets follow differences.
questions.teaches: The need for several parallel sets comes from regional difference; where regions share an ingredient, one shared class serves them all.

questions.q: A coffee chain wants consistent beans in every shop, but each country has different import rules. Which problem structure does this match?
options: Process variation with a single set of inputs
A static factory that every shop calls directly
Centralized supply with a separate set per region
A cache that stores the beans between shops
optionExplain: A single set of inputs does not fit, because the sets differ by region.
Static calls are not the structure here; the problem is central supply with regional sets.
Right: this matches the pizza ingredients, with centralized supply and a separate set per region.
A cache between shops is unrelated to the supply and regional-set structure.
questions.explain: Consistent beans from central supply, with a separate set for each country's import rules, has the same structure as the pizza ingredients: one control point and regional sets.
questions.rule: Central supply, regional sets.
questions.teaches: The ingredient problem is a general shape: a central party controls inputs, but each context needs its own matching set, which is what families of products later model.

questions.q: Which measures help keep pizzas consistent across franchises, according to the chapter's design? Select all that apply.
options: A shared ordering and preparation procedure
Regional ingredient sets supplied from a factory
Letting each franchise choose its own supplier
Removing the regional styles
optionExplain: Right: the framework keeps the ordering and preparation process the same.
Right: the franchiser controls what goes into each pizza through the factory.
Letting each franchise choose its own supplier invites the substitution problem.
Regional variety is a goal, not the cause, so removing regional styles does not help consistency.
questions.explain: Consistency needs control of both the process and the inputs: a shared procedure keeps the steps the same, and regional ingredient sets from a factory keep the franchiser in charge of what goes in.
questions.rule: Inputs and process.

questions.q: Franchises bake differently and also buy cheaper dough. Which pair of fixes does the chapter use?
options: A shared ordering routine that also controls which ingredients are bought
A factory that supplies ingredients and also dictates how they are baked
One national ingredient set for every region, with local freedom over the process
A shared ordering routine for the process, plus a factory supplying ingredients
optionExplain: A reader asks the routine to do both jobs; the ingredients need a source of their own.
A reader asks the factory to do both jobs; the process stays in the store framework.
A reader fixes the wrong thing; regions need different ingredients, and the process must be consistent.
Right: the framework controls the steps, the ingredient factory controls the inputs.
questions.explain: The ordering framework made the process consistent. The ingredient problem came after, and the franchiser solved it with a factory that supplies the ingredients.
questions.rule: Control the process with the framework and the inputs with a factory.

questions.q: True or false: Supplying ingredients from a factory also guarantees the franchises follow the baking and cutting procedure.
questions.explain: The ingredient factory controls what goes in. The shared ordering routine, built earlier, controls how the pizza is processed.
questions.rule: Inputs and process need their own controls.

questions.q: A pizza needs dough, sauce and cheese, and each region has its own versions of all three. What is the set of one region's versions called?
options: A singleton shared by every region
A decorator layered over the ingredients
A family of related ingredient classes
A proxy standing in for the ingredients
optionExplain: A singleton is a different concept about instance counts.
A decorator wraps an object to add behavior.
Right: the related parts needed for one region's pizza.
A proxy stands in for another object.
questions.explain: Dough, sauce and cheese are a set of parts that belong together for one region, and a set of related parts like that is a family. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: Family means parts that belong together.

questions.q: Which of these belong to the pizza ingredient family in the book? Select all that apply.
options: Dough
Sauce
Cheese
The franchise's phone number
The shop's opening hours
optionExplain: Right: dough is one of the ingredients needed to make a pizza.
Right: sauce is one of the ingredients needed to make a pizza.
Right: cheese is one of the ingredients needed to make a pizza.
A phone number has nothing to do with making a pizza, so it is not in the ingredient family.
Opening hours are not an ingredient, so they are not part of the family.
questions.explain: The ingredient family is everything needed to make a pizza, such as dough, sauce and cheese. A phone number and opening hours are not ingredients.
questions.rule: Family means all the parts.

questions.q: A theme-park app has WinterTheme with a white background, blue button and snowflake icon, and SummerTheme with matching summer choices. A screen uses the white background from WinterTheme and a summer icon. What is wrong?
options: The parts come from different families, so they may not belong together
Nothing is wrong, because a theme is only decoration for the screen
The screen should use more families so that the parts can be mixed
The icon should be removed, because only one icon is allowed
optionExplain: Right: parts from different families may not belong together, and mixing them breaks consistency.
A theme is more than decoration: its parts are designed to match, and mixing them spoils that.
Using more families so parts can be mixed would make the inconsistency worse.
The issue is mixing families, not the icon itself; each family has its own icon.
questions.explain: WinterTheme's background and SummerTheme's icon come from different families, which are designed so that their parts match. Mixing them breaks the consistency a family provides.
questions.rule: One family at a time.

questions.q: True or false: Two families may share an ingredient class, such as a Seattle family that reuses New York's dough.
questions.explain: What makes a set a family is that its parts belong together; individual parts can be reused across families.
questions.rule: Families may share parts.
questions.teaches: Families may share ingredient classes; what makes a set a family is that the parts are chosen to belong together, not that every part is unique to it.

questions.q: A car configurator offers a Sport package with stiff suspension, sports seats and low-profile tires, and a Comfort package with soft suspension, plush seats and tall tires. What is each package, in the book's terms?
options: A single large product
A static method call
A constructor parameter
A family of related parts
optionExplain: A package is not a single product; it is made of many parts chosen to go together.
A static method call is a code construct and does not describe a set of related parts.
A constructor parameter is a single value passed in, while a package is a set of parts.
Right: the parts are chosen to go together, so each package is a family of related parts.
questions.explain: Each package is a set of parts chosen to go together, such as suspension, seats and tires. That is a family of related parts in the book's sense.
questions.rule: Families are sets of related parts.
questions.teaches: A family is defined by the parts' relationship, not by the domain: any product built from several parts that must match each other forms one.

questions.q: A developer says: a family means all the products a class can possibly create. What is wrong?
options: Families only apply to food products such as ingredients
A family is a set of related parts that belong together
Families must have exactly three parts, like dough, sauce and cheese
Classes cannot create families, only single objects
optionExplain: Families apply to any related parts, not only to food products.
Right: a family is a set of related parts that belong together, and relatedness is what defines it.
A family can have any number of related parts; the three in the pizza example are only an illustration.
A class can create a whole family of related products, not just single objects.
questions.explain: A family is defined by relatedness: a set of parts that belong together, like dough, sauce and cheese. It is not simply everything a class can create.
questions.rule: Family means related.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: thin+marinara
thick+plum
thin+plum
A compile error, because the two kits cannot be mixed
optionExplain: A reader expects the dough's partner; the code asks the Chicago kit for the sauce.
A reader expects both parts from Chicago; the dough comes from the other kit.
Right: the dough comes from the New York kit and the sauce from the Chicago kit.
A reader expects the type system to stop mixing; both kits share an interface.
questions.explain: Nothing stops code from taking parts from two kits. A family should keep its parts together; mixing gives a pizza no region makes.
questions.rule: A family is a set of parts chosen to match.

questions.q: A franchiser must provide regional ingredient sets. Which approach lets any store get its region's ingredients through one common type?
options: One big class that uses an if for each region and each ingredient
An interface with a create method per ingredient and a factory per region
A static method for each ingredient that the store calls by name
A separate unrelated class for each region, with no shared type
optionExplain: Branches return the edit problem.
Right: one shared type, one implementation per region.
Static blocks swapping regions.
With no shared type the store would have to name each region.
questions.explain: A shared type with regional implementations is the shape. The card next lists the steps.
questions.rule: Interface plus one factory per region.

questions.q: What does the PizzaIngredientFactory interface declare?
options: A method that bakes the pizzas for each region
A single method that returns a whole pizza
A constructor for each region of the franchise
A create method for each ingredient in the family
optionExplain: Baking is not creation of ingredients.
Pizzas are built from ingredients.
Constructors belong to classes, not interfaces.
Right: the interface has one create method per product in the family.
questions.explain: PizzaIngredientFactory declares one create method for each ingredient in the family, such as createDough(), createSauce() and createCheese(). Each regional factory implements them.
questions.rule: One method per product.

questions.q: The theme-park app has ThemeFactory with createBackground(), createButton() and createIcon(). How many classes does a new AutumnThemeFactory implement?
options: One class, implementing all three create methods
Three classes, one for each create method
None, because it inherits from the winter factory
Two, covering background and button only
optionExplain: Right: one concrete factory class implements all three create methods for the whole family.
One factory covers the whole family, so there is no class per create method.
It does not need to inherit from the winter factory; it implements the ThemeFactory interface itself.
All three methods must be implemented, so covering only background and button leaves the family incomplete.
questions.explain: A concrete factory covers the whole family, so AutumnThemeFactory is a single class that implements createBackground(), createButton() and createIcon().
questions.rule: One factory, all methods.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a createSound() method to the factory interface requires every concrete factory to be updated.
questions.explain: Adding createSound() to the interface means each concrete factory that implements it must supply the new method, which is a real cost of this design.
questions.rule: Adding to the interface means updating all.
questions.teaches: Adding a product to a family changes the factory interface and so forces an update to every concrete factory, a real cost of this design.

questions.q: Put the steps of building regional factories for an office suite's dialogs in the order the authors' recipe suggests.
items: Define a UiFactory interface with createWindow, createButton and createMenu
Build one factory per platform that implements the interface
Write the control classes the factories return
Hook the factories into the application code
questions.explain: The recipe is interface first, then the regional factories and their parts, then the hookup.
questions.rule: Interface, factories, parts, hookup.
questions.teaches: The same three-step build, an interface, one factory per variant and shared parts, applies to any set of related products, such as controls per platform.

questions.q: The authors note that ingredient classes like RedPeppers can be shared among regions where appropriate. A developer says every region needs a complete set of its own classes. What is wrong?
options: Regions may share ingredient classes only if they also share one factory
Sharing is forbidden, so each region needs its own classes
Regions may share ingredient classes; only the factories differ
Factories are shared among regions, only the ingredients differ
optionExplain: Regions can share ingredient classes such as RedPeppers while keeping separate factories.
The authors allow sharing, so it is not forbidden.
Right: regions may share ingredient classes such as RedPeppers, and only the factories differ.
Each region has its own factory, so it is the factories that differ, not the ingredient classes.
questions.explain: Ingredient classes like RedPeppers can be shared among regions where appropriate, so each region does not need a complete set of its own. What differs by region is the factory.
questions.rule: Share parts where appropriate.

questions.q: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: The compiler rejects ChicagoFactory, which lacks the clam() method
It compiles, and clam() returns null at run time
It compiles, because the interface only suggests which ingredients to make
The compiler rejects the interface because it has too many methods
optionExplain: Right: every concrete factory must implement every create method.
A reader expects a missing method to be filled with null; interface methods must be implemented.
A reader treats the interface as advice; it is a contract.
A reader blames the interface size; the error is in the class that implements it.
questions.explain: An interface forces each regional factory to supply every ingredient. This is also why adding an ingredient later means editing every factory.
questions.rule: Every concrete factory implements every create method.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: thin+mozzarella thick+thick
thin+mozzarella thick+mozzarella
thin+thin thick+thick
A compile error, because two factories cannot share a class
optionExplain: A reader mixes up the parts; cheese does not depend on dough.
Right: each factory supplies its own dough, and they share the mozzarella class.
A reader assumes each kit uses its own dough for every part.
A reader expects every kit to need distinct ingredient classes; sharing is allowed.
questions.explain: The ingredient classes can be shared among regions where appropriate, so both factories use the Mozzarella class while differing in the dough.
questions.rule: Factories vary by region; classes may be shared.

questions.q: Two classes, NYCheesePizza and ChicagoCheesePizza, differ only in the ingredients they use. How can this be simplified?
options: Merge them into a single class that uses an if to choose the region
Delete the Chicago class and let New York style serve everyone
Add a third class that both regional classes can inherit from
Use one CheesePizza class that takes its ingredients from a regional factory
optionExplain: Branching returns the edit problem.
Deleting the Chicago class loses the Chicago style and does not simplify the design properly.
A third parent class adds a class and still leaves two classes that differ only in ingredients.
Right: one CheesePizza class takes its ingredients from a regional factory, which carries the regional difference.
questions.explain: When two classes differ only in their ingredients, one CheesePizza class can take them from a regional factory, which carries the difference.
questions.rule: Differ in parts, share the class.

questions.q: True or false: In the reworked design, the Pizza holds a reference to an ingredient factory.
questions.explain: In the reworked design the Pizza holds a reference to an ingredient factory and uses it to get its ingredients, so the pizza is composed with the factory.
questions.rule: Pizza has a factory.

questions.q: A LoginDialog that asks a ThemeFactory for its parts needs ____ dialog class(es) to serve both the Winter and Summer themes.
questions.explain: The ThemeFactory carries the differences between Winter and Summer, so LoginDialog is written once and serves both themes.
questions.rule: One class, parts from the factory.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a new Seattle region requires editing each pizza class.
questions.explain: The pizzas are decoupled from regional differences, so only a new ingredient factory and its parts are needed.
questions.rule: New region means new factory.
questions.teaches: A new region needs only a new ingredient factory and its new part classes, because the pizzas are decoupled from regional differences.

questions.q: A game has Wolf and Bear enemies in a Forest world and a Desert world, differing only in textures and sounds. How could the ingredient-factory idea reduce the class count?
options: Create a ForestWolf class and a DesertWolf class, one for each world
Use a single Wolf class with an if for each world's textures
A world factory supplies textures and sounds, so one Wolf class serves both
Delete the Desert world so that only one set of classes is needed
optionExplain: Making ForestWolf and DesertWolf gives two classes for one structure, which is the problem to avoid.
An if per world brings back the branching that a factory removes.
Right: a world factory supplies textures and sounds, so one Wolf class serves both worlds.
Deleting the Desert world loses content instead of reducing duplication.
questions.explain: Just as NYCheesePizza and ChicagoCheesePizza collapse into one CheesePizza, one Wolf class can take its textures and sounds from a world factory, so the class count falls.
questions.rule: Shared structure, different parts.
questions.teaches: When the products differ only in their parts, a family factory removes the need for one product class per family, so the class count grows with parts, not with products times regions.

questions.q: A developer says: our regions assemble pizzas in different orders, so one CheesePizza class with a factory is enough. What is the flaw?
options: Factories cannot supply sauce, only dough, in this design
The factory varies the parts, not the assembly steps
Pizzas cannot hold a reference to a factory, only stores can
Regions do not really differ in assembly order, so the premise fails
optionExplain: The factory supplies sauce as well as dough, so that is not the flaw.
Right: different steps would still need separate classes.
Pizzas can hold a reference to a factory, as the reworked design shows.
The developer states that regions do assemble in different orders, so the premise is given, not the flaw.
questions.explain: A factory varies the parts a pizza uses, not the order of its assembly steps. If regions assemble pizzas in different orders, they would still need separate classes.
questions.rule: Parts vary, steps stay.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: thin/marinara thin/marinara
thick/plum thin/marinara
thin/marinara thick/plum
A compile error, because one Pizza class cannot serve two kits
optionExplain: A reader assumes the first kit is shared by every pizza; each pizza holds its own.
A reader swaps the order; the first pizza gets the New York kit.
Right: the same Pizza class uses whichever kit it is composed with.
A reader expects one class per kit; composition removes that need.
questions.explain: One Pizza class serves both regions, since the regional differences live in the kit it is given. This is why the book needs no class per pizza per region.
questions.rule: One product class, many kits.

questions.q: Which problem is the Abstract Factory Pattern designed for?
options: Making sure that a class has only one instance anywhere in the program
Notifying many objects automatically when a single subject changes its state
Creating families of related objects without naming concrete classes
Wrapping an object with another one to add features dynamically
optionExplain: That belongs to a different pattern.
That describes the Observer pattern, not Abstract Factory.
Right: matching sets of products are the focus of Abstract Factory.
That describes the Decorator pattern, not Abstract Factory.
questions.explain: Abstract Factory is for creating families of related objects without naming concrete classes, like sets of ingredients. The other options describe Singleton, Observer and Decorator. The card next gives the definition.
questions.rule: Families of related objects.

questions.q: A client of an Abstract Factory knows only the ____ interface for creating products.
questions.explain: The client knows only the abstract factory interface, so the concrete factories and the concrete products stay hidden behind it.
questions.rule: Client sees abstractions only.

questions.q: A UI toolkit has a UiFactory interface with createWindow, createButton and createMenu, and WindowsUiFactory and MacUiFactory implement it. The app must now run on Mac. What changes?
options: The app is rewritten for Mac
Ifs are added to every control
WindowsUiFactory is edited
The app is passed MacUiFactory
optionExplain: Rewriting the app for Mac is exactly what the factory interface is meant to avoid.
Adding ifs to every control brings back the branching that the factory removes.
WindowsUiFactory is unrelated to running on Mac and needs no edit.
Right: the app is passed MacUiFactory, which swaps the factory and keeps the client unchanged.
questions.explain: The app takes a UiFactory, so running on Mac means passing it MacUiFactory. The client code stays the same and only the factory is swapped.
questions.rule: Swap the factory.

questions.q: True or false: A client that takes every control from one UiFactory makes mixing Windows and Mac controls hard to do by accident.
questions.explain: One factory means one consistent family; mixing would need the client to hold two factories on purpose.
questions.rule: One factory, one family.
questions.teaches: Because the client takes every product from a single factory, products that belong together stay together; mixing families becomes an effort rather than an accident.

questions.q: A furniture shop sells Modern and Victorian sets of chair, sofa and table. Customers want matching pieces. Which approach fits?
options: One class per piece of furniture, with an if to choose the style
A furniture factory interface, with one Modern and one Victorian factory
Three unrelated factories, one for each piece of furniture
A static method per piece that picks the style from a string
optionExplain: One class per piece with an if for the style brings back the branching a factory removes.
Right: each style factory produces a matching set of chair, sofa and table.
Three unrelated factories would let a Modern chair be mixed with a Victorian sofa, so mismatches become possible.
A static method that picks a style from a string blocks swapping and gives no guarantee of matching sets.
questions.explain: Matching Modern or Victorian pieces come from one factory per style, so a furniture factory interface with a Modern and a Victorian factory fits. This is a family problem, which Abstract Factory handles.
questions.rule: Family means abstract factory.
questions.teaches: The pattern fits wherever customers expect pieces to match: the guarantee of a consistent family is its main advantage over separate factories.

questions.q: A developer says: Abstract Factory is a pattern for making sure only one factory exists. What is wrong?
options: It is about limiting the application to one factory at a time, as a singleton does
It concerns families of products; how many factory objects exist is separate
Abstract factories cannot be shared between clients, so each client has its own
Abstract factories make only one product, which is why only one is needed
optionExplain: Limiting the number of factories is Singleton's job, not Abstract Factory's.
Right: Abstract Factory is about creating families of related products; how many factory objects exist is a separate concern.
A factory can be passed to several clients.
An abstract factory makes whole families of products.
questions.explain: Abstract Factory is about families of related products, not about how many factory instances exist.
questions.rule: Families of products.

questions.q: An app offers light, dark and high-contrast looks, each with its own matching buttons, menus and icons. Which design fits?
options: A static create(controlName) method that every screen calls to get any control
An abstract factory interface for the parts, with one concrete factory per look
Separate unrelated factories for buttons, menus and icons, each chosen on its own
One factory method on the screen that returns the whole look as a block of text
optionExplain: A reader reaches for the Simple Factory idiom; it does not keep parts of one look together.
Right: one family per look, created through one interface, so the parts match.
A reader splits the family; nothing then keeps the parts matching.
A reader collapses the family into one product; clients still need separate parts.
questions.explain: A family of matching parts is the case Abstract Factory is for. The authors name different regions, operating systems and look and feel as contexts for different factories.
questions.rule: One concrete factory per context, with parts that match.
questions.teaches: Different concrete factories can stand for different contexts such as regions, operating systems or looks and feels.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: win-window[mac-button] mac-window[win-button]
win-window[win-button] win-window[win-button]
mac-window[mac-button] win-window[win-button]
win-window[win-button] mac-window[mac-button]
optionExplain: A reader mixes the families; screen takes every part from one factory.
A reader assumes the first factory sticks; each call receives its own.
A reader reverses the call order; the Windows call is written first.
Right: screen builds every part from the factory it receives.
questions.explain: screen never names a concrete part, so the factory it is handed decides the whole look. Parts from one factory always match.
questions.rule: A different factory gives a matching family with no client change.

questions.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
questions.q: A customer orders from a New York store that uses an ingredient factory. Which step happens last?
options: The pizza asks the factory for its ingredients
The store creates the pizza
The customer orders
The pizza is baked, cut and boxed
optionExplain: Asking the factory for ingredients happens during preparation, which is before baking.
The store creates the pizza before it can be prepared, so creation comes earlier.
The customer's order starts the process, so it is the first step, not the last.
Right: processing follows preparation with factory ingredients.
questions.explain: Baking needs prepared ingredients, so the pizza is baked, cut and boxed after it has asked the factory for its ingredients. The card next fills in the flow.
questions.rule: Prepare before you bake.

questions.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
questions.q: Put these events of an order into a likely order.
items: A store for the region is created
orderPizza() is called
createPizza() builds the pizza with the regional factory
prepare() asks the factory for ingredients
The pizza is baked, cut and boxed
questions.explain: This is the flow the chapter traces: a store for the region exists, orderPizza() is called, createPizza() builds the pizza with the regional factory, prepare() asks the factory for ingredients, and the pizza is finished.
questions.rule: Store, order, create, prepare, finish.

questions.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
questions.q: In a UI example, a MacUiFactory is handed to a window when the window is created. When does the window ask the factory for its button?
options: When the window is built or drawn, as the pizza asks in prepare()
When the whole app starts up, before any window exists to need parts
Never, because the window already holds its buttons from the start
When the factory is discarded, after the window is closed again
optionExplain: Right: the product asks when it needs parts.
That is earlier than the window exists.
The window cannot already hold its buttons, because the factory is what supplies them.
Discarding the factory after the window closes is too late, because the button was needed earlier.
questions.explain: The window asks for its button when it needs the part, as the pizza asks its factory in prepare(). The factory is passed in at creation, but the request comes later.
questions.rule: Ask when you build.

questions.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
questions.q: True or false: If the New York store hands its pizza the Chicago ingredient factory by mistake, the pizza is made with Chicago ingredients.
questions.explain: The pizza uses whichever factory it is given, so the store's job of passing the right factory keeps a region consistent.
questions.rule: Wrong factory, wrong parts.
questions.teaches: The ingredients depend entirely on the factory the pizza is given, so the store's job of passing the correct regional factory is what keeps a region consistent.

questions.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
questions.q: A report builder is given a PdfParts factory and asks it for a header, a body and a footer. It is then given HtmlParts instead. What changes?
options: The builder code must be rewritten
Nothing, because parts do not depend on the factory
The same builder produces an HTML report
It fails to compile, because HtmlParts is a different class from PdfParts
optionExplain: The builder is written against the factory type, so it need not be rewritten.
The parts do depend on the factory, because the builder gets them from it.
Right: a different factory gives different parts, so the same builder produces an HTML report.
Both are factories of the same type, so the builder compiles and runs with either.
questions.explain: Handing the report builder HtmlParts instead of PdfParts changes the parts it receives, so the same builder produces an HTML report. The builder code is untouched.
questions.rule: Swap the factory, keep the builder.
questions.teaches: Handing the same client a different factory changes the family of parts it builds with, with no change to the client's code.

questions.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
questions.q: A trace states: orderPizza() asks the ingredient factory for dough. Where is the error?
options: The factory does not create dough; it only creates sauce and cheese
The store's createPizza() asks for the dough and passes it to the pizza
orderPizza() does not exist; the store calls prepare() directly
The pizza's prepare() asks the factory, not orderPizza()
optionExplain: The ingredient factory creates dough, sauce, cheese and the rest.
createPizza() hands the factory to the pizza; the pizza's prepare() is what asks it.
orderPizza() exists and is the routine that calls prepare().
Right: the pizza's prepare() is what asks the factory, while orderPizza() only calls prepare().
questions.explain: The pizza's prepare() asks the ingredient factory for dough, sauce and cheese, not orderPizza(). orderPizza() only calls prepare(), so the trace names the wrong caller.
questions.rule: Pizza asks the factory.

questions.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
questions.q: In the ingredient-factory design, what must a franchise store hand each pizza so that the pizza uses local ingredients?
options: The region's name as a string, for the pizza to look up the ingredients
A copy of each ingredient class the pizza needs
Nothing, because the pizza finds the right factory by checking its store
A reference to the store's own regional ingredient factory
optionExplain: A reader reaches for a lookup; the pizza would then need regional knowledge.
A reader hands over parts; the pizza asks the factory for them when it is prepared.
A reader makes the pizza search; a pizza is decoupled from regional differences.
Right: the store is given its local factory and passes it on to the pizzas it creates.
questions.explain: The authors tell us the stores need a reference to their local ingredient factories. Each store creates its pizzas with that factory.
questions.rule: The store supplies the factory; the pizza asks it for parts.
questions.teaches: Each franchise store holds a reference to its own local ingredient factory and gives it to the pizzas it creates.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: Which factory pattern creates objects by letting a subclass override a creation method?
options: Factory Method
Abstract Factory
Simple Factory
Singleton
optionExplain: Right: Factory Method works by inheritance, with a subclass overriding the creation method.
Abstract Factory works by composition, with a factory object passed in, not by overriding.
Simple Factory uses a separate object, not a subclass override.
Singleton controls how many instances exist and does not create products by overriding.
questions.explain: Factory Method creates objects by letting a subclass override a creation method, which is inheritance, while Abstract Factory hands a factory object to the client. The card next compares them.
questions.rule: Subclass means Factory Method.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: Match each factory approach to how it creates objects.
pairs: Inheritance: a subclass implements the factory method
Composition: a factory object is passed in
One class that builds products from a parameter
questions.explain: The mechanisms differ: Factory Method uses inheritance through a subclass, Abstract Factory uses composition with a factory object passed in, and Simple Factory is a single class building products from a parameter.
questions.rule: Inheritance, composition, idiom.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: A parser class is subclassed to supply createToken(), while a UI toolkit is handed a factory object that produces a window, a button and a menu. Which pairing is right?
options: Both use Factory Method, since both create products
Parser uses Abstract Factory; toolkit uses Factory Method
Parser uses Factory Method; toolkit uses Abstract Factory
Both use Abstract Factory, since both create products
optionExplain: The toolkit makes a family of products through a factory object, which is not Factory Method.
The parser uses subclassing, which is Factory Method, so this reverses the pairing.
Right: the parser uses subclassing, and the toolkit gets a family via a factory object.
The parser makes just one product through a subclass, so it is not Abstract Factory.
questions.explain: The parser gets createToken() from a subclass, which is Factory Method. The toolkit receives a factory object producing a whole family of window, button and menu, which is Abstract Factory.
questions.rule: Mechanism decides.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: True or false: The create methods inside an Abstract Factory are often implemented as factory methods.
questions.explain: The book says factory methods are a natural way to implement the product methods of an abstract factory.
questions.rule: Factory methods inside Abstract Factory.
questions.teaches: The two patterns compose: each create method inside an Abstract Factory is usually a factory method, so Abstract Factory is often built from Factory Methods.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: A game needs one Enemy per level type, and a separate need for matching sets of weapon, armor and shield per class. Which patterns suit the two needs?
options: Abstract Factory for the enemy and Factory Method for the gear
Factory Method for the enemy, Abstract Factory for the gear set
Simple Factory for both needs, since it is the simplest
Neither, because no factory pattern fits these two needs
optionExplain: That reverses them: the single enemy is a Factory Method job and the gear set is a family.
Right: a single enemy calls for Factory Method and a matching gear set for Abstract Factory.
Simple Factory is an idiom, not a pattern, and it neither supplies creation through subclasses nor creates families.
Each need matches a factory pattern: a single product and a family of products.
questions.explain: The enemy is a single product per level, which suits Factory Method, while matched weapon, armor and shield form a family, which suits Abstract Factory.
questions.rule: One product or a family.
questions.teaches: A useful rule of thumb is to count the products: one product points to Factory Method, a set that must match points to Abstract Factory.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: A developer says: Factory Method and Abstract Factory both create objects by inheritance in the same way. What is wrong?
options: Neither uses inheritance, because both patterns rely on interfaces alone
Both use composition, passing a factory object into the client
Abstract Factory uses composition, through a factory object passed in
Factory Method uses composition, with a creator object passed in
optionExplain: Factory Method does use inheritance, since a subclass supplies the creation method.
Factory Method uses inheritance, so it does not pass a factory object into the client.
Right: Abstract Factory uses composition through a factory object, which differs from Factory Method's inheritance.
Factory Method uses inheritance, with subclasses supplying creation, not a creator object passed in.
questions.explain: Factory Method uses inheritance, with a subclass supplying creation, while Abstract Factory uses composition, with a factory object passed in. They differ in mechanism.
questions.rule: Inheritance vs composition.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: Sort these descriptions by the pattern they fit.

items.t: Creation is done by a subclass that overrides one method
Creation is done by an object passed to the client
Usually makes a single product
Its interface has one create method per product in a family
The creator often holds code that uses the products it creates
Exists purely to create products

questions.explain: Factory Method relies on inheritance and a single product. Abstract Factory relies on composition and a family of products, and exists to create them.
questions.rule: Inheritance and one product, or composition and a family.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: What weakens this Abstract Factory client?
options: App keeps the factory in a field instead of passing it to each call
window() is called before the button is created
The button comes from new MacButton(), bypassing the factory's matching parts
UiFactory should be an abstract class instead of an interface
optionExplain: A reader dislikes the field; holding the factory is how a client is composed with it.
A reader worries about order; nothing in the pattern fixes one.
Right: one part bypasses the factory, so the parts need not match and a concrete class is named.
A reader blames the interface type; the authors say an abstract class is optional.
questions.explain: The client takes the window from the factory but builds the button itself. It loses the guarantee that parts match and names a concrete class again.
questions.rule: Take every part from the factory.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: A team's Abstract Factory interface has six create methods. What is the main cost of adding a seventh product?
options: Every concrete factory must be changed to implement the new method
Only the client changes, because it calls the interface
Nothing changes, because the new method is optional for factories
Only the products change, because the factories stay as they are
optionExplain: Right: interface growth ripples to every concrete factory, which must implement the new method.
The concrete factories also have to change, not just the client.
The method is not optional, so every factory must implement it.
The interface and the factories change too, not only the products.
questions.explain: Adding a seventh product means adding a method to the Abstract Factory interface, so every concrete factory that implements it must change. The card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: Growing the interface ripples.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: True or false: In the interview, Abstract Factory admits that adding new products means its interface has to change.
questions.explain: Abstract Factory says so in the interview: adding products changes its interface, and Factory Method points out the ripple to every subclass.
questions.rule: Interface change is the cost.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: A UiFactory has three methods and three platform factories. Adding createTooltip() changes ____ classes in total.
questions.explain: Adding createTooltip() changes the interface plus each of the three platform factories, so four classes in total.
questions.rule: Count the ripple.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: True or false: Abstract Factory is more attractive when a toolkit adds platforms often but adds new products rarely.
questions.explain: A new platform is a new factory with no interface change, while the costly change of adding a product is rare.
questions.rule: Which dimension grows?
questions.teaches: The cost of Abstract Factory depends on which dimension grows: adding a new family is cheap, while adding a new product to every family is expensive.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: A game needs to create one Enemy for each level, and nobody knows which levels will exist in two years. Which advice from the interview applies?
options: Use Abstract Factory, because it is built for unknown future classes
Use Factory Method, since not every concrete class is known in advance
Use Simple Factory, since it is the simplest way to switch on a level number
Use a singleton, so that only one enemy exists at a time
optionExplain: There is one product per level, not a family, so Abstract Factory is not the fit.
Right: that is the authors' advice.
Simple Factory would have to be reopened for each new level, which unknown future levels make likely.
A singleton limits instances; it does not help create a different enemy per level.
questions.explain: One Enemy per level is a single product, not a family, and the concrete classes are not all known in advance, so the advice points to Factory Method.
questions.rule: Unknown classes suggest Factory Method.
questions.teaches: The parting advice gives two triggers to remember: families that must match point to Abstract Factory, and unknown future classes point to Factory Method.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: A reader says: the interview proves Abstract Factory is a bad pattern. Where does the reasoning fail?
options: The interview praises only Factory Method, so its verdict is one-sided
It names a cost and a purpose; a cost alone does not make a tool bad
The interview never mentions costs, so none can be drawn from it
Patterns have no costs, so any criticism of one must be mistaken
optionExplain: The interview does not praise only Factory Method; it weighs both patterns, so one-sidedness is not the flaw.
Right: it names a cost and a purpose, and a cost alone does not make a tool bad.
The interview does mention costs, so costs can be drawn from it.
Patterns do have costs, which is why the criticism cannot be dismissed as mistaken.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the interview names a cost of Abstract Factory (changing the interface touches every factory) alongside its purpose of creating families. A cost alone does not make a tool bad.
questions.rule: Weigh cost and purpose.

questions.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
questions.q: How does Abstract Factory answer the charge that its interface is large and costly to change?
options: It creates whole families; Factory Method makes one product with one method
The interface is large only in the book's example, and real factories need one method
Changing it is harmless because the concrete factories do not implement it
A large interface lets a client create any product from any family
optionExplain: Right: the size follows from the job of creating a family.
A reader dismisses the size; a family needs a method per product.
A reader denies the cost; the interview agrees that the subclasses all change.
A reader confuses size with freedom; the point is that products belong together.
questions.explain: The interview has Abstract Factory concede the cost and explain it: a family needs a bigger interface.
questions.rule: A big interface is the price of creating a family.

questions.q: Which object is the strongest candidate for having only one instance in a program?
options: A report object that is created afresh for each customer request
A point object holding the x and y values of a single shape
The object that writes every message of the program to its log file
A temporary list that is built and discarded inside one loop
optionExplain: Plausible because it is important, but each request has its own report, so many are expected.
Plausible as a simple class, but thousands of points are normal and need no limit.
Right: logging is one of the chapter's examples, and several writers could garble one file.
Plausible as shared data, but it lives briefly in one place and nothing depends on its uniqueness.
questions.explain: Objects that coordinate one shared resource, such as a log, are the classic single-instance cases. The card next lists them and the trouble a second copy causes.
questions.rule: One shared resource, one object.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter names ordinary data records, such as one customer's order, among the objects that call for a single instance.
questions.explain: The authors' list has shared resources such as thread pools, caches, dialog boxes, settings, logging and device drivers. A record of one order is meant to exist in many copies.
questions.rule: Shared device or shared settings: one object.

questions.q: A grocery app has five kinds of objects. Which two would the chapter's reasoning support making single-instance?
options: The pool of connections to the product database
A receipt object created for each sale
The holder of the shop's saved preferences
A basket object for each shopper
A price label created for each item
optionExplain: Right: a pool of resources is one of the chapter's examples, and two pools would overuse connections.
A receipt belongs to one sale; many receipts are expected and independent.
Right: preference and registry settings are listed, and two copies could disagree.
Each shopper has a separate basket, so many baskets are expected.
Each item has its own label, so many labels are normal.
questions.explain: Objects that manage a shared pool or shared settings need one instance. Objects that represent one sale, shopper or item are meant to be many.
questions.rule: Ask whether two copies would disagree or double the resource use.

questions.q: In the chapter's interview, the Singleton says it would like more developers to know it. What reason does it give?
options: Many developers hit bugs from extra copies they do not know exist
Developers pay too much for each extra object, so memory runs out within minutes
Compilers cannot detect a second object, so every build fails and must be repaired
Most programs have no objects at all that need to be shared between classes
optionExplain: The interview says the bugs come from copies floating around unnoticed.
Overuse of resources is one of the three warned troubles, but it is not the reason the Singleton gives here.
Compilers do not check how many objects exist, but builds do not fail for that reason.
The chapter says the opposite: many common objects should exist once.
questions.explain: Duplicate objects often go unnoticed, which makes the resulting bugs hard to find. This is a reason to have the class itself prevent copies instead of relying on programmers to remember.
questions.rule: Hidden duplicates cause bugs.
questions.teaches: Bugs from duplicate objects are hard to find because the extra copies are unnoticed, so the class itself should prevent them instead of relying on programmers' care.

questions.q: Which statement about single-instance classes matches the chapter's advice?
options: Any class that many other classes depend on should be turned into a Singleton at once
The more Singletons a program has, the safer all of its shared state becomes
A class should become a Singleton as soon as it needs to expose any static method
Singletons are meant to be used sparingly; many in one design deserve a hard look
optionExplain: Dependence alone is not the test; the test is whether a second copy would cause trouble.
This treats the pattern as a safety net, but the authors warn about overusing it.
Static methods are a tool for building the pattern, not a reason to apply it.
The authors say to use sparingly and review designs with many.
questions.explain: The pattern solves a specific problem, so it should be applied where a second copy would hurt. A design full of Singletons suggests something else is wrong.
questions.rule: Use it where duplicates hurt, not by habit.

questions.q: A warehouse program has a class that sends commands to the one label printer on the packing bench. Which reason best supports giving it a single instance?
options: It uses the printer often, and any frequently used class must be made a Singleton
It stands for one physical device, and several controllers could conflict
It holds a lot of data, and large objects must be created only once in a program
It is written in Java, and Java classes with static methods must be unique
optionExplain: Frequency of use is not the criterion; what matters is that a copy would cause trouble.
One object per device avoids two senders giving conflicting commands.
Size does not decide it; a large report object can still be one of many.
Language features do not require uniqueness; the design need does.
questions.explain: An object that represents one physical thing is like the chapter's device drivers. Two controllers for the same printer could interleave or contradict each other.
questions.rule: One device, one controller object.
questions.teaches: An object that represents one physical device is a natural single-instance candidate, because two controllers for it can send conflicting commands.

questions.q: True or false: Making a class non-public guarantees that only one object of it can be created.
questions.explain: A non-public class can still be created by every class in its package, as often as they like. The card next explains what the constructor has to do with it.
questions.rule: Access to the class does not cap the count.

questions.q: A class that is not public can still be instantiated by the classes in the same ____.
questions.explain: The Socratic exercise reaches this point: a non-public class is open to its own package, and those classes can instantiate it more than once.
questions.rule: Narrower access, still many objects.

questions.q: Three classes in the package billing each call new on a non-public class Invoicer from the same package. How many Invoicer objects can exist?
options: Exactly one, because the class is not public
As many as those three classes choose to create
One per package, so one in total here
None, because non-public classes cannot be instantiated
optionExplain: Plausible because non-public sounds restrictive, but it restricts who, not how many.
Each new call builds another object, and nothing limits the calls.
A package is a circle of callers, not a counter of objects.
Non-public classes can be instantiated by classes in the same package.
questions.explain: Package-level access decides who may call new. It does not stop several callers, or one caller, from building several objects.
questions.rule: Restricting who is not restricting how many.

questions.q: A team agrees in writing that only the startup code will call new on a Cache class with a public constructor. A new hire builds a second Cache in a test helper. What does this show?
options: The new hire should have read the agreement, and one more written reminder would fix the design
Test code is exempt from the rule, so the design is working as intended in this case
The agreement was too weak, and adding a second signature on it would enforce it
A public constructor lets any caller break the agreement; the class enforces nothing
optionExplain: Reminders fail the same way again; a limit that depends on memory is not enforced.
Nothing in the class distinguishes test code from other code.
Signatures change the agreement, not what the compiler allows.
The agreement lives in people's heads, not in the class.
questions.explain: In the chapter's interview the Singleton says developers need not swear an oath not to instantiate it twice. The class prevents it by having no public constructor.
questions.rule: Enforce the limit in the class, not by agreement.
questions.teaches: A limit kept only by agreement among callers is not enforced; the enforcement has to live in the class, which in the interview needs no oath because it has no public constructor.

questions.q: A student argues: My class is package-level, so only one instance can exist. Which step of this argument fails?
options: Package-level access limits who can call new, but not how many times they call it
Package-level classes cannot be instantiated at all, so the count is zero
Package-level classes can be built by any class in the program, so the count is unlimited
The student should have used the word protected instead of package-level
optionExplain: Right: the premise limits callers, and the conclusion needs a limit on count.
Classes in the same package can instantiate them.
Only classes in the same package can build them; the failure lies elsewhere.
Changing the keyword would change the circle of callers, still not the count.
questions.explain: The argument moves from a statement about who may create objects to a statement about how many exist. The two are different.
questions.rule: Who is not how many.

questions.q: A concert hall has three doors. Order them from the widest circle of people who may enter to the narrowest, like the circle of code that can call new.
items: A door open to every ticket holder
A door open only to the staff of the hall
A door that only the hall manager can unlock
questions.explain: Constructor access works the same way: public admits any code, package-level admits the classes of one package, and private admits only the class itself.
questions.rule: Public, package-level, private: widening to narrowing.
questions.teaches: Access modifiers give nested circles of callers (public, package-level, private), and only private shrinks the circle to the class itself.

questions.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
questions.q: A class declares its constructor private. What is true of code in other classes?
options: It can use new, but only from classes in the same package
It can use new once per program run
It cannot use new on that class
It can use new, but only inside static methods
optionExplain: That describes a package-level class, not a private constructor.
Java has no per-run counter on constructor calls.
A private constructor is callable only from inside the class.
Where the call sits does not matter; other classes cannot call it.
questions.explain: Private means visible only inside the class. The card next shows how the class can still hand out an object.
questions.rule: Private constructor: no new from outside.

questions.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
questions.q: True or false: A static method can be called only after an object of its class has been created.
questions.explain: A static method belongs to the class, so it is called through the class name with no object. That is why MyClass.getInstance() works when no MyClass object exists.
questions.rule: Static methods need the class, not an object.

questions.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
questions.q: The class AuditTrail must let outsiders obtain its object but not build one. Which pair of declarations does that?
options: A public constructor and a public static method that returns an AuditTrail
A private constructor and a public instance method that returns an AuditTrail
A public constructor and a private static method that returns an AuditTrail
A private constructor and a public static method that returns an AuditTrail
optionExplain: The public constructor lets outsiders build objects themselves.
An instance method needs an object, and no outsider can create one.
This opens construction and closes the only way to ask.
Outsiders cannot use new, and they can call the static method on the class.
questions.explain: The private constructor blocks outside construction, and only a static method is callable without an object. Both are needed together.
questions.rule: Private constructor plus public static method.
questions.hint: Which method can an outsider call before any object exists?

questions.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
questions.q: A developer wants to write class FastSettings that extends Settings, whose only constructor is private. What happens?
options: It works, because a subclass can always call its parent's private constructor
It fails, because a class with a private constructor cannot be extended
It works, but only if FastSettings is in a different package
It works, but FastSettings must then also declare a private constructor
optionExplain: Privacy hides the constructor from the subclass too.
The authors state that you cannot extend a class with a private constructor.
Packages do not change what private allows.
The subclass's own constructor does not give it access to the parent's.
questions.explain: The same privacy that blocks outsiders blocks subclasses, because a subclass constructor must call a parent constructor. The chapter returns to this when it discusses subclassing a Singleton.
questions.rule: Private constructor means no subclass.
questions.teaches: A class whose constructor is private cannot be extended, because the subclass cannot reach the constructor it must call.

questions.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
questions.q: A class has a private constructor and no static method that builds or returns an object. Other classes cannot obtain any ____ of it.
questions.explain: No outsider can construct one and nothing hands one out. This is the chicken-and-egg dead end the Socratic exercise reaches, and the static method breaks it.
questions.rule: No static door, no object for outsiders.

questions.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
questions.q: A clerk at a ticket office asks the TicketCounter class for the counter object. Which description matches how a Singleton answers?
options: Each call builds a fresh object for that clerk alone, ready for the clerk's use
The call fails for as long as another clerk is still holding the object
The call may return an object that already exists and serves other callers
The clerk must register once with the class before any call can succeed
optionExplain: This would make many objects, which is what the pattern prevents.
Nothing in the pattern makes callers take turns to get it.
Asking is not creating: the interview says it may already be helping others.
The pattern needs no registration; any caller can ask.
