questions.explain: The interview's Singleton says you do not instantiate one, you ask for an instance, and it may already be helping other objects.
questions.rule: Ask the class; do not build.
questions.teaches: Asking a Singleton for its instance is not creating it: the object returned may already exist and be serving other callers.

questions.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
questions.q: Which set of Java features does the classic Singleton combine?
options: A private constructor, a static variable and a static method
A public constructor, an instance variable and a final method
An abstract class, an interface and a factory object
A protected constructor, a registry and a subclass
optionExplain: These three work together, as the chapter's bullet points say.
A public constructor lets anyone build objects.
These are other pattern ingredients, not what the Singleton uses.
Protected and registries come up only in the discussion of subclassing.
questions.explain: The chapter names a private constructor, a static method and a static variable. The card next shows how they cooperate.
questions.rule: Three pieces: private, static variable, static method.

questions.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
questions.q: In the classic implementation, the static method that hands out the object is conventionally called ____.
questions.explain: The chapter uses getInstance() throughout, and the interview's Singleton says you call it to get the instance.
questions.rule: getInstance is the door.

questions.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
questions.q: Put these steps in the order they happen on the very first call of getInstance in a classic Singleton.
items: The method finds the static variable empty
The private constructor builds the object
The object is stored in the static variable
The object is returned to the caller
questions.explain: The method checks the variable, builds with the private constructor, stores the result, and then returns it. Later calls skip the middle steps.
questions.rule: Check, build, store, return.

questions.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
questions.q: Why must the variable that holds the single object be static rather than an ordinary instance variable?
options: Instance variables live inside objects, and getInstance runs before any object exists
Static variables are faster to read, and the pattern needs speed on every single call
Instance variables cannot hold objects of their own class in Java at all
Static variables are kept in a registry that prevents a second copy from appearing
optionExplain: The static variable exists with the class, so getInstance can use it from the start.
Speed is not the reason; the reason is where the variable lives.
They can; the point is that no object exists yet to own them.
There is no such registry in the classic pattern.
questions.explain: A static variable belongs to the class, so the class can use it before any object exists. An instance variable would need the object that is not built yet.
questions.rule: Static variable: owned by the class, not by an object.
questions.teaches: The single object has to be held in a static variable because it belongs to the class and exists before any object does; an instance variable would need an object that is not built yet.

questions.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
questions.q: A developer writes getInstance so that it builds a new object on every call, then stores it in the static variable and returns it. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because the static variable ensures that only one object can exist
The method should be an instance method so that each object tracks its own copy
Each call makes another object, so the class no longer limits itself to one
The private constructor cannot be called from inside a static method of its own class
optionExplain: A variable holds one reference, but earlier objects may still be in use elsewhere.
This moves the problem to a place where no object exists yet.
The method must build only when the variable is empty.
A static method of the same class is allowed to call it.
questions.explain: Callers that received earlier objects still hold them, so several live at once. The empty-variable check is what keeps the count at one.
questions.rule: Build only when empty.

questions.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
questions.q: An airline app has a ReservationDesk Singleton that opens a large seat database. Nobody calls getInstance during a run that only prints timetables. When is the desk object built in the classic version?
options: When the program starts, since every static variable is filled at that moment
Not at all in that run, because it is built only when first requested
When the first thread is created by the program, whatever the thread does
When the class is compiled, before the program has started to run
optionExplain: In the classic version the variable starts empty and is filled on request.
The object is built by the first getInstance call, which never happens in that run.
Thread creation does not trigger the build.
Compiling produces code and builds no objects.
questions.explain: Because the classic version builds on first request, a run that never asks for the instance never builds it. The chapter returns to this advantage when it compares lazy and eager creation.
questions.rule: No request, no object.
questions.teaches: In the classic version the object is created only at the first request, so a run that never calls getInstance never builds it.

questions.q: True or false: Two controller objects for the same boiler can hold different beliefs about whether it is full.
questions.explain: Each object keeps its own record of what it has done, so their records can differ. The card next shows why this matters for the boiler.
questions.rule: Separate objects keep separate state.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says the boiler class is careful to prevent draining unboiled mixture, filling a boiler that is already full, and boiling an empty boiler.
questions.explain: These are the three mistakes named in the chapter's description of the controller.
questions.rule: Know the three guards.

questions.q: A hospital cabinet has a controller that refuses to unlock drawer 3 while drawer 3 is recorded as open. Two controller objects exist. Nurse A opens drawer 3 through controller one. Nurse B asks controller two to unlock drawer 3. What is the likely result?
options: Controller two refuses, because the cabinet itself remembers which drawers are open
Controller two refuses, because both controllers read from the very same record
Both controllers lock themselves until an administrator comes to reset them
Controller two may unlock it; it never learned that controller one saw the drawer open
optionExplain: The cabinet is not the one doing the checking in this scenario; the controllers are.
Separate objects do not read the same record unless they are the same object.
Nothing in the scenario triggers a lock-out.
Each controller checks only its own record.
questions.explain: The guard depends on state held in an object. With two objects there are two records, and the second does not know about the first drawer opening.
questions.rule: Two objects, two records.

questions.q: The boiler controller checks its state before every action. Why is that care not enough once a second instance exists?
options: The checks run too slowly to catch the fast changes made between two objects
A second instance removes the checks from the first instance's methods
Each instance checks only its own state, so neither sees what the other did
The checks are valid only for the first object created in the whole program
optionExplain: Speed is not the issue; the information is not shared.
Creating an object does not alter another object's methods.
The checks stay correct inside each object but miss what the other did.
Each object runs the same checks equally well on what it knows.
questions.explain: The code of the class can be careful and still fail when duplicated, because its correctness assumed that it alone holds the state.
questions.rule: Correct code can still need exactly one instance.
questions.teaches: A class can be carefully written and still fail when duplicated, because its correctness depends on its being the only holder of the state.

questions.q: True or false: If a controller kept no state and every command were safe at any time, a second instance would matter much less than it does for the boiler.
questions.explain: The boiler needed one instance because of its state. With no state to disagree about, a copy changes little, though resource-heavy objects may still deserve a single instance.
questions.rule: State is what makes duplicates dangerous.

questions.q: A bank's vault door controller keeps a record of which doors are open, and two controllers were created by mistake. Which two changes remove the root problem?
options: Let only the controller class create its object
Hand every caller the same controller object
Add comments to the code explaining the danger
Make each safety check stricter inside the controller
Give every caller its own controller to avoid sharing
optionExplain: Right: control of creation sits in the class, so no second object can appear.
Right: one shared object means one record of the open doors.
Comments do not stop a second object from being built.
Stricter checks still read a state that only one object knows.
Separate controllers multiply the records and the disagreement.
questions.explain: The fix is not better checks but ensuring one holder of the state, by letting the class control creation and hand out the same object. That is what the Singleton pattern does.
questions.rule: Fix duplicates by controlling creation.
questions.teaches: Duplicate-state problems are fixed by making the class control its own creation, not by tightening the checks inside the class.

questions.q: Which sentence best defines a Singleton?
options: A class with one instance and a global point of access to it
A class whose methods are all static, so that no object is ever needed
A class that cannot be subclassed or copied by any other class in the program
A class that creates one object for each thread that asks it for one
optionExplain: This is the authors' definition.
That is a different design, which the chapter treats separately.
Blocking subclasses is a side effect, not the definition.
That gives many objects, not one.
questions.explain: The definition has two parts: one instance and one global access point. The card next breaks them apart.
questions.rule: One instance, one access point.

questions.q: The Singleton Pattern ensures a class has only one ____ and provides a global point of access to it.
questions.explain: The authors' definition names the single instance first and the global point of access second.
questions.rule: One instance, global access.

questions.q: A tax office app stores its rate table in a global variable that any screen can read. Any screen can also build a second rate table with new. Which promise of the pattern is missing?
options: The promise of a global point of access
Both promises, because globals cannot hold objects
Neither, because one variable means one object
The promise that only one instance exists
optionExplain: Any screen can already read the global variable.
Globals can hold objects; the access promise is kept.
The variable holds one reference, but new can create others elsewhere.
The global variable gives access, but nothing stops a second table.
questions.explain: Access is covered by the global variable, but the class does not control its own creation. That is the first promise.
questions.rule: Access alone is not enough.

questions.q: How does the chapter describe the Singleton's class diagram, compared with its implementation?
options: The diagram is complex because it shows every thread, but the code is trivial to write
One class in the diagram, the simplest of any pattern, but several pitfalls in the code
Both are simple, so the chapter treats the pattern in a short paragraph
The diagram has two classes, one for the instance and one for the access
optionExplain: The reverse of the chapter's account.
The introduction says the diagram is simplest yet the code is hard to get right.
The chapter spends twelve pages on the pitfalls.
The diagram holds a single class.
questions.explain: Simplicity in the diagram does not mean simplicity in the code. The rest of the chapter is about the details that go wrong.
questions.rule: A short diagram hides a long list of pitfalls.
questions.teaches: A pattern's diagram can be very simple while its implementation is hard: Singleton code is hard to get right.

questions.q: True or false: If a class has a public static method returning a shared object but keeps a public constructor, the promise that only one instance exists is still kept.
questions.explain: The static method covers access only. With a public constructor, other code can build more instances with new.
questions.rule: Close the constructor to keep the first promise.

questions.q: A colleague says a news app's EditorsPick object is only a Singleton if it is built the first time someone asks for it. Which response fits the definition?
options: The colleague is right, because lazy creation is a part of the definition itself
The definition fixes only count and access, so building at class loading also qualifies
Neither is a Singleton, because the definition requires a global variable to exist
Only an eagerly built object qualifies, because only that kind is safe with threads
optionExplain: The definition does not mention timing.
Nothing in the definition says when the object is created.
The definition requires a global access point, not a global variable.
Safety with threads is a separate issue from the definition.
questions.explain: The chapter notes that the pattern can be implemented lazily, and later shows an eager version as another option. Both satisfy the two promises.
questions.rule: Timing of creation is an implementation choice.
questions.teaches: The definition says nothing about when the instance is built, so lazy and eager versions are both Singletons.

questions.q: A program creates a very memory-hungry object at startup and keeps it in a global variable. In which case is that wasteful?
options: When the program uses the object in every run
When the program reads the object from several classes
When the object is declared in the main class of the program
When the program ends up never using the object
optionExplain: Then the cost is spent on something needed.
Sharing does not add cost.
Where it is declared does not change the cost.
The cost is paid with no benefit.
questions.explain: Creation at startup spends resources whether or not the object is ever needed. The card next names the alternative.
questions.rule: Pay only for what is used.

questions.q: True or false: Lazy instantiation means the object is built when the program starts, whether or not anyone asks for it.
questions.explain: Lazy means the reverse: creation waits for the first getInstance call. Building at start is the eager choice.
questions.rule: Lazy: build on first request.

questions.q: A video editor has a 4K preview renderer used in about one session in twenty. Which approach spares the other nineteen sessions the cost?
options: Build the renderer as a Singleton when the first getInstance call asks for it
Build the renderer at launch and keep it in a global variable for every session
Build the renderer at launch and then share it through a Singleton afterwards
Build a renderer for each preview request and discard it when the request ends
optionExplain: Lazy creation means sessions that never ask never pay.
This is the up-front global the chapter names as wasteful.
Sharing does not change when it is built; it is still built at launch.
This makes many objects and repeats the cost.
questions.explain: Only lazy creation ties the cost to actual use. Early creation, even through a Singleton, spends resources in every session.
questions.rule: Tie the cost to the first use.

questions.q: Under lazy instantiation, who bears the cost of creating the object?
options: Every caller equally, because each call rebuilds part of the object
The program at startup, before any caller asks for the object
Whichever caller first requests it, and nobody if no one ever does
The class loader, which builds it when the class is first compiled
optionExplain: Later calls reuse the stored object.
That describes eager creation.
The first call builds it; later calls get it free.
Compilation builds no objects.
questions.explain: Laziness moves the cost from startup to the first request. A program that never requests the object avoids the cost.
questions.rule: Lazy moves the cost to the first request.
questions.teaches: Lazy creation shifts the whole creation cost onto the first requester, so one caller may see a delay while later callers see none.

questions.q: The application uses the Singleton in every run, right at startup. What happens to the advantage of lazy creation?
options: It grows, because the first request now happens earlier
It stays the same, because lazy creation always saves memory
It turns negative, because lazy creation makes the object slower to use afterwards
It disappears, because the object is built in every run anyway
optionExplain: Earlier use does not make lazy creation save anything.
The saving exists only for runs that never ask.
After the first request, lazy and eager objects behave the same.
There is nothing to save when the object is always needed.
questions.explain: Lazy creation saves only in runs that skip the object. If every run needs it, building early or late costs the same.
questions.rule: No savings when always used.

questions.q: Sort each object by whether lazy or early creation suits it better.

items.t: A 2 GB map index needed only by an admin screen
A rarely used export module with heavy fonts
A small clock helper that every page calls at load
A logger that every request writes to from startup

questions.explain: How often the object is needed and how costly it is to build decide the choice. Rarely used, expensive objects favour lazy creation; cheap or always-used ones gain nothing from waiting.
questions.rule: Use frequency and cost decide lazy or early.
questions.teaches: Frequency of use and cost of creation together decide the choice: rarely used, expensive objects favour lazy creation, while cheap or always-used ones gain nothing from waiting.

questions.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
questions.q: A classic Singleton passes every test, but in production the boiler is filled twice. What is the most likely cause?
options: The garbage collector destroyed the boiler and then built a second one in its place
Two threads each built an object, because check and build could overlap
The constructor was public, so another class was able to build a second boiler
A subclass shared the static variable and replaced the first object with its own
optionExplain: A real bug in old JVMs, but the chapter's problem here is threads.
This is the chapter's diagnosis.
The classic version already has a private constructor.
Subclassing is not part of this problem.
questions.explain: Threads can interleave the steps of getInstance. The card next explains how the interleaving yields two objects.
questions.rule: Interleaved steps can duplicate the object.

questions.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
questions.q: True or false: The multiple-instances problem in the chocolate boiler was caused by a public constructor that let other classes build a second boiler.
questions.explain: The chapter points to threads: it asks whether their addition could have caused it, then has the reader trace how two threads can get different objects.
questions.rule: Concurrent calls can split one object into two.

questions.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
questions.q: Two threads call getInstance on a ChatServer Singleton at about the same time. Put the events in an order that ends with two ChatServer objects.
items: Thread A checks the stored instance and finds it empty
Thread B checks the stored instance and also finds it empty
Thread A builds a ChatServer and stores it
Thread B builds another ChatServer and stores it
questions.explain: Both checks happen before either build, so both threads decide to build. The second store replaces the first, but thread A may still be using its object.
questions.rule: Both check before either builds.

questions.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
questions.q: A tester calls getInstance 1,000 times from a single thread and gets the same object each time. What does this show?
options: That the Singleton is safe, because repeated calls never produce a second object
That the Singleton is unsafe, because the first call took the longest
Only that the one-thread case works; it says nothing about overlapping threads
That the problem lies in the tester, which should use a larger number of calls
optionExplain: One thread cannot overlap with itself; other threads can.
Timing of the first call is not a sign of a race.
The failure needs two threads inside the method together.
More calls from one thread cannot expose the overlap.
questions.explain: A passing single-threaded test is consistent with a race. The bug appears only when two threads are inside getInstance in the unlucky order.
questions.rule: A passing test with one thread proves little.
questions.teaches: Passing single-threaded tests does not prove a Singleton safe, because the failure needs overlapping threads and may appear only rarely.

questions.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
questions.q: Thread B calls getInstance only after thread A has finished building and storing the object. What does B receive?
options: The same object A built, since the variable is no longer empty
A second object, because each thread builds an object of its own when it asks
Nothing at all, because B must wait for A to release the class before asking
A copy of A's object, made at the moment when B asks for it
optionExplain: The race exists only while the variable is empty.
Only a thread that finds the variable empty builds.
The classic version has no waiting.
The method returns the stored reference, not a copy.
questions.explain: The danger window is the time between the check and the store on the first call. Outside it, every thread sees the stored object.
questions.rule: The race exists only until the first object is stored.

questions.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
questions.q: Which situation has the same flaw as the Singleton thread problem?
options: Two threads check whether a username is free, see it free, and both register it
Two threads read the same fixed setting from the program and see the same value
One thread reads the username twice and sees that it is free both times it looks
Two threads write to two different files at the same time and both succeed
optionExplain: A shared check followed by an action, interleaved, gives two actions.
Reading unchanged data cannot conflict.
A single thread cannot interleave with itself.
No shared check decides between them.
questions.explain: The flaw is not specific to Singletons. Any shared check followed by an action can be interleaved so that both threads act.
questions.rule: Check-then-act on shared data can race.
questions.teaches: The Singleton problem is a general check-then-act race: any shared check followed by an action can be interleaved so that two threads both act.

questions.q: A shared check-then-create method is racing. Which Java keyword makes only one thread run it at a time?
options: static
final
synchronized
private
optionExplain: Static makes the method belong to the class and does not limit threads.
Final prevents overriding and does not limit threads.
It lets one thread at a time into the method.
Private limits who can call the method, not how many threads run it.
questions.explain: The chapter's fix is to make getInstance a synchronized method. The card next shows what it costs.
questions.rule: Synchronized: one thread at a time.

questions.q: True or false: Once the unique instance has been created, the synchronization in getInstance is still needed on later calls to protect its creation.
questions.explain: Only the first time through is relevant. After that, the lock is overhead.
questions.rule: The lock matters once.

questions.q: A game server's Leaderboard.getInstance() is synchronized and called by every player action. Which statement fits the chapter's reasoning?
options: Only the first call waits, because every later call skips the lock entirely
Every call waits its turn, though only the first call needed protection
No call waits at all, because the leaderboard has already been built once
Every call is slower only at the moments when the leaderboard is rebuilt
optionExplain: A synchronized method locks every time it is called.
The lock costs on every call after the first.
Synchronization applies whether or not the object exists.
The leaderboard is built once; the lock cost does not depend on rebuilding.
questions.explain: The lock is part of the method, so it is taken on each call. That is why a busy method pays repeatedly for a one-time need.
questions.rule: Lock on every call, need on the first.

questions.q: A developer synchronizes only the line that builds the object and leaves the empty-check outside the lock. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because building is the only step that actually creates objects
Threads would wait forever, because the lock is held outside of the check
The compiler will reject a synchronized block placed inside a static method
Two threads can both pass the check before either builds; two objects result
optionExplain: The check is where both threads decide to build.
Nothing in the setup makes threads wait forever.
Java allows synchronized blocks in static methods.
The protected region must cover both the check and the build.
questions.explain: The race lies between the check and the build. A lock that covers only the build still lets both threads decide to build, and they will build one after the other.
questions.rule: Lock both the check and the creation.
questions.teaches: The protected region must include both the check and the creation; locking only the creation leaves the gap that causes the duplicate.

questions.q: True or false: If getInstance is called once at startup from one place, a synchronized version adds very little cost.
questions.explain: The cost grows with the number of calls. With one call there is no queue and no repeated overhead.
questions.rule: Few calls, little cost.

questions.q: The overhead of a synchronized getInstance depends mainly on how ____ it is called.
questions.explain: The overhead comes from calls passing through the lock, so heavy traffic through getInstance matters most. The size of the object or the age of the program does not change the cost per call.
questions.rule: Cost follows traffic.
questions.teaches: Synchronization cost is paid per call that reaches the lock, so it matters only if getInstance is called often.

questions.q: A team has a correct synchronized getInstance and worries about speed. What is the most sensible first step?
options: Remove the synchronization now, since correctness can be repaired at a later date
Rewrite the class to avoid Singletons, since every lock is slow whatever it protects
Check whether the method is on a busy path, and leave it if it is not
Double the number of threads so that the lock is shared more evenly between them
optionExplain: This reopens the thread problem.
A lock is slow only where it is heavily used.
Only heavy traffic makes the lock matter.
More threads add contention.
questions.explain: Performance worries need evidence about how often the method runs. The card next gives the authors' first option.
questions.rule: Measure before changing.

questions.q: The authors warn that synchronizing a method can decrease performance by a factor of ____.
questions.explain: The chapter gives the factor of 100 as a warning for high-traffic code.
questions.rule: Up to a factor of 100.

questions.q: A weekly report job reads ReportConfig.getInstance() three times per run, and the method is synchronized. What would the authors suggest?
options: Leave it, because getInstance is not performance-critical here
Replace it with double-checked locking to save the cost of the lock on every call
Make every caller use a private copy of the object to avoid waiting for others
Remove the lock altogether, since only three calls cannot race with each other
optionExplain: Their first option is to do nothing in this situation.
The saving would be tiny and the technique adds complexity.
Copies break the one-instance rule.
Threads may still overlap during the first call.
questions.explain: With three calls per run the lock costs almost nothing. The straightforward fix is already adequate.
questions.rule: No pressure, no change.

questions.q: A developer says their small tool is single-threaded, so the unsynchronized classic version is fine. What do the authors advise?
options: Single-threaded tools need no care at all, so the classic version is correct for them
Use the classic version now and add threads and safety only when they are needed
Avoid Singletons in small tools altogether, since every Singleton needs locks
Consider every application multithreaded and choose a thread-safe version
optionExplain: The authors advise against assuming one thread.
Threads can be introduced later, and the bug would be hard to see.
Locks are not the reason to avoid the pattern.
The chapter's bullet points say to consider every application multithreaded.
questions.explain: Code outlives assumptions about it, and a race is hard to find. The authors tell readers to consider all applications multithreaded.
questions.rule: Assume threads.
questions.teaches: The authors tell readers to consider every application multithreaded, so a thread-safe Singleton is the default choice even for programs that look single-threaded today.

questions.q: True or false: If a correct synchronized getInstance moves from a nightly job to the request path of a busy site, it becomes incorrect.
questions.explain: Correctness is unchanged; only the cost per call multiplies with traffic. That is when the authors say to reconsider.
questions.rule: Traffic changes the verdict, not the correctness.

questions.q: An engineer replaces a working synchronized getInstance with a clever scheme in an app that calls it twice per hour, for speed. How do the authors' options bear on this?
options: They support it, because every gain in speed is worth the cost of making the change
They list doing nothing first, as the saving would be negligible and the cost real
They oppose it, because synchronized code must be left exactly as it was written
They are silent on it, because the chapter discusses only the chocolate boiler
optionExplain: They say to do nothing if performance is not critical.
The do-nothing option exists for exactly this case.
They do suggest changes when traffic is high.
The options are general advice on getInstance.
questions.explain: Replacing correct code for a gain nobody will notice adds risk. The authors rank doing nothing as the first option when speed is not critical.
questions.rule: Do not fix what is not slow.
questions.teaches: Leaving correct, simple code unchanged is a legitimate option: a faster scheme adds complexity that is not worth paying where getInstance is rarely called.

questions.q: A Singleton is cheap to build and every run uses it. Which approach needs no lock and no check in getInstance?
options: Synchronize the whole getInstance method
Build it when the class loads
Check twice and lock only if the instance is empty
Build it when the first thread asks
optionExplain: This has a lock on every call.
Nothing is left to decide at call time.
This has a check and a lock.
This needs a check at call time.
questions.explain: Building at class load leaves getInstance with nothing to decide. The card next names this eager creation.
questions.rule: Build early, return later.

questions.q: True or false: With eager creation the JVM builds the instance only when the first thread asks for it.
questions.explain: The authors rely on the JVM to create the unique instance when the class is loaded, which is before any thread accesses the static variable.
questions.rule: The JVM builds it first.

questions.q: Sort each object by whether eager creation at class loading suits it.

items.t: A small clock-format helper used by every page
A logger used from the first line of the program
A 3 GB offline map index used by a rare feature
A PDF exporter with heavy fonts that few users open

questions.explain: Eager creation suits cheap or always-used objects. Expensive objects that many runs never use should wait for a request.
questions.rule: Eager for cheap and always used.

questions.q: Why can two threads not create two objects under eager creation?
options: The JVM locks every call to getInstance for the whole time the program runs
Threads are forbidden from running at all while the class is being loaded
The compiler merges all of the threads into one when the class is declared static
The object is built once at class loading; no check-then-create step is left
optionExplain: The JVM builds the object early; it does not lock the calls.
Threads may exist, but none can use the variable before it is set.
Compilers do not merge threads.
The race is removed by removing the decision.
questions.explain: Lazy versions fix the decision with a lock. Eager creation removes the decision, because the object already exists when any thread asks.
questions.rule: Remove the decision to remove the race.
questions.teaches: Eager creation removes the race by removing the check-then-create decision, not by protecting it, so the lock and double check are both unnecessary.

questions.q: The Singleton's constructor opens an expensive network connection, and the feature is rarely used. What happens under eager creation?
options: Every run pays for the connection at class loading, even runs without the feature
Only the runs that use the feature pay, because the JVM delays the build until then
No run pays for it at all, because connections are free for static objects
The connection fails every time, because eager objects cannot open connections
optionExplain: Early creation spends the cost up front.
The JVM builds at class loading, not at first use.
Being static does not make the connection free.
Eager objects can open connections.
questions.explain: Eager creation is the wrong choice when the object is expensive and often unused. Lazy creation with a thread-safe check fits better.
questions.rule: Expensive and rarely used: stay lazy.

questions.q: A teammate who knows the standard lazy pattern reads a getInstance that only returns a variable. The instance is built at class loading. What is a reasonable response?
options: Rewrite it as lazy at once, since eager objects are wrong in threaded programs
Ignore the confusion, since a correct Singleton needs no explanation to anyone
Add a note saying the early build is deliberate, as the authors admit it may be less obvious
Replace it with an all-static class, which is obvious to everyone who reads it
optionExplain: Eager creation is thread-safe, as the chapter explains.
Correct code can still be hard to recognise.
The authors say eager creation may be less obvious to developers who know the standard pattern.
The chapter warns that all-static classes bring their own problems.
questions.explain: A correct choice can still surprise readers. The authors note that eager creation may be less obvious to developers familiar with the standard pattern, so a short note helps.
questions.rule: Explain choices that look unusual.
questions.teaches: A correct but unfamiliar version can surprise developers who expect the standard lazy pattern, so documenting the choice is part of choosing it.

questions.q: A lazy Singleton must avoid locking on most calls while staying thread-safe. Which idea could do that?
options: Lock only after the instance has been built and stored in the variable
Build a new instance on each call so that nothing has to be shared
Let each thread hold an instance of its own so that no thread has to wait
Check for the instance first, and lock only when it is missing
optionExplain: By then the race has already happened.
This makes many objects.
This breaks the one-instance rule.
Most calls find the instance and skip the lock.
questions.explain: The cost of the lock matters only when the instance already exists, so checking before locking skips it. The card next names the technique.
questions.rule: Check first, lock if needed.

questions.q: Put the steps of double-checked locking in order for a call that has to create the instance.
items: Check whether the instance already exists, with no lock
Enter the synchronized block
Check again whether the instance exists
Build and store the instance
questions.explain: The first check skips the lock on most calls. Inside the lock the check repeats, then the object is built.
questions.rule: Check, lock, check, build.

questions.q: A pricing service Singleton is heavy and wanted only on demand. It is called millions of times a second, on Java 17. Which option fits best?
options: Synchronizing the whole getInstance method
Double-checked locking
Building the instance at class loading
Doing nothing and keeping the classic version
optionExplain: The lock would be taken on every one of the millions of calls.
It keeps laziness and takes the lock only on the first calls.
The object is heavy and wanted only on demand.
The classic version is not thread-safe.
questions.explain: The constraints are lazy creation, high traffic and a modern JVM, which are the conditions that favour double-checked locking.
questions.rule: Lazy plus busy plus Java 5 or later.

questions.q: Why does double-checked locking check a second time inside the synchronized block?
options: The first check can be wrong, so the second check is there to correct the first
The second check keeps the lock from being held for too long a time
Another thread may have built the instance while this one waited for the lock
The language requires every synchronized block to repeat the condition it follows
optionExplain: The first check is right when it is made but may be stale by the time the lock is held.
The check does not shorten the lock time.
Threads that passed the first check queue at the lock, and each needs a recheck.
Java has no such rule.
questions.explain: Several threads can pass the first check together. Without a recheck, each would build an object in turn once it got the lock.
questions.rule: Recheck inside the lock.
questions.teaches: Threads that pass the unlocked check can queue at the lock, so the second check inside the lock stops each from building again.

questions.q: True or false: If the program must run on a JVM at Java 1.4, double-checked locking is a safe choice.
questions.explain: The authors warn that many 1.4 JVMs implement volatile in a way that allows improper synchronization, so another method should be considered.
questions.rule: Java 5 or later only.

questions.q: An engineer removes the first, unlocked check from a configuration loader and keeps only the check inside the synchronized block. What is the effect?
options: It stays correct, but every call takes the lock again, losing the saving
It becomes incorrect, because a single check cannot find an empty variable at all
It becomes faster, because there are now fewer checks for each call to make
It works only on Java 1.4 and earlier, where checks are handled differently
optionExplain: The first check is what avoids the lock on later calls.
One check inside the lock is enough for correctness.
Each call now waits for the lock.
The version issue is unrelated to this change.
questions.explain: The code is then equivalent to a synchronized method. The unlocked first check is the whole point of the technique.
questions.rule: The first check buys the speed.
questions.teaches: The unlocked first check is what saves the cost; removing it leaves a correct but fully locked method.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: The boiler has no performance concerns and is instantiated in every run. Which fix would the authors call overkill?
options: Double-checked locking
Synchronizing getInstance
Eager instantiation
All three fixes are equally overkill
optionExplain: It adds complexity and a Java 5 requirement for no needed gain.
They call it straightforward and a good choice.
They say it works as well as synchronizing.
They recommend two of them for this case.
questions.explain: Complex techniques are justified by needs the boiler does not have. The card next gives the full verdicts.
questions.rule: Match the technique to the need.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: Match each fix to the authors' verdict for the boiler.
pairs: Works as well, but may be less obvious to some developers
Overkill here, and needs Java 5 or later
questions.explain: Each verdict ties the fix to the facts: no performance concerns, always instantiated, and a version requirement.
questions.rule: Know each verdict and its reason.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: An airport tracker Singleton is heavy and needed in only some deployments. Scanners call it 100,000 times a second on Java 17. Which fix fits the authors' reasoning?
options: Synchronizing getInstance
Eager instantiation
Double-checked locking
Keeping the classic unsynchronized version
optionExplain: The lock would be taken 100,000 times a second.
The object is heavy and not needed everywhere.
It keeps lazy creation and avoids a lock on most calls.
It is not thread-safe.
questions.explain: The constraints reverse the boiler's: heavy traffic and an object that may never be needed. The same reasoning picks a different fix.
questions.rule: Different constraints, different fix.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: Which fact about the boiler makes eager instantiation harmless for it?
options: The boiler is a small object with only a little data
The code instantiates the boiler anyway
The boiler runs on Java 5 or later in the factory
The boiler is controlled by a single trained operator
optionExplain: Size is not the stated reason.
Early creation costs nothing extra if the object would be built regardless.
The version matters for double-checked locking, not eager creation.
Operators are not mentioned as the reason.
questions.explain: A verdict is only as good as the fact behind it. If the boiler were not always created, eager creation would waste the build.
questions.rule: A recommendation depends on its premise.
questions.teaches: A verdict is only as good as the facts behind it: the endorsement of eager creation depends on the boiler always being instantiated.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: True or false: If the boiler controller became a hot path with thousands of calls a second on Java 5 or later, the authors' reason for rejecting double-checked locking would no longer hold.
questions.explain: They rejected it because performance was no concern. When that premise changes, the verdict can change.
questions.rule: Change the premise, change the verdict.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: A colleague says: the authors chose synchronization for the boiler, so use it everywhere. Which reply fits the chapter?
options: They are right, because the authors would not give weak advice to their readers
They are wrong, because synchronization is always the slowest of the possible options
They are right, because the other fixes were shown to be incorrect in the chapter
Their choice rested on the boiler's facts; other constraints could favour another fix
optionExplain: Authority is not the test; the reasons are.
The chapter says it can be a good choice.
The chapter presents all three as working.
Advice is tied to the case it was given for.
questions.explain: A generalisation from one case needs the case's conditions to hold elsewhere. The authors stress examining performance and resource constraints.
questions.rule: Generalise only where the conditions match.
questions.teaches: A choice recommended for one case is not a rule for all cases; the recommendation holds only where the same constraints hold.

questions.q: A developer says a global variable does everything a Singleton does. Which gap is the real one?
options: It cannot be read from other classes, only from the class that declares it
It can only hold primitive values and cannot hold objects at all
It gives access to an object but cannot ensure only one instance exists
It is created at compile time, long before the program itself begins to run
optionExplain: Globals are readable from other classes.
Globals can hold objects.
Access is covered; the one-instance guarantee is not.
Objects are created when the program runs.
questions.explain: A global offers reachability. Nothing about it stops a second object from being built. The card next lists the authors' grounds.
questions.rule: Access is not control of the count.

questions.q: Which disadvantages of global variables does the chapter name or imply? Choose three.
options: The object may be created at startup even if it is never used
Nothing in a global variable prevents a second instance
They encourage polluting the namespace with many references
They can only be read by classes in the same package
They run noticeably slower than any method call
optionExplain: Right: the lazy-versus-eager problem the Guru raises.
Right: a global provides access but not the one-instance guarantee.
Right: the Q and A mentions namespace pollution with small objects.
Globals in Java are static references reachable from other classes; the chapter does not claim this.
The chapter makes no claim about speed against method calls.
questions.explain: The chapter's three grounds are startup creation, no guarantee of a single instance, and namespace clutter.
questions.rule: Three grounds against globals.

questions.q: A teammate proposes a global static reference to a 2 GB translation table filled at launch, saying it is the same as a Singleton. Which difference matters most?
options: The table is built at launch even in runs that never use it; a lazy Singleton waits
The global cannot be shared between classes, while a Singleton can be shared
The global is stored on disk, while a Singleton is stored in the memory
The global holds only one language, while a Singleton can hold several of them
optionExplain: This is the lazy-versus-eager difference the Guru names.
Globals are shared between classes.
Both live in memory.
Content is not what differs.
questions.explain: A global filled at launch spends the cost in every run. A lazily built Singleton spends it only when the table is first requested.
questions.rule: Cost at launch versus cost at first use.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Singletons can still be abused, even though they avoid some problems of global variables.
questions.explain: The authors argue for the pattern without claiming it is free of faults. A reader who accepts the grounds should still watch for abuse.
questions.rule: Better is not flawless.
questions.teaches: Singletons avoid some drawbacks of globals but not all: the authors warn that they can be abused, so the grounds for preferring them are comparative, not absolute.

questions.q: Which review comment gives a showable ground rather than a reaction?
options: Global variables feel sloppy to me, so I would avoid this design in new code
Everyone says Singletons are outdated, so we should drop it from this project
I have never liked static methods, so I think the design is weak overall
This object is built at startup though most runs never use it, wasting memory
optionExplain: A feeling, not a ground.
Popularity of an opinion is not a reason.
A dislike, not an argument about this case.
It points to a cost that can be checked in the code.
questions.explain: A good critique names something that can be shown wrong or costly in this design. Taste and common opinion cannot be tested.
questions.rule: Give grounds you can show.

questions.q: A small holiday-calendar object is cheap, used in every run at launch, and not duplicated in practice. Which of the authors' grounds still favours a Singleton over a global?
options: Avoiding the cost of building an object that is never used
The guarantee that no second instance can be built
Avoiding namespace pollution from many small references
None of them, since a global is better in every such case
optionExplain: The object is always used, so there is no waste.
The lazy-creation ground weakens, but the guarantee remains.
One object does not pollute the namespace.
The guarantee still differs.
questions.explain: When creation cost is irrelevant and only one object exists anyway, the remaining benefit is that the class enforces the count. Whether that is worth the pattern is a judgment.
questions.rule: Weigh which grounds apply to the case.
questions.teaches: Which grounds for a Singleton apply depends on the case: for a cheap, always-used object only the one-instance guarantee remains, so the benefit is smaller.

questions.q: True or false: A class whose members are all static can behave like a Singleton in some cases.
questions.explain: The authors say yes, if the class is self-contained and does not depend on complex initialization. The card next gives the catch.
questions.rule: It can work, but with conditions.

questions.q: According to the authors, the all-static approach can cause subtle bugs involving the ____ of initialization.
questions.explain: Static initialization across several classes can run in a hard-to-see order, which creates subtle bugs.
questions.rule: Initialization order is the hazard.

questions.q: Which scenario most strongly warns against an all-static class?
options: A text-formatting helper that holds no data and reads nothing when it loads
A configuration class whose static setup depends on the fields of three other classes
A constants class holding fixed numbers that are set directly in the code itself
A small utility with a single method that converts inches into centimetres
optionExplain: Self-contained with simple setup is the safe case.
Several classes with initialization dependencies are the risky case.
No dependencies, no ordering problem.
A self-contained utility is not at risk.
questions.explain: The warning applies when initialization is complex or spans several classes. A self-contained class avoids the ordering problem.
questions.rule: Dependencies create ordering bugs.

questions.q: Class A's static setup reads a static field of class B. What risk do the authors' warning point to?
options: A and B become one single object, so that both of their values are overwritten
B is created twice, once by itself and once more by the setup code of A
A cannot be loaded at all, because it depends on a static field of B
A may read B's field before B has finished its setup, giving a wrong value
optionExplain: Static classes do not merge.
Static classes are not instantiated.
Dependencies themselves are allowed.
This is an order-of-initialization bug.
questions.explain: When initializations depend on each other, the order decides the values. The bug is subtle because the code may work or fail depending on which class is loaded first.
questions.rule: Order decides the value.
questions.teaches: When one class's static setup reads another's, the order in which they initialise decides what is read, which is the subtle bug the authors mean by order of initialization.

questions.q: True or false: If the class is self-contained with no complex initialization, the authors say an all-static class would be the same as a Singleton.
questions.explain: The warning is conditional. With simple, self-contained setup, the authors accept the all-static design.
questions.rule: The warning depends on the conditions.

questions.q: A colleague says the authors condemn all-static classes outright. Which response is accurate?
options: They accept them when self-contained, and prefer a Singleton object otherwise
The colleague is right, since the authors call them far worse in every single case
The colleague is wrong, since the authors recommend all-static classes as the first choice
The authors do not discuss the topic anywhere in the whole of the chapter
optionExplain: The advice is conditional, not a ban.
The authors allow the self-contained case.
They recommend staying in the object world.
The Q and A addresses it directly.
questions.explain: A careful reader separates what an author says conditionally from what is claimed in general. Here the preference follows from the order-of-initialization risk.
questions.rule: Quote the conditions, not only the verdict.
questions.teaches: An author's preference can be conditional: the authors favour the object world because of initialization risk, while accepting that the simple self-contained case works.

questions.q: True or false: A Singleton has one instance no matter how many class loaders a program uses.
questions.explain: The chapter says that with several class loaders there can be several instances. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: One loader, one copy of the class.

questions.q: Each class loader defines a ____.
questions.explain: Because each loader has its own namespace, the same class can be loaded once per loader.
questions.rule: A loader is a namespace.

questions.q: A plugin host loads two plugins with separate class loaders, and both include the class PrefsStore, a Singleton. How many PrefsStore instances may exist?
options: Exactly one, since the class is a Singleton
Exactly one per plugin thread
Up to two, one for each loaded copy of the class
None, since the host refuses duplicate class names
optionExplain: The promise holds per loaded copy, not per name.
Threads are not the cause here.
Each copy of the class has its own Singleton.
The loaders do not refuse; each loads its copy.
questions.explain: The class name is the same, but two loaders mean two loaded classes, so each has its own instance.
questions.rule: One instance per loaded copy.

questions.q: What workaround do the authors mention for the class loader problem?
options: Declare the Singleton constructor protected
Make getInstance synchronized in every copy
Build the instance at class loading in every loader
Specify the class loader yourself
optionExplain: The constructor's access does not control which loader loads the class.
A lock inside each copy does not join the copies.
Each loader would still build its own.
The chapter says one way around it is to specify the class loader yourself.
questions.explain: If you control which loader loads the class, all code shares one copy and so one instance.
questions.rule: Control the loader to control the count.
questions.teaches: The authors' way around the class loader problem is to specify the class loader yourself, so that all code uses the same loaded copy of the class.

questions.q: True or false: In an application that uses a single class loader for everything, the class loader warning does not apply.
questions.explain: The problem is multiple copies of the class. With one loader there is one copy, so the promise holds.
questions.rule: One loader, no duplicate copy.

questions.q: A team synchronized getInstance yet still sees two instances in an application server with two class loaders. Why?
options: The synchronization was written incorrectly in the first copy of the class by the team
Synchronization coordinates threads within one loaded copy; there are two copies
Class loaders disable all of the synchronized methods in the classes they load
The server removes the private constructor when it loads the classes of the application
optionExplain: The cause is not a coding error in one copy.
Locks cannot join two separate copies.
They do not.
Nothing removes constructors.
questions.explain: Threads and class loaders are different causes of duplicates. A fix for one does not repair the other.
questions.rule: Match the fix to the cause.
questions.teaches: Synchronization guards against overlapping threads within one copy of a class; it cannot repair duplicates caused by two loaded copies of the class.

questions.q: On a very old JVM, a Singleton's state suddenly resets to its initial values. What could explain it?
options: Two threads built two objects at the same moment in the program
A subclass replaced the instance with an instance of its own class
The Singleton was collected, and a new one was built on the next request
The class loader loaded the class a second time and kept the new copy
optionExplain: That produces two objects, not a reset.
Subclassing is not involved.
This is the bug described before Java 1.2.
Class loaders cause duplicates, not resets.
questions.explain: A premature collection followed by a new build looks like a reset. The card next describes the bug.
questions.rule: Reset state can mean a rebuilt Singleton.

questions.q: True or false: Since Java 1.2 a Singleton needs a separate global reference to avoid being collected.
questions.explain: The bug was fixed in Java 1.2, and a global reference is no longer required.
questions.rule: Modern JVMs need no extra reference.

questions.q: A team maintains software on a JVM from before 1.2. Network connections held by a Singleton reset at random. Which diagnosis fits the chapter?
options: The Singleton is being collected; the next getInstance builds a fresh one
Two threads are building two different Singletons at exactly the same time
The constructor of the Singleton is public, so other classes build their own
The class is being loaded twice by two separate class loaders in the host
optionExplain: This matches the reset symptoms.
That gives two objects, not a reset.
That gives extra objects, not a reset.
That gives two objects living together.
questions.explain: The collector destroys the unreferenced Singleton, and getInstance quietly makes another with initial state.
questions.rule: A reset can mean a lost Singleton.

questions.q: On a JVM earlier than 1.2, how do the authors suggest defeating the collector?
options: Create a registry of Singletons
Make the constructor protected
Call getInstance twice at startup
Declare getInstance synchronized
optionExplain: The chapter's bullet points advise a registry of Singletons.
Constructor access does not affect collection.
Calling twice does not keep a reference.
Locks do not stop collection.
questions.explain: A registry keeps a reference to each Singleton, so the collector sees it as in use.
questions.rule: A registry keeps the instance reachable.
questions.teaches: On a JVM earlier than 1.2 the remedy is a registry of Singletons that keeps each one referenced so the collector does not reclaim it.

questions.q: On Java 8 no registry of Singletons is needed, because the garbage collector bug was fixed in Java ____.
questions.explain: The collection bug exists only on JVMs before 1.2, so later JVMs need no precaution.
questions.rule: Java 1.2 or later: no precaution.

questions.q: After hours of uptime on a very old JVM, a settings Singleton is back to defaults and no error appears. Why is this failure hard to notice?
options: The old object keeps running beside the new one and both answer callers
The JVM prints a warning that nobody reads when the object is lost
The next getInstance call quietly builds a new object, so callers see no error
The new object is a copy of the old state, so nothing visibly changes
optionExplain: The old object is destroyed.
The chapter describes confusing behaviour, not warnings.
The replacement happens silently.
It starts from initial values.
questions.explain: Because getInstance builds when the variable is empty, a lost Singleton is replaced without a signal. Only the changed behaviour reveals it.
questions.rule: Silent replacement hides the cause.
questions.teaches: The failure is silent: callers simply receive a fresh object and nothing signals that the earlier one was lost.

questions.q: Which two jobs does a Singleton class carry?
options: Creating its own subclasses and deleting its old instances over time
Managing its own single instance and doing its main role in the application
Handling several threads and handling several class loaders at once
Counting its callers and logging every one of the requests they make
optionExplain: Neither is part of the pattern.
Instance management is the added job.
These are hazards, not jobs of the class.
The pattern does not do this.
questions.explain: The Singleton does its ordinary job and also controls its own count and access. The card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: Two jobs in one class.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a Singleton can be argued to have two responsibilities.
questions.explain: They agree one could argue it manages its own instance and also performs its main role.
questions.rule: The authors admit the tension.

questions.q: Which two reasons do the authors give in defence of the Singleton against the one-responsibility objection?
options: A class managing its own instance makes the overall design simpler
Many developers are familiar with the pattern because it is widely used
The principle only applies to classes that use inheritance
Java requires every global object to manage itself
Responsibilities are not counted for static methods
optionExplain: Right: utility and simplicity are their first reason.
Right: familiarity is their second reason.
The authors do not say this; the principle applies to classes in general.
Java has no such requirement.
The authors give no such exemption.
questions.explain: The authors rely on simplicity and familiarity. Neither claims the principle is wrong.
questions.rule: Simplicity and familiarity.

questions.q: What do some developers do about the Singleton's second responsibility?
options: Give the class a second instance so that the two can share the work
Make every method of the class static so that no object is needed
Declare the constructor public so that access is spread to more classes
Abstract the Singleton functionality out of the class
optionExplain: This defeats the pattern.
This does not separate the responsibilities.
This weakens the pattern.
The chapter says some developers feel the need to do this.
questions.explain: Moving instance management elsewhere restores one job per class but gives up some of the simplicity the authors value.
questions.rule: Separate if the principle matters more.
questions.teaches: Some developers abstract the Singleton functionality into separate code, trading the simplicity of a self-managing class for one job per class.

questions.q: A reviewer says Singleton breaks the one-responsibility principle, so it is bad. Which reply is a reasoned reply rather than a reaction?
options: You dislike patterns in general, so your objection does not count for much here
Everyone uses Singletons, so the principle must not apply to this kind of class
It takes on two jobs, but self-managing simplifies the design, so the trade may be worth it
The principle is outdated and does not deserve to be taken seriously by a team
optionExplain: Attacks the person, not the argument.
Popularity does not answer the objection.
It concedes the point and weighs it.
An assertion with no reason.
questions.explain: A reasoned reply grants what is true in the objection and answers it with grounds. Dismissal and popularity are not grounds.
questions.rule: Grant what is true, then weigh.

questions.q: A team separates instance management from the main job of a Notifier class. What price do the authors' reasons suggest they pay?
options: They lose some of the simplicity of a class that manages its own instance
They lose the one-instance guarantee completely, whatever else the new code does
They lose the ability to use static methods anywhere in the new classes
They break the one-responsibility principle for the new holder class they create
optionExplain: This is the benefit the authors cite for the Singleton.
The guarantee can still be kept by the separate holder.
The separation does not forbid static methods.
The holder would have one job.
questions.explain: Every design choice here trades something. The authors name the simplicity of a class that manages itself as what the Singleton gains.
questions.rule: Each option has a price.
questions.teaches: Separating the instance management from the class's main job restores one job per class, at the price of the simplicity of a self-managing class.

questions.q: Several subclasses extend a Singleton base class built in the classic way. Why might they all share one instance?
options: Each subclass is forced to call the base constructor only once during a run
The compiler merges all of the subclasses of a Singleton into one single class
Subclasses of a Singleton are not allowed to have constructors of their own
The instance is held in one static variable that all of them share
optionExplain: Constructors are not limited this way.
Compilers do not merge classes.
They can.
Static variables belong to the base class, not to each subclass.
questions.explain: A single static variable in the base class is shared by everything derived from it. The card next explains the consequence.
questions.rule: One static variable, one shared instance.

questions.q: To let a subclass call the constructor, you must change it from private to public or ____.
questions.explain: The authors say the constructor must become public or protected, which weakens the Singleton.
questions.rule: Opening the constructor weakens the guarantee.

questions.q: A team makes the constructor of its SoundManager Singleton protected so that WinSound and MacSound can extend it. Which problems follow, according to the chapter?
options: None at all, since protected still blocks every class that lies outside the hierarchy
Other classes can instantiate it now, and the subclasses share one static variable
The subclasses cannot access getInstance, since static methods are never inherited
Only the loss of lazy creation, since protected forces the class to be created eagerly
optionExplain: The authors say that other classes can then instantiate it.
Both consequences are named in the chapter.
The chapter does not claim this.
Constructor access does not force eager creation.
questions.explain: Opening the constructor lets other classes build instances, and the static variable remains one shared slot.
questions.rule: Open constructor, shared variable.

questions.q: What do the authors say is needed to make subclassing a Singleton work?
options: A second static variable declared in each subclass by hand
A registry of sorts in the base class
A synchronized constructor
A public getInstance method in every subclass without any registry
optionExplain: The authors name a registry, not per-subclass variables.
The chapter says this is required.
Locks do not solve the shared variable.
Without a registry the shared variable remains.
questions.explain: A registry lets the base class track one instance per derived class. The extra machinery is part of the cost.
questions.rule: Subclassing needs extra machinery.
questions.teaches: Making subclassing work requires a registry of sorts in the base class, so that each derived class can have its own instance instead of sharing one static variable.

questions.q: True or false: If an application defines dozens of Singletons, the authors suggest taking a hard look at its design.
questions.explain: Singletons are meant to be used sparingly. A large number suggests the pattern is applied where it is not needed.
questions.rule: Use it sparingly.

questions.q: A team wants three variants of a Notifier Singleton that share behaviour. Which alternative do the authors' remarks point to?
options: Subclass one Singleton and let all three variants share its static instance variable
Make the constructor public so that all of the variants can reuse it directly
Replace the three variants with one all-static class that serves every purpose
Add the Singleton code to each class that needs it; the code is trivial to add
optionExplain: The shared variable is the problem they name.
This ends the Singleton guarantee.
The authors prefer to stay in the object world.
The chapter says Singleton code is trivial to add to any class.
questions.explain: Because the pattern code is small, repeating it in each class is a cheap alternative to a registry in a base class.
questions.rule: Ask whether repeating a little code is simpler than inheriting.
questions.teaches: Because Singleton code is trivial to add to any existing class, repeating it in each class is an alternative to subclassing and a registry.

questions.q: Sort each object by whether the chapter would list it as needing a single instance.

items.t: A thread pool
A cache
A dialog box
One customer order
A basket for each shopper
A temporary list inside one loop

questions.explain: The chapter lists thread pools, caches and dialog boxes next to settings, logging and device drivers. Per-customer or per-shopper objects and loop-local lists are meant to exist in many copies.
questions.teaches: The chapter's list of one-instance objects also includes thread pools, caches and dialog boxes, not only settings, logging and device drivers.
questions.rule: Give a class a single instance when a second copy would cause wrong behavior, wasted resources or inconsistent results.

questions.q: What does this program print?
options: true
false
It does not compile
It throws an exception at run time
questions.explain: Badge has an accessible constructor, so each new makes a separate object. The == operator compares references, and the two references differ.
optionExplain: Fits a belief that equal-looking objects are one object, but == compares references, not content.
Correct: two calls to new give two distinct objects.
The constructor is package-level and main is in the same package, so it compiles.
Nothing in the code can throw; creating two objects is legal.
questions.rule: Calls to new cannot be counted from outside, so limiting instances has to start with limiting who may call the constructor.

questions.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
questions.q: One statement in main stops this code from compiling. Which one?
options: Vault a = Vault.open();
The declaration of the private constructor
The static method open, which calls new Vault()
Vault b = new Vault();
questions.explain: Only code inside Vault may call its private constructor. The call in main is outside, so the compiler rejects it, while the same call inside open is allowed.
optionExplain: Asking the class for an object through its static method is exactly the allowed route.
A private constructor is legal; the error appears only where it is called from outside.
Code inside the class may call its own private constructor, so open compiles.
Correct: new Vault() outside the class cannot reach the private constructor.
questions.rule: Make the constructor private, then expose a static method so outsiders must ask the class for the object.

questions.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
questions.q: What does this program print?
options: 2 false
0 true
1 false
1 true
questions.explain: The first get call finds the variable empty and runs the constructor once. The second call returns the stored object, so both references point to it.
optionExplain: Would be right only if every call built a new object, which the null check prevents.
The constructor does run once on the first request, so the counter is not zero.
One construction is right, but the two references are the same object, so == gives true.
Correct: one construction, and both variables hold the same object.
questions.rule: Private constructor, static variable, static getInstance: build on the first request and return the stored object afterwards.

questions.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
questions.q: This class is meant to be a classic Singleton, yet main prints false. What is the flaw?
options: The static variable should be an instance variable
getInstance should be synchronized to give one object
The constructor is not private, so other code can build more
The null check should come after the assignment
questions.explain: Without private, any class in the package can call new Mailer, and that object differs from the stored one. The private constructor is one of the three parts of the classic version.
optionExplain: An instance variable cannot be read from a static method before any object exists.
Locking is about threads; this program has one thread and the extra object comes from new.
Correct: the open constructor lets outside code create a second object.
Checking after assigning would make the check meaningless and does not stop outside new.
questions.rule: Private constructor, static variable, static getInstance: build on the first request and return the stored object afterwards.

questions.q: Each call below uses a new Boiler object. What does this program print?
options: filling, then refused
filling, then filling
refused, then filling
refused, then refused
questions.explain: Each Boiler has its own full flag, so the second object never learns that the first one was filled. Its check passes and it fills as well.
optionExplain: Would be right if both calls used one Boiler, which is the Singleton fix.
Correct: separate objects keep separate records.
A new Boiler starts empty, so its first fill is not refused.
Both objects start not full, so neither refuses its first fill.
questions.rule: Safety checks that depend on an object's state only work if every caller shares the one object that holds the state.

questions.q: Match each part of the classic implementation to the job it does for the definition.
pairs: Keeps the promise that only one instance exists
Keeps the promise of a global point of access
Holds the single instance between calls
questions.explain: The private constructor blocks outside creation, the static method is the access point, and the static variable keeps the one object alive between calls.
questions.rule: Singleton means one instance, controlled by the class itself, plus one well-known way for anyone to reach it.

questions.q: What does this program print, line by line?
options: built, start, end
start, built, built, end
start, built, end
start, end
questions.explain: The object is built on the first get call, after start is printed. The second call finds it already stored, so built appears once.
optionExplain: This is eager timing; here nothing is built before the first request.
The null check stops a second build on the second call.
Correct: built once, on the first request, between start and end.
The first get call does build the object, so built does appear.
questions.rule: Create the single instance on first request when it is expensive and may never be needed.

questions.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
questions.q: Both threads pass the null check before either stores. What does this program print?
options: true
An exception
Nothing
false
questions.explain: Each thread builds its own Slow after the pause, and the two stores happen separately, so r[0] and r[1] refer to different objects.
optionExplain: Would hold if the check and store were one atomic step, which they are not here.
Nothing in the code throws; it simply builds two objects.
The program prints one line after both threads end.
Correct: the race produced two objects, so == is false.
questions.rule: A check-then-create sequence can be interrupted, so two threads may both see no instance yet and each build one.

questions.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
questions.q: A developer repeats the null check inside the first one to stop the race. Why does that not help?
options: The second check is true only on the first call of the whole program
Nested checks lock the class, so threads wait forever
Both checks run before any assignment, so two threads can still pass both
A repeated check makes the compiler drop the assignment
questions.explain: A check that is not protected by a lock can be passed by two threads before either assigns. A lock is what makes check and assignment one step.
optionExplain: That describes any empty variable, and it does not prevent two threads from seeing it empty at once.
An if statement takes no lock at all; only synchronization does.
Correct: with no lock, both threads can be past both checks before one stores.
The compiler keeps the assignment; the fault is in the timing.
questions.rule: A check-then-create sequence can be interrupted, so two threads may both see no instance yet and each build one.

questions.q: The same two threads run, but get is now synchronized. What does this program print?
options: false
true
An exception
It deadlocks
questions.explain: The second thread waits for the lock. When it enters, the first thread has stored the object, so the check fails and the same object is returned.
optionExplain: That was the unsynchronized result; the lock removes the overlap.
Correct: one thread at a time means one object.
Locking does not throw anything here.
The lock is released at the end of the method, so the second thread proceeds.
questions.rule: Declare getInstance synchronized to make the first-time check and creation safe, accepting a lock on every call.

questions.q: Synchronizing getInstance and eager creation both avoid the race. Which statement tells them apart?
options: Eager creation stays lazy but locks each call; synchronizing builds at class loading
Synchronizing stays lazy but locks every call; eager creation needs no lock and builds at class loading
Synchronizing removes the null check; eager creation keeps it
Eager creation can still produce two objects under threads; synchronizing cannot
questions.explain: Synchronizing keeps lazy creation and pays for the lock on every call. Eager creation has no check-then-create step, so no lock is needed, but the object is built even if unused.
optionExplain: This swaps the two approaches.
Correct: lazy plus a lock on every call, versus no lock plus early building.
Synchronizing keeps the null check; the lock only makes it safe.
The JVM builds the eager instance before any thread uses it, so one object results.
questions.rule: Declare getInstance synchronized to make the first-time check and creation safe, accepting a lock on every call.

questions.q: Order these ways of calling a synchronized getInstance from least to most reason to reconsider the lock.
items: Called once at startup
Called a few times an hour by a report job
Called on every request of a busy web page
Called thousands of times a second in a processing loop
questions.explain: The authors say to leave it alone when getInstance is not performance-critical and to reconsider when a high-traffic part of the code begins using it.
questions.rule: Keep the synchronized method while getInstance is off the busy path, and revisit the choice when traffic grows.

questions.q: The class builds its instance in a static initializer. Which lines does running main print, in order?
