options: Each must be edited to implement the hook
They keep working without any change
Each must be recompiled with a new template
Each loses the steps it had before
optionExplain: That would be true of a new abstract step.
Right: the default covers every existing subclass.
Recompiling is not an edit they have to make by hand.
Their steps stay as they were; adding a hook removes nothing.
questions.explain: A new hook comes with an empty default, so every existing subclass keeps compiling and behaves as before. Adding a hook is safe for old subclasses.
questions.rule: New hooks do not disturb old subclasses.
questions.teaches: Adding a hook with a default to a template leaves existing subclasses working, whereas adding a new abstract step breaks every subclass until it implements the step.

questions.q: What if a subclass overrides a hook but the template method does not call it?
options: The override runs anyway when the object is first created
The override takes the place of the template method
The language calls the override at the end of the algorithm
The override has no effect, since the template decides when hooks run
optionExplain: Nothing runs a hook by itself.
The template stays as it is.
There is no automatic call.
Right: a hook runs only where the template calls it.
questions.explain: The template controls the hook.
questions.rule: Hooks run when the template says so.

questions.q: True or false: A base class for bank transfers makes the debit step a hook with an empty default, because some subclasses may not need it.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a transfer that skips the debit cannot be right. The step is required, so it belongs among the abstract methods.
questions.rule: Required steps are abstract, not hooks.
questions.teaches: A step with no safe default must not be a hook, because an empty default would let a subclass silently skip essential work.

questions.q: How might a subclass use a hook to affect whether a step of the algorithm runs?
options: By deleting the step from the template method
By calling the step directly before the template starts
By overriding a hook whose answer the template checks
By declaring the step private in the subclass
optionExplain: Subclasses cannot edit the template.
The step belongs inside the sequence.
Right: the hook gives the subclass a say without changing the template.
Access modifiers do not decide whether the step runs.
questions.explain: The card next lists the uses of hooks.
questions.rule: The hook answers; the template acts.

questions.q: Match each use of a hook with an example.
pairs: A subclass implements the hook only if it wants that step
A hook like justReOrderedList runs after a list is reordered
A hook's answer controls whether the template adds condiments
questions.explain: The three uses are optional steps, reactions to events, and decisions that the template acts on.
questions.rule: Optional, react, decide.

questions.q: A card game's base class runs a turn: draw a card, play a card, then call a hook. A subclass for a shared-screen game uses that hook to hide the player's hand after each turn. Which use of a hook is this?
options: Reacting to a step that has already happened
Making a step optional
Deciding for the base class whether to run a step
Replacing the template method
optionExplain: Right: the hook runs after the turn and the subclass responds.
Nothing is skipped here.
The hook returns no answer for the base class to act on.
The template is untouched.
questions.explain: A hook after a step is a reaction.
questions.rule: After-step hooks are reactions.

questions.q: The condiment hook has a default answer in the abstract class. Why give a decision hook a default?
options: So subclasses with no opinion can leave it alone and the algorithm still works
So the template can skip calling the hook when it is in a hurry
So that subclasses are forced to override it before they work
So that the hook turns into an abstract method in the end
optionExplain: Right: the default is the common case.
The template decides to call it each time.
A forced override would make it abstract.
A default makes it a hook.
questions.explain: A decision hook needs a default.
questions.rule: Default to the common answer.
questions.teaches: A decision hook needs a sensible default, usually the common case, so that subclasses with no opinion still get a working algorithm.

questions.q: A subclass overrides the condiment hook so that it answers no. What does the template do?
options: It stops the whole recipe before the next step
It adds the condiments anyway and ignores the answer
It skips the condiment step and goes on with the rest
It asks the hook again until the answer is yes
optionExplain: Only one step depends on the answer.
The template honours the answer.
Right: the answer controls that one step.
The template asks once.
questions.explain: The hook's answer controls only the condiment step, so answering no skips that step and the recipe carries on with the rest.
questions.rule: No answer, no step.

questions.q: A checkout base class calls a hook wantsGiftWrap before a wrapping step. Which statements fit the book's use of a decision hook? Select all that apply.
options: The template calls wantsGiftWrap and wraps only when it answers yes
A subclass for a gift shop overrides wantsGiftWrap to answer yes
A subclass calls the wrapping step itself after checkout ends
Every subclass must override wantsGiftWrap
optionExplain: Right: the template acts on the hook's answer.
Right: the subclass supplies the answer.
The subclass would be running steps on its own and bypassing the template.
A hook is optional, so a default exists.
questions.explain: The subclass answers the question and the template does the acting.
questions.teaches: With a decision hook the subclass only answers a question, and the template keeps control of what to do with the answer.
questions.rule: The subclass answers; the template acts.

questions.q: A step of an algorithm is optional for some subclasses. How should the abstract class declare it?
options: As an abstract method, so every subclass is reminded of it
As a final method, so none can change it
As a private helper that the template skips
As a hook with an empty or default body
optionExplain: That forces every subclass to write it.
A final method cannot be overridden.
A skipped step would never run.
Right: optional steps suit hooks.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's rule.
questions.rule: Optional means hook.

questions.q: True or false: A concrete subclass has to implement every abstract method of the abstract class.
questions.explain: Each concrete subclass gives a complete implementation of the undefined steps.
questions.rule: Abstract means compulsory.

questions.q: A report base class has these steps: fetchRows (every report needs its own query), addWatermark (some reports want one) and formatTotals (every report formats differently). Which choice fits the book's rule?
options: All three abstract, so every report decides each one for itself
fetchRows and formatTotals abstract, addWatermark a hook
addWatermark abstract, and the other two steps hooks
All three hooks, so subclasses are never burdened at all
optionExplain: That would force an empty watermark in many reports.
Right: two steps are required and one is optional.
This reverses which steps are required.
Required steps with empty defaults would be skipped silently.
questions.explain: Required means abstract; optional means hook.
questions.rule: Ask whether the step is required.

questions.q: A team makes all ten steps of a template abstract, and most subclasses leave seven of them empty. What does this choice cost?
options: The template can no longer be declared final by the team
Subclasses lose the ability to vary any of the steps
Every subclass must write all ten, seven of them empty
The superclass can no longer call the steps it declares
optionExplain: Final and abstract concern different methods.
Subclasses can still vary all of them.
Right: abstract methods bind every subclass.
The template can still call them.
questions.explain: Abstract for optional steps burdens subclasses.
questions.rule: Do not use abstract for optional steps.
questions.teaches: The cost of a wrong choice is empty boilerplate in every subclass when abstract is used for optional steps, or silent omissions when a hook is used for required ones.

questions.q: What if a required step is made a hook with an empty default and a new subclass forgets it?
options: It compiles and runs, but silently skips that work
The subclass fails to compile until it adds the step
The template stops with an error at that step
The superclass supplies the missing work in its place
optionExplain: Right: the default hides the omission.
That happens for an abstract step, not a hook.
A hook default does not raise an error.
An empty default does no work.
questions.explain: A hook has a default, so a subclass that forgets it still compiles and runs, silently skipping the work. A hook cannot enforce a duty, which is why a required step should be abstract.
questions.rule: Duty needs abstract.

questions.q: A form-processing framework runs a template for each form type. Sort each step by whether the designer should make it an abstract method or a hook.

items.t: Parse the submitted fields (every form differs)
Log a message after saving (few forms care)
Choose the table to write to (no default exists)
Send an optional confirmation email
Show a custom error page (a standard page exists)
Validate the data (rules differ and are required)

questions.explain: Steps that every form must do, with no default, are abstract. Steps that few forms need, or with a standard default, are hooks.
questions.teaches: A useful test is whether a safe default exists: if the algorithm stays correct with an empty or standard step, a hook fits.
questions.rule: Ask whether a safe default exists.

questions.q: A designer splits an algorithm into thirty small abstract steps so subclasses can vary anything. What is the main drawback?
options: The template method can no longer be declared final
Each subclass must implement all thirty steps
Subclasses lose the ability to vary any of the steps
The superclass cannot call so many separate methods
optionExplain: Final and step count are unrelated.
Right: every abstract step is work for every subclass.
More steps give more flexibility, not less.
A method can call as many steps as it needs.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's advice.
questions.rule: Many abstract steps mean much work.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, making the steps coarser gives subclasses more flexibility.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: less granularity means less flexibility.
questions.rule: Coarse steps, less flexibility.

questions.q: A plugin template has 25 abstract steps, and most plugins vary only 3 of them. Which fix eases the burden while keeping the flexibility?
options: Make all 25 steps final
Merge all 25 steps into one abstract step
Drop the template and let each plugin write its own algorithm
Turn the 22 optional steps into hooks
optionExplain: Final steps could not be supplied.
That leaves subclasses little structure and removes the choice of what to vary.
That loses the reuse the template gives.
Right: hooks spare subclasses without removing the chance to vary.
questions.explain: Use hooks to lighten the load.
questions.rule: Optional steps become hooks.

questions.q: True or false: Merging three neighbouring abstract steps into one gives subclasses less work, and also less control over each of the three parts.
questions.explain: Coarser steps cut effort and control together, which is the trade-off the authors describe.
questions.rule: Coarsening cuts work and control together.
questions.teaches: Merging steps trades control for effort: the less granularity, the less flexibility.

questions.q: What if the algorithm had a single abstract step that covers nearly all of the work?
options: Subclasses write less code and also gain more control of each part
The template would gain more shared code to reuse among subclasses
The abstract step would turn into a hook with a default body
Subclasses write one method but redo nearly all the work, and the template shares little
optionExplain: Less work comes with less control, not more.
Less code is left in the template, not more.
Size does not turn a step into a hook.
Right: the coarsest step is easy to name and removes the benefit of the template.
questions.explain: A very coarse step leaves little to share.
questions.rule: Too coarse, little reuse.

questions.q: Rank these designs of one template from the least to the most flexible for subclasses.
items: One abstract step covering the whole algorithm
Three abstract steps
Seven abstract steps
Fifteen abstract steps
questions.explain: More steps give subclasses more places to vary. The same order also ranks the effort needed to write a subclass.
questions.teaches: The same order also ranks the effort of writing a subclass, so flexibility and effort rise together and the choice is a point on one scale.
questions.rule: Flexibility and effort rise together.

questions.q: In a layered system, what harm comes from high-level and low-level components that depend on each other in a tangle?
options: No one can easily see how the system is designed
Every call between the components runs more slowly
Components can no longer be inherited from by others
The compiler refuses to build a system with such calls
optionExplain: Right: the tangled dependencies hide the design.
Speed is not the issue the authors raise.
Inheritance is unaffected.
Tangled dependencies still compile.
questions.explain: The card next names this problem.
questions.rule: Tangled dependencies hide the design.

questions.q: The Hollywood Principle says: don’t call us, we’ll ____ you.
questions.explain: Low-level components wait to be called by high-level ones.
questions.rule: High-level components do the calling.

questions.q: A game engine, the high-level part, lets enemy scripts, the low-level part, plug in. Which arrangement follows the principle?
options: Each script calls into the engine's loop whenever it likes
The engine calls each script's update at the times it chooses
Scripts and engine call each other by name wherever convenient
Scripts start the engine and decide when each frame runs
optionExplain: That hands control to the low-level parts.
Right: the high-level part decides when the low-level part runs.
That is the tangle the principle warns about.
That also puts the low-level parts in charge.
questions.explain: The framework calls the plug-ins.
questions.rule: Plug-ins wait; the engine calls.

questions.q: A subclass step calls a method that it inherits from its own superclass. Is it breaking the Hollywood Principle?
options: Yes, because any call from a low level to a high level is forbidden
Yes, because inherited methods are always high-level components
No, since calling an inherited method is allowed; explicit cycles are the concern
No, because the principle applies only between unrelated classes
optionExplain: The principle does not go that far.
Inheritance itself does not make a component forbidden.
Right: low-level components often call methods above them through inheritance.
The principle applies within hierarchies too.
questions.explain: Inherited calls are fine; circular dependencies are the target.
questions.rule: Avoid explicit cycles, not every upward call.
questions.teaches: A low-level component often ends up calling a method defined above it through inheritance, and that is acceptable; the principle aims to avoid explicit circular dependencies between low-level and high-level components.

questions.q: A low-level component calls a high-level one, which in turn calls the low-level one back by name. Which problem grows?
options: Nothing, because both components are in the same system
Slower start-up, since both must be loaded first
Dependency rot, since each now depends on the other
Loss of the inheritance link between the two
optionExplain: Being in one system does not remove the tangle.
Loading time is not the concern.
Right: a circular dependency is the start of rot.
Inheritance is not affected.
questions.explain: When the low-level component calls the high-level one and the high-level one calls it back by name, each depends on the other, which is dependency rot. Cycles like this are what the Hollywood Principle helps avoid.
questions.rule: Do not let levels depend on each other.

questions.q: In a web server framework, sort each interaction by whether it follows the Hollywood Principle.

items.t: The framework calls a handler when a request arrives
A handler starts the framework's event loop
The framework decides when to load each plug-in
A plug-in calls three other plug-ins by name, which call it back
A page widget waits to be called when its section is drawn
A widget decides for itself when the framework draws it

questions.explain: The framework is in charge and calls your code at points it chooses. Code that takes control or forms call cycles breaks the principle.
questions.teaches: In a framework your code does not run the program; the framework does, and calls your code at the points it chooses.
questions.rule: The framework calls your code at points it chooses.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: In the CaffeineBeverage design, who decides when Tea's brew method runs?
options: The template method in CaffeineBeverage
Tea itself, when its own object is created
The client program, calling each step in turn
The Java runtime, when the program starts up
optionExplain: Right: the superclass calls the subclass step when its turn comes.
A Tea object does not start its own steps.
The client makes one call to the template.
The runtime does not know the recipe.
questions.explain: The card next ties this to the Hollywood Principle.
questions.rule: The superclass calls the subclass.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: Match each part of the drinks design with its role under the Hollywood Principle.
pairs: High-level component that controls the algorithm
Low-level components called when a step is needed
Don’t call us, we’ll call you
questions.explain: The superclass is high-level and in control, the subclasses wait for their turn.
questions.rule: High-level controls, low-level waits.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: A base class Job runs three steps: start, execute and finish. ReportJob supplies execute. Which statement shows the Hollywood Principle?
options: ReportJob's execute calls Job's start and finish in its own order
ReportJob starts Job and then supplies each step in turn
A scheduler calls execute directly and skips Job
Job's template calls ReportJob's execute when its turn comes
optionExplain: That puts the subclass in control of the order.
That also hands control to the subclass.
That bypasses the template that holds the structure.
Right: the high-level class decides when the low-level step runs.
questions.explain: The template calls; the subclass answers.
questions.rule: Template Method is Hollywood in action.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: How does the book relate the Hollywood Principle to the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: They are the same principle under two different names
Both aim at decoupling; Dependency Inversion is stronger and more general
The Hollywood Principle is the more general of the two
The Hollywood Principle is about concrete classes, the other about call order
optionExplain: They are related but not identical.
Right: they share a goal but differ in scope.
The book gives that role to Dependency Inversion.
This swaps the two: Dependency Inversion is the one about concrete classes, and the Hollywood Principle is about who calls whom.
questions.explain: Both principles aim at decoupling, but the Dependency Inversion Principle makes the stronger and more general statement about avoiding dependencies, while the Hollywood Principle is a technique for letting low-level components hook into a system. They share a goal but differ in scope.
questions.rule: Dependency Inversion is broader.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: What if a subclass called its superclass's steps itself, in an order it chose, instead of waiting for the template to call it?
options: Nothing would change, since the same steps would still run
The superclass would gain control of the order of the steps
Dependency rot would become impossible in the design
The subclass would hold the control, and the order would not be fixed in one place
optionExplain: The order would belong to each subclass.
The control would move away from the superclass.
It makes cycles more likely.
Right: whoever calls the steps owns the sequence.
questions.explain: If subclasses called the steps themselves, each would own its own sequence and nothing would fix the order in one place. The template keeps control by calling the subclass, not the other way round.
questions.rule: Keep control in the superclass.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: True or false: A subject that notifies its registered observers when its state changes follows the Hollywood Principle.
questions.explain: The observers do not poll the subject; the subject calls them when it chooses, which fits the principle.
questions.rule: Notification is calling, not being called.
questions.teaches: Other patterns use the principle too; the book names Factory Method and Observer as examples and asks the reader to find more.

questions.q: Java arrays cannot be subclassed, yet Arrays.sort needs a way to compare items. How did the designers supply the missing step?
options: Each array type gets its own subclass of Arrays
The items being sorted supply a comparison that sort calls
Sort guesses an order from the values themselves
The caller passes in the whole sorting algorithm
optionExplain: Arrays cannot be subclassed, which is the constraint here.
Right: the comparison is deferred to the items.
A guess could not order arbitrary objects.
The algorithm stays inside sort.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's account.
questions.rule: The items supply the comparison.

questions.q: To sort ducks with Arrays.sort, the Duck class implements the Comparable interface and its ____ method.
questions.explain: That gives sort the piece it needs to finish the algorithm.
questions.rule: Implement compareTo.

questions.q: You want to sort an array of Invoice objects with Arrays.sort. What must you do?
options: Make Invoice implement Comparable with a compareTo method
Write a subclass of Arrays that overrides the sort steps
Write your own sort that calls the library's swap
Make a subclass of the array type to hold the comparison
optionExplain: Right: sort needs the comparison from the items.
Arrays offers sort as a static method, not a class to subclass.
The library's sort already contains the algorithm.
A Java array cannot be subclassed.
questions.explain: Supply the missing step through the interface.
questions.rule: The items complete the algorithm.

questions.q: What if the Duck class does not implement the comparison that sort relies on?
options: Sort falls back to ordering the ducks by name
Sort orders the ducks by their position in memory
Sort lacks the piece it needs and cannot complete the ordering
Sort finishes, but the ducks stay in the original order
optionExplain: Sort has no such default.
Memory position is not an order the method uses.
Right: without compareTo the algorithm is incomplete.
The method does not silently succeed.
questions.explain: Without a comparison such as compareTo on Duck, sort lacks the piece it needs to order the ducks and cannot complete the ordering. The algorithm is incomplete without it.
questions.rule: The deferred step is required.

questions.q: A reviewer says Arrays.sort is a textbook template method. How does the book assess that claim?
options: It is textbook, because the sort method calls the comparison step
Not textbook, as it uses no subclassing, but it follows the spirit
It is not Template Method at all, because it has no abstract class
It is really Strategy, because it uses object composition
optionExplain: The textbook form uses a superclass and subclasses.
Right: the form differs, the intent is the same.
The book says it is in the spirit of the pattern.
The book answers that Strategy composes with a complete algorithm, and sort's is incomplete.
questions.explain: Judge a pattern by its intent as well as its shape.
questions.rule: Spirit over diagram.

questions.q: True or false: Because a Java array cannot be subclassed, a pattern that depends on subclassing cannot be adapted to arrays at all.
questions.explain: Arrays.sort keeps the idea of a fixed algorithm with a deferred step, and swaps subclassing for a static method and an interface.
questions.rule: Keep the intent and change the mechanism.
questions.teaches: When a language constraint blocks the textbook form, designers can keep the intent and change the mechanism; real code seldom matches a pattern's diagram.

questions.q: JFrame has a paint method that draws nothing unless you override it. What role does it play?
options: An abstract method that every frame must implement
A final template method that cannot be changed at all
A constructor that builds the frame and its contents
A hook where your own drawing joins JFrame's algorithm
optionExplain: It does nothing by default, so it is optional.
It is the thing you override, so it is not final.
It draws, it does not construct.
Right: a default that does nothing is a hook.
questions.explain: The card next explains the hook.
questions.rule: Empty default, so a hook.

questions.q: A JFrame's paint method does nothing by default because it is a ____, so an override is optional.
questions.explain: A method with an empty default that a subclass may override is a hook, so an applet or frame is not required to implement it.
questions.rule: Hooks are optional.

questions.q: A web framework's Page class calls an onLoad method, empty by default, each time a page is shown. Your ContactPage should focus the name field when it appears. What do you do?
options: Edit Page so it focuses the field
Call Page's display steps yourself from a constructor
Override onLoad in ContactPage
Override the method that shows the page
optionExplain: That would put your page's needs in the framework.
That bypasses the framework's control of when things run.
Right: the hook is where your code joins in.
That replaces the framework's algorithm.
questions.explain: Use the hook that the framework offers.
questions.rule: Override the hook.

questions.q: Why would a framework like Swing make paint a hook instead of an abstract method?
options: Most frames need no custom drawing, so it would burden subclasses
Hooks run faster than abstract methods when the frame is drawn
Abstract methods cannot be called from inside a template method
A hook can be called more than once for every frame drawn
optionExplain: Right: optional behaviour suits hooks.
Speed is not what separates them.
Templates call abstract methods all the time.
Call counts do not distinguish them.
questions.explain: Optional behaviour suits hooks.
questions.rule: Hooks for what most users skip.
questions.teaches: Frameworks lean towards hooks for behaviour most users never change, so that an ordinary subclass has nothing to write.

questions.q: True or false: Overriding a hook lets you change when the framework calls it.
questions.explain: The framework decides when the hook runs. You change only what happens there.
questions.rule: You choose the content, not the timing.

questions.q: A plugin host calls start() and stop() on every plugin, and the base class gives both empty bodies. Which description fits?
options: A template with hooks: the host sets the timing, and plugins override what they need
A set of abstract methods, because every plugin must implement both
A Strategy, because the plugins can be swapped at runtime by the host
A final template with no room for any plugin behaviour at all
optionExplain: Right: the host drives the life cycle and the plugins hook in.
Empty bodies mean the plugins are not forced.
Swapping is not the point here; the host calls at set times.
The hooks are the room for plugin behaviour.
questions.explain: Life-cycle callbacks are hooks.
questions.rule: The host calls; the plugin reacts.
questions.teaches: Life-cycle callbacks are a common form of hooks: the framework drives the stages and your code reacts at each one.

questions.q: Both Template Method and Strategy encapsulate algorithms. What is the difference in how they do it?
options: Template Method uses composition; Strategy uses inheritance
Both use inheritance, but at different depths of the hierarchy
Template Method uses inheritance; Strategy uses object composition
Template Method uses interfaces; Strategy uses static methods
optionExplain: This reverses the two.
Strategy composes objects instead.
Right: the chapter's summary says one encapsulates by inheritance and one by composition.
Neither is described that way.
questions.explain: The card next sets out the contrast.
questions.rule: Inheritance versus composition.

questions.q: Match each pattern with what the book says it does.
pairs: Subclasses decide how to implement steps in an algorithm
Encapsulates interchangeable behaviors and delegates to the chosen one
Subclasses decide which concrete classes to instantiate
questions.explain: The three are told apart by what is left open: a step, a whole behaviour, or which class to build.
questions.rule: Step, behaviour, class.

questions.q: A shipping calculator must let a user switch between Express and Economy pricing at runtime, and each is a whole pricing algorithm. Which pattern fits better by the authors' reasoning?
options: Template Method, since the pricing steps can be shared
Template Method, since it is the more flexible at runtime
Neither, since a runtime choice rules out both patterns
Strategy, since whole algorithms are swapped by composition
optionExplain: Shared steps do not help swap whole algorithms at runtime.
The authors give runtime flexibility to Strategy.
Strategy is built for runtime choice.
Right: runtime swapping is the strength of Strategy.
questions.explain: Swap whole algorithms with Strategy.
questions.rule: Runtime swapping points to Strategy.

questions.q: In the chat, which pattern is described as not depending on anyone else to do its algorithm, and why?
options: Template Method, because its superclass is abstract and complete
Strategy, because a strategy object can carry out the whole algorithm itself
Template Method, because its subclasses are always simple to write
Strategy, because it uses inheritance only for the first step
optionExplain: An abstract class still depends on what subclasses supply.
Right: Template Method depends on methods supplied by its subclasses.
Subclass size is not the issue.
Strategy relies on composition rather than inheritance.
questions.explain: Template Method depends on its subclasses' steps.
questions.rule: Template Method leans on subclass steps.
questions.teaches: Template Method depends on its subclasses to supply the missing steps, while a strategy object can run the whole algorithm alone, so Strategy carries less dependency.

questions.q: True or false: If every part of an algorithm is the same except one line, and runtime switching is not needed, the chat suggests Template Method's classes are the more efficient choice.
questions.explain: Template Method puts the duplicated code in the superclass, and the chat adds that it needs fewer objects.
questions.rule: Shared code and no runtime change favour a template.

questions.q: A reader argues that Arrays.sort is Strategy because it uses object composition. How does the book answer?
options: The reader is right, because composition alone settles which pattern it is, whatever else is true
Both patterns are identical in this case, so the label does not matter to anyone
In Strategy the composed class holds the whole algorithm; sort's is incomplete without compareTo, so it is nearer Template Method
The question has no answer, since the pattern depends on the programmer's view alone
optionExplain: Composition alone does not decide it.
The book gives a reason to prefer one.
Right: who owns the complete algorithm tells the two apart.
The book gives a reasoned answer, not a shrug.
questions.explain: Ask who owns the complete algorithm.
questions.rule: Complete algorithm, Strategy; incomplete, template.
questions.teaches: Telling the patterns apart depends on whether the composed piece implements the complete algorithm or only a missing step, not on whether composition appears on the surface.

questions.q: Which relation does the book state between Factory Method and Template Method?
options: Factory Method specializes Template Method
They are two different names for the same pattern
Template Method specializes Factory Method
They are unrelated apart from both using subclasses
optionExplain: Right: this is stated in the chapter's summary.
The book keeps them as two patterns.
The direction is the other way round.
The book links them closely.
questions.explain: The card next explains the link.
questions.rule: Factory Method specializes Template Method.

questions.q: In the specialization, the primitive operations are used to create and ____ objects.
questions.explain: The varying step builds an object and hands it back.
questions.rule: The varying step creates and returns.

questions.q: A base class DocumentApp has a template newDocument that calls a step createDocument and then opens a window. WordApp and SheetApp each decide which document class createDocument builds. What is the createDocument step?
options: A Strategy, since two subclasses choose different things
A Factory Method, which specializes Template Method
A plain step that creates nothing
Neither pattern, since it returns an object
optionExplain: Strategy swaps behaviours by composition.
Right: the varying step creates and returns an object.
It creates a document, so it is not a plain step.
Returning an object is what makes it a factory step.
questions.explain: A template step that builds an object is a factory step.
questions.rule: Creation step, Factory Method.

questions.q: True or false: Every template method has a step that creates and returns an object.
questions.explain: The brew step of the drinks example creates nothing. Factory Method is the special case where the varying step builds an object.
questions.rule: Only some templates have factory steps.
questions.teaches: The relation runs one way: a factory method is template-shaped, but most template methods, such as the drinks recipe, create no objects.

questions.q: A logging base class has a template log that formats a message, calls a step createSink to get an output channel, then writes. FileLogger returns a file sink and ConsoleLogger a console sink. Which statement fits?
options: log is the factory method, and createSink is the template
Both are factory methods, since both involve choosing a class
Neither is either, because a logger writes rather than builds
log is the template method; createSink is the factory-method step
optionExplain: This swaps the roles: log is the template and createSink is the step that builds a sink.
The template does not create objects itself.
createSink builds and returns a sink.
Right: the template calls a step that creates an object.
questions.explain: A template can call a factory step.
questions.rule: Template calls factory step.
questions.teaches: A template method and a factory method can sit in one class: the template is the algorithm, and the factory method is one of the steps it calls.

questions.q: A new rule says every run must also log a line after closing. In how many classes must the run method change?
options: None, because Doc already holds open and close for both classes
One: Doc, because the closing step is defined in that class
Two: Memo and Note, since each writes the order of calls itself
Three: Doc, Memo and Note, because all of them mention closing
optionExplain: Doc holds open and close, but the order in which they are called lives in the subclasses.
Editing close in Doc would log after every close, yet the rule is about the run sequence written in each subclass.
Right: the sequence open, body, close is written in each subclass, so both run methods need the edit.
Doc has no run method, so it needs no change to the sequence.
questions.explain: After the identical methods move up, the call order is still copied into Memo and Note, so a change to the sequence is made twice.
questions.rule: A change to a repeated sequence costs one edit per copy.
questions.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)

questions.q: Which pair of classes shows a shared algorithm, rather than only a shared method name or helper?
options: Two classes that each define a save method with the same name but unrelated work inside
Two classes that each validate, save and notify in that order, though the work in each step differs
Two classes that both extend one base class and each add several unrelated methods of their own
Two classes that call the same logging helper, at different points of otherwise different routines
optionExplain: A shared name is not a shared sequence; the two save methods may do unrelated things.
Right: the same kinds of step run in the same order, so one sequence can describe both.
A common parent says nothing about the steps the subclasses run or their order.
A shared helper called at different points does not make the surrounding routines one algorithm.
questions.explain: A shared algorithm is a shared ordered set of steps with the same roles, whatever the details of each step.
questions.rule: Look for a shared sequence of steps, not only for shared names.

questions.q: This base class is meant to serve both PDF and HTML exporters. What is wrong with its design?
options: openFile and closeFile should be abstract, because every file format needs its own opening and closing
export should be private, so that subclasses such as Html cannot call the sequence directly
Html must also override openFile and closeFile, because every subclass has to repeat them
The step name renderPdfPages describes one format, so the shared sequence is tied to PDF
optionExplain: Opening and closing are the same for both formats here, so they can stay shared in the base class.
Hiding export would stop clients from using the sequence, and the name problem would remain.
Shared steps are written once in the base class; repeating them would bring the duplication back.
Right: a step name should say what the step is for, so a neutral name such as render would serve both formats.
questions.explain: The sequence calls a PDF-specific name, so an HTML exporter would have to pretend to render PDF pages.
questions.rule: Name a step for its role, not for one variant.

questions.q: What does new Print().run() print, in order?
options: start, print, end
print, start, end
print only, since Print supplies the work
start, end, because step is abstract and is skipped
optionExplain: Right: the template in Job prints start, calls Print's step, then prints end.
Print's step is called from inside the template, after start, not before it.
Print supplies one step, but the template's own lines still run around it.
An abstract step is skipped by no one; the object's own version runs when the template reaches it.
questions.explain: The template method in the superclass fixes the order, and the subclass's step runs at its turn.
questions.rule: The template fixes the order; the subclass fills in a step.

questions.q: A team builds a plugin host that must control the workflow while plugin authors supply their own details. What does the book say suits this?
options: Strategy only, because plugins must be swapped for whole workflows
Copying the workflow into each plugin, so authors keep full control of it
Template Method, which the book calls a great tool for frameworks
A static helper that plugins call in whatever order they prefer
optionExplain: Strategy swaps whole algorithms; here the host wants to keep the workflow and let plugins fill in details.
Copies would repeat the workflow and hand control of it to every plugin author.
Right: the book says the pattern shows up so often because it is a great design tool for creating frameworks.
Letting plugins call in their own order gives them control, the reverse of what the host needs.
questions.explain: A framework keeps control of how something gets done and leaves the user to specify the details of each step.
questions.rule: Frameworks fit Template Method: they fix the workflow and leave the details.
questions.teaches: The book says Template Method is common in the wild because it is a great design tool for creating frameworks, where the framework controls how something gets done and the user specifies the details of each step.

questions.q: Tea overrides pour as well as brew. What does new Tea().make() print, in order?
options: boil, steep, pour
steep, boil, pour into mug
boil, pour into mug, steep
boil, steep, pour into mug
optionExplain: The shared pour in Drink is replaced by Tea's own, so the last line changes.
The order is fixed by make, so boil always comes before brew.
make calls brew before pour; Tea's overrides do not change the order.
Right: make still runs boil, brew, pour in order, but Tea's version of pour is the one that runs.
questions.explain: An override of a shared step changes what runs at that point, not the sequence set by the template.
questions.rule: The template sets the order; any overridden step runs its subclass version.

questions.q: In the fireside chat, why does Template Method say it is the most used pattern around?
options: It gives a fundamental way to reuse code while subclasses specify behaviour
It lets a client change algorithms at runtime by swapping objects
It needs no subclasses, so it never depends on other classes
It is the pattern with the fewest methods in any one class
optionExplain: Right: Template Method points to code reuse with subclasses specifying behaviour, and calls this perfect for frameworks.
That is Strategy's claim in the same chat, made through composition.
The reverse holds: the chat has Strategy point out that Template Method depends on subclasses.
Nothing in the chat counts methods per class.
questions.explain: The pattern claims its popularity from code reuse: shared code in the superclass, behaviour from subclasses.
questions.rule: Template Method is a technique for code reuse.
questions.teaches: In the fireside chat the Template Method character calls itself the most used pattern, because it provides a fundamental method for code reuse that lets subclasses specify behaviour.
questions.section: What did the Template Method get us?

questions.q: Fast overrides run and calls only write. Which statement about this code fits the pattern's definition?
options: Fast follows the pattern, since it redefines a step of the algorithm
Fast is correct as long as it also implements read and transform
Fast breaks the pattern's promise, since overriding run changes the structure
Fast breaks the pattern because read and transform have empty bodies
optionExplain: Fast does more than redefine a step: it replaces the sequence in run.
Implementing the steps does not help; the problem is that run itself was replaced.
Right: the pattern lets subclasses redefine steps, not the template method, so Fast changes the structure.
Empty bodies for steps are allowed; the issue is the overridden run.
questions.explain: Redefining steps is the pattern's purpose, but replacing the template method gives up the unchanged structure.
questions.rule: Subclasses redefine steps, never the template.

questions.q: What does new Bob().greet() print?
options: Bob here only, because closing is empty
Hello, Bob here, then closing
Nothing: it does not compile, since Bob does not override closing
Hello, then Bob here
optionExplain: open is concrete and runs from the superclass, so Hello comes first.
closing has an empty body; it prints nothing, whatever its name suggests.
A hook has a body already, so a subclass is free to leave it alone.
Right: open is a concrete step, body is Bob's, and closing is a hook with an empty body, so it prints nothing.
questions.explain: Concrete steps run as written, abstract steps run in the subclass, and an unused hook does nothing.
questions.rule: A hook that nobody overrides does nothing.

questions.q: Match each method declaration in an abstract class with the kind of method it is.
pairs: Concrete method, shared by every subclass
Abstract method, left for each subclass
Hook, empty by default and open to override
questions.explain: A body that the template relies on and subclasses cannot change is concrete, a declaration without a body is abstract, and an empty body that may be overridden is a hook.
questions.rule: Read the declaration: body and final means concrete, no body means abstract, empty and overridable means hook.

questions.q: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: A compile error: run in Quick cannot override run in Task, because that method is final
It compiles, and new Quick().run() prints quick
It compiles, and new Quick().run() prints run, since final wins at runtime
A compile error, because Task has no abstract method to override
optionExplain: Right: a final method cannot be overridden, and the compiler rejects the attempt.
Without final this would print quick, but final blocks the override.
The override is refused at compile time, so there is no runtime to decide.
A class needs no abstract method; the error is the override of a final method.
questions.explain: Final turns the promise of an unchanged template into a compile-time check.
questions.rule: A final template method cannot be overridden.

questions.q: What do new Counter().save() and then new Plain().save() print, in order?
options: save, counted, save, counted
save, counted, save
save, save, counted
counted, save, save
optionExplain: Plain does not override the hook, so its afterSave prints nothing.
Right: both call the template, which prints save then calls afterSave; only Counter's override prints counted.
counted belongs to Counter's run, directly after its own save, not at the end.
The template prints save before calling the hook, so save comes first each time.
questions.explain: A hook runs where the template calls it; an unchanged hook adds nothing.
questions.rule: Override the hook to join the algorithm; leave it and nothing happens.

questions.q: What do new Gift().pack() and then new Plain().pack() print, in order?
options: box, card, seal, box, card, seal
box, seal, box, seal
box, card, seal, box, seal
box, seal, box, card, seal
optionExplain: Plain overrides the hook to answer no, so its card is skipped.
Gift keeps the default, which answers yes, so the card is added for it.
Right: Gift keeps the default answer yes, so the card is added; Plain answers no, so the template skips it.
The two outputs are in the wrong order: Gift is packed first and adds the card.
questions.explain: A decision hook lets the subclass answer; the template acts on the answer.
questions.rule: The subclass answers the hook; the template decides what to do with it.

questions.q: Every order must be charged, yet charge has an empty body and one subclass forgot it. Which fix fits the book's rule?
options: Make wrap abstract as well, so that every step is covered by every subclass
Make charge abstract, because every subclass must provide it
Make process abstract, so that each subclass writes its own full sequence
Keep charge a hook and add a comment asking subclasses to override it
optionExplain: wrap is the optional step and stays a hook; making it abstract does not fix charge.
Right: the book says to use an abstract method when the subclass must provide the step.
Dropping the template gives up the shared sequence, and charge is still not guaranteed.
A comment is not enforced; a hook can be ignored, which is how the step was forgotten.
questions.explain: A required step declared as a hook can be skipped without notice; declaring it abstract makes the compiler demand it.
questions.rule: Required steps are abstract; optional steps are hooks.

questions.q: A template has twelve abstract steps and writing a subclass is a big job. Which moves does the book suggest? Select all that apply.
options: Merge neighbouring steps into coarser ones, accepting less flexibility
Declare the template method final so that subclasses have less to write
Turn the optional steps into hooks that subclasses may ignore
Split each step in two, so that every piece is small and simple
optionExplain: Right: the authors suggest steps that are not too granular, and call it a trade-off with flexibility.
Final protects the sequence; it does not reduce the number of steps to write.
Right: optional steps as hooks spare the subclasses from implementing them.
More, smaller steps mean more abstract methods to implement, the opposite of the aim.
questions.explain: Two moves ease the burden: coarser steps and hooks for optional parts. Splitting steps adds work, and final does nothing for effort.
questions.rule: To lighten subclasses, cut fewer steps or make optional steps hooks.

questions.q: Under the Hollywood Principle, which side decides when handle is called in this code?
options: Loop, the high-level side, which calls handle at the points it chooses
The lambda passed in from main, because it supplies the printing
Neither, because both run in the same thread and one call follows the other
The Handler interface, because it declares the method that is called
optionExplain: Right: Loop owns the loop and calls the handler on its own schedule, which is don't call us, we'll call you.
The lambda supplies content, but it never decides when or how often it runs.
Sharing a thread says nothing about who is in charge of the timing.
An interface only declares the method; it does not decide when it runs.
questions.explain: The low-level code waits to be called, and the high-level code decides when.
questions.rule: High-level code calls low-level code on its own schedule.

questions.q: Tea overrides brew so that it calls make again. What happens when new Tea().make() runs?
options: It prints boil once and then stops normally
It prints boil over and over until the stack overflows
It does not compile, because brew calls make
It prints boil twice, once for each call of make
optionExplain: Tea's brew calls make again, so it does not stop after one round.
Right: make calls brew, which calls make, so the two keep calling each other.
Calling an inherited method compiles; the trouble shows when the code runs.
Each call of make starts another, with no point where the chain ends.
questions.explain: A low-level call back up to the template makes a circular dependency, which the Hollywood Principle aims to avoid.
questions.rule: Do not make a low-level step call back into the template that calls it.
questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method

questions.q: What does this code print?
optionExplain: That is ascending order; this compareTo subtracts in the opposite direction.
A sort that stopped half way would give a mixed order; sort finishes the job with compareTo.
The original order is not kept; sort reorders using the comparison.
Right: sort runs its algorithm, and compareTo, written here to put larger widths first, decides the order.
questions.explain: The algorithm belongs to Arrays.sort, while the meaning of less than belongs to the items.
questions.rule: sort supplies the algorithm; compareTo supplies the comparison.

questions.q: According to the book, which method of java.io's InputStream is a template method, and which step must subclasses implement?
options: read(byte[], int, int) is the template method, and the no-argument read() is the step
The no-argument read() is the template method, and read(byte[], int, int) is the step
close() is the template method, and the no-argument read() is the step
InputStream has none, because the book offers sort as its only example
optionExplain: Right: the byte-array read is built on the read() that subclasses must implement.
This reverses the roles: the bulk read uses the single read() as its step.
The book names read in this role, not close.
The book says there are other template methods in the Java API and names this one.
questions.explain: The Java API holds more template methods than sort, such as the bulk read in InputStream.
questions.rule: Look for a method that is built from a step that subclasses must implement.
questions.teaches: The book names java.io's InputStream as another place: its read() is the step subclasses must implement, and the template method read(byte b[], int off, int len) is built on it.

questions.q: A developer adds a method drawLogo to a JFrame subclass and expects it to draw. Nothing appears. What is the likely reason?
options: paint is abstract, so the subclass must implement it before anything draws
Hooks work only in applets, so a JFrame cannot be extended this way
JFrame's algorithm calls paint, the hook, and never calls a method named drawLogo
The template is final, so JFrame blocks every new method in a subclass
optionExplain: paint is a hook with an empty body, not an abstract method.
JFrame has the paint hook, as applets have theirs.
Right: the framework decides when to call code, and it calls only the hooks it names, such as paint.
A new method is allowed; it is simply never called by the framework.
questions.explain: A method the framework does not call cannot take part in its algorithm; the way in is the hook.
questions.rule: Override the hook the framework calls; a new method is never called.
questions.hint: Think about who decides which methods run.

questions.q: Which statement describes how these two classes let the step vary?
options: A varies the step through composition, like Strategy; B through inheritance, like Template Method
A varies the step through inheritance, like Template Method; B through composition, like Strategy
Both vary the step through inheritance, but only A fixes the order of its steps
Both vary the step through composition, since each one calls a step method
optionExplain: This swaps the two: A is subclassed, while B holds an object.
Right: A has subclasses fill in step; B is handed an object that supplies the step.
B holds a Runnable and is not subclassed to vary its step.
A depends on subclasses overriding step, not on a composed object.
questions.explain: Inheritance versus composition is the book's way to separate the two patterns.
questions.rule: Template Method varies by subclass; Strategy varies by a composed object.

questions.q: Match each part of this code with its role in Template Method and Factory Method.
pairs: The template method that runs the steps
The step that creates and returns an object, the factory method
The subclass that decides which concrete class to instantiate
questions.explain: The template method order runs the algorithm; its step create returns an object, which is the Factory Method form; the subclass chooses what gets created.
questions.rule: Factory Method is a template step that creates and returns an object.

questions.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge
questions.q: Two shops merge. One keeps customer records in a spreadsheet, the other in a database, and neither will switch. What is the main trouble for a new app that reads both?
options: The records can never be shown together in one report, whatever the app does
The app must cope with two different ways of reaching the records
The app must be written in the language of whichever system is older
The shops must first agree on one shared company name before any app can work
optionExplain: Tempting, but a report can combine them; it just takes extra work today.
Right: the difference in storage shows up in whatever code uses both.
Language is not what differs here; the storage is.
Names are not part of the technical difficulty.
questions.explain: A client of two differently stored collections has to deal with both ways of reading. The card next shows how this plays out in the menus.
questions.rule: A client inherits differences it can see.

questions.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge
questions.q: True or false: In the merger story, the two menus use different MenuItem classes.
questions.explain: Both menus share the MenuItem class. What differs is the way each menu stores its MenuItems: an ArrayList in one, an array in the other.
questions.rule: The items agree; the containers differ.

questions.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge
questions.q: Two merged clinics keep appointments in different structures: an array in one, a hash table in the other. Neither team will rewrite. If nothing hides the difference, what must a new search page contain?
options: A rewrite of both clinics' storage before it can run
One shared loop that works on both with no extra help
Nothing special, since appointments look alike on screen
Separate code for reading each clinic's appointments
optionExplain: The teams refused to rewrite, and the page does not need them to.
A loop written for one structure does not fit the other.
How they look on screen is not how the page reads them.
Right: the page sees both structures, so it needs a way to read each.
questions.explain: The page reads storage directly, so it inherits both storage types. That is the situation the Waitress is in.
questions.rule: Visible differences must be handled by the client.

questions.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge
questions.q: Suppose both chefs had stored their items in an ArrayList. The difference in ____ would disappear, so one way of reading would serve both.
questions.explain: With the same type, the same reading code would fit both menus. The trouble comes from the mismatch of storage types.
questions.rule: No mismatch, no extra code.

questions.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge
questions.q: The chefs will not change their menu classes. Where, then, can a fix be placed?
options: Inside each menu, by editing how it stores its items and everything that relies on it
Nowhere; the only workable option is to undo the merger and separate again
Around the menus, in the client or a layer between them
In the MenuItem class, which both menus already use, so that it hides the storage
optionExplain: That is what the chefs have refused, so it is ruled out here.
Giving up is not forced; fixes outside the menus are possible.
Right: the menus stay as they are, so any fix is added around them.
MenuItem is not where the difference lies.
questions.explain: With the menus off limits, the fix has to be added on the client side or through something shared between client and menus.
questions.rule: Constraints on the parts push the fix to the seams between them.
questions.teaches: Because the owners will not change their menus, any fix has to be added around them, in the client or in a layer both menus can be reached through.

questions.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge
questions.q: True or false: A company merges two hospitals whose patient files use different layouts; both refuse to convert, and a billing tool must read both. The billing tool faces the same kind of problem as the Waitress.
questions.explain: The tool must read two layouts directly, as the Waitress reads two storage types. The same fix idea applies: hide the difference from the tool.
questions.rule: Spot the storage difference; hide it from the client.
questions.teaches: The same pattern shows up outside code about food: whenever merged sources differ and cannot be changed, the code that uses them carries the cost, so the useful move is to hide the difference from that code.

questions.q: True or false: A program that prints items from two collections of different types can use a single loop over both without any extra help.
questions.explain: A loop is written for one kind of container. Without help, two types need two loops. The card next shows what the Waitress does and what could change it.
questions.rule: Different containers mean different loops.

questions.q: A client that must print items from one ArrayList and one array needs ____ loops.
questions.explain: One loop uses the ArrayList's size and get methods; the other uses the array's length and subscripts.
questions.rule: One loop per kind of container.

questions.q: A hospital app has five report methods, each of which reads both a ward stored in an array and a clinic kept in a linked list directly. How many traversal loops do the five methods hold in total?
options: Two, one for each storage type, shared by all five methods
Five, one for each report method, whatever the storage
One, since a patient record is a single class used everywhere
Ten, as each method needs a loop for each storage type
optionExplain: Tempting, but the loops live in the methods and are not shared.
This counts methods but forgets each reads two storages.
Patient is the item class; the loops depend on the containers.
Right: five methods times two storage types gives ten loops.
questions.explain: Every method repeats the pair of loops, so the count is methods times storage types.
questions.rule: Loops multiply with methods and storage types.

questions.q: The hospital buys a third clinic that keeps patients in a hash table. The five methods still read storage directly. How many loops hold the traversal code now?
options: Fifteen
Ten, because the new clinic can reuse an old loop
Three, one per storage type
Five, one per method
optionExplain: Right: five methods times three storage types.
A loop written for an array or list does not fit a hash table.
That would need loops to be shared, which they are not here.
That would hold only if one loop could read every storage type.
questions.explain: The new storage type adds a loop to every method that reads items.
questions.rule: A new storage type touches every reading method.

questions.q: A developer says: the for-each loop removes the two loops, so the problem is gone. According to the authors, what does for-each fix?
options: It gives both menu classes a common interface they share, so the Waitress can use either
It removes the need to know the return types of each menu
It hides the loop syntax but not the client's knowledge of the menus
It makes adding a third menu cost nothing at all, however it stores its items
optionExplain: For-each does not change what the menu classes declare.
The client must still obtain items from each menu in its own form.
Right: the client is still tied to how each menu is built.
A third menu still has to be fetched and handled by name.
questions.explain: The authors say the real problem is that two menu implementations exist and the Waitress has to know each one. That is not her job.
questions.rule: Hiding syntax is not hiding implementation.
questions.teaches: A for-each loop hides the syntax of iteration but not the real problem: the client still has to know how each kind of menu is implemented, which is not the client's job.

questions.q: True or false: A report tool reads sales from one database only. The cost described in the card applies to it in full: it needs a loop for every one of the thousand sales it reads.
questions.explain: The cost counts distinct storage types read directly, not items or number of reads. One database means one way of reading, so no multiplication occurs.
questions.rule: Count storage types, not items.
questions.teaches: The cost grows with the number of different storage types a client reads directly; many items or many callers of one storage type add no new loops.

questions.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?
questions.q: A billing program reads orders from two systems, naming each system's class and looping over each in its own way. Which fault does it show most directly?
options: The orders are kept in the wrong systems for this purpose
It depends on concrete classes and on each system's storage
It uses more than one programming language at once
It processes the orders in the wrong sequence overall
optionExplain: Where orders live is not what the program does wrong.
Right: it is tied to details it should not see.
Nothing in the description mentions languages.
Sequence is not part of the description.
questions.explain: The program sees inside both systems, and that creates the dependency. The card next lists the faults the authors find in the Waitress.
questions.rule: Seeing inside creates dependencies.

questions.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?
questions.q: Which are faults the authors find in the Waitress that reads both menus directly? Select all that apply.
options: She codes to concrete menu classes instead of an interface
She must know how each menu represents its items
She repeats a loop for each kind of menu
She does not follow a standard waitress interface
She is not based on an XML menu format
optionExplain: Right: concrete references are the first fault.
Right: this violates encapsulation.
Right: duplicate loops are the third fault.
This is a distractor from the exercise; no such standard matters here.
Also a distractor; the design problem is not about file formats.
questions.explain: The three faults are concrete references, exposed representation and duplicate code.
questions.rule: Concrete, exposed, duplicated.

questions.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?
questions.q: A booking app reads hotels from two partners directly. Sort each observation.
groups: Not a fault of this kind

items.t: It names partner A's class and partner B's class in its code
It must know partner A uses a list and partner B an array
It repeats near-identical loops for each partner
Partner A keeps its hotels in a list
Partner B chose an array for its own reasons

questions.explain: The faults belong to the app that sees inside the partners. The partners' own storage choices are fine.
questions.rule: Fault lies in what the client knows.

questions.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?
questions.q: The Diner switches its storage from an array to a Hashtable. Which code must change?
options: Much of the client code that loops over the old array
Only the Diner class, since that is the one holding the data
Nothing at all, because the MenuItem class is unchanged
Only the other menu's code, so that it matches the Diner
optionExplain: Right: the authors note a lot of Waitress code would need to change.
The Diner changes, but so does everything that depended on its storage.
The item class is unchanged but the container is not.
The other menu has no reason to change.
questions.explain: Anything that saw the array has to be rewritten for the Hashtable.
questions.rule: Changes ripple to whoever sees inside.

questions.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?
questions.q: Which single repair would address all three faults together?
options: Merge both menu classes into one class with a single storage choice
Add comments above each loop explaining what it does and why
Make the Waitress keep her own copy of every item
Give the client one way to step through any menu, hiding its storage
optionExplain: The chefs refuse to rewrite, so merging the classes is not on offer.
Comments explain faults but leave them in place.
Copying items leaves the Waitress still reading both structures.
Right: it removes the concrete references, the exposed representation and the duplicate loops.
questions.explain: All three faults grow from the client seeing inside the menus. One uniform way to read any menu removes the dependency on classes, the exposed storage and the repeated loops.
questions.rule: One root cause suggests one repair.
questions.teaches: A repair that gives the client one uniform way to read any menu cures all three faults at once, because they share one cause.

questions.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?
questions.q: A reviewer reads a client for two warehouses, one a shelf grid and one a conveyor log, and writes: the fault is that the shelf grid is a poor data structure, so replace it. What is wrong with this diagnosis?
options: The conveyor log should be replaced with a better structure instead
The fault is in what the client knows of the storage, not the storage
A grid can never be a good data structure for any warehouse
Diagnosis should wait until a third warehouse arrives to compare
optionExplain: Replacing either structure repeats the same mistake.
Right: the grid may suit its job; the client should not see it.
A grid can be a good choice for its warehouse.
The faults exist with two warehouses already.
questions.explain: Place the fault where knowledge leaks, which is in the client.
questions.rule: Fix the leak, not the container.
questions.teaches: Diagnose by asking who knows what: the fault belongs where the knowledge leaks, not where the data happens to live.

questions.q: Two payment providers offer similar operations under different names. Which approach lets a shop's checkout stay unaware of which provider it uses?
options: Have checkout test the provider's name before every call
Copy one provider's code into the other and keep a single version
Offer both providers through one shared interface that checkout calls
Remove one of the providers so that only one remains to handle
optionExplain: This keeps the checkout aware of providers and adds conditionals.
Copying leaves the checkout dealing with whichever copy it has.
Right: the checkout depends on the shared interface only.
Dropping a provider avoids the problem rather than solving it.
questions.explain: A common interface hides which concrete class stands behind it. The card next applies this idea to the menus.
questions.rule: Depend on the shared type.

questions.q: The two menus differ mainly in the return type of ____.
questions.explain: Both menus have a method to get the items; only its return type differs.
questions.rule: Nearly identical methods suggest a shared interface.

questions.q: Two e-book stores each let you fetch a title list, one as a list and one as an array. A reader app should stop caring which store it uses. What do you want first?
options: A copy of both title lists stored inside the reader app itself
An interface both store classes implement, which the app uses
A rule forcing both stores to change over to arrays for titles
A separate reader app for each of the two stores
optionExplain: Copies would need refreshing and would not hide the stores.
Right: the app then depends on the interface alone.
Forcing a storage type is the rewrite the owners refuse.
Two apps would keep the stores' differences in front of the user.
questions.explain: The goal is a shared interface, not a shared storage.
questions.rule: Share an interface, not an implementation.

questions.q: True or false: If the Diner and Pancake House both implemented one shared interface, the Waitress could refer to menus through that interface instead of the concrete classes.
questions.explain: A shared interface lets the client name the interface and drop the concrete class names, which is the dependency that shrinks.
questions.rule: Interface replaces class names.

questions.q: Suppose both menus implemented one Menu interface, but getMenuItems() still returned an ArrayList in one and an array in the other. What problem would remain?
options: The Waitress would still need different loops for the two containers
The Waitress would still have to name two concrete menu classes
The chefs would have to rewrite how their menus store the items
The menus could no longer print their items for customers
optionExplain: Right: the items still arrive in different containers.
The shared interface would solve that part.
Storage need not change under this arrangement.
Printing is not affected.
questions.explain: The interface removes the class names but not the differing containers. A uniform way to step through items is needed as well.
questions.rule: Share the way of reading, not only the type name.
questions.teaches: A shared menu interface alone cures the concrete references but not the loops: the items still come in different containers, so a uniform way of stepping through them is needed too.

questions.q: A lamp class has turnOn() and a tax class has compute(). Would a shared interface for the two fit the card's idea?
options: Yes; any two classes at all can be given one shared interface
Yes, because each of the two classes has only a single method
No; the idea fits variations of one job, and these do two jobs
No; interfaces only work for classes that have the same storage
optionExplain: Sharing an interface for unrelated jobs forces odd methods onto both.
A method count says nothing about whether the jobs match.
Right: an interface should capture one job done in different ways.
Storage is not the test; the job is.
questions.explain: The menus fit because each one gives access to its items. A lamp and a tax class share no such job.
questions.rule: Interfaces unify variations of one job.
questions.teaches: A shared interface should capture one job done in different ways; unrelated jobs are not variations of one thing and gain nothing from a shared interface.

questions.q: A program reads scores from a table in one place and from a stack of cards in another. Applying encapsulate what varies, what goes into its own object?
options: The scores themselves, with their meaning and units
The name of the program and the screen it shows
The place where the total is finally printed out
The steps for walking through each container
optionExplain: Scores are the data, which is the same in both places.
The program name does not vary.
Printing the total is common to both cases.
Right: walking through each container is what differs.
questions.explain: The part that differs between the two sources is how to step through them. The card next gives the authors' idea.
questions.rule: Encapsulate what differs.

questions.q: According to the card, the part that varies in the menu code is the ____.
questions.explain: The menus differ in how their items are stepped through, because their collections differ.
questions.rule: What varies here is the iteration.

questions.q: A library app steps through books on a rack by position number and through boxed returns by taking the top one. Which design applies the card?
options: One stepping object per container, asked for the next book
One loop with an if on the container type in every method of the app that reads books
Moving all the books into one kind of container by hand before the app runs at all
A bigger switch statement inside the app that picks the container for each book
optionExplain: Right: the stepping is encapsulated in an object.
This keeps the stepping visible and duplicated across methods.
Rebuilding the containers is a rewrite, not an encapsulation.
A switch statement spreads the container knowledge further.
questions.explain: Each container gets an object that knows how to step through it. The app only asks for the next book.
questions.rule: One stepping object per container.

questions.q: After the stepping is encapsulated, the Pancake House changes to a different collection type. Which part changes?
options: Every client method that prints items
The MenuItem class
Only the iterator built for that menu
The interface the client uses to step through items
optionExplain: The client no longer touches the collection's own steps.
The items are the same as before.
Right: the knowledge of stepping lives in that one object.
The interface is what stays steady across collections.
questions.explain: The change is contained in the one object that knows the collection.
questions.rule: Encapsulation contains change.

questions.q: What must an iterator object remember between its calls to fetch the next item?
options: A copy of every item the collection holds
Its current position in the collection
The client's own code that calls it
The name of the menu it belongs to
optionExplain: Copying every item is not needed to step through a collection.
Right: it needs to know where it is in order to give the next item.
An iterator does not hold client code.
The name has nothing to do with stepping.
questions.explain: An iterator keeps track of where it stands. That is why it is an object and not a single function call, and why a fresh iterator starts a fresh traversal.
questions.rule: An iterator holds a position.
questions.teaches: An iterator holds the current position in the traversal, which is why it is an object rather than a single call; a fresh iterator starts a fresh pass.

questions.q: A teacher's app reads names from a seating chart (a grid) and from an attendance sheet (a list). Sort each part by whether it varies between the two.

items.t: How to step through the grid by row and column
How to step through the list by number
Counting off the grid's rows and columns
Printing each student's name
Greeting each student
The fact that every student has a name

questions.explain: Only the stepping differs. The work done with each item is common to both sources.
questions.rule: Encapsulate stepping; keep per-item work common.
questions.teaches: Only the stepping varies; what is done with each item is common, so the client's per-item work can stay in one place.

questions.q: A remote-control app must step through channels stored in a list or in a ring. Which minimal pair of operations lets one loop work for both?
options: Ask whether another channel remains; fetch the next channel
Ask for the container's size; read a channel by number
Return the whole container to the loop, to be read there
Sort the channels first, then read them one by one
optionExplain: Right: these two work for any container that can be walked.
Size and number work for lists but not for a ring or a hash map.
Returning the container hands the loop its details.
Sorting needs knowledge of the container and is not needed.
questions.explain: The pair that suits every container is have-more and get-next. The card next names them.
questions.rule: Two operations are enough.

questions.q: Match each name with its job.
pairs: The common type clients use to step through items
Knows how to step through one kind of collection
questions.explain: The interface fixes the client's view; each concrete iterator keeps the knowledge of its own collection.
questions.rule: Interface for clients, class per collection.

questions.q: A gardening app keeps plants in a list for beds and in a map for greenhouses. To print them with one loop, what should the loop take as its parameter type?
options: List
Map
Plant
Iterator
optionExplain: A list parameter would shut out the map.
A map parameter would shut out the list.
Plant is the item, not the thing you walk through.
Right: both kinds of storage can supply an iterator.
questions.explain: The loop should depend on the interface that every collection's iterator implements.
questions.rule: Loop over the interface.
