questions.q: A new collection type, a queue, is added. What must be written for the existing printing loop to work on it?
options: A new printing loop for queues
A concrete iterator for the queue
A new Iterator interface
A rewrite of the existing iterators
optionExplain: The printing loop is written for any iterator already.
Right: the loop is unchanged once it receives an iterator.
The interface is shared and stays as it is.
Existing iterators are unaffected by a new collection.
questions.explain: Adding a collection means adding one concrete iterator. Nothing else moves.
questions.rule: New collection, new concrete iterator.

questions.q: The chefs want some lunch items offered on Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday and others on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday. Where can this change be made without touching the Waitress?
options: In the Waitress's loop, by testing which day it is today
In the MenuItem class, by adding a field naming the day
In a new Diner iterator that returns the items for the day
It cannot be done without rewriting the Waitress and the menus
optionExplain: That would put menu knowledge in the client.
The item class cannot decide which items the loop receives.
Right: the Waitress sees only hasNext() and next().
The iterator approach allows it.
questions.explain: The authors describe an alternating iterator for the Diner menu. Because clients see only hasNext() and next(), a different iterator can change which items come out.
questions.rule: Change which items appear by changing the iterator.
questions.teaches: Because clients see only hasNext() and next(), a different concrete iterator can change which items come out, for example alternating items by day, with no change to the client.

questions.q: True or false: A contacts app stores tags in a hash-based set. An iterator over the set is guaranteed to return the tags in the order they were added.
questions.explain: The authors say iterators imply no ordering: order depends on the collection and on the implementation, and one should assume none unless the documentation says so.
questions.rule: Do not assume an order the collection does not promise.
questions.teaches: Iterators imply no ordering: order comes from the underlying collection and the implementation, so assume none unless the documentation says otherwise.

questions.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator
questions.q: Who is best placed to decide which kind of iterator walks a given collection?
options: The client, using a list of known collection types
The collection itself, as it knows its own storage
A central builder that knows about every collection
The Iterator interface, which all iterators implement
optionExplain: This ties the client to every collection type.
Right: the collection knows how it holds items.
A central builder would need updating for each new collection.
An interface only declares operations and builds nothing.
questions.explain: The owner of the storage knows how to walk it. The card next shows how the menus do this.
questions.rule: The owner of the storage builds the iterator.

questions.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator
questions.q: True or false: After the change, the Waitress calls the concrete DinerMenuIterator class by name to get an iterator.
questions.explain: She calls createIterator() on the menu and receives an Iterator. The concrete class stays hidden inside the menu.
questions.rule: Ask the menu; do not name the class.

questions.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator
questions.q: A museum has a Room class holding paintings in an array and a Vault class holding them in a linked list. Following the card, how does a guide app get an iterator for either?
options: Call a static builder in the app that checks the type
Ask each class for its array or list and wrap it in the app
Copy both collections into a new list and walk that list
Call createIterator() on the room or vault to get an Iterator
optionExplain: That puts type knowledge into the app.
Wrapping in the app exposes the storage again.
Copying defeats the point of leaving the classes alone.
Right: each class builds the iterator that fits.
questions.explain: The classes build their own iterators and the app calls the same method on each.
questions.rule: Same method, different classes.

questions.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator
questions.q: The Vault is rebuilt using a hash map. What changes for the guide app?
options: Nothing; only the Vault's own iterator code changes
Every place in the guide app that calls createIterator() on the Vault
The Iterator interface that every collection shares, since it must now cover hash maps
The Room class that holds the paintings in an array, since both should match
optionExplain: Right: the change stays inside the Vault.
The calls stay the same.
The interface is shared by all and stays put.
The Room has its own storage and is unaffected.
questions.explain: The Vault alone knows its storage, so only it changes.
questions.rule: Change stays with the owner.

questions.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator
questions.q: A developer declares createIterator() to return the concrete DinerMenuIterator. What is the drawback?
options: The method can no longer be called from the Waitress
The iterator can no longer hold a position in the menu
Clients become tied to a concrete class again
The menu loses all of its MenuItems
optionExplain: The method still works; the cost is the tie.
Position holding is unaffected.
Right: the declared type becomes the dependency.
Items stay where they are.
questions.explain: Returning the interface keeps the client dependent only on the shared type, the same lesson as programming to an interface.
questions.rule: Return the interface type.
questions.teaches: The declared return type matters: returning the Iterator interface keeps the client free of the concrete iterator class, while returning the concrete class would reintroduce the dependency.

questions.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator
questions.q: A transit app wants the stops of a bus line stored in an array. Put the steps in the order they happen.
items: The app calls createIterator() on the bus line
The bus line builds the iterator that fits its array
The bus line returns it typed as an Iterator
The app loops, asking hasNext() then next(), printing each stop
questions.explain: The loop is the same for any line. Only the second step differs from collection to collection.
questions.rule: Only the building step differs.
questions.teaches: In the sequence a client follows, only the step where the collection builds its iterator differs between collections; the client's calls and loop are identical.

questions.q: A print method takes an iterator as a parameter instead of a collection. What is the main effect for callers?
options: They must pass the collection's size along with the iterator
They can only print collections that are stored as arrays
They no longer have any say in what gets printed
They can print any collection that supplies an iterator
optionExplain: Size is not needed to walk an iterator.
Arrays are one case; the method fits others too.
Callers still choose what to pass in.
Right: the method depends on the iterator only.
questions.explain: The method no longer cares what lies behind the iterator. The card next shows the Waitress doing this.
questions.rule: Take the iterator, not the collection.

questions.q: The new printMenu() method takes an ____ as its parameter.
questions.explain: The method receives the iterator obtained from createIterator(), not the menu.
questions.rule: Parameter type is Iterator.

questions.q: A theatre app has printSeats(Iterator seats), called for the stalls (array) and the circle (list). Management opens a balcony stored as a queue. What does the app need?
options: A queue iterator and one more call to printSeats()
A new printSeats() written for queues
A rewrite of printSeats() that checks collection type
A conversion of stalls and circle into queues
optionExplain: Right: the method is unchanged; the balcony supplies an iterator.
The existing method already fits any iterator.
Type-checking would reintroduce the problem.
Conversion is not needed.
questions.explain: The method is reused as it is. Only a new iterator and a new call are needed.
questions.rule: Reuse the method; supply a new iterator.

questions.q: printMenu()'s loop body is changed to print the price as well. In how many places must the change be made?
options: Two, one for each menu
Three, including the test drive
One, inside the single loop
None, the iterators print for themselves
optionExplain: That was the situation before the change.
The test drive calls the method but does not repeat the loop.
Right: one loop serves all menus.
Iterators only supply items; they do not print.
questions.explain: With one loop, a change is made once.
questions.rule: One loop, one place to change.

questions.q: What does passing the iterator in, rather than building it inside printMenu(), buy?
options: The loop runs faster because less is checked
printMenu() need not name any menu class
Fewer items need printing on each call
The iterator no longer needs a hasNext() method
optionExplain: Speed is not the reason.
Right: the method stays free of any menu.
The number of items is unchanged.
hasNext() is still how the loop ends.
questions.explain: Whoever calls the method chooses the collection, so the method can be reused for every menu and for iterators written later.
questions.rule: Pass in what varies.
questions.teaches: Passing the iterator in, instead of creating it inside the method, keeps the method free of every menu class, so it can serve every menu and any iterator written later.

questions.q: True or false: A school app prints class lists with a method that takes an Iterator. When a class is added that is stored differently, no part of the app needs to change.
questions.explain: The print method stays as it is, but the app must still be told about the new class and call the method for it. The list of collections is a separate source of change.
questions.rule: Shared iteration does not remove the need to name each new collection.
questions.teaches: Even with a shared iterator, the client must still be told about each new collection, so the list of collections is a separate source of change.

questions.section: What have we done so far?
questions.q: True or false: A change that removes duplicate loops from a client also removes every dependency of that client on concrete classes.
questions.explain: Removing loops and removing dependencies are different gains, and one can happen without the other. The card next compares the two designs.
questions.rule: Check each dependency separately.

questions.section: What have we done so far?
questions.q: Match each design point with the description the authors give.
pairs: One for each kind of collection
One, for anything that implements Iterator
questions.explain: The comparison runs along the same lines in both columns: what the Waitress can see, and how many loops she needs.
questions.rule: Same dimensions, two columns.

questions.section: What have we done so far?
questions.q: Sort each item by whether iterators improved it or left it unresolved.

items.t: The Waitress knowing the array and ArrayList details
Needing two loops to print
Being bound to the collection types themselves
Being bound to two concrete menu classes
The menu classes sharing no common type

questions.explain: Iterators hid the storage and merged the loops. They did nothing about the menu classes having no shared type.
questions.rule: Iterators fix traversal, not typing.

questions.section: What have we done so far?
questions.q: The Waitress now receives iterators but still gets them by calling PancakeHouseMenu and DinerMenu directly. What happens when a third menu class arrives?
options: She must still name the new class in her code
Nothing; iterators handle new classes automatically
She needs another loop
The existing menus must change
optionExplain: Right: the concrete class names remain in her code.
Iterators do not remove the need to name the source of an iterator.
The loop is already shared.
The existing menus are unaffected.
questions.explain: The dependency on concrete menu classes was not touched by the iterator.
questions.rule: Name the source and you remain tied to it.

questions.section: What have we done so far?
questions.q: Two menu classes have methods with identical names and signatures, but neither implements a common interface. Can the Waitress hold either in a variable of one common type?
options: Yes; identical methods make them the same type
Yes, but only if the methods return an Iterator
No, because menus cannot share types at all
No; matching methods do not make a shared type
optionExplain: Matching shapes look like a shared type, but the language needs a declaration.
The return type does not change the rule.
Menus can share a type once both implement an interface.
Right: a common type needs a declared common interface.
questions.explain: The authors say the menu interfaces are exactly the same yet there is no common interface. Declaring one is the fix.
questions.rule: Declare the shared type.
questions.teaches: Matching interfaces are not a shared interface: two classes with identical method lists are unrelated types to a client until both declare a common interface.

questions.section: What have we done so far?
questions.q: A teammate writes: our report generator now loops once over any Iterator, so it no longer depends on concrete classes. What does this overlook?
options: Loops must run twice to cover both kinds of data source in the generator
It may still name concrete source classes elsewhere
Iterators cannot be used with reports of this kind, since reports need totals
Concrete classes are impossible to avoid in any design that reads real data
optionExplain: Nothing requires two passes.
Right: the iterator removed one dependency, not the others.
Iterators work with reports like any other consumer.
They can be avoided by depending on interfaces.
questions.explain: Removing a dependency in one place leaves any other naming of concrete classes in place.
questions.rule: Audit where each iterator comes from.
questions.teaches: Check where the iterators come from: a dependency removed in one place stays in any other place that still names the concrete classes.

questions.q: True or false: A design that fixes the most visible fault has therefore solved every problem it was meant to solve.
questions.explain: Fixing the most visible fault may leave others. The card next shows how to check what a solution has and has not covered.
questions.rule: Check each original problem.

questions.q: After adding iterators, the Waitress is still bound to two concrete ____ classes.
questions.explain: The menu classes have no declared common interface, so she still names both.
questions.rule: Name the gap.

questions.q: A team adds an index to speed up a slow search; searches are faster, but results are still stale. Judged by the card, what should the review say?
options: The fix is complete because speed was the main complaint
The fix failed because stale results remain and nothing else matters
One problem is solved; stale results remain open and are named
Both problems are solved because users can search again
optionExplain: A complete verdict ignores the remaining problem.
A failed verdict ignores what the index did achieve.
Right: it marks the solved problem and names the open one.
Searching again does not mean results are fresh.
questions.explain: Mark each original problem, solved or open, and name the open ones.
questions.rule: List, mark, name.

questions.q: Which comment names a precise gap rather than a vague one?
options: The design feels unfinished and could be tidied up in several places
The Waitress names two menu classes with no common interface
Iterators are complicated and hard to follow for newcomers
The code could be better in several ways that nobody has yet spelled out
optionExplain: A feeling does not say what is missing.
Right: it says exactly what is missing.
A complaint about complexity names no gap.
This could be said about any code.
questions.explain: A precise gap says what is missing and where.
questions.rule: Say exactly what is missing.

questions.q: The iterator design leaves the common-menu-interface problem open. What does that show about the iterator solution?
options: The Iterator pattern does not work for this case at all
The authors misjudged how well encapsulation was achieved
Iterators should be thrown away and the design restarted
It is incomplete, not mistaken about what it handles
optionExplain: The remaining gap is a different matter from whether iterators work.
Encapsulation of storage was achieved.
Nothing suggests discarding them; the authors build on them.
Right: it handles its part well and leaves another part unaddressed.
questions.explain: A gap can be real without making the solution wrong. The authors keep the iterators and add the shared interface on top.
questions.rule: Incomplete is not the same as wrong.
questions.teaches: A gap in a solution makes it incomplete, which is a different judgment from false: the authors keep the iterators and build the missing piece on top.

questions.q: A reviewer assesses a fix to a library's lending system. Which comments follow the card's advice? Select all that apply.
options: List the problems we started with and mark each solved or open
Say exactly which remain, for example that renewals still fail
Call the fix a failure because one problem is open
Say it is incomplete without saying how
Check that the original list of problems was itself complete
optionExplain: Right: this is the method.
Right: precision is the point.
One open problem does not make everything fail.
Without saying how, the comment cannot be acted upon.
Right: unlisted problems escape the review.
questions.explain: Complete judging lists problems, marks them and is precise. It also checks the list itself.
questions.rule: Check the list too.
questions.teaches: A review is only as thorough as its list of original problems, so also check that nothing was left off that list.

questions.q: A café chain's clients need one thing from each branch's menu: a way to walk its dishes. What should the shared interface for the branches contain?
options: A single method that supplies a walker over the dishes
Every method any branch menu offers
Each branch's storage details, so clients can pick the best loop
Nothing, since the branches differ
optionExplain: Right: it exposes just what clients need.
A large interface couples clients to every branch's quirks.
Storage details are what clients should not see.
Differences in storage do not rule out a shared interface.
questions.explain: A small interface keeps clients dependent on little. The card next shows the one the authors chose.
questions.rule: Share only what clients need.

questions.q: Match each part with its role in the new design.
pairs: Refers to menus through the interface
Creates the iterator for its own storage
questions.explain: The interface is the meeting point: menus implement it and the Waitress uses it.
questions.rule: Menus implement, clients use.

questions.q: A zoo app has Aviary and ReptileHouse classes with different storage. The app only prints the animals in each. Following the card, what should the shared interface offer?
options: Methods for adding, removing and counting animals as well
The storage structure of each house
A single method that returns an Iterator over the animals
A separate method for each species
optionExplain: Extra operations couple the app to more than printing requires.
The app should not see storage.
Right: it covers what the app needs and no more.
Species methods would fix the interface to today's animals.
questions.explain: The app prints animals, so one method that gives an iterator is enough.
questions.rule: Match the interface to the client's need.

questions.q: True or false: A new café class that implements Menu is added. The Waitress's printing code gains no new dependency on a concrete menu class.
questions.explain: She refers to the interface she already uses, so anything that implements Menu slots in.
questions.rule: New implementers slot in.

questions.q: The authors leave addItem() out of the Menu interface. What is the reason given?
options: So that the chefs keep control of their menus
Because menus have no way of adding any items at all
Because the Waitress would call it far too often in practice
Because iterators already take care of adding items
optionExplain: Right: adding stays with the chefs.
Menus can add items; they just do it outside the interface.
Frequency of calls is not the reason.
Iterators walk items; they do not add them.
questions.explain: An interface can be shaped deliberately to keep some operations out of clients' hands.
questions.rule: Leave out what clients should not do.
questions.teaches: An interface can deliberately leave out operations such as adding items, so that the owners of the collection keep control of its contents.

questions.q: A designer of a shared interface for several ticket machines includes each machine's coin-handling internals so clients can optimise. What does this do?
options: It makes the interface safer and easier for clients to use
It lets the machines change without any effect on their clients
It re-exposes hidden details and ties clients to them
It removes the need for separate classes for each machine
optionExplain: More exposure means clients can depend on more.
Clients depending on internals break when they change.
Right: the interface now carries the details clients should not depend on.
The machines still differ underneath.
questions.explain: A shared interface earns its value by staying small. Every extra operation is another thing clients may come to rely on.
questions.rule: A small interface keeps clients loosely tied.
questions.teaches: Everything in a shared interface is something clients may come to depend on, so an interface is worth most when it stays small.

questions.q: Your language's library has a standard iterator interface that its list classes support. You wrote your own for practice. What is the main benefit of switching?
options: Your own interface stops compiling once the library is used
Your classes work with library code already using the standard
Standard iterators run faster than any homegrown version
The pattern cannot work at all without the standard one
optionExplain: Your interface keeps compiling; the gain lies elsewhere.
Right: shared interfaces let code and classes mix.
Speed is not the point made in the card.
The pattern worked with your own interface.
questions.explain: Using the standard interface lets your classes join an existing ecosystem. The card next explains the authors' leverage.
questions.rule: Standard interfaces connect to existing code.

questions.q: An ArrayList already provides an ____() method that returns an iterator.
questions.explain: That is why the PancakeHouseMenuIterator class could be deleted.
questions.rule: Use the built-in when one exists.

questions.q: In a shop app, CatalogA keeps products in an ArrayList and CatalogB keeps them in a plain array. Which one needs a hand-written iterator class?
options: CatalogB, since arrays offer no iterator
CatalogA, since lists lack iterators
Both of them
Neither of them
optionExplain: Right: the array has no iterator of its own.
ArrayList has iterator(), so no class is needed.
Only the array lacks one.
The array still needs one.
questions.explain: Arrays do not support iterator(), so the class for the array must be written.
questions.rule: Write iterators for collections that lack them.

questions.q: True or false: The Diner replaces its array with an ArrayList. The team can then delete its homegrown iterator class and use the list's own iterator() method.
questions.explain: Once the storage supports iterator(), the extra class has no job.
questions.rule: Change the storage, reconsider the class.

questions.q: An older Java class offers hasMoreElements() and nextElement(). What do the authors suggest?
options: Prefer the older interface, since it was the original one and is the most stable
Prefer Iterator, which more classes support; an adapter converts
Rewrite the older class from scratch as a new class that uses the newer interface
Avoid the pattern altogether for such older classes, since it cannot be used with them
optionExplain: The older interface is the one that was replaced.
Right: the older Enumeration has been replaced by Iterator.
A rewrite is not needed if an adapter converts.
The pattern is not being avoided.
questions.explain: The authors point to Enumeration as an older version of Iterator, with an adapter in the chapter on adapters.
questions.rule: Prefer the widely supported interface.
questions.teaches: Enumeration is an older form of Iterator, with hasMoreElements() and nextElement(); the authors prefer Iterator because more classes support it, and an adapter converts between them.

questions.q: A playlist app needs to step backwards, which the standard Iterator lacks. What does the book's reasoning suggest?
options: Abandon iterators and go back to plain index loops
Copy the playlist into a reversed list on every pass
Extend the interface with extra methods, as ListIterator does
Require every collection to offer a first() method as well
optionExplain: Abandoning the pattern throws away its benefits.
Copying makes the client deal with storage again.
Right: the authors say you can add methods, and name ListIterator.
first() does not give backward stepping.
questions.explain: ListIterator adds previous() and more to the standard interface, and is supported by any Collection that implements List.
questions.rule: Extend the interface when you need more.
questions.teaches: Java's ListIterator extends Iterator with previous() and other methods, and is supported by any Collection that implements List.

questions.q: True or false: Because remove() is part of the Iterator interface, every iterator must be able to remove items.
questions.explain: The interface declares remove(), but the operation may be unsupported. The card next shows how the authors treat it.
questions.rule: Declared is not always supported.

questions.q: An iterator that does not support removal throws the runtime exception ____.
questions.explain: The Iterator documentation allows this exception from remove().
questions.rule: Unsupported means this exception.

questions.q: A read-only reporting iterator over audit logs must not delete anything. Following the card, what should its remove() method do?
options: Delete the item quietly without telling the caller
Be present and throw UnsupportedOperationException
Be left out of the class so that it fails to compile
Return normally and do nothing, as if it had worked
optionExplain: Deleting breaks the read-only promise.
Right: it honours the interface and signals it is unsupported.
The interface requires the method.
Doing nothing hides a failed request from the caller.
questions.explain: The method must exist because the interface declares it, and it should say plainly that it is not supported.
questions.rule: Fail loudly where unsupported.

questions.q: A client calls remove() on an iterator over a read-only collection and does not check for the exception. What may happen?
options: The compiler rejects the call before the program is run
The item is removed anyway, despite the collection
hasNext() starts returning false for the rest of the pass
An UnsupportedOperationException may surface when it runs
optionExplain: The method exists, so the compiler accepts it.
The iterator refuses the removal.
The exception has nothing to do with hasNext().
Right: it is a runtime exception.
questions.explain: The exception appears only when the call is made, not when the program is compiled.
questions.rule: Runtime exceptions show up at run time.

questions.q: While an iterator is in use, other code changes the underlying collection. What does the interface promise about remove()?
options: Its behaviour is unspecified, so concurrent use needs care
It removes from a private copy kept by the iterator
It always waits until the other code has finished its work
It restarts the traversal from the first element
optionExplain: Right: the authors warn about this.
No private copy is promised.
No waiting is promised.
No restart is promised.
questions.explain: The documentation leaves the behaviour open, so design for it instead of assuming.
questions.rule: Do not assume behaviour the contract omits.
questions.teaches: The behaviour of remove() is unspecified if the collection changes during iteration, so code that shares a collection between threads must be designed with care.

questions.q: A team uses a vendor's interface that declares several optional operations. Which habits match the card? Select all that apply.
options: Read the documentation for which operations are optional
Be ready for an unsupported-operation exception where one is allowed
Assume a declared operation always works
Treat every unsupported-operation exception as a library bug
Take care when collections are changed during use
optionExplain: Right: know what the contract leaves open.
Right: the authors say a good client checks for it.
A declaration does not guarantee support.
The exception is part of the contract here, not a bug.
Right: unspecified behaviour needs care.
questions.explain: A careful client treats optional and unspecified parts as risks to handle.
questions.rule: Handle the gaps in the contract.
questions.teaches: An operation declared in an interface is not a promise that it works: optional operations may signal at run time that they are unsupported.

questions.q: Which approach gives clients sequential access to a group of objects without revealing how the group is stored?
options: Publishing the group's internal array for clients to read
Copying the group into every client that wants it
Offering a stepping object that hands over elements one by one
Sorting the group before any client uses it
optionExplain: Publishing the array reveals the representation.
Copies leave each client with its own storage.
Right: clients see the elements but not the storage.
Sorting does not hide the storage.
questions.explain: A stepping object is the pattern's answer. The card next gives the official definition.
questions.rule: Hand out elements, not storage.

questions.q: The Iterator Pattern gives access to an aggregate's elements without exposing its underlying ____.
questions.explain: The definition speaks of the underlying representation, which the pattern keeps hidden.
questions.rule: Hide the representation.

questions.q: An airline app holds one day's flights in a table and a week's flights in a list. A schedule screen must show each flight in turn. Which design matches the definition?
options: The screen reads the table's rows and the list's items by number
Both are converted to text first
The screen asks the airline for sorted flights
The screen gets an iterator from each and steps through it
optionExplain: This exposes both representations.
Conversion to text loses the flights as objects.
Sorting is not the access the definition describes.
Right: the screen never sees the storage.
questions.explain: The screen asks each aggregate for an iterator and uses only that.
questions.rule: Ask for an iterator.

questions.q: True or false: The airline changes the week's storage from a list to a tree. If the schedule screen uses iterators, the screen code needs no change.
questions.explain: The screen was written against the iterator and not the list, so the representation can change behind it.
questions.rule: Hidden representations can change.

questions.q: A bag holds three copies of the same dish. What does an iterator over the bag do?
options: Skips the duplicates and returns each dish once
Fails because a bag is not allowed to have duplicates
Steps through each element, duplicates included
Returns the dish once, together with a count of copies
optionExplain: Skipping duplicates is not part of the definition.
Aggregates may contain duplicates.
Right: the iterator walks whatever the aggregate holds.
A count is not what the iterator returns.
questions.explain: The authors note that the underlying collection may be unordered, like a bag, and may even contain duplicates.
questions.rule: An iterator walks what is there.
questions.teaches: Aggregates may be unordered or contain duplicates; the iterator simply walks whatever the aggregate holds.

questions.q: A jukebox user wants track 7 immediately. What does the pattern's definition provide for that?
options: A direct jump to any track by its number on the list
Nothing by itself; it promises sequential access only
Backward stepping from the end back to the start
Automatic sorting of the tracks by their popularity
optionExplain: Jumping is not in the definition.
Right: stepping to track 7 means stepping through the earlier ones, unless an extension is added.
Backward stepping is an extension, not the definition.
Sorting is not part of the definition.
questions.explain: The definition promises sequential access. Anything more is an addition.
questions.rule: Sequential is the whole promise.
questions.teaches: Sequential access is the whole promise: anything beyond stepping forward through the elements, such as jumping to a position, is an extension rather than part of the definition.

questions.q: A method accepts an iterator and processes each item. With which collections can it be used?
options: Any collection that can supply an iterator
Only collections of the class its first caller used
Only arrays
Only collections that keep items sorted
optionExplain: Right: it depends on the iterator and nothing else.
Nothing ties it to a first caller's class.
Arrays are one case among many.
Sorting is not a requirement.
questions.explain: The method sees only the iterator, so any source of one will do. The card next names this idea.
questions.rule: The iterator is the only requirement.

questions.q: True or false: A method that takes an Iterator parameter must know whether the items come from an array or an ArrayList.
questions.explain: It sees only the iterator. Where the items come from is hidden.
questions.rule: Hidden source, shared loop.

questions.q: The photo app's countPortraits(Iterator photos) can count an online gallery's portraits with only one thing added: a call with the gallery's ____.
questions.explain: The existing method is reused as it is; the gallery only has to supply an iterator.
questions.rule: Reuse by supplying an iterator.

questions.q: The method must show a progress bar and so must know the number of photos before it starts. The Iterator offers hasNext() and next(). What follows?
options: The count is built into every iterator and can be read at no cost
The iterator alone cannot give the count; it must come from elsewhere
The method must be rewritten separately for every source that supplies photos
A progress bar cannot be shown at all with a design built on iterators
optionExplain: Counting is not in the interface.
Right: the interface has no count.
Rewriting per source gives up the benefit.
A bar can be built if the count comes from somewhere else.
questions.explain: The polymorphic code sees only the interface, so anything it needs beyond the interface must come from elsewhere.
questions.rule: The interface sets the limit.

questions.q: What does using the standard Iterator interface help with when mixing your own collection classes and library lists?
options: Library lists stop using iterators of their own
Your classes become faster than the library lists
Code written for the standard interface accepts both kinds
The two kinds can no longer be told apart by anyone
optionExplain: Libraries keep using their iterators.
Speed is not at stake.
Right: both can be passed to the same code.
The point is that the code need not tell them apart, not that nobody can.
questions.explain: The authors say a common Iterator interface makes it easier to mix your own aggregates with Java aggregates like ArrayList and Vector.
questions.rule: Standard interface, easy mixing.
questions.teaches: A common Iterator interface makes it easier to mix your own aggregates with library aggregates such as ArrayList and Vector.

questions.q: A lighting program has dimAll(Iterator lamps), used for lamps held in a ring and for lamp groups held in a tree. A developer proposes a second version for trees. Judged by the card, what is the response?
options: Needed, because trees cannot be walked by any iterator
Not needed if the tree can supply an iterator over the lamps
Needed, because rings are special and need their own method
Needed, because the method has the wrong name for trees
optionExplain: Trees can be walked by an iterator written for them.
Right: the method needs an iterator and nothing else.
Rings are handled by their iterator.
Names have nothing to do with it.
questions.explain: The test is whether a collection can supply an iterator, not what shape it has.
questions.rule: Shape does not matter; the iterator does.
questions.teaches: What decides whether polymorphic iteration works is whether the collection can supply an iterator, not its shape: even a tree can serve code written for iterators.

questions.q: A class holds a company's invoices and also has methods for walking through them forward, backward and by customer. Where should the walking live?
options: In the same class, since the invoices are held there already
In every client that happens to need a walk through them
In the Invoice items themselves, one walk for each
In separate walking objects, leaving the class to manage invoices
optionExplain: Convenient, but it burdens the class with a second job.
Every client would repeat the same code.
An invoice does not know its neighbours.
Right: walking is a separate job.
questions.explain: Keeping the walking separate lets each class do one job. The card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: One job per class.

questions.q: The Iterator Pattern takes the job of traversal away from the ____ and gives it to the iterator.
questions.explain: The aggregate stays focused on managing its collection.
questions.rule: Traversal leaves the aggregate.

questions.q: Sort each job for a Playlist class by whether it stays on the aggregate or moves to an iterator.

items.t: Add a song to the playlist
Report how many songs it holds
Hold the songs
Tell whether more songs remain in the pass
Hand back the next song in the pass
Remember which song the pass has reached

questions.explain: The playlist manages its songs. The iterator carries the state and steps of a pass.
questions.rule: Manage with the aggregate, walk with the iterator.

questions.q: The team wants a second way to step through the playlist: shuffled. Where does the change go?
options: In a new iterator; the playlist class is untouched
In new shuffling methods on the playlist class
In every client's loop that walks the playlist
In the song class that each track belongs to
optionExplain: Right: a new traversal is a new iterator.
That is the burden the pattern removes.
Clients keep the same loop.
A song does not control the order of a pass.
questions.explain: A new way of traversing is a new iterator, leaving the aggregate alone.
questions.rule: New traversal, new iterator.

questions.q: How does the aggregate's interface change when traversal moves to an iterator?
options: It gains one more method for each way of traversing
It must publish its internal array to the iterators
It shrinks to one method that creates the iterator
It loses the ability to add and manage elements
optionExplain: That is the situation before the move.
Publishing would defeat the purpose.
Right: createIterator() replaces traversal methods.
Managing elements stays with the aggregate.
questions.explain: The authors say the aggregate's interface and implementation are simpler. The menus gained only createIterator().
questions.rule: Simple interface, many iterators.
questions.teaches: The aggregate's interface shrinks to one method that makes an iterator, instead of growing a method for every way of traversing.

questions.q: True or false: Once an orchard app moves traversal into an iterator, the iterator can step through the trees without knowing anything about how the orchard stores them.
questions.explain: Each concrete iterator is written for one kind of aggregate and knows how it is built. The knowledge moved; it did not vanish. What is spared is the client.
questions.rule: The knowledge moves, it does not vanish.
questions.teaches: Each concrete iterator knows the structure of the aggregate it serves; the pattern moves that knowledge out of the clients and the aggregate's interface, not out of the design.

questions.q: An older book's iterator offers isDone(). Which method of Java's Iterator does it correspond to?
options: next()
remove()
createIterator()
hasNext()
optionExplain: next() returns an item; it does not test.
remove() deletes an item.
createIterator() belongs to the aggregate.
Right: both test for the end of the traversal, from opposite sides.
questions.explain: Both test whether the traversal has finished. The card next shows the other mappings.
questions.rule: Same job, different name.

questions.q: Match each classic or Java method with its counterpart.
pairs: No counterpart; Java gets a new iterator
questions.explain: Most classic jobs have a Java method; first() is replaced by getting a new iterator.
questions.rule: Map by job.

questions.q: A legacy photo library has start(), atEnd(), advance() and current(). Which mapping onto the Java interface is closest?
options: atEnd() is the reverse of hasNext(); advance() plus current() is next(); start() is a new iterator
start() is hasNext(), atEnd() is next(), and advance() is remove(), going by sound
All four are the same as next(), only with other names, because they all move along
current() is hasNext(), and atEnd() is remove() in the Java form
optionExplain: Right: each job finds its place.
This assigns the jobs to the wrong methods.
Four jobs cannot collapse into one.
current() reads an item; it does not test.
questions.explain: Match by job: test for the end, advance, read, start over.
questions.rule: Start, test, advance, read.

questions.q: A client that needs a second pass over a list with java.util.Iterator asks the list for a new ____.
questions.explain: Java gets a new iterator whenever a pass is wanted; there is no first().
questions.rule: New pass, new iterator.

questions.q: A method receives an iterator and walks it to the end. Another method then receives the same iterator object. What does it find?
options: A fresh pass starting again from the first item
No items remain, as the pass is used up
Only the first item again, then nothing more
A copy of the whole collection to start over
optionExplain: That would need a first() or a new iterator.
Right: the Java iterator cannot be rewound.
Nothing returns to the first item.
An iterator is not a copy.
questions.explain: Since there is no first(), a used iterator stays used. The state of the pass lives in the iterator.
questions.rule: A used iterator stays used.
questions.teaches: Because a Java iterator cannot be rewound, one that has been walked to the end is used up; the state of the pass lives in the iterator and a second pass needs a new one.

questions.q: A new graph library names its iterator methods begin(), finished(), advance() and value(). A colleague says it is a different pattern from Iterator. How should you respond using the card?
options: The names differ, but the jobs map: start, test, advance, read
They are right, since the pattern requires the Java method names
They are right, since four methods are too many for a pattern
Only the version for a hash map counts as the pattern
optionExplain: Right: recognise the pattern by its jobs.
The classic names differ too and are still the pattern.
The count of methods is not the test.
The pattern covers all kinds of aggregate.
questions.explain: Names change from library to library; the jobs stay the same.
questions.rule: Judge by jobs, not names.
questions.teaches: Recognise a pattern by the jobs it does and its intent, not by the names of its methods.

questions.q: In one design the caller asks for items one at a time. In another the caller hands over a task and the walker applies it to every item. In which is the caller in control of the iteration?
options: The second, where the walker applies the task
Both equally
Neither
The first, where the caller asks for each item
optionExplain: There the walker decides the pace.
The two differ in who steers.
In the first the caller does steer.
Right: the caller decides when to ask for the next item.
questions.explain: Who controls the iteration is what separates the two kinds. The card next names them.
questions.rule: Control marks the difference.

questions.q: Match each term with its description.
pairs: The client controls the iteration by calling next()
Steps through the elements itself and applies an operation passed to it
Less flexible, but easy to use
questions.explain: The two differ in who drives the traversal.
questions.rule: Who drives the traversal?

questions.q: Given the card, sort each need by the style that fits better.

items.t: Stop part-way when the loop body finds a match
Compare each element with the one before it
Walk two lists together, one item from each
Apply the same discount to every price
Print every row
Apply formatting to all cells

questions.explain: When the client must steer, it needs external iteration. When one operation applies to everything, handing it over is easier.
questions.rule: Steer: external. Apply to all: internal.

questions.q: A team wants to walk two lists together, taking one item from each in turn. Which style suits this?
options: Internal, since the iterator can see both lists at once
External, as the client decides when each iterator advances
Either one, since there is no difference between them
Neither style can walk two lists together at all
optionExplain: An internal iterator steps through one collection at its own pace.
Right: only the client can coordinate the two.
The styles differ in who controls the pace.
Two external iterators can be driven together.
questions.explain: Coordinating two walks needs the client in control.
questions.rule: Coordination needs control.

questions.q: Which kind of iterator has to remember where it is between the client's calls?
options: An internal iterator
Both, in the same way
An external iterator
Neither
optionExplain: An internal iterator runs its loop in one go.
The internal kind keeps its place inside its own loop.
Right: the client drives it by calling hasNext() and next().
An external iterator must hold its position.
questions.explain: An external iterator keeps its position so that an outside client can drive it, as the CompositeIterator will have to later.
questions.rule: External iterators carry state.
questions.teaches: An external iterator must remember its position between calls so that an outside client can drive it by calling hasNext() and next().

questions.q: A designer says internal iterators are better because they leave nothing for the client to get wrong. What does the card say against this?
options: They are slower than external iterators in every case, because they do all the work
They are less flexible: the client cannot steer the iteration
They cannot take an operation to apply to each element as they step through
They only work with arrays and never with lists or maps of any kind
optionExplain: Speed is not discussed.
Right: convenience is paid for with control.
Taking an operation is what they do.
They are not tied to arrays.
questions.explain: Convenience and control trade off: hiding the loop means giving up steering it.
questions.rule: Convenience costs control.
questions.teaches: Convenience and control trade off: hiding the loop saves work but gives up the ability to steer it.

questions.q: A Report class fetches data, formats it and prints it. A new printer type arrives, and later the data source changes. What is the likely problem?
options: Reports can no longer be created once printers differ
Printers and data sources must share a single type
The class has too few lines to do its work well
The class must be edited for two unrelated reasons
optionExplain: Reports can still be created.
Nothing forces a shared type.
Length is not the issue.
Right: two separate pressures hit the same class.
questions.explain: One class bearing two kinds of change is the situation the principle addresses. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Different reasons, same class.

questions.q: A class should have only one ____ to change.
questions.explain: That is the principle, which also says to give each responsibility to one class.
questions.rule: One reason to change.

questions.q: A Student class stores grades and also contains the code that formats a transcript for printing. Which pair of reasons to change does it have?
options: How grades are stored; how the transcript is laid out
The count of students and the names of the students
The school's location and the name of the school
The grades that are stored and the names that are stored
optionExplain: Right: storage and layout change for different reasons.
These are data values, not responsibilities.
These do not concern the class's jobs.
Both belong to storage and are one reason.
questions.explain: Storage and formatting are two areas of potential change.
questions.rule: Each job is an area of change.

questions.q: True or false: After the transcript layout moves into its own class, a later redesign of the layout touches only the transcript class.
questions.explain: With one class per responsibility, a change touches one class.
questions.rule: One change, one class.

questions.q: Which sign suggests that a class has two responsibilities?
options: The class has a long and complicated name
The class is used by a great many clients
The class has a private field holding some state
Changes of different kinds keep landing in one class
optionExplain: A name tells little about responsibilities.
Many clients do not mean many responsibilities.
Private fields are routine.
Right: the authors say to watch for signals that a class changes in more than one way.
questions.explain: The authors advise watching for signals of a class changing in more than one way as the system grows.
questions.rule: Watch how the class changes over time.
questions.teaches: A practical sign of mixed responsibilities is a class that is changed in more than one way as the system grows, so watch the history of changes.

questions.q: A teammate says the Menu class should also store the daily specials and print posters, since all relate to the menu. What does the principle suggest?
options: Poster printing changes for its own reasons and needs its own class
Keep them together, because they all share the subject of the menu
Add a printing method to every item on the menu
Split the class into a separate class for every method
optionExplain: Right: layout of posters changes for its own reasons.
Sharing a subject is not the test.
That spreads printing across items.
One class per method goes beyond the principle.
questions.explain: The test is whether behaviours would change for different reasons, not whether they relate to the same subject.
questions.rule: Ask what would make each part change.
questions.teaches: Relatedness in subject is not the test of one responsibility: the test is whether the behaviours would change for different reasons.

questions.q: True or false: A class with many methods must have low cohesion.
questions.explain: Cohesion depends on whether the functions belong together, not on how many there are. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: Relatedness, not count.

questions.q: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: How closely a class supports one purpose
A class has only one reason to change
questions.explain: Cohesion measures focus, the principle states the rule, and they usually go together.
questions.rule: Focus is cohesion.

questions.q: Rate each class sketch.

items.t: Stack: push, pop, peek, isEmpty
Thermostat: setTarget, readTemperature, heatOn, heatOff
LibraryCard: borrow, return, renew
Utility: sendEmail, computeTax, drawCircle, parseDate
Misc: compress, greet, convertCurrency
Order: addLine, total, applyDiscount, resizeWindow

questions.explain: Related functions give high cohesion. Unrelated functions in one class give low cohesion.
questions.rule: Do the parts belong together?

questions.q: A cohesive class gains a method that prints the weather forecast. What happens to its cohesion?
options: It rises, since bigger classes are more complete and useful
It stays the same, as only the old methods are counted
It drops, as the new function is unrelated to the purpose
It stays the same, since cohesion is only about naming
optionExplain: Size does not raise cohesion.
All of the class's functions count toward cohesion, not only the old ones.
Right: an unrelated function dilutes the purpose.
Cohesion concerns purpose, not names.
questions.explain: The forecast method has nothing to do with the class's purpose, so its functions no longer serve a single purpose and its cohesion drops.
questions.rule: Unrelated additions lower cohesion.

questions.q: A class is about one subject, say invoices, but changes both when the tax rules change and when the print layout changes. What does the principle point out?
options: It has high cohesion, so it will never need a change
It still has two reasons to change although the subject is one
It must be merged with another class on the same subject
It has no reason to change as long as its subject is one
optionExplain: Subject alone can hide two responsibilities.
Right: the principle asks about reasons for change, not subject.
Merging adds more mixed jobs.
It has two reasons to change, tax rules and print layout, so claiming it has none is wrong.
questions.explain: A class can look unified by subject and still carry two responsibilities, so the reasons for change are the check.
questions.rule: Check reasons for change as well.
questions.teaches: A class can look unified by its subject and still carry two responsibilities, so ask about its reasons to change as well as its subject.

questions.q: A Garden class has waterPlants, prunePlants, plantSeeds and printSeedCatalogueAsHtml. Which change raises its cohesion?
options: Move the catalogue printing into a class of its own
Add a method that sends greetings to the garden visitors
Add more printing formats to the Garden class as well
Merge it with a Weather class that tracks the forecast
optionExplain: Right: it removes the unrelated job.
Greetings are unrelated too.
More formats would deepen the mix.
Merging adds unrelated functions.
questions.explain: Cohesion rises by moving unrelated work out, not by adding things in.
questions.rule: Move unrelated work out.
questions.teaches: Cohesion rises by moving unrelated work out of a class rather than by adding more to it.

questions.q: A new menu stores dishes in a map from names to dishes. To get an iterator over the dishes only, what is the sensible way?
options: Ask the map's keys for an iterator over the dish names
Copy the dishes into an array and write an iterator for it
Convert the whole map to text and read the dishes from it
Take the map's values collection and ask it for an iterator
optionExplain: Keys are the names, not the dishes.
Copying is more work than needed when the values support iterators.
Text would lose the dish objects.
Right: the dishes are the values.
questions.explain: A map has two sets of objects, so you must pick the right one. The card next shows how the authors did it.
questions.rule: Pick the set that holds the elements.

questions.q: Which are among the three changes to fit the Café menu into the framework? Select all that apply.
options: Implement the Menu interface
Get rid of getItems()
Add createIterator() that returns an iterator over the HashMap's values
Rewrite the Waitress's loops
Switch the HashMap to an array
optionExplain: Right: the Waitress deals with menus through this interface.
Right: the framework hands out items through iterators.
Right: this is how the Waitress gets items.
The loop in the Waitress is already written against iterators.
The Café keeps its HashMap.
questions.explain: The three changes are the interface, removing getItems() and adding createIterator().
questions.rule: Interface, remove getter, add createIterator().

questions.q: A bakery menu class keeps items in a map from codes to items and exposes getBakeryItems(). Following the three changes, what does it end up with?
options: It keeps the getter, and the Waitress adds one more loop of her own for the bakery menu
It implements the shared interface, drops the getter, and iterates over the values
It copies everything into an array first, keeps the old getter, and also adds a new loop
It returns an iterator over the map's keys from createIterator() and drops the old getter too
optionExplain: Keeping the getter leaves the problem the framework solved.
Right: all three changes are applied.
Copying is not asked for.
Keys are not the items.
questions.explain: The same three steps work for any map-backed menu.
questions.rule: Same steps, new class.

questions.q: The Café's createIterator() returns the iterator over the map's values. What does the Waitress's loop receive on each call to next()?
options: A key
A key and value pair
A MenuItem
The whole map
optionExplain: Keys would come from a keys iterator.
Pairs would come from a different iterator.
Right: values are the MenuItems.
The map is the aggregate, not an element.
questions.explain: The iterator over values hands back the values one at a time.
questions.rule: Elements are the values.

questions.q: From the Waitress's side, how does the Café menu differ from the list-backed menu?
options: It needs a separate loop in the Waitress to read the items from the map
It does not differ; the iterator hides the route via the values
It needs a separate interface from the other menus, since its storage is a map
It must always be printed after all the others, since maps are slower
optionExplain: The Waitress's loop over an Iterator is shared by every menu, so no separate loop is needed.
Right: both hand over MenuItems through an Iterator.
Both menus implement the Menu interface, so the Café needs no separate interface.
Order of calls is unrelated.
questions.explain: The indirect route is invisible behind createIterator().
questions.rule: The route to the iterator is private.
questions.teaches: From the client's side, a menu backed by a map looks the same as one backed by a list: the iterator hides that the elements were reached indirectly through the map's values.

questions.q: True or false: A ticketing system keeps tickets in a plain array. The same three changes fit it into the framework without writing any iterator class, because arrays support iterators through their values.
questions.explain: Arrays offer no iterator at all, so an iterator class still has to be written, as the Diner needed. A map supports one indirectly; an array supports none.
questions.rule: Check whether the storage can supply an iterator.
questions.teaches: The three changes assume the storage can supply an iterator, directly or indirectly; when it cannot, as with an array, a concrete iterator must still be written by hand.

questions.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress
questions.q: A design is tested by adding a new variation. Which result shows it handles variation well?
options: The existing code is copied and then edited for the new variation
The new variation works only after every client has been changed
The same loop is duplicated again for the new variation
The new variation needs a small, local addition and no rewrite
optionExplain: Copy and edit leaves duplicated code to maintain.
Changing every client means the variation is not contained.
Duplication is the cost the design should avoid.
Right: change stays local.
questions.explain: Cost of the next addition is a good measure. The card next shows how the Waitress fared.
questions.rule: Measure the cost of the next variation.

questions.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress
questions.q: True or false: Adding the Café menu required a new traversal loop in the Waitress.
questions.explain: She already has one loop in printMenu(). The Café needed only another call to it.
questions.rule: One loop serves all menus.

questions.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress
questions.q: A news app prints articles from feeds with printFeed(Iterator). A podcast feed with its own storage is added. What is the smallest sufficient change?
options: Give the podcast feed a createIterator(), add one printFeed call
Write a new print routine for podcasts and keep it apart from the rest of the app
Convert the podcast feed's storage to match the other feeds in the app
Change printFeed so that it checks the type of each feed it is given
optionExplain: Right: that is the whole job.
A new routine repeats the old problem.
Conversion forces storage choices on the feed.
Type checks bring back the dependency.
questions.explain: A new feed needs only its own iterator and a call.
questions.rule: Small, local addition.

questions.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress
questions.q: After the Café, a fifth menu is added the same way. The Waitress needs about ____ more call to printMenu().
questions.explain: Each menu costs one call, so the cost per menu stays constant.
questions.rule: Constant cost per variation.

questions.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress
questions.q: What does decoupling the Waitress let the menu authors do?
options: Change the Menu interface freely whenever they want to
Skip implementing createIterator() in their own menu class
Print their own menus instead of the Waitress doing so
Choose any storage, if their menu supplies an iterator
optionExplain: The interface is shared and should be changed carefully.
createIterator() is what the Waitress calls.
Printing remains the Waitress's task.
Right: the Waitress does not depend on storage.
questions.explain: The authors of a new menu need not consult the Waitress about storage.
questions.rule: Decoupling frees the other side.
questions.teaches: Decoupling lets the author of a new menu choose any storage, provided the menu honours the shared interface, without consulting the author of the client.

questions.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress
questions.q: A clinic app adds each new ward through the iterator approach, and the team says the app is now closed to modification when wards are added. How should this claim be judged?
options: Not quite: the app is still opened to add a call per new ward
Correct: iterators remove the need for any edits at all
Not correct: the wards themselves must all be rewritten
Correct, because each new ward adds itself to the app
optionExplain: Right: the list of wards is still in the client's code.
Iterators remove the loops, not the list of collections.
The wards need no rewrite.
Nothing in the approach adds them automatically.
questions.explain: The Waitress still had to be edited to add the Café. The edit is small, but it is still an edit.
questions.rule: Small is not the same as none.
questions.teaches: Listing each collection by hand in the client is itself a modification at every addition, however small.

questions.q: A library groups its list, queue and stack classes under one shared interface for collections. What is the benefit for code that handles groups of objects?
options: All three become the same class behind the scenes, so that their code is shared
Their items are all stored together in one array that they take turns using
Code can treat them as one type and ask each for an iterator
Iterators are no longer needed for walking them, since the shared type does that
optionExplain: They stay separate classes behind a shared interface.
Storage differs by class.
Right: a shared type allows shared code.
Iterators are how code walks them.
questions.explain: A shared interface lets code treat different classes alike. The card next names the one in Java.
questions.rule: Share a type to share code.

questions.q: Which of these belong to the Java Collections Framework as the card describes? Select all that apply.
options: ArrayList
LinkedList
PriorityQueue
MenuItem
PancakeHouseMenu
optionExplain: Right: it is named in the card.
Right: it is named in the card.
Right: it is named in the card.
MenuItem is the book's item class, not a framework class.
That is the book's menu class.
questions.explain: The framework holds general collection classes; MenuItem and the menus are the book's own.
questions.rule: Framework classes are general.

questions.q: A school app keeps students in a LinkedList and teachers in a PriorityQueue. Both implement java.util.Collection. What does that let the app do?
options: Treat the two as though they were the same class, with identical behaviour inside
Use Collection's methods and get an iterator from either
Skip using iterators when walking either one, since Collection walks them itself
Store both of them together in one array and walk the array
optionExplain: They are still two classes.
Right: a shared interface offers shared operations.
Iterators remain the way to walk them.
Storage is unaffected.
questions.explain: The shared interface is the common meeting point.
questions.rule: Use the shared interface.

questions.q: True or false: A developer asks a map's keys for an iterator when the Items were wanted. The loop's elements turn out to be the keys, not the Items.
questions.explain: Which set of the map you take decides what the iterator returns.
questions.rule: Choose the right set.

questions.q: Where do the useful methods for manipulating groups of objects live, such as those beyond walking through them?
options: In the iterator that walks the collection
In the MenuItem class that holds one dish
In the Waitress class that prints the menus
In the Collection interface, not the iterator
optionExplain: The iterator offers hasNext(), next() and remove().
MenuItem is an element, not a group.
The Waitress is a client.
Right: the iterator only walks, Collection holds the group methods.
questions.explain: The iterator is for walking; the Collection interface is for working with the group.
questions.rule: Walk with iterators, manage with Collection.
questions.teaches: The iterator is for walking; the Collection interface carries the methods for manipulating the group, so the two have different jobs.

questions.q: A teammate says Hashtable does not support iterators at all, so a Hashtable-based menu needs a hand-written iterator class like the array did. How should you respond?
options: They are right, since Hashtable is not in the framework at all
It supports them indirectly: get the values first, then the iterator
They are right, since Hashtable has no collection of values
It supports them directly, with no extra step needed first
optionExplain: Hashtable can supply one, as the Café showed.
Right: no class needs to be written.
Hashtable does hold values.
The extra step is the indirect route.
questions.explain: No support at all (arrays) is different from support through another collection.
questions.rule: Direct, indirect, or none.
questions.teaches: There are three cases: direct support (ArrayList), indirect support through another collection (HashMap and Hashtable), and no support (arrays).

questions.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?
questions.q: True or false: Once every menu supplies an iterator, adding a new menu needs no change in the Waitress.
questions.explain: The loop is shared, but the Waitress is still told about each menu. The card next shows what the authors make of that.
questions.rule: Check what still needs an edit.

questions.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?
questions.q: The authors say opening the Waitress for each new menu violates the Open ____ Principle.
questions.explain: They name the Open Closed Principle for this repeated opening of the Waitress.
questions.rule: New menu, new edit: a sign.

questions.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?
questions.q: A hotel app has a Concierge class that calls printGuide(iterator) once for each of its eight partner services. A ninth is added. What does the authors' reasoning flag?
options: Nothing, because each guide already has an iterator of its own
The partners must all change their own classes
The Concierge must be opened to add a ninth call
printGuide must be rewritten for the new service
optionExplain: Iterators remove loops, not the list of calls.
The partners are untouched.
Right: the list of services lives in the Concierge.
printGuide is already general.
questions.explain: The same repeated calls that appear in the Waitress appear here.
questions.rule: Look for a repeated call per variation.

questions.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?
questions.q: True or false: The menus are put into one collection and the Waitress loops over it. When a new menu is added to the collection, the Waitress needs no change.
questions.explain: She loops over whatever is in the collection, so the per-menu call is gone.
questions.rule: Group to avoid per-variation edits.

questions.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?
questions.q: What is lost when the menus are put into one collection and the Waitress loops over it?
options: The items that each menu holds in its storage
The iterators that each menu supplies for itself
The Menu interface that all the menus implement
The menu names, unless each menu stores its own
optionExplain: The items are still there.
Each menu still supplies one.
The interface is still used.
Right: the separate calls carried the names with them.
questions.explain: The separate calls to printMenu() each knew which menu they were printing.
questions.rule: Grouping loses labels.
questions.teaches: A flat collection loses the labels that separate calls carried, so the names must be stored in each menu.

questions.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?
questions.q: A team removes repeated calls by putting every partner into a list and declares the design finished. By the card, what check is missing?
options: Whether the grouping handles needs like labels and nesting
Whether the list of partners is sorted in a sensible order for printing
Whether the partners like the new list arrangement, as they use it too
Whether the loop over the partners now runs faster than the old calls did
optionExplain: Right: grouping may fix one problem and cause others.
Sorting is not the concern.
Preferences are not the test.
Speed is not the question.
questions.explain: A fix should be tested against everything it must handle, not only the fault that prompted it.
questions.rule: Test a fix against all the needs.
questions.teaches: Test a grouping fix against needs beyond the repeated calls, such as labels and nesting.

questions.section: Just when we thought it was safe...
questions.q: A school timetable stores each day as an array of Lesson. The school adds modules that contain several lessons. What is the structural difficulty?
options: The array is too short to hold the lessons of a long day
Lessons cannot have names or any other descriptive details
A module is not a Lesson, so it cannot sit in a Lesson array
Modules need a different school to be taught in
optionExplain: Length is not the issue.
Names are not in question.
Right: the array's element type does not fit a module.
The school is not the issue.
questions.explain: The container assumes one kind of element, and the new requirement breaks that. The card next shows the same break in the menus.
questions.rule: Container types limit what fits.

questions.section: Just when we thought it was safe...
questions.q: True or false: The dessert submenu can be added by assigning it to the Diner's MenuItem array.
questions.explain: A menu is not a MenuItem, so it cannot be put in an array of MenuItem.
questions.rule: Types limit containers.

questions.section: Just when we thought it was safe...
questions.q: A file explorer stores a folder's contents as an array of File. A folder cannot go into that array because a folder is not a ____.
questions.explain: The array's element type does not fit a folder, so the structure itself must change, as with the dessert menu and the MenuItem array.
questions.rule: Different elements, different structure.

questions.section: Just when we thought it was safe...
questions.q: True or false: If the team patches only the dessert case, the patch would also cover a later breakfast submenu inside the pancake house menu.
questions.explain: A patch handles one case. The authors conclude the structure itself must be general enough for any submenu.
questions.rule: Patches handle cases; structure handles classes of cases.

questions.section: Just when we thought it was safe...
questions.q: Earlier the chefs would not change their menus. What do the authors now decide?
options: To leave the menus and add special cases to the Waitress
To drop the dessert menu and avoid the whole problem
To tell the chefs their menus will be reimplemented generally
To merge the diner and pancake house back into two shops
optionExplain: Special cases would repeat the older problem.
Dropping desserts avoids the requirement.
Right: an executive decision to rework.
Nothing suggests undoing the merger.
questions.explain: The earlier constraint was accepted while the cost of working around it was small. As complexity grew, it was revisited.
questions.rule: Revisit a constraint when the cost of keeping it outgrows its worth.
questions.teaches: A constraint accepted earlier, such as leaving the chefs' code alone, may be revisited when the cost of working around it grows large enough.

questions.section: Just when we thought it was safe...
questions.q: Which situation most justifies reworking the structure, as the authors did?
options: A single new item with a very long name on one menu of one restaurant
A recurring need for items inside items, across owners
A colour change on one page of a single menu in one of the restaurants
A typo in one label on one of the menus, spotted by a customer
optionExplain: That fits into the existing structure.
Right: the need is structural and recurring.
That is unrelated to structure.
That needs only a correction.
questions.explain: Rework is justified when the requirement is structural and will come again, not for a one-off.
questions.rule: Rework for the pattern, patch for the exception.
questions.teaches: A rework is justified when a requirement is structural and likely to recur, not when it is a one-off that fits the present structure.

questions.q: A new design must hold things nested inside things of the same kind. Which shape is the natural fit?
options: A tree
A flat list
A queue
A table with fixed columns
optionExplain: Right: nesting is what a tree represents.
A flat list cannot show nesting.
A queue orders items without nesting them.
Fixed columns cannot show variable nesting.
questions.explain: Nesting leads to a tree. The card next lists the authors' requirements.
questions.rule: Nested means tree.

questions.q: Which are among the requirements the authors list? Select all that apply.
options: A tree-shaped structure for menus, submenus and items
Traversal at least as convenient as the iterators now in use
The ability to traverse only one submenu or the whole menu including it
All items stored in a single array
Removal of the Menu interface
optionExplain: Right: the first requirement.
Right: the second requirement.
Right: the third requirement.
A single array cannot hold nested menus.
Nothing suggests removing the interface.
questions.explain: The three requirements are structure, convenience and flexible traversal.
questions.rule: Structure, convenience, flexibility.

questions.q: In a file explorer, sort each need by the requirement it expresses.

items.t: Folders that contain other folders
Files inside folders inside folders
A project root with several levels
Search only inside one folder
Search the whole drive including subfolders
List just the photos folder

questions.explain: Nesting calls for a tree. Choosing the starting point and reach of a pass is flexible traversal.
questions.rule: Shape versus reach.

questions.q: If the new design supported only whole-menu traversal, what could it not do?
options: Print the whole menu from the top
Hold menu items inside the structure
Hold the Diner menu as one of its parts
Iterate over only the dessert menu
optionExplain: Whole-menu traversal covers printing.
Holding items is part of the structure.
The Diner menu is part of the whole.
Right: that needs a traversal that can start inside the tree.
questions.explain: The third requirement is about traversing parts.
questions.rule: Parts need their own traversal.

questions.q: To iterate over only the dessert menu, where must a traversal be able to begin?
options: At the root, skipping everything that is not desserts
At the dessert menu, covering everything beneath it
At the first item of the whole Diner menu
At the last item of the whole menu tree
optionExplain: The root would cover too much.
Right: any node can be a starting point.
The first item is unrelated to desserts.
The last item is unrelated too.
questions.explain: Flexible traversal means any node can start a pass over its own subtree.
questions.rule: Any node is a starting point.
questions.teaches: Flexible traversal means any node can start a pass that covers everything beneath it, so every node must be able to supply a traversal.

questions.q: A music app has one flat playlist of songs with no groups. Does the tree requirement apply?
options: Yes; every collection of any kind must be a tree, however flat it looks
Yes; songs are always parts of albums that contain them, so a tree is needed
No; nothing is nested, so a flat collection will do
No; playlists of this kind cannot be iterated, so no traversal requirement applies
optionExplain: Only nesting calls for a tree.
Albums do not appear in this scenario.
Right: the tree answers nesting, which is absent here.
Playlists can be iterated.
questions.explain: The tree requirement came from menus inside menus. Without nesting, the requirement lapses.
questions.rule: Use a tree where there is nesting.
questions.teaches: The tree requirement answers nesting; where nothing nests, a flat collection with an iterator remains enough.

questions.q: A document contains sections, which contain sub-sections, which contain paragraphs. Which description fits best?
options: A flat list holding only the paragraphs
Parts inside wholes, forming a tree
A queue holding the sections in order
Two lists unrelated to each other
optionExplain: A flat list drops the sections.
Right: each level is part of the one above.
A queue shows order, not containment.
The two kinds of node are related by containment.
questions.explain: Parts inside wholes inside wholes is a hierarchy. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Containment is a tree.

questions.q: The Composite Pattern composes objects into ____ structures to represent part-whole hierarchies.
questions.explain: A tree is the shape of nested parts and wholes.
questions.rule: Parts and wholes form a tree.

questions.q: A travel app has trips made of legs, and legs made of stops. Which design applies the pattern?
