options: Three unrelated lists, one for each level of the trip
One array of strings describing every level of the trip in text
A separate app built for each level of the trip, with its own data
Trip, leg and stop nodes in one tree, same operations
optionExplain: Separate lists hide the containment.
Strings lose the structure.
Separate apps lose the whole.
Right: a tree with a uniform interface.
questions.explain: The levels nest, so they form a tree, and the same operations apply to each node.
questions.rule: Nest and treat alike.

questions.q: True or false: With the pattern in place, a client gets the travel time of a whole trip with the same call it uses on a single leg.
questions.explain: Nodes are treated uniformly, so one call serves any node.
questions.rule: One call, any node.

questions.q: A teammate says Composite is Iterator grown up. What do the authors say?
options: Composite replaces Iterator completely in the final design and the iterators are removed
Iterator is only a special case of the Composite Pattern, as they are related
No transformation links them; Composite is new and works well with Iterator
They cannot be used together in one design at all, as they solve the same problem
optionExplain: Iterator remains part of the solution.
No such relation is claimed.
Right: they are separate patterns that cooperate.
The authors show them working together.
questions.explain: The authors say not to look for a magical transformation, and that the two work very nicely together.
questions.rule: Different patterns, good partners.
questions.teaches: Composite is not a transformation of Iterator but a new approach; the two work very nicely together, with iterators used in a couple of ways inside the composite implementation.

questions.q: A flat playlist of songs has no folders. Should it use Composite?
options: Yes; every collection of objects should be a composite, whether or not it nests
Yes; each song is a whole made of many notes, which form a tree
No; playlists of songs cannot be traversed at all, so no pattern is needed
No need; nothing nests, so a plain collection fits
optionExplain: Only nested data calls for it.
The model does not include notes.
Playlists can be traversed.
Right: there are no parts and wholes here.
questions.explain: Use Composite where parts and wholes exist.
questions.rule: Match the pattern to the data.
questions.teaches: Use Composite only where the data has whole-part nesting; for flat groups, an Iterator over a plain collection suffices.

questions.q: A client holds a node that may be a single item or a whole group, and wants to print it. Which makes the client's code simplest?
options: Both kinds respond to the same print call
The client checks the kind, then picks the code
Only groups can be printed
The client prints items only
optionExplain: Right: no check is needed.
Checking the kind adds branches to the client.
Leaving items out is not what is wanted.
Groups would be left out.
questions.explain: A call that works on both removes the client's need to know. The card next explains this uniformity.
questions.rule: Same call, either kind.

questions.q: Match each phrase with its meaning in the menu tree.
pairs: A composition: it can contain menus and items
An individual object: it holds no other objects
questions.explain: Either kind responds to the operation; where it starts decides its reach.
questions.rule: Start point decides reach.

questions.q: In a drawing program, shapes are single (a circle) or groups (a face made of shapes). Following the card, how should move() be offered?
options: On groups only; clients move each shape of a group themselves
On single shapes only, never on groups of them, so groups are moved by hand
On both shapes and groups under one name
With a different name for groups than for single shapes, so each is clear
optionExplain: That pushes the work back to the client.
Groups could then not be moved.
Right: uniform treatment.
A different name means the client must know which it holds.
questions.explain: A shared operation lets the client move any shape without asking its kind.
questions.rule: Same name on both.

questions.q: A group contains three shapes and a smaller group of two shapes. The client calls draw() on the outer group. How many shapes are drawn?
options: Three
Five
Two
One
optionExplain: That leaves out the inner group's shapes.
Right: three shapes plus the two in the inner group.
That counts the inner group only.
That counts one call, not the shapes.
questions.explain: The operation spreads through every level of the group.
questions.rule: A call on the whole reaches every part.

questions.q: How does the client's code for printing a single dish differ from its code for printing a three-level menu tree?
options: It does not differ; it is the same call
It needs one extra loop for each level of the tree
It needs a type check at every level of the tree
It must be written twice, once for each kind of node
optionExplain: Right: the call is the same at any depth.
The loops are inside the nodes.
The pattern removes type checks.
One call covers both a single dish and a menu tree, so it need not be written twice.
questions.explain: The depth of the tree is the business of the nodes, not the client.
questions.rule: The client does not see depth.
questions.teaches: The client's code does not grow with the depth of the tree: the same call serves one dish and a deep tree of menus.

questions.q: In a gift-basket tree, sort each operation by whether it makes sense on both single gifts and baskets, or on baskets only.

items.t: Show the name
Report the weight
Print the contents
Add a gift inside
Get the third gift inside
Remove a gift inside

questions.explain: Uniform treatment covers operations both kinds can do. Managing children makes sense only for containers.
questions.rule: Child management belongs to composites.
questions.teaches: Operations that both kinds can do suit uniform treatment; child-management operations make sense only on composites.

questions.q: In a tree of folders and files, which are the leaves?
options: The root folder
Every folder
The folder with the most files
Files, which hold nothing else
optionExplain: The root is at the top.
Folders hold other items, so they are not leaves.
How many files a folder holds does not decide leaf status; holding nothing else does.
Right: leaves are the nodes at the ends.
questions.explain: Leaves are the ends of the branches. The card next names all three roles.
questions.rule: Leaves hold nothing.

questions.q: Match each role with its description.
questions.explain: Component is the general role, composite and leaf the two flavours.
questions.rule: Two flavours of component.

questions.q: In a company tree, sort each element by its role.

items.t: Division (holds departments)
Department (holds teams)
Team (holds employee records)
Employee record (holds nothing)
Contractor record (holds nothing)
Intern record (holds nothing)

questions.explain: What counts is whether the node can hold children.
questions.rule: Holds children or not.

questions.q: A new kind of node is added that holds a list of nodes of any kind. Is it a leaf or a composite?
options: A leaf, because it is a newly added kind
A composite, because it holds children
A leaf, because lists are simple structures
Neither, because it is a completely new kind
optionExplain: Newness does not decide the role.
Right: holding children makes a composite.
Simplicity does not decide the role.
Every node is one or the other.
questions.explain: The role follows from what the node holds.
questions.rule: Role follows from holding children.

questions.q: What type should a composite's list of children have so it can hold both menus and items?
options: Leaf
Composite
Component, the common type
Iterator
optionExplain: A list of leaves could not hold menus.
A list of composites could not hold items.
Right: both kinds are components.
An iterator walks; it does not hold.
questions.explain: A variable of the common type can hold either flavour.
questions.rule: Children are held as components.
questions.teaches: A reference of the common component type can hold either a composite or a leaf, which is what lets a composite's child list hold both.

questions.q: A web page is a tree of elements. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.
options: A div containing other divs is a composite
A paragraph of plain text with no children is a leaf
Every element is either a composite or a leaf
A leaf may contain composites
A composite must have at least one child to count as one
optionExplain: Right: it holds children.
Right: it holds nothing.
Right: those are the two flavours.
A leaf holds nothing, by definition.
Holding children is what matters, not currently having any.
questions.explain: The roles come from the capacity to hold children.
questions.rule: Capacity decides the role.
questions.teaches: A composite is defined by its capacity to hold children, not by currently holding any: an empty menu is still a composite.

questions.q: A base class has methods that some subclasses cannot sensibly support. What is a reasonable default for those methods?
options: Return a random value so that callers get something
Throw an exception saying the operation is unsupported
Delete the node that was asked to do it
Call the same method on a sibling node instead
optionExplain: A random value would hide the problem.
Right: it states plainly that the operation does not apply.
Deleting is destructive and unrelated.
A sibling's answer would be meaningless.
questions.explain: A default must say clearly that an operation does not apply. The card next shows the authors' default.
questions.rule: Say plainly that it is unsupported.

questions.q: The default implementation of an unsupported operation in MenuComponent is to throw ____.
questions.explain: Subclasses override what suits them and inherit the exception for the rest.
questions.rule: Default: unsupported.

questions.q: A shape tree has a Component class with add(child). A Circle is a leaf and does not override it. What does add() do on a Circle?
options: Adds a hidden child that nobody can see
Does nothing but reports that it succeeded
Fails to compile because Circle lacks the method
Throws an unsupported-operation exception
optionExplain: A leaf holds no children, so add() cannot hide one inside it.
Reporting success would be misleading.
The method exists on the common type, so it compiles.
Right: the inherited default applies.
questions.explain: The inherited default tells the caller the operation is unsupported at run time.
questions.rule: Inherit the default.

questions.q: A Menu class overrides add() but not getPrice(). A client calls getPrice() on a Menu. What happens?
options: The inherited default throws an exception
It returns zero as a neutral price
It sums the prices of all the items beneath it
The code does not compile for Menu at all
optionExplain: Right: Menu does not implement getPrice().
Nothing in the design returns a neutral zero; the inherited default throws an exception.
That would need an implementation.
The method exists on the common type.
questions.explain: The authors say Menu does not implement getPrice() or isVegetarian().
questions.rule: Unimplemented means default.

questions.q: What is a cost of putting both leaf operations and composite operations into one component class?
options: Leaves can no longer be created from this class, because it is abstract
Composites lose their children when it is used as the shared base
The class plays two roles, so some methods suit only some nodes
Iterators stop working on the tree altogether once methods are added
optionExplain: Leaves can still be created from the class, so that is not a cost.
Composites keep their children when the class is the shared base, so nothing is lost.
Right: the authors ask whether MenuComponent plays two roles.
Iterators are unaffected.
questions.explain: The authors note the class may play two roles, and deal with it by defaults.
questions.rule: One class, two roles.
questions.teaches: A single component class plays two roles, leaf and composite, so some of its methods make no sense for a given node, which is why defaults are needed.

questions.q: A file-system component has listChildren(), and a plain file does not support it. Which options do the authors name for methods that make no sense on a node? Select all that apply.
options: Do nothing
Return null or false
Throw an exception
Delete the node
Turn the leaf into a composite quietly
optionExplain: Right: sometimes you can do nothing.
Right: whatever makes sense in your application.
Right: being more proactive.
Nothing like that is suggested.
Nothing like that is suggested either.
questions.explain: The right choice depends on the application and the clients' willingness to check.
questions.rule: Choose by the application.
questions.teaches: There is a range of ways to handle a method that makes no sense on a node (do nothing, return null or false, or throw an exception), and the choice depends on the application.

questions.q: In a tree of folders and files, which class should implement an operation to add a child?
options: The file, which sits at the end of a branch
Both, in exactly the same way as each other
Neither, since trees cannot grow after being built
The folder, which can hold children
optionExplain: A file holds no children, so an add-child operation has no meaning on it.
Files would have no children to add to.
Trees can grow by adding to composites.
Right: only containers have children.
questions.explain: Only the class that holds children can add to them. The card next applies this to the menus.
questions.rule: Only containers manage children.

questions.q: Match each item with its role in the menu classes.
pairs: The composite class that holds MenuItems or other Menus
Not implemented; falls back to the default
Left to the inherited default as well
questions.explain: The leaf and composite each take the operations that fit them.
questions.rule: Each class takes what fits.

questions.q: A bundle tree has Product (leaf) and Bundle (composite). Product has getBarcode() and Bundle has addProduct(). Which assignment follows the card?
options: Product has getBarcode(), Bundle has addProduct(), others inherited
Both implement both methods in exactly the same way, to stay uniform
Bundle implements getBarcode() and Product implements addProduct(), swapped round
Neither implements anything and both inherit every default from the component
optionExplain: Right: each takes what fits and inherits the rest.
A product cannot add products and a bundle has no single barcode.
This swaps the classes.
Then nothing would work.
questions.explain: A barcode belongs to a product and adding belongs to a bundle.
questions.rule: Fit the operation to the class.

questions.q: A client calls getChild(0) on a MenuItem. Given the defaults, what happens?
options: It returns the item itself as its only child, for convenience
It returns null to say that there is no child at that position
The inherited default throws UnsupportedOperationException
It returns the first item of the parent menu instead
optionExplain: The item is not its own child.
Null is not what the default does.
Right: the leaf does not override it.
The parent is not involved.
questions.explain: The leaf inherits the throwing default.
questions.rule: Not overridden means default.

questions.q: Why does Menu leave getPrice() unimplemented?
options: Menus are free of charge, so there is no price to give for them
A Menu has no price of its own, so the operation fits poorly
getPrice() would be too slow to run for large menus with many items
Menus inherit the price of their first item, so a second price is pointless
optionExplain: The authors do not say menus are free; the reason is that a Menu has no price of its own.
Right: the authors say it does not make a lot of sense for a Menu.
Speed is not the reason.
No such inheritance exists.
questions.explain: Leaving an operation unimplemented is how the design says it does not apply to that kind of node.
questions.rule: Unimplemented means not applicable.
questions.teaches: Leaving an operation unimplemented in a class is how the design says that the operation does not apply to that kind of node.

questions.q: In a playlist tree with Song (leaf) and Playlist (composite), sort each operation by the class that implements it.

items.t: Report the track length
Report the artist
Add an entry
Remove an entry
Get the third entry

questions.explain: Data about one track belongs to the leaf. Managing entries belongs to the composite.
questions.rule: Data to leaves, children to composites.
questions.teaches: Child-management operations belong to composites only, while data about a single element belongs to leaves.

questions.q: A folder tree holds folders and files. A client calls listAll() on the root. How does listAll() reach the files deep inside?
options: Each folder asks its children to list themselves
The client loops over every level of the tree itself
The root copies every file into one array first
Each file asks its parent folder to list it
optionExplain: Right: the request passes down from each node to its children.
That makes the client walk the tree.
Copying everything is not how the call reaches the files.
Files do not initiate the listing.
questions.explain: Each node can do its own part and hand the rest down. The card next shows the authors' print().
questions.rule: Pass the request down.

questions.q: When a Menu meets another Menu while printing, that Menu's print() starts another ____.
questions.explain: The inner menu iterates over its own children in turn.
questions.rule: Each composite iterates over its own children.

questions.q: A root menu holds item A and then submenu S. S holds item B. Put the events of the root's print() in order.
items: The root starts iterating over its children
Item A prints itself
The root reaches S, whose print() starts its own iteration
Item B prints itself
questions.explain: Children are visited in order, and a submenu starts its own pass inside the root's.
questions.rule: Each composite runs its own pass.

questions.q: A sub-submenu is added inside S. Does Menu's print() code need to change?
options: Yes; it needs a loop for each level
Yes; the client must print the new level
Yes; MenuItem must change
No; the recursion covers any depth
optionExplain: No new loops are needed.
The client is not involved.
Leaves are unaffected.
Right: each Menu handles its own children.
questions.explain: The same code runs at every level.
questions.rule: Recursion handles depth.

questions.q: What role does an iterator play inside print()?
options: It prints the Menu's name at the top of the output and then stops
It steps through the children, calling print() on each
It holds the Waitress's position in the menu tree between her calls
It replaces the Menu as the composite in the tree during the print
optionExplain: The iterator does not print names.
Right: the authors say print() uses iteration internally.
The Waitress is not involved here.
The Menu is still the composite.
questions.explain: The composite uses an iterator internally to visit its children. Iterator and Composite cooperate.
questions.rule: Iterators work inside composites.
questions.teaches: A composite uses an iterator internally to step through its children; this is one of the ways the two patterns work together.

questions.q: A teammate writes printAll for a task tree: the root loops over its direct children and prints each. What goes wrong?
options: The root is printed twice, once at the start and once more at the end
Leaf tasks cannot be printed by a loop of this kind, as they have no children
Deeper sub-tasks go unprinted, as children do not print their own children
The loop never ends once it meets a nested task, as it keeps repeating
optionExplain: Nothing prints the root twice.
Leaves can print themselves.
Right: only one level is covered.
The loop ends after the direct children.
questions.explain: Recursion comes from each composite continuing the operation on its own children.
questions.rule: Each level must carry the request on.
questions.teaches: A loop over only the direct children covers one level; recursion arises when each composite child continues the operation on its own children.

questions.section: Getting ready for a test drive...
questions.q: A tree interface lets clients call any operation on any node without checking its kind. What is the main risk?
options: Clients must check types before every single call
A client may call an operation that does not fit that node
The tree can no longer hold leaves among its nodes
Operations run twice on every node they are called on
optionExplain: That is the cost of the opposite design.
Right: the interface allows calls that do not fit.
Leaves remain in the tree.
Calls are not repeated.
questions.explain: Freedom to call anything comes with the risk of calling something meaningless. The card next names the tradeoff.
questions.rule: Freedom costs safety.

questions.section: Getting ready for a test drive...
questions.q: Match each term with its meaning in the card.
pairs: The client cannot tell composite from leaf
Safer, but needs type checks and instanceof
questions.explain: The two designs sit at opposite ends of the same tradeoff.
questions.rule: Two ends of one tradeoff.

questions.section: Getting ready for a test drive...
questions.q: A CAD program has Part (leaf) and Assembly (composite). Designer A puts addPart() on the shared Component. Designer B puts it only on Assembly. Which statement is accurate?
options: A is safer for its clients, while B is more transparent to them in use
Both are equally safe and equally transparent to clients of the tree
Both give up transparency in exchange for safety in the interface
A gains transparency but loses safety; B gains safety but loses transparency
optionExplain: This swaps the two: placing the method on the shared Component gives transparency, while placing it only on Assembly gives safety.
Only B stops a call on a Part.
Only B gives up transparency.
Right: each gains what the other loses.
questions.explain: Placing addPart() on Component lets anyone call it on a Part; placing it only on Assembly means clients must know which they hold.
questions.rule: Gain one, lose the other.

questions.section: Getting ready for a test drive...
questions.q: True or false: Under a design where addPart() lives only on Assembly, a client holding a Component reference must check that the node is an Assembly, for example with instanceof, before adding a part.
questions.explain: The method is not on every node, so safety is bought with type checks in the client.
questions.rule: Safety costs conditionals.

questions.section: Getting ready for a test drive...
questions.q: A designer says getChild() should not exist on a leaf. Which perspective do the authors offer?
options: Leaves should be turned into composites whenever asked
Leaves should be removed from the tree entirely
See a leaf as a node with zero children, so the call fits
The call should crash on purpose to warn the client
optionExplain: Nothing suggests converting leaves.
Leaves are needed, because they are the nodes that actually hold the items.
Right: from that view, asking a leaf for children is meaningful.
A crash is not offered as a view.
questions.explain: A change of perspective can make an apparently inappropriate call reasonable.
questions.rule: Change perspective before changing design.
questions.teaches: A leaf can be seen as a node with zero children, so a child-related call on a leaf may be made meaningful by default rather than treated as an error.

questions.section: Getting ready for a test drive...
questions.q: Which sentence best states the authors' stance on the transparency and safety choice?
options: Transparency is the only choice the authors accept as valid for a composite
Safety is the only choice the authors accept as valid for a composite
Composite should be avoided because of this tradeoff between the two
Both are legitimate; it is a tradeoff chosen by watching effects
optionExplain: The authors describe the safe variant as still Composite.
They do not rule out transparency.
They present Composite as useful.
Right: principles guide, but the effects decide.
questions.explain: The authors say we are guided by principles but must observe their effects, and sometimes purposely do things that seem to break one.
questions.rule: Principles guide; effects decide.
questions.teaches: Principles guide design but their effects must be observed, and a principle may sometimes be set aside on purpose when the tradeoff favours it.

questions.q: A tree walker must pause after each node and resume when the client asks for the next. What must it keep between calls?
options: Its place in the tree and how to climb back up
A copy of the whole tree to walk through
Only the last node it returned to the client
The total number of nodes in the whole tree
optionExplain: Right: it must be able to carry on from where it stopped.
A copy is not needed to resume.
The last node alone cannot say where to go next.
A count does not give a position.
questions.explain: A walker that pauses must remember where it is. The card next shows how the book's iterator does it.
questions.rule: A paused walker needs a bookmark.

questions.q: True or false: Printing with print() uses iteration inside the component, while CompositeIterator is an external iterator.
questions.explain: print() steps through children itself; CompositeIterator is driven by a client calling hasNext() and next().
questions.rule: Internal for print(), external for CompositeIterator.

questions.q: A client wants every vegetarian item in a menu tree, wherever it sits. What does the book suggest?
options: Call isVegetarian() on the root menu once and use the answer for all items
Loop only over the direct children of the root menu and ignore submenus
Iterate over the whole composite with an iterator that covers child menus
Ask each chef to list the vegetarian items by hand and combine the lists
optionExplain: The root is a Menu and does not answer.
That misses nested menus.
Right: the iterator reaches every level.
That drops the structure.
questions.explain: An iterator over the whole composite lets the Waitress test every item.
questions.rule: Walk the whole tree.

questions.q: When the CompositeIterator finishes a submenu's items, it returns to the ____ level and continues from where it left off.
questions.explain: Its stored position tells it where to go; the stacks record the path back.
questions.rule: Stacks remember the way back.

questions.q: Why can print() recurse freely while CompositeIterator cannot rely on recursive calls to remember its place?
options: The client takes control between calls, so the iterator stores its position
Recursion is not allowed inside any kind of iterator, for safety reasons
Iterators have no access to the children of a node, only to the node itself
print() is faster than an iterator at the same job, so it can recurse
optionExplain: Right: the call stack is gone between calls.
The code can use recursion in other ways.
It can reach children.
Speed is not the reason.
questions.explain: In print() the language's call stack remembers where we are. An external iterator hands control back to the client after each item.
questions.rule: Control returns, so memory must stay.
questions.teaches: In a recursive print() the program's call stack remembers the place; an external iterator returns control to the client after each item, so it must store the place itself.

questions.q: A file-search tool walks folders, and the screen has a Next button that shows one file per press. Which implementation fits?
options: A recursive function that does the whole walk before it returns anything
A list of every file printed on screen all at once when the tool starts
Searching again from the start for each button press and skipping seen files
An external iterator that keeps its place, called on each press
optionExplain: A complete walk cannot pause for each press.
That ignores the one-at-a-time need.
That wastes the work and loses place.
Right: it can pause between files.
questions.explain: A step-by-step interface needs a walker that can pause and resume.
questions.rule: Pausing needs an external iterator.
questions.teaches: A step-by-step user interface needs an external iterator that can pause and resume; a one-shot recursive walk cannot stop after each item.

questions.q: A method must return a list of results but sometimes has none. Which return value spares callers from checking?
options: null
An empty list
An error message string
The method's own name
optionExplain: Callers would need to check for null.
Right: callers can loop over it as usual.
A string is the wrong type.
A name is the wrong type.
questions.explain: An empty answer of the right type needs no checks. The card next shows the authors' version for iterators.
questions.rule: Return an empty object, not null.

questions.q: The NullIterator's hasNext() returns the same value on every call: ____.
questions.explain: It always reports that no items remain, so any loop ends at once.
questions.rule: Always false.

questions.q: In a folder tree, Document is a leaf with a createIterator() method. Using the book's better choice, what should Document return?
options: null
An iterator over the document's parent folder
An iterator whose hasNext() always returns false
An iterator that throws an exception on every call
optionExplain: Null forces checks onto the client.
That would visit unrelated nodes.
Right: the client's loop simply finds nothing.
That would force a try/catch around every loop.
questions.explain: A harmless empty iterator keeps the client free of special cases.
questions.rule: Empty iterator, no checks.

questions.q: True or false: A leaf returns the NullIterator. The Waitress's loop finds nothing to step through for it and moves on without special code.
questions.explain: hasNext() is false at once, so the loop ends for that node.
questions.rule: No items, no problem.

questions.q: NullIterator is an example of which wider idea, per the authors?
options: The Strategy pattern
The Observer pattern
The Factory pattern
The Null Object pattern
optionExplain: Strategy swaps behaviours.
Observer notifies on changes.
Factory creates objects.
Right: the authors name it so.
questions.explain: A Null Object is a stand-in with neutral, do-nothing behaviour, which lets clients avoid testing for null.
questions.rule: Stand in a harmless object for nothing.
questions.teaches: A Null Object is a stand-in object with harmless do-nothing behaviour, used so that clients need not test for null.

questions.q: A logging component returns a NullLogger that discards messages when logging is off. A developer worries that a missing log could hide a problem. How should this be judged?
options: A fair concern: use them where nothing is a legitimate result
No concern: do-nothing objects can never hide a missing signal
No concern, since returning null would be the safer way
The idea should be dropped for every use in all designs
optionExplain: Right: it fits cases where nothing is normal.
A quiet empty result can hide a missing signal.
Null forces checks and is no safer.
It is useful where nothing is a normal answer.
questions.explain: A do-nothing object removes a signal. Use it where nothing is a legitimate result, as with a leaf.
questions.rule: Use it where nothing is normal.
questions.teaches: A do-nothing object also removes the signal that something is missing, so reserve it for cases where nothing is a legitimate result.

questions.q: A tree operation does not apply to some nodes. A client wants to call it on all nodes without checking kinds, and wants the answer to say plainly that it is unsupported. Which approach does that?
options: The node returns false whenever it is asked
The client checks the type of the node first
The node throws an unsupported-operation exception
The node removes itself from the tree when asked
optionExplain: False looks like a real answer.
Checking the type is the client's burden.
Right: it says unsupported and needs no check.
Removing itself changes the tree.
questions.explain: An answer that says unsupported differs from a value like false. The card next gives the authors' reasoning.
questions.rule: Unsupported is not the same as false.

questions.q: Match each approach with what the authors say about it.
pairs: Says clearly the operation is unsupported
Meant for error handling, not program logic
questions.explain: Each choice has its own price and benefit.
questions.rule: Each choice has a price.

questions.q: In a shipping tree of Boxes (composite) and Parcels (leaf), isFragile() is meaningful for parcels. A manager says boxes should return false. Under the authors' reasoning, what is lost?
options: Transparency, since boxes would be treated differently from parcels by clients
The ability to call it on parcels as well as on boxes in the same way
Nothing, since returning false means the same thing as being unsupported
The difference between not fragile and not applicable
optionExplain: Returning false keeps transparency.
Parcels are unaffected.
False and unsupported say different things.
Right: false looks like a real answer.
questions.explain: A false answer cannot be told from a real false. The exception keeps the difference visible.
questions.rule: False hides the unsupported case.

questions.q: True or false: If isVegetarian() is later implemented for Menu, the existing Waitress code keeps working with it.
questions.explain: The authors list this as a benefit of the exception design: someone can implement a sensible method and have it work with existing code.
questions.rule: Unsupported leaves room to grow.

questions.q: In the Waitress's code, what does the caught exception signal?
options: A bug in the Menu class that must be fixed
A failure of the iterator while it walked the tree
An expected case: the node does not support the operation
A corrupted tree that can no longer be walked
optionExplain: The Menu behaves as designed.
The iterator worked fine and walked the whole tree.
Right: it is routine here.
The tree is intact, and the exception only marks an unsupported operation.
questions.explain: Here the exception stands for a normal answer, not a fault.
questions.rule: Say why the exception is routine.
questions.teaches: In this design the caught exception is an expected answer, not a fault, so the code should say so, since readers expect try/catch to signal errors.

questions.q: A critic says exceptions should not be used for program flow at all. Which reply uses the authors' reasoning?
options: Exceptions are fine for program flow in every case, with no real cost to clarity
Concede the general point, then compare the costs of the alternatives
Exceptions are only meant for syntax errors in code, and for nothing else
The authors ignore the matter and do not discuss it anywhere in the chapter
optionExplain: The authors concede it is not the intended use.
Right: it accepts the rule and shows the cost of the alternatives.
This is not what they say.
They address it directly.
questions.explain: A fair defence concedes what is true and names the tradeoff.
questions.rule: Concede, then compare costs.
questions.teaches: A fair defence of a design concedes the general rule it bends and names the costs of the alternatives.

questions.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...
questions.q: In a tree, you hold a reference to a node and want to delete it. What helps most?
options: A link from each node to its parent
A copy of the whole tree kept beside the original
A second tree built from the same nodes
A counter of the nodes in the tree
optionExplain: Right: the parent can remove the child.
A copy does not help delete.
A second tree doubles the work.
A count does not locate the parent.
questions.explain: Removing a node means changing its parent. The card next lists this and other issues.
questions.rule: Deleting needs the parent.

questions.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...
questions.q: Which issues does the interview raise? Select all that apply.
options: Parent pointers
Ordering of children
Caching of results
Replacing the tree with a table
Allowing only the safe interface
optionExplain: Right: they ease traversal and removal.
Right: order needs a careful scheme.
Right: it saves repeated traversals.
No such proposal appears.
The interview treats it as one variation, not a rule.
questions.explain: The interview names parent links, ordering and caching.
questions.rule: Parents, order, cache.

questions.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...
questions.q: In a slide-deck tree (deck, sections, slides), a word count for a section is slow because the section is re-traversed on every keystroke. Which point applies?
options: Add a parent pointer to every slide
Sort the slides alphabetically
Switch to the safe interface
Cache the total at the section node
optionExplain: Parent links do not avoid the traversal.
Sorting does not save traversals.
The interface choice is unrelated.
Right: the result is expensive to compute repeatedly.
questions.explain: A result computed by constantly traversing the structure is a candidate for caching.
questions.rule: Cache costly repeated results.

questions.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...
questions.q: Slides must stay in a specific order. What follows for adding and removing slides?
options: Nothing; any composite keeps the order of its children itself
A more careful scheme for managing and walking the children
Order is lost whenever any child is removed from it
Slides become leaves instead of staying as they are
optionExplain: Order needs explicit handling.
Right: the interview says so.
A careful scheme can keep order.
Slides stay as they are.
questions.explain: Order adds work to child management and traversal.
questions.rule: Order adds care.

questions.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...
questions.q: Is a version of Composite with separate interfaces for leaves and composites still the Composite Pattern?
options: No, it is a different pattern with another name
No, since composites need exactly one shared interface
Yes, a safer version, though clients check types and cast
Yes, and it needs no type checks or casts at all
optionExplain: The interview calls it a safer Composite.
A single interface is the transparent variant, not the only one.
Right: the interview says so.
The checks are the price of safety.
questions.explain: The safer variation requires the client to check the type of every object before a call so the object can be cast correctly.
questions.rule: The safe variant is still Composite.
questions.teaches: A version of Composite with separate interfaces for leaves and composites is still the Composite Pattern, a safer one, but the client has to check types and cast.

questions.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...
questions.q: True or false: A rarely used tree of a few dozen nodes should still cache every computed result in each composite.
questions.explain: Caching pays when the structure is complex or expensive to traverse and is traversed repeatedly for the same result. A small, rarely used tree gains little.
questions.rule: Cache where traversal is costly and repeated.
questions.teaches: Caching suits a structure that is expensive to traverse and traversed repeatedly for the same result; elsewhere it adds work for little gain.

questions.q: A pattern is described as: clients treat collections of objects and individual objects uniformly. Which pattern is it?
options: Facade
Composite
Adapter
Observer
optionExplain: Facade simplifies an interface.
Right: it matches the description.
Adapter changes an interface.
Observer notifies of state changes.
questions.explain: Each pattern has a purpose that sets it apart. The card next lists the ones from this chapter.
questions.rule: Know patterns by purpose.

questions.q: Match each pattern with its purpose.
pairs: Clients treat collections of objects and individual objects uniformly
Traverse a collection without exposing its implementation
Simplifies the interface of a group of classes
Changes the interface of one or more classes
Notifies a group of objects when some state changes
questions.explain: The purposes are distinct, which is how patterns are told apart.
questions.rule: One purpose each.

questions.q: A team must print every entry of a catalogue that one team keeps in arrays and another in lists, without learning their storage. Which pattern?
options: Composite
Facade
Observer
Iterator
optionExplain: Composite is for part-whole trees, and nothing nests here.
Facade does not give uniform traversal.
Observer is about notification.
Right: traversal without exposure.
questions.explain: The need is traversal of differently stored collections.
questions.rule: Traversal calls for Iterator.

questions.q: A tool needs folders that contain folders and files, with size() working on either. Which pattern shapes the structure?
options: Composite, for the nesting and the uniform size()
Iterator, because the folders hold files and other folders
Adapter, because folders have a different interface from files
Facade, because the tool is large and has many parts
optionExplain: Right: nested parts and wholes with uniform operations.
Iterator helps walk the structure but does not build it.
Folders and files share one interface in a composite.
Size of the tool is not the reason.
questions.explain: Composite is about structure and uniform operations, while Iterator is about walking.
questions.rule: Structure versus walking.

questions.q: How do the two patterns relate to each other in the chapter?
options: Iterator replaced Composite in the final design, so one of them was dropped
Composite replaced Iterator in the final design, so one of them was dropped
They cooperate: Composite builds the structure, Iterator walks it
They cannot be combined in one design, since they solve different problems
optionExplain: Iterator stays in the final design.
Composite does not remove iterators.
Right: the chapter uses both together.
The chapter combines them.
questions.explain: The vegetarian menu uses a composite and an iterator over it together.
questions.rule: Structure plus walking.
questions.teaches: The two patterns are partners rather than rivals: Composite builds the structure and Iterator provides ways to walk it.

questions.q: Sort each need by the pattern that addresses it.

items.t: Hiding whether items are in a list or an array
Stepping through items one at a time
Keeping traversal out of the aggregate class
Treating a group of shapes like one shape
Menus inside menus
One call applying to a whole tree

questions.explain: Iterator concerns access to a sequence. Composite concerns structure and uniform operations.
questions.rule: Access versus structure.
questions.teaches: Iterator is about access to a sequence of elements; Composite is about the structure of parts and wholes and about operations that apply uniformly.

questions.q: A client totals the items of both menus with this code. What happens when it is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints 3, because both menus are collections of items
It does not compile, because an ArrayList has no length field
It does not compile, because an array has no length field to read
It compiles but fails when run, because the two types differ
optionExplain: Tempting because both hold items, but the code never gets as far as running.
Right: an ArrayList is asked with size(), while the array has a length field.
Arrays do have a length field; it is the ArrayList that lacks one.
The mismatch is caught earlier, when the code is compiled.
questions.explain: The array is read with its length field and the ArrayList with size(). Each container has its own way of being read, so code written for one does not fit the other.
questions.rule: Each container is read in its own way.
questions.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge

questions.q: Both loops run to the end, so this code prints the number ____.
questions.explain: Two items are counted by the loop written for the ArrayList and three by the loop written for the array. Both loops are needed, and a third storage type would bring a third.
questions.rule: One loop per storage type.

questions.q: Match each symptom in a client with the design fault it shows.
pairs: It names PancakeHouseMenu and DinerMenu in its code
Coding to concrete classes, not an interface
It knows one menu keeps an array and the other an ArrayList
It repeats a near-identical loop for each menu
questions.explain: The three faults the authors list are concrete references, exposed representation and duplicate code. Each symptom points at one of them.
questions.rule: Name the fault from the symptom.
questions.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?

questions.q: Both menus are meant to share this Menu interface. What does the compiler say about DinerMenu?
options: Nothing; the method names match, so DinerMenu is a valid Menu
It is only a warning, because the array can be turned into a list
Error: the return type is not compatible with the one in Menu
Error: an interface may not declare a method with a return type
optionExplain: Matching names are not enough; the signature must fit as well.
Java does not convert an array into an ArrayList by itself.
Right: the menus differ in the return type of getMenuItems(), and that blocks a shared interface.
Interfaces may declare return types; this is not the problem.
questions.explain: The authors note that the menus are close to sharing an interface, except for the return type of getMenuItems(). That one difference stops a shared interface in the current form.
questions.rule: A shared interface needs matching signatures.

questions.q: What does this code print?
options: tea true
jam true
pie false
jam false
optionExplain: That would be the second item with more to come; two calls were made before the print, not one.
The third item is right, but the walker has already reached the end.
The walker does not start over; it keeps its place between calls.
Right: after two calls, the third call returns jam and leaves nothing more.
questions.explain: The walker remembers its position. Two calls move it past pie and tea, the third returns jam, and then hasNext() reports false.
questions.rule: An iterator holds its own position.

questions.q: What does this loop print?
options: tea;pie;jam;
pie;jam;
jam;
tea;
optionExplain: The first item was already taken by the call before the loop.
Right: next() consumed tea, so the loop starts from the second item.
The loop would print only jam if two items had been consumed.
The loop does not stop after the item already taken.
questions.explain: Each call to next() moves the iterator on. The call before the loop used up tea, so the loop prints the rest.
questions.rule: next() moves the iterator on.

questions.q: A Diner iterator hands out every second day. What does this loop print?
options: mon;tue;wed;thu;fri;
tue;thu;
mon;wed;
mon;wed;fri;
optionExplain: That is what a one-step iterator would print; this one moves two steps.
The first call returns mon before the position moves, so tue is skipped, not shown.
The position reaches the last day too, because index 4 is still inside the array.
Right: the positions are 0, 2 and 4, and the loop ends when the position passes the end.
questions.explain: The client loop is the usual one, yet the output differs because this concrete iterator moves two places at a time. Changing which items come out needs no change to the client.
questions.rule: The iterator decides what comes out.

questions.q: Each shelf builds its own iterator. What does this loop print?
optionExplain: The shelves are visited in list order: the two-item shelf first.
The loop restarts for each shelf and prints a count for each, not a total.
The second shelf holds three items, not two.
Right: the loop body is the same, and each shelf supplies the iterator that fits it.
questions.explain: The client code is identical for both shelves; only the iterator each one creates differs. That is why the client never needs to name a concrete iterator class.
questions.rule: The loop is shared; the iterator is the shelf's own.
questions.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator

questions.q: One loop body serves two kinds of collection. What does this code print?
options: a;b;x;y;
b;a;
x;y;b;a;
b;a;x;y;
optionExplain: Nothing in the loop sorts the items; they come out as the collection holds them.
The second call also runs, so its items are printed too.
The calls run in the order written, so the list comes first.
Right: one loop prints the first collection, then the second, each in its own order.
questions.explain: The loop only sees an Iterator, so it prints whatever each collection hands out, in the order each collection gives it. Two calls of one method replace two loops.
questions.rule: One loop, many sources.

questions.q: A reviewer claims this Waitress no longer depends on concrete menu classes. Which part shows the claim is wrong?
options: The parameter types of print(), which name both menu classes
The while loop, which calls hasNext() and next() on each iterator
The return type of createIterator(), which is Iterator in both menus
The for loop, which handles two iterators from one list
optionExplain: Right: the signature still binds the Waitress to two concrete menu classes.
The loop works through the Iterator interface, which is the improvement.
Returning the interface type is what keeps the iterator class hidden.
One loop for several iterators is the gain, not a dependency.
questions.explain: The iterators removed the dependency on storage and the duplicate loops. The Waitress still names PancakeHouseMenu and DinerMenu, which is the problem left for the next step.
questions.rule: Check what the client still names.
questions.section: What have we done so far?

questions.q: Put the steps of the authors' review of the iterator work in order.
items: List the problems: storage exposed, duplicate loops, and the Waitress bound to concrete menu classes
Mark exposed storage and duplicate loops as solved by the iterators
Name the open problem: the Waitress still names two concrete menu classes
Fix the open problem by giving the menus a shared interface
questions.explain: The review starts from the list of problems, marks which are solved, names the one that is open, and only then repairs it.
questions.rule: List, mark, name, then fix.

questions.q: The Café should join the framework through this Menu interface. What does the compiler report for CafeMenu?
options: Nothing; addItem() is enough to make the class a valid Menu
Error: CafeMenu does not implement createIterator()
Error: addItem() must first be declared in the Menu interface
Only a warning, since the interface has only one method
optionExplain: A class that implements an interface must supply all its methods.
Right: each menu takes on the job of creating its own iterator, so it must supply createIterator().
A class may have methods beyond the interface; the interface is only the common part.
The size of the interface does not soften the rule.
questions.explain: The Menu interface asks each menu to create the iterator that suits its storage. A class that does not supply that method cannot stand in for a Menu.
questions.rule: Implementing Menu means supplying createIterator().

questions.q: Sort each item by whether the Waitress depends on it or it stays hidden from her.

items.t: The Menu interface
The Iterator interface
The MenuItem class she prints
The array inside DinerMenu
The HashMap inside CafeMenu
The body of createIterator() in each menu

questions.explain: She uses the two interfaces and the items she prints. How each menu stores items, and how its iterator is built, are the menus' own business.
questions.rule: Depend on the interface; hide the rest.

questions.q: A developer expects an iterator from a plain array this way. What does the compiler say?
options: Nothing; every Java collection and array has iterator()
Error: the array's items would first have to be sorted
Warning only; the iterator is empty until items are added
Error: an array has no iterator() method, so one must be written
optionExplain: ArrayList has iterator(), but an array does not.
Sorting plays no part in getting an iterator.
The code does not compile at all, so there is no empty iterator.
Right: the DinerMenu needed its own iterator class because it relies on an array.
questions.explain: The authors point out that the Diner needs its own iterator because an array supports neither iterator() nor any other way to create one.
questions.rule: Arrays need a hand-written iterator.
questions.code:
String[] diner = {"blt", "soup"};
Iterator<String> it = diner.iterator();

questions.q: An iterator over an unmodifiable list is asked to remove. What does this code print?
options: removed
Nothing; the program ends with a compile error
unsupported
Nothing; remove() quietly does nothing
optionExplain: That needs an iterator that allows removal; this list does not.
The call compiles, since remove() is declared in the interface.
Right: the iterator provides remove() but signals that it is not supported.
A silent no-op would hide the problem; the interface allows the exception instead.
questions.explain: remove() is part of the interface but optional. An iterator that does not allow it throws UnsupportedOperationException, and a careful client catches that.
questions.rule: Provide remove(), and say when it is unsupported.

questions.q: Which member of this class breaks the promise in the Iterator Pattern's definition?
options: getItems(), which hands out the ArrayList and so exposes the representation
createIterator(), which gives clients sequential access to the items
The items field, which is private and holds the elements
The class as a whole, since it declares two methods
optionExplain: Right: any client holding the ArrayList can see and rely on how the items are stored.
This is the pattern doing its job: access one after another, with the storage hidden.
A private field is how the representation stays out of sight.
The number of methods is not the issue; what they reveal is.
questions.explain: The pattern gives sequential access without exposing the underlying representation. getItems() hands that representation to every client.
questions.rule: Give a way to step through, not the container.

questions.q: A teammate calls this method polymorphic iteration. What is wrong with that claim?
options: The loop prints the dishes one at a time instead of all at once
Its parameter is a concrete collection type, so it cannot serve other collections
Methods that use a for loop can never be called polymorphic
The method returns nothing, so no caller can use its result
optionExplain: Printing one at a time is what any traversal does.
Right: polymorphic iteration means taking an Iterator, so that any collection able to supply one can be used.
The kind of loop is not the point; the parameter type is.
Returning nothing has no bearing on polymorphism here.
questions.explain: Polymorphic iteration is a method that takes an Iterator. This method accepts only an ArrayList, so a menu stored in an array or a map cannot use it.
questions.rule: Take the Iterator, not the container.

questions.q: The pattern moves traversal out of this aggregate. Which members would move to an iterator? Select all that apply.
options: The pos field that marks the place in a pass
hasNext()
next()
add()
size()
optionExplain: Right: remembering where a pass has reached is part of traversal.
Right: telling whether more items remain is traversal.
Right: handing back the next item is traversal.
Adding songs is managing the collection, which stays with the aggregate.
Reporting how many songs it holds is also managing the collection.
questions.explain: Position, hasNext() and next() are the stepping through. Adding songs and counting them are the aggregate's own job.
questions.rule: The aggregate holds; the iterator walks.

questions.q: ListIterator adds previous() to the standard interface. What does this code print?
options: a
c
b
Nothing; it throws an exception
optionExplain: That would need three steps back from the end of the second item.
c is the next item ahead, not the one just passed.
Right: two next() calls pass a and b, and previous() returns the item just passed, b.
Both moves are legal here, so no exception occurs.
questions.explain: previous() returns the element the iterator has just stepped over. After a and b were passed, that element is b.
questions.rule: previous() steps back over the last item.

questions.q: Here the list steps through its elements and applies the operation handed to it. What kind of iteration is this?
options: External, since the client supplies the code run on each price
Internal, since the iterating is controlled by the list, not the client
Both at once, since the client and the list each do some of the work
Neither, since a list is a collection and not an iterator
optionExplain: Supplying the operation is what an internal iterator needs; the client does not drive each step.
Right: the client hands over an operation and the iterator does the stepping.
An iteration has one driver; the question is who calls for each next element.
The list performs the iteration here; it plays the iterator's part.
questions.explain: With an internal iterator you pass the operation and it does all the work. An external iterator would leave the client calling next() for each element.
questions.rule: Who drives each step?
questions.code:
List<Integer> prices = List.of(3, 5, 8);
prices.forEach(p -> System.out.print(p + ";"));

questions.q: Applying the principle, what does a reviewer report about this Invoice class?
options: One reason to change, since every method concerns invoices
No fault, since the class has only three short methods
Several unrelated reasons: the total rules, the layout and the storage
Two reasons, since only total() and saveToDisk() can ever change
optionExplain: Sharing a subject does not make one reason to change.
Length is not the test; the number of areas of change is.
Right: how totals are worked out, how the invoice looks and where it is kept can each change on its own.
The layout in toText() can change on its own as well.
questions.explain: Each responsibility is an area of potential change. This class takes on calculation, presentation and storage, so a change in any of them lands in the same class.
questions.rule: Count the areas of change.

questions.q: A lead says a Customer class that also saves itself to a file has one responsibility, since both concern customers. Why is this slip easy to make?
options: The principle applies only to classes of more than a hundred lines
Saving to a file is not counted as a responsibility at all
Our minds group behaviours together even when they are really separate responsibilities
Tools usually rename classes that carry two responsibilities
optionExplain: The principle has no size threshold; it concerns reasons to change.
Storage is one of the commonest separate responsibilities.
Right: the authors say we are too good at seeing behaviours as a set, so careful examination is needed.
No tool is mentioned; the authors rely on diligence.
questions.explain: The authors say separating responsibilities is one of the hardest design jobs because our brains group behaviours that are really two or more responsibilities. The remedy is to examine designs diligently.
questions.rule: Look past the shared subject.
questions.teaches: Separating responsibilities is hard because our brains group behaviours together even when they are two or more responsibilities, so designs need diligent examination.

questions.q: A team splits a class that billed customers and printed posters into two classes, each following the Single Responsibility Principle. What does the book say about their cohesion?
options: It tends to be high, and such classes are more maintainable
It stays the same, because cohesion ignores responsibilities
It drops, because each class now has fewer methods
It cannot be judged, because cohesion applies to modules only
optionExplain: Right: classes that follow the principle usually have high cohesion and are easier to maintain.
The two ideas are closely related, not unrelated.
Fewer methods do not lower cohesion; unrelated functions do.
The book applies cohesion to a class or a module.
questions.explain: The book calls cohesion the more general concept and links the two closely. Classes that follow the principle usually have high cohesion and are easier to maintain.
questions.rule: One responsibility usually means high cohesion.
questions.teaches: Cohesion is the broader idea; following the Single Responsibility Principle usually yields high cohesion and easier maintenance.

questions.q: The Café keeps dishes in a map and iterates over its values. What does this code print?
optionExplain: That adds the lengths of the keys, b1 and s2, not the dishes.
That counts only the longer dish; the loop visits both.
Right: the iterator over values returns both dishes, 13 and 4 characters long.
That is the number of entries, not what the loop adds up.
questions.explain: Taking the map's values and asking them for an iterator gives the dishes, not the keys. The two dishes have 13 and 4 characters.
questions.rule: Values first, then the iterator.

questions.q: Sort each future change by whether the iterator design absorbs it with one new iterator and one more call, or needs a structural change.

items.t: A new menu that keeps its dishes in a linked list
A new menu that keeps its dishes in a hash map
A fourth menu that keeps its dishes in an array
A dessert menu that must sit inside the Diner menu
Menus nested several levels deep
A menu whose elements are other menus

groups: Absorbed by a new iterator and a call
questions.explain: A new storage type is just another menu that supplies an iterator. Menus inside menus break the assumption that a menu holds only items, so the structure itself has to change.
questions.rule: New storage fits; new nesting does not.
questions.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress

questions.q: A developer wants an iterator over the dishes of a map-based menu this way. What does the compiler say?
options: Error: a HashMap has no iterator() method of its own; get its values first
Nothing; the iterator walks the keys and values together
Error: only arrays are allowed to supply iterators
A warning, because the map has no collection of values
optionExplain: Right: a map holds keys and values, so you retrieve the values Collection and ask that for the iterator.
Neither this call nor a pairing of keys and values exists on the map itself.
Arrays are the ones that cannot supply iterators.
A map does have a collection of values; that is the route to take.
questions.explain: HashMap supports Iterator only indirectly. It holds two sets of objects, so you first retrieve the Collection of values and then obtain its iterator.
questions.rule: For a map, ask the values.
questions.code:
HashMap<String, String> menu = new HashMap<>();
Iterator<String> it = menu.iterator();

questions.q: The Waitress loops over a collection of menus. What does this code print?
options: eggs;toast;
eggs;soup;
breakfast: eggs;toast; lunch: soup;
eggs;toast;soup;
optionExplain: The loop goes on to the second menu.
Each menu's dishes are all printed, not just the first.
The data holds no menu names, so none can be printed.
Right: one loop covers every menu in the collection, but no menu names appear.
questions.explain: Putting menus in a collection removes the repeated calls: a new menu needs no new line. The output also shows what was lost, because the names are not part of the data.
questions.rule: A collection removes the calls, not the labels.
questions.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?

questions.q: A teammate wraps the three printMenu() calls in a helper called printAllMenus(), with the three calls still inside. Does this fix the problem the authors describe?
options: Yes; the Waitress's other methods now make a single call
No; adding a menu still means opening code to add another call
Yes; the helper makes the Waitress closed to modification
No; a helper is not allowed to call printMenu()
optionExplain: It hides the calls from other methods, but the helper itself still has to change.
Right: each new menu still means opening the Waitress and adding a call.
Closed to modification means a new menu needs no edit, and here it still does.
Helpers may call printMenu(); that is not the objection.
questions.explain: The authors object that every new menu forces the Waitress to be opened and more code added. A helper moves the three calls but leaves that cost where it was.
questions.rule: Moving the calls does not remove them.
questions.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?

questions.q: The Diner stores elements in an array of MenuItem and tries to add a dessert Menu to it. What happens when this is compiled?
options: It compiles, because the array has room for two elements
It compiles, and the Menu is converted into a MenuItem
It fails only when run, because the array is already full
It does not compile, because a Menu is not a MenuItem
optionExplain: Room is not the issue; the element type is.
Java does not turn one class into an unrelated one.
The mistake is caught before the program runs.
Right: the array holds MenuItems only, and a menu cannot be assigned to it.
questions.explain: The authors note that a dessert menu cannot be assigned to a MenuItem array. The container assumes one kind of element, which is why a more general structure is needed.
questions.rule: The element type limits what fits.
questions.section: Just when we thought it was safe...

questions.q: Put the authors' line of reasoning in order.
items: The Diner asks for a dessert submenu
A menu cannot be assigned to the array of MenuItem
The authors decide to rework the chefs' implementation into something general
They list what the new design needs: a tree, convenient traversal and flexible traversal
questions.explain: The request exposes the limit of the array, the limit forces a rework, and the rework starts from a list of requirements.
questions.rule: Request, limit, decision, requirements.

questions.q: One cost() call works on a whole tree and on a single item. What does this code print?
optionExplain: That counts only the first item of the tree.
The single item costs 5, not the cost of the tree.
That leaves out the item at the top level, which costs 2.
Right: the inner box costs 7, the outer box adds 2 to give 9, and the lone item costs 5.
questions.explain: The same call works on any node. A box asks its parts to report their cost, and a part may itself be a box, so the call reaches every level.
questions.rule: One call, any node.

questions.q: A GUI toolkit has a Panel holding buttons and other panels. In the pattern's terms, what happens when the top-level Panel is told to display?
options: Only the Panel is drawn, and each button must be displayed by the client
The client checks the type of every part before displaying it
The Panel is first turned into a flat list of buttons
The Panel tells its components to display, and any that hold components do the same
optionExplain: That would leave the client walking the structure, which Composite avoids.
A composite spares the client such type checks.
Nesting is kept; nothing is flattened.
Right: a composite displays itself by telling all its components to display.
questions.explain: In the authors' GUI example, you tell the top-level component to display and count on it to display all its parts. A composite does this by passing the request to its components.
questions.rule: Tell the whole; the whole tells the parts.
questions.teaches: GUI toolkits are a typical home for Composite: a top-level Frame or Panel holds other components, and telling it to display makes it tell all its parts to display.

questions.q: A node with no children counts as a leaf. How many leaves does this tree have?
optionExplain: That misses one of the two leaves under b.
Right: a, c and d have no children; root and b are composites.
That counts b, which holds c and d, so it is a composite.
That counts every node, composites included.
questions.explain: Leaves are the nodes that hold no children: a, c and d. The root and b hold children, so they are composites.
questions.rule: No children means leaf.

questions.q: A leaf inherits the default add() of the component class. What does this code print?
options: added
? cannot add
Nothing; it does not compile
leaf cannot add
optionExplain: The inherited default throws, so the line printing added is never reached.
The leaf overrides name(), so it reports leaf, not the default.
The call compiles because the method exists on the shared type.
Right: the default throws, the catch runs, and name() is the leaf's own.
questions.explain: The leaf implements only what suits it and inherits the throwing default for add(). The call is legal to write, but it fails at run time.
questions.rule: Inherited defaults say unsupported.

questions.q: A developer says MenuItem is finished because it stores a price. What happens when getPrice() is called on a new MenuItem?
options: It prints 2.5, because the field holds the price
It prints 0.0, the neutral value for a price
It throws UnsupportedOperationException from the inherited default
It does not compile, because getPrice() is not implemented
optionExplain: A field is not a method; the call still goes to the inherited getPrice().
The default does not return a neutral value; it throws.
Right: the leaf never overrode getPrice(), so it falls back on the exception default.
The base class supplies a body, so the code compiles.
questions.explain: The leaf must implement the operations that fit it. MenuItem is the class that should implement getPrice(); until it does, the inherited default throws.
questions.rule: The leaf must override what it supports.

questions.q: Each menu prints its name and then asks its children to print. What does this code print?
options: menu;pie;desserts;cake;
menu;pie;desserts;
cake;desserts;pie;menu;
menu;desserts;cake;pie;
optionExplain: Right: each node prints itself, then its children in order, so desserts is followed by its own child.
That stops at the first level and omits the child of desserts.
That is the reverse order; each node prints itself before its children.
Children are visited in the order they were added, so pie comes before desserts.
questions.explain: Each print() prints the node and then calls print() on each child, so a submenu prints its own contents inside the parent's pass.
questions.rule: Print yourself, then your children.

questions.q: This print() was meant to print a whole menu tree. What does it print for the tree shown?
options: menu;pie;desserts;cake;
menu;pie;desserts;
menu;
menu;pie;desserts;cake;pie;
optionExplain: That needs the children to print their own children, and here they do not.
Right: the loop prints the names of the direct children but never calls print() on them.
The loop does print the direct children after the name.
Nothing in the code prints a name twice.
questions.explain: The loop covers one level only. Recursion arises when each child continues the operation on its own children, so cake is never reached.
questions.rule: Call print() on the child, not just its name.

questions.q: A safe design keeps add() only on Menu. What happens when a client holding a Component calls add()?
options: It compiles, because the object really is a Menu
It compiles but throws an exception when run
It does not compile; the client must check the type and cast first
It does not compile, because a Menu cannot hold a Component
optionExplain: The compiler checks the declared type, which is Component.
A missing method is caught before the code runs.
Right: safety is bought with type checks in the client, and transparency is lost.
Menu can hold Components; the call fails because the declared type lacks add().
questions.explain: Separating the interfaces catches inappropriate calls, but the client can no longer treat every node alike. It needs instanceof and a cast before it may add.
questions.rule: Safety costs transparency.
questions.section: Getting ready for a test drive...

questions.q: In a toolkit, Button and Panel implement unrelated interfaces. By the Composite's reasoning, what must a client do to treat them?
options: Nothing; unrelated interfaces already make the client's code transparent
Wrap every Button inside a Menu before calling it
Make every Button a subclass of Panel
Check which interface each object implements before calling it
optionExplain: Without a shared interface the client has to tell the objects apart.
A wrapper does not give the objects a common interface.
That is a drastic change and not what the pattern asks for.
Right: with different interfaces the client must worry about which one each object has, which defeats the purpose.
questions.explain: For a composite to work transparently, all its objects share one interface. Otherwise the client has to know which interface each object implements.
questions.rule: Transparency needs one interface for all.
questions.teaches: For transparency, every object in the composite must implement the same interface; otherwise the client has to worry about which interface each object implements, which defeats the purpose.
questions.section: Getting ready for a test drive...

questions.q: A walker keeps its place in a stack instead of recursing. What does this code print?
options: menu;pie;desserts;tea;
menu;tea;desserts;cake;pie;
menu;pie;desserts;cake;tea;
pie;cake;tea;
optionExplain: That leaves out cake, the child of desserts.
Children are pushed in reverse, so the first child is popped first, not last.
Right: the stack walks each submenu fully before returning to the next sibling.
Menus are visited as well as their items, so their names appear.
questions.explain: The stack records the path back up. A submenu's children are pushed on top, so they are all visited before the walker returns to the remaining siblings.
questions.rule: The stack remembers the way back.

questions.q: A leaf returns null from createIterator(), and the client loops without checking. What happens when this runs?
options: The loop ends at once and prints nothing
It prints null once and then stops
It does not compile, because null is not an Iterator
It fails with a NullPointerException on the first hasNext()
optionExplain: That is what a no-op iterator would do; null does not behave that way.
Nothing is printed, because the loop condition fails first.
null is accepted wherever an object type is expected, so it compiles.
Right: the client needs a null check, which is why the authors prefer an iterator that is already finished.
questions.explain: Returning null forces conditional code on every client. An iterator whose hasNext() always returns false lets the same loop end quietly.
questions.rule: Return an empty iterator, not null.

questions.q: The loop skips any node whose isVeg() throws. How many vegetarian items does this code count?
optionExplain: That counts the submenu or a non-vegetarian item as vegetarian.
That counts every node, including the one that does not support the question.
Right: two items answer true, one answers false, and the submenu is skipped.
The exception is caught per node, so the loop carries on to the others.
questions.explain: The exception from the submenu is caught inside the loop, so the walk continues. Two items report true and are counted.
questions.rule: Catch per node and carry on.

questions.q: A section caches its word count. How many times is the count worked out by this code?
optionExplain: That would be the count without a cache; each call would repeat the work.
The first call finds nothing cached and does compute.
120 is the stored result, not the number of computations.
Right: the first call does the work and stores it, and later calls reuse the result.
questions.explain: Caching saves traversals when a result is requested repeatedly. Only the first call computes; the other two return the stored value.
questions.rule: Compute once, reuse after.
questions.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...

questions.q: A report is a tree of sections inside sections, and a tool must step through every paragraph in order. Which statement fits the chapter?
options: Iterator alone, because stepping through items needs no tree
Composite alone, because a tree already includes its own traversal
Neither, because a report is a document and not a collection
Composite for the nesting and Iterator for stepping through it
optionExplain: Nesting needs a structure; the iterator walks it but does not build it.
The authors add an iterator to walk the whole composite.
A report with sections is a collection of parts and wholes.
Right: the two patterns cooperate, one for the structure and one for the walk.
questions.explain: Composite gives a structure in which sections and paragraphs are treated alike, and an iterator over it provides the step-by-step access. They work well together.
questions.rule: Composite builds; Iterator walks.

questions.q: A teammate says Facade is the pattern that changes the interface of one or more classes. Which pattern has that purpose?
options: Strategy
Observer
Adapter
Composite
optionExplain: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable behaviours and uses delegation.
Observer notifies a group of objects when some state changes.
Right: Adapter changes the interface of one or more classes, while Facade simplifies the interface of a group of classes.
Composite lets clients treat collections and single objects uniformly.
questions.explain: The chapter's match list gives each pattern a purpose. Facade simplifies the interface of a group of classes; changing an interface is the work of Adapter.
questions.rule: Facade simplifies; Adapter changes.

questions.q: In a state diagram, what does an arrow between two circles show?
options: A message sent from one object to another object
The move from one state to another that an action causes
The order in which the states were first designed
The data that the first state hands to the second
optionExplain: Arrows can look like message passing, but circles are states of one machine, not objects.
An arrow is a transition: an action happens and the machine ends up in a different state.
Design order is not drawn in the diagram.
States are behaviors, not containers that pass data along.
questions.explain: Arrows are transitions between states. The card next sets out the vocabulary.
questions.rule: Read a machine as states, which say how it behaves now, and transitions, which are the actions that move it between states.

questions.q: A move from one state to another, caused by an action such as inserting a quarter, is called a ____.
questions.explain: The chapter calls each arrow a state transition: the machine changes state because of an action.
questions.rule: Arrows are transitions; circles are states.

questions.q: After a gumball is dispensed, the machine goes either to No Quarter or to Out of Gumballs. What picks between the two?
options: Which of the four actions the customer chose to perform last
The state the machine was in before the quarter arrived
A fixed rule that always sends the machine to No Quarter before anything else
