A count of the gumballs that remain, which the machine keeps as well
optionExplain: The action is the same dispense in both cases, so it cannot tell the exits apart.
The earlier state is the same in both cases, so it cannot tell the exits apart.
A fixed rule would never reach Out of Gumballs.
Dispensing is the only action with two exits, and the count of remaining gumballs chooses the exit.
questions.explain: Judy points out that the machine must track the number of gumballs: the count is tested to choose the next state.
questions.rule: Some choices between arrows depend on data the machine remembers.
questions.teaches: A state machine often remembers a quantity beside its state, such as a count, and tests it at the moment of an action to choose between arrows leaving the same state.

questions.q: A document system moves a file through its life. Sort each item as a state or as a transition.

items.t: Draft
Submit for review
In Review
Approve
Published
Reject

questions.explain: Draft, In Review and Published are conditions the file can be in. Submitting, approving and rejecting are the events that move it between them.
questions.rule: States are conditions; transitions are the moves between them.

questions.q: Joe notes that nonsensical actions can happen, such as ejecting a quarter in No Quarter. What does that mean for a machine drawn with only the sensible arrows?
options: The designer must still decide what the machine does in those cases
The machine cannot receive those actions, so no decision is needed for them
The machine moves to a new state chosen at random for them
The machine treats them like the closest sensible action instead
optionExplain: Joe and Frank agree these cases have to be taken care of, so the missing arrows do not settle them.
A real customer can still do them, so an absent arrow does not remove the action.
Nothing in the chapter suggests random choice.
Nothing in the chapter treats a wrong action as another action.
questions.explain: A diagram lists the intended moves; unintended actions still arrive and need an answer.
questions.rule: Missing arrows are not answers.
questions.hint: Think of what a customer can physically do.

questions.q: A pedestrian crossing light cycles Red, Green, Flashing Green and back to Red. One action, the timer expiring, causes every move. How many transitions does its diagram have?
options: One, because only one action is involved in the cycle
Four, because there is one for each state plus the start
Three, because each state has one arrow leaving it
Six, because every pair of states could be joined
optionExplain: The gumball example shows the count of transitions can differ from the count of actions.
The start is not an extra state here; the cycle has three states.
Transitions are counted as arrows, and each of the three states has one arrow out.
Arrows are drawn only for moves that can occur.
questions.explain: Four actions gave five transitions in the gumball machine, so the two counts need not match.
questions.rule: Count arrows, not actions.
questions.teaches: Transitions are counted as arrows: a single action can account for several arrows (one per state it applies in), and one state can hold two arrows for the same action.

questions.q: True or false: In a procedural state machine, each state is written as its own class.
questions.explain: In that style the states are plain values, and one class does all the branching. The card next shows the four steps.
questions.rule: Procedural machines store states as values.

questions.q: Put the chapter's four steps for building a state machine in order.
items: Gather up the states
Create an instance variable for the current state with a value per state
Gather up the actions that can happen
Write a method per action that uses conditionals on the current state
questions.explain: The first two steps set up the states and where to hold the current one, the third lists the actions, and the last writes the methods around them.
questions.rule: States first, then the variable, then actions, then one method per action.

questions.q: In a procedural machine, where would you read the full behavior of the state Has Quarter?
options: In one place, in a single method that is named after that state
In the constant that holds the state's value, together with its replies
In a branch inside each of several action methods, beside other states
In a separate class that holds only that one state's behavior and nothing else
optionExplain: That layout would be states first; the recipe organizes by action.
The value only names the state; it holds no behavior.
Behavior is organized by action, so each action method carries a branch for every state.
That describes the State Pattern, which comes later.
questions.explain: Reading one state means visiting every action method.
questions.rule: The recipe groups code by action, not by state.
questions.teaches: In the conditional recipe the code is grouped by action, so the behavior of a single state is split across every action method.

questions.q: A parking gate has states Closed, Open and Broken and actions car arrives, car leaves and repair. Under the four-step recipe, where does the code for car arrives go?
options: In one method for that action, with a branch for each of the three states
In three methods, one for each state, each of which handles all the actions
In the Broken constant, since that state is the exception to the usual case
In a separate class created for every state of the gate
optionExplain: There is one method per action, and the method branches on the current state.
That swaps the layout round; the recipe has one method per action.
A constant only names a state and carries no code.
Separate state classes are the later redesign, not this recipe.
questions.explain: One method per action, one branch per state.
questions.rule: Method per action; branch per state.

questions.q: The parking gate needs a fourth state, Maintenance. Under the recipe, what must change?
options: Only one new method is needed, for the Maintenance state
Nothing else changes, since the variable accepts any value that is given to it
Only the method for the repair action needs editing, as repair ends the new state
Each action method needs a new branch, as well as a new state value
optionExplain: There are methods for actions, not for states, in this recipe.
The variable holds the value, but the methods still need to know what to do with it.
Car arrives and car leaves also have to answer for the new state.
Every action must say what it does in Maintenance, so each action method is edited.
questions.explain: A new state touches every branching method.
questions.rule: New state, edit every action method.
questions.hint: Which methods must know about each state?

questions.q: A smart thermostat has modes Idle, Heating and Cooling. Match each part of the four-step recipe with the part of the thermostat code.
pairs: Idle, Heating and Cooling as named values
Instance variable for the current state
A field that records the current mode
Temperature rises, temperature falls, user switches off
A method that checks the mode when temperature falls
questions.explain: Each step of the recipe has a counterpart: the modes are the states, the field holds the current one, and each event gets one method that branches on the mode.
questions.rule: The recipe applies to any device with modes.
questions.teaches: In the recipe, states are only values and actions are methods, so the structure follows the actions; this matches how the diagram's events are listed.

questions.q: True or false: A state machine only needs code for the actions that make sense in each state.
questions.explain: Actions that make no sense can still be performed, so they need an answer too. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Unexpected actions need decisions.

questions.q: True or false: According to Joe and Frank, the gumball code must also deal with a customer who inserts two quarters.
questions.explain: They list odd actions such as a second quarter or ejecting when none is in, and say the code has to take care of them.
questions.rule: Plan for actions that make no sense.

questions.q: In the solution to the book's sold-out exercise, what does the machine do when the crank is turned in the Sold Out state?
options: It moves to No Quarter and waits there for the next customer to arrive
It prints a message that there are no gumballs and stays where it is
It dispenses the last gumball that the machine keeps in reserve
It does nothing, with no message of any kind
optionExplain: Moving on would not fit a machine that is still empty.
The solution shows a printed message that says the crank was turned but there are no gumballs.
The machine is sold out, so no gumball is left.
The solution gives every action a visible reply, even this one.
questions.explain: A refusal that changes nothing is a defined response.
questions.rule: Answering with a refusal counts as handling the action.
questions.teaches: A refusal that prints a message and changes nothing is a valid defined response; an action that makes no sense in a state is answered, not skipped.

questions.q: A ticket barrier has 3 states and 3 actions. How many state and action pairings need a defined response?
options: Three
Six
Twelve
Nine
optionExplain: That counts only one response per state or per action.
That adds the two counts instead of multiplying them.
That multiplies in a fourth factor that is not there.
Each of the 3 states needs a response to each of the 3 actions, which is 3 times 3.
questions.explain: States times actions gives the pairings.
questions.rule: Pairings equal states times actions.

questions.q: The ticket barrier gets one new state and keeps its 3 actions. The number of new pairings that need a defined response is ____.
questions.explain: The new state must answer each of the 3 actions, so 3 new pairings appear; the existing pairings keep their responses.
questions.rule: A new state adds a row of responses.
questions.hint: Count the actions, not the states.

questions.q: A ticket kiosk has states Idle and Paid. Sort each pairing by whether the response moves it to a different state or leaves it where it is.

items.t: Pay while Idle
Pay while Paid
Print while Paid
Print while Idle
Refund while Paid
Refund while Idle

questions.explain: Only paying while Idle, printing while Paid and refunding while Paid change the state. The other three pairings do not make sense and refuse.
questions.rule: Many pairings refuse, but each still needs its own response.
questions.teaches: In a typical machine most pairings of state and action produce no transition; they only refuse, and a design should make those refusals cheap to write.

questions.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!
questions.q: A first version passes every test and the customer is pleased. What does that tell you about how easily it will accept a new feature?
options: A great deal, because well-tested code is easy to extend
Little, because passing tests and ease of change are separate questions
That the next feature will need only a small and safe edit to the code
That the code was built with the right method, so change will be cheap
optionExplain: Tests check behavior, not structure.
Tests show the present behavior is correct; they say nothing about the cost of the next change.
Nothing links passing tests to the size of future edits.
A method is not a guarantee either; the chapter's design used one and still struggled.
questions.explain: Correct now is not the same as easy to change. The card next follows the authors' argument.
questions.rule: Judge a design by how a new requirement changes it, not only by whether it passes today's tests.

questions.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!
questions.q: True or false: In the chapter, Mighty Gumball's testers found problems with the first version before the contest request arrived.
questions.explain: They found it fine, and asked for the next level of features. The trouble appears only when the change is considered.
questions.rule: The first version was well received.

questions.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!
questions.q: Before any code is written for the contest, the authors ask the reader to draw a state ____ that includes the new behavior.
questions.explain: The design puzzle asks for a new diagram as the first step, so the size of the change is visible before code is touched.
questions.rule: Express a change in the diagram first.
questions.teaches: A change request is best first expressed as a change to the diagram, new states and arrows, which shows how big the change is before any code is edited.

questions.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!
questions.q: A team reviews a booking app that works well. Which question best tests how good its design is?
options: How many places would need to change to add one new booking status?
Do all of the existing automated tests still pass after each release?
Was a recognized design method followed when the app was written?
Has the app run for a full month without any complaints from users?
optionExplain: The count of places a new requirement touches measures how well the structure takes change.
Passing tests shows current correctness only.
A followed method did not save the gumball design.
Complaint-free use shows the present, not the future.
questions.explain: Ask what the next requirement would touch.
questions.rule: Measure a design by the cost of change.

questions.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!
questions.q: True or false: If a program stays fixed after delivery, it pays little for being hard to extend.
questions.explain: The weakness concerns the cost of extension. A machine that never changes never pays that price, so the rule applies where change is likely.
questions.rule: The rule applies where change is likely.
questions.hint: What kind of cost did the authors point to?

questions.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!
questions.q: A quiz app can add a question type either by adding one new class and editing one setting, or by editing five existing methods. Which is more likely to break features that already work?
options: Adding one class, because new code has not been tested in use yet
Both are equally risky, as the feature set is the same
Editing the five methods, as each edit touches working code
Neither is risky, since the tests will catch any fault in either case
optionExplain: New code has risk, but it leaves the working code alone.
Risk depends on how much existing code is edited, not on the feature.
The more working code a change edits, the more chances to break it. A new class touches little that exists.
Tests help but do not remove the risk the authors worry about.
questions.explain: Frank and Judy want changes localized so a change to one state does not risk the rest.
questions.rule: Smaller edits to working code mean smaller risk.
questions.teaches: The risk of a change grows with how much working code it edits, so a good structure confines a new requirement to new code and a few small edits.

questions.q: Several behaviors share one block of conditional code. A change to one behavior is needed. What is the main danger?
options: The edit may disturb the other behaviors that share the same code
The edit will make the program run more slowly than a new class would
The edit cannot be made without moving to a new programming language
The edit will remove the need for tests
optionExplain: Shared code means a fault in one branch can affect the branches around it.
Speed is not the worry the authors raise.
Nothing needs a new language.
Testing is still needed; the point is the risk.
questions.explain: Shared code spreads risk. The card next gives the authors' reasoning.
questions.rule: When one change must edit code that other behaviors share, separate the behaviors.

questions.q: Judy says the redesign should localize the ____ of each state.
questions.explain: She wants each state's behavior in one place so a change to one state leaves the rest alone.
questions.rule: Put each state's behavior in one place.

questions.q: What does Frank's call to refactor the code ask for?
options: New features added on top of the old structure, with no other change
A faster version of the same conditional logic, with the same layout
A rewrite that also changes what the machine does
A new structure that behaves the same way but is easier to change
optionExplain: Adding features is the contest request, a separate matter.
Speed is not the goal Frank gives.
Changing what the machine does would be a new feature.
Refactoring reshapes the code; the behavior customers see stays as it was.
questions.explain: The goal is easier maintenance and modification with unchanged behavior.
questions.rule: Refactor to change structure, not behavior.
questions.teaches: Refactoring changes the structure and keeps the behavior, so its success is judged by two things: existing behavior stays the same and later changes become easier.

questions.q: A fitness app has one function for workout types run, swim and cycle, with branches for each. A tweak to swim lap counting broke cycling. Following Judy's reasoning, what should change?
options: More checks are added inside the shared function
Each workout type gets its own place for its behavior
The three types are merged into fewer branches
A comment is added above each branch to warn editors
optionExplain: More checks treat the symptom while the sharing remains.
Separate places mean a tweak to swimming cannot touch cycling.
Fewer branches still share code.
A comment warns but does not separate.
questions.explain: Separate behaviors that change on their own.
questions.rule: One place per behavior that changes on its own.

questions.q: True or false: If the payment behaviors stay fixed, the case for separating them is weaker than if they change often.
questions.explain: The argument is about the risk of change. Without change the risk stays small, so the benefit of separating is smaller.
questions.rule: The argument depends on change being likely.
questions.hint: What event makes shared code dangerous?

questions.q: A report tool has one export function with branches for PDF and CSV. Adding Excel means editing that function. Which principle does this go against?
options: Favor composition over inheritance, since no subclass is used
Program to an interface, since no interface is declared for the formats
The Open Closed Principle, as a new format forces edits to working code
Keep the interface small, since the export function has grown so large
optionExplain: Composition is about how objects are assembled, not about edits.
An interface is not the issue here; the edit is.
That principle asks for new behavior to arrive as new code, leaving working code closed to edits.
The size of an interface is a different matter.
questions.explain: Later the chapter says the new design closes each state for modification and leaves the machine open to extension.
questions.rule: Add behavior by adding code, not by editing working code.
questions.teaches: The Open Closed Principle says a design should be open to extension and closed to modification, so new behavior comes as new code and working code stays untouched.

questions.q: An object acts differently in each of five modes, using big branches. Which move best follows the advice to encapsulate what varies?
options: Give the five modes shorter and clearer names
Move each mode's behavior into its own class
Add one more branch for each new mode
Copy the whole object once for each mode
optionExplain: Renaming leaves the branching where it is.
What varies is the per-mode behavior, so it goes into separate classes.
More branches keep the varying part mixed in.
Copies would duplicate the code that does not vary.
questions.explain: Pull out what varies. The card next shows the authors' two moves.
questions.rule: Pull what varies into its own classes.

questions.q: Match each principle or remark from the cubicle conversation with what it justifies.
pairs: Each state's behavior goes into its own class
The machine holds a state object and delegates to it
A new class and a few edited transitions
questions.explain: The first principle explains the class per state, the second explains the delegation, and Judy's remark says what a later addition costs.
questions.rule: Each principle justifies one move.

questions.q: Judy expects a new state to need a new class and some changed transitions. Which existing classes are the likely ones to change?
options: Every state class, since each one implements all actions
Only the machine's constructor, which builds the state objects
The states that have a transition leading into the new state
None of them, as a new state is fully independent
optionExplain: Each state implements all actions, but only some need to move the machine to the new state.
The constructor creates the new object, but the neighbors still need to reach it.
A transition into the new state is code in the neighbor state that sends the machine there.
A state with no arrows to or from it is unreachable.
questions.explain: Only neighbors on the new state's arrows change.
questions.rule: Change spreads only along the arrows.
questions.teaches: Because states hold their own transitions, adding a state edits only the states whose arrows lead into it, along with the new class itself.

questions.q: A video game character can be Standing, Jumping or Ducking. Which design does the authors' reasoning lead to?
options: The character has one input method with a branch for each state
Each state class is a subclass of the character class
The character class is copied once for every state
The character holds a state object and passes each input to it
optionExplain: That is the conditional design the authors move away from.
Frank favors composition over making states subclasses.
Copies would duplicate the code shared by all states.
The character delegates input to the current state object, which holds the behavior for that state.
questions.explain: Hold a state object and delegate.
questions.rule: Hold a state object and delegate to it.

questions.q: True or false: After the machine swaps its current state object, the next action is still handled by the old state object's code.
questions.explain: Delegation goes to whatever object is current, so after the swap the new state's code answers the next action.
questions.rule: The swap is how behavior changes over time.
questions.hint: Which object does the machine call?

questions.q: A developer moves each state's behavior into its own class, but the machine still tests a state number to choose which class's method to call. Which part of the authors' advice is only half applied?
options: Delegation: the machine should hold a state object and forward calls to it
Encapsulation: the behavior has stayed inside the machine and was never moved
Closure: the machine can no longer be extended by anyone at all
Naming: the state classes must be named after their actions
optionExplain: The behavior is separated, but the branching remains, so the conditionals have only moved.
The behavior has already been moved out into classes.
The machine can still be extended; the issue is its branching.
The classes are named after states, as in the chapter.
questions.explain: Separating behavior is not enough; the machine must hand the call to the current state object.
questions.rule: Separate the behavior, then delegate to it.
questions.teaches: Moving behavior into classes does not remove the conditionals unless the machine also forwards calls to the current state object; otherwise the branching just relocates.

questions.q: Code is reshaped to use state objects. What happens to the conditionals that tested the current state?
options: They stay, but move into the state classes unchanged
They are replaced by a second set of conditionals in the machine
They are removed, and the machine delegates to the state object
They are kept as a fallback in case a state object fails
optionExplain: The state classes only answer for their own state, so they need no state tests.
A second set in the machine would keep the problem.
Delegation replaces the branching: the current state object does the work.
Nothing in the plan keeps a fallback set of conditionals.
questions.explain: The state objects take over the choosing. The card next lists the three steps.
questions.rule: Make one State interface with a method per action, one class per state, and have the machine delegate instead of branching.

questions.q: Put the authors' three steps in order.
items: Define a State interface with a method for every action
Implement a State class for every state of the machine
Replace the conditional code by delegating to the current state
questions.explain: The interface comes first so the classes can implement it, and delegation comes last when the state classes exist to delegate to.
questions.rule: Interface, state classes, delegation.

questions.q: Why must the State interface have a method for every action the machine can receive?
options: Each state class is copied from the interface at compile time
The interface lists the actions in the order in which they happen in use
The customer's actions call the interface directly
Any state must accept any action, as the machine does not know the state
optionExplain: Implementing an interface is not copying.
The interface lists actions, not their order.
The machine receives the actions, not the interface.
Delegation hands an action to whichever state is current, so all states must accept all actions.
questions.explain: A uniform interface lets the machine forward calls without knowing the state.
questions.rule: One interface method per action.
questions.teaches: Delegation needs one uniform interface: the machine forwards the same call to whichever state is current without testing which one, so every state must accept every action.

questions.q: A help desk ticket is Open, Assigned or Closed, with actions assign, resolve and reopen. Which list matches the three steps?
options: An interface of the three actions, a class per state, and a delegating ticket
A class for each action, with each class branching over the three states of a ticket
An interface with one method per state, and one class for each action of the ticket
One ticket class with a status number and a single large method that holds everything
optionExplain: That matches the plan: actions in the interface, states as classes, and delegation from the ticket.
That arranges the code by action, as in the old design.
That swaps the roles of states and actions.
That is the conditional design the plan replaces.
questions.explain: Actions become methods; states become classes.
questions.rule: Actions become methods; states become classes.

questions.q: The help desk adds an action, escalate. How many of the three State classes must gain an escalate method?
options: Only Assigned, as that is where escalation makes sense
All three, as each class implements every interface method
None, because the ticket class itself handles the new action alone
Two, as Closed tickets are never escalated
optionExplain: Open and Closed still have to answer escalate.
Each class implements the whole interface, so each must reply to escalate, even if the reply is a refusal.
The ticket only forwards the call.
Closed has to reply too, even with a refusal.
questions.explain: A new action touches every state class.
questions.rule: Make one State interface with a method per action, one class per state, and have the machine delegate instead of branching.
questions.hint: Think about what implementing an interface requires.

questions.q: A door lock has states Locked, Unlocked and Alarm and actions swipe card, push and tamper. Which pieces does the three-step plan call for? Select all that apply.
options: An interface with swipeCard, push and tamper methods
A class for each of the three states implementing the interface
A class for each action containing branches over the states
A lock class that holds the current state object
optionExplain: Actions become methods of the interface.
Each state becomes a class that implements it.
That groups code by action, the old arrangement.
The lock stays as the object that holds the current state and forwards calls.
questions.explain: The plan keeps the lock class as the holder and forwarder, with state classes behind it.
questions.rule: States become classes and actions become methods.
questions.teaches: The machine class stays in the design as the object outsiders talk to; it holds the current state object and forwards calls, while the state classes work behind it.

questions.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes
questions.q: True or false: In a State Pattern design, two different state classes can each have an insertQuarter method that behaves differently.
questions.explain: The interface fixes the method names, but each class decides what the method does. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Same name, different behavior per class.

questions.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes
questions.q: Match each method of the book's sold-out state with its reply, described in words.
pairs: Says it cannot accept a quarter because the machine is sold out
Says it cannot eject, as no quarter was inserted
Says the crank was turned but there are no gumballs
Says that no gumball was dispensed
questions.explain: The sold-out state answers all four actions, and each answer is a refusal of some kind.
questions.rule: Every action gets a reply in every state.

questions.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes
questions.q: The book's SoldOutState is created with the GumballMachine as an argument. What is that for?
options: It lets the state copy the machine's code into itself when it is created
It lets the state reach the machine's data and set the next state
It makes the state a subclass of the machine
It stops other machines from using the same state object
optionExplain: Reaching the machine is not copying its code.
A state that holds the machine can call it, for example to change the current state.
The relation is held by reference, not by inheritance.
Sharing is discussed separately, and has nothing to do with this argument.
questions.explain: States keep a reference to the machine.
questions.rule: A state keeps a reference to the machine it serves.
questions.teaches: Each state object holds a reference to the machine, so it can read the machine's data and ask it to switch to the next state.

questions.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes
questions.q: A dishwasher has states Idle, Washing and Done, and actions start, openDoor and finish. How many methods does the Washing class implement?
options: One, for the action that ends the washing
Two, for the actions that make sense while washing
None, as the dishwasher class itself holds that behavior
Three, one per action, even the ones that refuse
optionExplain: Only one action would leave the other two without a reply.
Actions that make no sense still need a refusal.
The behavior of a state sits in the state class.
Each state class implements the whole interface, so Washing answers all three actions.
questions.explain: The class covers every action.
questions.rule: Every state covers every action.

questions.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes
questions.q: A gumball machine in No Quarter state is given two quarters in a row. What happens?
options: The first is accepted and the second rejected, as the state changed
Both are accepted, as the machine has no limit on the number of coins
Both are rejected, as the machine starts out in a state that refuses coins
The first is rejected, and then the second is accepted instead
optionExplain: The first quarter moves the machine to Has Quarter, whose insertQuarter refuses a second coin.
That ignores the state change after the first coin.
The No Quarter state is where a coin is accepted.
The order is the other way round.
questions.explain: The state at the moment of each action decides the reply.
questions.rule: Each state class implements every action of the State interface, answering correctly for its own state.
questions.hint: What state follows the first quarter?

questions.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes
questions.q: A Cancelled state in a subscription service is a class that refuses most actions. Which statements fit the State Pattern design? Select all that apply.
options: Its post and comment methods refuse the action
It still has a method for every action of the interface
It can be left out of the design, as it does nothing
Its resubscribe method may send the account back to Active
optionExplain: Refusing is a defined reply.
Every state class implements the whole interface.
A state that mostly refuses is still a real state with its own class.
The few actions it accepts are its exits.
questions.explain: A state that mostly refuses is still a class that answers all actions; its few accepted actions are the ways out.
questions.rule: Even a refusing state is a full state class.
questions.teaches: A state that mostly refuses is still a real state with its own class; the few actions it accepts are its exits, as refilling is for a sold-out machine.

questions.q: In the redesigned gumball machine, who changes the machine from No Quarter to Has Quarter?
options: The customer, by picking the next state directly from the machine's panel
A table kept outside the machine and the states
The No Quarter state object itself, when it accepts the quarter
The test harness, which sets the state before each call
optionExplain: Clients do not set states directly.
No outside table appears in the chapter.
In the authors' design the state classes carry the transitions.
A harness only drives the machine from outside.
questions.explain: The state class does it. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: State classes carry out the transitions.

questions.q: In the authors' gumball design, the ____ classes decide which state comes next.
questions.explain: The chapter notes that in the gumball machine the states decide the next state, although the context could do so.
questions.rule: In this design the states own the transitions.

questions.q: How does a state object in the chapter get hold of the next state object it should switch to?
options: It creates the new state object itself, each time a move is needed
It receives the object from the customer's action on the machine
It asks the machine for it through a getter method on the machine
It looks the object up in a global list of states
optionExplain: Creating objects in each state would tie it to the concrete class.
Customers act on the machine and never pass state objects.
The authors use getter methods on the context rather than naming concrete state classes.
No global list appears in the chapter.
questions.explain: The machine hands out its state objects.
questions.rule: Ask the machine for the next state object.
questions.teaches: A state object reaches the next state through getter methods on the machine rather than naming concrete state classes, which keeps the state classes less tied to one another.

questions.q: In a video player, the Paused state receives the play action. What does the design have the Paused class do?
options: Resume the sound and make Playing the player's current state
Resume the sound and leave the current state of the player as Paused
Do nothing, as the player class decides the next state
Create a second player object that begins its life in Playing
optionExplain: The state answers the action and then sets the player's current state.
That leaves the player in the wrong state afterwards.
In this design the states decide.
A second player is not part of the design.
questions.explain: Answer, then move on.
questions.rule: Answer the action, then set the next state.

questions.q: The sold state dispenses the last gumball, so the count is now zero. Which state follows?
options: No Quarter
Has Quarter
Sold again
Sold Out
optionExplain: That is the exit when gumballs remain.
A quarter was just used up, so the machine does not hold one.
Nothing in the diagram sends the machine from Sold back to Sold.
With no gumballs left the machine goes to Sold Out; otherwise it goes to No Quarter.
questions.explain: The count picks the exit.
questions.rule: A state class answers an action for its own state and, when the machine should move on, sets the machine's current state to the next state object.
questions.hint: What does the diagram say about the empty case?

questions.q: A parking gate is designed like the gumball machine. Sort each item by whether it belongs inside a state class or inside the machine.

items.t: Reply to car arrives while Broken
Count of cars currently inside
Which state object is current
Choice of next state after a car leaves
Getter that returns the Open state object
Refusal when repair is requested while working

questions.explain: Replies and the choice of next state are behavior of a state. The data and the state objects themselves belong to the machine.
questions.rule: States own behavior and moves; the machine owns data and the state objects.
questions.teaches: The machine keeps the data and the references to its state objects, while the state classes keep the behavior and the moves between states.

questions.q: After the rework, what does the machine's insertQuarter method do?
options: It tests an integer and then runs the matching branch of a conditional
It calls insertQuarter on the object that represents the current state
It creates a new state object for each coin that is inserted
It stores the coin and waits for the customer
optionExplain: That describes the first design.
The machine delegates, and the current state object decides.
States are created once and swapped, not created per coin.
The machine does not decide; its state does.
questions.explain: It forwards to the current state. The card next explains.
questions.rule: The machine forwards each action to the current state.

questions.q: In the reworked machine, the variable for the current state holds a state ____ instead of an integer.
questions.explain: The integer constants are replaced by objects of the state classes.
questions.rule: State is held as an object.

questions.q: The same insertQuarter call behaves differently in two states. What now makes the difference?
options: A conditional that sits inside the machine's own insertQuarter method
A flag that each customer action sets in the machine before the call
The order in which the state objects were created when the machine started
The class of the current state object, which has its own insertQuarter
optionExplain: The conditionals have been removed from the machine.
Customers do not set flags.
Creation order plays no part in dispatch.
The choice that conditionals made is now made by which object is current.
questions.explain: Which object is current decides the behavior.
questions.rule: The current object's class decides.
questions.teaches: The decision the conditionals used to make is now made by polymorphism: the same call runs different code depending on the class of the current state object.

questions.q: A music player is in the Paused state and the user presses play. Put these steps in order.
items: The player's play method is called
The player forwards play to its current state object
Paused resumes the sound
Paused sets the player's current state to Playing
questions.explain: The call arrives at the player, is forwarded to the state, and the state does the work and then moves the player on.
questions.rule: Call, forward, act, move.

questions.q: A state class resumes the sound but forgets to set the player's current state to the next state. What happens on the next action?
options: The player works out the right state by itself without being told to
The player still delegates to the old state, so nothing changes
The player stops accepting any further action until it is restarted
The old state hands over to the right state by itself
optionExplain: Nothing in the design lets the machine infer a state.
The machine only knows its state through the variable; if it is not updated, the old object keeps answering.
The machine keeps working with the old state.
The state objects do not move the machine on unless told.
questions.explain: A transition is only real when the current-state variable changes.
questions.rule: The context holds one object per state and a variable for the current one, and each action method calls the same action on that object.
questions.hint: Which object does the player call next?

questions.q: A kiosk's pressStart calls the current state's start and then also calls its finish. In the Idle state finish refuses. What is the result in Idle?
options: No harm is done, but the second call is unnecessary
The kiosk finishes a job that was never started in the first place
The kiosk moves to the Printing state
The kiosk fails because finish is not allowed
optionExplain: The state refuses finish, so the extra call has no effect; it only signals a wrinkle in the design.
A refusing finish starts nothing.
No transition follows a refusal.
A refusal is a normal reply, not a failure.
questions.explain: The authors suggest returning a boolean or using exceptions as ways to avoid the unneeded call.
questions.rule: Refusing states make extra calls safe, not necessary.
questions.teaches: Because every state answers every action, an extra call is safe, but the authors still see it as untidy and mention a boolean return value or exceptions as ways to avoid it.

questions.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...
questions.q: True or false: A refactoring that changes a program's structure must also change what the program does.
questions.explain: Refactoring reshapes the structure while the behavior stays the same. The card next lists the authors' claims.
questions.rule: Refactoring keeps behavior.

questions.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...
questions.q: Which gains do the authors list for the reworked machine? Select all that apply.
options: Each state's behavior is localized in its own class
The troublesome if statements are removed
The structure maps more closely to the state diagram
The machine needs fewer classes than before
optionExplain: This is the first gain they list.
They say the conditional code that was hard to maintain is gone.
They say the structure is easier to read as a result.
The authors say elsewhere that the pattern increases the number of classes.
questions.explain: Three of the four are claimed gains; the number of classes goes up, not down.
questions.rule: More classes are part of the price.

questions.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...
questions.q: Why does the authors' reworked code map more closely to the state diagram?
options: The diagram was drawn from the finished classes after the code was done
The code now uses the same colors and symbols as the diagram does
Each circle became a class and each arrow a call that sets a state
Each arrow has become a separate class of its own
optionExplain: The diagram was drawn first and the code follows it.
Colors are not a matter of code.
The structure mirrors the diagram: circles to classes, arrows to state changes inside them.
Transitions are calls inside state classes, not classes.
questions.explain: The diagram can be read off the code.
questions.rule: Circles become classes; arrows become state changes.
questions.teaches: The step from diagram to code is nearly mechanical in this design: a circle becomes a class and an arrow becomes a call that sets the next state.

questions.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...
questions.q: A team refactors a billing module. Which result shows success in the authors' sense?
options: The same invoices as before, with each billing rule in its own class
New discount rules added to the module, so that invoice totals now differ
Fewer classes and one longer method with more branches
Faster runs, although a few invoices come out different
optionExplain: Behavior is unchanged and the structure is better localized.
Changed totals mean the behavior changed.
A longer branching method goes the other way.
Different invoices mean the behavior changed.
questions.explain: Same results, better structure.
questions.rule: Same behavior, better structure.

questions.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...
questions.q: Mighty Gumball reruns its old tests on the reworked machine. What do the authors expect?
options: Different results, as the structure of the code is now different
The tests cannot run at all, as the classes have changed so much
Better results, since the code is cleaner
The same results, since the machine is functionally unchanged
optionExplain: Structure and behavior are separate.
The machine's outside calls are unchanged.
Cleaner code does not change the outcomes.
The authors say the new machine is structurally different but functionally exactly the same.
questions.explain: Behavior is held constant.
questions.rule: A good refactoring keeps behavior and changes structure so that behavior is localized, branching shrinks and extension is easy.
questions.hint: Which part did the rework leave alone?

questions.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...
questions.q: A shipping calculator is being improved. Sort each change as structural, which leaves the quotes the same, or functional, which changes what customers see.

items.t: Move each carrier's rules into its own class
Add an express delivery option
Rename helper methods for clarity
Change the free-shipping threshold
Remove a duplicated rate lookup
Send an email when an order ships

questions.explain: Structural changes leave every quote as before. The others change the output or the behavior customers meet.
questions.rule: Keep structural and functional changes apart.
questions.teaches: A change is structural when nothing visible to users differs afterwards; the authors rework the structure first and add the contest afterwards, so that each step can be checked on its own.

questions.q: What does the State Pattern let an object do?
options: Copy its behavior from another object at the time it is created
Change its behavior when its own internal state changes
Hide its data from every other object in the whole program
Share one class between many objects that are unrelated to each other
optionExplain: Copying at creation is a different matter and is not about change over time.
The pattern is about behavior that follows internal state.
Hiding data is encapsulation in general, not this pattern.
Sharing a class is not what the definition says.
questions.explain: Behavior follows internal state. The card next gives the definition.
questions.rule: Behavior changes with internal state.

questions.q: In the State Pattern, the ____ gets its behavior by delegating to the state object it currently holds.
questions.explain: The object whose behavior changes, such as the gumball machine, is called the Context.
questions.rule: The context delegates to its current state.

questions.q: In the gumball machine, inserting a quarter is accepted in one state and rejected in another. What does this show about the definition?
options: The machine has been given two different classes by its maker at the factory
The customer has chosen which behavior the machine will use
The same request gives different results because the internal state differs
The machine has been rewritten by the program while it was running
optionExplain: The machine is one class; the difference sits in the state objects.
Customers do not choose behavior in this pattern.
Different outcomes for the same input, depending on state, is the first half of the definition.
Nothing is rewritten; the state object in use changes.
questions.explain: Different outcomes for one request point to state-dependent behavior.
questions.rule: Same request, different outcome, because of state.
questions.teaches: State-dependent behavior is recognized by the same request producing different outcomes at different moments, with nothing else about the request changed.

questions.q: Which scenario shows the State Pattern at work?
options: A call object picks a ringtone once, when created, and never changes it
A call reacts to the hold button differently when Ringing than when Connected
A call class has one subclass for each phone carrier that connects it
A call object stores a list of the numbers it has dialed so far
optionExplain: That is behavior fixed once, which is not state-driven.
The same input gets different behavior as the call's own state changes.
Subclasses per carrier fix behavior by type.
Storing numbers is data, not changing behavior.
questions.explain: Look for behavior that follows state.
questions.rule: Look for behavior that follows internal state.

questions.q: True or false: If a context's internal state stays fixed after it is created, its behavior under this pattern stays fixed as well.
questions.explain: The behavior changes only because the current state object is replaced. With no state change there is nothing to swap.
questions.rule: No state change means no behavior change.
questions.hint: What causes the context to use different code?

questions.q: A report exporter picks PDF or CSV when it is created and keeps that choice for life. Why does the State Pattern fit poorly?
options: It has too few classes for any design pattern to be applied to it
It does not hold a reference to any other object at all
Its behavior does not change as its own state changes over time
It needs a database to be in place before a state can exist
optionExplain: The number of classes is not the test.
Holding references is not the issue here.
The pattern is about behavior that moves with internal state; a choice made once is not that.
No database is involved in the definition.
questions.explain: Fit depends on behavior changing with state, not merely on having alternatives.
questions.rule: State fits behavior that follows internal state.
questions.teaches: Having interchangeable behaviors is not enough for the State Pattern; the behavior has to change as the object's own state changes over time.

questions.q: A client uses an object whose behavior changes completely over time. What might the client reasonably conclude?
options: That the object has been deleted and has not been replaced
That the client's own code must have been changed behind its back
That the object has secretly turned into a database of records
That the object seems to have come from a different class
optionExplain: Nothing has been deleted; the same object keeps answering.
The client's code is unchanged.
A database is not involved.
Completely different behavior looks like a different class from outside.
questions.explain: From outside it looks like a new class. The card next says what really happens.
questions.rule: Behavior change can look like class change.

questions.q: In reality, when its state changes, a context under the State Pattern keeps its own ____ and only references a different state object.
questions.explain: The authors say the appearance is produced by composition, with the context referencing different state objects.
questions.rule: The class stays; the referenced state object changes.

questions.q: According to the authors, what produces the appearance of a class change?
options: Composition, with the context referencing different state objects
Inheritance, with the context becoming a subclass of the state class
Cloning, with the context making a copy of itself each time
Reflection, with the context renaming its methods at run time
optionExplain: The context keeps the same class and points at another state object.
The authors favor composition over inheritance in this design.
Nothing is copied.
Methods are not renamed.
questions.explain: Swap the referenced object, and the behavior swaps with it.
questions.rule: Composition gives the appearance of a class change.
questions.teaches: The illusion rests on two things at once: the context keeps its identity and class, and only the object it delegates to is replaced.

questions.q: A chat user object has states Online, Away and DoNotDisturb, and messages are handled differently in each. What really happens when the status changes?
options: The user object is replaced by a new instance of some other class
The user class is rewritten by the program while it runs
The user object keeps its class and points to another status object
A new subclass is generated for every incoming message
optionExplain: Replacing the object would break everyone holding a reference to it.
Classes are not rewritten at run time in this design.
Only the referenced status object changes.
No subclasses are generated.
questions.explain: Same object, different delegate.
questions.rule: Same context, different state object.

questions.q: True or false: After a state change, a client that asks which class the context belongs to would find the same class as before.
questions.explain: The context was never replaced by an object of another class; only the state object it references changed.
questions.rule: The class does not change.
questions.hint: What exactly was swapped?

questions.q: Clients call pause on a media player. A new state class, Buffering, is added to the player. What must the clients change?
options: Every call to pause, so that it names the new state
Only the clients that run on slow networks, where buffering is common
The clients must be recompiled with a copy of the state classes
Nothing, since they talk only to the player, not to its states
optionExplain: Clients never name states in their calls.
Network speed is not the matter.
States are internal to the context.
Clients deal with the context, which hides the state objects.
questions.explain: The context's hiding of states lets states change freely.
questions.rule: Clients depend on the context, not its states.
questions.teaches: Because clients see only the context, states can be added, removed or reshuffled without client code changing.

questions.q: True or false: The State and Strategy patterns have noticeably different class diagrams.
questions.explain: Their diagrams are essentially the same; what differs is the intent. The card next sets out the difference.
questions.rule: Same diagram, different intent.

questions.q: Match each question with the answer for the two patterns.
pairs: Strategy: who usually picks the behavior object?
State: who changes the current object over time?
The context, as its own state changes
Strategy: it is a flexible alternative to
State: it is an alternative to many
questions.explain: In Strategy the client configures; in State the context moves through states. The last two pairs name the problems each replaces.
questions.rule: Strategy is client-configured; State is context-driven.

questions.q: A context holds an interface reference with several implementations. Does that diagram alone tell you which pattern it is?
options: No, both patterns have this shape, so the intent has to decide
Yes, because only the State pattern uses an interface reference
Yes, because only the Strategy pattern lets the object be swapped
No, because neither pattern makes use of an interface at all
optionExplain: The structure is shared, so you must ask who sets the object and why.
Strategy has an interface reference too.
State swaps objects as well.
Both patterns use an interface.
questions.explain: Look at how the object is chosen and changed.
questions.rule: Ask who picks the object and why.
questions.teaches: A class diagram cannot identify a pattern whose twin has the same shape; to name it you ask who sets the delegate and whether it changes along fixed transitions.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it is closer to Strategy or to State.

items.t: A route planner is given a walking or driving method by the user and keeps it
A parcel answers cancel differently as Packed, Shipped or Delivered
A sorting tool is given a comparison rule by its caller
A vending panel moves itself from Idle to Paying to Dispensing
A text box is configured with a spell-check method at setup
A loan file moves from Submitted to Reviewed to Approved by itself

questions.explain: Where the client chooses a method, it is Strategy. Where the object moves through stages by its own transitions, it is State.
questions.rule: Client-chosen is Strategy; self-driven is State.

questions.q: A context starts with one behavior object, and as events occur each object hands over to the next along a fixed set of transitions. Which pattern's intent is this?
options: Strategy, because the behavior objects share an interface
State, because behavior changes along well-defined transitions
Neither, because a context is not able to swap its behavior objects
Strategy, because swapping is done at run time
optionExplain: Sharing an interface is true of both patterns.
Moving along defined transitions as internal state changes is the mark of State.
A context can swap objects in both.
Strategy can swap at run time, but does not rely on transitions.
questions.explain: Fixed transitions point to State.
questions.rule: Same structure, different intent: in Strategy the client configures the behavior, in State the context moves itself through states.
questions.hint: Which pattern builds in well-defined transitions?

questions.q: A game enemy is given an aggressive or cautious plan by a level designer and keeps it. Later the designers want it to switch plans by itself, depending on its health, along set rules. How does the design's intent change?
options: It stays Strategy, as the plans are still interchangeable objects
It moves from Strategy toward State, as the enemy drives its transitions
It moves from State toward Strategy, as the plans are objects
It stops being a pattern at all, as the enemy now decides for itself
optionExplain: Interchangeable plans are in both; the new part is self-driven switching.
Once the object moves itself between behaviors by rules, the intent is State.
The designer no longer picks, so it moves the other way.
An object that decides for itself is exactly the State intent.
questions.explain: Self-driven switching along set rules is State.
questions.rule: Self-driven switching along set rules is State.
questions.teaches: The same code can move from Strategy to State when its requirement shifts from behavior assigned from outside to transitions driven by the object itself.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is Strategy mainly a flexible alternative to?
options: Interfaces, because an interface cannot hold any code of its own
Conditionals, because states are not allowed in that pattern
Factories, because they tend to create too many objects
Subclassing, because inheritance fixes behavior in place
optionExplain: Strategy uses interfaces itself.
Conditionals on state are what State replaces.
Factories are not discussed here.
Inheritance leaves you stuck with the inherited behavior; Strategy lets you swap it.
questions.explain: Strategy replaces inheritance for behavior. The card next adds State's counterpart.
questions.rule: Strategy is an alternative to subclassing.

questions.q: The authors call State an alternative to lots of ____ in the context.
questions.explain: Encapsulating behavior in state objects replaces the conditionals that tested the state.
questions.rule: State replaces state conditionals.

questions.q: What does the Q&A say happens to an application with a lot of state if separate state objects are not used?
options: It ends up with large conditionals that are hard to maintain
It ends up with faster code, but with more memory in use at run time
It ends up with fewer classes and no loss of clarity
It ends up with states that the clients must set for themselves
optionExplain: Large conditionals are the alternative the authors warn against.
Speed is not the point made.
Fewer classes is true, but clarity is lost.
Clients do not set states in either case.
questions.explain: Objects make states explicit and easier to follow.
questions.rule: Objects make states explicit.
questions.teaches: Representing each state as an object makes the states explicit in the code, which reduces the effort of understanding and maintaining it.

questions.q: A tax calculator has one subclass per country, and a user needs to switch country while the program runs. Which approach does the authors' reasoning point to?
options: State: add conditionals that test the country each time a rule is used
More subclasses: one subclass for each pair of countries involved
Strategy: hold a rules object for the country and swap it by composition
Neither: the user should restart the program to change country
optionExplain: Conditionals are what State is meant to replace.
More subclasses keep the behavior fixed by type.
Inheritance locks the country in; composing with a rules object lets it change.
Run-time change is exactly what Strategy supports.
questions.explain: Inheritance sticks; composition swaps.
questions.rule: Compose when behavior must change.

questions.q: True or false: If the tax calculator's country is chosen once and does not need to change, the case for replacing subclassing weakens.
questions.explain: Being stuck with a behavior is a problem only when the behavior has to change.
questions.rule: The argument applies where change is needed.
questions.hint: When is inheritance a problem?

questions.q: A document editor has modes Editing, ReadOnly and Locked. A colleague proposes subclasses of Document for each mode. Why is State objects the better fit?
options: Subclasses cannot override any method that the base class defines
State objects need fewer classes than the subclass approach does
One document can change mode over time; a creation-time subclass cannot
Modes are only data, so they must not be made into classes
optionExplain: Subclasses can override methods.
State usually needs more classes, not fewer.
A subclass fixes the mode when the object is created; swapping a state object lets the same document change mode.
The chapter treats states as classes.
questions.explain: The mode must change while the object lives.
questions.rule: Use state objects when the same object must change mode.
questions.teaches: Subclassing ties a mode to the creation of the object, whereas swapping a state object lets one and the same object change mode during its life.

questions.q: In the State Pattern, where can the logic for state transitions live?
options: In the context or in the state classes; the pattern allows either
Only in the state classes, as the pattern requires it of every design
Only in the context, as clients need to see where it goes next
Only in a separate table that neither of them owns
optionExplain: The authors' design puts it in the states, and they say the context can do it instead.
The authors say states do not always decide.
Nothing requires the context to decide.
No separate table is described.
questions.explain: Either place works; the card next explains how to choose.
questions.rule: Transitions can live in either place.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, only the concrete state classes can decide which state comes next.
questions.explain: They say the alternative is to let the Context decide the flow.
questions.rule: States are one option, not a requirement.

questions.q: A team keeps all transitions in the context. A new state is added. Which class is edited to add the arrows into and out of it?
options: Every existing state class, since each one has arrows
Only the client that uses the context
None, because the new state class holds its own arrows
The context, since it holds all the transitions
optionExplain: Existing states would hold no transition logic in that design.
Clients do not hold transitions.
The new class cannot hold arrows from other states.
With transitions in the context, the context changes and the state classes stay closed.
questions.explain: The place of transitions decides what is edited.
questions.rule: The home of the transitions is what you edit.
questions.teaches: The home chosen for transitions decides which classes stay closed to modification as the system evolves: the context if they live in the states, the state classes if they live in the context.

questions.q: A transit system is being designed. Sort each need by where its transitions suit best, using the authors' guideline.

items.t: A door that always goes Closed, Opening, Open, Closing
A lift that picks its next move from live requests
A fixed boarding sequence of check-in, security, gate
A ticket gate whose next state depends on a card balance
A signal that cycles Red, Green, Yellow on a timer
A booth that closes when the queue count reaches zero

questions.explain: Transitions that follow a fixed order suit the context; those that depend on run-time data suit the state classes.
questions.rule: Fixed order to the context; run-time choice to the states.

questions.q: A traffic light with a fixed Red, Green, Yellow cycle now skips Yellow when an emergency sensor reading arrives. Where do the transitions best go now?
options: In the context, as the cycle of the light is still mostly fixed
In the state classes, as the next state depends on run-time data
In the clients, who are the ones that know when an emergency occurs
In a global file that every light in the city reads
optionExplain: A choice that depends on data no longer fits a fixed order.
Once the next state depends on live data, the guideline moves the choice to the states.
Clients should not drive the states.
A global file adds no support.
questions.explain: The guideline depends on whether transitions are fixed.
questions.rule: Put fixed transitions in the context and dynamic ones in the states, and weigh the dependencies that each choice creates.
questions.hint: Is the order of states still fixed?

questions.q: Two developers disagree: one wants transitions in the states for locality, the other wants them in the machine for fewer dependencies. What is the most useful way for them to settle it?
options: Let the more senior developer decide the matter, since the choice is only one of taste
Count how many lines each placement takes in code, then pick the shorter one
Try both placements and ship whichever of them the first client prefers
Name what is at stake and compare the changes you expect
optionExplain: Seniority gives no reasons, and the choice is a trade-off, not taste.
Line count is not the issue the authors raise.
Clients do not judge internal structure.
The authors treat it as a trade-off with stated costs, so the issue should be defined and reasons weighed.
questions.explain: A disagreement about design is settled by defining the issue and weighing reasons.
questions.rule: Define the issue, then weigh reasons.
questions.teaches: A design disagreement is settled by defining the issue and weighing reasons against the changes you expect, not by declaring one placement the winner.

questions.q: True or false: In the State Pattern, clients usually call the state objects directly.
questions.explain: Requests to the states come from the context, not from clients. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Clients talk to the context only.

questions.q: Under the State Pattern, requests to the state objects come from the ____, not from clients.
questions.explain: The context oversees its state and does not want a client changing it without the context's knowledge.
questions.rule: The context owns its state.

questions.q: Under what condition can many contexts share the same state objects?
options: When every context is in the same state at the same time
When the state objects keep no internal context of their own
When all of the contexts are created within a single second of one another
When the state objects are created by the clients that use the contexts
optionExplain: Sharing does not require contexts to match.
A state that remembers nothing about a particular context can serve all of them.
Timing plays no role.
Clients do not create state objects.
questions.explain: The states must be free of per-context data.
questions.rule: Shared states hold no per-context data.
questions.teaches: A shared state that needs the context's data or methods must be handed the context as a parameter on each call, since it cannot hold a reference to just one.

questions.q: A game has 500 enemies, each in Idle, Chase or Flee states, and memory is tight. Which design follows the authors' advice?
options: Make each state object once, share it, and pass the enemy into each call
Make three new state objects for every single enemy that spawns in the game
Make one state object per enemy and let the clients set it directly
Make one Enemy class per state and then copy each of them 500 times
optionExplain: Shared state objects save memory and receive the enemy as a parameter.
That is 1,500 state objects, where 3 would do.
Clients do not set states directly.
Copying classes does not suit the pattern.
questions.explain: Share the state objects, pass the context.
questions.rule: Share states and pass the context.

questions.q: A shared Chase state keeps a field recording which enemy it last chased. Two enemies share that object. What goes wrong?
options: The state object cannot be created a second time for the other enemy
Both enemies stop accepting any action from the game loop
Data about one enemy leaks into the behavior of the other
The field is cleared when the enemy is destroyed
optionExplain: Only one object is created in a shared design.
Actions still work, but with wrong data.
A shared object with per-context data mixes up the contexts.
No such clearing occurs.
questions.explain: Shared states must not remember a context.
questions.rule: Clients talk only to the context, and state objects can be shared among contexts if they keep no context data of their own.
questions.hint: How many enemies does the field describe?

questions.q: A toll plaza system has many booths, each Open, Busy or Closed, and shares its state objects. Which statements fit the authors' advice? Select all that apply.
options: The state objects are stored in static variables
Each state method receives the booth it acts on
A state object keeps a count of cars for its booth
Drivers may set a booth's state directly
optionExplain: Shared states are typically assigned to static instance variables.
The booth is passed in so that the shared state can reach its data.
A per-booth count must stay in the booth, not in a shared state.
Clients are not meant to set the state of a context.
questions.explain: Sharing works when per-booth data stays in the booth and is reached through the reference passed in.
questions.rule: Per-context data stays in the context.
questions.teaches: Sharing turns state objects into stateless helpers: anything that differs between contexts, such as a count, must be kept in the context and reached through the reference passed in.

questions.q: True or false: Using the State Pattern usually increases the number of classes in a design.
questions.explain: Each state becomes a class. The card next shows how the authors weigh this cost.
questions.rule: More classes are part of the cost.

questions.q: The authors describe the extra classes as the price you pay for ____.
questions.explain: They grant that the pattern adds classes and call this the price of flexibility, worth paying for code that will last.
questions.rule: Grant the cost, then weigh it.

questions.q: How can the extra state classes be kept out of the way of clients?
options: By making them package visible, so only the package sees them
By merging all of the state classes into the context class again
By giving every state class exactly the same name as the others
By having the clients create the state classes only when they are needed
optionExplain: What matters is the number of classes clients see, and package visibility hides the rest.
Merging would bring back the problem the pattern solved.
Names would collide and add confusion.
Clients are meant to stay out of the states.
questions.explain: Hiding turns a visible cost into a private one.
questions.rule: Hide the extra classes from clients.
questions.teaches: The cost of extra classes falls mostly on clients who must learn them, so hiding the state classes behind the context makes the cost of the pattern largely private.

questions.q: A developer is writing a script for a trade-show demo that will be discarded afterwards. It has three states. What would the authors' advice suggest?
options: State classes are required, as the pattern always pays back its cost
State classes are forbidden, as scripts have to be kept in one file
State classes are needed only if the clients are able to see them
State classes are optional, since the code will not live to be changed
optionExplain: The advice assumes the code will live and change.
The authors forbid nothing of the kind.
Visibility affects cost, not the choice for a throwaway.
The authors' advice has an exception for one-off code that will be thrown away.
questions.explain: Predict the code's life before paying for flexibility.
questions.rule: Pay for flexibility when the code will change.

questions.q: True or false: A throwaway script that unexpectedly lives for years and gains new states makes the extra state classes more worthwhile.
questions.explain: The exception applied to code that is thrown away; with repeated change the benefit of flexibility grows.
questions.rule: The verdict follows the code's expected life.
questions.hint: What did the exception for one-offs depend on?

questions.q: A critic says: State is bloat, six classes where one would do. Which reply is best argued?
options: It denies the cost and says that the six classes come entirely free of charge
It grants the cost, then compares it with the alternative's cost
It dismisses the critic as someone who is inexperienced with design patterns
It repeats that design patterns are better than plain code in every case
optionExplain: Denying a true cost loses credibility.
A fair reply admits what is true in the objection and weighs it against the alternative.
Attacking the critic gives no reason.
A blanket claim does not answer the particular cost.
questions.explain: Concede the real cost, then compare costs.
questions.rule: Concede what is true, then weigh.
questions.teaches: A fair reply to an objection about cost grants the cost and compares it with the cost of the alternative, instead of denying the cost or attacking the critic.

questions.q: Why did the authors implement State as an interface in the gumball machine?
options: Interfaces are faster than abstract classes in every case that comes up
An abstract class cannot be extended or used by any state class
They had no common functionality to put into an abstract class
The pattern forbids the use of abstract classes in its diagram
optionExplain: Speed is not the reason given.
States can extend an abstract class.
With nothing shared, an interface was all that was needed.
The diagram actually shows an abstract class.
questions.explain: Nothing to share, so an interface. The card next explains when that changes.
questions.rule: Use an interface while states share no code, and an abstract State class when they repeat default behavior or methods may be added later.

questions.q: True or false: The State Pattern's class diagram shows State as an abstract class, although the gumball code used an interface.
questions.explain: The authors note this difference and say you might prefer an abstract class in your own implementation.
questions.rule: The diagram and the code may differ in this detail.

questions.q: What benefit does an abstract State class have over an interface, in the authors' Q&A?
options: It lets the context choose its states without using any delegation
Methods can be added later without breaking the concrete state classes
It stops the clients from ever calling the state objects directly
It removes the need for there to be any concrete state classes
optionExplain: Delegation is still needed.
An abstract class can supply a default for a new method, so existing states still work.
Hiding states from clients is a separate matter.
Concrete states are still the ones that give behavior.
questions.explain: A default body means old subclasses need no edit.
questions.rule: A default method body protects existing subclasses.
questions.teaches: An abstract base class can supply a default body for a new method, so adding a method does not force every existing state class to be edited.

questions.q: A notification module has states Queued, Sending and Failed. Four of five actions get the same generic reply in nearly every state. What do the authors suggest?
options: Keep an interface and copy the same reply into each of the state classes
Merge the three states into a single class that uses branches
Make State an abstract class holding generic replies for states to inherit
Give every client that uses the module its own copy of the reply
optionExplain: Copying keeps the duplication.
Merging brings back the conditionals.
The duplicated replies move into the base class as defaults.
Copying to clients spreads the duplication wider.
questions.explain: Shared default replies go in a base class.
questions.rule: Move repeated default replies up.

questions.q: A new action is added to a State interface implemented by ten state classes. The number of classes that must be edited is ____.
questions.explain: An interface method must be implemented by every class, so all ten are edited; with an abstract default, none would have to be.
questions.rule: An interface forces every implementation to change.
questions.hint: Who supplies the body for the new method?

questions.q: A banking app's states refuse actions with messages that customers read. Is one generic inherited message adequate?
options: Yes, since a generic message suits every customer in every state
Yes, since refusals are not shown to anyone who uses the app
No, since an abstract class is not able to hold any messages
Not necessarily; customer-facing refusals may need wording per state
optionExplain: The authors' reasoning rested on the message not being seen.
Here the messages are shown.
An abstract class can hold default replies.
The authors justify a generic reply because customers will not see it; if they do, the case weakens.
questions.explain: The generic reply suits messages nobody reads.
questions.rule: Generic replies suit messages that nobody reads.
questions.teaches: Generic inherited replies are justified when no user sees them; when refusals are user-facing, a base class should supply only a default that states can override.

questions.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game
questions.q: In the redesigned machine, what is the main step in adding the 1-in-10 game?
options: Add a state class for winners and a transition into it
Add a branch to each of the existing action methods
Add an integer constant and edit the machine's conditionals
Add a second machine class that handles only the contest
optionExplain: A new behavior is a new state, plus a way to reach it.
That is how the first design would have been edited.
Integers and conditionals belong to the first design.
That duplicates the machine instead of adding one state.
questions.explain: Add a state. The card next shows the details.
questions.rule: Add a state class and a transition into it.

questions.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game
questions.q: Match each part of the contest change with where it went.
