pairs: The new behavior of releasing two gumballs
The random draw and the transition to winning
The has-quarter state, where the crank is turned
The way the machine knows the new state
A new state variable in the GumballMachine class
questions.explain: The behavior has its own class, the draw sits where the crank is turned, and the machine holds the new state object.
questions.rule: New state class, new link, new variable.

questions.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game
questions.q: Why is the chance game placed in the has-quarter state?
options: It is the state that holds the largest number of gumballs
It is the only state class that has a constructor in the design
That is the state in which the customer turns the crank
It is the oldest state class that was written in the design
optionExplain: Gumball counts are not the reason.
Every state class has a constructor.
The draw decides what the crank does, so it goes where the crank is handled.
Age plays no part.
questions.explain: Put the decision where the action is handled.
questions.rule: Put the new transition where the triggering action is handled.
questions.teaches: A new transition belongs in the state that handles the triggering action, which decides whether to go to the old next state or the new one.

questions.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game
questions.q: A parking meter has states Waiting, Paid and Expired. A promotion lets one payer in twenty park free. What does the authors' approach suggest?
options: Add a flag to the meter and then test it in every action method
Rewrite Paid so that it sometimes charges the driver nothing
Add a new meter class for every promotion that is run
Add a FreeParkState, reached by a chance draw in Waiting
optionExplain: A flag tested in every method brings back the scattered conditionals.
That mixes two behaviors in one state.
A meter class per promotion does not follow the design.
A new state for the new behavior, reached from the state that handles the coin.
questions.explain: New behavior, new state.
questions.rule: New behavior means a new state.

questions.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game
questions.q: The promotion changes to one payer in five. The number of state classes whose chance code changes is ____.
questions.explain: The odds live in the one state that does the draw, so only that class changes.
questions.rule: A local rule changes in one place.
questions.hint: Where does the draw live?

questions.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game
questions.q: The parking meter now needs a new action that every state must answer, such as extend time. How much of the design is edited?
options: Every state class gains a method, a larger change than adding a state
Only the new state class, as with the promotion
Only the meter class, which forwards the call to its state
None, since the interface adapts to new actions by itself
optionExplain: A new action touches the whole interface and all of its implementations.
The promotion added a state; this adds an action.
The meter forwards but each state must answer.
Interfaces do not adapt by themselves.
questions.explain: The design makes new states cheap and new actions costly.
questions.rule: New states are cheap; new actions touch every state.
questions.teaches: The state design makes adding a state cheap but adding an action costly, because a new action means a new method in the interface and in every state class.

questions.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.
questions.q: Two state classes differ only in that one releases two gumballs rather than one. What is the best argument for merging them into one class?
options: It makes each state easier to read
It removes duplicated code
It gives each class a single responsibility
It makes the contest easier to remove later
optionExplain: Merging mixes two cases and lowers clarity.
Merging saves the near-identical code in two classes.
Merging gives the merged class two responsibilities.
A merged class makes removal harder.
questions.explain: Merging saves code but costs something. The card next names the cost.
questions.rule: Treat one state class or two as a trade-off between duplicated code and a class with two responsibilities, and decide with reasons.

questions.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.
questions.q: Which costs do the authors name for merging the winner behavior into the sold state? Select all that apply.
options: One class would represent two states, so clarity suffers
The sold state would take on two responsibilities
The merged class would run noticeably slower
The merged class could no longer be compiled
optionExplain: They say the winner and non-winner states would be mixed in one class.
They cite the principle one class, one responsibility.
Speed is never raised.
Compilation is not raised.
questions.explain: The costs are about clarity and responsibility, not speed or compilation.
questions.rule: Merging costs clarity and single responsibility.

questions.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.
questions.q: The authors ask what happens when the promotion ends. What does the question test?
options: Whether the machine can still dispense a single gumball to a customer
Whether contest code must be removed from a class serving ordinary sales
Whether the customers will remember the contest after it has ended
Whether the random draw of the winner can be made more fair
optionExplain: Single gumballs are not the issue.
If the contest code is mixed into the sold state, ending the contest means editing the state that serves everyone.
Customer memory is not the issue.
Fairness of the draw is a different matter.
questions.explain: Ask what happens when the requirement ends.
questions.rule: Ask what happens when the requirement ends.
questions.teaches: Asking what happens when a temporary requirement ends is a quick test of whether it deserves its own class, since a separate class can simply be removed.

questions.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.
questions.q: A store app has a Checkout state, and a Black Friday Checkout that differs only in a 20 percent discount. Which argument fits the authors' reasoning for keeping it separate?
options: The two checkouts have almost the same code, so they must be kept separate
Separate classes run faster than merged ones do in every program
A discount cannot be applied inside a class that holds other rules too
The discount is temporary, so its class can be removed when the sale ends
optionExplain: Near-identical code is the argument for merging, not for separating.
Speed is not part of the authors' reasoning.
A discount can be applied wherever the checkout is.
A promotion that will end is a reason to isolate it.
questions.explain: Isolate what will end.
questions.rule: Isolate behavior that is expected to end.

questions.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.
questions.q: True or false: If the contest were permanent and its stakes stayed fixed, the argument for a separate winner class would lose some of its force.
questions.explain: The authors' question about the promotion ending would no longer apply, leaving clarity as the main reason.
questions.rule: The weight of the argument depends on expected change.
questions.hint: Which of their questions would stop applying?

questions.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.
questions.q: An email tool has a Sent state and a SentWithReceipt state that differs by one extra step. Which statement judges the trade-off best?
options: Merging saves code but mixes two cases; ask how likely the receipt step is to change alone
Merging is correct, because duplicate code is the worst fault a design can have
Separating is correct, because having more classes is always the better choice
Neither choice matters at all, because the tool still works for its users
optionExplain: It names both sides of the trade-off and a fact that would settle it.
That treats one cost as decisive without argument.
That treats one benefit as decisive without argument.
Working code today does not settle the cost of change.
questions.explain: Name both costs, then ask which change you expect.
questions.rule: Name both costs, then ask which change you expect.
questions.teaches: When two considerations pull in opposite directions, the deciding fact is which change you expect, so a sound judgment names that expected change instead of ranking one consideration above the other.

questions.q: In the state design, where does a new refill action go?
options: Into the machine class only, with a branch for each of the states
Into the sold-out state only, since it alone needs it
Into the State interface, and each state class implements it
Into the clients, who then call each of the states directly
optionExplain: That brings back the branching.
The other states must still answer if the machine delegates.
A new action is a new interface method, so every state must answer it.
Clients do not call the states.
questions.explain: Every state answers every action. The card next shows the authors' solution.
questions.rule: A new action goes into the State interface and every state answers it, while the context updates its data and then delegates.

questions.q: Put the steps of the authors' refill in order.
items: Code calls refill on the machine
The machine adds the gumballs to its count
The machine calls refill on its current state
If the machine was sold out, that state moves it to No Quarter
questions.explain: The machine updates the count and delegates to the state, which decides whether the state changes.
questions.rule: Count first, then delegate.

questions.q: Why does the machine's refill both update the count and call the state's refill?
options: The state cannot read any data, so the machine has to do it all itself
Calling the state is optional, and is only done for the purpose of logging
The count belongs to the machine; what a refill means depends on the state
The count must be stored in two places, for safety
optionExplain: States can read the machine's data through its reference.
The call to the state is where the state changes.
Data stays in the context and behavior goes to the state, as in the rest of the design.
Nothing suggests duplicating the count.
questions.explain: The context handles data; the state handles meaning.
questions.rule: Data in the context, meaning in the state.
questions.teaches: A new action usually splits into a data part handled by the context and a behavior part handled by the state, which is how the design keeps data and behavior apart.

questions.q: A ticket kiosk gains addPaper. Following the authors' solution, what happens?
options: addPaper joins the interface; OutOfPaper moves to Idle; others stay put
addPaper is added to the kiosk only, with a branch for each state
Every state moves the kiosk to Idle when paper is added to it
OutOfPaper alone implements addPaper, as no other state needs it
optionExplain: Every state implements the new method; only the dead-end state reacts.
That brings back state branching.
A mid-print state would be disturbed.
The interface requires every class to implement it.
questions.explain: Only the dead-end state reacts.
questions.rule: Only the dead-end state reacts to the recovery action.

questions.q: True or false: If refill is called while the gumball machine is in the has-quarter state, the count rises and the state stays the same.
questions.explain: Only the sold-out state moves the machine on; the has-quarter state does nothing for refill.
questions.rule: Outside sold out, refill only adds gumballs.
questions.hint: Which state reacts to refill?

questions.q: A pantry app's restock(n) first calls the current state's restock, which moves from Empty to Ready only if the count is above zero, and then adds n to the count. What goes wrong?
options: The state is called twice and so it moves to Ready twice over
The count rises twice, once per call
Nothing goes wrong at all, since the order of the two steps does not matter
The state sees the old count of zero and may stay Empty
optionExplain: The state is called once.
The count is updated once.
Here the state's decision uses the count, so order matters.
The authors update the count first, then delegate, so the state sees the new data.
questions.explain: Update the data first, then delegate.
questions.rule: Update the context's data first, then delegate.
questions.teaches: When a state's decision depends on context data, the context must update that data before delegating, so that the state acts on the new value.

questions.q: A turnstile moves only on the pairings its code lists. What does this program print?
options: OPEN OPEN LOCKED LOCKED
LOCKED OPEN OPEN LOCKED
LOCKED OPEN LOCKED OPEN
LOCKED OPEN OPEN OPEN
optionExplain: Picks this if every action is believed to cause a move. The first push, in LOCKED, matches no pairing and changes nothing.
Right: push while LOCKED and coin while OPEN match no pairing, so the state stays; the other two actions move it.
Picks this if the turnstile is believed to toggle on every action. The second coin, in OPEN, has no pairing and changes nothing.
Picks this if the last push is believed to be refused. Push in OPEN is a listed pairing, so it moves to LOCKED.
questions.explain: The method returns a new state only for the pairings LOCKED with coin and OPEN with push. Any other pairing returns the current state, so the printed states are LOCKED, OPEN, OPEN, LOCKED.
questions.rule: A transition exists only where a state and an action are paired; every other pairing needs its own decision.

questions.q: Trace the conditional machine below. What does this program print?
options: ok ok back none
ok no back back
ok no back none
ok no none none
optionExplain: Picks this if a second quarter is believed to be accepted. In HAS_Q the insert method takes its else branch and prints no.
Picks this if eject is believed to work in any state. After the first eject the state is NO_Q, so the else branch prints none.
Right: the first insert moves to HAS_Q, the second is refused, eject moves back, and the second eject finds no quarter.
Picks this if eject is believed to fail after a refused insert. The state is still HAS_Q then, so the first eject succeeds.
questions.explain: Each action method tests the single state variable. Insert from NO_Q prints ok and sets HAS_Q; insert from HAS_Q prints no; eject from HAS_Q prints back and resets; eject from NO_Q prints none.
questions.rule: In the conditional recipe, the state variable plus the branches inside each action method decide everything.

questions.q: The machine has four states: No Quarter, Has Quarter, Sold, Sold Out. What is the fault in insertQuarter?
options: It sets the state before the message prints, so a customer might never see the message
It tests HAS_Q before NO_Q, so the second branch can never be reached in any state
It prints a message in the HAS_Q state, where a customer should not be told anything
It has no branch for SOLD or SOLD_OUT, so in those states the action gets no response
optionExplain: Picks this on the order of the lines. The order does not matter here; the state is set and the message is printed in the same branch.
Picks this on the order of the tests. The two tests exclude each other, so both branches can run.
Picks this on the idea that refusals are silent. A message is a defined response; silence in other states is the gap.
Right: a response must be defined for every state, and a refusal message is also a response.
questions.explain: The method answers only two of the four states. In SOLD and SOLD_OUT nothing is printed and nothing changes, so the pairing was never decided.
questions.rule: Every action needs a defined response in every state; silence is a gap, not a choice.

questions.q: In the first, conditional design, the contest adds a Winner state. What does that cost?
options: Every method that branches on state needs a Winner case
Only the turn-crank method changes, because the draw happens there and nowhere else
Nothing in the old methods changes, because a new constant is enough for them
Only the dispense method changes, because two gumballs are released there
optionExplain: Right: the code is grouped by action, so a new state adds a branch to each method that has to answer for it. Our reading, from the recipe.
Picks this because the draw is in the crank. The other actions must still say what they do in Winner.
Picks this because adding a constant looks like a small edit. Methods that do not know the new value cannot answer for it.
Picks this because the visible difference is in dispensing. The other methods must still answer in the new state.
questions.explain: In the conditional recipe the code is grouped by action, so a new state needs a branch in every action method. Joe's reminder that every action must be checked against the state points the same way. This is our reading of the recipe, not a figure from the book.
questions.rule: When behavior is grouped by action, a new state touches every action method.
questions.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!

questions.q: Match each fault of the first design with the repair the cubicle conversation points to.
questions.explain: Each fault has a matching repair: separate the states, make additions local, and delegate instead of branching.
pairs: Changing one state risks breaking the others
Localize each state's behavior in its own class
A new state would mean many edits to working methods
Add a class and edit only a few transitions
The machine branches on a number to pick behavior
Delegate to an object for the current state
questions.rule: Match the fault to the repair: separate what varies, then delegate to it.

questions.q: Sort each move by the principle it applies: encapsulate what varies, or favor composition.
questions.explain: Moving behavior out of the machine is encapsulation. Holding an object and passing calls to it, or swapping it, is composition.

items.t: Give Paused its own class
Hold a reference to the current state object in a field
Move the reply for an ejected quarter out of the machine branches
Forward play to the object held in that field
Swap the held object to change behavior at run time
Keep Standing and Ducking behavior apart from the rest of the character code

questions.rule: Encapsulation separates the behavior; composition connects the machine to it.

questions.q: A developer applies step two to a door with open and close actions. What happens when this code is compiled?
options: It compiles, and close does nothing in Locked unless someone overrides it
It compiles, and calling close fails with an error only at run time
It compiles, because a state needs only the actions that make sense in it
Compilation fails, because Locked does not implement the close method
optionExplain: Picks this from languages where a missing method is skipped. A Java class that implements an interface must define every method.
Picks this by expecting a late failure. The missing method is caught when the class is compiled.
Picks this from the idea that refusals are optional. Every state must answer every action, so the refusal has to be written.
Right: a state class must implement every method of the interface, even if its reply is a refusal.
questions.explain: Step one gives the interface a method per action, and step two requires each state class to implement all of them. Locked leaves out close, so the compiler rejects it.
questions.rule: A state class answers every action of the interface, including the ones it refuses.

questions.q: Three slots with different states each get an insert call. What does this program print?
options: accepted accepted accepted
rejected accepted rejected
rejected rejected rejected
accepted rejected accepted
optionExplain: Picks this if every insert is believed to run the same code. The class of each object decides the reply.
Right: each call runs the insert method of the object held, and Full and Empty answer differently.
Picks this if the first reply is believed to carry over. Each object answers for itself.
Picks this by reversing the two classes. Full rejects and Empty accepts, in the order the array lists them.
questions.explain: The loop calls insert on three objects. Full prints rejected, Empty prints accepted, and Full prints rejected again.
questions.rule: The same method name, called on different state classes, gives different behavior.
questions.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes

questions.q: States set the next state themselves here. What does this program print?
options: no coin taken refused sold no coin
no coin taken refused sold sold
no coin taken taken sold no coin
taken refused sold no coin no coin
optionExplain: Right: crank in NoQuarter refuses; insert moves to HasQuarter; the second insert is refused; crank sells and returns to NoQuarter; the last crank refuses.
Picks this if the machine stays in HasQuarter after a sale. The sale sets the state back to NoQuarter.
Picks this if a second insert is accepted. After the first insert the state is HasQuarter, which refuses.
Picks this by skipping the first crank. The first call is crank, and the machine starts in NoQuarter.
questions.explain: The state object answers each call and, when needed, replaces the machine's state. The printed words follow the state held at each call.
questions.rule: Each state reply may also set the machine's next state; the next call uses the new one.

questions.q: The machine forwards every call to its state. What happens when this program runs?
options: It prints a refusal, since a machine with no state refuses every action
It does nothing, since a call on an unset state is skipped by Java
It throws a NullPointerException: no current state was set
It fails to compile, because the state field is declared without a value
optionExplain: Picks this from the idea that a missing state means a refusing one. An unset field holds no object that can answer.
Picks this by expecting a quiet skip. Java throws an exception when a method is called on null.
Right: the delegating method calls a method on a state that was never assigned.
Picks this by expecting the compiler to catch it. A field may stay unset, and the problem appears only at run time.
questions.explain: Delegation needs a current state object at all times. The machine must set its starting state, as the book's constructor does, or the first forwarded call fails.
questions.rule: A delegating machine needs a current state object from the start.

questions.q: The authors say each state is now closed for modification while the machine stays open to extension. What does that mean for a new state?
options: Every state class is edited so that it knows about the new state in the design
The machine is rewritten with another branch added for the new state's behavior
New behavior arrives as a new class, and the finished states keep their own behavior
The old state classes are deleted and generated again with the new state included
optionExplain: Picks this from the idea that all states are linked. Only the transitions that lead into the new state may change.
Picks this from the first version. The reworked machine only forwards calls, so it has no state branches.
Right: the authors list this among the gains of the rework.
Picks this from the idea that extension means regeneration. Closed for modification means the opposite.
questions.explain: Closed for modification, open for extension means that new behavior comes as new code. The finished state classes are not reopened to add a state beside them.
questions.rule: New behavior arrives as new state classes; finished ones stay closed.
questions.teaches: The authors list one more gain: each state is closed for modification, and the machine stays open to extension by adding new state classes.
questions.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...

questions.q: A developer says this Document class uses the State Pattern. What is missing?
options: State objects: the mode is a number tested by an if, with no delegation
A getter for the mode, so clients can read which mode the document is in
One subclass of Document for every mode that the document can be in
A static counter that records how many documents have been created so far
optionExplain: Right: the pattern needs the context to hold a state object and delegate to it.
Picks this on encapsulation. A getter does not change how behavior is chosen.
Picks this because subclassing changes behavior too. That is the inheritance route the pattern avoids.
Picks this on bookkeeping. The count has no part in how behavior follows state.
questions.explain: The behavior changes with the mode, but the Document tests a number inside its own method. The pattern puts each mode in a state class and delegates to the current one.
questions.rule: State-dependent behavior alone is not the pattern; the context must delegate to state objects.

questions.q: Ctx swaps its state object. What does this program print for its two lines?
options: Ctx A, then Ctx A
Ctx A, then B B
A A, then B B
Ctx A, then Ctx B
optionExplain: Picks this if flip is believed to do nothing. It assigns a new B object to the field.
Picks this if the context itself is believed to turn into B. The context object keeps its class.
Picks this by expecting both names to track the state. The first name is the context's own class.
Right: the context keeps its class, and only the class of the state object it references changes.
questions.explain: getClass on the context gives Ctx both times. getClass on the referenced state gives A and then B after the swap.
questions.rule: The context keeps its class; the swapped state object only gives the appearance of a change.

questions.q: A reviewer sees a Strategy diagram and a State diagram with identical boxes and arrows and calls one a copy error. What is wrong with that call?
options: Nothing is wrong, because two matching diagrams show the same pattern drawn twice
The patterns share a structure and differ in intent, so matching is expected
The diagrams differ in the interface name, which the reviewer should have compared
State diagrams carry a counter that the Strategy diagram leaves out of its boxes
optionExplain: Picks this by reading a diagram as the pattern. The diagrams match, but the patterns do not.
Right: the authors say the two class diagrams are essentially the same.
Picks this by looking for a label difference. The authors place the difference in intent, not in naming.
Picks this by inventing a visible mark. The authors point to no such feature of either diagram.
questions.explain: The authors admit the class diagrams are essentially the same. They tell the patterns apart by intent: who picks the behavior object and whether it changes along set transitions.
questions.rule: Same diagram, different intent: ask who sets the delegate and why.

questions.q: A caller hands Duck its behavior when creating it, and nothing changes it afterwards. Which pattern's intent is this?
options: State, since Duck delegates to a field whose type is an interface
Strategy, since the client picks the behavior and the Duck keeps it
State, since two classes implement the interface that the Duck holds
Neither, since the Duck class has no subclasses and uses no conditionals
optionExplain: Picks this from the shared structure. Delegation to an interface appears in both patterns.
Right: in Strategy the client usually specifies the object the context is composed with.
Picks this from the number of implementations. Both patterns have several implementations.
Picks this by taking the missing subclasses as no pattern. Composition with an interchangeable object is Strategy.
questions.explain: The creator chooses the behavior and the Duck never swaps it by itself along transitions. That is the Strategy intent, even though the structure matches State.
questions.rule: If the client chooses the delegate and it stays, think Strategy; if the context moves along transitions, think State.

questions.q: An order page has long if chains over Placed, Paid and Shipped in each handler. Which pattern does the authors' reasoning point to?
options: Strategy, since handlers could be swapped by the page for each order
Strategy, since subclassing orders by status would lock in the behavior
State, since conditionals on the order's own state pile up
Neither, since conditionals are the authors' preferred remedy for statuses
optionExplain: Picks this because Strategy also swaps objects. Here the order's own state, not the client, drives the choice.
Picks this from the subclassing problem. The order must move between statuses, which subclassing cannot do.
Right: the authors present State as the alternative to lots of conditionals in the context.
Picks this by reversing the authors' view. They warn about very large conditionals that are hard to maintain.
questions.explain: The problem is conditionals on the object's own state, spread over several handlers. The authors name State as the alternative to such conditionals.
questions.rule: Conditionals on internal state call for State; behavior fixed by inheritance calls for Strategy.

questions.q: Which are consequences of putting the transitions in the state classes, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Dynamic moves, such as one that depends on the gumball count, suit the states; the price is dependencies between state classes. Clients play no part, and the context still holds the current state.
options: It suits dynamic moves that depend on run-time data, such as the gumball count
It creates dependencies between the state classes
Clients must choose each next state for the machine
The context no longer needs to hold a current state
optionExplain: Right: the authors give the gumball count as the case where the states decide.
Right: the authors name this as the disadvantage of the placement.
Fails: clients do not change the state of a context.
Fails: the context still holds the current state object; only the decision moved.
questions.rule: Transitions in the states suit dynamic moves, at the price of coupling the states.

questions.q: One Open object is shared by all booths and keeps a car count. What does this program print?
options: A1 B1 A2
A1 B1 A1
A3 B3 A3
A1 B2 A3
optionExplain: Picks this if each booth is believed to have its own count. There is only one Open object, so one cars field.
Picks this if the count is believed to reset on each call. The field keeps its value between calls.
Picks this by printing the final count each time. Each line prints the count at that moment.
Right: the single shared object keeps one count for all booths.
questions.explain: All three calls reach the same object, so cars rises from 1 to 3. Data about one booth ends up mixed with the others, which is why shared states must not hold such data.
questions.rule: A shared state object must not keep data that belongs to one context.

questions.q: In package lib, GumballMachine is public and SoldState has no modifier. Which of them can code in another package use?
options: Only GumballMachine, so clients never see the state classes
Both, since every class in a library is open to all of its users
Only SoldState, since the state classes are the library's main interface
Neither, since a class has to be named in an import before it is usable
optionExplain: Right: package visibility hides SoldState from other packages, which is how the authors hide extra classes.
Picks this by assuming that classes are open by default. A class without public is limited to its own package.
Picks this by mixing up the roles. Clients talk to the context, and the states are the hidden part.
Picks this from the import rule. An import works only for public classes.
questions.explain: A class without a modifier is package visible, so code outside lib cannot name SoldState. Clients use only the public GumballMachine, and the extra classes stay private to the package.
questions.rule: Package visibility hides the extra state classes from clients.

questions.q: Sending overrides only insert. What does this program print?
options: refuse insert, then refuse eject
take, then nothing at all
take, then a compile error for eject
take, then refuse eject
optionExplain: Picks this if the base replies always win. A subclass method replaces the default.
Picks this if an unoverridden method does nothing. An abstract class with a body gives subclasses a default.
Picks this from the interface rule. An abstract class with an eject body needs no override.
Right: Sending supplies its own insert and inherits the default eject.
questions.explain: Abstract State holds default replies. Sending replaces insert and inherits eject, so a state only writes the methods that differ.
questions.rule: An abstract State class lets states inherit defaults and override only what differs.

questions.q: Put the steps of one crank turn with the contest in order.
questions.explain: The has-quarter state handles the crank, runs the draw, and sets the next state; the chosen state then releases the gumballs.
items: The crank is turned while the machine is in the has-quarter state
The has-quarter state runs the chance draw
On a win it sets the current state to the winner state
The winner state releases two gumballs
questions.rule: The draw lives in the state that handles the crank; the winner state does the extra dispensing.
questions.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game

questions.q: The authors want winner and sold kept as two classes, yet the two repeat code. What do they suggest?
options: Merge them after all, because duplicate code is the worse of the two costs
Make State an abstract class with default behavior that both states inherit
Copy the repeated lines into the machine so both states call them from there
Delete the winner state's methods and let the sold state answer for both
optionExplain: Picks this by ranking duplication first. The authors call the choice a trade-off and offer a way out of it.
Right: the sanity check proposes this to clean up duplicate code in the sold and winning states.
Picks this to centralize the code. The authors place the shared defaults in the State type instead.
Picks this to cut size. That is the merge, with the loss of clarity the authors warn about.
questions.explain: Merging and keeping apart are not the only choices. An abstract State class holds the shared defaults, so each state class stays small and the duplicated replies are written once.
questions.rule: Before merging states to cut duplication, move the shared code to a base class.
questions.teaches: The trade-off between duplicated code and clarity is not forced: the authors suggest making State an abstract class with default behavior, so two states can stay separate and still share code.
questions.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.

questions.q: The machine starts sold out and refill(5) is called. What does this program print?
options: to NoQuarter, 5
to NoQuarter, 0
to NoQuarter, 10
optionExplain: Right: the machine adds to its count first and then forwards the call to its state.
Picks this if the state is believed to be skipped. refill ends with a call to the state.
Picks this if the state is believed to run before the count changes. The count line comes first.
Picks this if the amount is believed to be added by both parts. Only the machine changes the count.
questions.explain: The data part (count) is updated in the machine and the behavior part is delegated to the current state. The SoldOut state reports the move to NoQuarter, then main prints the count.
questions.rule: The context updates its data, then delegates the action to the current state.

questions.q: A developer lets the has-quarter state's refill set the machine to No Quarter. A customer's quarter is already in. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing goes wrong, because every state should reset the machine when refilled
The count is lost, because the state replaces the count held by the machine
The inserted quarter is forgotten, since only sold out should move on
The compile fails, because only one state may implement the refill method
optionExplain: Picks this from the exercise wording about resetting. The authors reset only from the sold-out state.
Picks this by mixing data and behavior. The count belongs to the machine and is not touched by a state change.
Right: only the sold-out state moves on refill; elsewhere it does nothing. Our reading of the effect on the quarter.
Picks this by confusing the interface. Every state implements refill.
questions.explain: The authors make refill do nothing in every state except sold out. Moving a has-quarter machine to No Quarter would drop the inserted quarter from the machine's story, which is our reading of the effect.
questions.rule: A new action should change state only where it means something.

questions.q: Has creates its next state with new Sold(). Which change follows the authors' way of limiting dependencies between states?
options: Make Has extend Sold, so that it can reach the Sold class directly
Move crank into Machine and delete Has, so that no state names another
Ask the machine for it with m.getSoldState() and pass that to setState
Call m.setState(null) so that the machine picks a state by itself later
optionExplain: Picks this to avoid new. Inheritance couples the two classes even more tightly.
Picks this to remove the coupling. That returns to a machine that holds the behavior.
Right: the authors fetch state objects through getters on the Context instead of naming concrete classes.
Picks this to hand over the choice. A null state breaks delegation, as the machine then has nothing to forward to.
questions.explain: Naming Sold in the code ties Has to a concrete class. A getter on the machine returns the shared object, so Has needs to know only the machine.
questions.rule: Fetch the next state through a getter on the machine rather than naming its class.

questions.q: Match each phrase of the definition with what it means in the gumball machine.
questions.explain: The definition has three phrases: behavior alters, because the internal state changes, and the class only seems to change.
pairs: The same insert request is accepted in one state and rejected in another
The machine delegates to a different state object
A client sees an object that acts as if it came from another class
questions.rule: The three phrases map to a different response, a different state object and an apparent new class.

questions.q: True or false: To report a machine's gumball count and state, the monitor needs the machine to gain brand-new methods for both.
questions.explain: The machine already offers methods for count and state, so only a location is new. The card next shows how the monitor uses them.
questions.rule: Reuse what the object already offers.

questions.q: To let the CEO tell machines apart, the authors add a ____ field to the GumballMachine class.
questions.explain: The report prints each machine's location along with its inventory and state.
questions.rule: Add only the data the report lacks.

questions.q: What does a GumballMonitor need in order to produce its report?
options: A copy of the machine's source code to read its fields
A reference to a machine whose methods it can call
A list of every machine location stored in the monitor itself
A subclass relationship with GumballMachine
optionExplain: The monitor never reads the source; it calls methods.
Right: the monitor is handed a machine and works through its methods.
The location comes from each machine, so no list is stored in the monitor.
Monitoring is a separate class; inheritance from the machine is not needed.
questions.explain: The monitor depends only on the methods of whatever it is given.
questions.rule: Keep reporting in a separate monitor class that is given a machine and reads it through the machine's existing methods.
questions.teaches: Because the monitor touches the machine only through its methods, any object that offers the same methods could be handed to it in the machine's place.

questions.q: A garden centre has a Greenhouse class with methods for humidity and lamp status. Following the chapter's approach, how should daily reports be produced?
options: Add the report printing and formatting code into the Greenhouse class itself
Make GreenhouseMonitor a subclass of Greenhouse so it can read fields
Copy the humidity and lamp data into a daily file that a script reads
Write a GreenhouseMonitor that is handed a greenhouse and calls its methods
optionExplain: That mixes reporting into the machine; the chapter keeps it in a monitor.
A monitor needs a reference to a greenhouse, not to be one.
A copied file would go stale and bypass the methods the object already offers.
Right: reporting lives in its own class and uses the methods that already exist.
questions.explain: A monitor is given the object and calls its methods.
questions.rule: Give the monitor the object; let it call the methods.

questions.q: True or false: If the report must also show a new field, such as a model number, the monitor class has to change so that it asks for and prints it.
questions.explain: The monitor decides what appears in the report, so a new line in the report means a change there, as well as a getter on the machine.
questions.rule: What the report shows is decided in the monitor.

questions.q: A building has twelve Thermostat objects in one program. How can one ThermostatMonitor report on all twelve, using the chapter's design?
options: Hand it each thermostat in turn, since it uses only shared methods
Create twelve separate monitor subclasses, one for each thermostat
Merge the twelve thermostats into one combined object first
Store every thermostat's readings inside the monitor
optionExplain: Right: a monitor tied to methods, not to one object, can be given any number of thermostats.
One class already handles any thermostat; subclasses add nothing.
Merging loses each thermostat's own location and state.
Stored readings go stale and duplicate what the thermostats already know.
questions.explain: One monitor class can serve many objects with the same methods.
questions.rule: Keep reporting in a separate monitor class that is given a machine and reads it through the machine's existing methods.
questions.teaches: A monitor written against methods, not a particular object, can serve any number of objects that offer those methods.

questions.q: A monitor reads an oven only through its methods. What does this program print?
options: bake at 180
Hot at 220
bake at 220
A compile error, because report expects an Oven and gets a Hot
questions.explain: The monitor calls methods on the object it is given. Hot answers getTemp() with 220 and inherits getMode(), so the report reads bake at 220.
optionExplain: Tempting if the monitor read a fixed value, but it calls getTemp() on the object it was handed, and Hot overrides that method.
The class name is never printed; the report text comes from getMode() and getTemp().
report calls getTemp() on whatever object it receives. Hot overrides it to return 220, and getMode() is inherited as bake.
A Hot is an Oven, so it can be passed where an Oven is expected; nothing fails to compile.
questions.rule: A monitor depends on the methods an object offers, not on one particular class.

questions.q: The first monitor printed correct reports in testing, but the CEO was not satisfied. What is the likeliest reason?
options: The report left out the gumball count
The monitor printed state names in the wrong order
He wants to watch them from his desk
The machines had no location field
optionExplain: The count is part of the report.
Order is not the complaint in the story.
Right: the content is fine; the monitor and the machines share one JVM.
The location field was added for this report.
questions.explain: The card next shows what stands between the CEO and his desk.
questions.rule: Correct code can still be in the wrong place.

questions.q: In Joe's proposal, what happens to the GumballMonitor class?
options: It is rewritten to open network connections itself
It is split into a CEO part and a store part
It stays as it is and is handed a proxy of a machine
It is replaced by the machine's own report method
optionExplain: Joe wants no network code in the monitor.
No split is proposed; the monitor stays one class.
Right: the whole point is to reuse the monitor unchanged.
The machine does not take over reporting.
questions.explain: Keep the monitor; change what it is given.
questions.rule: When working code is in the wrong place, keep it and give it a stand-in for the distant object.

questions.q: Besides leaving the monitor alone, which two jobs does Joe say remain? Select two.
options: Make the gumball machine able to act as a service that accepts network requests
Give the monitor a way to get a reference to a proxy object
Move every machine into the CEO's JVM
Rewrite the machine's state classes
optionExplain: Right: the real machine must listen for requests.
Right: the monitor needs a proxy to be handed.
Moving machines would defeat the point of remote monitoring.
The state classes are not part of Joe's list.
questions.explain: Joe names two remaining tasks: the machine must accept network requests, and the monitor needs a proxy.
questions.rule: When working code is in the wrong place, keep it and give it a stand-in for the distant object.
questions.teaches: Remote access needs work on both ends: the real object must be reachable as a service, and the client needs a way to obtain its stand-in.

questions.q: A hospital's BedReport class prints each Bed's identifier and status inside the ward server program. A manager wants it on a PC in another building. Following Joe, what is the best first move?
options: Keep BedReport and hand it a stand-in for the beds in the ward
Copy every Bed object onto the manager's PC in the other building
Rewrite BedReport so that it opens sockets to the ward by itself
Move the printing code into the Bed class and call it from there
optionExplain: Right: the report logic stays and only the object it reads is replaced by a stand-in.
Copies would go stale and are not the real beds.
That puts network code into code that was fine.
Printing in Bed moves the problem; it does not cross the gap.
questions.explain: Reuse the client code; swap the target for a stand-in.
questions.rule: Swap the target, not the client.

questions.q: True or false: If the monitor and the machine both ran in the same JVM, the monitor would still need a proxy to produce its report.
questions.explain: The first test worked exactly because both were in the same JVM. The proxy is needed once they are apart.
questions.rule: The need for a stand-in comes from distance.

questions.q: A ReportPrinter reads the private fields of a machine object directly instead of calling methods. Why would handing it a stand-in not work as in the monitor story?
options: A stand-in cannot be created for any Java class
The stand-in would be slower than the machine
The printer would have to move to the CEO's JVM
A stand-in offers methods, not inner fields
optionExplain: Stand-ins can be made; the problem is what they offer.
Speed is not the barrier here.
Moving the printer does not solve missing fields.
Right: the story works because the monitor uses only methods.
questions.explain: A stand-in can only provide what the real object advertises as methods.
questions.rule: When working code is in the wrong place, keep it and give it a stand-in for the distant object.
questions.teaches: A stand-in can offer only the methods of the real object, so code that reaches into the object's inner details cannot be handed one.

questions.q: Mon.show only calls getCount(). What does this program print?
options: count=7 twice, once for each call
count=7, then nothing because Stand keeps no count
count=7, then count=0 because Stand starts empty
count=7, then a compile error because Stand is not a Real
questions.explain: Stand has the same method as Real and forwards each call to it, so the monitor prints count=7 both times without any change to Mon.
optionExplain: Stand implements Gum and forwards getCount(), so both calls report 7. The monitor cannot tell the stand-in from the real object.
Stand keeps no count of its own, but it asks the object it holds and returns the answer.
Stand never stores a count to start from; every call is passed to the object it holds.
Mon.show accepts any Gum, and Stand implements Gum, so there is no type problem.
questions.rule: Hand an unchanged monitor a stand-in with the same methods and it works as before.

questions.q: True or false: A remote proxy runs on the same machine as the real object it represents.
questions.explain: It sits near the client. The card next shows where the proxy lives and what it does.
questions.rule: The proxy is local to the client.

questions.q: A remote proxy is a local ____ for an object that lives in another JVM.
questions.explain: The book calls it a local representative: you call local methods and they are forwarded.
questions.rule: Local face, remote body.

questions.q: Where does the remote proxy object itself live?
options: In the remote JVM, next to the real object
In the client's own heap, next to the client
In a third JVM shared by all clients
Half in each JVM, joined at the network
optionExplain: Then the client would still need a remote reference.
Right: the client calls an object in its own memory.
No third JVM is involved in the definition.
An object lives in one heap.
questions.explain: The proxy is a heap-local object that handles the low-level network details.
questions.rule: A remote proxy is a local object that forwards each call to an object in another JVM.
questions.teaches: The proxy is an ordinary object in the client's own heap, which is why the client can call it with normal local method calls.

questions.q: A payroll program in London calls a TaxLookup object, held by a JVM in a Mumbai office, through an object in London's own program that forwards each call. Which statement names the roles correctly?
options: The London object is the proxy and the Mumbai one is the remote object
The London object is the remote object and the Mumbai object is the proxy
Both objects are remote objects because they are far apart
Neither is special; any forwarding object is a remote object
optionExplain: Right: the forwarding local object is the proxy.
That swaps the roles; the real work lives in Mumbai.
Distance alone does not make the proxy remote; it is local to its caller.
Forwarding to another JVM is what makes it a remote proxy.
questions.explain: The local forwarder is the proxy; the far object is the remote one.
questions.rule: Proxy near the caller, real object far away.

questions.q: True or false: If the real object ran in the same JVM as the client, it would still count as a remote object.
questions.explain: A remote object is defined by living in a different JVM or address space.
questions.rule: Remote means a different address space.

questions.q: Two Java programs run on one laptop, each in its own JVM. Program A calls a method on a local object that forwards the call to Program B. Does the remote proxy idea apply?
options: No, since remote requires a separate physical computer to be involved
No, since proxies are only able to work inside a single JVM
Yes; remote means a separate address space, not a separate computer
Yes, but only if both programs share one heap between them
optionExplain: The book says a different address space is enough.
Proxies are used exactly to cross between JVMs.
Right: the definition rests on the address space.
Sharing a heap would make the object local.
questions.explain: Two JVMs on one machine are still remote to each other.
questions.rule: A remote proxy is a local object that forwards each call to an object in another JVM.
questions.teaches: 'Remote' describes a different address space, not distance in kilometres, so two JVMs on one computer are remote to each other.

questions.q: A teammate calls ProfileProxy a remote proxy. Why does it not fit the chapter's idea?
options: It implements an interface, and remote proxies must be classes
It holds a field, and proxies may not keep any data
It returns a saved value and never forwards a call to anyone
It sits in the same package as Profile, so it counts as local
questions.explain: ProfileProxy never contacts any object elsewhere; name() returns a stored string. A remote proxy would forward the call and return what the remote object answers.
optionExplain: A remote proxy shares the real object's interface, so implementing Profile is expected.
Holding a field is allowed; what matters is that a saved value stands where a forwarded call should be.
A remote proxy forwards each call to the real object in another address space. This one only returns a stored string.
Package placement is not the test; the real object's address space is.
questions.rule: A remote proxy is defined by forwarding calls to a remote object, not by its name.

questions.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
questions.q: True or false: In Java, a variable can be assigned an object that lives in a different JVM's heap, as long as the type matches.
questions.explain: A reference is tied to the heap of the running code. The card next shows what to use across JVMs.
questions.rule: A reference stays inside one heap.

questions.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
questions.q: RMI stands for Remote ____ Invocation.
questions.explain: Remote Method Invocation lets code find objects in another JVM and call their methods.
questions.rule: RMI calls methods across JVMs.

questions.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
questions.q: What does the book say RMI gives you?
options: A way to copy a whole remote heap into the local one
A faster network format for sending large files
A way to merge two separate JVMs into one
A way to find remote objects and call their methods
optionExplain: Heaps are not copied across.
RMI is not about file transfer.
The JVMs stay separate.
Right: finding and invoking is what the chapter needs.
questions.explain: RMI finds remote objects and calls their methods.
questions.rule: RMI finds remote objects and lets you call them.
questions.teaches: The chapter works in three stages: a detour to learn RMI, making GumballMachine a remote service, then building a proxy over RMI so the CEO can monitor any number of machines.

questions.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
questions.q: A client JVM wants to call postMessage(text) on a Room object that lives in a chat server's JVM. Which approach matches the chapter?
options: Declare a Room variable and assign the server's object to it
Obtain a proxy through a mechanism such as RMI and call it locally
Copy the server's heap contents into the client at startup
Rename the packages so both JVMs share one heap
optionExplain: A variable cannot point into another heap.
Right: a local proxy does the crossing.
Copying the heap gives stale duplicates, not the real room.
Package names do not merge heaps.
questions.explain: Use a proxy to call across heaps.
questions.rule: Cross heaps with a call, not a reference.

questions.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
questions.q: True or false: If client and object were in the same heap, an ordinary variable reference would be enough to call the object.
questions.explain: The limit applies only across heaps; inside one heap a reference works.
questions.rule: The reference limit appears only across heaps.

questions.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
questions.q: A warehouse JVM must be made reachable by a dispatch program in another JVM. Put the chapter's three stages in order.
items: Learn how RMI works
Make the warehouse object a remote service
Build a proxy that talks to it through RMI
questions.explain: The chapter learns the tool first, then makes the real object callable, then builds the proxy that uses it.
questions.rule: Learn RMI, make the object remote, then build the proxy.
questions.teaches: Making an object reachable remotely changes the real object as well as the client, so both sides take part.

questions.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
questions.q: x and y refer to one object in a single heap. What does this program print?
options: gum
gumball
gumballgum
ball
questions.explain: Both variables point to the same object in one heap, so the append through y shows when x is printed. A variable cannot be given an object that lives in another heap.
optionExplain: Would be right if y were a separate copy; here y is another name for the same object.
y = x copies the reference, not the object, so appending through y changes what x shows.
Nothing in the program joins the text to itself; append adds once.
The append adds to the end of the text, so the output cannot start with ball.
questions.rule: Within one heap a reference reaches the object itself; across heaps it cannot be obtained.

questions.q: When client code calls service.doBigThing() on a remote service, what likely happens first?
options: The client opens its own socket inside the doBigThing call
The remote object copies itself into the client's memory
The compiler turns the call into network code by itself
A local look-alike receives the call and forwards it
optionExplain: The client code stays unchanged and holds no socket code.
The service stays where it is.
The compiler does not decide to cross a network.
Right: a look-alike object takes the call.
questions.explain: The card next describes the two helpers.
questions.rule: A look-alike receives the call.

questions.q: Match each part to its job.
pairs: Pretends to be the service and forwards the call
Unpacks the request and calls the real service
Does the actual work of the method
questions.explain: Each part has one job; only the real service holds the logic.
questions.rule: Forward, unpack, do the work.

questions.q: From the real service object's point of view, who calls its method?
options: The remote client directly across the network
The service helper, so the call is local
The client helper, over a socket
The network card driver
optionExplain: The client never reaches the service itself.
Right: the service helper makes a normal local call.
The client helper talks to the service helper, not to the service.
Drivers are not part of the story.
questions.explain: The service cannot tell the call came from far away.
questions.rule: The service helper makes a plain local call on the real service.
questions.teaches: The real service cannot tell that its caller is remote, because the service helper makes an ordinary local call to it.

questions.q: A hotel app calls unlock(412) on LockHelper, which sends the request to a server component that calls unlock(412) on a Door object. Which part holds the code that actually opens the door?
options: LockHelper, because it has the unlock method
The server component, because it makes the call
The Door object
Both helpers share the code between them
optionExplain: Having the method does not mean having the logic.
It only unpacks and forwards.
Right: only the real service has the logic.
Neither helper contains the real logic.
questions.explain: Helpers forward; the service does the work.
questions.rule: The logic lives only in the real service.

questions.q: True or false: If the client helper did not offer the same methods as the service, client code written against the service could still call it unchanged.
questions.explain: The client helper works because it advertises the same methods; without them, the client's calls would not match.
questions.rule: A look-alike must match the methods.

questions.q: A branch app has SeatMapHelper, which offers getFreeSeats() and book(seat) like the central cinema's SeatMap. What should getFreeSeats() inside the helper do?
options: Send the call to the central side, then return the reply it gets
Count free seats from a list stored in the helper itself
Ask the cinema's database directly and skip SeatMap altogether
Throw an error until the branch has its own SeatMap object
optionExplain: Right: the helper forwards and returns the result.
A local list would be a second copy of the logic.
That bypasses the real service.
The helper exists so no local copy is needed.
questions.explain: A helper can stand in for an object it does not contain.
questions.rule: The look-alike helper ships the call and returns the reply.
questions.teaches: The client helper is the proxy idea in miniature: it carries the service's methods but none of its logic, which is why it can stand in for an object it does not contain.

questions.q: A teammate calls LockHelper the client helper for a remote door. Which part of the chapter's description does it break?
options: It prints a message, which only the service object is allowed to do
It has the same unlock method as Door, which a helper must not have
It takes an int argument, which cannot be shipped across a network
It holds the unlocking logic instead of forwarding the call to a server
questions.explain: The client helper should send the method name and arguments to the server. LockHelper just prints, so the real Door is never reached.
optionExplain: Printing is not the rule; the fault is that the helper holds the logic at all.
Having the same method as the service is exactly what a client helper must do.
Primitives such as int can be shipped across the network.
A client helper has the service's method but none of its logic; it contacts the server and waits. LockHelper does the work itself.
questions.rule: A client helper looks like the service but holds none of its logic.

questions.q: Which step comes last when a client makes a remote call through helpers?
options: The service helper invokes the real method on the service object
The client helper hands the results to the client object
The client calls its method on the client helper object
The service helper packages up the result
optionExplain: That is the middle of the trip.
Right: the answer must come back to the client first.
That is the first step.
That is step five, before the return reaches the client.
questions.explain: The card next lays out the six steps in order.
questions.rule: The call ends back at the client.

questions.q: Put the steps of a remote call in order.
items: Client object calls the method on the client helper
Client helper packages the call and ships it over the network
Service helper unpacks it and invokes the real method
Service object returns a result to the service helper
Service helper packages the result and ships it back
Client helper unpackages the result and returns it to the client object
questions.explain: The call goes out through the client helper, runs on the service and returns by the same route.
questions.rule: Out, run, back.

questions.q: Who decides which method to invoke, and on which object, at the service end?
options: The client object, by choosing which socket to send it on
The real service object, once the call has reached it
The network, by routing the packet to the right method
The service helper, using what the client helper sent
optionExplain: The client object has no knowledge of sockets here.
The service object is not called until the helper has decided.
A network moves bytes and does not choose methods.
Right: the packaged call tells the service helper what to do.
questions.explain: The service helper reads the package and finds the target.
questions.rule: A remote call is a round trip: call, package, ship, unpack, run, package, ship, unpack, return.
questions.teaches: Packaging happens twice in each round trip, once for the request and again for the result, and the service helper is the one that turns a package into an actual method call.

questions.q: A weather app asks a remote service getForecast for Oslo. Which of these happen between the request leaving the client helper and the result reaching the client object? Select three.
options: The service helper unpacks the request
The real getForecast method runs on the service object
The service helper packages the forecast to send back
The client object unpacks the packet from the network
The client helper invokes the real getForecast
optionExplain: Right: unpacking is the service helper's first job.
Right: the real method runs on the service object.
Right: the result is packaged before it is shipped back.
The client helper, not the client object, does the unpacking.
The client helper has no logic to invoke.
questions.explain: The server side unpacks, runs and repackages; the client helper handles the return.
questions.rule: Each side packs and unpacks.

questions.q: True or false: If the service helper did not ship a result back, the client helper would keep waiting for a return from the server.
questions.explain: The client helper contacts the server and waits for a return, so a missing reply leaves it waiting.
questions.rule: The client helper waits for the return trip.

questions.q: Sort each action by the side that performs it.

items.t: Packages up the method name and arguments
Unpacks the request to find the method
Invokes the real method
Unpackages the returned values
Ships the result back over the network
Calls the method on the helper

questions.explain: Each side both packs and unpacks: the client packs requests and unpacks results, the service side does the reverse.
questions.rule: A remote call is a round trip: call, package, ship, unpack, run, package, ship, unpack, return.
questions.teaches: Each side both packs and unpacks, so every value that crosses the network is converted twice, once in each direction.

questions.q: The packet holds a method name and two arguments. This code plays the service helper. What does it print?
options: reply:5
reply:add
reply:2,3
reply:23
questions.explain: Splitting the packet is the unpack step and the addition stands for the real method; the helper then packages the result as reply:5.
optionExplain: The helper unpacks the packet, performs the call (here an addition) and packages the result: 2 + 3 gives reply:5.
The method name sits at index 0; the code reads indexes 1 and 2.
The code does not print the arguments back; it computes with them.
The two arguments are parsed as numbers and added, not joined as text.
questions.rule: The service helper unpacks, runs the real method, then packages the result.

questions.q: In RMI vocabulary, what is the client helper called?
options: A stub
A skeleton
A registry
A service
optionExplain: Right: the stub is the client-side helper.
The skeleton is the service-side helper.
The registry is the lookup service.
The service is the real object.
questions.explain: The card next gives both names.
questions.rule: Stub client side, skeleton service side.

questions.q: Match each RMI term to its meaning.
pairs: Where a client finds remote objects
questions.explain: The stub and skeleton are the two helpers; the lookup service helps the client find the remote object.
questions.rule: Learn the three names.

questions.q: True or false: Since Java 5, programmers should generate static stubs and skeletons with the rmic tool.
questions.explain: Static stubs and skeletons are deprecated; they are now generated dynamically.
questions.rule: Stubs and skeletons are generated dynamically now.
questions.teaches: Before Java 5 static stubs and skeletons were made with rmic, but now they are deprecated and generated dynamically, and the stub is really a java.lang.reflect.Proxy instance.

questions.q: A developer uses RMI for a bank client that calls account.getBalance(). Which job does RMI take off her hands?
options: Deciding which methods remote clients are allowed to call
Making her own argument classes Serializable
Writing the networking and I/O code between the helpers
Starting the registry on the server
optionExplain: She still decides what the remote interface offers.
Serializable stays her job.
Right: RMI builds the helpers, so she writes no networking code.
The registry is started by her in a later step.
questions.explain: RMI builds the plumbing; you decide the interface.
questions.rule: RMI handles the wire, not the design.

questions.q: True or false: If a team wrote its own helpers without RMI, the networking and I/O code between them would be theirs to write.
questions.explain: RMI's benefit is that you do not write that code yourself.
questions.rule: RMI removes the need to write network code.

questions.q: The book still draws both stub and skeleton although the skeleton is no longer a separate generated class. According to the authors, why?
options: The skeleton is still generated as a separate class file
Both are required before the client program can compile
It helps you see that something carries the call
The registry cannot run without a separate skeleton file
optionExplain: The RMI runtime now dispatches directly using reflection.
The client compiles against the interface.
Right: the authors keep them for understanding.
No such skeleton file is required.
questions.explain: The diagram is conceptual, even where the code differs.
questions.rule: RMI generates the stub, the skeleton and a lookup service, so you write ordinary calls instead of network code.
questions.teaches: The authors keep drawing the stub and the skeleton because the picture helps you see that something under the covers carries the call, even where the runtime now does it with reflection.

questions.q: A reviewer says the skeleton lives in the client and the stub on the server. Which correction fits RMI's vocabulary?
options: Both belong to the registry, which hands the right one to each caller
The stub is the client helper and the skeleton is the service helper
Neither exists any more, because Java 5 removed both ideas from RMI
They are two names for the client helper, used on different JVMs
questions.explain: The stub stands in for the service on the client side and the skeleton receives requests on the service side. The reviewer had them swapped.
optionExplain: The registry only hands out the stub; the skeleton is on the service side.
In RMI's words the client helper is a stub and the service helper is a skeleton.
Since Java 5 they are generated dynamically; the idea remains and the book keeps drawing both.
They are different helpers, one on each side of the network.
questions.rule: Stub means client helper; skeleton means service helper.

questions.q: True or false: A remote call made through RMI is as safe as a local method call, since it looks the same to the client.
questions.explain: It involves a network, and networks can fail. The card next shows what the client must do.
questions.rule: Looks local does not mean is local.

questions.q: Networking and I/O are risky because they can ____.
questions.explain: They can fail, and so they throw exceptions.
questions.rule: Remote calls can fail.

questions.q: What must the client do about the risk of a remote call, according to the authors?
options: Nothing, since RMI hides every failure from the client code
Acknowledge it by handling or declaring the exceptions
Ask the compiler to ignore exceptions in remote code
Restart the registry before making each call
optionExplain: Transparency does not cover failures.
Right: the client must acknowledge the risk.
The compiler is what makes the client acknowledge.
The registry is not a per-call matter.
questions.explain: Handle or declare the remote exceptions.
questions.rule: A remote call looks local but is not; the client must acknowledge that it can fail.
questions.teaches: Declared exceptions force the callers' hands: any code that calls a method on a reference of the interface type must handle or declare them, so the type system makes the risk visible.

questions.q: A mobile app calls cloud.getInventory() on a proxy that looks like a local object. Which review comment matches the book?
options: No handling is needed because the call looks like a local one to it
Move the app to the server so it never fails
Replace the proxy by a local copy of the whole inventory
Handle failure of the call, since it only looks local
optionExplain: Looking local is exactly the trap.
Moving the app does not remove other failures.
A copy would not be the live inventory.
Right: the failure still has to be handled.
questions.explain: Handle the failure at the call site.
questions.rule: Make the risk visible to the caller.

questions.q: True or false: If an interface's methods declare no exceptions, callers are not forced by the compiler to handle remote failures.
questions.explain: The compiler forces handling only when the interface declares exceptions, which is why the remote interface does.
questions.rule: The declaration is what forces the handling.

questions.q: A reviewer writes, 'Remote proxies make remote calls indistinguishable from local calls, so error handling can be skipped.' What is the main flaw?
options: It treats how the call looks as the whole truth about it
It mistakes a proxy for a stub in the RMI vocabulary
It assumes that every remote call needs a registry first
It overlooks that proxies are slower to write than local code
optionExplain: Right: transparency is incomplete as a description.
The vocabulary is not the issue.
Registry use is not the flaw in the claim.
Writing effort is not the point.
questions.explain: Judge a claim by what it leaves out.
questions.rule: A remote call looks local but is not; the client must acknowledge that it can fail.
questions.teaches: Full transparency hides a difference that matters, so a good remote design keeps a visible mark of the network, such as declared exceptions, on purpose.

questions.q: Quote.price() declares a checked exception. What happens when Shop.cost is compiled?
options: It compiles, and the exception is ignored at runtime
Compilation fails: the exception is neither handled nor declared
It compiles with a warning that the exception may be thrown
It compiles, because return passes the exception on automatically
questions.explain: This is the mechanism that makes remote risk visible: a caller of a method with a declared exception must handle or declare it, or the code will not compile.
optionExplain: The compiler does not let checked exceptions slip through; the code must deal with them before it will compile.
Any code calling a method that declares a checked exception must handle or declare it. cost does neither.
This is an error, not a warning.
Nothing passes an exception on unless the method declares it.
questions.rule: Declared exceptions force callers to acknowledge the risk.

questions.q: What kinds of values can be passed as arguments to a remote method?
options: Any object, since the stub copies its fields
Primitives and objects that can be serialized
Only strings and integers
Only objects defined in the same package as the service
optionExplain: The stub cannot copy arbitrary objects.
Right: values must be shippable across the network.
Many types are allowed, not just these two.
Package location is not the rule.
questions.explain: The card next explains the three rules.
questions.rule: Arguments must be shippable.

questions.q: Select the three rules for a remote interface.
options: It extends java.rmi.Remote
Every method declares RemoteException
Arguments and return values are primitive or Serializable
Every method is static
It is declared as a class
optionExplain: Right: this makes it a remote interface.
Right: the stub does networking and I/O.
Right: values are shipped by serialization.
Static methods are not part of the rules.
It is an interface, not a class.
questions.explain: The three rules are Remote, RemoteException and shippable values.
questions.rule: Remote, RemoteException, Serializable.

questions.q: Which two things implement the remote interface?
options: The skeleton and the registry
The client and the stub
The registry and the actual service
The stub and the actual service
optionExplain: The skeleton calls the service; the registry stores a stub.
The client only uses the type.
The registry stores a stub; it is not a service.
Right: the client uses the interface as the type and both ends implement it.
questions.explain: The stub looks like the service because both implement the same interface.
questions.rule: A remote interface extends Remote, declares RemoteException on every method, and uses only primitive or Serializable types.
questions.teaches: The stub is a stand-in that works wherever the service type is expected because both implement the same remote interface.

questions.q: A PrinterService remote interface has printJob(Job j) returning a Receipt. Job and Receipt are the developer's own classes. What must she ensure?
options: Both classes are Serializable and printJob declares RemoteException
Job and Receipt are both declared as static nested classes
Only Job implements Serializable, because Job is the part sent first
printJob is declared final so that nobody can override it later
optionExplain: Right: arguments and return values must be shippable, and the method must declare the exception.
Static nesting does not make a type shippable.
The return value is also shipped back.
Final is not in the rules.
questions.explain: Check the argument, the return and the exception.
questions.rule: Both directions are serialized.

questions.q: True or false: A list of Strings can be passed as an argument without any extra work to make it Serializable.
questions.explain: Strings and most API types, including collections, are already serializable.
questions.rule: API types are mostly fine already.

questions.q: A teammate's remote interface Thermostat extends Remote and has getReading() returning a custom class Reading. Which changes do the book's rules require? Select two.
options: getReading declares RemoteException
Reading implements Serializable
Thermostat becomes a class
getReading becomes static
optionExplain: Right: remote calls can fail, so the method declares it.
Right: Reading is shipped back, so it must be serializable.
It stays an interface that clients type against.
Static methods are not remote calls on an object.
questions.explain: The exception and the serializable return type are the two missing rules.
questions.rule: A remote interface extends Remote, declares RemoteException on every method, and uses only primitive or Serializable types.
questions.teaches: Serialization is what moves a value over the wire, so a custom type becomes usable in a remote method only when it opts in by implementing Serializable.

questions.q: Scale extends Remote and compiles. Which rule for a remote interface does weigh() break?
options: Its return type double is not Serializable
Its String argument must be wrapped in a custom class
It does not declare RemoteException
It should be in a class that implements Remote
questions.explain: The interface extends Remote and uses permitted types, but weigh() declares no RemoteException. The compiler accepts it; RMI's rules do not.
optionExplain: Primitives such as double are allowed as return values.
Strings can be sent as they are.
Every method of a remote interface must declare that it throws RemoteException, because the stub does networking and I/O.
The book says an interface extends Remote; a class does not take its place.
questions.rule: Every method of a remote interface declares RemoteException.

questions.q: True or false: A class whose superclass constructor throws a checked exception can leave that exception out of its own constructor declaration.
