questions.explain: The superclass constructor always runs, so the exception reaches the subclass constructor. The card next applies this to RMI.
questions.rule: A throwing constructor passes its exception down.

questions.q: The simplest way to make an implementation class remote is to extend ____.
questions.explain: UnicastRemoteObject supplies the remote functionality.
questions.rule: Extend UnicastRemoteObject.

questions.q: What does subclassing UnicastRemoteObject also trigger?
options: Automatic registration with the registry
Automatic Serializable checks at compile time
Dynamic generation of the stub and skeleton
Automatic start of the rmiregistry process
optionExplain: Registration is a separate step.
Compile-time checks do not exist for this.
Right: stubs and skeletons are generated automatically.
The registry is started by hand.
questions.explain: The extension both makes the class remote and triggers generation.
questions.rule: A remote implementation implements the remote interface, extends UnicastRemoteObject and declares RemoteException on its constructor.
questions.teaches: Subclassing UnicastRemoteObject is what causes the stub and skeleton to be generated dynamically, so no separate generation step is needed.

questions.q: A developer writes ParcelTrackerImpl, implements the remote interface and extends UnicastRemoteObject. The compiler reports an unreported exception from the constructor. Which fix matches the book?
options: Remove the extends clause from the class declaration
Catch the exception inside the UnicastRemoteObject superclass
Add a no-arg constructor that declares RemoteException
Make the constructor private so nothing can call it
optionExplain: That would drop the remote functionality.
The superclass is not yours to edit.
Right: the implementation needs a place to declare the exception.
Access does not remove the exception.
questions.explain: Declare the exception in your own constructor.
questions.rule: Declare what the superclass throws.

questions.q: True or false: A class that offers the right methods but does not implement the remote interface can still serve as the remote service.
questions.explain: The service has to implement the remote interface, the type the client uses.
questions.rule: The service must implement the interface.

questions.q: Sort each requirement under the part that carries it.

items.t: Extends java.rmi.Remote
Methods declare RemoteException
Types are primitive or Serializable
Implements the remote interface
Extends UnicastRemoteObject
Has a constructor declaring RemoteException

questions.explain: The interface is the contract; the implementation does the work and supplies the remote machinery.
questions.rule: A remote implementation implements the remote interface, extends UnicastRemoteObject and declares RemoteException on its constructor.
questions.teaches: The job splits in two: the interface is the contract clients type against, and the implementation holds the work and the machinery that makes it remote.

questions.q: A superclass constructor runs whenever a subclass is instantiated. What does this program print?
options: impl, then base
impl only, since the subclass hides Base
base only, since Impl has no body to run
base, then impl
questions.explain: The same rule explains why a remote implementation must declare the exception of UnicastRemoteObject's constructor: that constructor runs first.
optionExplain: The superclass constructor runs first, not second.
The superclass constructor still runs; the subclass cannot skip it.
Impl's constructor body also runs, after the superclass one.
new Impl() calls Base() first and then runs Impl's own body.
questions.rule: Instantiating a class always runs its superclass constructor first.

questions.q: What must already be running when a service registers itself?
options: The rmiregistry
The client that will use the service
The skeleton as a separate process
A second copy of the service
optionExplain: Right: registering puts the service into the registry.
Clients can start later.
No separate skeleton process exists.
A second copy is not needed.
questions.explain: The card next shows the full order.
questions.rule: Registry before service.

questions.q: Put the four steps of making a remote service in order.
items: Make the remote interface
Make the remote implementation
Start the rmiregistry
Start the remote service
questions.explain: The code comes first, then the registry, then the service that registers itself.
questions.rule: Registry before service.

questions.q: What does the system put into the registry when you register the implementation object?
options: The service object itself
The skeleton
The source code of the interface
The stub
optionExplain: The real object stays in the service JVM.
The skeleton stays on the service side.
Source code is not stored.
Right: the stub is what a client needs.
questions.explain: The registry holds what clients will call.
questions.rule: Start the registry before the service, then register the service by name so clients can find it.
questions.teaches: RMI puts the stub, not the service object, into the registry, because the stub is what the client really needs.

questions.q: A developer starts TicketServiceImpl's main() before rmiregistry and sees a failure on the registering line. What explains it?
options: The service had too many methods to be registered at once
The registry was not running when the line executed
The client had not looked the service up yet
The interface was not declared as a class
optionExplain: The number of methods has no effect on whether a service can be registered.
Right: the registry must be running when the registering line executes, or the line fails.
Registration happens before any client looks the service up, so the lookup is not the cause.
The remote interface is meant to be an interface, so that is not the cause.
questions.explain: The registering line needs the rmiregistry to be running already, so starting main() before it fails there. In such a failure the first thing to check is the start order.
questions.rule: Registry running before registration.

questions.q: True or false: Starting the registry after the service is acceptable, as long as both are running before the first client call.
questions.explain: The registration line fails if the registry is not running when it executes.
questions.rule: Order matters at registration time.

questions.q: A company intranet has a staff directory where you look up a name and get contact details. Which part of the RMI setup plays the same role?
options: The rmiregistry
The skeleton
The remote interface
The UnicastRemoteObject
optionExplain: Right: the registry maps names to what a client needs.
The skeleton handles calls, not names.
The interface describes methods.
The superclass makes the class remote.
questions.explain: The rmiregistry maps names to what a client needs, like a directory where you look up a name and get contact details. It is the white pages of the RMI setup.
questions.rule: The registry maps names to stubs.
questions.teaches: A registry is a lookup point: it holds names and hands back what a client needs to reach a service, in the way a phone book gives a number instead of the person.

questions.q: Match each RMI piece to the job it does in the setup.
pairs: Called by the service to register itself
Called by the client to get a stub
questions.explain: The registry is started first from a terminal. The service calls rebind() to register itself, and the client calls lookup() to get a stub.
questions.rule: Registry first, service rebinds, client looks up.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: What does a client get back from a registry lookup?
options: The service object itself, moved into the client
A copy of the service's source code
A stub it can call as if it were the service
A list of the service's method names
optionExplain: The service stays in its own JVM.
No source code is shipped.
Right: the client calls the stub.
The stub does more than list names.
questions.explain: The card next shows the lookup.
questions.rule: Lookup returns the stub.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: The client does a ____ on the RMI registry, giving it a name.
questions.explain: Naming.lookup returns the stub for that name.
questions.rule: Look up a name to get the stub.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: How does the stub arrive in the client JVM?
options: The client builds it from the interface by hand
It is compiled into the client program ahead of time
The service pushes it into the client when it starts
RMI deserializes it for the client automatically
optionExplain: No hand building is needed.
The stub is obtained at runtime.
The registry hands it out on lookup.
Right: it comes back as the return value and is deserialized for you.
questions.explain: The stub travels as a serialized object.
questions.rule: The stub arrives from the registry lookup, deserialized for the client.
questions.teaches: The stub itself travels as a serialized object, which is why the client receives it ready to call without building anything.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: A kiosk must reach the CatalogService, registered as Catalog on host 10.0.0.5. Which lookup matches the book's pattern?
options: Naming.rebind("rmi://10.0.0.5/Catalog")
Naming.lookup("rmi://10.0.0.5/Catalog")
new CatalogService("10.0.0.5")
Naming.lookup("Catalog.class")
optionExplain: Rebind is the service's registration call.
Right: lookup with an rmi address and the name.
The client does not construct the service.
A class file is not a registry name.
questions.explain: Use lookup with the address and the name.
questions.rule: Address plus name.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: True or false: If a service had been registered under the name RemoteHello, a lookup for a different name would return its stub.
questions.explain: The registry maps names to stubs; a different name finds a different entry.
questions.rule: The name selects the stub.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: A service must be reached over the Internet by many unknown clients. What do the authors say will be needed?
options: No registry, since the Internet finds objects itself
A second copy of the stub in every client program
A rewritten remote interface
Some kind of locator service
optionExplain: The registry is one such lookup tool.
Copies would be stale.
The interface is not the issue.
Right: they note that an Internet design needs a locator service.
questions.explain: Finding the service is its own problem.
questions.rule: Plan how clients find the service.
questions.teaches: The registry in the example is a simple locator; a system used across the Internet would need some kind of locator service of its own.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: Put the client's three steps in order.
items: The client does a lookup on the RMI registry
The registry returns the stub
The client invokes a method on the stub as if it were the real service
questions.explain: The client looks up the name, the registry returns the stub (deserialized by RMI), and the client then calls methods on it.
questions.rule: Lookup, receive the stub, call the stub.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: True or false: The compiler warns you when a remote method uses a type that is not Serializable.
questions.explain: The compiler does not detect it. The card next names the two common mistakes.
questions.rule: A clean compile proves little.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: One common RMI mistake is starting the service before the ____ is running.
questions.explain: The registration line fails when no registry is running.
questions.rule: Registry before service.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: When does a non-serializable argument type show up?
options: At compile time, as a type error
At runtime, not at compile time
When the registry is started
Only when the service is registered
optionExplain: The compiler does not detect it.
Right: you will not know until runtime.
The registry does not check types.
Registration is not where it fails.
questions.explain: Test remote calls to find these.
questions.rule: Start the registry first, and make every remote argument and return type serializable.
questions.teaches: A clean compile says nothing about serializability, so only a real remote call exercises the check.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: A new remote ticket service compiles and starts. The first client call fails because the Seat class is not Serializable. Which common mistake is this?
options: Forgetting to start the registry first
Forgetting to extend Remote in the interface
Forgetting to make a type serializable
Forgetting the lookup name
optionExplain: That would fail at registration.
That mistake would show up differently.
Right: it matches the second mistake.
A wrong name fails in lookup.
questions.explain: Runtime failures on first call point to types.
questions.rule: First call fails: check Serializable.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: True or false: Starting the service before the registry produces a compile error.
questions.explain: The registration line fails when it runs, not when it is compiled.
questions.rule: Order errors appear at run time.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: A CI server compiles a remote project with zero warnings. A reviewer concludes serialization is fine. What is the flaw?
options: A clean compile proves nothing about serializability
Zero warnings means the registry must have started fine
Serialization is checked only at the moment the stub is made
Warnings are produced only for types declared as static
optionExplain: Right: only running reveals it.
Compilation does not start the registry.
The check is at run time of a call.
That does not explain the gap.
questions.explain: Do not trust the compiler for this.
questions.rule: Start the registry first, and make every remote argument and return type serializable.
questions.teaches: Some remote-design errors surface only when the program runs, so tests that make real remote calls matter.

questions.section: How does the client get the stub object?
questions.q: Sort each symptom by the mistake that causes it.

items.t: The registering line fails as the service starts
Everything compiles and starts, but the first call returning a Seat fails
Naming.rebind() finds no registry listening
A custom argument class fails when the call is sent
Fixed by starting rmiregistry in the classes directory
Fixed by adding implements Serializable to a class

questions.explain: A missing registry shows when the service tries to register. A non-serializable type shows only when a call carries it.
questions.rule: Registry problems appear at start-up; serializable problems at call time.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: To let remote clients call GumballMachine's methods, where should those methods first be listed?
options: Inside the GumballMonitor class
In a new remote interface for the machine
In the RMI registry's configuration
In a copy of the machine on the CEO's computer
optionExplain: The monitor is a client, not the home of the list.
Right: the remote interface lists what clients can call.
The registry holds names and stubs.
A copy would not be the real machine.
questions.explain: The card next lists all three tasks.
questions.rule: List remote methods in an interface.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: Put the three tasks for making GumballMachine a service in the order the book lists them.
items: Create a remote interface for the machine
Make the interface's return types serializable
Implement the interface in a concrete class
questions.explain: The interface comes first, then its types are checked, then the class implements it.
questions.rule: Interface, types, implementation.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: Which return type in the machine's remote interface was not Serializable?
options: The String used for location
The int used for the count
The GumballMonitor class
The State class
optionExplain: String is serializable, so the location return type was fine.
An int is a primitive, and primitives are serializable, so it was fine.
The monitor is not returned by the machine.
Right: State was the return type that was not Serializable, so it had to be fixed.
questions.explain: Of the machine's return types, String and int are already serializable and the monitor is not returned, so the State class was the one that was not Serializable and had to be fixed.
questions.rule: Give the existing object a remote interface, make its return types serializable, and implement the interface in the existing class.
questions.teaches: The authors check the interface return type by return type, and the one that fails is State, because getState() returns a State object.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: A CoffeeKiosk interface has getCups() returning an int, getSite() returning a String and getStatus() returning a custom Status object. Which return type needs attention?
options: Status
The int, since primitives cannot be shipped
The String, since text is large
None, since the interface is declared remote
optionExplain: Right: a custom type has to be made Serializable.
Primitives are allowed.
Strings are serializable.
Declaring remote does not make types serializable.
questions.explain: Custom return types need checking.
questions.rule: Check every return type.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: True or false: If the interface's methods returned only ints and Strings, the serialization step would need no extra work.
questions.explain: Primitives and Strings are already shippable.
questions.rule: Built-in types need no work.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: A ParkingLot class already works locally. In the chapter's way, which describes the work to offer it as a remote service?
options: Rewrite ParkingLot from scratch as a client stub for the other side
Replace each of its methods by hand-written network calls
Add a remote interface, make returns serializable, implement it
Move ParkingLot into the program that runs the monitor
optionExplain: A stub is the client side, not the lot.
The helpers handle the network.
Right: the existing class is kept and adapted.
Moving it would not make it a service.
questions.explain: Adapt the existing class; do not redesign it.
questions.rule: Give the existing object a remote interface, make its return types serializable, and implement the interface in the existing class.
questions.teaches: The existing class is kept and made to implement the new remote interface with a few additions; the real object is not rewritten.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: MachineRemote compiles. Which part would the chapter's checklist flag for a remote interface?
options: getState() returns State, which is not Serializable
getCount() returns int, which cannot be shipped
MachineRemote extends Remote instead of implementing it
Both methods declare RemoteException
questions.explain: Only State fails the serializable check. The authors found exactly this: it is the one return type of the machine that was not Serializable.
optionExplain: The checklist asks that all return types be serializable, and State is the one that is not.
Primitives are allowed in a remote interface.
An interface extends Remote; that is the rule.
Declaring RemoteException on every method is required, not a fault.
questions.rule: Check every return type of a remote interface for Serializable.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: True or false: Serializing an object that holds a reference to another object can send that other object across as well.
questions.explain: Serialization follows what the object refers to. The card next shows why this matters for State.
questions.rule: Shipping an object may ship what it points to.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: The machine's getState() returns a ____ object, which was not Serializable.
questions.explain: State was the return type that had to be fixed.
questions.rule: State needed attention.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: Why is making State Serializable not the end of the problem?
options: State is too large to be sent across a network at all
State has no methods that could be serialized at all
Each State points at the machine, which would go along
State cannot be created in the JVM on the CEO's desk
optionExplain: The size of State is not the reason the chapter gives for the problem.
Methods are not what serialization is about here.
Right: the reference to the machine is the issue.
Whether State can be created on the CEO's JVM is not the issue; its reference to the machine is.
questions.explain: Each State holds a reference to the gumball machine, so serializing it would drag the whole machine along. Making State Serializable is therefore not enough; the reference to the machine is the problem.
questions.rule: Before marking a type Serializable, check what it points to, because shipping it can ship them too.
questions.teaches: A State needs its machine only to call the machine's methods locally, so that reference is a local convenience, not data that should be shipped.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: A remote method returns an Order object. Order holds a reference to the full StoreDatabase so it can look up prices. What problem does the chapter's reasoning predict?
options: The order object could not be created at all by the client
The whole database could travel with the order
The method would no longer compile in the remote interface
The database would be deleted when the order is sent
optionExplain: The client can create the order object without trouble; the problem is what it points to.
Right: references are followed.
Nothing about the reference stops the remote interface from compiling.
Sending an order deletes nothing; the problem is that more than the order is sent.
questions.explain: Serialization follows references, so an Order holding the full StoreDatabase could send the whole database along with it. Look at what an object points to before returning it remotely.
questions.rule: Check the references.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: True or false: If State objects held no reference to the machine, the second problem would not arise.
questions.explain: The extra problem comes from the reference to the machine.
questions.rule: No reference, no extra baggage.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: A team must return a Session object to remote clients. The session points to a connection pool. Which question should they ask before marking it Serializable?
options: How many methods does the session class have in total?
Is the connection pool written in a different language?
Can the session class be declared as a static class?
What else would travel with it through its references?
optionExplain: Method count does not decide it.
The language of the pool does not decide what travels with the session.
Whether the class is static is unrelated to what its references carry.
Right: references decide what ships.
questions.explain: Marking a type Serializable also decides what it carries.
questions.rule: Before marking a type Serializable, check what it points to, because shipping it can ship them too.
questions.teaches: Marking a type Serializable is a decision about everything it points to as well as about the type itself.

questions.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
questions.q: St holds a Machine and both are Serializable. St is written out and read back. What does the program print?
options: null
A NotSerializableException
Leeds
It does not compile
questions.explain: The reference travels with the object: the copy of St still reaches a Machine with the site text. That is the effect the authors do not want for State.
optionExplain: The Machine is not dropped; serialization copies what the object refers to.
Both classes are Serializable, so nothing is thrown.
Serializing St also serializes the Machine it points to, so the copy still reaches it.
Nothing in the code is invalid; it compiles.
questions.rule: Serializing an object ships what it refers to as well.

questions.q: True or false: A remote service that has not been registered can still be found by clients through the registry.
questions.explain: The registry knows only what is registered. The card next shows where the machine registers.
questions.rule: Register to be found.

questions.q: So that clients can locate the machine, it is registered with the RMI ____.
questions.explain: The registry is the lookup point for stubs.
questions.rule: Register with the registry.

questions.q: Where do the authors put the registration code?
options: In the test drive that starts the machine
Inside every one of the State classes
In the GumballMonitor class on the CEO's desk
In the client's call that looks up the stub
optionExplain: Right: they add a little code to the test drive.
States do not register anything.
The monitor is the client.
Lookup is the client's job.
questions.explain: Start-up code does the registering.
questions.rule: A finished service is invisible until it is registered with the registry.
questions.teaches: Registration is start-up code kept outside the machine class, so the machine's own logic stays free of it.

questions.q: A developer finished ScoreBoardImpl and started it, but clients' lookups find nothing. Which step is likely missing?
options: Adding more methods to the interface
Registering the service with the registry
Making the monitor a subclass
Running the monitor on the same machine
optionExplain: Extra methods would not help lookup.
Right: unregistered services cannot be found.
A subclass does not help lookup.
Location of the client is not the cause.
questions.explain: A missing registration explains an empty lookup.
questions.rule: Started is not the same as findable.

questions.q: True or false: If the registry is not running when a machine tries to register, the registration fails.
questions.explain: The registry must be running when the registering line executes.
questions.rule: Registry first.

questions.q: A monitor must reach any of ten identical packing-machine services. By the chapter's design, what must each service do at startup?
options: Send its stub to the monitor by email
Open a socket for each other machine
Copy itself into the monitor program
Register itself with the registry
optionExplain: Stubs are found through the registry.
Machines do not need to know each other.
Copying defeats the service.
Right: each registers and the monitor looks each up.
questions.explain: Each running service registers itself.
questions.rule: A finished service is invisible until it is registered with the registry.
questions.teaches: The same monitor code can serve any number of machines because every running machine registers itself and the monitor looks each one up.

questions.q: A machine service starts without errors, yet the monitor finds nothing under the name it asks for. Select two consistent causes.
options: The machine never registered with the registry
It registered under a different name than the monitor uses
GumballMonitor has no location field of its own
getCount() returns an int
The monitor holds a proxy instead of the machine
questions.explain: A service that was never registered cannot be found, and one registered under another name is not found by the monitor's name.
optionExplain: Without registration the registry has nothing to return.
The lookup is by name, so a different name finds nothing.
The monitor does not need its own location; it reads the machine's.
int is an allowed return type.
Holding a proxy is the design; it does not hide the service.
questions.rule: Lookup finds only services registered under that exact name.

questions.q: True or false: To monitor remote machines, the authors rewrite GumballMonitor so that it contains the network code itself.
questions.explain: They reuse the monitor and give it proxies. The card next shows what changes.
questions.rule: Reuse the client.

questions.q: Instead of a local machine, the monitor is handed a ____ to a remote machine.
questions.explain: The proxy forwards the monitor's calls across the wire.
questions.rule: The monitor is handed a proxy.

questions.q: What must the monitor still worry about when it uses proxies?
options: Remote exceptions raised by network failures
Which JVM each machine runs in
How to serialize each State
Where the registry stores stubs
optionExplain: Right: calls can fail on the network.
It does not know or care where machines run.
Serialization is handled by the helpers.
The registry is not its concern.
questions.explain: It cares only that calls can fail.
questions.rule: Hand the unchanged client proxies instead of local objects, and let it deal with remote exceptions.
questions.teaches: A call through the proxy hands back ordinary values, a String for the location, an integer for the count and a State object, so the monitor's code reads the same as before.

questions.q: A fleet program has a TruckReport class that works on local Truck objects. Trucks now live in other depots. Which change fits the chapter?
options: Copy every truck object over to the report machine
Rewrite the report so it opens a socket for each depot
Give it truck proxies and handle remote exceptions
Make Truck a subclass of TruckReport
optionExplain: Copies would go stale.
Network code belongs in helpers.
Right: proxies and exception handling.
Inheritance reverses the relation.
questions.explain: Proxies in, exception handling added.
questions.rule: Proxies in, exceptions handled.

questions.q: True or false: Using a proxy removes the monitor's need to deal with remote exceptions.
questions.explain: The monitor does not know or care that calls are remote, apart from having to worry about remote exceptions.
questions.rule: Failure handling stays.

questions.q: Inside the monitor's code, which statement tells it whether a particular machine is local or remote?
options: The location field in each machine
The type of the State it receives
None; it neither knows nor cares
The order in which it calls methods
optionExplain: The location is data, not a flag for remote.
The State type is the same.
Right: the proxy hides the difference.
The order of method calls says nothing about whether a machine is local or remote.
questions.explain: The monitor calls the same interface on every machine and the proxy hides the difference, so local and remote look the same to the client.
questions.rule: Hand the unchanged client proxies instead of local objects, and let it deal with remote exceptions.
questions.teaches: The monitor can report on any mix of local and remote machines, because nothing in its code reveals which is which.

questions.q: The monitor code stays the same for both calls; the second stand-in fails. What does the program print?
options: count=9, then a crash with a stack trace
count=9, then count=0
unreachable, then count=9
count=9, then unreachable
questions.explain: The monitor code does not change between a working and a failing stand-in, but it must be ready for the failure. That readiness is what remote exceptions require.
optionExplain: The monitor catches the failure, so the program does not crash.
A failed call returns no value, so count=0 is never printed.
The calls run in the order written, so count=9 comes first.
The first call prints count=9. The second throws, which the monitor handles by printing unreachable.
questions.rule: The client code is unchanged but must still handle failure.

questions.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
questions.q: What does the proxy do with the State that comes back from the remote machine?
options: It deserializes the State and returns it to the monitor
It prints the State and forwards the text to the monitor
It stores the State and returns nothing to the monitor
It sends the State straight back to the machine again
optionExplain: Right: the monitor gets an ordinary object.
The monitor needs an object, not text.
It returns the value to the caller.
The machine already has its State.
questions.explain: The card next walks through the whole trip.
questions.rule: Proxy returns an ordinary object.

questions.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
questions.q: Put the trip of a getState() call in order.
items: The monitor calls getState() on the proxy
The proxy forwards the call to the remote service
The skeleton passes the request to the gumball machine
The machine returns the state to the skeleton
The skeleton serializes it and sends it back to the proxy
The proxy deserializes it and returns it to the monitor
questions.explain: The request goes out through the proxy and skeleton and the answer returns by the same route.
questions.rule: Out through the proxy, back through the skeleton.

questions.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
questions.q: Which object serializes the State for the return trip?
options: The monitor
The proxy
The registry
The skeleton
optionExplain: The monitor receives an object.
The proxy deserializes it.
The registry only stores stubs.
Right: it packages the state on the service side.
questions.explain: Serialize at the service end; deserialize at the client end.
questions.rule: Proxy forwards, skeleton delivers, the machine answers, the skeleton serializes, the proxy deserializes.
questions.teaches: Serialization happens at the service end before the state is sent, and deserialization at the proxy before it is returned, so the two helpers mirror each other.

questions.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
questions.q: A parcel-locker monitor calls getFreeSlots() on a proxy. In RMI's vocabulary, what receives the request on the locker's side?
options: The stub
The skeleton
The registry
The monitor
optionExplain: The stub is the client-side helper.
Right: the skeleton is the service-side helper.
The registry is a lookup service.
The monitor started the call.
questions.explain: Service-side helper is the skeleton.
questions.rule: Stub client side, skeleton service side.

questions.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
questions.q: True or false: If the monitor calls getCount() instead of getState(), the call travels through the same proxy and skeleton.
questions.explain: The walk-through applies to each of the three calls.
questions.rule: Same path for each call.

questions.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
questions.q: Sort each task by the side that does it.

items.t: Forwards the call to the remote service
Receives the request
Deserializes the returned state
Serializes the returned state
Returns an object to the monitor
Passes the request to the machine

questions.explain: The proxy and skeleton mirror each other.
questions.rule: Proxy forwards, skeleton delivers, the machine answers, the skeleton serializes, the proxy deserializes.
questions.teaches: The proxy and skeleton are mirror images: one sends the request and deserializes the answer, while the other receives the request and serializes the answer.

questions.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
questions.q: A trace of getState() says the skeleton deserializes the State and returns it to the monitor. What is wrong?
options: The skeleton serializes the State; the proxy deserializes it and returns it
The monitor should have forwarded the call to the machine itself
The skeleton must contact the registry before it can answer any call
The State is not serialized anywhere on the way in this trace
questions.explain: On the way back the skeleton serializes and the proxy deserializes. The trace puts deserializing on the wrong end.
optionExplain: The skeleton sends the state back serialized and the proxy turns it into an object for the monitor.
The monitor only calls the proxy; the proxy forwards.
The registry is used to obtain proxies, not on each call.
The state must travel over the wire, so it is serialized on the way.
questions.rule: Skeleton serializes the answer; proxy deserializes it.

questions.q: What does the Proxy Pattern provide for another object?
options: A surrogate that controls access to it
A faster copy that replaces it
A subclass that adds new features
A registry that lists its methods
optionExplain: Right: a surrogate or placeholder for control.
A copy would not be the object.
Adding features describes decorating.
A registry is a lookup point.
questions.explain: The card next gives the definition.
questions.rule: Surrogate that controls access.

questions.q: The Proxy Pattern provides a surrogate or ____ for another object to control access to it.
questions.explain: Surrogate and placeholder describe the same stand-in role.
questions.rule: A stand-in that controls access.

questions.q: In the gumball example, how did the remote proxy control access?
options: It refused calls coming from unknown monitors on the net
It delayed building the machine until a request needed it
It handled the network details that the monitor could not
It added a new report format to each call it forwarded
optionExplain: Refusing is the protection kind.
Delaying is the virtual kind.
Right: it made the remote machine reachable.
Adding behaviour is not its role.
questions.explain: Control can mean making something reachable.
questions.rule: The remote proxy hid the network from the monitor.
questions.teaches: Controlling access is wider than refusing: for a remote proxy it means making an object that is far away reachable for a client that does not know how to reach it.

questions.q: A video app shows a grey box where a film poster will appear and swaps in the real image once it is downloaded. How does the box fit the definition?
options: It is a subclass of the image with extra methods
It is a registry that keeps a list of poster names
It is a copy of the finished poster
It is a placeholder that controls use of the image
optionExplain: It does not extend the image class.
It does not look up names.
It exists before the poster is ready.
Right: a placeholder with control.
questions.explain: A placeholder that controls access is a proxy.
questions.rule: Placeholder plus control.

questions.q: True or false: If the monitor already knew how to talk to remote objects, the access control the proxy provided in the book's example would not be needed.
questions.explain: The book says the proxy was needed because the client could not talk to a remote object.
questions.rule: The need came from the client's gap.

questions.q: Which of these is a proxy, going by the chapter's definition?
options: A subclass that overrides one method to print extra log lines
An object that stands in for a report and builds it on first use
A utility class made only of static helper methods and constants
A snapshot copy of an object's data kept for later use
optionExplain: That alters behaviour without standing in.
Right: it stands in and controls access.
A utility class represents nothing.
A snapshot is not a stand-in with control.
questions.explain: A proxy stands in and controls access.
questions.rule: A stand-in that builds on first use controls access.
questions.teaches: Being a wrapper is not enough; the test for a proxy is whether it stands in for the object and controls access to it.

questions.q: A student writes: the Proxy Pattern gives an object extra features by wrapping it. Which part of the definition does this miss?
options: That the wrapper must be created by a factory
That the wrapper must be remote
That the wrapper must be a subclass of the object
That the wrapper controls access to the object
questions.explain: The student described a decorator. The Proxy Pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.
optionExplain: A factory is one way to hand out proxies, not part of the definition.
Remote is one variant; the definition covers other forms.
The proxy shares an interface; it is not defined as a subclass.
The definition is a surrogate or placeholder that controls access. Adding features is the Decorator's purpose.
questions.rule: A proxy controls access; a decorator adds behavior.

questions.q: Why can a proxy be used anywhere the real object is expected?
options: The proxy is a subclass of the real object
The compiler treats proxies specially
The proxy copies the real object's fields
Both implement the same interface
optionExplain: The structure uses a shared interface.
No such compiler rule is involved.
Copying fields is not the structure.
Right: a shared interface allows substitution.
questions.explain: The card next gives the structure.
questions.rule: Same interface, so substitutable.

questions.q: Match each role to its description.
pairs: The interface shared by the real object and the proxy
The object that does the real work
The object that holds a reference to the real one and controls access
questions.explain: The three roles fit together through one interface.
questions.rule: Subject, RealSubject, Proxy.

questions.q: Who may create and destroy the RealSubject in some cases?
options: The Subject interface
The Proxy
The client directly
The registry
optionExplain: An interface creates nothing.
Right: the Proxy may be responsible.
In this structure the client goes through the Proxy.
The registry is RMI specific.
questions.explain: The proxy can manage the real object's life.
questions.rule: The Proxy and the RealSubject implement the same Subject interface, and the Proxy holds a reference to the RealSubject.
questions.teaches: The Proxy may be responsible for creating and destroying the RealSubject, so the real object can come and go behind a Proxy the client keeps.

questions.q: A bank app has an interface Account, a class SavingsAccount that does the work, and a class AccountGuard that implements Account and holds a SavingsAccount. Which class is the Subject?
options: The SavingsAccount class
The AccountGuard class
The Account interface
The bank app
optionExplain: That is the RealSubject.
AccountGuard implements Account and holds the real object, so it is the Proxy.
Right: the Subject is the interface.
The bank app uses Account, so it is the client of the pattern.
questions.explain: The Subject is the shared interface, Account, which both SavingsAccount (the RealSubject) and AccountGuard (the Proxy) implement. The bank app is just the client.
questions.rule: Subject = shared interface.

questions.q: True or false: If the Proxy did not implement the Subject interface, it could still be substituted anywhere the RealSubject occurs.
questions.explain: Substitution works because both implement the same interface.
questions.rule: No shared interface, no substitution.

questions.q: In a virtual proxy the Proxy stands in before the real object exists. What does that say about the Proxy's reference to the RealSubject?
options: It may be empty until the Proxy creates the object
It is always filled in when the Proxy is built
It points to the client that is calling the proxy instead
It is replaced by a copy of the Subject interface itself
optionExplain: Right: the Proxy can exist first.
That fails when creation is deferred.
The client is not the subject.
Interfaces are not copied.
questions.explain: The Proxy can exist before the thing it represents.
questions.rule: The Proxy and the RealSubject implement the same Subject interface, and the Proxy holds a reference to the RealSubject.
questions.teaches: A Proxy can exist before the RealSubject does, so its reference to it may be empty until the Proxy creates the real object.

questions.q: Prox implements Subject and holds a Real. What does this program print?
options: via-proxy:real
real
via-proxy
A compile error, since a Prox is not a Real
questions.explain: The client holds a Subject and cannot tell which implementation it has. Prox forwards to its Real and adds its own prefix.
optionExplain: Prox adds a prefix and then returns what the Real answers.
The prefix is added by Prox before the Real's answer.
The Real's answer is appended, so the text does not stop at the prefix.
The variable is typed as Subject, and Prox implements Subject, so it is accepted.
questions.rule: A proxy is used through the shared Subject interface.

questions.q: Prox has the right method but does not declare implements Subject. What happens when Demo is compiled?
options: It compiles, because Prox holds a Real that implements Subject
Compilation fails: a Prox cannot be converted to Subject
It compiles, and fails with an exception when run
It compiles, since any class with req() counts as a Subject
questions.explain: Prox has the same method but not the same type. The chapter's substitution depends on the Proxy implementing the Subject interface.
optionExplain: Holding a Real does not make Prox itself a Subject.
Substitution works through the shared interface; without implements Subject, Prox cannot be used as one.
The error is found at compile time, before anything runs.
Java does not treat classes with matching method names as the same type.
questions.rule: Without the shared interface, no substitution.

questions.q: Which kind of proxy controls access to a resource that is expensive to create?
options: A remote proxy
A virtual proxy
A protection proxy
A caching proxy
optionExplain: Remote proxies guard remote objects.
Right: virtual proxies guard expensive resources.
Protection proxies guard by rights.
Caching is a further variant.
questions.explain: The card next names all three.
questions.rule: Virtual guards the expensive.

questions.q: Match each proxy to what it guards.
pairs: A resource that is expensive to create
A resource based on access rights
questions.explain: Each variant guards one kind of resource.
questions.rule: Remote, virtual, protection.

questions.q: Which of these is another variant the book names?
options: A dispatching proxy
A factory proxy
A lazy singleton proxy
A caching proxy
optionExplain: Not named in the book.
Not named in the book.
Not named in the book.
Right: the toolbox mentions caching proxies, along with synchronization, firewall and copy-on-write.
questions.explain: The toolbox mentions caching proxies, along with synchronization, firewall and copy-on-write proxies, and the list of variants is open. The other options are not named in the book.
questions.rule: Pick the proxy by what it guards: a remote object, an expensive resource or a resource needing rights.
questions.teaches: The book also lists caching, synchronization, firewall and copy-on-write proxies, so the three named forms are only part of the family.

questions.q: Match each scenario to the proxy that fits.
pairs: A scheduling app reaches a calendar object on another continent
A gallery loads a huge picture only when it is opened
Interns can read a file but not delete it
questions.explain: Match the guarded thing to the proxy.
questions.rule: Match by what is guarded.

questions.q: True or false: The three named variants are the only forms the Proxy Pattern takes.
questions.explain: Many other variants exist, such as caching proxies.
questions.rule: The list is open.

questions.q: A proxy keeps the results of earlier requests and returns them instead of fetching again. Which family does the book place it in?
options: A caching proxy, a specialised virtual proxy
A protection proxy that decides based on access rights
A remote proxy that forwards calls to a cache in another JVM
A decorator that adds behaviour
optionExplain: Right: the book calls it a caching proxy.
It does not check rights.
Remote is not the point.
It controls access, not adds behaviour.
questions.explain: Caching is a form of virtual proxy.
questions.rule: Pick the proxy by what it guards: a remote object, an expensive resource or a resource needing rights.
questions.teaches: A caching proxy is a specialised virtual proxy that keeps previously created objects and returns them when it can.

questions.q: Remote and virtual proxies look different. According to the book, what do all proxy variants share?
options: They all defer creating the subject until it is needed
They all hold a remote object that lives in another JVM
They all add new behavior to the subject they stand for
They intercept the client's method call on the subject
questions.explain: All variants intercept the method invocation the client makes on the subject. That indirection is what lets them do different jobs.
optionExplain: Only the virtual proxy defers creation.
Only the remote proxy does that.
Adding behavior is the Decorator's purpose.
The shared feature is interception of the call, whatever the proxy then does with it.
questions.rule: Every proxy variant intercepts the client's call.
questions.teaches: All proxy variants share one trait: they intercept the method invocation the client makes on the subject, and that level of indirection lets them dispatch to a remote subject, stand in for an expensive one, or decide which clients may call which methods.

questions.q: What does a virtual proxy often do about creating an expensive object?
options: It creates the object twice, once as a safety copy
It creates the object in another JVM on the network
It delays creating the object until it is needed
It declines to create the object, whether needed or not
optionExplain: Duplicates are not the idea.
Another JVM describes a remote proxy.
Right: deferred creation.
The object is still created when needed.
questions.explain: The card next describes before and after creation.
questions.rule: Defer the cost.

questions.q: A virtual proxy often ____ creating the object until it is needed.
questions.explain: Deferring creation is the common use.
questions.rule: Defer creation.

questions.q: Once the real object exists, what does a virtual proxy do with requests?
options: It keeps answering them itself with its stand-in text
It destroys the real subject
It delegates them directly to the real subject
It refuses them until the client asks again
optionExplain: Its stand-in role ends once the object exists.
It does not destroy what it just built.
Right: after creation it passes requests on.
It has no reason to refuse.
questions.explain: Stand in first, delegate later.
questions.rule: A virtual proxy stands in until the costly object is needed, creates it then, and afterwards passes requests straight through.
questions.teaches: A virtual proxy changes its behaviour over time: first it is a stand-in, then a plain pass-through to the real subject.

questions.q: A map app's RoutePlanner takes seconds to build, yet the screen must open at once. Which design matches a virtual proxy?
options: A planner proxy sends every request over the network to a planner in another JVM
A planner proxy answers at once, then builds the planner when a route is asked for
A planner proxy refuses to give routes to users who have no paid plan
A planner proxy logs every request it receives and then does nothing more
optionExplain: That is a remote proxy.
Right: stand in, create on demand, then delegate.
That is a protection proxy.
Logging alone does not stand in.
questions.explain: Match the symptom to the variant.
questions.rule: Costly creation suggests a virtual proxy.

questions.q: True or false: If no request needs the real object, a proxy that defers creation would not build it.
questions.explain: Deferring means creating only when needed.
questions.rule: No need, no creation.

questions.q: A proxy stands in for a report object that does not exist yet when the proxy is first used. Which statement fits?
options: That fits a remote proxy, whose subject must already exist elsewhere
That fits a protection proxy, whose subject must already be created
That cannot be a proxy, since a proxy needs an existing subject
That fits a virtual proxy, whose subject may not exist yet
optionExplain: A remote proxy's subject exists elsewhere.
Protection does not concern creation.
A virtual proxy can precede its subject.
Right: a virtual proxy can come first.
questions.explain: A virtual proxy can exist before its subject.
questions.rule: A virtual proxy stands in until the costly object is needed, creates it then, and afterwards passes requests straight through.
questions.teaches: A remote proxy's subject already exists elsewhere, whereas a virtual proxy's subject may not exist yet.

questions.q: Lazy stands in for a Heavy object. What does this program print?
options: built, start
start, built, built
start
start, built
questions.explain: Lazy defers creation until the first request needs the real object, and afterwards passes calls straight through.
optionExplain: Building would come first only if Heavy were created when Lazy was.
The second show() reuses the Heavy that already exists.
show() creates the Heavy on its first call, so built is printed.
Nothing builds Heavy until show() is first called, and later calls reuse it.
questions.rule: A virtual proxy builds the costly object once, when first needed.

questions.q: What should a CD viewer do while a cover image is still downloading?
options: Show a placeholder message and stay responsive
Freeze the whole window until the image arrives
Skip the cover and leave the space empty for good
Download every single cover before showing any screen
optionExplain: Right: placeholder and responsiveness.
Freezing hangs the app.
The cover should eventually appear.
That makes the wait longer.
questions.explain: The card next shows how a proxy delivers this.
questions.rule: Show something, stay responsive.

questions.q: While the image loads, the proxy displays a message asking the user to ____.
questions.explain: The proxy displays Loading CD cover, please wait... until the image arrives.
questions.rule: A placeholder message covers the wait.

questions.q: In the Swing design, what does the virtual proxy take the place of?
options: The menu of CD titles in the application
The icon that would load the image
The online service that supplies the covers
The network connection used for the download
optionExplain: The menu of CD titles is a separate part of the application and is not replaced.
Right: it stands in for the icon.
The service stays where it is.
The connection is not replaced.
questions.explain: In the Swing design the virtual proxy stands in for the icon that would load the image, so it fills the icon's place until the cover has arrived.
questions.rule: The virtual proxy stands in for the slow icon.
questions.teaches: The proxy takes the icon's place, so the viewer treats it as an ordinary icon without knowing about the loading.

questions.q: A recipe app shows one photo per dish, and the photos load slowly. Which design matches the chapter's approach?
options: The app loads every one of the photos before showing any screen
The app shows no photos at all until a later release
The app moves all photo files onto the user's phone first
A stand-in per photo shows a message and loads in the background
optionExplain: That is exactly the freeze to avoid.
The photos are still wanted.
Moving files does not address the wait.
Right: stand in and load in the background.
questions.explain: Stand in, load, then hand over.
questions.rule: Placeholder now, real thing later.

questions.q: True or false: If the viewer loaded the image directly inside the display call, the whole application could hang while it waits.
questions.explain: The authors say they do not want to hang up the entire application while it waits.
questions.rule: Waiting in the display call risks hanging.

questions.q: Sort each task by who does it.

items.t: Shows the loading message
Paints the finished image
Manages the loading in the background
Holds the downloaded picture

questions.explain: The proxy handles the waiting; the real icon handles the finished picture.
questions.rule: The proxy handles the waiting; the real icon handles the picture.
questions.teaches: The work divides in two: the proxy covers the period before the image exists, and the real icon takes over once it does.

questions.q: The covers arrive over a network, yet the viewer uses a virtual proxy. Why not a remote proxy?
options: Remote proxies cannot be used inside programs that draw with Swing
The proxy hides an icon that is slow to create, not a remote object
The covers are held in the viewer's own JVM after the first download
A remote proxy would not show a message while the image is loading
questions.explain: The same structure serves both. What differs is the reason the real object is hidden: here it is the cost of creating the icon.
optionExplain: Swing is not what decides the kind of proxy.
The same structure serves both; what matters is that the proxy hides an icon that is expensive to create because its data must be fetched, not an object living on another machine.
The covers come from an online service, not from the viewer's JVM.
The message is a detail; the deciding question is what the proxy guards.
questions.rule: The proxy kind depends on what is guarded, not on whether a network is involved.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: What happens when the user asks for a new CD cover?
options: A new proxy is created and the process starts over
The old proxy swaps in the new URL and carries on
The old image is kept and the new request is ignored
The whole application restarts from the beginning
optionExplain: Right: a new proxy for a new image.
The book creates a new proxy.
The new request is honored.
The application does not restart; only a new proxy is created for the new cover.
questions.explain: A request for a new CD cover creates a new proxy, and the process starts over. The card next gives the four steps.
questions.rule: New image, new proxy.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: Put ImageProxy's four steps in order.
items: Create an ImageIcon and start loading it from the URL
Display the loading message while bytes arrive
Delegate all calls to the icon once it is loaded
Create a new proxy when the user asks for a new image
questions.explain: The proxy moves from loading to delegating, then starts over for a new image.
questions.rule: Load, show message, delegate, restart.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: Once the image is loaded, which calls does ImageProxy delegate to the icon?
options: Only paintIcon(), since painting is its main job
Only the calls that would change the loaded image
All calls, getWidth() and getHeight() included
None, since the proxy paints the image by itself
optionExplain: Sizes are delegated too.
Nothing here changes the image.
Right: after loading, the proxy forwards every call, getWidth() and getHeight() included.
The proxy does not paint the image itself.
questions.explain: Once the image is loaded, ImageProxy forwards every call to the real icon, getWidth() and getHeight() as well as paintIcon().
questions.rule: Once loaded, the proxy delegates every call.
questions.teaches: After loading, the proxy forwards every call to the icon, sizes included, and not only the painting.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: A slideshow shows a large PDF through a proxy that has finished loading. The user selects a different PDF. By the chapter's design, what happens next?
options: The existing proxy is reused with a different address
The finished PDF is deleted from memory first
A new proxy is created for the new PDF
The application waits for the old proxy to expire
optionExplain: The book creates a new proxy.
Deletion is not described.
Right: a new proxy per image.
No expiry is described.
questions.explain: The design uses one proxy per image: when the user selects a different PDF, a new proxy is created for it rather than reusing the finished one.
questions.rule: One proxy per item.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: True or false: While the bytes are still arriving, calls such as paintIcon() are delegated to the finished ImageIcon.
questions.explain: Before loading is complete the proxy shows its loading message; delegation starts after.
questions.rule: Delegation starts after loading.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: A music app's TrackProxy offers the same methods as Track and hides a track that is still downloading. How does its structure compare with a remote proxy's?
options: The structure is the same; what differs is why the real object is hidden
The structures differ, because a virtual proxy has no real subject
The structures differ, because a virtual proxy changes the interface
The structures are the same, and so is the reason
optionExplain: Right: same structure, different reason.
A virtual proxy has a real subject.
Both implement the same interface.
The structures are the same but the reasons differ: one hides loading delay, the other hides distance.
questions.explain: A virtual proxy has the same structure as a remote proxy: it implements the real subject's interface and holds a real subject. What differs is why the real object is hidden, because it is still loading rather than on another machine.
questions.rule: Same structure as a remote proxy, but the reason for hiding differs.
questions.teaches: The class diagram looks like the remote proxy's; the difference is that the proxy hides an object that is expensive to create, not one that lives elsewhere.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: Cover shows a message until loaded is set, and a new Cover starts unloaded. What does this program print?
options: Loading..., image, image
image, image, image
Loading..., image, Loading...
Loading..., Loading..., Loading...
questions.explain: The same cover shows the message, then the image once loaded. A new image means a new proxy, which starts with the message again.
optionExplain: A new proxy starts over; it does not inherit the finished state.
The first call happens before loading completes, so it shows the message.
The first Cover is not loaded, then loaded is set, and the third is a new Cover that starts unloaded again.
Setting loaded changes the second call.
questions.rule: A new image gets a new proxy that begins in the loading phase.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: The layout asks ImageProxy for its width before loading has finished. What does the book's proxy answer?
options: It returns 0 so that nothing is drawn until the image is ready
It waits for the download and then returns the image width
It throws an exception for every size request until loading completes
A fixed default width, because the icon's size is not yet known
questions.explain: The proxy keeps answering sizes while the icon does not yet exist. After loading it delegates the size questions to the icon.
optionExplain: A zero width would make the placeholder message vanish.
The proxy must not block the interface while the download runs.
The layout would break; the proxy keeps answering.
Until the ImageIcon exists, ImageProxy answers size questions itself with fixed defaults.
questions.rule: Before loading, the proxy answers for the missing icon.
questions.teaches: Until the ImageIcon exists, ImageProxy answers size questions itself with fixed default values (800 wide, 600 high); once loaded it delegates getIconWidth() and getIconHeight() to the icon.

questions.q: Which pattern does the book suggest for tidying ImageProxy's conditionals?
options: The Decorator Pattern
The Template Method Pattern
The Adapter Pattern
The State Pattern
optionExplain: Decorating adds behaviour.
Template Method fixes a sequence.
Adapter changes an interface.
Right: ImageLoaded and ImageNotLoaded become states.
questions.explain: The card next gives the redesign.
questions.rule: Two situations suggest State.

questions.q: In the redesign, the proxy starts in the ImageNotLoaded state and moves to ____ once the ImageIcon is retrieved.
questions.explain: The state changes when the image has been retrieved.
questions.rule: Start unloaded, then switch.

questions.q: What moves into the two state classes?
options: The network connection to the image server
The code from the if statements
The URL of the image to be loaded
The menu of titles in the viewer
optionExplain: The network connection stays with the proxy and is not moved into the states.
Right: the code from the if statements moves into the states, so each state holds its own case.
The image URL stays with the proxy, which the states use when they need it.
The menu of titles is part of the viewer outside the proxy, so it does not move.
questions.explain: The code from the if statements moves into the two state classes, so each state holds its own case and the proxy delegates to the current one.
questions.rule: When one internal condition is tested in several methods, consider moving each condition's behaviour into a state.
questions.teaches: Each state class holds the behaviour for one situation, so the repeated condition checks disappear.

questions.q: A document-upload widget repeats an if-uploaded-else check inside four methods. Which clean-up fits the puzzle?
options: Move each situation's behaviour into its own state class
Merge the four methods into one long method with a switch
Add a fifth method that checks the flag for the others
Copy the widget into two subclasses that repeat its code
optionExplain: Right: states replace the checks.
A long method keeps the condition.
Another check adds more.
Subclasses duplicate code.
questions.explain: State replaces repeated conditions.
questions.rule: Repeated condition, consider State.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's solution the image proxy has two states, ImageNotLoaded and ImageLoaded.
questions.explain: The book's solution gives the image proxy an ImageNotLoaded state and an ImageLoaded state.
questions.rule: The image proxy swaps between two states.

questions.q: A ticket class repeats the same check of whether it is paid inside four methods. What does the puzzle suggest?
options: Four methods need four separate conditions
The ticket class should be turned into a proxy for another object
The same check in every method signals state-dependent behaviour
The paid flag should be removed from the class and the checks dropped
optionExplain: Four separate conditions would miss the point: the repeat of one condition is the clue.
Turning the ticket into a proxy for another object does not address the repeated check.
Right: this is the State signal.
Removing the flag loses information.
questions.explain: The same paid check repeated in four methods signals state-dependent behavior, which the State pattern removes by giving each state its own class. Spot the repeated condition.
questions.rule: When one internal condition is tested in several methods, consider moving each condition's behaviour into a state.
questions.teaches: A condition tested in every method is a sign that the object's behaviour depends on its state, which is where the State Pattern fits.

questions.q: In this State redesign the loader calls done() when the image arrives, yet paint() still prints Loading. Why?
options: Shown.paint() should return Loading instead of Image
done() never moves the proxy to the Shown state
A state class must be declared abstract to work
Prox must be created only after the image has arrived
questions.explain: The states are right, but nothing switches s from Loading to Shown. The book moves the proxy to ImageLoaded once the ImageIcon is retrieved.
optionExplain: Shown correctly returns Image.
The redesign needs a transition: the proxy starts in the not-loaded state and moves to the loaded one when the icon is retrieved. done() is empty.
These states implement an interface, which is fine.
The proxy exists first so that it can show the message while loading.
questions.rule: A state redesign needs a transition to the next state.

questions.q: When does the real image replace the loading message?
options: At the instant the user picks a title from the menu
Before the download of the image has begun
Only after the whole window has been closed
At the next paint after the ImageIcon is created
optionExplain: At the instant the user picks a title nothing has loaded yet, so there is no image to show.
Before the download has begun there is no image to show, so that is too early.
Waiting until the window closes is too late, because the image should appear as soon as it is ready.
Right: the image replaces the message at the next paint after the ImageIcon is created.
questions.explain: The real image replaces the loading message at the next paint after the ImageIcon is created, not before the download begins or after the window closes. The card next walks through it.
questions.rule: Next paint after loading.

questions.q: Put the events in order.
items: paintIcon() is called and the proxy starts a thread
The thread retrieves the image
The ImageIcon is fully created
The next paintIcon() delegates to the ImageIcon
questions.explain: The first paint starts the work; the later paint shows the result.
questions.rule: Start, load, create, delegate.

questions.q: Why can the user resize the window while the image is loading?
options: The window is closed for the duration of loading
A separate thread does the loading work
The image has already been loaded by that time
The proxy deletes the loading message from the screen
optionExplain: The window stays open.
Right: the thread keeps the window responsive.
The image has not arrived yet.
The message is still shown.
questions.explain: A thread keeps the display alive.
questions.rule: The first paint starts a background load; the first paint after it finishes shows the real image.
questions.teaches: The retrieval runs in a separate thread, so the window stays responsive while the image loads.

questions.q: A photo finishes loading at 3 seconds. The display next paints at 5 seconds. When does the real photo appear?
options: At 3 seconds, before any paint
At the first paint, before loading
Only when the proxy is recreated
At the 5 second paint
optionExplain: Arrival alone does not paint.
That paint showed the message.
No recreation is needed.
Right: the next paint after loading.
questions.explain: The paint call delivers the image.
questions.rule: Paint delivers the image.

questions.q: True or false: If loading ran on the same thread that paints the display, the window could hang while waiting.
questions.explain: That is the hang the thread avoids.
questions.rule: A thread avoids the hang.

questions.q: In a virtual proxy, who decides when the costly real subject gets created?
options: The remote registry creates it as soon as the program starts
The proxy creates it itself, once the first real need arrives
The client must create it before it builds the proxy
The real object creates itself and then tells the proxy
optionExplain: A registry belongs to remote proxies; it does not decide when a virtual proxy's subject is created.
Right: the proxy owns the decision and creates the real subject only when the first real need arrives.
If the client created it first, the creation cost would be paid up front and the proxy would have nothing to delay.
The real object does not exist yet, so it cannot create itself or tell the proxy anything.
questions.explain: The virtual proxy owns the creation decision: it stands in at first and creates the real subject only when a real need, such as the first paint, arrives. That is how it avoids the creation cost until then.
questions.rule: The virtual proxy decides when to create the real subject.
questions.teaches: A virtual proxy itself decides when to create the real subject, doing so on the first real need instead of at construction.

questions.q: paintIcon() can run many times while an image loads. In the book's code, what stops each paint from starting another thread?
options: A flag, retrieving, set when the first thread starts
The ImageIcon refuses repeated requests
The Swing window blocks paints until loading completes
The proxy discards its URL after the first paint
questions.explain: ImageProxy keeps a boolean flag. Only the first paint sees it false, starts the thread and sets it, so later paints just show the message.
optionExplain: The proxy checks the flag before it starts a thread and sets it the first time.
The ImageIcon is created inside the thread, not asked repeatedly.
Painting continues during loading; the window stays usable.
The thread needs the URL to load, so the proxy keeps it.
questions.rule: A guard flag keeps repeated paints from repeating the load.
questions.teaches: ImageProxy keeps a boolean retrieving, set when the first loading thread starts, so repeated paints during the wait show the message without starting more threads.

questions.q: A decorator and a proxy both forward calls to another object. What mainly separates them?
options: Their position in the class hierarchy of the program
Whether they implement an interface of their own
Their purpose: one adds, the other controls access
The number of methods that they forward to the subject
optionExplain: The hierarchy does not decide it.
Both implement the same interface.
Right: intent decides.
Method count does not separate them.
questions.explain: The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Intent separates them.

questions.q: A decorator adds ____ to a class, while a proxy controls access to it.
questions.explain: Adding behaviour is the decorator's job.
questions.rule: Decorator adds; proxy controls.

questions.q: Which statement fits the authors' view of the loading message in ImageProxy?
options: It adds behaviour, but its main role is controlling access
It makes ImageProxy a decorator, since it adds behaviour
It shows that the proxy has no real subject of its own to guard
It proves a proxy must change the interface
optionExplain: Right: the main role is access control.
The authors say the more important role is access control.
ImageProxy does have a real subject to guard, which is the icon it loads.
The proxy keeps the interface.
questions.explain: ImageProxy's loading message adds behavior, but the authors see its more important role as controlling access to the icon, so it remains a proxy rather than becoming a decorator.
questions.rule: The authors judge by main intent: access control.
questions.teaches: The proxy decouples the client from the icon: the client need not wait for each image before painting its whole interface.

questions.q: One wrapper adds spell-check highlights to any text box. Another wrapper checks that the user has edit rights before passing a call to the text box. Which is which?
options: The first is a proxy and the second is a decorator
The first is a decorator; the second is a proxy
Both are decorators, since both wrap an object
Both are proxies, since both control access
optionExplain: That swaps them: the highlighting wrapper adds behavior and the rights check controls access.
Right: adds behaviour versus controls access.
The second wrapper controls access, which makes it a proxy, so both cannot be decorators.
The first wrapper adds behavior, which makes it a decorator, so both cannot be proxies.
questions.explain: A wrapper that adds spell-check highlights adds behavior, so it is a decorator, while one that checks edit rights before passing a call on controls access, so it is a proxy.
questions.rule: Behaviour is decorating; rights are proxying.

questions.q: True or false: Because a decorator and a proxy both implement the same interface as the object they forward to, the interface alone shows which one you have.
questions.explain: Both share the interface; the purpose tells them apart.
questions.rule: Purpose separates them.

questions.q: Sort each wrapper by the pattern it is.

items.t: Adds a timestamp to every message
Hides that the service runs on another machine
Shows a placeholder while a photo loads
Adds compression to a data stream
Restricts a record to its owner
Adds toppings to a drink order

questions.explain: Adding behaviour is decorating; controlling access is proxying.
questions.rule: Sort each wrapper by its intent.
questions.teaches: A proxy does not always wrap an existing object: its subject can be on another machine or not yet created, so wrapping is only an informal word for it.

questions.q: In the fireside chat, what does the Proxy say you should do if you are wrapping something ten times?
options: Replace each wrapper with a decorator
Go back and re-examine your design
Keep going, since depth has no cost
Put a factory in front of the outer wrapper
questions.explain: In the chat, the Proxy says it is seldom seen wrapping a subject several times, and that wrapping something 10 times calls for re-examining the design.
optionExplain: The chat does not offer that as a cure.
The Proxy says wrapping a subject several times is seldom seen with proxies and is a reason to re-examine the design.
The Proxy treats deep wrapping as a warning, not as free.
A factory helps clients obtain proxies, not reduce wrapping.
questions.rule: Many proxy layers around one subject are a signal to re-examine the design.
questions.teaches: The Proxy remarks that a proxy seldom wraps a subject several times, and that wrapping something ten times is a sign to go back and re-examine the design.

questions.q: A wrapper creates its inner object on the first call, then passes every call to it. Which pattern fits best?
options: A facade, since it hides how the inner object is created
A decorator, since it passes every call to an inner object
An adapter, since it changes how the inner object is created
A proxy, since it controls when the real object is created
questions.explain: Deferring creation controls access to the inner object, which is the proxy's purpose. Nothing here adds behavior or changes the interface.
optionExplain: A facade simplifies the interface of several objects.
Passing calls on is common to both; a decorator adds behavior and does not control when the object exists.
An adapter changes the interface, and this wrapper keeps it.
Deferring creation until needed is how a virtual proxy controls access to an expensive object.
questions.rule: Control of access, such as lazy creation, marks a proxy.

questions.q: Which pattern changes the interface of the object it wraps?
options: Proxy
Decorator
State
Adapter
optionExplain: A proxy keeps the interface.
A decorator keeps the interface.
State is not a wrapper in this sense.
Right: an adapter converts the interface.
questions.explain: The card next compares the four.
questions.rule: Adapter changes the interface.

questions.q: Match each pattern to its description.
pairs: Wraps an object and adds behaviour
Wraps several objects to simplify their interface
Wraps an object to control access to it
Wraps an object and gives it a different interface
questions.explain: Each pattern has its own purpose.
questions.rule: Know the purposes.
