questions.explain: The book says that when you adapt a pattern it never hurts to document the difference. Freedom to adapt is a reason to document it, so others can follow.
questions.rule: More freedom, more reason to document.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: This team adapted a classic pattern and noted the change in a comment. What does the program print?
options: true true, since the class still allows only a single instance overall
false false, because every call to of builds a brand-new object
false true, since asking for the same name gives a new object
true false, since each name gets one instance
optionExplain: That is the classic one-instance design; this adapted version keeps one per tenant name.
computeIfAbsent stores the first instance and returns it again for the same key.
The same key returns the stored object, so the first comparison is true.
Right: x returns the same object twice, and y gets a different one.
questions.explain: The same tenant name returns the same instance and a different name returns another, so the output is true false. The comment tells the next developer how this version differs from the classic one-instance design.
questions.rule: Adapt the pattern, and write the difference down.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Priya says: our version departs from the classic design, so we must stop using the pattern's name. What does the book's advice say?
options: She is right, since a changed pattern has become a different pattern
She is right, because a pattern name implies the classic structure exactly
She is wrong, since the pattern may be adapted and the change noted
She is wrong, since the book says adapted patterns need no documentation
optionExplain: The book calls patterns guidelines, not laws, so a departure does not make a new pattern.
The book allows alteration; the note on differences is what keeps the name honest.
Right: adapt it to fit, and write down how your version differs from the classic design.
The book says it never hurts to document differences, and recommends doing so.
questions.explain: The book says patterns are guidelines you may alter. It suggests documenting the difference, which keeps the name useful, not dropping the name.
questions.rule: Keep the name, and document the difference.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A pattern catalog describes each pattern with the same set of sections. What is the main benefit of that?
options: Every pattern ends up looking equally suitable for your problem
You know where to look for the same information in every entry
You can skip reading the sections that describe consequences
The patterns are guaranteed not to overlap with one another
optionExplain: A template organises information; it does not make patterns equally suitable.
Right: a fixed template means the answer to a given question is in a known place.
The consequences section is one of the most useful, so skipping it defeats the purpose.
Related patterns are described precisely because patterns relate and can overlap.
questions.explain: A shared template makes entries comparable and lets you jump straight to the part you need. The card next lists the sections.
questions.rule: Same template, same place to look.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Match each catalog section to what it tells you.
pairs: What the pattern is, like a definition
When and where the pattern might be used
The classes in the design and their roles
The good and bad effects of using the pattern
questions.explain: Intent says what the pattern is, Motivation and Applicability say when it fits, Participants name the classes and roles, and Consequences list the effects.
questions.rule: What, when, who, cost.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: You are choosing between two patterns and want to understand how they differ. Which part of a catalog entry helps most?
options: The sample code section showing how one version is written
The list of participants and the roles they play in the design
The pattern's name and the picture of its class diagram
The section on how the pattern relates to other patterns
optionExplain: Sample code shows one implementation, not how patterns compare.
Participants list classes and roles of this pattern only.
A name labels the pattern but does not compare it.
Right: the book says each entry describes the relationship to other patterns, such as how two patterns differ.
questions.explain: Entries describe relationships to other patterns, which is why the book calls this one of the most useful sections for telling similar patterns apart.
questions.rule: Look under related patterns to compare.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A catalog entry lists the bad effects of a pattern as well as the good ones. What does that make possible?
options: A reader can ignore the intent section
A reader can alter the pattern without documenting it
A reader can guarantee the pattern has no side effects
A reader can decide not to use the pattern
optionExplain: Intent remains the first check of what the pattern is.
Documentation of differences is a separate need.
Listing effects shows them; it does not remove them.
Right: an entry that shows costs supports a choice against the pattern.
questions.explain: Consequences cover both sides, so reading them is how you find unintended effects before committing. A pattern's benefits come with costs.
questions.rule: Read the costs before the code.
questions.teaches: A catalog entry lists the bad effects of a pattern next to the good ones, so reading it can lead you to choose against the pattern.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A gardening guide lists each plant with the parts below. Match each part to the catalog section it resembles.
pairs: What the plant is good for
Soils and climates where it thrives
questions.explain: The guide has the same kinds of parts as a pattern catalog: name, purpose, where it applies and what it costs. Any collection of reusable solutions can use such a template.
questions.rule: A template travels beyond software.
questions.teaches: Any collection of reusable solutions can be organised with the same kind of template: a name, a purpose, where it applies and what it costs.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Sort each question by the part of a catalog entry that answers it.

items.t: Does my situation fit this pattern?
Where might I use it?
Will it add effects I did not intend?
What will I pay in complexity?
When was the pattern meant to be used?
What are the drawbacks of applying it?

questions.explain: Motivation and Applicability say when and where the pattern fits. Consequences say what comes with using it, good and bad.
questions.rule: Fit before cost: applicability, then consequences.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Besides the class design, a catalog entry offers evidence from practice. Which part of the template does that?
options: Intent, which states what the pattern is like a definition
Examples of where it has been used in real systems
Motivation, which says when the pattern might be wanted
Participants, which lists the classes and their roles
optionExplain: Intent defines the pattern; it does not show it in use.
Right: the template includes examples from real systems.
Motivation says where and when to use it, which is a reason, not evidence from practice.
Participants describes the roles of the classes, not real-world use.
questions.explain: The template also gives examples of where the pattern has been used in real systems. This lets a reader see the pattern at work before adopting it.
questions.rule: Known uses show the pattern in real systems.
questions.teaches: A catalog entry has a section of examples where the pattern has been used in real systems, which shows it at work.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: You think a catalog pattern fits your problem. What should you check before working it into your design?
options: Its motivation, applicability and consequences
Its sample code, in order to copy it into the design
Its name, to see if it sounds right for the problem
Its class diagram, to count the classes it will add
optionExplain: Right: confirm the fit and the effects before investing in details.
Sample code is a later step and is not a test of fit.
A name may suggest a fit but does not confirm one.
The structure matters after the fit is confirmed.
questions.explain: A fit check comes first. The card next gives the whole sequence.
questions.rule: Fit first, details later.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Put the steps of Jim's routine in the order he follows them.
items: Get familiar with the patterns and their relationships
Check Motivation and Applicability
Review Consequences
Read Structure and Participants
Work the pattern into your design with alterations
Review Implementation and sample code
questions.explain: Jim confirms the fit and effects first. Only after that does he study the structure, work it into his design and read the implementation notes.
questions.rule: Fit, effects, structure, adapt, implement.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: An engineer reading a catalog of building-safety patterns finds one that might suit a stairwell. Following Jim's routine, what comes before studying the diagrams?
options: Copying the sample solution straight into the plan as drawn
Checking where the pattern applies and what effects it has
Asking colleagues which pattern is the most popular these days
Building a small model first to see how the structure looks
optionExplain: Sample solutions come at the end of the routine.
Right: motivation, applicability and consequences come before structure.
Popularity is not part of the routine.
Models come later, if at all, after the fit is checked.
questions.explain: Jim reads the diagram and participants only after he knows the pattern is right and what it will do to the rest of the design.
questions.rule: Is it right? What will it do? Then how is it built?
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Why does Jim review the Consequences section before he reads the structure?
options: Because the structure section cannot be understood without it
Because the consequences section also contains the sample code
To rule out unintended effects on his design before details
Because the catalog forbids anyone from reading structure first
optionExplain: Structure is understandable on its own; the order is about risk.
Consequences list effects, not code.
Right: he wants to be sure there will be no unintended effect on his design.
The routine is Jim's habit, not a catalog rule.
questions.explain: Reading effects early protects the rest of the design: if the costs are unacceptable, the details never need studying.
questions.rule: Check the costs before the details.
questions.teaches: Reviewing consequences before adopting a pattern is how you protect the rest of the design from unintended effects.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A paramedic memorises emergency protocols before any call. In the call, a quick look at a card confirms which to use. Which part of Jim's routine is this like, and why does it help?
options: Reviewing consequences, so that no protocol is ever used in practice
Getting familiar first, so a lookup only has to confirm a choice
Reading sample code, so that each protocol is copied exactly as written
Alteration of the structure, so that every protocol is changed
optionExplain: Consequences are reviewed to avoid bad effects, not to avoid using protocols.
Right: prior familiarity means that, when a need arises, you already have an idea of what to look up.
Samples are a late step and the paramedic is not copying code.
Alterations come when working a choice into a design.
questions.explain: Jim gets to know all the patterns and their relationships first, so that when a need arises he has some idea of what he is looking for and the catalog confirms it.
questions.rule: Learn the options before the need.
questions.teaches: Knowing the options in advance turns a catalog from something you search blindly into something that confirms a choice you already have in mind.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: True or false: After Jim confirms a pattern is right, he works it into his design, making any alterations needed to make it fit.
questions.explain: In the dialogue he works the pattern into his design, making any alterations needed to make it fit. Adapting the structure is part of the routine.
questions.rule: Adapt the structure to your design.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Lee opens a catalog only when a need arises and reads every entry from scratch. Which step of Jim's routine is missing?
options: Reviewing the sample code and implementation notes before choosing a pattern
Getting familiar with all the patterns and relationships beforehand
Reading Structure and Participants before Motivation and Applicability
Skipping Consequences so that the design stays as simple as possible
optionExplain: Jim reads Implementation and sample code last, once he knows the pattern is right.
Right: Jim studies the patterns and their relationships first, so a need points to a candidate.
Jim reads Motivation and Applicability first to check fit, then Structure.
Jim reviews Consequences to avoid unintended effects, so skipping them is not part of his routine.
questions.explain: Jim first gets familiar with all the patterns and their relationships. When a need appears, he then has some idea of what to look for.
questions.rule: Learn the patterns and their relationships before the need arises.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: How do a fundamental patterns catalog and a domain-specific one differ?
options: Fundamental catalogs are written for beginners, domain ones for experts
Domain catalogs describe anti-patterns, fundamental ones describe patterns
Domain catalogs cover one area, fundamental ones cover general design
Fundamental catalogs cover only creational patterns
optionExplain: Audience level is not the distinction the book draws.
Anti-patterns are a different topic; both kinds of catalog describe patterns.
Right: scope is the difference.
The fundamental catalog covers several categories of patterns.
questions.explain: The difference is scope: general design versus a specific area. The card next gives the classic example.
questions.rule: Fundamental catalogs are general; domain catalogs are specific.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: The classic GoF catalog lays out ____ fundamental patterns.
questions.explain: The GoF catalog lays out 23 fundamental patterns.
questions.rule: GoF: 23 fundamental patterns.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A team building a service that handles many simultaneous users wants patterns for that kind of system. Which kind of catalog does the book suggest?
options: Only the GoF catalog, since it has every pattern ever described
A catalog of anti-patterns, since concurrent systems are risky
None; patterns do not exist for systems of that kind
A domain-specific catalog, such as one on concurrent systems
optionExplain: The GoF catalog holds fundamental patterns, not every domain's.
Anti-pattern catalogs warn about bad solutions; the team wants good ones.
The book says domain catalogs are being published.
Right: the book says catalogs exist for domains such as concurrent systems.
questions.explain: Domain-specific patterns concern problems in specific domains, and catalogs for them exist.
questions.rule: Domain problem, domain catalog.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: What does the book say about catalogs other than the fundamental one?
options: None exist yet, so the fundamental catalog is all there is to use
They replace the fundamental patterns with newer, improved versions of them
New ones are appearing for areas such as enterprise and business systems
They are limited to a single programming language or platform
optionExplain: The book says the opposite.
They add domain patterns; they do not replace the fundamentals.
Right: the book says many catalogs are starting to be published in such areas.
The book names areas of work, not languages.
questions.explain: The book mentions enterprise software, concurrent systems and business systems as areas where catalogs are starting to appear.
questions.rule: The catalog shelf keeps growing.
questions.teaches: Catalogs are being published for areas such as enterprise software, concurrent systems and business systems, so the set of catalogs is still growing.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A law student owns a textbook of general contract principles and a handbook on shipping contracts only. Which book plays the part of a domain-specific catalog?
options: The shipping handbook, because it covers one area's problems
The general textbook, because it is the most definitive of the two
Neither, because law has no recurring problems to document
Both, because any book on a topic is a catalog
optionExplain: Right: scope to one area is what makes a catalog domain-specific.
The general book plays the part of the fundamental catalog.
Law has recurring problems, which is why handbooks exist.
Scope, not being a book, is what defines each kind.
questions.explain: A narrow handbook mirrors a domain catalog and a general textbook mirrors a fundamental one. You turn to the narrow one when the area has recurring problems of its own.
questions.rule: General first, specific when the area demands it.
questions.teaches: Turn to a domain catalog when your area has recurring problems of its own that general patterns do not address.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: True or false: A designer meets a recurring problem in a specialised area that none of the 23 GoF patterns addresses. This means the problem cannot have a pattern.
questions.explain: The GoF catalog covers fundamental patterns only. Domain-specific catalogs exist for problems particular to an area.
questions.rule: Not in GoF is not the same as no pattern.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Sort each pattern set by the kind of catalog it belongs to.

items.t: Strategy
EJB patterns
Decorator
Patterns for concurrent systems
Factory Method
Patterns for business systems

questions.explain: Strategy, Decorator and Factory Method are among the fundamental GoF patterns. EJB, concurrent-systems and business-systems patterns come from domain-specific catalogs.
questions.rule: Fundamental catalog or domain catalog: choose by scope.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: According to the book, how do design patterns come into existence?
options: They are invented at a desk by experienced designers and then tested
They are voted on each year by the publishers of catalogs
They are generated step by step from the design principles
They are discovered in solutions that recur, then described
optionExplain: Invention is the opposite of the book's view.
Publishers collect and publish patterns; they do not make them.
Principles guide design, but patterns are found in practice.
Right: the book says patterns are discovered, not created.
questions.explain: The book says patterns are discovered, not created. The card next adds who can discover one and why few do.
questions.rule: Patterns are found, not made.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, anyone can discover a pattern and write its description, although it takes commitment.
questions.explain: The book says anyone can discover a pattern and write its description, though it is not easy and takes commitment.
questions.rule: Anyone can, but it takes commitment.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A hospital pharmacist notices that the same safe-dispensing routine solves a problem that recurs on many wards. How does the book describe her situation?
options: She has created a pattern, since she thought of the routine and wrote it down
She has nothing, because only software can have patterns at all
She has a pattern as soon as she gives it a name of her own
She has found a possible pattern in practice; describing it takes commitment
optionExplain: The book speaks of discovery, not creation.
The idea of patterns started outside software.
A name is only one need; the other tests still apply.
Right: it is a candidate found in recurring practice, and writing it up is real work.
questions.explain: A routine that works and recurs is the raw material of a pattern. Describing it well and testing it still lie ahead.
questions.rule: Found in practice, proven later.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: The book says the majority of people do not write patterns; they use them. What follows?
options: People who use patterns without writing them have not really understood them
Using patterns without writing one is the normal way to benefit
Only people who write patterns can contribute to the pattern community
Using patterns is a stage everyone must pass before writing
optionExplain: Understanding does not depend on authoring.
Right: the book presents using as the common, fine way to take part.
The book lists other ways to take part, such as joining the community.
Nothing in the text makes writing a required next step.
questions.explain: Writing is a choice with a cost, not a duty. Most people gain by using what others have written.
questions.rule: Use first; write only with a reason.
questions.teaches: Using patterns without writing any is the normal way to benefit; authoring is optional and worth doing only for a reason.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Which of these would the book count as good reasons for someone to start writing patterns? Select all that apply.
options: Having found a solution to what seems a recurring problem
Working in a specialised domain where new patterns would help
Wanting to join the patterns community and add to its work
Wanting a name for a one-off fix to spare the effort of documenting it
optionExplain: Right: a recurring problem with a solution is the raw material.
Right: the book names specialised domains as a reason.
Right: contributing to the growing body of work is a reason.
A name for a one-off fix does not meet the recurring test, and avoiding documentation is not a reason the book gives.
questions.explain: The book lists three reasons: a specialised domain, a recurring problem with a solution you found, and wanting to be part of the community.
questions.rule: Write with a reason.
questions.teaches: The book gives three reasons to write patterns: a specialised domain, a found solution to a recurring problem, or wanting to join the community.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Which statement matches the book's view of where a new pattern comes from?
options: A writer notices a solution already recurring in practice and describes it
A writer designs a new structure first and then looks for problems it solves
A writer renames an existing pattern and publishes it as new
A writer asks a community which patterns it would like
optionExplain: Right: patterns are discovered in recurring solutions.
Designing first is creating, which the book says is not how patterns arise.
Renaming does not discover anything.
Patterns come from practice, not wish lists.
questions.explain: Discovery starts from practice: a recurring problem and a solution people already use. The writer's job is to see it and describe it.
questions.rule: Start from practice, not from the drawing board.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Maya plans to invent a brand-new pattern by Friday. Which part of her plan conflicts with the book?
options: She wants to contribute to the patterns community, which the book discourages
She plans to write it down, although writing should wait until a catalog exists for it
She treats a pattern as invented on demand, though it is discovered slowly
She aims at a new pattern, although the book says no new pattern can ever be found
optionExplain: The book lists wanting to join the community as a reason to write patterns.
The book wants candidates written down so that others can try them.
Right: the book says patterns are discovered, not created, and it does not happen quickly or often.
The book says new ones can be found; it only says that most apparently new ones are variants.
questions.explain: The book says patterns are discovered, not created, and that finding one is not easy, does not happen quickly and does not happen often.
questions.rule: Patterns are discovered in recurring practice, not invented to a deadline.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: According to the book, when can a candidate solution be called a design pattern?
options: As soon as its author documents it in a standard template
When a catalog publisher accepts it for publication
After it has been applied once, successfully, in one large project
After it has been applied in real solutions at least three times
optionExplain: Documentation is needed but is not the test of being a pattern.
The book does not tie being a pattern to a publisher.
One use does not show a solution recurs; the rule asks for three.
Right: the Rule of Three sets this test.
questions.explain: The book gives a numeric rule. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Three real-world uses.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A candidate can be called a pattern only if it has been applied in a real-world solution at least ____ times.
questions.explain: The Rule of Three: at least three applications in real-world solutions.
questions.rule: Rule of Three.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A teacher has used her classroom routine in two real classes and it worked both times. A colleague says she can publish it as a pattern. What does the Rule of Three say?
options: Yes: two successes show that the routine recurs in practice
Yes: a routine used by its own author counts as a pattern
Not yet: it needs at least three real-world applications
No: routines used in classrooms can never be patterns
optionExplain: Two is below the minimum in the rule.
The book says others should have used it and found it works.
Right: two uses fall short of three.
The rule is about the number of applications, not the subject area.
questions.explain: The rule sets three real-world applications as the minimum before a candidate is called a pattern; two are a good start but not enough.
questions.rule: Two is a good start, not the threshold.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Why does the rule ask for applications in real-world solutions?
options: Real-world solutions are always simpler than classroom examples would be
Three is the number of categories in the standard scheme of patterns
Publishers only accept patterns that already appear in shipping products
A pattern is shown by use that worked, not by an author's confidence
optionExplain: Complexity is not the reason.
The number of categories is unrelated.
Publishing is not what the rule is about.
Right: the book says you do not have a pattern until others have used it and found it to work.
questions.explain: A candidate becomes a pattern through proof in use. Real-world use shows that it solves the problem under real constraints.
questions.rule: Proof comes from use.
questions.teaches: The rule treats pattern status as earned by successful use in real conditions; the author's belief that the design is good does not count.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A chef's technique works well in her own kitchen only. Which step would move it toward pattern status in the book's sense?
options: Other cooks use it in real kitchens, at least three times
The chef gives it a catchy name and lists it on the menu of her restaurant
The chef demonstrates it three times in her own kitchen for guests
Critics write praise of the dishes that the technique produces
optionExplain: Right: others applying it in real settings is what the rule asks for.
A name helps, but use is the test.
Her own kitchen is one place; the book says others have to use it.
Praise is not the same as being applied by others.
questions.explain: The book ties pattern status to others having used the solution and found it works. Three demonstrations in one kitchen are one setting repeated.
questions.rule: Others, in real settings.
questions.teaches: The uses that count come from others, in separate real solutions; repeating a technique in the author's own setting does not meet the standard.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: True or false: A candidate has been applied successfully in two real-world solutions, and a third is under way. It has not yet met the Rule of Three.
questions.explain: The rule asks for at least three applications that have happened. Until the third is done and found to work, the candidate has not passed.
questions.rule: Count completed, successful uses.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Sort each candidate by whether it meets the Rule of Three.

items.t: Applied in three real-world solutions
Applied in two real-world solutions
Used once by its author, in a pilot
Applied in five real-world solutions
Believed good by its author but never applied
Applied in four real-world solutions

questions.explain: The rule asks for at least three applications in real-world solutions. Two uses, a pilot, or an idea that was never applied fall short.
questions.rule: At least three real-world applications.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A developer believes she has found a brand-new pattern. What does the book expect to be true of most such finds?
options: They turn out to need a new category of their own in the catalog
They turn out to be correct and complete as first written
They turn out to be variants of patterns that already exist
They turn out to be too complicated for any catalog to hold
optionExplain: Nothing in the text suggests new categories are the usual outcome.
The book expects patterns to need refining.
Right: the book says most apparently new patterns are variants.
Complexity is not the issue the book raises.
questions.explain: A newcomer's find usually has an older relative. The card next explains why that matters before writing anything.
questions.rule: Most new patterns are variants.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Most patterns that appear to be new are, in fact, ____ of existing patterns.
questions.explain: The book says most apparently new patterns are variants of existing patterns.
questions.rule: Variants of known patterns.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: An architect thinks she has invented a new way to arrange hospital wards for recurring emergencies. What does the book's advice to would-be writers say to do first?
options: Publish it quickly before someone else publishes the same idea
Learn the existing arrangements, since hers may be a variant
Replace the older arrangements with hers on every ward at once
Wait to see whether anyone else notices the same problem
optionExplain: Speed is not the book's concern; being well versed is.
Right: study first, since most new-looking patterns are variants.
Replacing existing patterns is not part of the advice.
Waiting is not the advice; the book says to study and to reflect.
questions.explain: A well-versed writer can tell whether the idea is new or a variant, and learns how it relates to existing ones.
questions.rule: Know the field before claiming to extend it.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A designer has found a solution that recurs, but only in a very unusual circumstance. What may be true of it, according to the book?
options: It qualifies automatically because it has been seen to recur
Its applicability may be too narrow to count as a pattern
It qualifies only if it is renamed with a catchy label
It must be combined with another existing pattern to qualify
optionExplain: Recurring is necessary but the book also asks for broad enough applicability.
Right: the book warns that a new-looking pattern may be too narrow.
A name does not widen applicability.
Combination is not in the text.
questions.explain: Recurring is not the whole story: a design must apply widely enough to be worth calling a pattern.
questions.rule: Recurring and broad enough.
questions.teaches: A solution can recur and still be too narrow in applicability to qualify as a real pattern.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A nurse keeps a journal of handover problems and the fixes she used, and rereads it each month looking for designs that come back. Which advice to writers does this follow?
options: Studying existing patterns before writing a new one of her own
Reflecting on experience, where ideas for patterns are born
Having other developers try the pattern and give feedback
Waiting for the Rule of Three to be satisfied before writing
optionExplain: That step is about reading others' work; the journal is her own experience.
Right: combing your own record for recurring designs is the reflecting step.
Nobody else is involved in her journal yet.
The rule applies later, to test a candidate.
questions.explain: The nurse is mining her own record of problems and solutions for designs that recur.
questions.rule: Keep a record, then comb it.
questions.teaches: A written record of your own problems and fixes, reread for designs that recur, is a practical way to turn experience into pattern candidates.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: True or false: Because most new-looking patterns are variants, the book rules out the discovery of any truly new pattern.
questions.explain: The book says most apparently new patterns are variants, not all. It also warns that a genuinely new find may be too narrow to qualify.
questions.rule: Most, not all.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A developer skips studying existing patterns and spends months on her own design. What risk does the book name?
options: Her design may be too broad, because the book says patterns must be narrow
She may reinvent the wheel and solve what a pattern already solves
Her design may break the Rule of Three before anyone has even used it
She may lose the right to call any of her solutions a pattern for good
optionExplain: The book warns that applicability may be too narrow, not too broad.
Right: the book says studying patterns prevents reinventing the wheel.
The Rule of Three concerns real-world uses, not whether she studied.
The right to call something a pattern depends on use, not on study.
questions.explain: Studying existing patterns, the book says, prevents you from reinventing the wheel. Without it, a developer may rebuild what a known pattern already solves.
questions.rule: Study first, so you do not reinvent the wheel.
questions.teaches: Studying existing patterns also keeps you from reinventing the wheel.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: After finding a pattern candidate, what does the book say about getting the first description right?
options: Keep it private until the description is perfect in every way
Publish the first version unchanged to start a wider discussion
Expect to refine it with feedback, not to get it right at once
Avoid templates so that the description feels fresh and original
optionExplain: Perfection is not reached; feedback is part of the method.
The book wants it tried and refined, not frozen.
Right: the book calls the pattern a work in progress.
The book recommends using established templates.
questions.explain: The book expects several rounds. The card next gives the steps.
questions.rule: Refine and refine some more.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Put the writer's steps in the order the book gives them.
items: Do your homework on existing patterns
Reflect on your own experience
Put your ideas on paper in a form others understand
Have others try the pattern and refine it
Check that it has been applied three times in the real world
questions.explain: The book's advice runs from study and reflection to writing, to trial by others and refinement, with the Rule of Three as the closing reminder.
questions.rule: Study, reflect, write, refine, check.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A teacher has written up a classroom routine and wonders whether to invent her own format. What does the book suggest?
options: Use an established template such as the one in the GoF catalog
Invent a new format so that the description is entirely original
Skip the format and let readers ask the author questions later
Use only code listings and leave out any prose description
optionExplain: Right: a lot of thought has already gone into how to describe patterns.
The book says you do not need to invent your own method.
Readers must be able to use it without asking.
The book mentions descriptions others can read, not code only.
questions.explain: Template reuse saves effort and helps readers, who already know where to look.
questions.rule: Reuse a template.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Why does the book say it is a good idea to get a candidate into the hands of other developers?
options: It transfers responsibility for the pattern to those testers
It makes the pattern an official part of the next GoF catalog
It shows how many other developers like the author's style
It brings feedback and the real uses the Rule of Three needs
optionExplain: The author remains the writer; others test it.
Catalog membership is not what trials achieve.
Popularity is not the aim.
Right: others' trials both improve the text and supply the applications.
questions.explain: Handing it over does two jobs: the feedback improves the description, and the successful uses count toward the Rule of Three.
questions.rule: One step, two payoffs.
questions.teaches: Giving a candidate to others serves two purposes at once: feedback for refining the description, and the real-world applications that the Rule of Three requires.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A hospital drafts a new protocol. Which process best matches the book's picture of improving a pattern description?
options: Staff on several wards try it, report back, and the authors revise
The authors polish the draft alone until they feel sure it is right
One ward adopts the draft and nobody revises it afterwards
The authors publish the draft at once and refuse any changes
optionExplain: Right: try, feedback, revise, try again.
The book says others should review and try it.
Without revision there is no refinement.
Refusing changes ignores the feedback.
questions.explain: The loop is try, feedback, revise, try again. The author does not decide alone when the description is clear enough.
questions.rule: Let readers' trouble guide the revision.
questions.teaches: The review loop is try, feedback, revise, try again; the author does not decide alone when the description is clear enough, because readers' trouble shows where it is not.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Sam plans to write a pattern. Which parts of the plan conflict with the book's advice? Select all that apply.
options: Invent a private notation for the description
Skip the Rule of Three, since the draft reads well
Show it to nobody until it is perfect
Treat the draft as a work in progress
optionExplain: Conflict: the book says you need not invent your own method.
Conflict: the authors remind writers not to forget the Rule of Three.
Conflict: the book wants others to try it and give feedback.
No conflict: this is the book's own advice.
questions.explain: Three of the four steps contradict the advice. Treating the draft as a work in progress is exactly what the book recommends.
questions.rule: Template, feedback, Rule of Three.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A pattern description does not have to be ____ before it is shared; it has to be solid enough for other developers to read and understand.
questions.explain: The book does not expect a perfect description on the first try. It expects one that others can read, understand and apply.
questions.rule: Aim for understood by others, not perfect.
questions.teaches: A description need not be perfect; it has to be solid enough for other developers to read and understand.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Why do pattern catalogs partition patterns into classifications?
options: To make sure that each pattern belongs to exactly one group only
To avoid having to learn how the patterns relate to each other
To organise them, narrow a search and compare within a group
To rank the patterns from the best to the worst overall
optionExplain: The book says patterns often seem to fit more than one category.
The book says knowing the relationships is the most important thing.
Right: these are the reasons the book gives.
Categories group patterns; they do not rank them.
questions.explain: Categories serve three purposes. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Organise, narrow, compare.

questions.q: Which are benefits of classifying patterns that the book names? Select all that apply.
options: Organising a growing collection
Narrowing a search to a subset
Comparing patterns within a group
Removing the need to study how patterns relate
optionExplain: Right: classification organises the collection.
Right: you can search one group rather than all patterns.
Right: members of a group can be compared with each other.
The book says the relationships among patterns remain the most important thing to know.
questions.explain: Classification organises, narrows and enables comparison. It does not replace knowledge of the patterns and their relationships.
questions.rule: Organise, narrow, compare.

questions.q: A hardware shop has 3,000 tools. Which use of its aisles matches the way the book says categories help?
options: A customer picks tools in the order the shop bought them
A customer assumes every tool belongs to exactly one aisle
A customer goes to the drill aisle to compare drills
A customer ignores aisles to avoid learning the products
optionExplain: Order of purchase says nothing about use.
The book notes that patterns often seem to fit several categories, so exact fit is not the benefit.
Right: narrowing to a group and comparing within it.
Categories help only when you use them to narrow and compare.
questions.explain: Going to one aisle narrows the search, and the drills there can be compared with one another.
questions.rule: Pick the group, then compare inside it.

questions.q: A designer says: we need a creational pattern here. She has not named a particular pattern. What do categories let her do?
options: Skip checking whether any pattern in the group really fits
Talk about a set of patterns as a group before choosing one
Treat all creational patterns as if they were interchangeable
Prove that no structural pattern could ever work here
optionExplain: Fit still has to be checked.
Right: the category lets a team discuss a group without naming a member.
Members of a group differ; comparing them is a purpose of categories.
A category names a group; it does not prove anything about others.
questions.explain: The Student in the dialogue makes this point: we might know we need a creational pattern without knowing which one, and still talk about creational patterns.
questions.rule: Name the group first, then pick the member.
questions.teaches: A category lets a team talk about a whole group of patterns before it has chosen a member.

questions.q: A music teacher says: I need a slow piece for beginners, and among slow pieces this one is the most graceful. Which two uses of categories does this show?
options: Ranking all the pieces on one single scale from worst to best
Proving that the piece belongs to no other group at all
Replacing the need to know the pieces in each group
Narrowing a search to a group, then comparing within it
optionExplain: Within-group comparison is not a ranking of everything.
Fitting several groups does not matter to these uses.
Knowing the members is still needed.
Right: slow pieces narrows the search, and most graceful compares within it.
questions.explain: Categories make the narrowing and the comparison easy to say: the best structural pattern for a given job is a statement about one group.
questions.rule: Compare a member with its group.
questions.teaches: A category gives a standard for comparison: a member can be called the best of its group, such as the best structural pattern for changing an object's interface.

questions.q: True or false: The most important thing about categories, according to the book, is to know the patterns and the relationships among them.
questions.explain: The book says the most important thing is to know the patterns and the relationships among them, and to use categories when they help.
questions.rule: Patterns and relationships first.

questions.q: Match each remark to the benefit of categories it shows.
pairs: I only need to look at the creational patterns
Narrowing a search to a subset
Adapter is the best structural pattern for changing an object's interface
The catalog files all its patterns under three headings
questions.explain: Looking only at one group narrows a search, naming the best member of a group is a comparison within it, and grouping a long list organises it.
questions.rule: Organise, narrow, compare.

questions.q: The best-known classification scheme sorts patterns into three categories. On what basis?
options: Their age
The number of classes they use
The language they are written in
Their purposes
optionExplain: Age is not the basis.
Class count is a property of a design, not its purpose.
Patterns are language-independent designs; language is not the basis.
Right: the three categories are based on purpose.
questions.explain: The scheme groups patterns by what they are for. The card next names the three.
questions.rule: Category = purpose.

questions.q: The three categories are creational, behavioral and ____.
questions.explain: The first catalog's scheme: creational, behavioral and structural.
questions.rule: Creational, behavioral, structural.

questions.q: A designer has a pattern whose main job is to govern how objects communicate and are interconnected. Which category fits it by the book's description?
options: Behavioral
Structural
Creational
None, since categories apply only to classes
optionExplain: Right: behavioral patterns are about communication and interconnection between objects.
Structural patterns are about how classes and objects are composed.
The book describes creational patterns by name only, and the job given is not about creation.
Patterns are classified by purpose, whether about classes or objects.
questions.explain: Communication and interconnection between objects is the book's wording for behavioral patterns.
questions.rule: Communication: behavioral. Composition: structural.

questions.q: A student finds that several patterns seem to fit more than one category. What does the book say about this?
options: It shows the student has misread the patterns, and should reread
It is common, so categories are guides, not verdicts
It shows the scheme is wrong and should be dropped altogether
It happens only with structural patterns, never the others
optionExplain: The book says don't worry; everyone finds it hard.
Right: the book says the difficulty is normal.
The book still recommends using categories when they help.
The book does not limit the difficulty to one category.
questions.explain: Placement is hard because patterns have several aspects. The book treats the scheme as helpful, not as an exact sorting.
questions.rule: Expect borderline cases.
questions.teaches: Difficulty placing a pattern is normal: categories are guides, and many patterns seem to fit more than one.

questions.q: A librarian shelves books by subject, but some books fit two subjects. Which feature of pattern categories does this resemble?
options: Each item belongs to exactly one group, with no doubt at all
Sorting by one attribute forces borderline cases, so groups are aids
The librarian needs no knowledge of the books to shelve them
The number of subjects is fixed by nature, not by choice
optionExplain: The overlap shows the opposite.
Right: any partition by a single attribute leaves items near the border.
Placing a book requires knowing it.
The number of groups is a choice.
questions.explain: Whenever items are partitioned on one attribute, some fit two groups. The book accepts this for patterns and keeps the scheme as a helpful aid.
questions.rule: Single-attribute sorting leaves borderline cases.
questions.teaches: Any scheme that sorts items by a single attribute will leave borderline items, which is why the book treats categories as aids.

questions.q: Sort each description by the category it belongs to in the book's wording.

items.t: How classes and objects are composed to create new structures
How objects communicate with one another
Composing objects to gain new functionality
The interconnection between objects
How classes are assembled into larger structures
The way objects talk to each other

questions.explain: Composition into structures or functionality is structural. Communication and interconnection between objects is behavioral.
questions.rule: Composed: structural. Communicating: behavioral.

questions.q: Which statements about the GoF scheme conflict with the book? Select all that apply.
options: Patterns are placed by their purpose
Every pattern fits one category without argument
Three is the only possible number of categories
Structural patterns concern how classes and objects are composed
optionExplain: This is the book's statement of the scheme, so it does not conflict.
The book says many patterns seem to fit more than one category, so this conflicts.
The book says others have suggested four, five or more, so this conflicts.
This matches the book's description of structural patterns.
questions.explain: The book says the scheme is based on purpose, and that many patterns seem to fit more than one category. It also notes that others propose four, five or more categories.
questions.rule: Purpose-based, convenient, and not exclusive.

questions.q: Match each category or pattern to what the book says about it.
pairs: How classes and objects are composed into new structures or functionality
questions.explain: Structural patterns concern composition, behavioral patterns concern communication between objects, and the Gang of Four place Decorator among the structural ones.
questions.rule: Structural: composition. Behavioral: communication.

questions.q: Decorator adds behavior to objects, yet the GoF scheme calls it structural. What is the reason?
options: It changes the classes of the program rather than its objects at run time
It was one of the first patterns ever discovered and catalogued
Its focus is on how objects are composed, not on how they communicate
It never changes what the program does from the user's view
optionExplain: It composes objects dynamically; nothing in the book says it changes classes.
Age does not decide the category.
Right: the focus on composition makes it structural.
It adds new functionality, so it does change what the program does.
questions.explain: The category follows the pattern's focus, not the effect it has on behavior. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: Look at the focus, not the effect.

questions.q: The ____ of a pattern is often the key to understanding which category it belongs to.
questions.explain: The book says that the intent of these patterns is different, and that is often the key.
questions.rule: Intent places the pattern.

questions.q: Pattern X wraps one object in another so the wrapper adds a feature. Pattern Y sets up how objects communicate. By the book's reasoning, which is which?
options: X is structural and Y is behavioral
X is behavioral and Y is structural
Both are behavioral, since both change behavior
Both are structural, since both involve objects
optionExplain: Right: wrapping is composition, and communication is the behavioral concern.
This reverses the book's reasoning for wrapping.
Adding behavior is an effect; category follows focus.
Communication between objects is what behavioral patterns address.
questions.explain: Wrapping to add functionality is composition, as in Decorator. Setting up communication is the behavioral concern.
questions.rule: Wrap and compose: structural. Communicate: behavioral.

questions.q: Which question best places a pattern in the book's scheme?
options: Is its focus composing objects, or having them communicate?
Does the finished program behave differently from before?
How many classes does the pattern need in its diagram?
How well known is the pattern among most developers today?
optionExplain: Right: the focus of the pattern separates structural from behavioral.
Nearly every pattern changes what a program does, so this separates nothing.
Class count does not decide the category.
Fame does not decide the category.
questions.explain: The test is about the pattern's focus. A visible change in behavior is the wrong test because Decorator would fail it.
questions.rule: Ask about the focus.
questions.teaches: To place a pattern, ask what its focus is, composition or communication, and not whether it ends up changing behavior.

questions.q: A kitchen manual groups techniques as how ingredients are combined into a dish, and how cooks hand work to each other. Layering sauces on a base to add flavor goes where?
options: Under handing work to others, since it changes the taste
In neither group, since it only adds flavor to the dish
In both groups equally, since it does both jobs
Under combining ingredients, since it is composition
optionExplain: The effect on taste does not make it a hand-over technique.
The groups are about focus, not about effect.
Its focus is composition; equal placement ignores that.
Right: layering is composition, even though its effect is new flavor.
questions.explain: As with Decorator, the visible effect, new flavor or new behavior, does not decide the group. The focus does.
questions.rule: Effect misleads; focus decides.
questions.teaches: The same visible effect, such as new functionality, can come from techniques with different focuses, so the effect is a poor guide to category.

questions.q: True or false: The book treats the placement of Decorator as settled and says nobody disagrees with it.
questions.explain: The book reports that lots of developers say Decorator should be behavioral, then explains the GoF reasoning. It also admits many people are confused by the categories.
questions.rule: Placements can be disputed.

questions.q: Bold wraps another Msg, and the wrapping is done at run time. What does this program print?
options: hi, since only Plain holds the text and wrappers cannot change it
*hi*, because only the outer wrapper takes effect on the text
A compile error, since Bold wraps a Msg and a Plain is not one
**hi**, since each wrapper adds asterisks
optionExplain: Plain holds the text, but each wrapper adds to what it returns.
Both wrappers call inner.text(), so both add asterisks.
Bold takes a Msg, and both Plain and Bold are Msg, so it compiles.
Right: Plain returns hi, the inner Bold gives *hi*, and the outer Bold gives **hi**.
questions.explain: Each Bold adds an asterisk on both sides of the inner text, and two are nested, so the output is **hi**. The behavior comes from composing objects by wrapping, which is the structural focus the Gang of Four saw in Decorator.
questions.rule: Wrapping composes objects: that is the structural focus.

questions.q: True or false: The three-category scheme by purpose is the only way patterns have been classified.
questions.explain: Other schemes exist, including one by whether a pattern deals with classes or objects. The card next describes them.
questions.rule: More than one scheme exists.

questions.q: Patterns are often classified by a second attribute: whether the pattern deals with ____ or objects.
questions.explain: The second common attribute is whether a pattern deals with classes or objects.
questions.rule: Classes or objects.

questions.q: A team groups the patterns it uses into decoupling patterns and extension patterns on its wall chart. Is this acceptable by the book's view?
options: No: only the three GoF categories are permitted in a team
Yes, but only if the team publishes the chart to others
Yes: other schemes exist and you may make your own
No: grouping should be by classes or objects and nothing else
optionExplain: The book says the three categories are not the only scheme.
Nothing requires publication.
Right: the book says to feel free to create your own scheme.
Class-or-object is one scheme, not the only one.
questions.explain: The book welcomes custom groupings when they help understanding, and mentions decoupling patterns as a subcategory example.
questions.rule: Use the grouping that helps you.

questions.q: A pattern is described as structural and as dealing with objects. Which statement is right?
options: The labels come from different schemes and can both apply
The labels contradict each other, so one of them must be wrong
Structural patterns can only ever deal with classes, not objects
The labels mean the same thing, so one of them is redundant
optionExplain: Right: the schemes classify on different attributes.
They answer different questions, so they can coexist.
The book says nothing of the kind.
One is about purpose, the other about classes or objects.
questions.explain: A pattern can carry one label from each scheme because the schemes use different attributes.
questions.rule: Different attributes, different labels.
questions.teaches: Classification schemes that use different attributes can be applied together, giving each pattern one label from each.

questions.q: A library classifies books by subject and also by format, print or digital. How does this resemble the schemes for patterns?
options: One attribute decides everything there is to know about an item in stock
Only the format scheme is allowed, since print is the original
The two schemes must give the same answer for every book in the library
Separate attributes describe the same item, each answering a question
optionExplain: The example shows that one attribute is not enough.
Both are in use, as with patterns.
They answer different questions.
Right: subject and format are separate attributes, like purpose and class-or-object.
questions.explain: Subject and format are independent attributes. In the same way purpose and class-or-object are independent ways to describe a pattern.
questions.rule: One item, several labels.
questions.teaches: Several independent attributes can describe one item, each answering a different question about it.

questions.q: True or false: If a team's own grouping of patterns helps them understand the patterns better, the book says they are free to use it.
questions.explain: The book says to feel free to create your own scheme if it helps you understand the patterns, while still knowing the common ones.
questions.rule: Use what helps.

questions.q: Sort each label by the scheme it belongs to.

items.t: Creational
Deals with classes
Structural
Deals with objects
Behavioral

questions.explain: Creational, structural and behavioral come from the scheme based on purpose. Whether a pattern deals with classes or with objects is the second attribute.
questions.rule: Purpose is one attribute; class or object is another.

questions.q: Besides organising and comparing, what other use of categories does the book's Master give?
options: Proving that a pattern is correct before anyone has used it
Deciding which of the patterns in a group is the oldest
Launching into new territory by building on how groups relate
Avoiding the need to learn the patterns and their relationships
optionExplain: Categories do not prove correctness.
Age is not a use the Master mentions.
Right: the Master says categories can launch us into new territory.
The book says knowing the patterns remains the main thing.
questions.explain: The Master names a further use. The card next describes it.
questions.rule: Categories also point to new territory.

questions.q: True or false: Others have suggested more than three categories, such as four or five.
questions.explain: The Master says three is a convenient number, and that others have suggested four, five or more.
questions.rule: Three is a convenience.

questions.q: A florist sorts her arrangements into wedding, funeral and table groups and notices that none suits an office lobby, so she designs one. Which use of categories is this?
options: Using the groups to prove her arrangements are best
Using the groups to avoid thinking about customers
Using the groups to narrow a search
Using the groups to explore new territory
optionExplain: Nothing in the example proves quality.
The example involves a customer need.
She is not searching existing arrangements; she is extending them.
Right: the groups reveal where something new could go.
questions.explain: Seeing the shape of the groups led her to a gap, which is the launch into new territory the Master describes.
questions.rule: Groups can reveal gaps.

questions.q: How can categories help a person who hopes to find new patterns?
options: They guarantee that every new pattern will fit into exactly one group
Seeing how patterns in a group relate lets them extrapolate
They show that all the possible patterns are already known and listed
They replace the need for studying the existing patterns
optionExplain: The book admits placement is often unclear.
Right: the Master says categories give us a way to extrapolate to new patterns.
The field has grown, and the book expects more patterns.
The writer's advice begins with studying patterns.
questions.explain: Relationships within and between groups suggest what a missing member might do.
questions.rule: Gaps in a group suggest new members.
questions.teaches: Seeing how patterns within a group relate lets you extrapolate to patterns that have not been written yet.

questions.q: Which proposals fit the book's attitude to categories? Select all that apply.
options: Refusing to compare patterns from different categories
Adding a fourth category for decoupling patterns
Dropping a scheme that does not help your team
Insisting that exactly three categories are correct
optionExplain: Does not fit: categories exist to help comparison, including across groups.
Fits: others have suggested four or more, and subcategories exist.
Fits: use categories when they help.
Does not fit: three is a convenience, not a fact.
questions.explain: The book treats categories as tools. The number is flexible and a scheme that does not help can be set aside.
questions.rule: Categories serve you.
questions.teaches: Because the number of categories is a convenience, a team can add, drop or merge categories when its needs change.

questions.q: True or false: A student struggles with the categories, so the book tells her to memorise which category each pattern belongs to before doing anything else.
questions.explain: The book says many people are confused by the categories and that the most important thing is to know the patterns and their relationships. When categories help, use them.
questions.rule: Use categories when they help.

questions.q: Which remark uses categories to launch into new territory, as the Master describes?
options: I need a creational pattern here, though I have not yet chosen which one
Adapter is the best structural pattern for changing an object's interface
Show me only the behavioral patterns in this whole catalog of patterns
What would a pattern be that offers structural power at a behavioral cost?
optionExplain: This talks about a whole group without naming a member, which is a different use.
This compares one member to the rest of its category.
This narrows a search to a subset.
Right: it uses known groups to imagine something new, as the Master's sports-car remark does.
questions.explain: The Master names launching into new territory as a use of categories: from known groups you extrapolate to something new, like a sports car at an economy price. The other remarks talk about a group, narrow a search or compare members.
questions.rule: Categories can point at gaps for new designs.

questions.q: What does the book mean by thinking in patterns?
options: Naming a pattern for every single class found in a design
Memorising the definitions of all the patterns in a catalog
Starting every design by listing the patterns it could use
Seeing where patterns fit a design and where they do not
optionExplain: Labelling every class would force fit where none exists.
Memorising definitions is knowledge, which the book says is not enough alone.
The book warns against starting from patterns.
Right: the skill is judging fit in both directions.
questions.explain: The book frames it as a skill of seeing fit. The card next gives the reason practice matters.
questions.rule: Thinking in patterns is judging fit.

questions.q: True or false: The book says that understanding the theory of patterns without experience in using them will not make much difference.
questions.explain: Knowledge matters, but without experience and practice it makes little difference to your work.
questions.rule: Knowledge needs practice.

questions.q: A junior engineer has memorised the definition of every pattern in a catalog but has not used any. What advice follows from the book?
options: Memorise the relationships among patterns before touching any design
Practise on real designs, looking for where patterns fit or not
Wait to use patterns until the definitions can be recited without notes
Replace theory with practice and stop reading catalogs
optionExplain: More memorising adds knowledge, which is not the missing piece.
Right: practice turns the knowledge into judgment.
Reciting does not give the experience the book asks for.
The book says the knowledge is important; it asks for practice on top of it.
questions.explain: She has the knowledge; she lacks experience. Working on real designs, looking for fit and non-fit, builds the skill.
questions.rule: Add practice to knowledge.

questions.q: Which of these belong to thinking in patterns, as the book describes it? Select all that apply.
options: Seeing where a pattern does not belong
Seeing where a pattern fits a design
Fitting a pattern to every design by adapting it
Judging fit from experience, not only from definitions
optionExplain: Belongs: the book names where patterns do not fit as part of the skill.
Belongs: this is the first half of the skill.
Does not belong: forcing a fit everywhere is the opposite of seeing where patterns do not belong.
Belongs: the book contrasts experience with academic knowledge.
questions.explain: The skill has two halves, fit and non-fit, and it is built from experience.
questions.rule: Learn to say no as well as yes.
questions.teaches: Thinking in patterns includes recognising where a pattern does not belong; a designer who sees only where patterns fit is half trained.

questions.q: A chess coach says: knowing the names of the openings is not the skill; the skill is seeing, in a live game, when an opening suits the position. Which point in the book does this echo?
options: Naming the openings is the key skill in a live game
Beginners should avoid studying until they have played much
Knowledge needs practice before it changes results
Only masters may use the known openings in a real game
optionExplain: The coach says names alone are not the skill.
The coach does not dismiss study; the point is practice on top of it.
Right: knowing names or definitions is not the same as judging fit in practice.
The book encourages use at all levels.
questions.explain: Judging fit in a live situation is a skill that grows with practice and cannot be replaced by memorised names or definitions.
questions.rule: Judgment comes from live cases.
questions.teaches: Judgment of fit grows by working through live cases, which memorised names or definitions cannot supply.

questions.q: True or false: Because practice matters most, the book tells readers that the theory of contexts, forces and catalogs is not worth learning.
questions.explain: The book says the theory is important and that knowledge is power. Its point is that theory without experience and practice will not make much difference.
questions.rule: Theory plus practice.

questions.q: A lead says: to think in patterns, first count how many patterns could be applied to the design. What does the book say instead?
options: Count them, since every design should use as many patterns as it can hold
Look at the design and see where patterns fit and where they do not
Memorise the whole catalog, since recall alone decides where patterns fit
Avoid patterns, since practice matters more than any pattern ever could
optionExplain: The book warns that using more patterns is not what makes a better design.
Right: the skill is seeing fit and non-fit in a design.
The book says knowledge without practice makes little difference.
Practice includes using patterns where they fit; it does not mean avoiding them.
questions.explain: The book describes thinking in patterns as looking at a design and seeing where patterns fit naturally and where they do not, which is a judgement, not a count.
questions.rule: Judge where patterns fit and where they do not.

questions.q: According to the book, what should be your goal when you design?
options: Simplicity, not applying a pattern to the problem
Using as many patterns as the design can hold
Flexibility for every change you can imagine
Matching the classic structure of a catalog pattern
optionExplain: Right: the book puts simplicity first.
The book warns that more patterns do not mean better design.
Flexibility for imagined change is the hypothetical reason it warns against.
Adapting patterns is allowed, and matching is not the goal.
questions.explain: Simplicity comes first and a pattern comes in only if it helps. The card next adds the exception.
questions.rule: Simplicity first.

questions.q: Your goal should be ____, not how can I apply a pattern to this problem.
questions.explain: The book's goal for design is simplicity, summed up as KISS.
questions.rule: Keep it simple.

questions.q: A team must email a weekly summary to ten colleagues. One member proposes a pluggable report framework built from several patterns. What does the book's advice suggest?
options: Adopt the framework to show the team is sophisticated
Start simple, and add a pattern only when a need appears
Build the framework now in case the weekly email grows
Avoid sending the summary until the design is finished
optionExplain: The book says you need not use patterns to be seen as a sophisticated developer.
Right: simplicity first; patterns on need.
Building for a possible future is the temptation the book warns about.
Delaying the job is not the advice.
questions.explain: Nothing about a weekly email calls for a framework. The simplest solution can be revisited if a real need appears.
questions.rule: Start simple; let need add structure.

questions.q: A junior developer worries that skipping patterns will make her look unsophisticated. What does the book say?
options: Other developers appreciate and admire a simple design
Skipping patterns shows she has not studied them
A sophisticated developer uses a pattern in every design
Sophistication is judged by the number of classes
optionExplain: Right: the book says simplicity is appreciated.
The book says to choose simplicity even for those who know patterns.
The book says the opposite.
The book does not measure sophistication by class count.
questions.explain: The book says you should not feel unsophisticated for solving a problem without a pattern; a simple design earns respect.
questions.rule: Simple is respectable.
questions.teaches: Skipping a pattern does not make a developer less sophisticated, because other developers appreciate a simple design.

questions.q: A school secretary tracks late homework in a spreadsheet column. Later, the school asks her to record homework for 30 teachers and to send alerts to parents. What does the book's attitude suggest?
options: Switch to a fully custom system right away, because more change is coming
Stay with the spreadsheet in every case, because a simple design is final
Avoid the alerts, as they would complicate the design of the sheet
Keep the simple solution while it works; use a pattern once a need appears
optionExplain: Building ahead of a need is the temptation the book warns about.
The book says a pattern is sometimes the best way to stay simple and flexible.
Alerts are a requirement; the design should meet them.
Right: simplicity is judged against the need, which can grow.
questions.explain: KISS is relative to the need. When the need grows, the simplest design that meets it may change, and a pattern can then be the simplest answer.
questions.rule: Simplest for the need you have.
questions.teaches: Simplicity is relative to the need: when requirements grow, the simplest design that meets them may change and may include a pattern.

questions.q: True or false: A design that uses a pattern can still fit the book's idea of simplicity, if the pattern answers a real need.
questions.explain: The book says that sometimes the best way to keep a design simple and flexible is to use a pattern. The test is whether the pattern answers a real need.
questions.rule: Judge the pattern by the need.

questions.q: This program prints 7. If addition is the only operation the app will ever need, which advice does the design ignore?
options: Favor composition over inheritance, as in the book's first duck example
Solve things in the simplest way possible; simplicity is the goal
Document how the version differs from the classic pattern design in the catalog
Give each pattern a name that joins a shared team vocabulary of designs
optionExplain: The code does use composition, and nothing in it breaks that principle.
Right: three types wrap a single addition that never varies.
Nothing here departs from a classic pattern in a way that needs a note.
Names help communication, but the problem here is needless structure.
questions.explain: Calc, Op and Add wrap one addition in three types. If nothing will vary, the book's aim of the simplest possible solution says to write 3 + 4.
questions.rule: Simplest first; the pattern must answer a need.

questions.q: Sort each choice by whether it fits the book's advice on simplicity.

items.t: Using a plain loop to total five numbers
Building a plug-in framework to print one fixed report
Adding a pattern because a likely change needs it
Choosing a pattern first and then looking for a problem for it
Keeping the design simple because it meets every stated need
Adding three layers so the design looks sophisticated

questions.explain: The book wants the simplest solution that does the job, with a pattern when the need appears. Choosing a pattern first, or adding layers for show, breaks that.
questions.rule: Need first, then the simplest design that meets it.

questions.q: True or false: Because design patterns are well tested by many developers, a team can plug one in without thinking about the rest of its design.
questions.explain: The book says patterns are not a magic bullet. The card next explains what still has to be thought through.
questions.rule: Tested is not the same as fits.

questions.q: Design patterns aren't a magic ____.
questions.explain: The book's phrase is that patterns are not a magic bullet; in fact they are not even a bullet.
questions.rule: No magic bullet.

questions.q: A hospital IT team installs a well-known scheduling pattern, then finds that the new queue slows the billing system. Which point of the book does this illustrate?
options: A well-tested pattern cannot cause slowdowns in other parts of a system
A pattern has consequences for the rest of the design to think through
Patterns should be avoided whenever systems are connected to each other
Slowdowns show that the pattern was misnamed in its documentation
optionExplain: The book says the opposite: a tested pattern can still affect other parts.
Right: the book asks you to think through the consequences for the rest of your design.
The book does not say to avoid patterns.
Naming has nothing to do with slowdowns.
questions.explain: The scheduling pattern may be sound in itself, but it sits inside a larger system. Thinking through its effects on that system is the team's job.
questions.rule: Check what it does to the rest.

questions.q: Which risk does a pattern's long track record reduce?
options: The risk that it will affect the rest of your design
The risk that your requirements will change
The risk that other developers will not recognise it
The risk that the solution idea itself is unsound
optionExplain: That risk is specific to your design and still needs checking.
A track record says nothing about future requirements.
Recognition comes from the shared vocabulary, not from the track record.
Right: many developers have solved the problem with similar techniques.
questions.explain: Other people's experience tells you the idea works in general. How it behaves in your design is a separate question.
questions.rule: General evidence, local check.
questions.teaches: A pattern's track record lowers the risk in the solution idea, but the fit with your own design remains your responsibility.

questions.q: A medicine passes many trials, and a doctor still checks how it interacts with the patient's other medicines. Which idea in the book is this like?
options: A pattern must be tested by every single user before anyone can rely on it
A solution that works for most people is unsafe for everyone
Patterns should be tested for several years before they are described
A pattern's general success does not replace checking it on your system
optionExplain: The book does not ask for tests by every user.
The book trusts tested patterns for the general case.
The testing of patterns is not at issue.
