Right: general evidence does not settle the local question.
questions.explain: Test results about a treatment in general do not tell you about a particular patient, just as a pattern's record does not tell you about a particular design.
questions.rule: General evidence, local check.
questions.teaches: Evidence that a solution works in general does not replace checking how it interacts with your specific system.

questions.q: A team adopts a pattern without thinking through its consequences. Which outcomes does the book's warning point to? Select all that apply.
options: A guarantee that the pattern fits because it is well tested
Unintended effects on other parts of the design
A design that no longer needs a shared vocabulary
More classes and layers than the problem needed
optionExplain: Not supported: tested patterns carry no guarantee of fit.
Likely: effects on the rest of the design are what the book asks you to think through.
Not supported: the vocabulary is a benefit unrelated to checking consequences.
Likely: patterns can add classes and layers, which the book lists as costs.
questions.explain: Skipping the check risks effects on the rest of the design and extra structure; being well tested does not rule either out.
questions.rule: Think through the consequences.

questions.q: A pattern has a long track record, but your design has an unusual constraint. What does the book's warning say about the fit?
options: The record settles the fit, because many developers have used the pattern
The record is irrelevant, since a tested pattern is never worth using
You must still think through its consequences for your design
You should wait until three developers have used the pattern in your area
optionExplain: The book says patterns are not a magic bullet: you cannot plug one in and walk away.
The book values the track record; it does not call tested patterns useless.
Right: the pattern is well tested, but your design's consequences are yours to check.
The Rule of Three decides when a candidate counts as a pattern; it is not a test of fit.
questions.explain: The track record is about the solution in general. How the pattern affects your own design still has to be thought through.
questions.rule: A track record does not replace checking your own consequences.

questions.q: A designer sees a problem in her design. According to the book, what comes before choosing a pattern?
options: Browsing the catalog for the newest pattern
Splitting the problem into as many classes as possible
Considering whether a simpler solution would work
Announcing the pattern name to the team
optionExplain: A catalog survey comes after a simpler solution is ruled out.
Splitting into classes is a design move, not a first check.
Right: the book says to give a simpler solution consideration first.
Naming comes after a choice is made.
questions.explain: Simpler first. The card next gives the full sequence.
questions.rule: Simpler first.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: Put the steps of deciding to use a pattern in the order the book gives them.
items: Be sure there is a problem in your design that a pattern addresses
Consider a simpler solution
Consider the problem together with its constraints
Match it to a pattern, surveying catalogs if you need to
Check that the consequences are ones you can live with
Study the effect on the rest of the design
questions.explain: The book runs from checking the need and the simpler options, through matching with constraints, to checking consequences and effects.
questions.rule: Need, simpler, constraints, match, consequences, effects.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: A city IT office wants to let residents report potholes through a web form. A planner suggests picking a pattern before looking at the form's needs. Which first step does the book recommend instead?
options: Choose the pattern that is used by similar systems in other cities
Draw the class diagram of the planner's own favourite pattern
Give a simpler solution a chance, then look at the constraints
Ask residents which patterns they would prefer for the form
optionExplain: Choosing by popularity skips the need and the simpler option.
Structure comes after a match is confirmed.
Right: simpler first, then constraints.
Residents do not choose design patterns.
questions.explain: The need and constraints decide, and the simplest working solution goes first.
questions.rule: Need before pattern.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: A designer has found a pattern that matches her problem. What decides whether she adopts it?
options: Whether the consequences are acceptable for the rest of the design
Whether the pattern is listed in a famous and widely read catalog
Whether other developers have used it before
Whether it makes the design look more sophisticated to its reviewers
optionExplain: Right: the book says to make sure you can live with the consequences and to study the effect on the rest of the design.
A listing shows the pattern exists but not that it suits her design.
Use by others is the track record, which is not the local check.
The book warns against using patterns for sophistication.
questions.explain: A match on the problem is not the end. The book adds a check on consequences and effects before the final go-ahead.
questions.rule: A match is not yet a decision.
questions.teaches: Even after a pattern matches the problem, the decision is open until you have accepted its consequences and studied its effect on the rest of the design.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: A manager sees slow onboarding of new hires and does not know of a ready-made method. Which approach mirrors the book?
options: Rule out a simple fix, then survey programs by purpose and where each applies
Adopt the most famous onboarding program at once, since fame signals a good fit
Wait for the new hires and their teams to propose their own programs
Copy the onboarding program of the nearest competitor in the field
optionExplain: Right: simpler first, survey by intent and applicability, then check consequences.
Fame does not show fit.
The book describes an active survey, not waiting.
A competitor's context may differ.
questions.explain: When you do not already know a match, you survey candidates by their intent and applicability, much as a catalog invites.
questions.rule: Survey by intent and applicability.
questions.teaches: If you do not already know a match, survey candidates by what each is for and where it applies, and let broad familiarity shorten the survey.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: Nina chooses a pattern like this. Which parts of her process conflict with the book? Select all that apply.
options: She studies its effect on the rest of the design
She picks the pattern first because she likes it
She checks the pattern's consequences
She does not consider a simpler solution
optionExplain: No conflict: the book asks for this too.
Conflict: need and constraints should drive the choice.
No conflict: the book asks for this.
Conflict: the book says to consider the simpler solution first.
questions.explain: Two steps are reversed or missing. Checking consequences and effects is exactly what the book recommends.
questions.rule: Need first, check last.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: True or false: After a designer is sure that no simpler solution will meet her needs, the book says to consider the problem together with the constraints it must operate under.
questions.explain: Those constraints help match the problem to a pattern. The order is: rule out the simple solution, then problem with constraints, then a pattern, then its consequences.
questions.rule: Constraints are what match a problem to a pattern.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: A designer knows no pattern that fits her problem and wants to survey candidates. Which catalog sections does the book name as particularly useful for that?
options: Implementation and sample code
Structure and Participants
Intent and Applicability
Consequences and Known uses
optionExplain: Implementation notes help after the pattern is chosen, not while choosing.
Structure shows the class design; it comes after the fit is confirmed.
Right: they say what each pattern is for and where it applies.
These help judge a chosen pattern's results and track record, not survey the candidates.
questions.explain: The book says the intent and applicability sections of the catalogs are particularly useful for surveying patterns that might solve the problem.
questions.rule: Survey by intent and applicability.
questions.teaches: When surveying patterns that might solve a problem, the intent and applicability sections of the catalogs are particularly useful.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: In which one situation does the book suggest using a pattern even if a simpler solution would work?
options: When the team enjoys using patterns in its designs
When you expect aspects of your system to vary over time
When the design will be shown to customers and managers
When the simple solution is already working well enough
optionExplain: Enjoyment is not a reason in the book.
Right: expected variation is the stated exception.
Audience is not a reason in the book.
A working simple solution is the case for staying simple.
questions.explain: There is one exception to simplicity first. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Expected variation is the exception.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: Add patterns for practical change that is likely, not for ____ change that may happen.
questions.explain: The book contrasts practical change that is likely with hypothetical change that may happen.
questions.rule: Practical, not hypothetical.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: A tax-software shop knows that rates change by law each year. A toy shop thinks it may one day change its colour scheme. Which case supports adding flexibility with a pattern?
options: The toy shop, because any possible change calls for a pattern
The tax software, because change is expected and practical
Both, because every system may change at some later date
Neither, because simpler solutions always win in the end
optionExplain: A possible colour change is hypothetical.
Right: yearly legal change is likely.
If every possibility counted, the practical-versus-hypothetical rule would mean nothing.
The book makes an exception for expected variation.
questions.explain: Rates changing yearly is practical change. A colour scheme that might change someday is hypothetical.
questions.rule: Likely change earns flexibility.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: Which activity helps a designer find where patterns may be needed?
options: Counting how many classes and objects the design has in total
Listing every pattern that a catalog describes, in order
Identifying the parts of the design likely to change
Asking which parts of the design look the simplest today
optionExplain: Class count does not show where change will occur.
A list of all patterns is not tied to the design.
Right: areas of change are a sign that a pattern may be needed.
Simple parts rarely need a pattern.
questions.explain: Look at the design for the places that will vary; that is where a pattern may be worth its cost.
questions.rule: Find the change, then find the pattern.
questions.teaches: Looking for the parts of a design that are likely to change is a practical way of finding where a pattern may be needed.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: A restaurant changes its menu every season. The owner also imagines opening branches in other countries someday. Which of the two justifies a flexible ordering design now?
options: The seasonal menu, because that change is known and recurring
The imagined branches, because bigger plans need more flexibility
Both equally, since both involve change
Neither, because restaurants never change
optionExplain: Right: expected, practical change.
Imagined plans are hypothetical, and unneeded flexibility adds complexity.
The book separates likely from hypothetical.
The seasonal menu does change.
questions.explain: The book says to design for change that is likely to happen. Seasonal changes are certain; the branches are only imagined.
questions.rule: Build for what is coming, not for what is imaginable.
questions.teaches: Building for change that only may happen adds complexity for a benefit that may never come, which is the cost the next ideas warn about.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: True or false: A pattern added for a change that does not occur still adds complexity to the system.
questions.explain: The book says unneeded patterns only add complexity, and that you might never need them. The complexity is paid whether or not the change comes.
questions.rule: The cost is paid up front.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: Sort each possible change by whether it is practical or only hypothetical.

items.t: Tax rates are revised by law every year
The company might one day be bought by a larger firm
A new payment provider is already contracted for next month
Users could someday ask for a dark mode
Delivery partners are swapped each season
The product may one day be sold on Mars

questions.explain: The book supports a pattern for practical change that is likely to happen. Change that merely may happen does not justify one.
questions.rule: Likely change justifies a pattern; imagined change does not.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: A dev says: our app might be sold abroad someday, and the book says to use a pattern wherever aspects may vary. What does she misread?
options: She misreads nothing, since any possible variation justifies a pattern
She treats change that may happen as if it were change that is likely
She uses a pattern at design time, which the book allows only at refactoring
She forgets that the book forbids patterns once a simpler solution exists
optionExplain: The book separates practical change from hypothetical change.
Right: the exception covers aspects you expect to vary, not any imaginable change.
The book allows patterns at design time and at refactoring time.
The book names one exception: when you expect aspects of the system to vary.
questions.explain: The book's condition is expected variation, practical change that is likely to happen. It warns against hypothetical change that may happen.
questions.rule: Likely, not merely possible.
questions.section: You know you need a pattern when...

questions.q: What is the goal of refactoring?
options: To add new features to the code and improve its speed
To make the code run faster at any cost to readability
To replace the existing code with a pattern throughout
To improve structure without changing behavior
optionExplain: New features change behavior.
Speed is not the stated goal.
A pattern is a possible means, not the goal.
Right: structure improves while behavior stays.
questions.explain: Refactoring changes organization, not behavior. The card next ties this to patterns.
questions.rule: Structure, not behavior.

questions.q: Match each sign or idea to what the book says about it.
pairs: May signal the need for the State pattern
Not the only time to introduce patterns
questions.explain: The book gives two signs for patterns during refactoring. The goal of refactoring is structure, and design time is not the only moment for patterns.
questions.rule: Signs: conditionals, concrete dependencies.

questions.q: A pharmacy's order handler has twenty conditional statements that depend on an order's status. What might this signal, according to the book?
options: The handler needs more conditionals to cover all cases
A Factory is the only possible cure for that kind of code
The State pattern might organize the code better
The code should be rewritten with new behavior added
optionExplain: More conditionals would add to the problem.
A Factory is the book's suggestion for concrete dependencies.
Right: conditionals are the book's sign for State.
Refactoring does not change behavior.
questions.explain: A clutter of conditionals on state is the sign that State may help. The refactoring must keep what the handler does.
questions.rule: Conditionals: think State.

questions.q: At what times does the book say patterns may be introduced into a design?
options: Only at design time, before any code has been written
At design time and also later, when refactoring
Only after the code is finished and has been shipped
Only when a catalog recommends it for that very code
optionExplain: The book says design time is not the only time.
Right: design time is not the only time.
The book says refactoring is a good time, which can come before the end.
Catalogs do not recommend; the designer decides.
questions.explain: Patterns can come in after the fact. Looking at existing code with fresh eyes may show a better structure.
questions.rule: Patterns can arrive late.
questions.teaches: A pattern can be introduced after the code exists, as a result of refactoring, and not only while first designing.

questions.q: A team asks whether this chapter covers everything about refactoring with patterns. How does the book treat the topic?
options: As a topic that is fully covered by the two signs in this chapter
As something that only beginners need to study before design
As a large subject of its own, with entire books written on it
As outside the scope of design patterns, so not worth study
optionExplain: The two signs are examples, not complete coverage.
The book says it is something to study as skills grow.
Right: the book says entire books have been written on it.
The book links refactoring to patterns.
questions.explain: The chapter gives two signs and sends you to further study; refactoring with patterns is a subject in itself.
questions.rule: The signs are a start.
questions.teaches: Refactoring with patterns is a substantial subject with entire books written on it, so the two signs are a start, not the whole.

questions.q: True or false: A team adds a new feature while it refactors the code with a pattern. The book counts this as refactoring.
questions.explain: Refactoring improves structure without changing behavior. A new feature changes behavior, so it is not refactoring.
questions.rule: Same behavior, better structure.

questions.q: Door has a chain of conditionals on its state. Pushing twice, what does this program print?
options: opens, then opens
opens, then already open
already open, then opens
locked, then locked
optionExplain: After the first push the state is open, so the second push cannot open it again.
Right: closed becomes open and returns opens; the second call returns already open.
The door starts closed, so the first push opens it.
locked is the fallback for unknown states; this door only has closed and open.
questions.explain: The first push finds closed, sets open and returns opens. The second finds open and returns already open. A chain of conditionals on a state is the sign the book gives for the State Pattern.
questions.rule: Conditionals on a state value may signal State.

questions.q: True or false: Once a pattern has been added to a design, the book says it should stay.
questions.explain: The book says not to be afraid to remove a pattern when it is not needed. The card next says when.
questions.rule: Patterns can be removed.

questions.q: Remove a pattern when the ____ you planned for isn't needed.
questions.explain: The book says remove a pattern when the system has become complex and the flexibility planned for is not needed.
questions.rule: Unused flexibility is a cost.

questions.q: A courier firm built a plug-in system for ten delivery types. Three years later only one type is used, and the plug-in layer confuses new staff. What does the book advise?
options: Consider replacing it with a simpler solution
Keep it, because removing patterns is blasphemy
Add more plug-ins to justify the system
Document the layer and leave it alone
optionExplain: Right: unneeded flexibility with added complexity is the case for removal.
The book jokes about this feeling and says adults can take it.
Adding more would increase the cost.
Documentation helps, but the problem is the complexity itself.
questions.explain: The flexibility planned for is not needed, and the pattern's complexity is now a cost, so a simpler solution would be better.
questions.rule: Unused flexibility goes.

questions.q: A team keeps an unused pattern because removing it feels wrong. How does the book see that reluctance?
options: As proof that the pattern is still valuable to the team that built it
As good practice, because patterns are proven in so many other systems
As a rule that tested designs must not be touched or altered once built
As a feeling, not a reason: the test is whether the flexibility is needed
optionExplain: A feeling does not show that the flexibility is used.
Proven in general is not proven for this design.
The book says the opposite.
Right: the book jokes about blasphemy, then gives the real test.
questions.explain: The book names the feeling, that removal seems to be blasphemy, and then replaces it with a test about the flexibility.
questions.rule: Judge by need, not by attachment.
questions.teaches: Reluctance to remove a pattern is attachment, not a design reason; the test is whether the flexibility is still needed.

questions.q: A museum set up a complex booking process for rare group tours that did not take place. Staff now struggle with it. Which principle in the book applies?
options: Complexity shows that the museum is careful and professional
A booking process must never be simplified once it has been built
Complexity for unused flexibility is a cost worth removing
Rare events always need complex processes to handle them well
optionExplain: The book does not equate complexity with quality.
The book invites removal when needed.
Right: the planned flexibility is not needed, so a simpler way is better.
The book warns against building for rare imagined cases.
questions.explain: Unused flexibility has a cost in confusion and effort. The same logic that applies to patterns applies to any machinery built for change that never came.
questions.rule: Unused machinery costs people.
questions.teaches: The cost of machinery built for change that never arrives falls on the people who must work with it, in patterns and in any other system.

questions.q: True or false: If the flexibility a pattern was added for does turn out to be needed, the pattern has earned its place and should stay.
questions.explain: Removal is for a pattern whose planned flexibility is not needed. A pattern that handles real change is doing its job.
questions.rule: Keep what earns its place.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it is a reason to remove the pattern or to keep it.

items.t: The planned flexibility is never used and the layers confuse newcomers
Three delivery types are in use and a fourth arrives next month
A simpler solution without the pattern would now be better
The pattern still handles real, recurring change
The interface and its only class never vary
The pattern makes the code easy to extend as requirements change often

questions.explain: The book says to remove a pattern when the flexibility planned for is not needed and a simpler solution would be better. A pattern that handles real change keeps its place.
questions.rule: Remove when the flexibility is unused; keep it while it earns its place.

questions.q: A developer sees how a pattern could prepare her code for many possible future changes, none of which is required yet. What does the book advise?
options: Add the pattern now, so that later changes cost the team nothing
Add the pattern now in a simplified form to limit its cost
Ask the team to vote on which future changes seem the most likely
Resist, because a hypothetical reason only adds complexity
optionExplain: Building ahead of need is the temptation it names.
A simplified pattern still adds complexity for no present need.
Voting does not turn a hypothetical reason into a practical need.
Right: the book says to resist and that the pattern may never be needed.
questions.explain: The book calls the pull to over-build a temptation. The card next gives its reason.
questions.rule: Resist hypothetical flexibility.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, a pattern added for a hypothetical reason adds complexity and may go unused.
questions.explain: The book says that if the reason is only hypothetical, the pattern is only going to add complexity, and you might never need it.
questions.rule: Hypothetical need, real cost.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: The owner of a clinic's booking app says: maybe one day we will be a chain, so build multi-branch support now. What does the book advise?
options: Wait until a practical need for multiple branches appears
Build multi-branch support right away, to avoid rework later on
Build half of the multi-branch support now, as a compromise
Refuse to discuss any plans for growth with the owner
optionExplain: Right: a maybe is a hypothetical reason.
The book says to resist building for hypothetical change.
Half of an unneeded feature is still unneeded.
The book asks for restraint, not silence.
questions.explain: A chain is a possibility, not a requirement. The book's rule is to act on practical needs today.
questions.rule: Practical need, not possibility.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: Why does the book call the urge to build flexible architectures a temptation?
options: Because the pull comes from liking elegant designs, not from a need
Because flexible architectures are not useful in any real project
Because developers should avoid being creative in their designs
Because the book bans every design that is ready for later change
optionExplain: Right: developers naturally love such architectures, and that liking is not a requirement.
The book allows flexibility for practical change.
The book does not tell developers to avoid creativity.
The book allows patterns for needed change.
questions.explain: The book is not against flexibility. It points out that the pull toward elegant, change-ready designs can come from taste, so a developer should check whether a need stands behind it.
questions.rule: Check taste against need.
questions.teaches: The urge to over-build comes from developers liking elegant architectures, so it must be checked against a present need.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: A cook buys equipment for every dish she might ever make. Which statements fit the book's reasoning? Select all that apply.
options: Equipment bought in advance always pays for itself
Buying only what current menus need is the safer approach
The benefit may never arrive
The cost is paid now, in space and upkeep
optionExplain: Does not fit: the book says hypothetical additions may never be needed.
Fits: act on practical need today.
Fits: the book says you might never need it.
Fits: unneeded additions bring present costs, as complexity does.
questions.explain: The costs of extra capacity arrive immediately while its benefits depend on events that may not occur.
questions.rule: Costs now, benefits maybe.
questions.teaches: The cost of unneeded flexibility is paid immediately, while its benefit depends on events that may never occur.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: Suppose the clinic's lawyers confirm that the owner will open a second branch next quarter. What does the book's reasoning say now?
options: The reason is still hypothetical until the second branch actually opens
A practical need exists, so a pattern may now be justified
Nothing changes, since patterns are only meant for the present
The change should be handled by removing existing patterns
optionExplain: A confirmed plan is not an imagined one.
Right: a change you are quite sure is coming is a practical need.
The Master allows patterns for future requirements you are quite sure about.
Removal is for unneeded flexibility, not for a coming need.
questions.explain: The test is how sure you are. Confirmed plans turn a possibility into a practical need.
questions.rule: Sure and coming counts.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: A notification module sends only email today. Which reason supports adding a pattern for channels, by the book?
options: A teammate says other channels would be nice to have someday
Other teams in the company use many different channels
The owner confirmed that SMS ships next sprint
Patterns make the module look more professional to reviewers
optionExplain: This is a hypothetical reason; the book says do not add the pattern for it.
Other teams' needs are not this module's practical need.
Right: SMS is a change the module has a practical need for.
Appearance is not a need; the book says patterns add complexity when not needed.
questions.explain: The book supports a pattern for a practical need to support change now. A confirmed SMS launch is that need, while a wish, other teams' habits or looks are not.
questions.rule: Practical need, not hypothetical.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: Where does the Master say a design should start?
options: From a list of the patterns that the whole system will use
From design principles and the simplest code that works
From the most flexible architecture available on the market
From a catalog's scheme for classifying the patterns
optionExplain: The Master says building from patterns should not be the goal at the start.
Right: start simple from principles; patterns emerge.
Flexibility for its own sake is the temptation to resist.
Classification helps comparison but does not start a design.
questions.explain: The Master puts principles and simple code first. The card next gives the rest.
questions.rule: Principles first, patterns on need.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: Let patterns ____ from the needs of your design, instead of starting from them.
questions.explain: The Master says patterns should emerge naturally as the design progresses, rather than being the starting point.
questions.rule: Let patterns emerge.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: A new project lead wants to assemble the architecture from a list of patterns before writing any code. What would the Master say?
options: Start with principles and simple code; let patterns emerge as needed
Good plan; patterns make a design strong and flexible from the start
Use only the three most famous patterns, whatever the need
Skip patterns entirely and write plain code from now on
optionExplain: Right: patterns emerge from need.
Building from patterns should not be the goal of a design's start.
Fame is not a reason.
The Master does not tell the Student to avoid patterns.
questions.explain: The Master would ask for the simplest code first and add a pattern when the design shows it is needed.
questions.rule: Need first, pattern second.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: What value does the Master still see in patterns?
options: They make code more complex, which is the surest sign of real skill
Proven experience that avoids mistakes, plus a shared vocabulary
They should be used in every design for maximum power and flexibility
They replace the need for design principles and for simple code
optionExplain: Complexity is a cost, not a value.
Right: the Master names both as their value.
The Student asked about this and was told no.
Principles remain the starting point.
questions.explain: Patterns are valuable when needed. The Master's caution is about timing, not worth.
questions.rule: Valuable when needed.
questions.teaches: Patterns are valued as proven design experience that helps avoid common mistakes and as a shared vocabulary, which is why they are worth adopting when a need appears.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: A carpenter starts with measurements and basic joints, and reaches for a specialised jig only when a joint will not work any other way. Which attitude does this resemble?
options: Avoiding specialised tools entirely, even when basic means have failed
Choosing the jig first and then fitting the work to it
Letting a specialised tool emerge from need, after basic means
Using every tool in the workshop on each and every job
optionExplain: The carpenter does use the jig when needed.
That reverses the order.
Right: the specialised tool enters when basic means fall short.
That is the overuse the book warns about.
questions.explain: The basic tools come first and the specialised one earns its place when the basic ones fall short.
questions.rule: Specialised tools earn their place.
questions.teaches: A specialised tool should earn its place by a demonstrated need, after the basic means have been tried.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: True or false: The Master tells the Student to avoid design patterns entirely.
questions.explain: The Master says patterns are a tool to use when needed, and that when the need emerges the Student should use one. The caution is about timing.
questions.rule: Use them when needed.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: A project starts with the simplest code. Halfway through, the design shows the need to vary behavior by state. What does the Master's advice suggest?
options: Rewrite from the pattern catalog, since the design should have started there
Refuse the pattern on principle, since the code was begun without one
Wait until three developers confirm the pattern before using it
Use the pattern now, since the need has emerged in the design
optionExplain: The Master says not to make building from patterns the goal at the start.
The Master says to use a pattern when you see the need emerge.
The Rule of Three is for calling something a pattern, not for using a known one.
Right: start simple and use a pattern once the need is clear.
questions.explain: The Master says to let a pattern emerge: start from principles and simple code, and use a pattern when the need appears.
questions.rule: Start simple; adopt a pattern when the need emerges.
questions.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.

questions.q: What does the book's beginner believe about design patterns?
options: Patterns should be used only where they are needed
The more patterns used, the better the design
Patterns are laws that cannot be adapted
Patterns are not worth learning
optionExplain: That is a lesson the beginner has not yet learned.
Right: this is the beginner's belief, which the beginner will learn is not so.
That is closer to the intermediate's struggles, and the book allows adapting.
The beginner uses patterns everywhere.
questions.explain: The beginner is keen and thinks more is better. The card next shows what experience teaches.
questions.rule: More patterns is not better design.

questions.q: Match each stage to its description in the book.
pairs: The more patterns used, the better the design
Starts to see where patterns are and are not needed
Still tries to fit square patterns into round holes
questions.explain: The beginner is eager and believes more is better. The intermediate begins to judge fit but still forces some.
questions.rule: Beginner: everywhere. Intermediate: starting to judge.

questions.q: A new hire adds a plug-in system to a script that prints one report. Which description from the book fits her?
options: The intermediate, who is starting to see where patterns are not needed
Neither, because plug-ins show careful planning for change
Neither, because a short script cannot make use of any patterns
The beginner, who believes more patterns mean a better design
optionExplain: An intermediate designer is starting to see where patterns are not needed.
Planning for change is justified only by practical need.
Scripts can use patterns; the question is need.
Right: the beginner uses patterns everywhere.
questions.explain: A plug-in system for one report is pattern use without a need, the beginner's mistake.
questions.rule: A pattern with no need behind it marks the beginner.

questions.q: The book calls the beginner's use of patterns everywhere good. Why?
options: It makes the beginner's designs simple and easy to read
It proves that using more patterns makes better designs
It teaches the beginner exactly when not to use patterns
It gives the beginner lots of experience and practice
optionExplain: The book says such designs are not simple.
The book says the belief is mistaken.
That comes later, as the beginner learns.
Right: practice is valuable even when the belief behind it is wrong.
questions.explain: The behavior is useful for learning even though the belief is wrong. Experience then shows where patterns are not needed.
questions.rule: Practice is good; the belief is not.
questions.teaches: Using patterns everywhere is good practice for learning, even though the belief that more patterns mean better design is mistaken.

questions.q: A student photographer applies the rule of thirds to every photo. After a year, she starts to notice shots where a centred frame works better. Which change in the book's account does this resemble?
options: Moving from the intermediate stage back to the beginner
Giving up the use of guidelines altogether from now on
Moving from the beginner stage toward the intermediate stage
Proving that the rule of thirds is wrong for every photo
optionExplain: The direction is toward more judgment.
She still uses the guideline; she is learning when not to.
Right: noticing where a guideline does not fit is the shift the book describes.
The rule still works in many photos.
questions.explain: The shift comes from experience: using the guideline everywhere teaches where it stops helping.
questions.rule: Experience shows the edges of a rule.
questions.teaches: Progress from beginner to intermediate comes from experience that shows where a pattern is not needed.

questions.q: Which statements reveal the beginner's belief that more patterns make a better design? Select all that apply.
options: The more patterns we use, the stronger the design
I looked for a simpler way and a pattern turned out unneeded
I adapt the pattern where the classic design does not fit
I need a pattern for this print statement
optionExplain: Reveals the belief directly.
Does not: this shows judgment.
Does not: this is the intermediate's growing skill.
Reveals it: a pattern for the simplest task.
questions.explain: The first two statements treat patterns as a measure of quality. The others show the judgment that experience brings.
questions.rule: Count of patterns is not a measure of quality.

questions.q: Match each sample thought to the mind that has it.
pairs: I need a pattern for Hello World
Maybe I need a Singleton here
This is a natural place for Decorator
questions.explain: The beginner wants a pattern even for Hello World, the intermediate wonders whether a Singleton belongs, and the Zen mind sees a natural place for Decorator.
questions.rule: Beginner: everywhere. Intermediate: maybe here. Zen: where it fits.

questions.q: Which description matches the Zen mind in the book?
options: It seeks simple solutions and uses a pattern where one fits
It uses a pattern in every design to keep all designs uniform
It avoids patterns to stay free of all their costs and layers
It applies each pattern exactly as the classic design shows
optionExplain: Right: simplicity and principles first, patterns where they fit.
That is the beginner's habit.
The Zen mind uses patterns when they are the natural answer.
The Zen mind knows a pattern may need adaptation.
questions.explain: The Zen mind is not obsessed with patterns. The card next lists its habits.
questions.rule: Simple first; pattern where it fits.

questions.q: Which are traits of the Zen mind in the book? Select all that apply.
options: Tries to fit as many patterns as possible into a design
Not obsessed with using patterns
Thinks in terms of object principles and their trade-offs
Looks for simple solutions that best solve the problem
optionExplain: Not a trait: that is the beginner's habit.
Trait: it is not obsessed with patterns.
Trait: principles and trade-offs guide the thinking.
Trait: simple solutions come first.
questions.explain: The Zen mind puts the problem, principles and trade-offs first and uses patterns when they fit.
questions.rule: Problem, principles, trade-offs.

questions.q: Four reviewers comment on a design. Which one shows the Zen mind?
options: Add three patterns now, in case the design grows later and needs them all
Patterns are a waste of effort in this design; remove every one of them
Keep it simple, and adapt a fitting pattern for the part that will change
Every class should be named after a pattern it might one day follow
optionExplain: That is the beginner's belief that more is better.
The Zen mind uses patterns when they fit.
Right: simple, principled, and a pattern where it fits, adapted.
That forces patterns into every class.
questions.explain: The Zen mind weighs simplicity, change and fit, and adapts the pattern it chooses.
questions.rule: Weigh simplicity, change and fit.

questions.q: The book says the Zen mind is also a beginner mind. What does it mean by that?
options: It does not let its pattern knowledge overly sway its decisions
It knows no patterns at all and relies on instinct alone
It uses patterns everywhere in each design in order to gain practice
It stops learning anything new once it has mastered the patterns
optionExplain: Right: it keeps the open, simple view of a beginner while knowing the patterns.
The Zen mind knows many patterns.
That is the beginner's behaviour, not the Zen mind's.
The book says learning is lifelong.
questions.explain: The Zen mind combines knowledge with a beginner's openness: knowledge informs the decision without driving it.
questions.rule: Knowledge informs; it does not drive.
questions.teaches: The Zen mind keeps a beginner's openness: it knows many patterns but does not let that knowledge overly influence a design decision.

questions.q: An experienced cook knows how two similar sauces differ in purpose and picks the one the dish needs. Which trait of the Zen mind does this resemble?
options: Using one pattern for every dish that she cooks each day
Seeing how similar patterns relate and differ in intent
Following the classic recipe without any change, whatever the dish
Avoiding all known methods and cooking by instinct alone
optionExplain: That is the beginner's habit.
Right: the book says the Zen mind understands the subtleties of difference in intent between related patterns.
The Zen mind knows adaptation may be needed.
The Zen mind uses patterns when needed.
questions.explain: Telling apart related designs by their intent is part of the Zen mind. The cook's choice between sauces by purpose is the same skill.
questions.rule: Know related patterns by their intent.
questions.teaches: The Zen mind sees the relationships between similar patterns and understands the subtle differences in their intent.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, the Zen mind avoids patterns.
questions.explain: The Zen mind applies a pattern when a need for one naturally arises. What it avoids is obsession with using them.
questions.rule: Not obsessed is not opposed.

questions.q: A reviewer with the Zen mind meets a simple design that meets the need and contains no pattern. What does she do?
options: She adds a pattern anyway, to show the team what she knows
She asks which classic pattern the design most closely resembles
She sends it back until a suitable pattern is introduced
She accepts it, since a simple solution that works is enough
optionExplain: That is the Beginner's belief that more patterns make a better design.
Matching the design to a classic form is not the Zen mind's aim.
The Zen mind is not obsessed with using patterns.
Right: simplicity that solves the problem is what the Zen mind looks for.
questions.explain: The Zen mind looks for simple solutions that best solve the problem and is not obsessed with using patterns, so it accepts the simple design.
questions.rule: The Zen mind prefers the simplest design that works.

questions.q: Kim says: I know all 23 GoF patterns, so I have the Zen mind. What does the book's description suggest?
options: Kim is right, since knowing every pattern is the mark of the Zen mind
Kim is right, but only if she also knows the domain catalogs
Kim is wrong, since the Zen mind avoids all pattern knowledge
Kim is wrong, since the Zen mind is shown by how it applies patterns
optionExplain: The book describes the Zen mind by attitude and judgment, not by how many patterns are known.
Breadth of catalogs is not what marks it.
The book says it is also a beginner mind that does not let pattern knowledge overly influence it, not that it lacks the knowledge.
Right: it applies a pattern where it fits, with simplicity and principles first.
questions.explain: The Zen mind is about how patterns are used: where they fit, with simplicity and principles first, and without letting pattern knowledge overly influence decisions. Knowing many patterns does not give it.
questions.rule: Knowing patterns is not the same as the Zen mind.

questions.q: Which are downsides of using design patterns that the book names? Select all that apply.
options: They make the design impossible to change
They can add layers, which adds inefficiency
They often add classes and objects
They stop other developers from recognising the design
optionExplain: The book does not say this.
Named: layers add complexity and inefficiency.
Named: more classes and objects add complexity.
The book lists recognition as a benefit.
questions.explain: The book names added classes and objects, added layers, and the risk of overkill. The card next gives the full list and the benefits.
questions.rule: More classes, more layers.

questions.q: Design patterns often introduce additional ____ and objects, so they can increase the complexity of your designs.
questions.explain: The book says patterns often introduce additional classes and objects and can increase complexity.
questions.rule: Patterns add classes and objects.

questions.q: A team adds three layers of abstraction to route a simple request, and the page now loads more slowly. Which downside from the book is this?
options: A pattern has been misnamed in the project's documentation
The shared vocabulary has failed to reach the whole team
Patterns cannot be adapted to fit the needs of the design
Extra layers add complexity and inefficiency to each request
optionExplain: Names do not slow pages.
The vocabulary is not the issue.
Adaptation is not the issue.
Right: the book says patterns can add layers, which bring complexity and inefficiency.
questions.explain: More layers mean more work for each request and more to understand. This is the cost the book warns of.
questions.rule: Layers cost complexity and speed.

questions.q: A pattern would solve a problem, but a design principle gives a simpler solution to the same problem. What does the book say?
options: Use the simpler solution and do not fight it
Use the pattern because it is better known by developers
Combine both so that no effort is wasted in the design work
Wait for a senior developer to decide the matter
optionExplain: Right: the book says to use the simpler solution.
Being better known is a benefit, not a reason to add cost.
Combining adds the costs of both.
The book asks the designer to decide.
questions.explain: Principles can often solve the same problem simply. In that case the pattern is overkill and the book says not to fight it.
questions.rule: If a principle is enough, use it.
questions.teaches: Design principles can often solve a problem more simply than a pattern, and when they do, the simpler principle-based solution should be used.

questions.q: A warehouse buys a sorting robot, a conveyor and a routing app to handle five parcels a day. Which idea in the book does this illustrate?
options: Shared vocabulary among the workers of the warehouse
The benefit of well-tested equipment that others have used
Overkill: machinery whose cost far outweighs the need
The need to document differences from a standard layout
optionExplain: Nothing here concerns vocabulary.
Tested equipment is a benefit; the problem is the scale.
Right: the cost is far above the need.
Documentation is not the issue.
questions.explain: A pattern, like a machine, has costs. When they exceed what the need justifies, the solution is overkill.
questions.rule: Match the machinery to the need.
questions.teaches: Overkill means the cost of the machinery, in complexity and layers, exceeds what the need justifies.

questions.q: True or false: Although patterns have costs, the book says that when a pattern is the right tool for the job, the advantages are many.
questions.explain: The book says that when a pattern is the right tool for the job, the advantages are many. The costs are a reason to weigh the choice, not to avoid patterns.
questions.rule: Weigh, do not reject.

questions.q: Each Wrap adds a layer and prints w. What does this program print?
options: 5, since the wrappers add nothing visible
w 5, as only the first layer prints
w w w 5, with each layer printing once
5 w w w, as the layers print after Real
optionExplain: Each Wrap prints w before it delegates.
There are three Wrap objects, and each prints.
Right: three layers print w three times, then the number 5 is printed.
The print happens before the call to in.get(), so w comes first.
questions.explain: Three Wrap layers each print w before passing the call on, then Real returns 5. The book notes that patterns can add layers, which adds complexity and inefficiency.
questions.rule: Each layer adds work and complexity.

questions.q: Besides providing solutions, what does the book call one of the biggest benefits of patterns?
options: A guarantee that any code using them runs faster
Freedom from needing to learn design principles
A shared vocabulary for talking with other developers
A way to avoid documenting designs for other people
optionExplain: Patterns can add inefficiency.
The principles remain the foundation.
Right: the shared vocabulary is the benefit the book stresses.
The book recommends documenting.
questions.explain: The human side of patterns matters. The card next explains what it brings.
questions.rule: Patterns are also a vocabulary.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Patterns give you a ____ vocabulary with other developers.
questions.explain: The book names a shared vocabulary as one of the biggest benefits of patterns.
questions.rule: A shared vocabulary.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Two developers both know the pattern names in their catalog. One says: let us make the report screen an observer of the data. What is the direct benefit?
options: A whole design is conveyed in a few words, avoiding misunderstandings
The screen will be faster automatically, because the design is named
The design no longer needs a review, because both developers agree
The other developer need not know any patterns for the name to work
optionExplain: Right: the name stands for a design both understand.
Names do not change speed.
A shared name does not replace review.
The benefit depends on both knowing the name.
questions.explain: A shared name is a compact way to describe a design and keeps misunderstandings down.
questions.rule: A name carries a design.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: How do the OO design principles help when you meet a pattern that is new to you?
options: You can skip reading the new pattern's catalog description entirely
You can assume the new pattern is sound without checking its fit
You can understand the pattern's motivation and workings from them
You can rename the pattern to suit the habits of your own team
optionExplain: The principles help you read the description; they do not replace it.
Understanding is not the same as assuming it is sound.
Right: the book says the principles let you understand the motivation and workings of any new pattern.
Renaming would damage the shared vocabulary.
questions.explain: Principles are the common ground behind the patterns, so a new pattern can be read in their light.
questions.rule: Principles unlock new patterns.
questions.teaches: The OO principles give you a base from which to understand the motivation and workings of any new pattern.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Jazz musicians call a chord sequence by a name, and a band of strangers can play it at once. Why does the book say it is worth spreading pattern names to colleagues?
options: Names are valuable only to the person who first coined them
Its value rises as more of your colleagues know the names
Spreading names replaces the need to learn the patterns
A name works even if nobody else on the team knows it
optionExplain: The point of a vocabulary is that it is shared.
Right: a shared vocabulary improves as more people share it.
Names stand for patterns that must still be learned.
The vocabulary needs shared knowledge.
questions.explain: The musicians' name works because everyone knows it. The book says to spread the word so that more colleagues can use the vocabulary.
questions.rule: Spread the vocabulary.
questions.teaches: Sharing the vocabulary is itself worthwhile, since its value rises as more colleagues know it.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: True or false: A developer who is the only person on a team who knows the pattern names gets the full benefit of a shared vocabulary.
questions.explain: A shared vocabulary needs more than one person who shares it. The book urges you to spread the word so that fellow developers use it too.
questions.rule: A vocabulary needs speakers.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: A developer names a class FeedObserver, though it does not notify anyone of changes. What does this do to the shared vocabulary?
options: Nothing, since a name is only a label and carries no meaning
It helps, since any familiar name speeds up the reading of code
It misleads readers who know the name and expect its behavior
It raises the Rule of Three count of the Observer Pattern by one
optionExplain: The value of a name is that it carries a design with it, so a wrong one carries the wrong design.
Familiar names help only when they are true of the code.
Right: readers will expect an observer and find something else.
The Rule of Three concerns real applications of a pattern, not class names.
questions.explain: Our reading, from the book's advice that class names reveal the patterns underneath: a name only helps if it is accurate. Colleagues who know the name will expect behavior the class lacks.
questions.rule: A pattern name must describe what the code really does.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: What does the book say using patterns in design meetings helps a team do?
options: Skip discussion of the requirements and move straight on to code
Stay in the design longer without getting bogged down in details
Finish meetings sooner by having everyone vote on which patterns to use
Avoid the need for any documentation of the design afterwards
optionExplain: Requirements still need discussion.
Right: the vocabulary keeps the talk at the level of design.
Voting is not part of the advice.
Documentation is a separate setting for the vocabulary.
questions.explain: Pattern names lift a discussion above implementation detail. The card next lists all five settings.
questions.rule: Patterns keep talk in the design.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Match each setting to what the book says patterns do there.
pairs: Keep the team in the design and prevent misunderstandings
Reduce the amount of documentation needed
Let readers quickly see the pattern behind the code
Share knowledge, for example in a brown-bag lunch
questions.explain: Each setting has a benefit: staying in the design, shorter documentation, quick understanding of code, and wider knowledge.
questions.rule: Five settings, five benefits.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: A developer names a class after the pattern behind it and notes the pattern in a comment. Which of the book's five ways is this?
options: Design meetings, where the team talks
Code comments and naming conventions
Architecture documentation for the whole system
Talks to groups of interested developers
optionExplain: Meetings are a spoken setting.
Right: the book recommends naming and commenting to reveal the pattern.
Architecture documents are separate from code.
Talks are to groups.
questions.explain: Names and comments in code reveal the pattern, so later readers understand the implementation quickly.
questions.rule: Let names reveal patterns.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Why does mentioning a pattern in architecture documentation reduce the amount of writing needed?
options: The reader is expected to guess the design from the name and context
Patterns cannot be described in writing, so documents leave them out
The documentation replaces the code as the real source of the design
The name stands for a design the reader knows, so fewer words suffice
optionExplain: Guessing is the opposite of a shared vocabulary.
The catalog describes patterns in writing.
Documentation supports code; it does not replace it.
Right: a shared name carries a design in a word.
questions.explain: The name does work that sentences would otherwise do, provided the reader knows it.
questions.rule: A name saves words.
questions.teaches: A pattern name in documentation conveys a whole design in a word, so fewer words give the reader a clearer picture, if the reader knows the name.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: A hospital procedure manual names its routines, such as a two-person check, and uses those names in forms and on wall charts. Which advice in the book does this resemble?
options: Hiding the procedure behind general terms that suit every ward
Writing nothing in the manual and teaching by word of mouth
Using a different name for the same routine on every ward
Choosing names that reveal what is underneath so readers understand
optionExplain: Hiding is the opposite.
The book asks for documentation.
Different names would break the shared vocabulary.
Right: names that reveal the pattern help readers understand quickly.
questions.explain: Where a name appears in the places people read, the vocabulary does its job. The hospital's checks work like pattern names in code and comments.
questions.rule: Put names where readers look.
questions.teaches: Where a shared name appears in the places people actually read, such as comments, class names and charts, it lets readers understand the structure at once.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: A developer's plan for sharing patterns has these parts. Which conflict with the book's advice? Select all that apply.
options: Offer a short talk to a local user group
Never mention patterns in comments
Name every class Manager, whatever pattern it follows
Explain pattern names in design meetings
optionExplain: No conflict: this is the book's fifth suggestion.
Conflict: the book says to identify patterns in comments.
Conflict: the book says to choose names that reveal the pattern underneath.
No conflict: this is the book's first suggestion.
questions.explain: The first two parts hide the patterns, which defeats the vocabulary. The others follow the book.
questions.rule: Reveal, do not hide.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: A developer explains patterns to colleagues in daily chats. What benefit does the book give for sharing the vocabulary like this?
options: It replaces the need for a patterns catalog on the team
It makes the design simpler inside the code itself
It saves time on code reviews alone and nothing else
It helps others learn patterns and builds a community
optionExplain: Catalogs stay useful; the vocabulary complements them.
The vocabulary helps communication but does not change the code's structure.
The book names other benefits for conversation; time is not the main one.
Right: the book says other developers learn about patterns and a community builds.
questions.explain: The book says using patterns with other developers helps them learn about new patterns and builds a community.
questions.rule: Share with colleagues to spread patterns and build a community.
questions.teaches: Using patterns in conversation with other developers helps them learn about new patterns and builds a community.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Which person is a member of the Gang of Four?
options: Erich Gamma
Christopher Alexander
Ward Cunningham
Elisabeth Robson
optionExplain: Right: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides are the GoF.
Alexander was the architect with whom patterns began, a different group.
Cunningham runs the Portland Patterns Repository.
Robson is a co-author of this Head First book.
questions.explain: The GoF are four authors of the first catalog. The card next names them and their book.
questions.rule: GoF: Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: The GoF book, Design Patterns, kicked off the field of design patterns when it was released in ____.
questions.explain: The book says the GoF book kicked off the field in 1995.
questions.rule: The GoF book appeared in 1995.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: A colleague says: check what GoF says about this before we decide. What is she pointing you to?
options: A catalog of the anti-patterns found in many real projects
A catalog of domain-specific patterns for a single named industry
A list of the coding standards used across the whole company
The first and most definitive catalog of fundamental patterns
optionExplain: Anti-patterns are described elsewhere.
The GoF catalog covers fundamental patterns, not one industry's.
The GoF catalog is about patterns, not standards.
Right: GoF means the Gang of Four's catalog.
questions.explain: GoF is shorthand for the authors and their book of 23 fundamental patterns.
questions.rule: GoF = the first catalog.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: What is the relation between the GoF book and the patterns in this Head First book?
options: This book replaces the GoF set with a newer set of patterns
The two books share no patterns, as they cover different fields
The GoF book is the basis for the patterns used here
This book describes only the patterns the GoF left out
optionExplain: It uses the GoF set, not replaces it.
They share the patterns.
Right: the book says GoF is the basis for its set.
It covers the GoF patterns.
questions.explain: The book builds on the GoF catalog and points you to it for the full treatment.
questions.rule: This book is based on GoF.
questions.teaches: The patterns taught in this book are drawn from the GoF catalog, which is why the GoF book is the natural next read.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: A new field has a founding textbook that is still the standard reference decades later. What attitude does the book's description of GoF suggest toward such a text?
options: Treat it as the last word on patterns, so nothing further is needed
Treat it as outdated and ignore it in favour of newer, shorter books
Treat it as useful only to its authors and the people who know them
Treat it as the definitive starting point, expecting later growth
optionExplain: The book says it is not the last word.
It remains a recommended start.
It is for all readers of the field.
Right: the book calls GoF first and most definitive, but not the last word.
questions.explain: A founding text is a good start. Its value does not shut out later work.
questions.rule: Start with the founders; keep reading.
questions.teaches: A founding text deserves reading as the starting point of a field, and later work should be expected to extend it.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: True or false: The book presents the GoF book as the last word on design patterns.
questions.explain: The book says the field has grown substantially since the GoF book was published; it is the first and most definitive, but not the last word.
questions.rule: First, not last.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: Match each name to what the book says about it.
pairs: A professor of architecture at Berkeley
Kicked off the field of design patterns
questions.explain: The GoF are Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, Alexander was a professor of architecture at Berkeley, and the 1995 book kicked off the field.
questions.rule: GoF: first catalog. Alexander: the origin.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: Where did the idea of patterns begin?
options: In the GoF book of 1995, which gathered the first catalog
In building architecture, with Christopher Alexander
In the Portland Patterns Repository wiki run by Ward Cunningham
In the first multi-tier systems built for the early web
optionExplain: The GoF book brought patterns to software but did not begin them.
Right: patterns started with Alexander's work on buildings.
The wiki is a later community resource.
The book says patterns started in architecture of buildings, not systems.
questions.explain: Patterns began outside software. The card next names the source.
questions.rule: Patterns began in building architecture.

questions.q: Match each resource to what the book says about it.
pairs: A wiki run by Ward Cunningham where anyone can take part
A central resource for patterns work, with articles, books, mailing lists and tools
A conference called Pattern Languages of Programs
The ACM Conference on Object-Oriented Systems, Languages and Applications
questions.explain: The wiki and the Hillside site are online resources. PLoP and OOPSLA are conferences.
questions.rule: Wiki, site, two conferences.

questions.q: A software developer asks why she should read A Pattern Language, a book about towns and buildings. What does the book give as the reason?
options: It lists the 23 fundamental software patterns with sample code
It replaces the GoF catalog with a newer and much fuller catalog
It teaches the object-oriented principles behind the software patterns
It shows the true beginnings of patterns and analogies with software
optionExplain: That is the GoF catalog.
It is not a software catalog.
Principles are taught elsewhere.
Right: the book recommends it for the origins and the analogies.
questions.explain: Alexander's books are the roots of the idea. Reading them shows what software patterns borrowed.
questions.rule: Read the roots.

questions.q: What does it suggest about patterns that their originator was an architect rather than a computer scientist?
options: The idea of patterns is not tied to software
Software patterns are older than architectural ones
Patterns apply only to buildings
Computer scientists should not write patterns
optionExplain: Right: patterns began outside software.
The book says patterns started in architecture.
The book lists several domains.
The book invites participation.
questions.explain: Because patterns began in architecture, the concept carries to other fields, as the next idea shows.
questions.rule: Patterns are not only for software.
questions.teaches: Patterns began in building architecture, so the concept is not tied to software and can carry to other fields.

questions.q: A hospital manager wants to discuss shared routines with people from many fields, on a site where anyone can take part and every topic can be raised. Which resource in the book fits?
options: The Hillside Group conference list
The GoF book
The Portland Patterns Repository
The Timeless Way of Building
optionExplain: The Hillside site lists conferences and resources, not an open wiki.
The GoF book is a catalog, not a discussion site.
Right: it is a wiki open to anyone, with threads on every topic related to patterns and OO systems.
That is a book by Alexander.
questions.explain: Of the resources named, the wiki is the open discussion space.
questions.rule: An open wiki for open discussion.
questions.teaches: The Portland Patterns Repository is an open wiki, so anyone can join discussions on patterns and object-oriented systems.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, Christopher Alexander was a computer scientist who invented software patterns.
questions.explain: The book says Alexander was an architect, a professor of architecture at Berkeley, who invented patterns for buildings and towns.
questions.rule: Alexander was an architect.

questions.q: A colleague says the Gang of Four invented the idea of patterns. What is the best correction according to the book?
options: Patterns began with Alexander on buildings; the GoF compiled the first software catalog
Patterns began with Ward Cunningham, who started the Portland Patterns wiki as a home for them
Patterns began in concurrent systems, and the GoF later collected them in one book
The colleague is right, since all patterns began with the GoF book of 1995
optionExplain: Right: the idea began with Alexander, and the GoF compiled the first patterns catalog for software.
Cunningham runs the Portland Patterns Repository wiki; he did not start patterns.
Concurrent systems are one domain-specific area, not the origin.
The book says directly that patterns did not start with the GoF.
questions.explain: Patterns started with Christopher Alexander, who wrote about living architecture. The GoF put together the first patterns catalog in software and started a movement there.
questions.rule: Alexander started patterns; the GoF catalogued them for software.

questions.q: Which of these does the book's Patterns Zoo include as a domain of patterns? Select all that apply.
options: Compiler optimisation patterns
User interface patterns
Business process patterns
Organizational patterns
optionExplain: Not in the book's zoo.
Included: designing interactive software.
Included: interaction between businesses, customers and data.
Included: structures and practices of human organizations.
questions.explain: The zoo covers more than code design. The card next lists each domain.
questions.rule: Patterns reach beyond code.

questions.q: Match each pattern domain to what it addresses.
pairs: Interaction between businesses, customers and data
Structures and practices of human organizations
questions.explain: Each domain applies the pattern idea to a different kind of recurring problem.
questions.rule: Domain, then problem.

questions.q: A designer wants guidance on laying out an interactive screen for a mobile app. Which pattern domain in the zoo covers this?
options: Architectural patterns
Business process patterns
User interface patterns
Domain-specific patterns for real-time systems
optionExplain: Architectural patterns concern buildings and towns.
Business processes concern interactions between businesses and customers.
Right: designing interactive software is the user interface domain.
Real-time systems are a different specific domain.
questions.explain: User interface patterns address how to design interactive software programs.
questions.rule: Screens: user interface patterns.

questions.q: What does the book say about application patterns?
options: They concern only buildings, towns and cities, where patterns first began
They concern system-level architecture; MVC has been known to pass for one
They are the same as the creational patterns in the GoF classification
They are limited to concurrent systems and other real-time software
optionExplain: That is the architectural domain.
Right: this is the book's description.
Creational is a different, purpose-based category.
That is a domain-specific example.
questions.explain: Application patterns work at the level of the whole system, and the book notes that MVC can pass for one.
questions.rule: Whole-system architecture: application patterns.
questions.teaches: Application patterns work at the level of the whole system, and MVC has been known to pass for an application pattern.

questions.q: Sort each concern into the kind of pattern the zoo would file it under.

items.t: Problems of concurrent systems
How to make and communicate decisions effectively
Problems of real-time systems
Interaction between businesses and customers
Problems particular to a specialised technical field
How data and decisions flow between a business and its clients

questions.explain: Domain-specific patterns concern a particular technical domain. Business process patterns concern how businesses, customers and data interact.
questions.rule: Technical field, or business interaction?
questions.teaches: Patterns can describe how people and companies work together, as well as how code is built.

questions.q: True or false: The book's Patterns Zoo lists every domain in which patterns can be used.
questions.explain: The book says the zoo shows a few domains, and leaves space for the reader's own field notes.
questions.rule: The zoo is a sample.

questions.q: A software firm wants guidance on how to organise its teams and who reports to whom. Which zoo domain fits best?
options: Business process patterns, which cover interactions among businesses, customers and data
Application patterns, which cover system-level architecture
User interface design patterns, which cover interactive programs
Organizational patterns, which cover the structures of human organizations
optionExplain: Business process patterns are about interactions with customers and data, not team structure.
Application patterns are about system architecture, not people.
User interface patterns are about the design of interactive software.
Right: team structure is the structure of a human organization.
questions.explain: Organizational patterns describe the structures and practices of human organizations. Business process patterns describe interactions between businesses, customers and data.
questions.rule: People and structures: organizational. Customers and data: business process.

questions.q: What does an anti-pattern tell you?
options: How to remove a pattern from a design safely
How to test whether a pattern is correct in code
How to name a pattern so others can find it
How to go from a problem to a bad solution
optionExplain: Removing patterns is a separate topic.
Testing a pattern is a different job.
Naming is a feature of patterns and anti-patterns alike.
Right: it documents a recurring bad solution.
questions.explain: An anti-pattern is the mirror of a pattern. The card next explains why it is worth writing.
questions.rule: Anti-pattern: problem to bad solution.

questions.q: Avoiding bad solutions can be as ____ as finding good ones.
questions.explain: The book says documenting bad solutions prevents others from repeating the mistake, which is as valuable as finding good solutions.
questions.rule: Avoiding is as valuable as finding.

questions.q: A finance team keeps applying the same Friday patch that fixes this week's complaint and breaks next week's reports. A colleague writes up why the patch keeps being chosen and why it fails. What is the write-up closest to?
options: An anti-pattern: a recurring bad solution, documented to be avoided
A design pattern, since the patch does solve the weekly complaint
A refactoring, since it changes the structure of the finance reports
A catalog, since it lists each of the reports that the patch breaks
optionExplain: Right: a recurring, attractive bad solution documented to prevent repetition.
A pattern is a good solution; this one fails.
Refactoring improves structure; the write-up changes no code.
A catalog describes many patterns.
questions.explain: The patch recurs, looks good up front and fails later. Documenting it so others can avoid it is the anti-pattern's job.
questions.rule: Recurring and attractive and bad.

questions.q: Which statement about anti-pattern types is supported by the book?
options: Like patterns, they come in several types, such as organizational ones
They exist only for development work in large software companies today
They exist only for organizations, the teams inside them, and management
They exist only for one programming language and its libraries
optionExplain: Right: the book lists these types.
The book names more than one type.
The book names more than one type.
The book names areas of work, not a language.
questions.explain: Anti-patterns mirror patterns, which also exist in many domains.
questions.rule: Anti-patterns have domains too.
questions.teaches: Anti-patterns, like patterns, exist in several domains: development, object-oriented design, organizations and specific fields.

questions.q: Airlines publish reports on recurring pilot errors and on the conditions that tempt crews into them. Which idea in the book does this resemble?
options: Removing a pattern from a design once its flexibility is no longer needed
Documenting recurring failures and why they tempt, so others avoid them
Reading a catalog's consequences section before using a pattern in a design
Spreading a shared vocabulary in meetings, documents and code comments
optionExplain: Removal is about unneeded flexibility.
Right: a recurring failure documented as a warning.
Catalog reading is about choosing patterns.
Vocabulary is about communication.
questions.explain: The reports turn individual mistakes into shared lessons, which is what documenting an anti-pattern does.
questions.rule: Failures documented are lessons shared.
questions.teaches: Documenting recurring failures as carefully as successes turns individual mistakes into lessons that others can use.

questions.q: True or false: Any bad solution, even a one-off, counts as an anti-pattern.
questions.explain: An anti-pattern is a recurring bad solution to a common problem, documented so that others avoid it. A one-off mistake does not recur, and so does not qualify.
questions.rule: Recurring is required, here too.

questions.q: Sort each description by whether it fits a design pattern or an anti-pattern.

items.t: A general solution to a recurring problem in a context
Shows how to go from a problem to a bad solution
Looks like a good solution, then turns out bad when applied
Documented so that others can apply it
Documented so that others can avoid it
Resolves the goal and constraints it is applied to
